This is all about timing and device control (controller/keyboard/mouse, whichever you choose). You move your little square around the screen avoiding the obstacles. You need a delicate touch.
Minimal visuals and gentle, atmospheric music during gameplay along with only a couple of timed levels makes it a nice relaxing experience with no pressure.
Cross-platform which, as a Linux user, is always a big plus for me. Being in Windows makes me permanently irritated.
Each level has a name (Bridge, Gas Pump, Industrial Zone etc) and on completion you're rewarded with a nice monochrome photo of said title - my favourite was the breaching whale. I found myself wondering where they were taken - I'm assuming all over the world because the game description mentions Samsara (worldly wandering). There was a windmill in one so maybe that was Holland, and was that a statue of Lenin? There are tons of language options so perhaps it's designed so that everyone can recognise at least a couple of pictures. Who knows?
Some of the levels are hard (30+ attempts for me) but it's not rage-quit territory. You always feel like you can succeed with a few more tries.
X marks the spot of your last (failed) attempt. This is very useful because normally you would have to try and remember the spot which would result in a lot of unnecessary repetition, so this feature serves to keep the game fresh.
On the credits menu there's an 'Our Games' heading with 5 apparently clickable icons. I enjoyed Cubway and I'd like to check out these other games but nothing happens when you click them.
You can only see each picture on completion of the level. It would be nice to have an accessible gallery of all the pictures once you've completed the game.
I used the triggers on my Steam controller, I found it to be the most accurate method. The only trouble is that they're the wrong way round - right trigger moves left and vice versa. I tried switching them over via the Steam settings but then the up/down switches too which is equally confusing. This only really matters on level 26 (timed + direction-oriented) but still, it needs fixing.
Currently 36 levels (~2 hours) with no replay value due to only one difficulty setting. At the moment I'd say 'good' value. However, there is a free update on the way with 19 more levels and 3 difficulty settings. When that comes along it will become VERY good value.
13 achievements which keep popping up with gratifying regularity. Finishing the game gets you 100% achievements without any further faffing about. Trading cards are also on the way with the upcoming free update. Cloud support for people who move around.
Cubway tests your dexterity and timing with a satisfying level of difficulty and a nice relaxing ambiance. Thoroughly recommended, especially if you're looking for a different type of game from your usual common genres.

A simple RPG with an incredibly touching story about two doctors who essentially access a dying man's memory in order to allow him to achieve the one wish he had. To go to the moon.  Admittedly, the controls and game map were a little funky but the story itself more than made up for it.

WTMG's Heidi Hawes writes: "To the Moon is a beautifully told story of two doctors who use futuristic technology to grant the last wish of a dying man. Using advanced machinery, they can artificially alter his memories and make it so he can live out his heart’s greatest desire during his final moments. Upon meeting him within his mind, he tells them his deepest desire is to go to the moon, but he cannot remember exactly why that is his biggest wish. In order to solve the mystery, the doctors must regress further and further into his memories to try to pin point the source of the longing.
Overall, I’d have to say that To the Moon is definitely a game worth playing if you like story driven games. Its lack of any innovative type of gameplay is forgivable due to the deep storyline, wonderful characters, and fantastic musical score. I found the premise of the game to be a refreshing change to many of the other point and click style adventures."

I should start off with I got To the Moon during the winter sale so there would be less pressure on the game from me as far as expectations went. I checked off that I would recommend this game as I would for those who like a very linear story told in a unique way of collecting memories in a reverse chronological order. Although in spite of that I wasn't particularly fond of the game. That is, while I thought it was well done, I didn't love it.
Dr. Rosalene and Dr. Watts are both likeable characters for different reasons. Dr. Rosalene is more level-headed, serious, and logically driven, which I appreciated during certain situations in the story. Dr. Watts is the comedic relief, which while entertaining at times, could be a little vexing at others. It's only towards the end in Arc 3 where you truly see how their different personalities affect their standpoints on what the job demands of them with the request they must fulfill in To the Moon of getting their patient, well, to the moon. That's where they both became much more enjoyable to me. Up until that moment their commentary was more of side commentary while the player pieces together what is going on for themselves. Clues are given to you through the fragmented memories, but nothing is explictedly stated, which I did like.
The overall plot of To the Moon was certainly an intriguing one and what initially caught my attention. The way the story is preseted to the player during actual gameplay (if you can really call it that, but I'll get to that a little later) fits with the jobs of both doctors and having the reader experience it any other way would feel off-putting. The writing was serious, funny, vague -- if not maybe little too vauge at times for some -- and perhaps for some almost sorrowful, but at the end of the day it was well executed.
Although repetitive, dare I say even a little too much at some points, in a more obvious way than other games text adventure games (I wouldn't consider it a VN due to the many player-controlled moments), the soundtrack was lovely. The tense moments had befitting sound accompaniment as did the tranquil ones. The main title music, which serves as To the Moon's main theme, is beautifully composed.
Gameplay was the player controlling either Dr. Rosalene or Dr. Watts as they walk through a given memory. In Arc 1 you're searching for memory links and the locked momento, which is accessable once you find the other memory links first, and breaking the surrounding barrier of the momento. The player is then prompted to complete a puzzle by flipping over a row or column of tiles whose completed image is that of the now-unlocked momento. The memory link searching doesn't stop in Arc 1, but unlocking momentos does. Arc 2 is more story and memory links returns in Arc 3. No matter where you are in the story, it's a lot of walking. I saw some call To the Moon a walking simulator in reviews just as it is also tagged as such if you click on the "User-defned tags". I don't care for a lot of walking if there's not much or any element of exploration involved, but I decided to give To the Moon a chance nonetheless. I don't regret it, but don't misunderstand that as I'm enamoured with this game. I'm still not.
With all that being said, I must return to my main point of I didn't love this story. I wasn't blown away by it and it wasn't as much of a rivetting experience to go through as it seemed to be for others whose reviews I read before buying this game. The story, as beautifully written and well executed as it was, just didn't do it for me. There was something about it that fell short. I wasn't all that invested in Johnny and his story, which took a huge blow out of enjoyment for me even with all that his memories revealed about his backstory from childhood until the near-present just before the doctors arrive to fulfill the job they'd already signed on to do. While the banter between Dr. Rosalene and Dr. Watts provided entertainment, I found half of it necessary and half of it unecessary and merely there to fill an otherwise silent walk. There was, of course, the soundtrack playing in the background in general though not always, but their conversations felt more like filler moments than offering much in the way of progress or necessary information to the story. While witty conversations is still enjoyable and not everything has to be serious and of the utmost importance at all times, there were moments where I wish I could silence them.
In Arc 3, there is a moment of awkward gameplay while revisiting one of the patient's memories that didn't feel like it fit at all. I know why it was implemented as far as character motives went, but it felt like it could've been better done to tie in more with what was going on. The segment felt more like filler than anything else in order to extend the game. That was another hit to my appreciation for To the Moon.
All in all, it was a charming and lovely story with interesting characters (the doctors) taking the spotlight and leading the player through the patient's memories. Perhaps I'm not an emotional enough person to really appreciate the emotional moments, but often I didn't feel very much and was underwhelmed by it all. It was only at the very end when you see all your work come together where I became a little more invested and in turn interested, but because it was right at the end the feeling didn't last very long.
I can't say I'll be playing the sequel, Finding Paradise. To the Moon was good enough for me, and I also can't honestly say I'd have paid for it had I been only able to purchase the game at full price. I recommend waiting for sale (I got it at 75% off for $2.49) and it will either feel like a huge steal or something more fair for a well put together story yet without being enthralling or a waste of money.

There are many different ways to play your character and all are fun if used correctly. The only downside I can find is that some of the time sensitive platforming puzzles can be frustrating and I've experienced glitched and game crashes. In terms of glitches I'll have enemies fall outside of the map while still aggroed onto me making it impossible to proceed in the mission. Other times you will fall off a platform and land on a ledge that shouldn'r have collision, making you respawn in a place that you cannot advance from. After getting the Soul Splitter, the game will crash if you ALT+TAB out. Even so these problems are extremely rare and they don't detract fom the overall experience. Darksiders 2 is an amazing and addictive game and it's my opinion that it's a must have for any RPG fan.
Overall I give it a 9/10

If you like controlling one guy in a huge battlefield where lots of stuff is going, choose what weapons to carry, and choose what you want to do or what objectives you want to carry out, buy this game. To me, it feels like a top-down Planetside 2, but the strategy and mechanics are much more polished.
You control one soldier on a vast battlefield. You're not the best or the worst soldier. You're just another dude that can rank up just like everybody else. As you rank up, you get access to other weapons and more NPCs join your squad.
The game is split up into campaigns and matches and the vast majority of enemies and allies are NPCs (something Planetside I think should've had).
Each match/round is generally a territory control system with several minor objectives you can carry to help the territory control initiative.
All of the Movement, cover, and shooting mechanics are simple, but also have little nuances that you can master over time.
You can choose the role you want to play and play it. It's a very satisfying/challenging/fun game and I can't wait to play it again. In a world full of gimmicky games, this one focuses on fun first. Wish there were more AAA games that did that.

I truly enjoy and reccomend this game, however would hold off on buying it IF you are looking to play for more than a few hours in a single save. If you buy it now, you are buying for a taste of what is to come.
I would like to preface this review by saying, the devs are very very responsive and are working very hard on getting bugfixes and updates out. They do listen to the community, and this does not seem like a studio that will do the whole alpha and abandon.
Gameplay and Mechanics: 5/10 - It is a lot of fun to build the different zones in your airport and continue developing terminals, gates and upgrades as your airport grows. Now, that being said, end game comes way too quick. Within maybe 2-3 hours on a save, my airport was making 500k+ a day, and I had run out of things to put in. Now with this being a very early alpha, it is understandable that there are some lacking features. However in its current state, there really isn't much to do.
The core unlocks and gameplay is way too easy. Customer satisfaction is always high, even with low amounts of facilities. The airline contracts come way too easy, and there isn't (a visible one anyway) any kind of relationship status with the airlines. Sure they will cancel on you for some reason, but I can't see a way how to check why. It is frustrating to lose 20k in termination fees and not really see how to improve. Many times you're only losing contracts due to game breaking bugs which will be discussed further in the review.
In its current state, the gameplay here is really fix the default airport by adding facilities and staff until you have 3-4 gates going and its endgame. You can't even use all of the features the game has due to bugs, such as the restriction of food court/cafe right now.
Bugs: The game is broken in many many ways. Simple things just dont work. I.E Food court. But there are also smaller bugs such as passangers blobbing at the end of queues and getting stuck, causing bottlenecks. Construction also creates weird zones (with secure/nonsecure zones) sometimes and requires reloading to fix.
The real game breaking bugs are the ones that I cannot see workarounds to. Such as gates being available and flights being cancelled because the game does not register it. So you end up scheduling flights 3-4 hours apart and still have issues sometimes. Or traffic on the roads. Why does a bus carrying passangers stop blocking both lanes of traffic to drop them off when he could just block one. Also, why does a garbage truck take 3-4 hours to pickup trash? Seems silly.
All bugs aside, there is the huge lag issue. I have a gtx 980, and a new gen I7 paired with 16 gigs of ram. Aaand its on a SSD drive. So there is absolutely no reason this game should be running at less than 10 FPS when I have 2 747 class airplanes, and 2 767's at the same time. So theres that.

This is not a game that's easy to review for me as it's easily the most internally polarizing game I've ever played. It's a game that I both love and hate in equal measure, one that makes the most obvious, horrible mistakes, while still managing to dazzle you with its heart.
The game starts off really well with a beautifully rendered slide-show cutscene that looks as if it were painted by hand. It does a perfect job of setting up a mood and introducing our protagonist, and is immediately followed by a very simple and easy tutorial. It's a tutorial that nearly lies to you though, starting you off with a couple of puzzles, only to then bind you to what comes to be something like two hours of primarily dialogue, wandering about and looking at things.
The game is slow. It's insane how slow it is. The story gives you almost no hooks to catch you with other than the hope that you'll enjoy the characters and the -promise- of a mystery enough to continue. The actual puzzles in the first two chapters are all very simple. The game does a good job of telling you what you need to do in order to progress, and as you figure out the methods, it'll hint towards the means. They're (mostly) well designed and a joy to unlock, but they never quite feel like they're the main focus of the game.
The main focus is the story. It's not a bad story either, it's sweet, it's got its mystery and its build up, but the pacing is glacial. Finishing the first two chapters took me about four hours and in that time I learned extremely little. Yes, you do find out tidbits about both Sam (the protagonist) and Dr. Styles (her employer), but none of it is surprising and none of it carries the shock that the writers seemed to intend. The 'accident' is mentioned very quickly in the game and you're told not to ask people about it (and the game doesn't let you, either), but when it's finally revealed what happened -- it's completely predictable and almost disappointing. A cutscene shows Sam responding to it with shock, surprise, grief and empathy, whereas the player's reaction is more likely that of; "That's it? Really? That's the big reveal?"
Yet, like I said, the story isn't bad. It's just not good. The characters are fine, admittedly even if they feel like they're taken out of a teen romance story, with the orphaned sorta-gothic tough girl acting as the lead, who ends up living with a dark, mysterious and secluded, brooding man with a dark secret and-- yeah. You see where that's going. Along the way she gathers around herself a group of social stereotypes, all of which feel entirely two dimensional. Yet, again, they're not bad. They're entirely likeable even.
Then there's the graphics. Another point that really has me struggling to make a decisive judgement on it. It's gorgeous. Mostly. All the environments you go to are beautifully rendered, clearly handmade with so many little touches. I can only think of a couple of locations where I actually wasn't impressed with what I saw. Some of the locations are straight up amazing, even. Check the screenshots and you'll see exactly what I mean. Yet I did say that they're gorgeous, mostly. Mostly. See, all this amazing art is actually given to you at a surprisingly low resolution. Playing at 1920x1080 I was exposed to gorgeous art that had been muddied by being stretched out across the screen. It felt like such a waste. It's only a 5gb game too, it's heart breaking that they didn't just up the size and add higher resolution backgrounds.
This is then combined with another good & bad, the character models. They actually look just fine. The resolution is high enough and the details are good enough. The lighting in the scene illuminates them well and the shadows are actually rather pretty. Yet despite this, the fact that you have a high resolution 3D character in a lower resolution environment causes them to pop out horrendously. Not a single character in the game ever looks like they're a part of the world they live in. You're constantly reminded by how the world is nothing but a 2D plane. To make matters worse is that every once in a while the models are given idle animations that are way, way too exaggerated. One scene has the American sitting on the grass, constantly going between leaning back and sitting forward, with him kicking his leg into the air in between. As the conversation goes, he'll do this constantly.
Another up and down is the voice acting. The voice actors themselves were very likeable. Their voices fit their roles and they did their lines well. The downside is that this game is stuck with the ye olde adventure game type of talking. It's the kind where as they talk, a box of subtitles pop up. Once the character has finished speaking those lines, they stop. The subtitles go away and a new box opens. Then the character continues. Every time this happens there's this weird and awkward pause that completely snaps you out of it, and really shouldn't be happening in a modern game like this. Conversations should be fluid, especially with such a lovely cast; people should actually talk like they're talking to each other. Not like they're by themselves and reading subtitle boxes one at a time.
So what's the verdict? Honestly, despite everything, I want to like this game. I do. Every part of it just shines with heart and effort. You can tell that on every front, the developer put their heart and soul into the game. They worked -hard- on it, and that fact gives it so much charm and likeability. This shows best in the art I believe, but also in the puzzles themselves. They're rather simple, I admit, but they're a joy to solve. They're fun! I wish the game had more of them, a LOT more. It's fantastic to chase after Daedalus clues! It's equally fun to flip through the book of magic tricks to apply them to a situation, then map out the choreography. Simple, yes. Easy, yes. But fun. Charming, clever and full of character.
So I really believe I can suggest this game to people that enjoy adventure games. If you're okay with slow pacing, if you enjoy an easy story and you'd rather have fun puzzles instead of difficult ones, this is a game I can recommend to you. Like I said, this game is a labour of love and I want to see more from the talent behind it. :]

Well I think it's safe to say this is easily the best adventure game in the last 15 years.  Nothing even comes close, sorry Broken Age you are terrrrrrrrrrrrible (although not as bad as Broken Sword!).  I may be a bit biased as the Laura Bow adventure games were my favorite adventure games as a child and this has a very similar feel.  The central plot is a murdery mystery/ghost story/mad scientist/magicians cult story!  Personally, I loved the plot.  That doesn't mean it didn't have it's problems as it had a ton.
However, the noir atmosphere and just the way the art direction infused almost every scene and environment with dread was excellent.  Even more props should go to the artist who did all the graphic novel cutscenes, I much preferred these to a surely more hideous and costly 3d rendered cutscene.  The magicians club graphic novel scene was particularly well done.  As I said though, the game did have a lot of problems.  It's divided into 8 chapters, howevers it was painfully obvious who the murderer was by chapter 4.  Which maybe could have been handeled better, but the main character (Samantha) simply could not figure it out.  This made almost every dialogue scene cringe worthy as she interrogated characters and kept coming to ludicrous conclusions.
I find it impossible to believe anyone who plays this game would be stumped, so the main characters bumbling I would expect would annoy everyone.  This would have been bad enough, but I found it even more frustrating that she started off as a bright and clever woman and then you have to watch her devolve into this lunatic dummy was extremelyyyyyyyyy disappointing.  I guess I understand what the writer was doing, she was trying to hide who the murderer was by throwing in so many red herrings that you get confused.  What ends up happening is that you just shake your head in sadness as your character losses all sense of reason and makes ludicrous proclamations.  She started off as the Hercule Poirot of this game, but by the end she was really the Captain Hastings...she literally didn't even solve the mystery at the end and and it was left up to a much wiser character.
As I said though, despite all of this I loved the game and I still enjoyed the story for the atmosphere alone and even with the easily solveable murder questions still remained that you could focus on instead keeping things still interesting.  Also as good as the music was, 3 songs is not enough to make a musical score for a 15 hour game, at least have for 4 songs geez!  Even being the best adventure game in the last 15 years it's still an adventure game so #Worth $10

Even though I am a huge FF fan, my favs being 7 and 12, this one just rubs me the wrong way in several ways. The combat just is imo not very good for a FF game. The 13 day time limit is not fun at all. It reminds me of Dead Rising 2 where if you fail to complete the main mission in time you can start over with your saved stats. I don't want to do that in any game, ever. I just feel very stressed and rushed while playing. Hopefully this is the last time they ever put a time limit in a FF game. I felt so incredibly rushed, especially with Hope chiming into my earpiece every couple minutes telling me to hurry up, that while on the first real main mission where you have to find the pass code symbols I got stuck and couldn't find the fourth one, which in itself is incredibly stupid mission gameplay for any game let alone a FF game. Even more confusing is the gear system and discovering robots early on that have what feels like billions of hp and take me about 5 minutes to beat per battle doesn't help. It says they are weak against lightning but aero and blizzard do twice as much dmg to them than lightning does. It says use lightning to stagger them but lightning, no matter how many times I cast it, won't stagger them. The schemata system is awkward to say the least. Should I have a fire spell in the red schemata slot, a lightning in the yellow slot, and blizzard in the blue? Or can I do like one person I read online and make the red assault, the yellow for debuffs, and put all magic spells in the blue schemata? What a stupid, ill conceived mess.
Don't get me wrong, the more I'm playing the more I think that I might be getting the hang of it. I may just restart the game on easy and try that since normal is hard like folks have said. Then again probably not since, poor performance aside, this game absolutely ♥♥♥♥ing blows.

No Man's Sky is best enjoyed with others, allowing you to tell your own story of what you personally have seen.  In a practically endless (1.8 quintillion planets) universe, You will quickly find that a lot of it does look the same.  But you will also find landscapes that are truly one in a million. Have patience, look around, and keep in mind: It's about a journey with no destination.

This game is an interesting experience.
You play a randomly named soldier, who is put in a battlefield has to try to survive with a bit of amunition and maybe 1 or 2 grenades. Your goal is to capture a certain tatical location and than move on to the next til you have finally pushed back the enemy far enough that he retreats and your side is victorious. To help you the games gives you a good variaty of weapons and some armours or even vehicles to choose from or to buy with points you getting from taking this locations. You also have lots of comrads over witch you can take command when you rank up and can even call in airstrikes and such.
The problem for you is, that pretty much every bullit kann kill you. It doesn't have to but it can and more often than not the tide will shift and you found yourselfe surroundet by enemies. That means that you will (probably) die quite often and get a new random named soldier to fight for your country.
Good thing though, your ranks and weaponpoints will (with a little penalty) go to your next charakter, so you don't loose everything.
Oh you can play in singleplayer in some sort of campain or something (doesn't seem to have a story though) or in skirmish missions. Or you can play it online in coop vs a botarmy or vs other players.
There is also a workshop and some mods that can enhance your experience.
Overall the game is relativly simple so gameplay can get boring at some point. But the maps vary in a way that force you to change your tactis from time to time, so it won't happen to fast. There are also special weapons that cannot be bought witch can be collected (and stored for later use) or used (and than probably dropped after death^^).
In my experience the game is best enjoyed with some friends. Playing with one friend won't do you much good, but playing with 2 or more will give you some advantages that you can really feel.
So if your and your friends are looking for a little game to play in larger groups where you can play good together even if your skilllevel is quite different this could be a game for you.

This game is outstanding! You play as a single soldier in a battlefield full of... how many soldiers? I have no idea. The AI controls a lot of them, and when you are playing Coop, the AI controls both opposing factions plus whatever soldiers on your side who are not human. If, no wait, scratch that WHEN you die, and YOU WILL DIE A LOT, you respawn in a random point somewhere near the battlefield your previous soldier fell in. You gain rank by earning XP through killing enemies and caprturing objectives. You can buy weapons with Resource Points, or RP, which you earn by capturing objectives, selling dropped items, or selling rare weapons.The combat is fun, the enemies are relentless, and the battles are intense, to say the least. The graphics are a bit minimalist, but I think it works out for the best, as there is so much going on all the time that it would be very easy to lose track of yourself and your teammates if things were more realistic.
Here's a list of pros and cons.
PROs:
1- Great diversity of weapons, including factions specific guns
2- Roles of weapons are important. For example, if you have a grenade launcher, you'll have a hard time in close quarters.
3- Body armor and ghilly suits are available, to increase survivability or decrease visibility, respectively, and they actually work!
4- Want to use a vehicle, but have no one to drive it? No problem! The AI is actually pretty good at piloting the vehicles, but sort of ruthless when it comes to running people over...
5- The people who play the game are, for the most part, pretty cool. They understand it's a team effort, and there are clans out there who take pride in blitzing entire maps with tank rush tactics.
Now for the CONS:
1- Some realism issues...
- M79 grenades arm too close to the launcher. The 40mm grenade should not arm until the projectile is beyond the lethal blast radius. Having the grenade explode in the wielder's face if someone happens to walk in front of him while firing is frustrating and unrealistic. The actual RL grenade travels a full 30 meters from the tube, even if that is straigh up in the air, so it is still theoretically possible to arc the grenade in such a fashion as to land right beside the launcher, thus killing the wielder. And while you're at it, do something about the "spread." I have personally fired the M79 hundreds of times and can tell you unreservedly that it is FAR more accurate than you have depicted here.
- One the subject of weapon accuracy, how is it that a pistol is more accurate at a distance than a combat rifle?
- Why is it I can empty an entire magazine at an enemy and hit him 12 times, and while I reload, he pops me once and I die?
- Hand grenades: EVERY SINGLE TIME a grenade is thrown from a crouch behind cover, the grenade will stick to the top of the cover right in front of the wielder. This causes TKs in every match. Seriously, devs. This should be easy to fix.
- The AI is good. TOO GOOD. Like Agent Smith bullet-dodging good. Running With Rifles is a top-down sandbox shooter designed with emphasis on cooperation, squad leading and being a tiny soldier in a big war. The events take place on an open world battlefield divided between two factions, each trying to capture bases from the opposite side until the enemy has been wiped out from the area. The player takes the role of a private and fights along his/her comrades controlled by AI, slowly gaining influence over fellow soldiers through rank promotions from success in battles.
When the influence grows, AI soldiers begin to follow the player starting as a combat pair, ultimately forming a 10-member squad. The AI squad commanding has been made as transparent as possible to avoid micromanagement and excess amount of keys or menus. The AI squad members e.g. find cover on leader’s signal from crouching, they spot enemies on their own and open fire if it fits the situation. When the leader uses a suppressed weapon for stealth approach, the squad will engage in fight only if the enemy manages to alert the surroundings by shouting or shooting.
The soldiers die quickly, and the player’s soldier makes no exception. The game uses the simplest possible die-or-don’t bullet hit model, which makes the gameplay extremely intense and challenging. Caution, frequent usage of covers, suppressing fire to buy time and staying with the group is highly encouraged; the heroic movie hero-style risk-taking will likely lead only to a quick death ... it’s a beautiful way to go though.

The story occasionally craps itself when the characters do something completely against their established personality, which makes it difficult to immerse yourself when you just can't understand why anyone acts like they do and eventually you just have to give up and observe everything at a distance, which is a shame.
The game also commits the cardinal sin of objects you've already looked at suddenly changing function when you poke at something else somewhere else that magically furthers the story, without letting you know. Which means you're constantly running around rechecking every clickable thing you've already clicked, looking for the one thing that'll now allow you to continue.
Gameplay is frustrating, but that's par for the course for most adventure games. It's story touches your heart, and speaks to you, whatever walk of life you're on. You really need to experience it, at least once. As bittersweet as it may be at some points, it leaves you feeling good and warm and fuzzy, and it makes life seem a bit more lovely, even for just a few moments.
Going into a bit more depth, the game is really well developed in general.
- The pixel art is really well made, the characters are very expressive and manage to convey the emotions they might be feeling at any given time, even if their faces consist of a few pixels. And the backgrounds and locations look amazing in general.
- The soundtrack is just... superb. Such a big part of the game. It really completes the experience.
- There is a very well managed contrast between the humour and the more touching or sad moments in the game, they sometimes even work together to great effect.
- The gameplay itself is very minimalistic, don't expect much more than your typical point-and-click, it's really just a vehicle to drive the story. Functional, but that's it. There are some tiny little things that spice it out but it's nothing worth mentioning.
- It's really a bargain. It's not too lengthy (about 4 - 5 hours) and it's deffinitely worth every penny.
- Just play it. Honestly, you should have more than enough reasons at this point, just buy it and play it. Trust me, it's well worth it~

To the Moon was a rollercoaster experience. Not necessarily on the emotional level as its reputation demands but in the dread, cringe, and relief at its story elements and writing.
Up the ride goes as we climb a steep incline of intrigue about the life of an old man’s guilt. Down it comes with a tonally dissonant and awkward delivery of humour from a couple of doctors who can’t seem to decide what kind of characters they are. Up it goes again with a genuinely touching moment between the endearing central couple. Atop the precipice of expectation the ride stops with anticipation that the big reveal is going to be some cliched garbage that the old man’s mother used to sing him a song about the moon or some♥♥♥♥♥♥ Onward it goes as the truth becomes ever more complex.
Such was my experience with to the moon. Though I actually ended up quite liking the story and found it to be very interesting. But it’s poor use of language at times continuously made me nervous that it would devolve into some nonsense that the true meaning of life is the power of friendship. And that would have been ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Thankfully, the game surprisingly tells a unique and original story whose arc is birthed from the struggles of communication. There’s some meta appreciation then in the fact that some of the communication in the game is expressed rather clumsily. However I doubt the game is trying to be that clever and is simply a result of inexperience.
It occurs to me though that there may not be a non-pretentious way to criticise this game or games like it. It’s almost entirely a narrative experience with very little gameplay and so the essence of the experience is in the engagement of the plot and the presentation of its dialogue.
At a basic level if you like the story then you like the game since that’s all there really is to it. And while the writing is effective in getting its point across resulting in large quantities of the feels being mined from the chests of unsuspecting players, it definitely lacks some polish and comes off as more of a first draft than a finished product.
But if it succeeds in almost universally touching the hearts of it’s players is there any value in pointing out its shortcomings?
Well much like the inexplicable desire of the central character to go to the moon, I’m equally compelled to point out the flaws in my games wherever they exist in an ultimately meaningless gesture to find fulfilment where none can possibly exist.

Like Final Fantasy XIII, Lightning Returns isn't a bad game, but i was very disappointed with it. The best aspect of this game is definitely the combat system, mixing the XIII and XIII-2 style with a more action-RPG style, but being neither of those in the end. It's fun to play, but somewhat cluncky. You have 3 garbs in which you assign 4 abilities (for each face button), and using them consumes your ATB. You'll need to switch often (with the shoulder buttons) to ensure that you have actions to perform and don't get stuck without options. The garbs and abilities are highly customizable, which is a plus. The combat isn't great, but it's good. The rest of the game however, is mediocre. This time you have an open world to roam, but it's bland and you only have 3 settings: 2 cities, forest and desert with ruins. That's it. Sounds good, but in practice means little. And then there's the time limit mechanic. I hate it. I admit that the game gives you plenty of time to do all the main quests and plenty of side quests, but if you want to do everything then the time limit will freak you out. And speaking of side quests, that's how you get stronger this time. Fighting enemies gives you less rewards, and sometimes is a bad ideia to fight, making the new combat system less important. What i really hate about this game is the way it's designed: the game almost forces you to play multiple playthroughs, especially if you're a completionist. Even if there wasn't a time limit, you must replay the game at least 3 times to collect "everything" (it's very subjective here). Problem is, the game becomes boring after that. Getting "100%" in this game is a chore. Most of the side quests are boring. Travelling is boring. And it shouldn't be that way. The rest of the game isn't great either: the graphics are just OK, the music isn't memorable, and the story sucks. Like i said, playing the game once (and on easy difficulty) is OK. Replaying it isn't. The combat is good, but doesn't make up for the rest of it. I even prefered XIII over this one in the end. The PC port this time is actually decent, but i won't praise it because all PC games should be optimized in the first place. I recommend it on sale with caution for completionists.

I'll start off by saying this game does not have many of the bugs and issues that people are saying in other reviews, I'm guessing they're reviewing the original game and not the deathinitive edition since this version of the game does work pretty well. There are one or two bugs here and there but nothing completely gamebreaking. For example the game sometimes crashes when you minimize, Bringing up the steam ui sometimes breaks the controls for some reason and that's a bit messy, there's a couple parts in the game where your progress is blocked by an invisible wall but if you just go back to the main menu or restart the game that usually fixes it. Aside from that no other problems here.
First of all I want to talk about the improvements over the first game. There are many. The climing is a lot better, the combat is a lot better, the abilities aren't as annoying to use and switch out, the game overall feels a lot more complete, it's a much bigger open world, lot more to do, side quests here and there. Just overall Darksiders 2 improves everything over the first game. There are a whole load more weapons in the game and armor and just loads of different item drops that you can use to make yourself stronger, there are a lot more moves you can learn from different characters. Those are a just a few of the cool new things in the game.
The story seems to be parallel to the first game, as in it takes place at the same time and it is cool to see another one of the four legendary horsemen. It has a lot of new characters and a few returning characters, it's a pretty good story really. Like I said the gameplay is very good and much improved over the original. Not too much bad to say about the game.
There are however still a few bad things to say about the game. First of all the keyboard controls aren't very good at all. They're all mapped weird. For example in all the menus you have to press space bar on most of it and then if you want to fast travel you have to hover your mouse over a place and then press enter even though you press space in the rest of the menus, and then in-game space is just jump so it can get confusing. Some of the puzzles are quite annoying too, maybe they're just difficult but some are just a pain in the a$$, not fun to figure out. The graphical options aren't much, and the shadows on the characters are terrible, all pixelly and whatnot. There is a dodge roll but it's really annoying cause if you do it 3 times in a row you'll do a super roll that leaves you vunerable for a second and slows you to a hault, that's very annoying especially in boss fights where you need to dodge a whole load of times.
Overall this game is decent, much better improvement over the first game and a must play if you have played the original, there are some problems but nothing game breaking. I'd give it a solid 8/10.

Short review: It's awesome. Get it.

For those who haven't played Half Life 2, play this update. It's the definite way to go. For those of us who have played Half Life 2 before: play this update, especially if you have not opened this game since you beat it back in 2004. Half Life 2:Update provides a welcome lighting update that may not seem like much at first, but I found myself being constantly impressed by how gorgeous it looks in the 16:9 with proper lighting and sharper shadows. The Citadel level at the end of the game is greatly improved with the cinematic lighting, it definitely adds to the theatric appearance that Valve was shooting for originally.
The commentary along the way is for the most part very good. The commentary near the beginning was excellent, and a lot of mention of the narrative reasons how the levels were designed is useful to know. There is a handful of commentary that does stray too much to the generic side of game design and level design, rather than containing pertenant information. My only gripe is that the commentary plays over and drowns out cinematic moments. I found myself often rushing to deactivate the commentary bubble while important in-game moments were occuring. It would have been much nicer if they could have paused the cinematic moments while the commentary played. They were able to pause enemy behaviour when the commentary was active, but not the cinematic moments.
Highly recommend this free fan made mod. It definitely made me remember why I still regard HL2 as one of the most important modern-day video games.
It goes without saying that this is one of the greatest video games ever made...

What a hard game to recommend.
I can say that throughout the whole game I was entranced by it's design and ingenuity, but now that sit here having finished the game I have no idea what to think of it.
If you have ever drawn comics as a kid, chances are that you tried your hands at some meta storytelling, like having a character from a panel reaching out to another panel to interact with another character and breaking the 4th wall in the process.
Well, Gorogoa is pretty much that idea explored to it's fullest.
The game is pretty much all about moving 4 panels around in order to create interconnectivity between them so you can make progress. The situations very quickly take a turn into the abstract and dream-like architecture and force you to play around with perspectives and scales to reach the desired outcomes.
The game has a great sense of progression and focus that manages to keep you invested on whats going on and feeling like you are constantly travelling deeper into the mystery.
I have seen this game being compared to Children of Men somewhere on the internet, and I think it's a fair observation.
The game never breaks the continuity, even if that means making you travel through time and space. One panel will always lead to another panel.
The problem then resides on what exactly you want out of this game. It's 15 bucks, and it takes an hour and a half to beat. Unfortunately it has that puzzle game characteristic of being a lesser game once you know what th solutions are. So does the presentation and uniqueness of it make it worth replaying?
I havent replayed the game yet, but I honestly dont feel the urge to do so.
The story goes for obtuseness and non-linear structure, and it does seem to take the format of the game design as a storytelling device, but I had trouble getting invested in it mainly because I couldnt grasp whatthe hell was going on and was more interested in the puzzles themselves.
I have yet to see any kind of discussion about the way Gorogoa handles its story, but the main consensus so far seems to be a big "?????".
I usually cheer for different ways of storytelling, but this one in particular left me kind of in the dark, and left me no desire to jump back in to find out more.
But maybe thats the desired intent. The game really feels like you are constantly diving into a deeper dream, and the meaning of it is what you decide of it.
As for the puzzles, we enter the subjective arena once again. While I did find some puzzles that took a few minutes to guess the solution to, alot of them were very easy and not that demanding. But for me thats actually a good decision, considering how the pacing of the game is it's main strength, and having you bash your head into a wall because of a hard puzzle would kinda break that sense of continuity the game goes for.
But others might not feel the same way for a 15 buck game. They might want a serious challenge. And then there are other people who will find Gorogoa more challenging than I do.
I would put in the category of Portal 1: Less than 2 hours to beat, some challenging puzzles, the presentation carries the rest.
So yeah, thats Gorogoa. I enjoyed my time with it while playing, but it hasnt left me thinking that much about it after finishing it.
It was worth the 15 bucks for me, but will it be the same for you?

This game is outstanding! You play as a single soldier in a battlefield full of... how many soldiers? I have no idea. The AI controls a lot of them, and when you are playing Coop, the AI controls both opposing factions plus whatever soldiers on your side who are not human. If, no wait, scratch that WHEN you die, and YOU WILL DIE A LOT, you respawn in a random point somewhere near the battlefield your previous soldier fell in. You gain rank by earning XP through killing enemies and caprturing objectives. You can buy weapons with Resource Points, or RP, which you earn by capturing objectives, selling dropped items, or selling rare weapons.The combat is fun, the enemies are relentless, and the battles are intense, to say the least. The graphics are a bit minimalist, but I think it works out for the best, as there is so much going on all the time that it would be very easy to lose track of yourself and your teammates if things were more realistic.
Here's a list of pros and cons.
PROs:
1- Great diversity of weapons, including factions specific guns
2- Roles of weapons are important. For example, if you have a grenade launcher, you'll have a hard time in close quarters.
3- Body armor and ghilly suits are available, to increase survivability or decrease visibility, respectively, and they actually work!
4- Want to use a vehicle, but have no one to drive it? No problem! The AI is actually pretty good at piloting the vehicles, but sort of ruthless when it comes to running people over...
5- The people who play the game are, for the most part, pretty cool. They understand it's a team effort, and there are clans out there who take pride in blitzing entire maps with tank rush tactics.
Now for the CONS:
1- Some realism issues...
- M79 grenades arm too close to the launcher. The 40mm grenade should not arm until the projectile is beyond the lethal blast radius. Having the grenade explode in the wielder's face if someone happens to walk in front of him while firing is frustrating and unrealistic. The actual RL grenade travels a full 30 meters from the tube, even if that is straigh up in the air, so it is still theoretically possible to arc the grenade in such a fashion as to land right beside the launcher, thus killing the wielder. And while you're at it, do something about the "spread." I have personally fired the M79 hundreds of times and can tell you unreservedly that it is FAR more accurate than you have depicted here.
- One the subject of weapon accuracy, how is it that a pistol is more accurate at a distance than a combat rifle?
- Why is it I can empty an entire magazine at an enemy and hit him 12 times, and while I reload, he pops me once and I die?
- Hand grenades: EVERY SINGLE TIME a grenade is thrown from a crouch behind cover, the grenade will stick to the top of the cover right in front of the wielder. This causes TKs in every match. Seriously, devs. This should be easy to fix.
- The AI is good. TOO GOOD. Like Agent Smith bullet-dodging good. When an enemy soldier is hiding behind a rock, he will often make such effective use of cover that it is impossible to hit him without sending soldiers to BOTH flanks. You can see the AI commanding the soldier to move, and he literally changes direction so fast that he looks like Agent Smith from The Matrix. The AI should not know the position of every soldier on the battlefield, nor should it know the source, trajectory, speed, and impact location of every bullet, shell, and grenade. I have seen AI soldiers hop out of the way of incoming grenades and artillery shells as if they were psychics looking into the future. Fix that crap.

2- THE LOOT SYTEM: This is a BIG ONE. Remember when I said most fo the people in the game are cool? Well, there are more than a few ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, too. When you die, and you WILL, any weapons and items you were carrying drop onto the ground. You can retrieve them, if you get back to your corpse fast enough, but there is always a substantial chance that some drop farming d-bag will steal your guns while you're running back to get them. Sometimes, if you catch them in the act, they will give them back. Sometimes. Most of the time, they just act like you don't exist. If you see a guy with a riot shield wandering around and not shooting anything, he's probably a drop farmer and will most likely steal your♥♥♥♥♥♥ DEVS: Implement some kind of loot protection! Allowing any random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to steal a super rare off of my corpse is infuriating, to say the least. Set up a loot system that allows players to protect their loot (i.e., permission settings so they can allow trusted players only to collect their guns when they die), or maybe even add the option to altogether disable loot loss on death! I have been through mulitiple games now where I end up losing ALL of my RP because some drop farming shitbag steals everything.
CONS aside, this game is still a LOT of fun. I highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys intense, fast paced, and relentless battles.
Just don't try the final missions on your own.... YOU WILL DIE.

Running With Rifles is a top-down sandbox shooter designed with emphasis on cooperation, squad leading and being a tiny soldier in a big war. The events take place on an open world battlefield divided between two factions, each trying to capture bases from the opposite side until the enemy has been wiped out from the area. The player takes the role of a private and fights along his/her comrades controlled by AI, slowly gaining influence over fellow soldiers through rank promotions from success in battles.
When the influence grows, AI soldiers begin to follow the player starting as a combat pair, ultimately forming a 10-member squad. The AI squad commanding has been made as transparent as possible to avoid micromanagement and excess amount of keys or menus. The AI squad members e.g. find cover on leader’s signal from crouching, they spot enemies on their own and open fire if it fits the situation. When the leader uses a suppressed weapon for stealth approach, the squad will engage in fight only if the enemy manages to alert the surroundings by shouting or shooting.
The soldiers die quickly, and the player’s soldier makes no exception. The game uses the simplest possible die-or-don’t bullet hit model, which makes the gameplay extremely intense and challenging. Caution, frequent usage of covers, suppressing fire to buy time and staying with the group is highly encouraged; the heroic movie hero-style risk-taking will likely lead only to a quick death ... it’s a beautiful way to go though.

Not the highest budget, best looking, or most fun handling racing game ever made, for sure, but fairly enjoyable nonetheless. Personally I've never been a fan of games that drift by turning sharper, as opposed to using a button, as it feels like you have less control. However, this game manages to still feel controllable most of the time, despite not feeling as responsive as a game like Sonic & SEGA All Stars Racing Transformed (which personally has my favorite driving mechanics of any racing game).
I have yet to figure out if there's anything I can do to gain boost meter or if it just refills over time. The boosting doesn't always feel as fast as I'd like, but it changes handling interestingly and is frequently refilled, which is nice. I also haven't played many off-road racing games, so this is a nice change of pace, with lots of bumps and such along the way that can challenge you and send you flying, which is quite fun. Speaking of, the car models, designed to look off-roady, are a nice change of pace from the kinds of racing games I usually play. The AI likes to PIT you and force you into obstacles, but trying to return the favor is more difficult than it seems it should be.
If you're a fan of racing games and don't mind a mediocre-but-competent fun little racing game, Insane 2 isn't a bad choice. I wouldn't spend more than $5-10 on it.

Sigh.. another JRPG gone awry. For me at least.
It's one of those "this one thing" is a non-starter for me, and that is, drumroll please badadadadadadada tss, lack of mouse support.
Seriously gaming with two hands on the keyboard is something I have never done. I suppose with enough ,practice I could find the right flow, and it would come natural, but after 15 years of gamin, this is something I've only seen done when two dudes were playing a flash game together. What compounds this process is that when you change schematics, they come with abilities that are binded to their own button. So, you can have 3 schemes at a time, and switch between them. So i set guard as the F button on two, only it moves to space bar on the 3rd. I go to that one, hit F to guard and OOPS, hit in the face because I can't establish any kind of muscle memory for the controls. Believe me, I tried different configs, nothing feels natural, comfy, or something I could see myself getting used to without 40 hours of practice.
So the actual game. Time limit that is inconsequential with some basic understanding of an ability called cronofreeze. Lots of combat that looks flashy but feels hollow for some reason. Great art style, dialogue. Solid plot it would seem, and hollow world exploration. Everything just feels, kinda empty.
Should you buy this game? Do you own a pad? Then maybe it'll be boatloads of fun, I dunno. I keep re-installing and uninstalling in the same day.

Despite the Stupid name "LIGHTNING RETURNS™: FINAL FANTASY® XIII" is the best game in the thirteen series and doesn't shame the long overall-series.
Final Fantasy XIII was supposed to be huge open areas, but offered mostly a pipe dream. LIGHTNING RETURNS™ aknowledges the faults of previous installations and offers this time only four areas that are considerably sizeable compared to one big area fo the original FF XIII.
To be more dethful LIGHTNING RETURNS™ has a 13 day cycle. Unfortunately the days don't really vary, just mostly add more quests. So the game doesn't come anywhere near the (very old) gloriousness of the Majora's Mask where every day was unique and the fates of inhabitants were genuinely touching. The writing team seems to be aware of this and really like to emphasize how Lightning has lost all of her humanity and empathy and is a do-gooder only for quest-rewards, or something.
One thing that really shines in the game is the voice acting. The game is full of sounds and every line that is said is voice acted. This might come close to 20 hours of voice acting both in japanese and english. This partly remedies the lifelessness of the game world and the game is more vivid than Final Fantasy XII, which had the series record in this field.
Despite the critique of the world I had two reasons for complaining. Another them is a stupid and addicting cheat code called chronostasis that should be NEVER used, the game would have been better without. I think time restrainment in rpg is a very cool idea especially if failing makes you stronger (and smarter). Another complaint is that the guy responsible for dress attributes should have been fired. He effectively ruined the very awesome work of this very awesome person that made a huge effort for Lightning's pretty <3 dresses.
Forgot to mention: Controller is mandatory!

No mouse use in game? Really SquareEnix? Your controls are ♥♥♥♥ing garbage. With literally no way to change them. Except choosing type 1 or type 2 controls. With zero explanation as to the bindings for either. Are you all absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or did you just spaz out for a minute or two while porting this game? FFS.
If you havn't got a controller don't even waste your time. Wouldn't buy it for a dollar.

Old school point-and-click game with a context of magic and paranormal activity.
The game is played through two main characters, much like in the Gabriel Knight series, also created by Jane Jensen. The gameplay is known for most: pointing, clicking and discussing all the way. This works of course as well as it should  and there wasn't much to complain about. The story is divided into chapters each having its own puzzles and goals. The puzzles are relatively clear and not too difficult. Compared to the Gabriel Knight series, this game involves also a fair share of fantasy elements and nods to mythology, which suits the story just fine. However, as a negative side note, the game is not too long and the story seems leave a couple loose plot lines unresolved. Maybe there was a sequel planned, which never came about?
All in all, this is a good game with nice features for those wanting to solve yet one more mystery through excessive molesting of the mouse. However, the game is not the best in its genre, missing a few unforgettable moments.

The first Insane game (also spelled 1nsane) was released in 2001. While not insanely successful (as far as i know), it was a fun off-road arcade racer with lots of game modes and tons of maps and cars to choose from. (It even had a cop car and a hover-craft sci-fi racer thingy)
Insane 2 continues this line, being far from a realistic racing game, but immensely fun, if you don't take it too serious. Expect lots of jumps and brutal crashes. The game has quite a few cars, maps and racing modes (from classic racing to capture the flag).
Gameplay-wise, Insane 2 isn't too difficult. The AI has some dumb moments, but luckily, these are relatively few and far-between. The Physics can seem strange to someone expecting a simulator, but their do their job. Ice and mud will make you glide around, for example. One annoying thing is, that the car will turn into rubber when you're carrying the flag (during CTF and RTF games). While the cars do take damage, it seems mostly cosmetic until the car breaks down completely, when a reset will fix it and bring you right back into the action.
The game looks very satisfying and seems well optimized, running very well even on mid and low-end machines. Graphics-wise there's very little to complain about, really.
I can't really say much about the multiplayer, as i have yet to test it.
All in all, the game is well worth your time, IF you don't expect a realistic racing game and if you enjoy over the top races.
Probably the biggest downside, is the current price on Steam. If you can get a better deal, take it!

Insane 2 offers a number of innovations in the off-road racing genre. Besides the traditional time trial mode, the game features 9 other game modes, including the popular “Capture the flag”, “Gate hunt” and “Pathfinder”, as well as some new competitions, such as bonus hunting, territory control and helicopter pursuit. All of these modes are also available in multiplayer, with up to eight players participating simultaneously.
More than one hundred and fifty races combined into championships and cup competitions take place in Europe, America, Africa and the Antarctic. The game has an enormous variety of long distance tracks: sand and snowy deserts, high-speed roads and impassable cross-country paths, African beaches and deserted Antarctic stations.
The game features 18 vehicles of different classes, from buggies to monstrous “Bigfoots”, as well as an additional prototype class. Rating points won in the races can be used to upgrade any of the vehicles, from a selection of 15 running gear, body or engine upgrade alternatives. Each vehicle is furnished with a detailed destruction system. Reaching the end of a course without suffering any losses is an enormous challenge that only a select few are able to accomplish. The opponents, who constantly create extreme situations, aren’t the only danger: players also need to watch out for railway crossings, heavy tanker trucks and even lightning in stormy weather.

I enjoyed this game. My main motivation for and why I even played it was to get some closure on 13-2's ending and Serah and Lightning. I approached it with the mindset of completing it as quickly as possible to see the story, but I found myself enjoying it more the farther I got.
So first, things I liked. I loved the environments. Such an improvement from 13-2 in terms of size and utility. There was much more to see and do in the world that felt a lot more expansive. I liked how there were a greater variety of NPCs you could interact with (whether as vendors, quest givers, or just random people) It also looked a lot nicer than 13-2, particularly the Wildlands and the Dead Dunes. Side quests are a MASSIVE improvement over 13-2's. I'm not talking about the side AREAS in 13-2 like the Vile Peaks or the extra Oerbas that had a side story (they were well done and we SO needed more of those), I'm talking about those meaningless fetch quests with pretty much zero interaction and take up the 80% of the side quest datalog. In LR, there are more side quests, and a good portion of them have interesting stories and actually feature our protagonist INTERACTING with the quest givers. Not perfect, but a major improvement. I actually liked how this game took a bit more of a personal tone with the protagonist, really delving into Lightning as a person and character. I wish 13-2 treated Serah in the same way. Maybe because this series is pretty much just about Lightning :/.
Moving onto things I didn't like:
The time system. It's awfully frustrating and inconveniencing. How I have to wait for a specific time to access some area or a particular quest. There are some quest givers that only appear during certain times of the day and some parts of any main or side quest can only be done at certain times of the day. And once you're finished your quest and go to turn it in? Oh sorry, the NPCs aren't there anymore and you have to wait till the next day... It's annoying, especially when you have a THIRTEEN DAY TIME LIMIT. You have to painfully wait for some quests to progress because of the time while having a constant reminder of the short amount of time you have left. It's stupid. I know there should be enough time to complete most of the side quests, but it's stressful to have to worry about what time of the day I can do what while being reminded that time is running out. I understand how the time limit imposes a sense of urgency that's more realistic, but it could have been far less annoying and restrictive. Maybe I just want to take my time, enjoy the environments and explore as much as I can.
The combat. I liked having a real time battle system (it's what I'm used to), I liked being able to time my attacks, my dodges, and my guards. It made fighting more immersive. But what I liked even more was the more strategic-based combat system in 13-2. I liked the paradigm system where I was able to choose my strategy, assign roles to party members. Every move felt like it had some thought and planning put into it. I usually like real time combat, but for some reason, it felt off in this game. Nothing bad about it, it's just a personal preference, I guess.
The story for the most part felt rather incoherent and messy. There wasn't some underlying path Lightning was treading on to reach her goal. Her journey felt all over the place. There wasn't anything significant tying each chapter of her goal to save Serah. It felt like she was just visiting the areas to do busywork, taking part in the irrelevant lives of others. Yes, she was working to save the souls of her close friends, but it wasn't tied to her ultimate goal. It feels like the work she's doing throughout those thirteen days didn't advance any part of the overarcing plot: to save Serah. The final encounter did not have enough buildup from the plot at all, which made it feel rather incohesive with the rest of the story. I still enjoyed Lightning's reunion with her friends throughout her story, however, especially the Snow part (one of the sections where you could really feel the connection to the plot). Sections like that maintain the game's continuity from its predecessors.
The villain was a disappointment. He wasn't much of a character. He basically had no presence in the whole game until the very end. He had zero development and didn't feel like a threat at any point in the game, because he was missing for like 95% of the game. You couldn't really feel his influence on the story at all, it's like he came out of nowhere and conviently makes an appearance to take the physical form as a target who the good guys need to unleash their weapons at.
This brings me to my biggest complaint: how the characters were handled. My ultimate motivation for playing this game is to get some closure on what was left behind in FF13-2. Mostly on the characters. For the most part, the characters were handled well throughout the story. It was how they wre concluded that left me really disappointed. Serah, the person that Lightning starts this whole journey for, the centerpiece behind her motivations, and the person who was the main drive for her actions and story, is basically non-existant in the game. And what little there is of her takes form mostly in a fake Serah they created. I thought this was a neat concept (especially how this fake developed to harbor feelings for Lightning) but WHY NOT use what little characterization and development time there was on the REAL character? You know, the one Lightning talks about for the WHOLE GAME. But the biggerst letdown was how the journey for Serah concluded. There is basically no satisfactory closure on her relationship with Lightning. What did Serah want to say to Lightning after being revived? Did she forgive Light for her death in 13-2 (we should all know the answer but I would've liked to hear it from her)? Did she and Light have anything to say to each other after 500 years that showed the power of their will to be together again? Did she have any words about how she felt about everything that happened and being together with Light again? Did she even acknowledge Snow? Her fiance??? Nope, it ends just like that. She utters maybe three lines (that weren't all that memorable) before the game ends. Lightning has spent THREE WHOLE GAMES trying to get her back, even defeated a god. Then it's like she came back and it doesn't even matter at all. I mention Serah, and not so much the other characters, because I really felt like Lightning and Serah were the two most important characters in the trilogy (on how every game has been about them trying to be together), with everyone else a whole level below in terms of significance. If that is to be the centerpeice of your trilogy, it better be well developed and concluded, which I felt that it was not. Not only that, closure on the other characters were scarce too. It's like how everyone is leaving behind their old lives and homes, and no one cares. This game needed better, more satisfying closure on the characters than that last cutscene. It's supposed to be a happy ending, which is good, but there's no reason that a happy ending like this can't be more satisfying.
Overall a decent game that I enjoyed my time with, despite frustrating things, mostly because of the return of characters I grew into, even though in some cases they may have been inconsistent or lacking. The gameplay held its own well enough for me, though on a mechanical standpoint, this game really doesn't have much going for it, as there isn't anything all that special about it. The game is mostly carried by the characters built from the two precious games, and their stories. If you like the character or generally like Final Fantasy or JRPG style characters, then this may be your thing. If you don't care about the characters or the story beyond 13-2, I would say this isn't worth the time.

For a Free to Play game, this has to be one of the most chilling and exhilarating experiences I've had in a horror game. Although it has a simple game mechanic of (literally) walking through 1000 rooms to get to the end, it has you at an almost constant feeling of dread, knowing that you could be hunted down and pursued at any given moment. Every new specimen you meet has a unqiue origin and a really cool reference to other horror games. (Ex: Specimen 13 references to the water enemies in Amnesia.)
Having beat the main story and the DLC, I, sadly, don't have much of a reason to play this game as often anymore unless I get in the mood for a good adreniline rush. The Endless Mode does give me that fix, though there were a few frustrating moments of collision issues, a bit of texture glitches and enemies that I really hate encountering *cough*specimen6*cough*.
All in all, I highly recommend this game if you like the cute, humorous charm blended with macabre elements. Though I will say that I have friends that have tried this game and didn't take a liking to it, so of course, it's not for everyone.

Half Life 2 is the follow-up to the revolutionary, genre-defining game, Half Life.
For those who have never played either game before, but have played plenty of FPS', Half Life 2 wont be as big a deal to you as it was for those who played it when it was new. This game is a run-and-gun shooter with a variety of weapons and environmental puzzles to try and advance to the end of the game. There are no levels or cutscenes, rather, the idea in this game is immersion in the events that are unfolding around you. The gameplay is generally only interrupted by pauses so the game can load the next segment of the map.
There is no map, or objective marker, rather the game funnels you in a direction without feeling like you are just going through narrow corridors. Sometimes, you will get stuck trying to figure out what to do or where to go next, but this is rarely a concern.
Overall, this is a game that a PC gamer probably should play at some point in their lives. But so many games seem more action-packed or fun because of the ideas created by the original Half Life that have been used over and over as a standard for games today. It is still well worth a play through, but you certainly wont be excited by the gameplay today.

I must recommend for puzzle enthusiasts due to its unique, albeit short indie experience.

I love point-and-click adventure games and have played loads, and Gray Matter is now one of my most favorites. That's not to say it's perfect though, but it's defintiely one of the best.

Pros:
- beautiful art
- great music
- a well-done and interesting story, if a bit cliche and cheesy (in an addictive I-have-to-know-what-happens-next sort of way)
- a unique and fun gameplay mechanic with magic tricks, which had me wishing I could do more with it (hoping that if there's a sequel they expand and enhance this feature! it was a lot of fun). I've never played, or heard of, a game featuring a magician (as in, a stage magician, where the magic isn't really magic) and it felt different and exciting and was a lot more fun than I expected!
- the puzzles feel intuitive and fun but still provide a challenge. I really, really like the implementation of highlighting locations depending on what can/has been completed there. The progress list was also very helpful for the once or twice when I would get stuck and not know what to do, and be able to suss it out based on what my progress list said was only partially completed.
Cons:
- the quality of the voice acting varies, and took me out of the game a few times when it made me go "huh?". Occasionally a character said something in an odd inflection or with no emotion. It reminded me a lot of Cole Phelps interviewing people in LA Noire, where his reactions didn't always fit the technique choices of 'truth', 'doubt', and 'lie'.
- the animations surprised me by being lower quality than expected. I've recently replayed The Longest Journey, a game that came out in 1999, and Gray Matter's animations reminded me a lot of TLJ. I guess the screen shots made my expectations higher? Certainly not awful, but not what I expected from a game in 2014.
- I experience no bugs/glitches EXCEPT one that effectively prevented me from continuing the game, forcing me to reload a save from hours earlier. I recommend making at 2-3 saves per chapter and keeping them, just in case. This was the only time I was forced to consult walkthroughs, in order to try to figure out what went wrong. Eventually determined it was not necessarily due to me but something just went wrong in the game... I suspect I did something in an odd/unexpected order and messed something, a la King's Quest. Don't expect this to be something that happens often though, as when I looked into it it seemed like a rare problem (but it's still a problem that exists, and a big one at that).
I got the game on sale for ~$3 and felt like I got way more than my monies worth, honestly. Even with what I consider to be 'cons', I'd have happily paid the full price for the game and am recommending it to my friends. I really hope there's a sequel someday!

An enjoyable story, with minor puzzles
I find point and click adventures to be generally enjoyable, but the older I get the more interest I have in the story they tell than the puzzles.
So when I finally started playing Gray Matter, which I received for very cheap as part of a bundle, my main focus was on the story. Having now put almost 12 hours into it (having let the game run a bit, it was probably closer to 11), I have to say I ultimately enjoyed the game, and might seek out more of Jane Jensen's works (a writer on the game).
The game follows Sam/Samantha as she interacts with David and the other characters we meet. As she is a magician, the puzzles mostly involve her performing tricks or solving puzzles as she gets closer to her goal of becoming a master magician. However, the focus of the game is not on the tricks, but rather the story.
There are some interesting twists as the story progresses, and it had me shivering in a few spots. I definitely recommend this game if you're looking for an interesting story, and have at least a passing enjoyment of point and click adventures.
Gray Matter gets 4 of 5 stars, only because of very slight control issues in a handful of scenes.
