Edit (mainly an update and response to Mike's comment):
Mike, since this review I processed for a refund, but have been avidally keeping up to date with the game. Undeniably, the dev/s are doing an amazing job providing regular updates to the game, already fixing (or on their way to fixing) things that really ruined the experience (like not being able to assign flights to specific gates). That is the nature of early access and from that front the dev/s comittment is really nice to see.
Whether I know game design or not, I'm sure I'm not the only one who feels that there's early access and 'early access' (where the former is a diamond in the rough with some issues, and the latter is something that has fundamental flaws and is basically unplayable - a money grab). Upon its release, I would say SimAirport sat somewhere uncomfortably between the two. It was playable, but had fundamental flaws, and at the time (and still does to some degree) lack a large amount of content or depth to make the game truly replayable. I'm sure there are people gagging for a game like this and are willing to pay just to get early access. I'm not one of them. I'm willing to support a game, especially one that has commited developers like this one, but I don't buy something purely based off commitment or what will be. I take into account the current state of the game.
As someone who likes the idea of the game, but could also be fine without it, I would say ~£20 is a little steep. I'm confident that the majority of negative reviews for this game are not about it's playability but infact that for the state the game was in when they purchased it, the price is pretty extornionate. Everyone has an idea of value that is their own. You may see the potential this game has, as well as there being no other alternative as good reason to spend £20, there are many like you from a glance of the steam reviews. But equally, I see that while the game has potential, if I were to buy it now, it's currently not worth anywhere near £20 in my opinion, and similarly from reading the steam reviews I can see many that share my view. This is why I discussed other early access games charging less at the start, that way they can appeal to both you and I. While they are getting more money from people like you (assuming you are like that), they're losing out more on people like me. Who know's what price is the 'right' price, the best blend so to speak.
None-the-less, with the rate the game is improving I can see myself slowly starting to justify the current price, but just not yet, there's still some way to go.
Original review:
Right, I'm going to reflect the same opinions of many other critical reviews, but here goes.
The game has an interesting concept, and generally executes what has been implemented quite well. Unfortunately, as of writing this review, very little of the game seems actually present (or at least I hope that's the case). In my playtime (2-3 hours), I accomplished most of what the game had to offer. Currently this game has very little replayability value. The game also has quite a few incredibly distracting bugs, and occasionally crashes.
All this would probably be fine, if it wasn't for the fact that the developers are asking the full game price despite the games current state with both lack of content and strong presence of bugs. Early access isn't a banner you can hide behind and say "Well, it's early access, so of course it's broken" or "Well, it's early access, so of course there's very little to do" while still justifying full price. I've bought games in the past, such as Minecraft and KSP when they were in their early access (/pre-release phases). I think both cost around £7, which is easily half the price of the full release version if not less. And yet, compatively, even in their state at the time of purchase, they were far more complete than SimAirport is.
And that's really it. The game isn't a bad premise (although I am aware it's not the only game meant to be coming out in this genre), but at the moment, it's buggy... with little content... at full price.
I can't help but feel that the 'greed' of the developers will actually backfire. I'm sure they would have more takers if they price the game appropriately, in turn, they'll recieve more feedback, and the customers would be happier and not feel completely ripped off. I would geniunely struggle to justfiy spending £10 on this game at the moment, and they're asking for almost double that, pffft.

Having adored the other Annapurna Interactive title released this year -
is my GOTY - I decided to pick
up despite not being a fan of puzzle games. I was rewarded with a mindblowing experience.
The game is built around the intriguing premise of solving puzzles through finding similarities between disparate scenes. Throughout the whole game, the gimmick never got stale, making it a pleasure to search for how one object could magically transform into another in ways I would never have imagined. I'm not a huge fan of puzzles, as I'm usually too obtuse to get far, but even for an inexperienced player like myself, I found that the solutions flowed quite easily. I didn't look anything up - just experimented until it clicked.
The narrative is told completely through images and music, making it a puzzle of its own, but I found it fairly easy to understand. There was even a plot twist that actually shocked me (in hindsight, maybe I should have saw it coming?), so I'd say that the story is itself simple and effective.
is short and sweet, beautifully illustrated, and wonderfully fun to play around with. I'd definitely recommend this game to anyone - it's highly unique and was clearly a labour of love. Even non-puzzle-lovers will find something to enjoy. It's left me with a yearning for more games like it.

Also had not been a fan of typically what the studio has pumped out, but I was reading the best of 2017 games lists that are out there and this consistently was showing up. So I thought I'd give it shot. Holy crap am I glad I gave it a shot. This game was incredible! BUY! BUY! BUY! I really enjoyed learning about Norse mythology and psychosis. Again, BUY! BUY! BUY! And when you go to play be sure to play with headphones like it suggests. First of all, I have to admit that I simply assumed that auditory hallucinations are commonly experienced like one might hear the voice of a person standing some distance away, akin to visual hallucinations which seamlessly blend into the field of vision, since a whisper directly in your ear would seem to be more easily identifiable as unreal. From the documentary included with the game I did learn however that mental illness, who would've guessed, does not conform to common sense logic in this way and while there are of course many forms of schizophrenia, the game does indeed give an accurate representation and is not improperly overdramatized in this fashion.
Aside from that, there are a few technical points of criticism which I have not seen commonly addressed. While Senua's model is truly terrific (in terms of animation as well, but especially the realism of her eyes and skin/hair texture), so much so that one might feel, much more than might usually be the case, invited to occasionally spend a few minutes simply staring at her, this is not the case for much of the environment. While ground vegetation looks decent, tree leaves are generally poorly cropped, low-resolution sprites, which irritatingly stand out from the background unless so far away as to be completely blurred by the depth of field effect. Worse still, the texture of very obvious foreground objects, especially flat surfaces of rock, wood or metal, are often so low resolution that it's pixelated even at a distance. Screenshots somewhat obscure this with filters (available via the built-in photo mode, a really nice feature), but while playing I found this particularly jarring because of the discrepancy between Senua and the background.
On that note, I'd like to mention that "post-processing" is one single option that encompasses several filters like depth of field, motion blur and film grain, possibly among others, which do make the background look much nicer, but unfortunately cannot be disabled seperately. Since motion blur gives me a headache, I had to turn this entire option off, even though I would have liked to leave film grain on. (Note that this only improves the above-mentioned texture quality insofar as it blurs the distand background. While standing still and looking at a nearby surface, it does nothing.)
The performance is stable, but optimization is not impressive as turning all the options down makes everything look utterly atrocious, but does not improve the framerate anywhere near what would be justified. (Then again, The Talos Principle would probably be one of the very few games I would call well-optimized.)
What I also rather disliked was the use of live-action video in cutscenes. Somewhat ironically, the heavily distorted, but obviously real footage right next to Senua's pristine presence didn't quite fit in my opinion (even though they only appear in flashbacks and visions).
Gameplay-wise the only complaint I have is that for a story-based game, no matter the price tag, it's really short, especially since the combat is very easy even on hard (similar to Tomb Raider e.g.), especially if you use the 'focus' (i.e. bullet-time) mode, which you are forced to do regularly, and due to the linearity of the narrative there isn't really any replay value. That being said, I very much appreciate that there are no in-game achievements, unlockables, talents or any similar nonsense that doesn't belong in this kind of game. It might have been a sensible decision to avoid overextending the admittedly limited level and enemy design variety, but unlike some others mentioned, I didn't find it tiring as is. In fact, I really liked the combat. While the camera does lock on to enemies, it works much better than in other console-oriented games. Despite being appropriately slow and weighty, the abilities work nicely and don't feel sluggish or unresponsive. One fantastic plus in my opinion, which by itself makes controls feel far better than other 'cinematic-combat' games, is the ability to cancel attacks. You can still interrupt a sword swing in order to evade (and the animation is not too jerky either).
[On a sidenote, like other games of this kind, it obviously lends itself very well to a longplay, in case one prefers and actual movie over a highly cinematic game.]
Voice acting was quite good, but, even though this is certainly not an objective flaw, I found it somewhat distracting that all the voices have different accents for no good reason. While it would seem somewhat sensible to give the Picts a Scottish accent, only one of the voices uses one. This would not bother me in a modern setting, but presumably Senua comes from a small village where everyone has the same dialect and she wouldn't have any other references (aside from maybe the Vikings, who she wouldn't be able to understand though). The writing is generally good, but occassionally uneven. Terms like 'dad' or 'teenager' just don't fit here.
Finally, I fundamentally disagree with the existential philosophy presented here and this did somewhat detract from my enjoyment of the story, particularly the ending, since I've been noticing growing increasingly averse to unsound ideologies compared to my willingness to suspend judgement years ago. Nonetheless it was a genuinely beautiful composition. Despite the much darker theme of 'Hellblade', I think it can very well be compared to 'The Fountain' (despite that not being a game), while I would mention 'SOMA' and 'Bioshock Infinite' as positive contrasts in terms of writing.
Overall, I give the game an 8/10. A 7 would feel a bit harsh, but the graphical inconsistency and lackluster story do dampen my excitement a bit.

Very nice game.  There's a three-fold progression.
First the tutorial, which takes you through the basics of the game: moving and shooting.
Next comes the progression to commander, where you take missions to gain ranks, either invading a planet, attacking a space station, defending a space station or bounty hunting.  In addition to spending money on upgrading your ship and your soldier, you also gain skill points and partake in the Prophecy missions.
Finally, once you attain the rank of commander, YOU decide what YOUR faction will do next.  You can exterminate another faction's colony to build your own, which earns you resources, or attack another faction's space station to make room for your own.  This has a 4x feel to it.
Once you get into the game, it becomes difficult to stop playing.

This game may not offer much in sense of graphics, but it makes up for it in gameplay for sure. It brings together a couple of genres, exploration/space sim/3rd person shooter/rpg in a very unique and entertaining way. Not something I have seen done succesful before.

I’ll be honest with you. I bought Lightning Returns primarily for the dress up, and my expectations weren’t high. While I wasn’t a fan of FF XIII, and even less of a fan of it’s confused, malformed sequel, you couldn’t fault either game for their excellent selection of high quality, glossy lipped and slightly dead eyed Japanese dolls. The producers of Lightning Returns seem to have realised this and baked it into the marketing campaign with all the subtlety of a cruise missile aimed at a nunnery.
What will come as something of a surprise to many then is that the game is not the car crash disaster it by all rights should have been, though it is heavily flawed. Lightning Returns is a good example of why steam needs a middle ground rating – I can’t honestly give it a thumbs up, not without serious caveats but dismissing it entirely is every bit as unjust.
The core conceit in particular is both original and compelling – God is going to end the world in seven days in order to create a new one, being evidently based on the bored bi-polar sociopath of the Old Testament. You as the hero can do nothing to stop this – all you can do is save as many souls of those in this world as you can, so that they may be reborn in the next. There’s a further wrinkle to this - no-one has been born in 500 years, but equally no-one can die of old age. However, people may still be killed by other traditional means such as disease, misadventure or good fashioned suicide. This sets up a nihilistic Children of Men-esque world covered in a thick malaise of apathy, offset by a tense race against time as you do what you can to save what little hope is left.
This being based on the characters and premises of FF XIII, this potential is of course completely squandered. The story is borderline incomprehensible at best, a train wreck with no survivors at worst. Set 1000 years after the first game, Lightning is awoken from cryosleep by God and has agreed to be the world’s soul collecting saviour with the hook that her sister Serah is reborn in the next world. But she’s also had her emotions removed, the reasons of which are never adequately explained, so why she should be moved by this emotional plea is unclear. Removing your main character’s personality as well as driving motivation doesn’t sound like a recipe for entertaining drama without a careful writer at the helm. Sadly the writing is roughly on par with the last two games – which is to say it’s crushingly, wincingly awful. All of the characters you either loathe or barely remember make their melodramatic, floppy haired return, and chew their way through dialogue so purple it would make Anne Rice blush.
Word of advice – set the language to Japanese. All credit to the English voice actors, they do the best they can with the material they’re served but this is hot, George Lucus tier garbage and not understanding the words being spoken adds a comforting, brain shielding barrier between player and script. Your comlink companion Hope (also thankfully de-emotioned) never shuts the ♥♥♥♥ up either, and in English his repeated dialogue goes from irritating to excruciating very quickly indeed.
So it’s down to the mechanics to save the whole show, and I personally found the game quite compelling in spite of its shortcomings. The impact of the time limit on this game can not be overstated. Make no mistake, this is an absolute core part of the game that cannot be ignored in any way, shape or form. You have six in game days to finish the whole thing, with an hour of game time being roughly equal to a real-world minute. You have a limited supply of EP (I forget what it actually is, so I’m going to assume it refers to Lightning’s collection of Emerson Lake & Palmer records) that can be used to stop time for about three real world minutes – EP is regained slowly, typically by killing baddies. Time management is absolutely crucial, and it is a massive barrier to relaxed exploration. If this sounds like a deal breaker to you, I would not recommend this game regardless of how much you want to see Lightning in her knickers.
In terms of freedom, Lightning Returns finally gets the balance right after the hand holding corridor of FFXIII and the borderline cryptic non-linearity of the sequel. There are four large areas, each containing their own main quest as well as a series of side quests that can be tackled in any order, though enemies do get tougher in the larger, more open sections. The side quests are of particular import – Lightning does not level up by fighting monsters (the lazy cow) and instead gains flat bonuses by completing these quests. They’re of a variable quality – there is a literal “find my dog” quest, but there are some nice multi-tiered interwoven quests that don’t inhale dong in there as well. The time limit alongside a general lack of waypoints can make this aspect of the game quite frustrating, and I feel that they should have made these more optional – you will have to complete a sizable number if you want to have hope of beating the bosses or even some of the tougher basic enemies.
A word of warning - The game is surprisingly difficult, and demands you learn its mechanics quickly. You will need to learn how to block quickly, or you will die, frequently and unceremoniously to even the lowliest of enemies. You will not be able to muddle through things on the default difficulty –Every loss results in a loss of a precious hour from the in game clock. The first boss in particular is a wake up call, and they only get harder from there – seriously consider starting on easy if action games are not your forte, though it should be noted that if you do so your future descendants will feel your gaming shame.
The battle system is fantastic once you get the hang of it though. This is by far the most action orientated of any of the FF games, with nary a menu to be seen. You control only Lightning this time, but she can switch between three different costumes at will – when one is in use, the ATB gauges of the others will recharge faster. While each costume has different abilities and stats, you’re largely free to customise their active abilities as you wish. There’s a bewildering number of costumes and accessories available, and those wanting skimpy bikinis might want to temper their expectations- while those exist, they’re vastly outnumbered by the range of much more tasteful outfits. This is probably for the best, as Lightning is built like a 15 year old boy with two oranges in a bra – her bottom is Isaac Clarke levels of flat. Flatter than Master Chief. Flatter than Sigourney Weaver in Alien. I’m not some kind of badonkadonk zealot, but this is heartbreaking stuff.

Lightning Returns is easily my favorite Final Fantasy XIII game.  Given my opinion of the other two games that's not saying all that much, but I genuinely like this one.
The battle system is the best thing to happen to a Final Fantasy game in years, it's a fantastic hybrid between direct character control and picking commands from a menu and it's something I've never seen before.  It's possible it was ripped from some MMO I don't know about, but it was very fresh concept to me and it took me by surprise how much I'm digging it.  The battle system alone is enough to put this game ahead of the other games in the series for me.
I also really like the character customization system.  I wasn't sure how I'd feel about basic abilities like attack and guard being limited, equipable items, but it works.  The garb (aka dress) system also works because, whether we admit it or not, we all like playing dress up with our virtual action figures (they're totally not dolls! :) - whether it's putting spiked pauldrons on a barbarian or a highly impractical "armor" on Lightning.
Beyond the combat systems, I like the general structure of the game too, even though it's exceptionally basic.  Sadly none of the quests are all that compelling by themselves, they're still all Fedex and monster hunts, but I like the regulated nature of having a bunch of quests and gradually working through them.  It keeps me going in Bethesda RPGs where most quests are similarly hollow and mechanical in nature, and it kept me going here.
The time limit did worry me quite a bit.  Basically you have a limited about of time to accomplish a particular number of tasks in game, and if you fail to do so, you get a bad end and have to restart.  The notion that I could play the game for 20+ hours only to get a bad ending and have to start over seemed ridiculous.  However, it turns out it's a complete nonissue. I decided to play the game on easy because I was so worried about that and I ended up completing all main quests and like 90% of the side quests by the game's half way point without looking at a guide once.
The story is the one area I'm pretty disappointed with the game.  The plot is nonsense, but that's no different than the other FFXIII games...or Final Fantasy games in general for that matter.  However, in other FF games you at least get some degree of enjoyable spectacle in how the story is presented - big set piece moments and scenes.  Apart from the always cool opening cinematic, I've only come across one other scene that I thought was cool.  Other than that, the game doesn't even get its anime drama-on properly.  All the series main characters have like 2- 5 minute cameos at best, during which they try to cram in entire emotional arcs and it comes as especially absurd how quickly characters change from one viewpoint to another and resolve their conflict.
So the story is a wash like the other games and the spectacle that was the saving grace of the original FFXIII isn't there, but I like playing the damn thing more than any other game in the series.  It goes without saying that you shouldn't bother playing this unless you suffered through the other FFXIII games, but if you do, you might just find is a nice way to finally be done with that chapter in FF history.

This adventure game signed the legendary Jane Jensen (Gabriel Knight series) was Jane's first since parting ways with Sierra. It had a long and troubled development over many years but the end result is VERY good. And now it's finally avalible on Steam.
Weaving one of her signature stories that blends the paranormal with the contemporary, in this case neurobiology and the unused potential in the human mind. When street magician Samantha "Sam" Everett gets waylaid by a broken motorcycle on her way to London and in need of shelter and money decides to pose as the new assisstant for the reclusive neurobiology researcher Dr. David Styles in his gothic mansion outside Oxford. Pretty soon strange events are afoot and you play as both Samantha and Dr. Styles to try and get to the bottom of it.
The game offers interesting puzzles of varying difficulty, especially when Sam has to use her street magic to manipulate people and objects to progress. The soundtrack by Robert Holmes is gothic and hauntingly beautiful, especially the songs by The Scarlet Furies.  They really helps to set the mood of the story.
If adventure games and good stories are your thing, this one is an instant buy. I don't think you'll regret it.

Overall, my experience has been positive (though not great).
BUGS: I have yet to experience a game-breaking bug, though I haven't tested the Cafe yet (which many people complain that it can seriously create havoc in your game and have to start over). Yes, you do get people/vehicles stuck, but you can continue playing if you don't mind seeing that odd baggage cart stuck on the tarmac.
LAGGING: I try to avoid scheduling big aircraft to avoid the lagging. V-SYNC has helped alot (on ADM, open Vision Control centre, go to Gaming, then to 3D Application Settings and scroll down to "wait for vertical refresh"). I can easily handle 1.000 people. Reloading the game every now and then also seems to help quite alot. Then again I have a pretty good machine. Avoid if your computer is not up for it. This is definitely an area they need to work heavily on. People want to build big airports. You should be able to handle 5.000 passengers even on a descent (not great or even good) PC.
CONTENT: There isn't much content yet, so no, you won't be able to recreate Dubai or LHR with shops, restaurants, underground and overground transport, garages, etc. No shops, for example (apart from the Cafe). Scheduling is very very basic (the Timetable is where, i believe, most people will spend their time and needs major changes). You don't even see where the Aircraft come from or go to.
PRICE: 22EUR is quite alot. Should have been around 15EUR.
Although I ticked the "yes" box, my recommendation is to wait as there is another airport game coming out soon.

Alright, I posted a review back when I got the game and wanted to post a new updated one. A lot of the bad reviews seem to stem from people forgetting the idea that this game is early access. However, this is probably one of the most intriguing games I've seen for a while. Buyers beware, at this stage you are not getting a complete game....YET! Yes it may not be complete but it definitely is a fun game to play at this stage. Here are some more specifics into it:
Likes:
1. As far as managing, you have a lot of different ways to control your airport.
2. Fairly realistic, I am an aviation enthusiast and granted there are some unrealistic things about this game but overall, especially with the background ATC chatter and the airport equipment, I am pretty happy with the current result.
3. Developers are ACTIVE. SimAirport is receiving updates monthly if not weekly. The developers have listened to the community, and are working their way to the finished product.
4. A lot of different aspects of the airport. Everything from security to the baggage conveyors to a separate café. The airport is intricate.
Dislikes:
Once again this is an early access so most of these I overlook. However, you may experience these issues.
1. AI bugs. Lots of bugs with the AI. In the current stage of my airport the AI will get "stuck." Now once again, we are expecting this to be fixed in the near future so stay tuned.
2. Frame rates and stability are not great. Running 10x speed with 3,000 moving objects in the airport does take a toll on your computer. So be aware of this aspect when it comes to the game.
3. Scheduling isn't the best. Out of all the things, the aircraft are set to arrive at a certain time and you can almost guarantee the busier the airport gets, there's going to be a delay for any larger airlines. Especially those 747s and the A380s.
Overall I do suggest this game. However, for those who are on edge and don't want to commit now, I would suggest maybe waiting a little more to see more of those features come out. I am happy with the current game and I am looking forward to see what it brings in the future. Hope you guys enjoyed this review!

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is one of those games where it is gripping and engaging for every second. While it only has about an 8-10 hour playtime, the fact that it is all interesting and important to the story makes Hellblade an amazing game.
You play as Senua, a lone Celtic warrior. She suffers from psychosis and hears voices telling her things throughout the game. You seek to battle through various Norse gods in order to free your dead husbund from the depths of hell, while sacrificing yourself in his place.
Senua's Sacrifice has a great balance between its philisophical aspects and the raw, adrenelin-pumping action, and that's something that makes it special.  You won't get burned out from the stress of the horrific combat (too much), and you also won't feel like the game is just talking at you. All in all the game has great pacing, great art, and a great message so you should probably get it if you can

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice, A game I am pretty disappointed with purchasing.
When I first looked at this game, I had a gut feeling it wasn't worth the price or time, but sadly, might gut is never wrong. Thankfully, I bought this on a sale.
FIrst off:
The game itself is very misleading in both title and thematics. Hellblade Senua's Sacrifice sounds like a total mythological action game and sadly there's almost no actual action. No, This game made the mistake of being a psychological thriller with small action based fighting. If I had to compare the gameplay, It would be Ryse Son of Rome, A game that's gameplay is surprisingly similar if not identical. Basically a game with a marginally fixed 3rd person view when it comes to fighting. Although I did enjoy Ryse, Hellblade is definitely not the same cup of tea.
Hellblade has the misfortune of basing the entire game around Norse Mythology without any actual mythological presence, but rather the psychological representation of them encased in a fear driven woman whose carrying around a severed head of a mad man. And while again, Ryse kind of did the same with Roman mythology, There was actual gameplay to it that could be grasped and accomplished. Every time I die in this game, I feel like it was done cheaply and without explanation. It doesn't make it hard, It just makes it annoying. Granted, I learn from my mistakes and the game itself runs on a pseudo-Lives system. So rather than every time you die, you lose a life, its every time you die, you gain a permadeath meter which when first explained sounded stupid to some people, but its basically a redecorated "lives" system and I just like saying "get gud" to those wannabes out there, but we all know that some gamers like being spoon fed.
Sadly, Its not even that the gameplay is hard. Its just really simple and annoying. 90% of the time, youre just basically looking for shapes to captivate a OCD disorder for opening stupid doors.  That's right, Most of this game is a boring run around looking for SHAPES.... I mean really? Can I please just enjoy a game about killing without someone adding in "psychological BS" into a game? The worst part is that you hear her inner thoughts and thinking process in whispers that  make you wonder why did they do this in the game? So you would probably lose your mind. Even before you start the game, They exclaim on an entire page: "best experienced with headphones on" so you can have those whisper drowning in your ear all damn day as you try to find shapes... The only thing the whispers are actually good for are to tell you when to block your enemies when you can see them because as I said earlier: THE CAMERA IS LOCKED 3rd PERSON. Meaning, I cant move it, As if I am actually the person fighting these weird looking guys with a deer head on throughout the entire game. WHERES THE VARIETY?! OH wait: Boss battles.... 5 boss battles.... These bosses are the closest thing to an actual mythology and I am just sitting here saying: I could be playing something else...
But is it bad? Well.... Its not a bad game, Its just not a good game. I do enjoy the mechanics to some degree, but the game teases me with actual mythology just to play this game. I feel like I am going to get far more Norse Mythology from God of War 4 than this game and that's kind of sad. I own an entire book on norse mythology and this game doesn't teach me anything I cant read out of that, but it is nice to see Runes placed in a game other than fantasy games, So I am not too bummed out.
Have I been too hard on this game? No, People claimed this was close to a AAA game on an independent level and that sounds about right if we include it in the same idea of Bioware owned by EA as the AAA part(Just an example, obviously the indie company here did better than EA). The thing about Senua's Sacrifice, I don't feel like it was trying to be a game as much as a movie that you can briefly interact with and I think this would make a better movie in general. The concept is good, but psychological parts mixing with combat, just seems rather mixed and trying to be both horror and action. The game is a must get if you like psychology mixed with some combat and definitely if you liked story driven games like Ryse or Heavy Rain.
I dont recommend this game on a personal level simply because the gameplay was lacking for me. If you like psychological thrillers, this game is for you, on a professional and unbiased level, This is a good game for psychological thrill seekers.Again,  I personally dont because I find this stuff boring even with the recommended headphones on. Im a gamer that has his likes and dislikes, but I still wanted to try this out for myself and I have to say, I dont regret playing this one. It definitely has something, but I wish they worked on it more for better fighting gameplay.

The puzzles (if you could even call them that) leave a lot to be desired for me though.  It's all about lining up tile art, which in most cases are solvable with brute force - clicking around and dragging tiles until you spot the way tiles should line up. It started to feel a little tedious to me halfway through once you understand how the game works.
There's also a really disjointed story buried in here, but the gameplay fractures the narrative significantly, making it really difficult to care about. What would you say to a platformer where you have to roll around a square? Not push, roll. The concept has been done well elsewhere, like with your slick technicolor cube in EDGE, but you have to admit it's not the most appealing pitch in the world. You need a really sharp presentation or some enthralling puzzles to make that sort of awkwardness sing, and I suppose on some level Gravilon tried to do that. It tried, but it definitely did not succeed.
Gravilon is a puzzle platformer where you roll a square around a bunch of floating lines. Other than some floaty movement and dots you can touch to reverse gravity, the rolling is just as clunky as you're imagining. You can build up momentum to cross gaps, which you'll need to do pretty much all the time, but it makes your box extremely difficult to control. And that's a pretty core problem with the game, because not half a dozen levels in it gets blisteringly hard. You'll start being expected to make long precision jumps and clutch gravity flips, and falling off the level or touching deadly yellow lines starts the whole level over.
There are a few extra tools you have to overcome these difficulties, like a slow-motion button and the fact that when you die or reset, your previous square remains in the level. But rather than supporting your efforts, these mechanics become required before even warming you up to how they work. All of this takes place in a gray void with the next and previous levels visible in the back and foregrounds, which sounds cool except they're all made of the same black lines and blend together into a visual mess. Add a plain-text menu that looks like fifteen minutes of placeholder programming, and you have an unpolished, unbalanced ball of frustration on your hands. And it doesn't even roll right.
I'll be the first to sing the praises of a fresh take on the vast platformer genre, even if it doesn't pan all the way out. But Gravilon is a transparently lazy attempt at using a gimmick to push a poorly-designed game. Anyone with functioning eyes should see the problem with the layered levels right away, and if you somehow get past that you really, really should be questioning the fun factor of precision maneuvering with a rolling square. No one seems to have caught these fatal flaws and so Gravilon sits here, mired in its failings like a wagon with square wheels.

I really want to like Salvation Prophecy. It has an amazing concept, a really good storyline with two distinct endings, and plenty of great lore. However, I can't like it. The beginning of the game? Awful. It's mostly grindy, you feel very not powerful, and the like. The middle? Amazingly fun, complex tactical simulation. The ending? Tedious, and even more grindy than the beginning. Without spoiling anything, you can spend the entire game carefully building up an entire empire only to watch it be tore down, with little you can do. Some of the most fun I've had in recent gaming history has been in the middle section of this game, but I honestly don't feel like I can recommend it.
In addition to my other hesitations, the game is very glitchy. There are also missions exclusive to sections of the game, with know way of knowing in advance which missions will vanish. I had to replay the campign just to get some achievements that I missed because I didn't realize the missions would be inaccessible later. The graphics are also wanting, with absolutely no customization available -- and it definitely feels like it's missing.
Overall, Salvation Prophecy is an amazing attempt. I feel like if it had been given the funding it needed, it could have become an amazing game, similar in caliber to the other space epics but distinct, bringing its own unique perspective on the space sim. But it wasn't. It felt far too much like an indie game that desperately wanted to become something mainstream, it just needed the funding.

Let me give you a quick summary:
Graphics:
- Indie budgets shows right away. Textures are low res, location are reused, models are ridiculous sometimes.
- Animations are hilarious
+ Space combat effects are decent
+ Very few obvious bugs to speak about
+ unique planetary missions have amazing locations
Sound:
- your own music recommended
- voice acting is ridiculous
- actually not that many sound effects
+ doesn't get annoying
+ space travel effects amazing
+ no bugs detected
+ ambient sound effects help immersion
Gameplay:
- simplistic in every area
- little choice of items, most useless
- difficult to understand why are you promoted to faction leader so soon
- otherwise unbalanced (AI and Aliens)
- land combat AI sucks (worst part of the game actually)
- shallow story line, some ridiculous moments especially with runes
- arcade minigames in warp tunnels and wormholes
+ story is presented in interesting manner and despite being quite simple is properly explained and transparent, you can tell the reason for the ongoing war
+ missions. Mass fighter jumping in and out of combat is just the most amazing thing this game has (I say this as FreeSpace veteran)
+ simplified arcade combat - not necessary a good thing but at least it is made in proper way (does not annoy)
+ side missions, hilarious pirate descriptions
+ multiple aspects (well, not that many) of faction to manage
+ ending better than Mass Effect 3, despite very ♥♥♥♥♥♥ final boss battle(considering mission length this battle is actually a good thing)
+ overal feeling and atmosphere is a combined shadow of Homeworld, FreeSpace and Mass Effect titles. It is quite simply good.
Conclusion:
Love and care is visible in each and every part of the title. It is properly done, relativelly bug free, not badly imbalanced jewel that makes it obvious - developers really wanted to deliver but were short on funds. These are the pople who seem to know what they are doing and where they are heading, just didn't head the means to make the journey.
You will not be disappointed if you get this game on sale, even tho it is short you will enjoy this.
And perhaps showing your support will prompt people responsible for Salvation Prophecy to create a sequel.

Ah, Wanderlust: Rebirth. It's been too long since I played you, and I still have good memories...
But, every time I try to go back to playing Wanderlust: Rebirth (WR from now on), I end up remembering why I stopped playing it in the first place. Let me just get one thing out of the way: I do consider this game to be particularly good for what it is, a 2D top-down beat'em-up RPG. WR would be even better had the developpers not centered its gameplay on co-op with other players. And so I start explaining why I don't recommend WR...
First, as the entire game was developed with co-op in mind, there is actually content of the game that can't be accessed in solo gameplay. Yes: because everyone likes playing with randoms or, even better, can convince his friends to play a game only he seems to like.
The first point segues into the second: playing alone you get AI team-mates, but they are just a sliver short of being useful. The reason for this is that the AI teamsters tend to get killed incredibly easily by certain enemy types while not amounting to doing any real damage (or healing) to contribute, in a general way. They are also clearly not balanced to help you in the higher difficulties, meaning that it does end up as if they weren't really there. It even gets insulting when, as the Paladin, you can't even use your skills to bring them back to life, AS WOULD HAPPEN IF THEY WERE A REAL PLAYER INSTEAD. What's the point? Are the developpers telling us that only some classes work for playing solo?
Third, for a game with WANDERLUST as its name, you don't tend to wander much at all. Exploration is minimal, having most scenarios (or chapters, if I remember how the game calls it correctly,) being linear and driven by a quest that is very cliché. I'll admit that you DO wander
a somewhat varied diversity of caves and forests, and that perhaps the setting of the game has a worthy backstory that ends up either unseen by the player or forcefully fed at him depending on perspective and situation, but you would expect initially to have a little more freedom exploring a world full of annoying monsters for you to beat up.
Fourth, the enemies. Maybe if this point was a little more balanced in favour of the single player or by how many players there are in the game, the earlier three points wouldn't stand out as much. But come on! Some enemies are plain ludicrous in their balance. Blood slimes, even if "rare" in the campaign, are about the most annoying thing in the arena game mode if you can't finish them off quickly, or rather, quicker than they can leech off your useless AI budies' health into their own; blood slimes can also one-shot you, given the right conditions. And this is simply the enemy that pops to mind as the most unbalanced: poisoning spiders and the annoying elf casters also come to mind, if you really want a list of sorts.
Fifth... is definitely the grind. You would not believe how much you have to grind in this game... and you'll hate why, too: you need 3 of the previous tier of items to craft a next-tier item. And you also need tons of crappy small parts semi-randomly to craft things. And you need a "blueprint" of the item you're crafting. And the ingame currency as well, lots of it. And then this consumes space in your already limited and otherwise useless inventory. See where I'm getting at? You're not even grinding to become more powerful, oh no: you're grinding to raise a few numbers just a little, so that coming across an elf mage isn't immediately lethal at least. Leveling up is instead done by how well you scored on a chapter, which then gives you X of a total of Y skillpoints that the chapter can give. Meaning that playing alone is much harder in addition to the lackluster AI buddies, especially when you have to rely on them since most other things in the game are broken. Heck, the only way it could be worse was if you decided to actually play WITHOUT the AI buddies, which I believe you can, but why would you? It's better to have 3 meatshields and possibly a buff or two for 10 seconds than to die in those 10 seconds just because everthing was targetting you and you didn't kill the most dangerous things as fast as you could.
Also, that I know of, the multiplayer scene is practically dead. Maybe you can get into a game with a stranger, MAYBE. Timezones apply, of course. Be wary of desynchs, too: those can be quite annoying, with everyone stuck waiting for something that will never happen because the other person doesn't have the exact same data.
So, why did I bother making this review? Simple reasons. Primarily to warn you not to buy this game, but also to tell you that most of the things I listed are promised not to be issues with the sequel of this game, the (as of the time) yet unreleased Wanderlust Adventures. Seriously, DON'T BUY THIS GAME. You'd do the developpers more of a favour to buy the next game and extra copies if you care about them (thus creating a larger player base for an inherently better game by gifting the extra copies) than if you bought this game right now, or ever.
(Edit: the Steam store finally has the aforementioned Wanderlust Adventures here,
, in case you were wondering.)

tl;dr- If you like puzzles, music and exploring, I recommend giving the game a try. I like the abstract nature and lack of handholding, and I especially recommend this game to my programming cohort ;).
I grabbed this game in a bundle- and this game single-handedly influenced my decision to go ahead and get the bundle. This game is at first glance, sheer EYE-CANDY! Although, as I will go on to explain, it is much more than that. As a person who loves point-and-click games- this game is a 3D adventure/exploration with puzzles and P&C without the inventory.
I want to quote the developer here, "Fract is not just about exploring a world or solving its puzzles, but it's about taking a journey of musical discovery". I feel this statement is so true. As a self-proclaimed music and puzzle aficionado, I thought the combination of lights and sound was an excellent foundation, and the abstract nature of this game did not slow me down at all. Some people may feel the game begs the question "what do I do?” to which I pose the answer- try stuff. The game has a good feedback loop- you will realize the game is not linear and it is not a sandbox. The game will respond to "correct actions" by lighting stuff up, which should naturally incline you to try more of that stuff. The finale of the game culminates into a musical puzzle symphony experience.
The game has some replay value- (in fact, I’m feeling the urge to go and replay after posting this review-  keep in mind it’s been a few months since I played last). You can also go into your “studio” and make your own beats and loops- even though that’s not my “thing” that’s still a pretty cool feature . All in all a great game, and I recommend you give it a try.

The best game of the Final Fantasy 13 trilogy! This conclusion to the trilogy has better, more fast-paced gameplay, more clothing, more accessories, and more lore than the first two games. Speaking of lore, the main quests and sidequests are a joy to do because they give you more insight into the world, and quite a few of them provide comic relief!
The name of the game in Lightning Returns is the Stagger gauge. Many enemies will be difficult (or impossible) to defeat unless staggered. Character development will quickly focus on builds (called "schemata") designed to stagger enemies and keep them that way.
I strongly recommend starting the game in Easy mode, as in Normal mode you cannot regenerate HP and enemies are far more difficult to kill.
This game features a monster genocide option. If you kill enough of a certain species, you will permanently remove that monster from the game. This option makes it easier to explore areas, but I found the emptiness... disturbing.
Do not worry about managing your time in this game, because it features New Game Plus. You will not only be able to finish the quests you couldn't, but do over every quest in the game if you so desire. This will allow you to reach apocalyptic levels of might as a one-woman army. Of course, you can use New Game Plus just to run around and take in the view!
If you have never played any game from the Final Fantasy 13 trilogy, I strongly recommend Lightning Returns. Like the leading lady herself, this game stands on its own with its gorgeous graphics, beautiful music and rich story.

If I have anything good to say about it, it's that Square Enix finally produced a rather good port of their in-house made game. Other than that, you will like this game only in case you: a) like Lightning as a model (not as a character) b) like what they done to the combat c) like fetch quests in MMOs.
If not, this game is an incredible dissapointment and probably the worst part of the XIII trilogy. The premise and ideas are absolutely fantastic - the world is ending, events of XIII and XIII-2 just postponed/lessened the impact of what the main antagonists were trying to do, but they essentially got what they wanted. People lived for 500 years stuck at the age they were when the ending of XIII-2 happened, no new people are being born. All that is left is that Lightning, as a Savior, saves the chosen souls to be reborn in the new world, where people can live, die and be born again. Sounds amazing, doesn't it? Sadly, the actual events to follow up on this are just horribly dumb.
Instead of a brilliant dark but hopeful ending to the trilogy we get stupidly boring retread on the previously done stories. Story has flashes of brilliance in terms of ideas, but never seems to understand what to do with them. Cutscenes are horribly and sometimes amateurishly directed, dialogues (often monologues) are boring and often poitnless. mini-stories in side-quests are sometimes interesting, but tied to most boring fetch quests you can imagine with most intriguing and involved quests in the entire game being the very first one you get. Things often just happen, get dropped, kinda picked up by the end, but there's no unifying feel to any of it. Everything is just *there*.
Same goes for the combat/RPG systems. Yes it is more involved and action-y than other XIII games, but it's still boring and often pointless. It's no Vagrant Story of Parasite Eve II. In terms of the soul saving, time restricted mechanics it's no Valkyrie Profile either, despite Tri-Ace working on the game. Also some features that could make first playthrough fights at least a bit less pointless are locked away until NG+ and some stay locked unless NG+ is played on Hard. Because reasons.
It's a game with a great premise that fails in devlivering on it. That has features and mechanics that have been used in much better and more fun games. That has an unsatisfying story, that could bring an interesting end to the trilogy, but instead goes for a "Lightning wet-fantasy fanfic" feel, that often reminds of Metroid: Other M in terms of how boring, self-indulgent, repetitive and stupid it is. Such a shame.

This is the most unique, thoughtful and well-designed puzzle game I've ever played. The creator worked on this for seven years, and while the end result is short, it's incredibly astounding in every aspect. The puzzles aren't so much about difficulty as they are about getting you to think in different terms.
The four panels can be dragged around, and they are like layers of reality that not only have depth but are linked to each other in some way. You'll find this by zooming into or out of one panel, then dragging it around to find it leaves a cutout window in the image. In another panel, you'll have the color/shape you need, and can overlap the cutout onto it, linking the two together and allowing a third panel to join in where your protagonist can now venture into. It's nuts, and I highly recommend it.
It is very short, 80 min for me. But if you enjoyed the demo, you really should buy it.

This game is a genuine diamond in the rough. It's an engaging third person action/adventure title laced with Celtic/Nordic influences and mythology that tells the story of a woman, named Senua, searching for a way to free the soul of her beloved, held captive by the goddess of Hel. The puzzles, exploration and combat all have a twist - that Senua suffers from a mental disorder called Psychosis, which causes her to hallucinate and see the world from a different, although troubling, perspective.
The game's visual and audio design is astounding, considering the developers worked with a budget fit for an indie game. All the models and environments in the game are rendered beautifully and with insane amounts of detail - combine this with Nvidia ANSEL or the built in photo mode and you're ready to take great screenshots with minimal effort, The game's use of audio to immerse yourself in Senua's world is amazing to say the least. Music and  sound effects fit the themes of the game, and dialogue between characters are a treat. When using headphones,the voices in Senua's head makes you feel like somebody is standing behind/beside you and speaking directly into your ear! It's unsettling and I loved it.
The game also features audio logs in the form of "Lore Stones" where another character's voice tells you stories about Norse mythology, which ties directly to Senua's quest in one way or another. They're told wonderfully and are highly entertaining if you enjoy the subject matter.
The only issue I have with the game is the combat difficulty, which wasn't too difficult if you're patient and have decent reaction times (I only died three times in the game, two of which were due to exploration). The puzzles do get a little boring after some time, but the game isn't long enough to drag them on forever, so that's okay.
2017 saw a lot of big budget "AAA" video game releases that ultimately fell flat because publishers focused too much on monetisation and shoving loot boxes down your throat, because they feel that the "single player model is boring and dying". Yet here is proof that a great single player experience can be found when developers pour their heart and soul into creating it - and you don't
a greedy publisher to help you to do it.

Salvation Prophecy is an enjoyable space game that starts out as an action game with slight RPG elements but at some point suddenly becomes a strategy survival (kind of) game.
For the content this game packs, it can be played through fairly quickly (took me about 12 hours, although I mostly neglected bounty hunting that run). Still, however, some parts of the game become repetitive quickly, and it is especially annoying that later in the game you still have to partake in the same kinds of missions you take on in the beginning. The only difference then basically is that you're in control of where these missions take place, but delegating (as you would expect to be able in a commanding position) is not a thing here.

Welcome to Star Trek Online minus the ability to dodge. It will drive you nuts but not nuts enough to not buy the game (for a sale price of course :).
The tutorial first and fore most is great. Absolutely, it will walk the gamer through everything you need to know and will even politely say where to go next.
As stated, this game is essentially STO. You are able to walk around your station (and other planets) and participate in raids or a take over of a planet. There are two aspects to the game : 3rd person over the shoulder and controlling a spaceship. The spaceship aspect is pretty cool as you get to be in control of space jumps. There will be missions where the player will need to travel quite a distance in a short period of time. This is done by initiating wormholes or the jump drive. This in itself is a mini-game that could potentially make the game better, or drive someone nuts. The player is also able to take part in major fleet missions involving destroying another rivals space station. This game is very controller friendly and make navigating through wormholes and warp jumps easy. This game does a good job allowing you to control exactly where you go - however some may find wormholes and the warp jumps annoying. Armor, stim packs, and even weapons for your character become modifiable. You are also able to choose between 4 races.
I got this game as a gift and would likely only buy on sale. I would rather play Star Trek Online though as I feel it has more depth to it. This game tries but that little extra freedom of being able to walk around your own ship or wherever is not there. The gameplay itself (movement and action) is alright at best. A lot more could have been done in these regards. I mean cmon, you get to invade a planet!
RATING : 7/10

Before I get into my review, let me start off by saying: This game is in EARLY ACCESS. This means that it is nowhere close to being finished, it is subject to crashes, subject to bugs, and some things just don't work as they should. Some things just don't work at all. That will change as the game progresses. If you're not a patient person, then skip this title. Don't buy the game expecting everything to work and leave a bad review when you realize just how far off it is from being complete.
Now, with that out of the way, I can continue my brief review. SimAirport is going to be an amazing game once it is completed. I am enjoying the little bit we have now to play around with, and I am certain there will be more to enjoy with each update that is released. I am not going to knock the game for having bugs or crashes, or having things that simply dont' work (at the time of this review, Cafes don't work properly - which is going to change). The only thing I will knock about the game is the price, even then it is hard to criticize the price because I know at some point here in the near future, there will be enough content that merits it.
If you enjoy games like this, and want to help the Dev team out, pick it up. If you are patient, willing to deal with crashes, bugs, and the like, pick it up. Even though there is not much to do yet, there is enough to keep me playing. And as things get added, taken away, expanded upon, improved upon...that is oinly going to increase the amount of time I give this game.
The graphics aren't the best, and they don't have to be. I know some people have compared SimAirport to Airport CEO, which are similar in a lot of ways, but also vastly different. I’m pretty surprised by the hate this game still gets.  As someone who has played 100 hours over the last 9 months or so, I’d like to give a more balanced review.  My account says 16 hours, but I was playing on a friend’s copy before purchasing it more recently on sale for $26 CAD, and I transferred over my save.
With 100 hours in I still haven't done most of the story, no side quests, and haven't even done base building, which is a huge aspect of the game.  I've also barely gotten into ship battles, and haven't gotten a freighter or more ships.  There is so much to do in this game at this point, it's overwhelming.
Sure, it started out with issues and a high price and it should have been released as a beta for the first year.  The devs absolutely made a mistake on that one, but to me it is not worth writing off a game forever, and I think it is unfair to still crap on it now for those issues from the past.  I get not trusting the company anymore, but it's not legit to post bad reviews of a game in its current state based on dislike of past company decisions.  They treated it like a beta afterward and have updated it regularly since, and now it is a very complete game.  And they have done better than many devs in that they actually directly change things asked for by the players, which I have noticed on all updates so far.  Also, while the price is high, it seems to go on sale at least once every 3-4 months for 66% off.
Graphical and other glitches used to be a problem but are now down to virtually non-existent for me (GTX 1070).  I get no random frame rate drops anymore, which used to plague the game.  I get a graphics driver crash that crashes the game maybe once every second time I play if I'm playing for a 2-4 hours.  I haven’t wanted to spend the time to resolve this, but it can likely be solved with a driver tweak.  Otherwise it runs nicely at 1440p on ultra.
The controls have been significantly improved, and although some people disagree over the user interface, it's really pretty good at this point.  Many of the things that used to be tedious can now be done quickly, and they now allow you to skip most "waiting" times in menu selections and whatnot.
I'm not going to try to convince anyone to like this type of game as it's simply not for everyone, but for the type of game it's aiming to be, it's a really good game.  That's why I'm surprised at the recent bad reviews.  Past the last major update, there really isn't much to complain about.  And they keep adding free content.  I feel like people are judging the game based on this built up hate for it from earlier, or just because it became vogue to crap on it.  It's like there is a conspiracy against it.  It's not a straight mining/building game, FPS, RPG, racing game, dedicated space fighter, or pure survival game.  I can see why some people don't like that it is kind of all of these things without fitting nicely into one genre, and without being the best in any of these areas.  But it is by far the best exploration/sandbox game I have ever played, and visually the most appealing (even if it doesn't have the most top of the line graphics).  I have had so many moments of complete awe while playing this game at the environment around me.
Many people complain about not finding enough variety in the game.  I will concede that the creatures are not done all that well, and unless you examine them closely, which you don’t normally do during the course of the game, they begin to all seem the same.  I’m not sure how they could resolve this exactly.  After playing for this long I have seen quite a variety, but you have to look closely.  Planet feature variety is great, but you can occasionally hit a rut in which you find many planets with similar features in close succession.  I can see why someone who has not played very long could begin to think there is not much variety of animals and plants and general landscape features.  It’s out there, but you do have to move along and potentially visit hundreds of planets to see a lot.  It really is random, so you can have bad luck when it comes to finding good planet variety.
Areas that definitely need fixing are: the economy system, flight dynamics, and navigation.  While flight has improved, it still doesn’t feel like you can really control your ship all that well.  I’m not sure how realistic this is, but regardless, I’d like better control.  They seem to have tried to introduce more of an economy system in the 1.3 update, but it still feels really basic and trading on the market feels static and pointless.  A really good economy driven by player trading could improve this massively.
As for navigation, it seems that they are trying to present the feeling that you are alone in the universe and travelling around exploring, never really knowing where you are.  I kind of like this at first, but after a while it becomes really annoying that you can’t at least set easy way points, or mark star systems with notes, etc.  There are great 3rd party tools out there for mapping where you are, tracking where you’ve been, and intentionally navigating to different areas of the galaxy, but they are almost overkill as they allow too much information and easy navigation.  I like the feeling of being a small drop in a vast and largely unknown universe, but I want to at least be able to easily track where I’ve been, mark anything I want to note, and fairly easily navigate back to anywhere I’ve marked/been.  The portal system improves this somewhat and it looks like it will ultimately offer the ability to warp to virtually any planet in the game, but then you have the whole pain in the♥♥♥♥♥of not having your ship with you.
Base building seems impressive, but I haven’t bothered with it yet because you can only build one base, and I am more of an explorer.  The game would be vastly improved if you could build as many bases as you want, or even better, build structures and shape the land anywhere on any planet, perhaps minus a few blocked off areas where there are other structures that shouldn’t be messed with.  This could lead to some cool things, like players cooperating on building huge interconnected cities on planet that could even be visible from space.
Speaking of that sort of thing, as a distant improvement, it would be great to see more varied intelligent life, with NPC’s roaming around on planets, life-filled cities, and much better AI with creatures that might roam in packs and live a more realistic existence.  Currently all NPC’s are stationary and creatures on planets seem to be kind of randomly dispersed and just walk around aimlessly, sometimes killing each other, but not doing much of anything else.
Many people have commented that they get bored after a while playing the game as it becomes a grind.  I suppose this is a fair criticism, but that is really a subjective matter.  Almost any game becomes a grind if you happen to find it boring.  Many highly rated mining/building games and RPGs have substantial grinding to them.  I suggest just exploring like crazy and trying not to focus too much on any one thing you want to build or upgrade, and eventually you’ll stumble across everything you need.  It’s best to have multiple projects/quests on the go.
All in all, it’s a great game, and most of the areas I’d improve it are not really criticisms, but just things I’d love to see added, either to this game or future games of this genre.  It's kind of that type of game, where it is so vast and covers so many genres that it begs to be updated and modded.  I feel like people are getting really petty with this game, and at its core, there is nothing wrong with the game, and I think it is just not what some people wanted or expected, even after being updated.  And that's fine, but I suggest going in with reasonable expectations.  This is a great first stab at this type of game, and I really think it deserves a better rating.

All in all, Darksiders 1 is a better game, if only because there aren't so many required sidequests. And I enjoyed the story a lot more for the same reason. War has more of a personality than Death does.
The combat and dungeons in Darksiders 2 are great. But the whole game is essentially a giant fetch quest (except killing instead of fetch). To reach one objective, you must kill 3 things in 3 separate dungeons. Then you put them into a statue, and have to kill something else. Then you are told you have to kill three more things. Then you're told to go to a new zone and kill more things.
I'm probably 2/3 through the game at this point. 26 hours of completionist-style play (more counting deaths and idle time). And you know what? The *whole* game I've been trying to complete one quest, but there are a zillion required distracting sidequests to do that first thing. This wouldn't be so bad, except you never make progress on the main quest until you complete a dozen sidequests.
I wouldn't care so much if there was time not spent in a dungeon, but this game is 90% dungeons. The dungeons themselves are good, the puzzles the right level to slow you down a little. Basically, if you try to play this aggressively, you'll probably get sick of the dungeons, because this game is dungeons and minibosses the whole way through.
Dungeon after dungeon after dungeon after dungeon. And you'd better like sifting through loot, too.
That said, as long as you don't play too much at once, it's a good game. The combat is solid (although the skill tree is kinda iffy. I like passives more than abilities, and I forget to use the abilities regularly, since I don't really have to.)

Finally posting my review of this because it saddens me to still see so many negative ones on its page.

Currently though, with the game still receiving major content updates(and I am talking HUGE here, each one seems to transform the whole game again) there is a lot more to do! Base building has become a big aspect of the game, there's planet ground vehicles, trading has been reformed, space combat aswell, there's questing now and a lot more upgrade and customization options for the Multi-Tool(your weapon, terraforming and mining tool), new ships, you can own a space freighter, the story mode has been overhauled...
If you're looking for a game with a great deal of freedom and content, this is the game for you. And if you were disappointed with it when it came out because it lacked deeper playstyle options or motivations to try different things, give it another try aswell!

Fract OSC is a beautifully minimalistic puzzle-exploration game. The puzzles and layout of the world are seperated into three main areas; blue/cyan, green, and red/pink. They vary wildy from block puzzles that test spatial awareness, to connecting conduits ala Pipe Dream. At the end of each main puzzle is a step synth music puzzle. the main puzzles were really well thought out, and the final puzzzles in each section involve interesting clues and solutions.
The visual astetic of the game is wonderful and reminds me of Tron. Neon colored lights, mostly monotone base colors make it look very 90's cyberpunkesce. The music is not as present as I thought it would be. The music that is there though, it is really immersive and does come to life because of your actions. That is really cool.
The step synth puzzles were a little annoying, because they required a bit too much trial and error. Outside of the main areas there is not much to do. The game is also a bit on the short side. It does'nt have much replayability other than to mess with the in game music maker. I would recommend this game if you like point and click adventure games or something like Antichamber. If you don't like obtuse puzzles in games then this is not for you, but if you love exploration and ambiance, then you will love it like I did.

It's really hard to describe this game, part exploration, part puzzle, part incredible soundtrack/sounds, part abstract art. The exploration part is really good, no hand holding or arrows showing you where to go, just HUGE jumps fueled by your curiosity.
The puzzles are music based, they're really creative and fun. After you complete them the music comes alive and it goes hand in hand with the abtract Tron inspired landscapes really well. It also has a sprint button and great virtual synthesizer to play around with.

Rock-band, tron and DeadCore had a baby, and called it Fract. A clever blend of puzzles and platforms where the things you do make music, and the music affects the world. Genuinely challenging at times, though it would have benefited from more fluid and faster movement... and a jump button.[6.0]

I love chillout games. I love Flower on the PS3 and Journey as well (though that's less chillout, more heartrending/warming adventure, though it is beautiful). I also have a fondness for exploration games, hence why I really enjoyed Gone Home and I quite liked Proteus. It's part of why I like ARK Survival Evolved and also why I liked Minecraft too. There was this great exploration element, as you discovered cool little neat things and such.
The problem I find though is if there's nothing else but exploration, it gets really, really dull, really really fast. Proteus has this problem. It's beautiful and relaxing and charming but there's ♥♥♥♥all to DO whilst you explore. You might as well load up some ambient music and put on a few random visualisations on Winamp or WMP or something. Much the same experience.
Here's where FRACT OSC gets it right though. IT GIVES YOU♥♥♥♥♥♥TO DO. Oh my god it gives you♥♥♥♥♥♥to do. It's an exploration game at heart, and a music game. It's both, and its married perfectly together. The world is made up of, controlled by, and explored through music. The music the game creates for you, the music YOU can later create with the synthesiser part of the game. But here's the thing, you can't DO that until you get some instruments. How do you get instruments? you unlock them in game. How? by rebuilding the broken down and out of order sound based tech in these ruins you find yourself in.
How do you do that? by SOLVING PUZZLES WITH YOUR AWESOME INTERACTO-PUZZLEVISION :D
There's no enemies, no real threats. You can "die" but that boots you immediately back to the nearest checkpoint you got to. Handy, convenient, and if you don't "die" when you fall off something, chances are you are meant to get there or there's a way back out of it. Fall damage doesn't seem to exist, there doesn't appear to be a way to get irreversably trapped (and if there is you can always press ESC and boot back to last station again, always possible), you can fast travel between stations...
Everything is done through symbols and holographic screens, no words, no voiceover expositing things to you. You gotta work it out yourself, and that's where the game truly shines, not just through the beautiful soundscapes that unlock as you solve puzzles, but because this is at once a fiendish and rewarding first person puzzler, but also a fantastic way to relax and chill out.
I have worked out puzzles and whilst I would be fist pumping and cheering about how I feel like a genius, I'm too chilled the hell out to do so. I merely smile to myself, nod in time to the awesome music, and get started on FINDING the next puzzle, which in itself could be a puzzle!
This is the perfect exploration/ "walking simulator" -puzzle game combination. You won't regret it. It's challenging, it's difficult, it's often obtuse, it is however both super relaxing, super fun, and super cunning. Get it.

If I have anything good to say about it, it's that Square Enix finally produced a rather good port of their in-house made game. Other than that, you will like this game only in case you: a) like Lightning as a model (not as a character) b) like what they done to the combat c) like fetch quests in MMOs.
If not, this game is an incredible dissapointment and probably the worst part of the XIII trilogy. The premise and ideas are absolutely fantastic - the world is ending, events of XIII and XIII-2 just postponed/lessened the impact of what the main antagonists were trying to do, but they essentially got what they wanted. People lived for 500 years stuck at the age they were when the ending of XIII-2 happened, no new people are being born. All that is left is that Lightning, as a Savior, saves the chosen souls to be reborn in the new world, where people can live, die and be born again. Sounds amazing, doesn't it? Sadly, the actual events to follow up on this are just horribly dumb.
Instead of a brilliant dark but hopeful ending to the trilogy we get stupidly boring retread on the previously done stories. Story has flashes of brilliance in terms of ideas, but never seems to understand what to do with them. Cutscenes are horribly and sometimes amateurishly directed, dialogues (often monologues) are boring and often poitnless. mini-stories in side-quests are sometimes interesting, but tied to most boring fetch quests you can imagine with most intriguing and involved quests in the entire game being the very first one you get. Things often just happen, get dropped, kinda picked up by the end, but there's no unifying feel to any of it. Everything is just *there*.
Same goes for the combat/RPG systems. Yes it is more involved and action-y than other XIII games, but it's still boring and often pointless. It's no Vagrant Story of Parasite Eve II. In terms of the soul saving, time restricted mechanics it's no Valkyrie Profile either, despite Tri-Ace working on the game. Also some features that could make first playthrough fights at least a bit less pointless are locked away until NG+ and some stay locked unless NG+ is played on Hard. Because reasons.
It's a game with a great premise that fails in devlivering on it. That has features and mechanics that have been used in much better and more fun games. That has an unsatisfying story, that could bring an interesting end to the trilogy, but instead goes for a "Lightning wet-fantasy fanfic" feel, that often reminds of Metroid: Other M in terms of how boring, self-indulgent, repetitive and stupid it is. Such a shame.

10/10 would recommend this purely for its story, music, and graphics -- but then I'm a complete sucker for beautiful pixel art, emotional soundtracks, and immersive storylines, so I guess I might be a bit biased.
Although To the Moon does -- to an extent -- deliver on its overwhelmingly positive response, there's much room for improvement with regards to its controls and gameplay.
Controls are limited to either pointing, clicking, and using the arrow keys to move around and spacebar to interact, and there isn't any option to change the key settings. Rather, there aren't any options or settings at all available to customize.
Gameplay feels less adventure game-ish and more upgraded visual novel-ish. You progress through the entire story in a routine fashion, completing each stage by collecting key memories and solving a fairly easy standard puzzle. There are a handful (Note: I mean this literally -- there are just around five non-routine things to do) of neat, quirky deviations from the norm, but that's it.
On a more positive note, the soundtrack is wonderful and adds so much atmosphere to the story, although it isn't the most memorable and hasn't really stuck to my head like other game OST's. The art is stunning, and there are many wallpaper-worthy scenes. Again, I'm biased because PIXELS <3.
The best thing about To the Moon is its story. It's rich and refreshing, and the script, albeit some of its cheesy and clichéd lines, is decent. There were a few particular moments I enjoyed, divided between some of the sentimental parts of the memories and some of the humorous banter of the doctors you play as. My only real qualm with the story aside from the cheese is that based on majority of its reviews, I was expecting to bawl, but I didn't.
TL;DR: To the Moon is a good game.
Is it overhyped? Yes.
Did it make me cry? No.
Did I still feel feelings? *calms heart down* Y-yes.
Is it still worth playing? Definitely!
Would I play it again? Hell yes.
Rating: 8/10

This game is pretty straight-forward: you enter a spooky mansion full of Jump Scares. BUT: The deeper you descend into the spooky mansion, the spookier it gets. Are you ready to uncover the secrets within these walls? Are you prepared for a dangerous adventure?
