Salvation Prophecy's vision is clear; put together the strategy, shooter, and space dogfights in space sims into one game. The execution is poor.
In the shooter portions of the game you will be riding a dropship down to a planet's surface and killing the opposing force. The foot controlls w,a,s,d to move, right click to aim (no over the shoulder here, it just makes your reticule appear) and left click to shoot. That's it. No crouch, no cover mechanic, just trading fire until you or your opponent die. There are slight variations in the different races weaponry, but their skill trees are all the exact same.
dogfights are the better portion of the game. You can fight using three weapons, laser fire, missles, and emp bursts which destroy incoming missles. The fighting is intense and challenging. The real problem with the ship combat is the navigation. to jump from area to area in the game you will need to warp and use black holes. warping is a mini-game in which you will be avoiding electric beams that do damage to your ship. black holes have you flying through a tunnel and avoiding the sides, operation style. often you will have to navigate two or three of each to get to your mission. The black holes are the most frustrating as damage is unavoidable and and you will need to use your healing items before a battle even starts.
The strategy portion of the game I never got to and before you cry foul let me explain the ranking system in the game. You will start out as the lowest ranking in your military installation only being able to do shooter missions. after doing a couple of those you will rank up and have access to  star fighter missions and exploration. There are about ten ranks in the game and the very last rank is the one that gives you access to the strategy portions. I am about 4 hours in and have moved up to about rank three. The strategy missions could be the most amazing thing to happen to gaming, but I would have to wade through at least 5 more hours of mediocrity to get there.
I cannot recommend Salvation Prophecy unless you are a hardcore space sim fan and even then I would wait until it drops to bargain price.

I'm doing this for 2 reasons:
1. The Steam Awards badge.
2. The game recently dropping to Mixed recent reviews.
Basically, people who haven't touched the game since launch are now sending negative reviews just to get the badge without really thinking what's going on with this game. Even after the backlash, Hello Games continued to update its game with tons of content, including a first step into
. There's also the problem of people that expected something different for what it was. The game is a space exploration / survival at its core, but it seems people expected a high caliber action game keeping them busy and  when it wasn't advertised as such ever. I knew well what I was getting and I sure enjoyed it.
That part might get deleted after the whole Steam Awards is done. So, to make an actual review of the game:
No Man's Sky is a space exploration game. You go from planet to planet gathering resources and upgrading your equipment. I could cut it short there and I'd probably be describing the release version of the game.
Thankfully now, it doesn't stop there; there's relationships to build with the different races, various side storylines to discover, construction of your own base and farm to get resources easier, vehicles to make getting around places and mining easier (plus, they're extra fast and fun), more diverse and impressive landscapes on
planets, treasure hidden everywhere on a planet and if you reach end game you could be the owner of an entire fleet.
Let's say its an Elite Dangerous for more casual people that just want to relax while going around space.
Recommended? If you like the "Walking Simulator" genre and anything to do with space, you'll probably love this one. If you're into survival games, the game gives you a gamemode which makes it harder. It is definitely worth a try for the experience.

All things considered this is a surprisingly nice game. It has some rough edges, but it's totally worth playing through. It's slightly difficult to recommend to anyone who's not already into JRPGs or familiar with Final Fantasy (which for all intents and purposes are rather 'Westernised' and not particularly 'hardcore' JRPGs anyway), but that kind of goes without saying. It's a niche genre game and a great one at that. I know people have been critical about the FFXIII games, but from the few hours I've spend on this game so far (about 11 hours) I'd generally disagree with most of the critique. It got me hooked fairly easily, despite a few flaws.
PROS:
-excellent voice acting, both in Japanese and English
-great sountrack
-great combat system with surprising depth in strategy because of the Schemata you can customise and abilities you can upgrade.
-your clothing (garbs), weapons and items determine a large portion of the damage you do, health you have and so on, which makes for a very good combat system
-no XP level up nonsense grind here, although you can upgrade general stats from around half-way through the game
-defeating monsters actually requires skill and blocking / evading
-the game's difficulty is excellent and higher difficulties will really make this a tough challenge for experienced players, people new to JRPGs should probably start on Easy as to not get frustrated
-main quest missions are great and actually make you want to play on and on
-side quest missions are not too much of a grind or fetch quest IMHO
-locations are great, varied and generally just very interesting, something that can't be said about many recent games these days that suffer from open-world generic-ness and problematic recycling of content
-despite the somewhat lazy port, PERFORMANCE is excellent at all times, with combat being a joy at full HD resolution (or higher) @ 60 fps. I'd say it's required for a game like this, as you do have to respond rather quickly in combat
-graphics in general look great, even despite texture resolution not really being entirely current generation quality. It's hardly a problem in a game that looks like an anime anyway
-amazing cutscenes (that kind of make you wish the entire game looked like that, but lets not forget this is a PS3 port)
CONS:
-sidequests aren't entirely optional, you kind of need to gather as much souls, gil credits/weapons/garbs/etc as possible in order to stop 'time' and have acceptable stats to progress through the main quest. I'd say one to three side quests per zone (or chapter I suppose) seems to be the minimum. thankfully there's a variation in difficulty of said side quests.
-speaking of time, the game has a day and night cycle which includes a mandatory trip to a futuristic spin on 'Noah's Ark', which is actually kind of immersion breaking and annoying. They probably should have made that optional. Trainers do exist to mod the game and turn the timer off though, but I didn't really found that necessary.
-story line is kind of a biblical affair with the player being 'the savior' in a fairly literal way, this might be off putting to some. Without spoiling too much, you've struck a deal with God and need to gather as many souls as possible within the  5 days left before an inevitable apocalypse.
-the game could use a few more voice overs for the taunts or commentary of the player, there are only a few different lines and she uses them a lot. Same goes for voice over loops of announcers in some areas that keep telling you you're a wanted criminal.
Some nitpicking:
-there's a downside to how some enemies have rather varied weaknesses, which means your most successful 'build of Schematas (which defines your attacks, blocks, evasions, magic attacks or heals or any kind of bonuses in combat) tends to be more of a generalised build, instead of specialising which results in far more powerful more interesting builds. I wouldn't say the game is ever unfair here, but don't be too surprised if you need to change your Schematas in order to beat specific types of enemies, which otherwise take forever to beat with your weaker attacks that happen to be the kind they aren't immune to. I suppose to many people this is a good thing, because it means the game requires some skill / stragey in building effective Schematas
-you'll see the same enemy types a lot, but with the combat being rather exciting it's a minor gripe. You'll also figure out how to deal with the strengths and weaknesses of each specific type fairly soon. Don't get me wrong, there are plenty of different enemies in total, but 10 hours in I've only seen less than a dozen so far
-keyboard control is rebindable which is great, but the default lay-out makes zero sense. You'll be using BackSpace, M, . and all kinds of keys across the keyboard to control the game; I've played thusfar on keyboard, but I'm sure using a Gamepad of some kind would work way better
-no mouse camera control /in-menu control as far as I can tell, but you'd best play this with a controller anyway
-don't be too surprised to find literal references to the PS3, because it's actually a fairly lazy port all around.
I've got no doubt some people think this game is pushing it's whole 'savior story' a bit too much, which is kind of true, but there's plenty of great content to be found regardless with the new combat system being a big pro. I recommend the game, especially on a discount.

I don't usually enjoy puzzle games but this one captivated me. It's difficult to explain the central concept but I'll try my best: What if you had four panels of artwork and could arrange them in certain ways to progress a story? What if, for example, one panel showed a locked door and by zooming more closely into another panel, you could make out a key-shape etched into the bark of a tree? What if you pulled the key loose from that one panel and used it to unlock the door in the other?
There's a wonderful sense of dream logic to the entire game, aided by the music which plays, but the puzzles always make sense and are never so taxing that you want to give up. It only took me three hours to complete the game but it was a really fun experience. Take a chance and pick this up if you're considering it. There isn't another game like it on the market.

Honestly I don't normally write reviews seriously but this game shocked me with how beautiful and imaginative it was. The puzzles felt fun and original and it neither felt like I was reusing old solutions nor was the main core mechanic of each set being under-used (i.e. being introduced then taken away for another mechanic).
The exploration is really nicely done, it felt like that nicer type "do it yourself, we're not giving you a map or anything", and while it was confusing at first until you realise how pathing works, it made me feel a lot more free and immersed within the game.
The artstyle is something I was a big fan of, very Tron like yet it wasn't sickening with neon. The colours stood out and made key areas and visuals clear, as the rest of the game is rather dark in shading.
The music was atmospheric and beautiful, and probably the game's highlight. Every little part of the game, from the puzzles (which I noticed changed either modulations or notes on the main synthesizer) to the little expanding platforms changes the music in some way and makes the world feel magical and mysterious. The atmosphere it creates is one that enchanted me from the beginning to the end.
The little unlockables at the end that unlock parts of the synth to use are probably one of the most desirable unlockables I've ever come across in any game. Unlike Crackdown's orbs or Meat Boy's bandages (both games I enjoyed but did not feel invested in the collectables, even though they changed the game in some way), this game goes for short but sweet collectables that add modulations and functions to the additional synthesizer which can be used to make pretty tracks without needing too much experience in music design itself. In fact, the game sort of teaches you about certain aspects of music design and effect through its puzzles, like one for instance which works on timing decay.
If I had to say there was something lacking, it would be the loss of (at least I don't think there is) a story or underlying message. But in this element I feel perhaps a directed story may have spoiled the looser narrative of exploring the world. Also, there isn't much replayability outside of the synth, but the synth does kind of make up for that by itself.
All in all I had a great time playing this game and I continue to play around with the synth. I would absolutely recommend buying this game if you can, it's well worth your time and money.

This is to the last two Wolfenstein games what Arkham City is to Arkham Asylum. It's an upgrade on every front to an already excellent base game. It's not so much that there's more, but that it's also better. Again, the formula is very much the same with the core mechanics and game design untouched. Subtle things like the characters, animations, voice acting and movement is so natural it's unbelievable. Watching the characters talk and move feels so much more natural and realistic than any other video game I've ever played. The added abilities and perks and upgrades are very welcome, as is the more immersive story and brutal violence. This is Wolfenstein on steroids, with some Saints Row level crazy antics. It's shocking. It's comical. It's badass. It's a rich game world (some of the collectibles' references to Donald Trump are hilarious). It's fast-paced and action-packed. What more could you want!?
On a technical level, the game also runs well and looks great, though it requires some tweaking to get the best out of it. After much experimentation, I'm managing to achieve a stable 60 FPS using mixed settings (mostly on Ultra) with a GTX 1060 6GB, i5-3470, 12GB DDR3-1600 MHz RAM at 4K (2160p) resolution (albeit with 42% resolution scale)! Though to be honest, the game doesn't look significantly better than Wolfenstein The New Order, and that's coming form someone who played it on Xbox One (though it was one of the first and only shooters to achieve 1080p60 on console, at least at the time). The only real complaint with the graphics is the unsually low texture quality. Perhaps this is a bug or some graphics setting but the textures are definitely inconsistent in quality both between and within levels.
Finally I have to give this game much praise for something absurdly simple yet practically a godsend: the loading times. I have it installed on an external 7200 RPM hard drive, and it is a big game obviously. Yet after disabling the intro movies (easily done by renaming the video file), from the moment I press "Play" on Steam I can be in the level within 20 seconds. Better yet, when you die (which will happen quite often on the hardest difficulties), you'll be thankful that the game doesn't mess about with ridiculously long death animations. It immediately reloads the last save when your health goes to 0. And guess how long this takes on a mechanical hard drive? About 2 or 3 seconds. Combine this with the ability to save the game at literally any moment along with your progress saving between deaths for things like perk unlocks, collectibles, upgrades etc. and you have a game where you can easily die a hundred times on the same checkpoint and not feel frustrated whatsoever!
I don't usually write reviews for games before I finish at least the main campaign, but for Wolfenstein: The New Colossus I don't feel I need to see any more to warrant a recommendation. With so many disappointments and shady business practices in the current gaming industry, Wolfenstein II is a shining beacon that reminds us how simple it is to make a great video game. You don't need to re-invent the wheel or do anything drastically different. With incremental improvements in many areas and continuing the story (and without censorship!), improving the game world and not littering the game with microtransactions, whilst keeping features which add value such as challenge modes (and not shovelling in a half-baked multiplayer just because it's a first-person shooter), Wolfenstein II is surely the de-facto standard for modern single-player first-person shooters. It stays true to its legacy yet moves the franchise forward; arguably more so than the similar DOOM (2016). At some points in the game I just wanted BJ to have nightmares about killing monsters in DOOM and actually play a modern DOOM level, kind of like the previous game with old Wolfenstein levels (which, by the way, are in Wolfenstein 2!). Perhaps that would some meta for the next game.

Sad to say I am disappointed after finally getting to play this.  I bought a Humble Bundle almost exclusively because I saw Wanderlust in the list of games (would never have heard of it otherwise).  I really do like almost everything about the game, but for a couple of small things and one big one.  For small things, the lack of explanation of significant concepts (like the mage runes and their cooldowns) made just jumping in kind of frustrating.  Also, the videos make it look like a great dual-stick shooter combined with RPG elements; in reality, the mage is the only character that uses the mouse.  The rest are one hand for movement and the other for 4 attack hotkeys.  I just couldn't enjoy the Rogue because of how quickly enemies respond to dash (9/10 times they turn around too fast to backstab them), and how if you tried to change direction mid-dash to attack behind yourself at the end, you would mostly get stuck attacking in the same direction you had dashed until you tapped the opposite direction again.  So, you dash thru an enemy and end up attacking air with them behind you.
The big issue: the advancement system.  Earning CP (skill points) based on your performance rank of each level.  This could really be a very nice idea, and add great replayability.  My big problem is that most of the scoring is based on combos (getting consecutive hits without taking damage).  Oh sure, it was easy to ace the first few levels with the mage; you just stand back and snipe/dodge while allies distract.  But with the other (melee) characters...unless you're 1v1 with an enemy (RARE), there's too much in the way to see when they're going to attack in order to doge or block.  So I just don't see advancing being very easy for the other characters.  For Rogue, I wanted to be a good dash backstabber, but ended up just using potions nonstop because you could actually stay mobile with dash/bomb/dash and not get hit by enemies swarming on 3 sides.  I couldn't even hit and run because of the dash/direction bug above.  I see the Warrior as the class where you stand and block while your allies wail on the enemies...but where will you get your combo points?  In short, if I didn't feel like it would be a chore to ace each level (essentially unlocking the last HALF of your stat points because you get x points for x% completion + an extra 100 points for 100%), I would be playing all the way through this.  If I feel the urge to play something similar, I think I'll have to go back and boot up Secret of Mana.

As a side note I had the graphical settings set to ' Best' which I then changed to Fastest. Which didn't seem to have any effect on performance whatsoever.
I can understand their disclaimer at the start that tells you NOT to use the 'Start From Scratch' option that is available.

On the whole a nice game with massive potential, quirky style and generally quite promising. There are plenty of features I would like to see added and a lot of what already exists I would like to see adapted to work slightly differently.

The Mount and Blade-like dynamic war is innovative, but doesn't really mean anything as the races tend to keep a stalemate until you reach the faction commander level.  The writing for the opening and the "timeline" pieces are amazing, but almost none of that color reaches the gameplay portions.
I got it for 10 bucks, but if I paid more for it, I would have been angry.  Bottom line is that the graphics are circa 2006 and the gameplay is shallow and gets repetitive fast.  It's not a bad game, it's just that there are so many other good games out there you should be playing instead.

My thoughts on this game.
Pros:
- Engaging mystery as once you start you'll want to know how it ends.
- You follow the history of various items over a long period of time.
- The twists were interesting, though some people may see them coming.
Cons:
- Puzzles were annoying, you could only sumbit memories one at a time, and after preparing a memory you had to click on it again to use it.
- The doctors are often vague because the plot demanded it. For example the doctors don't explain what River's condition is or what they saw in John's room, even though there's no reason to be vague when talking to each other.
- River's condition (most likely a form of autism) was used however the plot needed it to be used to keep things mysterious, rather than an accurate representation of autism. While River's teenage years did reflect how someone with autism would act as a young child she had no problems communicating, as the plot needed her to tell John something, even though she'd have the most trouble communicating at this age. By contrast as an adult she was able to hold a conversation yet chose to make hundreds of rabbits rather than talk to John about things. Either River's condition prevents her communicating or it doesn't, you can't switch between them to keep the plot vague.
- Given that this whole story was set in the memories of a comatose man who was going to die in a few days I didn't care that they were trying to remove River from his memories since it wouldn't have any effect on anything in the real world. Likewise there was no reason for Wyatt to care about this since he was supposed to have manipulated the memories of many people before John, which would cause the person to forget many people due to the different path they took in life.

I wanted to like this game. I wanted, so badly, to like this game.
An entire strange world to explore? Based around music? With loads of puzzles and mysteries to solve? Count me in.

I mean what kind of bland, unoriginal idea for a puzzle is that?
The gameplay basically boils down to this:
-enter new area
-solve puzzle
-compose song to open doors/power lasers
-rinse and repeat until all completely identical puzzles are complete
-go back to first part of the area
-realise you have to go back to each and every puzzle to find a combination code for the final puzzle
-get out some ♥♥♥♥ing paper
-fly back to all the previous puzzles and write down the code
-go back to the first part again
-input the code
Yeey area done. Just do that two more times, and then the game is over.
The visuals and sound are gorgeous, I can't deny that. But what's the point in exploring and sucking up the atmosphere of this strange landscape when everything looks the same?
Not worth your time or your money, even on sale.
The in-game sythesiser is pretty nice and suprisingly complex, but it's just an extra feature and doesn't save the game at all.
Keep in mind that I don't just say this because I want to be a funny little troll and hate on a game just because lots of other people like it. I really, really wanted to enjoy this game, and came into it with a very positive and optimistic attitude.

Gravilon is equal parts fascinating and frustrating.  I absolutely love the minimalistic style - its very unique and I haven't come across anything else like it.  The controls are simple - left and right.  Instead of using the spacebar to jump, you use it to slow time - another really cool and unique feature that I enjoyed.
As with all platformers, the goal is simple - make it to the end of the level.  But unlike a sidescrolling platform, your world is smaller and gravity works both ways.  You navigate lines by either rolling on top of them or floating under them, depending on your gravity situation.  Sometimes your exit portal is right beneath you, but you have to manuever around in a circle hitting several gravity switchers to make it to your destination.
As someone who isn't great at puzzle games, I found the levels very difficult.  This game takes patience to hit small targets precisely and to control the speed of your moving block.  Holding down the A or D button even a second too long would build too much momentum and I would fly off course.
The lack of music, the minimal look (almost like modern art), the simple controls and the cool gravity switcharoo make this a game that's easy to return to, even for just a couple of minutes.  But be prepared for a challenge!

Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus isn’t a game that makes sense. It’s one step forward, ten steps back now let’s cut off our legs.
While people are complaining about the performance and how it doesn’t run well, this game actually ran perfectly fine for me with the settings cranked up to max and the frame rate smooth as butter. So I basically got to run through 12 hours of what must be the worst sequel while everything looked nice, how wonderful.
The graphics are great but it’s like lighting up a block of wood with a diamond chandelier. Yes, all the effects are nice, but the levels are all the same colour and same aesthetic. Remember in the last game how each level had a theme and unique colour palette that helped elevate the design of each level? How each level was designed in accordance with the setting? The castle was designed like a castle, the ward was designed like a ward, the moon base was designed like a moon base. Here all the levels not only look like hot garbage, but they’re designed that way as well. It’s either a variation of ruined urban areas or industrial buildings that are a mishmash of stairs and catwalks or just long hallways of nothing. Even the hub in the last game was better than anything in this game. It had personality, each room was unique and designed to represent the individual that inhabited it. Here the hub is a long sterile hallway of rooms with no personality at all, not to mention it’s too big. Like I said it also looks the same as every other level, it looks like the base on Venus which looks like the Auzmerzer. Manhattan is just a ruined urban area that looks like New Orleans which looks like Roswell. The only interesting level is Mesquite which is mostly just boring walking around pressing buttons to activate cut scenes of B.J.’s childhood and just as it gets good the level is over.
Cutscenes are everywhere, each level is a host to button prompts that trigger cutscenes. In the previous game you were the one that executed the main villains. Here all you do is press or hold E to activate a cutscene where we get a sequence where B.J. kills someone, taking away that perspective of us doing the dirty work makes it feel boring. Even the last ‘boss’ is walking across a room and pressing a button which cues the cutscene that sets up the inevitable sequel because of course they do. I wouldn’t mind the cutscenes perhaps if they were shorter and actually decent. All the characters from the previous game that were good are pushed aside to make way for cartoon characters with cringe-worthy dialogue. The jokes in this are juvenile which would be okay if this were Shadow Warrior, clearly it isn’t. The tone conflicts itself many times. A serious discussion will be followed by a poop joke, moments of activity are offset by prolonged series of drunk gags, it’s all boring and out of place humor. Even the morose character arc and background of B.J. is one that develops separately from the story and with long-term effect. Boohoo he had a bad childhood, it makes for some tense C u t s c e n e s but it doesn’t change anything in the story, B.J. develops for a bit and then kills Nazis for the rest of the game that’s it, no one else has an arc and no one else develops, Grace probably has the most dialogue and she does nothing but serve as the strong woman who replaces Carol as the leader, that’s it. Then why did Carol die in the first place if we’re just going to get a more annoying version of her anyway?

Gameplay is where they really spayed the dog. All the wonderful things about the gameplay in the last game are rolled back in favour of superfluous and unnecessary changes. The guns, every gun in this game is fun to shoot. They sound and look great and that’s about it. It was the same case as the last game but in the last game your assault rifles were also rocket launchers, the marksman rifle, absent here, was also a laser weapon. Here the upgrades are bigger mags, integrated silencers and armor piercing rounds. Wow the weapon variation is not only less interesting but it’s also tame and boring like a cookie-cutter modern-warfare shooter. The only notable improvement on a weapon would be the shotgun which I will admit is fantastic in this game and better than the previous one. In addition to this the first chunk of the game caps your health at 50 while compensating with 200 armour though this does nothing to offset how quickly you die in this game. I played New Order on one of the harder difficulty settings. Here I actually turned the difficulty down because of how ridiculously fast you die. It’s a criticism I’ve seen everywhere but for a guy built like a brick♥♥♥♥♥♥house made up of smaller brick♥♥♥♥♥♥houses inside an armour of other♥♥♥♥♥♥houses he is made of absolute glass and while this makes sense in the context of the story it ruins the gameplay. How wonderful that your GAME is ruined in favour of a mediocre tale. Later on this is corrected to 100 health and 100 armour but the first part of this game is such an abortion to get through. The graphical effects actually impair your vision. While the soft shadows, dust, particle effects and HDR all look nice, they all clash to occupy the same space and all the effects are so visually invasive that it makes it impossible to see anything when they’re all in play. It makes for a pretty scene to look at but during the game’s more intense fights it just makes it harder to get anything done.
I don’t understand what went wrong, whether you enjoy this game is up to you and perhaps if I had played this prior to the prequel I would have found it okay, but it is an objectively worse game than its predecessor and even its fantastic expansion. It’s a baffling mish-mash of conflicting mechanics and design choices that even without considering New Order as a comparison makes for a mediocre FPS. Anyone claiming that this is ‘more of the same’, whether as a positive or a negative, must not have the cognitive ability to comprehend fundamental design concepts and perhaps may even be blind to make a claim so broad.
Not on sale and certainly not at full price, avoid entirely.

Having picked up Wolfenstien 2: The New Collossus (TNC) for 50% off its base price and getting all DLC for $40, I must say I'm quite happy with my purchase.
I kept up with a lot of the news that came out about the game while carefully avoiding spoilers which is something I highly recommend that potential players do if they want to get the most out of TNC.  From the very beginning ID would explain that TNC was going to be a far more outrageous experience than the previous installments which I feel like is a promise they delivered on.  The game truly does have some "WTF" moments that illicit laughter or a sly smirk, but none of it goes so far that it made me roll my eyes in irritation.  After all this is a game where Nazis have seized control of the world, super sodiers shoot lasers and in previous installments had you fighting zombies.
TNC begins simply enough with Billy being rescued by his comrads and being in a coma for several months.  The player is then treated some flashbacks of Billys past which does a good job of building up his character.  It doesn't take long to get into the action however when General Engle attacks.  At this point the player is given control of Billy, however after being in a coma for so long he doesn't have an easy time of getting around so your going to have to do your Nazi killing in a wheelchair.  Getting through this leads to a cutscene that establishes Engle as one of the most interesting villains that I've encountered personally in a video game.  It hasn't been since Farcry 3's Vaas, that I've been so entertained by a games antagonist.
This is something that TNC fleshed out a little more.  Characters and story.  Which seems to be a point of contention for a lot of people that played this game.  I feel like TNC struck a good balance between story and gameplay.  I never felt like the narrative was barging its way in and ruining my good time.  In fact I feel like the game could have used more story.  The plight of the resistance is quite interesting and reading through the collectible documents and letters in the game gives you a deeper sense of that plight.  Simply put, the world building is quite good.  Not to mention the excellent acting and dialogue that went into it.  Which is shame why I feel like the story doesn't go far enough.  Engle is such an amazing villain that it's criminal that she doesn't get more screen time.  The back story for Billy when he was young is built up but ultimately ends on a slightly weak note.
Much of TNC's story parts are clearly built up for a 3rd installment.  I just wish we could have had more for THIS installment.
Much of the gameplay remains the same for TNC with a few minor additions and changes.  One of the strangest quirks TNC has is that leaning is kind of a janky mess.  I don't know what happened here but from what I recall TNO did not have this problem.  For example in TNC you want to peak around the corner to see what's there.  Well, pressing the ALT key and doing so works so long as you don't move a muscle.  The second you try to peak around further by moving the mouse the camera will snap back and forth in the most disorienting way.  This is probably my biggest issue with the game as I like to play stealthy sometimes and the leaning mechanic simply doesn't work as intended.
Speaking of stealth, TNC's is pretty much the same as TNO's.  Which is a huge bummer because the game clearly wants you to have that option.  For starters it's really unforgiving.  For example I'm crouched behind a crate and a Nazi is on the other side but is facing towards my only path to him.  So I decided to rush up to him and do a take down.  The Nazi didn't yell out or fire his gun, yet somehow the two commanders were alerted and sounded the alarm for back up.  Another example is if a Nazi finds a downed comrad they all become WAY more skilled at noticing your location, even when crouched.  If only you could pick up bodies and place them in other places...   Say what you want about Ubisoft and the "busy work" Farcry series, but damn it, they know how to stealth.
A few new additions to the game include contraptions which alter how you move through a level.  There's the Contrictor, Ramshackles, and Battle Walker.  The Constrictor Billy to crawl through narrow tubes or vents.  The Ramshackles allows him to crash through certain walls and into enemies and the Battlewalker allows him to stand on stilts and reach higher locations.  These honestly don't add much to the game except for letting you choose which path you want to take through a level.  They do have their own special kill executions which is nice.
There are plenty of weapons with which to inflict pain onto Nazis with.  You have throwable axes, a machine gun, a rifle, shotgun, a grenade pistol and a few other consumable heavy weapons.  All of the weapons you can carry can be upgraded to have different effects.  I would have liked a few more interesting weapons but I was mostly happy with the weapon selection.
One more aspect to talk about when it comes to TNC.  I've seen, through forums and other outlets, that quite a few people have said this game has an "SJW" or "Liberal" agenda.  After putting in 20+ hours on this game (getting collectibles and DLC), I must say I have no idea where people are getting this from.  I can only assume that's because of a news article from a few months ago that stated that TNC was "upsetting conservatives".  A quick google search will lead you to some easy to find searches.  Honestly I never once felt like TNC was pushing ANY kind of political view point.  So I think that worry, if you happened to have had it, can be put to rest.
Overall though, TNC offers a really solid and fun FPS experience that is definitely worth picking up, especially for %50 off.

I'm not usually one for time management games or dating sims, but CTHCC drew me in with its anime sensibility and comedic promise, before completely shattering my expectations.
Befitting its comedy club premise, the dialogue is regularly chuckle-worthy, with moments of pure absurdist brilliance. (One example: "I see now ... So that's why I like cannoli. That makes sense." "Wh... What are you talking about?" "It makes total sense." "Don't just end a conversation like that!")
That said, each of the major characters also has their own full story arc with actual emotional weight, ranging from coping with loss to coping with corporate encroachment. These topics are handled with surprising sensitivity, and display Mairu (Miley in the Westernized version) as more than a mere player avatar, with her own vulnerabilities occasionally surfacing... and then she'll make a lesbian joke, because deflecting is fun.
The gameplay itself is broken down into distinct turns (seen here as morning/afternoon/evening), in which the player can explore the town freely before deciding on their "move" for that particular round. Thankfully, the developers provided enough content to avoid turning the skill-building process into a grind. Dozens of NPCs populate this world, some appearing only at specific times, and each spawning new dialogue on a daily or weekly basis, giving incentive to wander a bit before reading the next magazine or earning more yen.
There are some minor bugs, such as character portraits being displayed with an incorrect outfit or NPCs referring to the previous week's guest lecturer as forthcoming. I played the deWesternized version, yet characters would sometimes lapse into their Westernized names, which is momentarily distracting but not nearly gamebreaking.
You will most likely need at least a second playthrough in order to experience all six storylines, so the replayability is sufficient to justify the non-sale price, and I encountered new dialogue responses throughout my second run. I'm planning to try a third, attempting to generate the "best" ending without the benefit of the New Game+ option, before diving into the sequel... recruiting was just the beginning...
Honestly, this is quite a quick visual novel, but a fun one. Worth it if it's under sale and trust me, you'll have a good laugh, if you understood the jokes.

Simple puzzle game with intuitive gameplay and nice aesthetic, with a very limited amount of levels, no real replayability and a lack of difficulty even in the later levels. You are introduced to the concept of the game in the first few levels, and nothing gets added - just a slowly increasing amount of waypoints you have to pass through to get to the goal - the only real step up in difficulty is about half way through the second set of 16 levels when you start to get two pairs of waypoints of the same colour, although in most cases it tends to be fairly clear which ones pair together, but this mechanic does allow a few more interesting levels late in the game.
In terms of the interface it is mostly fairly good - the menu is simple to use, and in the game I used arrow keys to move around and enter for the next level (saving having to switch to mouse until the set of 16 had ended). The main frustration I had was the animations for colouring up/down and the goal descending, which jar the flow of the game every time you get to a checkpoint on your route.
So overall if you want a quick relatively simple puzzle game that can be finished in an hour or two you should be okay here, but don't expect too much.

I held off on this game for a long time, in fact it was the first Final Fantasy game I decided I would not bother getting - and having been a fan of the series for almost my entire life that was a huge deal. The reason for this of course was the dreaded "timer".
Well, the game has been out a while, it was on sale for 8 Euro, I figured id keep an open mind and try it out! And I gotta say.. I misjudged it. Don't get me wrong, I still don't like the time management aspect as it stresses me out, it makes me rush more than i'd like in an RPG, some of the zones are pretty huge and i'd love to just go exploring for a while - but I can't because i'll game over if I do. Im a completionist and this game doesn't allow it. With that said I gotta say for what it is, the time aspect is well done - it's actually bareable even for someone who hates that sort of thing, the timer pauses in conversations, cutscenes, menu's - and when you chill at your base (ark) in between days, stopping to take a breather or tinkering with your gear/shopping is really not an issue which is great! The timer will only run when you are running around the map exploring and moving about.. It even pauses in combat, and the more combat you do the more "EP" you collect, which you can use to cast Chronostasis which freezes the timer for a while. You can also extend your total time by several days when you do certain quests, so in short.. You have plenty of time. I haven't finished the game at the time of writing this but I am quite confident that i'll be able to do most if not all things that I want too during my first playthrough with some management, and with the game being built around multiple playthroughs (like Type-0) anything I do miss i'll be able to check out the next time around, and there seems to be plenty of reasons to play through a second time.
Alright, im ranting on so i'll move away from the timer topic and get into the game itself. The story has been referred to as lighthearted but I think that's incorrect, it's not as deep as what you are used too from the main series of games, but was any spin-off sequal ever? Think X-2, yes it has a few more lighthearted moments and some obvious fan service, but the story do have a serious tone as well as it wraps up the series.
The performance of the game is great, it looks pretty and runs smoothly and I haven't run into any bugs or crashes. The only thing that I would complain on from a technical standpoint is the controls, they are really weird and you can't set everything as you want which makes it feel like an obvious console port, for an example your map button and one of your attack buttons shares a key, and similarly with the menu button and a second attack, etc. So if you want your map on M and your menu on say Tab or Esc like in a typical PC game, you would have to do combat with those two keys as well which is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥and 20 houres in im still not used to the controls and I probably won't ever be, so i'd definetly recommend trying a controller if you have on since the game is obviously built for that!
Lastly the gameplay itself, combat is suprisingly fun although some of the random monster encounters can be a bit annoying, either they will knock you to the ground all too often, or die too easily, when you to get around to a boss you are rewarded for strategy. You can play the game button mashing, but the game rewards you if you choose to play better, as an example - you can hold the block button to block things, but if you simply press block at the right moment you might knock back and stagger your enemy, and there's also tactical strategies as using vulnerabilities against enemies.
You do not get to level up in the traditional way which im not sure if I like or not.. Instead you are rewarded with permanent stats for each quest you complete, another reason to replay the game, as you can increase in power endlessly (?). You also get quite alot of new equipments and you can equip multiple setups to switch between in batte, and you can upgrade your spells - and from what I hear your equipment too once you unlock hard mode, so despite not leveling up you still have plenty of ways to increase in power and you get quite a few ways to customize your Lightning the way you like her.
That should cover the basics so i'll just TLDR; The time management is annoying but ok, it sounds worse than it is - the game is not as serious as the previous two installments but doesn't screw around with it's story, don't go into it expecting another main series game, with an open mind though you should definetly have alot of fun and get a nice conclusion to the story.
And most of all - get ready to repeat these words regularly every time you play.. SHUT UP, HOPE.

Didn't expect that this would become my 2nd favorite Final Fantasy game of all time (VII being the best), especially not after having just finished the god-awful XIII-2. Lightning Returns is probably the first truly open-world FF game and rather than having an incoherent mess of locations like XIII-2 did, it instead has just four but each one is different from the gloomy European Luxerion and the vibrant, festive Yusnaan to the more open and diverse spaces of the Wild Lands and the Dead Dunes, each of which has a different atmosphere depending on the time of day (the day-night cycle is dynamic for the first time in the series). The battle system is the best in the series, being less about cheap and tedious grinding and more about precise timing, exploiting enemy weaknesses and having the right kind of schemata. The game's most notorious feature, the clock, is perhaps also its best feature, encouraging you to be efficient with your time, and allowing you to feel good about yourself at the end of a productive day. (It's also quite generous; after having finished nearly every available quest on Normal, I still had almost a week left on the clock.) And then there's Lightning, the icing on the cake if there ever was one and a reason in itself to buy the game. You may dress her in all kinds of cool outfits ("garbs"), which really makes the game the ultimate Waifu Dress-Up Simulator. Note that there are some jarring fps drops especially in the cities, a "feature" of the graphics engine, but that's pretty much my only complaint.

FRACT OSC is a pretty great and unique game. It's an adventure/puzzle game (sort of like Myst) with great visuals and music. The music is the central element of this game. Each puzzle creates music that builds up as progress is made, creating the soundtrack for that area. There's very little direction or instruction in the game, but it's usually not a problem. The puzzles are satisfying to solve, but aren't too difficult.
There's also a studio mode that gradually opens up if you want to use the synths and sequencers to make music or mess around. It's fairly limited, but pretty easy to use and songs can be exported (as WAV) or uploaded to youtube.
FRACT OSC is great and I definitely recommend it if you like the graphics & music. It's not a very complex or long (~4 hours, maybe) game, but it's a unique experience that's well worth it.

Fract OSC is one of the most moving gaming experiences I have ever had the privilege of having. For me, it evoked feelings that only a select few first-person exploration games, like Metroid Prime or STALKER, have managed before. The sheer scale of Fract's world provided me some legitimate awe as I scampered through its crumbling mega-structures and coaxed ancient, dilapidated machinery back to life.
In addition, the game has, perhaps, one of the best finales I've ever seen in a game, with all of your solutions to previous puzzles coming together and building on one another to a very satisfying climax.
Add to that a ♥♥♥♥♥ing soundtrack by MogiGrumbles, and you have a game I'm going to revisit often.

Fract OSC is the 80s lovechild of Tron and Myst. This auditory odyssy offers an Alice in Wonderland ride that, while it delights the senses, ultimately makes little sense from a traditional storytelling perspective. The only explanation the player receives about the story is before you ever buy the game or install. After that, the player is subjected to a variety of sights and sounds in what seems like an immense world, but how all of these pieces tie together leaves a player more puzzled than satisfied. But, if the player can suspend disbelief and the need for a strong narrative, the game does impress the senses.
Offering a midi style toolbox (i.e., 'the studio') with which to build tracks, Fract pays homage to the demo scene of the 80s and 90s. Tools within the studio can be unlocked organically by making progress in the single player game, or a player can opt to bypass the story and unlock all components of the studio immediately.
My only complaint is a compliment to the game-- I enjoyed it so much, I wish there was more to the single player story. (I only got 8 hours out of the game, using no walkthroughs.)
I highly recommend Fract if the game is on sale. I still recommend the game at its "normal" price point, although that recommendation is not as strong at full price due solely to the limited story content.
Either way-- Fract is a game that won't soon be forgotten.

Well, I just finished FRACT OSC, and I can safely recommend it. If you were a big fan of the MYST series, like I was, then this is perfect for you.
There is no real story behind this game, and it invites you to use your imagination, to explain why everything is what it is. From the visual and aural feasts you are given, you draw your own conclusions as to what the civilization was like. There is virtually no text within the actual game, instead relying on pictures and diagrams to relay information. Music is heavily used for artistic effect, though many of the puzzles
This game requires an awful lot of backtracking, so be prepared.
Beware, to run this at a constant framerate you need a decent rig, or to turn down the view distance. However, your mileage may vary. The options menu is rather sparse, lacking even a rebind keys option, which forces you to use the default bindings.
This game uses flat textures and polygonal shapes to create the terrain and buildings, and personally, I think it pulls off the look quite well. For such a simple design, it is quite beautiful.
The music creation tool is not something I have experimented with, but if you have any experience with music editing programs, you may find use in some of its synths. Again, your mileage may vary.
In my opinion, this game does not neccesarily warrant more than one playthrough, but if you have the patience to finish the game, you should have the patience to find and collect the achievements. I'm going to be searching for them myself, as I haven't perfected the game yet.
In conclusion, this game is beautiful. The art style is wonderful, but the puzzles are not for the impatient. Many of them require fine tuning and experimentation, and some of the later ones require backtracking. The options menu could do with more, but it is forgivable by a game so pretty.

In any case i know this company has moved on to some new trucker games and at this point I have just downloaded a new one that was on steam sale. I do have high hopes so we will see

Quite honestly a huge disappointment. The developers very obviously rushed the game, and didn't do any research. The following are my complaints about the game.
Guns feel inaccurate and underpowered compared to New Order and Old Blood. Laser gun had everything removed from it that was good, and now it's another generic gun.
No stealth mechanics, and the maps feel rushed and poorly made. Ubercommander missions are good, however implimented badly.
"AMERICA, YEEAAHH!" Boring, and could do without the side story about Blazkowizc's dad.
More unrealistic than can be expected from a game like this, and a clear lack of research.
What I loved most about New Order and Old Blood was the gunplay. The guns felt accurate, varied, and fun to shoot! I would sit back in levels and pop the heads of Nazi's from across the map with my assault rifle or my pistol, and it was satifying to do so. In this game, the guns are dumned down to waving all over the place, heads feel smaller so you can't headshot from across the map, and there are only 2 scopes in the game! One on your assault rifle, basically turning it into a sniper rifle, and another on your "upgraded" (in the words of set) laser gun.
One of the key weapons in New Order was the laser gun. It allowed you to cut through thin metal, gave you a scope to shoot multiple Nazi's at once, and actually recharged over time. All this was removed in place of an OP 1 shot kill gun, that isn't fun to use. The mechanic of cutting holes in metal was also removed in place of just destroying any bit of metal you target instantly.
The variation in guns was also reduced to a pistol, SMG, assault rifle, shotgun, grenade gun, and the laser gun. Throughout my entire playthrough, I pretty much only used my pistol for trying to be stealthy, assault rifle if I got caught, and laser gun for taking down mech units. The upgrades to the weapons also don't provide any variability, and are almost not worth getting.
Gameplay didn't feel much like a wolfenstein game at all. As mentioned in the Gunplay section, the weapons just felt inaccurate and lacking damage. The stealth mechanic was non existant. There are only a few situations in which an alternative route is present, and they are very minor get-arounds.
The maps are designed poorly in that you have a big area, but no little routes around like vents. As the game progresses, these big areas just get filled up with large units which you can't headshot with your pistol, forcing you to go into open combat, and alerting the commanders. Additionally, the maps are pretty awful to look at. They're either a generic underground base, or a blown up city, with a tiny colour palette, consisting mostly of brown.
Without any spoilers, all I can say here is it's so poorly thought out. You go around and recruit about 20 resistance fighters, and expect to take back America with that. And so, I can sum it up with just "America, YEAHHH!!".
Quite honestly, it would have made more sense (to me at least) to liberate Europe, or maybe Russia, which are closer to Germany and probably have more resistance groups, and then try to bring back a war that way. The whole idea behind the Wolfenstein games is fantastic! An alternative world where the Nazi's won WW2. However, America isn't really what anyone things of when they think of the Nazi's. Instead, they think of Germany (obviously), the occupation of Europe, the siege on England, the struggle for Russia, etc. There are so many oppertunities the developers could have taken, and I honestly feel they picked the worst one.
The concept of the ubercommanders is good, but so badly implimented. The maps which you go through in the main story are just reused, which feels really cheap.
Additionally, the whole side story with Blazkowicz's dad is completely unnecessary, and feels like it was only included to say "Hey look, even though Blazkowicz grew up in a time where people were racist towards black people and Jews, he wasn't!! Oh, and he also had Daddy issues!". This whole side story just made me cringe, and hate the game even more.
Oh god, as a physics student, I cringed too much at the lack of reseach the developers did in this section! Simple things such as radiation, now acts like a gas. Go to a nuclear bomb drop site with a gas mask, and oh boy, look, you're alright!
Even bigger issue than that though was with Venus. The game didn't mention the Nazi's had terraformed Venus, otherwise I wouldn't have had any issues. Anyway, Venus in this game is made out to be just the top of a Volcano. A bit hot, but all good. In actual fact, the surface of Venus is 90 times that of Earth's atmosphere, and with a temperature of about 470 degrees C. Under this pressure, the cute little suit Blazkowicz wears will instantly get crushed, and although Blazkowicz migth be able to withstand the outside pressure, it would be too heavy on him to allow him to breathe. Additionally, the massive base the Nazi's build on the surface of Venus would also be crushed under the atmospheric pressure.
After finishing the game, I was underwhelmed. It felt like a rip off of Doom, except without the awesome kill animations, the really fast paced action, and the fun variation of guns. I quite honestly regret playing this game, and look forward to playing New Order though again.

The worst part about Hellblade is that it can sometimes be extremely slow-paced. For a short game (6-7 hours if you play straight through) this is a pretty big problem. Slow movement and lots of very similar puzzles make this effect even worse.
Without spoilers, I can say that the ending left me confused and unsatisfied at first. This game's story is a lot to digest, and if you're not willing to truly attempt to understand the protagonist, it probably won't be an enjoyable experience.
The devs clearly wanted to make a game exploring psychosis and how it can affect a person, and if you're not looking for something like that, it'd be best to spend your money elsewhere.
Also, the combat system is pretty fun, one of the better parts of the game for me. It has rather simple controls, but still leaves room for the player to employ certain strategies or styles of combat.
Since I knew what I was getting into, I enjoyed the game, and can definitely recommend it to anyone who is willing to invest a little time into understanding Senua.
Summary, plus some other little tidbits:

+ Plot is entirely unique
+ Protagonist (well, the actor really) portrays real emotion
- Relatively short (6-7 hours)
- Slow-paced at times
- CANNOT be rushed through. Understanding the protagonist takes effort
- Is not particularly well-optimized. Framerates can dip even with strong hardware

Rating 7.5/10
Overview: Third Person Action RPG
The Good:
+ If you love Legend of Zelda dungeons then you will love this game. Between the main game, side quests and DLC there are roughly 20 dungeons to complete. The dungeons provide a good mix of puzzle solving, platforming and combat with a decent boss battle at the end.
+ 2 skill trees to develop your character. One skill tree focuses more on offensive abilities while the other focuses more on summoning and defensive abilities.
+ Lots of different loot to customize your character. Loot has different modifiers to fit your playstyle, i.e health on kill, fire damage, ice damage etc. Mix and match different loot to get the best results.  Special weapons can be upgraded allowing you to customize what attributes it gets.
+ Combat is fast and fluid making good use of all your combat abilities.
+ The story is somewhat minimal but does a good job of further fleshing out the story of the horseman
+ The crucible allows you to play 100 waves of fighting enemies that get progressively harder with each wave. After every 5 waves, you have a choice of accepting loot or quitting. The higher the waves the better the loot.
+ The additional DLC is also worth playing, providing more dungeons, unique enemies and weapons.
+ Fantastic soundtrack and voice acting
The Average:
+/- Bigger doesn’t always mean better. What this game makes up for in size it lacks in focus. The open world is big but also feels a bit empty. The open design of each world feels ‘segregated’.
+/- Graphics have been updated and the new lighting looks impressive but like the first game, I’m not so sure it’s a reason to replay the entire game over again.
+/-  Given the vast amount of loot given, I would have liked a better UI to manage everything. It would have been nice to have an option to put items in a junk pile and then sell everything to a vendor all at once rather than having to select every individual piece of loot.
The Bad:
- The side quests are atrocious. Almost all of them is some sort of collect-a-thon requiring a walk-through to find every little piece. To make matters worse, to complete one side quest you must complete another first, so you must collect everything. Many of these collectibles can add a permanent boost to your stats. The good news however is that these side quests are completing optional.
- The game suffers from technical performance. The game crashed on me a few times, experience some odd glitches etc. Its been well over a year since the last update. The developers have promised a new patch but that still remains to be seen.
Conclusion:
Like its predecessor, this game borrows different elements from different games and puts it together in one cohesive package. Its an action RPG with the platforming from Prince of Persia with level design from Legend of Zelda. A solid recommendation for anybody interested in the genre.

Didn't expect that this would become my 2nd favorite Final Fantasy game of all time (VII being the best), especially not after having just finished the god-awful XIII-2. Lightning Returns is probably the first truly open-world FF game and rather than having an incoherent mess of locations like XIII-2 did, it instead has just four but each one is different from the gloomy European Luxerion and the vibrant, festive Yusnaan to the more open and diverse spaces of the Wild Lands and the Dead Dunes, each of which has a different atmosphere depending on the time of day (the day-night cycle is dynamic for the first time in the series). The battle system is the best in the series, being less about cheap and tedious grinding and more about precise timing, exploiting enemy weaknesses and having the right kind of schemata. The game's most notorious feature, the clock, is perhaps also its best feature, encouraging you to be efficient with your time, and allowing you to feel good about yourself at the end of a productive day. (It's also quite generous; after having finished nearly every available quest on Normal, I still had almost a week left on the clock.) And then there's Lightning, the icing on the cake if there ever was one and a reason in itself to buy the game. You may dress her in all kinds of cool outfits ("garbs"), which really makes the game the ultimate Waifu Dress-Up Simulator. Note that there are some jarring fps drops especially in the cities, a "feature" of the graphics engine, but that's pretty much my only complaint.

FRACT OSC is a game completely based on exploration. You are thrust into an electronic world with puzzles and an amazing art style. Its a slow-pased game where there is no REAL objective, but it includes discovering new places, and uncovering secrets and locations. While this may get boring to most people, it is worth a try. It took a few failed attempts before I finally really got into this game, but I'm so glad I stuck with it. FRACT does not go out of its way to tell you what you're meant to be doing or how you're meant to do it, and indeed my first hour was spent utterly lost and wandering around the (admittedly very pretty) landscape, accomplishing absolutely nothing. That frustration led me to put it aside for a few months. But if you stick with it, you'll eventually begin to figure out this game's secrets. By the end of my playtime with FRACT I could start it up knowing exactly what I wanted to do, where I wanted to go, and how I was going to do it.
In FRACT, you're plunged into the trippy, Tron-like world of a gigantic yet dormant synthesizer. As you progress further and further, you'll gradually begin to bring the beast online, unlocking more and more of its features that can ultimately be put to use in an actual sequencer (your studio, as the game calls it) which you can visit at any time. This is a game where completing all the puzzles presents you with an actual reward - a fully functional digital audio workstation that is simple to play with, yet deceptively powerful under the hood.
If you liked Portal's method of first-person-puzzling, and in particular if you enjoyed the dynamic nature of Portal 2's music which adapted to your progression through the puzzles, you'll likely enjoy this game. It does require a bit of initial time and patience, but it pays off in spades.

Overall:  You're inside some sort of machine that makes music as you activate its various parts by solving puzzles.
My rants and raves:
* Brilliant, original idea.  I love the music-machine feel to the game.
* The puzzles do not give any sort of instruction, and give little indication of whether or not you're getting closer to the proposed solution.  You are given a toy that is 100x more complex than a Rubik's Cube™.  With no instructions and no idea what the winning conditions are.  Good luck.
* The developers tell you to explore this vast world in order to activate the machine totally... but give you no map.  I recommend Youtube walkthroughs if you're a completist.  The Steam achievements for this game are not very clear, either.
* The game, with its Tron-like feel, at times resembles Las Vegas.  Everything is lit up like an arcade and you have no idea where you are supposed to go next, or what is activated and what is not.  The lack of communication (e.g., score, progress, direction) with the player is terrible.
Unfortunately, while the game scores great originality points with me, there was far too much else that I found lacking or frustrating so I cannot recommend it.  I hope to see a sequel or expansion with some of these issues addressed.

Similar Games:
Mass Effect, Mount & Blade, and to a lesser degree Dynasty Warriors
The Good:
Varied gameplay mechanics that primarily focused on third person ground combat and space flight, but layers of strategy & RPG were there as well
Ground combat had a Mount & Blade/Dynasty Warriors feel to it, so the player would be fighting alongside his/her comrades in massive ground battles
Space flight and combat had a similar feel to the ground portions, but much more open and interesting
Space travel was unique in its use of wormholes and hyperjumps, which were refreshing and a nice change of pace
When needing to get a far off area in space, “hyperjumping” gets you there faster through the use of a quite fun mini-game that involves avoiding electric bolts strewn across a tunnel (See image)
A similar mini-game is present when using “wormholes”, which require you to stay in the center of the tunnels without hitting the sides (See Image)
Four different character races that each have different looks, starting areas, ships, and equipment loadouts
An RPG progression system that rewards you with skill points for accomplishments in battle (both space & ground)
This allows the player to tailor their character to their specific play styles (offensive, defensive, etc…)
A giant living, breathing world with a deep backstory and lore
Conversation trees are welcome and add a bit of needed flavor to character interactions
Numerous choices and options that are not only present in character and story development, but also in the game interface
Character interactions are amusing and keep a sense of humor about them (I was reminded of GlaDOS during certain points of the tutorial)
Sound design is well done and helps to immerse the player in battles or space travels
The Bad:
The beginning of the game is not indicative of the full package
The player will spend a good thirty minutes of slogging through a mediocre tutorial/basic combat section that has a very “been there, done that” feel to it
Graphics are very dated and can really ruin the great immersion the story creates
Animation and physics when it comes to combat sequences is very limited
Example: explosions all look the same and do not have a physics engine behind the particles (at least it is perceived that way)
Example: the death animations on the ground combat sections are all the same as well, with no variation based on the chosen weapon or vehicle of death
Not enough variation in indoor textures
When traveling to different space stations it is not uncommon to see the same textures and/or room setups within the same race
It feels like the game tries to do too much in scope and would benefit on focusing on one of its styles (space combat was my personal favorite)
Can you play it while the children are awake?:
I think so.  With the dated graphics and basic death animations, the game didn’t scream inappropriateness to me.
Did I make time to complete it?:
I did not.  However, I found the scope and gameplay compelling and worth the time spent in the game world.  This small team should be proud of their ambitious project and I look forward to their future endeavours.

Salvation Prophecy seems to me to be the reaction of a programmer saying "You know what needs to be redone and improved? Star Wars: Battlefront 2's sandbox mode." In this persuit there were some successes and some failures.
Successes:
In general, the game does a good job of making you feel like an important piece in your army, but not necessarily the whole army. If you work with your units rather than doing your own thing you'll be more successful, but it also seems at the end of every battle (especially land battles) that had you not been there, the odds of winning would have been zero.
The game takes a while to get warmed up, but once you reach "Faction Commander" status, some strategy elements become highly entertaining, Managing resources to create well-placed armies and defences is interesting, and working with or against the other factions is the best part of the game, in my opinion.
Space battles are fun, and upgrades for your ship really feel important and obvious (rather than some games where upgrades make such a minor difference you can hardly tell they've been installed). While the space battle system isn't completely intuitive to veteran space simulator pilots, its fairly easy to learn the new rules and becomes a new and interesting challenge. Furthermore, piloting your craft through wormholes and hyperspace turns out to be an important skill, though I do wish that computer players coming out of hyperspace would exhibit some amount of damage, as you often do.
Failures:
The biggest failure of this game are the land battles which are incredibly repetitive. After finishing a battle you will likely need to take 5 minutes for your trigger finger to relax after it had been held down non-stop for 15 minutes or so. While the factions are each unique, each member of a faction plays practically identically, but perhaps with different skill levels. The game could have added significantly more depth with different weapons (other than "Standard Blaster, Melee, and Faction-Specific).
Some factions are simply better than others. The Salvation, after which the game is named, have an ability to heal themselves, and also have an ability to throw up a reflecting shield making a skilled human player practically invincible. Meanwhile, the amusing Wyr are large targets with almost no defensive capabilities.
The main plot of the game is fairly unimaginative. Factions fighting in space, check, prophesy and chosen one, check, inexplicable and inevitable galactic doom, check. I didn't feel like I was very invested in the plot, and the only reason I was motivated to finish it was that if I spent any more time not finishing it, I would have eventually lost.
The worst part about the plot was that it was carried through by plot-specific missions which mostly involved you trudging around alien planets toward a puzzle solution. There are alien beasts on these planets, but solo combat basically involves standing there, holding down the "fire" button, and waiting. You'll always win, so the monsters seem less like a tactical roadblock and more like a waste of time. I think these missions could have easily been shortened to just the puzzle sections to be much more effective.
Some of the mechanisms of the game are also broken. If another faction destroys a third faction's base, its totally within your power to build a new base there instantly, as it is within your power to instantly rebuild any base destroyed by your enemies. This makes losing battles more of a bother than a tactical setback, and it makes winning seem awfully easy. If you're like me, by the time you unlock diplomacy, two of the factions have already been reduced to one or 2 bases, and their surrender is easy to coax.
I hesitate to reccomend this game because the issues do keep parts of the game from being fun (especially by the end of your campaign when the last thing you want to do is another damn land battle), but there's also so much good in this game. I would love to see a sequel with some more depth, and maybe a little more production value.
If this game is on sale, it is probably worth checking out.

This, in many respects, is the most minimalistic game I've played. The stunning environments, sounds (as mentioned in the previous paragraph, there is no music), and controls all contribute to make this a seemingly less-is-more experience—minding, I'm not even sure yet as to how many levels there are total!
• The controls are about more minimal than the levels themselves. This, using Unity's system for launch, there is adequate customization for the controls. The levels, on the other hand, are intricately designed, and, as this game's own sypnosis says it, thought-provoking! I literally did stop at a few moments to think about the path I was trying to move across, and as accurate to that path as possible! Alongside the levels and controls, there's also the physics, which surprisingly, to myself, did actually make it a lot easier to move, whether it's 'climbing' on top of one the lines or flying across the level—unless, of course, you instead fly
the level.
Got it for $0.21. Still probably wouldn't recommend it at that price.

I bought all three Wolfensteins (made by Bethesda) during the Autumn Sale a few months back. Altogether I paid about what this game would normally cost without a sale. That being said, The New Order is by far my favorite out of the tree (fiddy). I played each directly after the other with no break between (took a couple weeks to do since I played on the hardest difficulty each time). I highly recommend buying the first two games while they are on sale as those two games are extremely good in my opinion. This game was still pretty good but there were some aspects which really set back the game in my opinion. For instance when throwing hatchets, if you were not in an open area (with no lowhanging door ways or cover beside you) there was a very strong possiblity for the hatchet to not even be thrown in the same direction you were looking - it would richochet off some wall and go the other way and go luck finding it because it'll literally be glitched into the ground and impossible to see. Really sucks during stealth play throughs. Also there were not that many orignial weapons in the game (that you can carry on you), but I absolutely loved the heavy weapons you can use periodically.
But I digress...
Here are my conclusions on this game, hopefully they will help you make a decision about purchasing it.
- This is the only wolfenstein to my knowledge that out of the gate lets you play at higher than 60fps. (I have a 1440p, 144hz monitor with a gtx 1080 rarely did i experience dips below 130fps during the game running mostly everything on high or ultra)
- I HATE when you dont have maxed out ammo for a gun and when you pull that gun out, it does NOT have a full magazine even if you have sufficient ammo for a full magazine; this game will do you dirty like that during those missions were ammo is scarce. So before you start shooting make sure you reload!
- Story was very good! Much less outlandish than the Old Blood but that outlandish factor in the Old Blood really set it apart. There were times in the game were I would find myself chuckling to myself about some of the shenanigans i would do in game and some shenanigans that i See BJ do during the cutscenes (my favorite is when he turns around with a hatchet in his hand after completely wrecking something, youll know what im talking about when you play through it).
- Would definately NOT recommend buying this game at full price, I do not feel as though the campaign justifies that price, but for half off it is a great title to own.
- All in all i would rate this game a 7/10 would be higher if the on sale price was more than 50% off but still a great game for the money (which should be half off lol)

This is a prequel review, so you guys can get it on sale.
Decisive to say, I think you should get it at this stage. I'm not altogether that far through the game, but from what I've seen so far I'm blown away. The design is seriously good. It feels like nothing I've played. It seems educational too. Graphically I've no complaints. It's presented brilliantly. You will be pleased I assure you. Sound is outright impressive. The voices in the Senua's head give me an insight into how it must be like to suffer from mental difficulties like this. Scary stuff in places, but somewhat useful in game. It's an affliction but a sort of super power if you look at it from a weird angle. Ah, weird angles... that reminds me, the puzzles in the game are brilliant, if not a bit frustrating at times.
Combat wise the game has a simplistic approach in regards to the enemies, when they appear, etc., but the annimation flow of Senua's different strikes is almost 'Dead or Alive' class. Really responsive, enabling me to control my destiny. Wrap all this up into a rouge like game (I can't say why, spoiler) where your performance can lead to total failure and I'm hooked. Overall, there's a damn lot I love about this game already and not much I can complain about either. It seems to be an experience rather than a trash game to witter away the hours.
Enjoy!

Probably one of the best games I have ever played. The game is even more interesting if you are interested in psychology by any chance. In this game you are Senua a Nordic warrior-woman (perhaps a shield maiden). Senua suffers from severe pyschosis and from what I understood from the game you are one of the voices in her head (presumebly the most dominant one. ps: this is my own theory). What I really loved about the game is that you can really emphatize with the character and really be the character. The 3-D sound technique is implemented so good that the developers depicted what pyschosis in the most vivid way possible. The combat may seem dull but I don't think that its very important because its the mental challange which is most important in this game rather than the physical one. I really recommend watching the Hellblade feature in the game, it really gives you a really firm grip of how the game was made and how its really close to reality. Also you will learn a lot about Norse Mythology. PS: Use good headphones if you want to experience the game at it's peak. Thanks Ninja Theory for this amazing experience and helping us understand the people who suffer from psychosis.
