Cherry Tree High Comedy Club is an interactive visual novel/adventure game where you play as Mairu, a girl during her last year as a student of Cherry Tree High, who is trying to reopen the Cherry Tree High Comedy Club. The game alternates between visual novel scenes and your own interactions with the world around you in side-scrolling fashion, as you level up your abilities and try to persuade at least 3 other people to join your club, in accordance with school rules. Buy magazines, go out for lunch, converse with others as level up your relationships, but hurry because you are running out of time for the submission deadline. Thumbs up to a fun interactive anime-type visual novel.

Cherry Tree High Comedy Club is what I would consider a time-management visual novel.  You manage a limited amount of time/actions to improve your skills and then use those skills to overcome challenges.  It is a good time for the short game/novel it is.  About 3-4 hours of unique content with a second playthrough pretty much needed to see the stories of the all characters.  After seeing the content however, the game loses all replay value.  Nothing random happens and the majority of the events have maybe 1-2 versions depending on your progress at that point in the game.  I would recommend to pick it up on sale if you have interest in these types visual novels.  However, it won't convince anyone to be a fan of the genre.  Keep in mind there is a new game+ that allows you to carry over your stats if you "beat" the game to allow easier recruitment on future plays.
Note: I played the non-westernized version.
Pros:
+Decent characters - I liked them.  They were trope heavy, but they were well written and I enjoyed the banter.
+Great Art - I really do enjoy the art-style of the game.  Between the pixel art characters and the  cartoony overworld, you will be enjoying the colorful town.
Meh:
~Short - Common for this genre, but depending on your reading speed it is easy to finish the first time in 2.5-3.5hrs.  I completed the game 3 times in my 5.5hrs and saw everything this game has to offer.
~Music - Nothing wrong, nothing noteworthy.
Cons:
-No dialogue skip - Most visual novels have the ability to skip over text you have already read, if you plan on playing 2-3 times to either see the other characters or recruit all 6 this feature is sorely missing.
-Poor graphics options - Full screen stretches and the default resolution is pitiful.  Would benefit from either bars on full screen or the ability to scale the game window.
-Short - Common for this genre, but depending on your reading speed it is easy to finish the first time in 2.5-3.5hrs.  I completed the game 3 times in my 5.5hrs and saw everything this game has to offer.
TL;DR - Short time-management visual novel, but worth picking up on sale.

Static washes out your vision, slowly fading away to reveal large and impossible geometric objects reaching up and out as far as you can see. Dead machinery jutting out from pastel colored ground and rock. You don’t know how exactly you got here nor how any of these strange constructs were built. Your legs carry you across the land, poking your head into enclosed buildings that might as well be giant tombs. At last, you come across an object that emits a strange hum. You touch it and the hum changes pitch slightly in reaction. You move it around and it changes tempo and pitch respective to where it was before. You don’t know what is going on but you sure as hell are nodding your head.
FRACT OSC is like a Fantasia for the dance-minded music fans. IDisneylandM, if we were to give it a genre tag in our music player. Much like the Aggro-crag, every area on the map is color coded according to the theme of the sounds you’ll expect to hear. Pink acts as your bubbling leads, blue as your bass and green as the airy pads. Each instrument has its own dedicated area in the mountain area FRACT takes place in. The leads come from such towering heights, the pads sit in the middle and the bass rumbles on from down below. There are other, smaller details which show themselves to musician and non-musician alike which key you in to each place’s role in the overall scheme of what is going on.
Exploration is only one part of what makes FRACT tick. The tock of the metronome comes from the game’s puzzles. Each instrument has a specific puzzle type which increases in difficulty as you progress through them. The block movement and pad rotation puzzles were fine, but the last laser puzzle in the bass area had me tearing at my hair a while. Overall though I didn’t find any of them prohibitively difficult (though the ease of a majority of them may disappoint hardcore puzzle game fans) and FRACT always allowed me the freedom to leave any given puzzle to explore at my leisure. I would have to come back to it eventually if I wished to see the end, but the lack of pressure really goes a long way towards making even the hardest puzzles easier to forgive. I’m glad to see games like FRACT and Ether One taking this stance.
The way the sound design is so keenly and closely tied together with the puzzles was enough to make me smile as every solution came together. Starting off in an area, the puzzles were very basic and the sounds those areas produced once fully activated reflected that. By the time you’ve hit the end of the series of puzzles for a given color/instrument, the puzzles have added new mechanics over time and the resulting sounds that blast forth have additional layers of complexity. It really builds up a feeling of progression. Instead of a simple pat on the back for completion and shoving the player towards the next goal, you’re allowed to enjoy the fruits of your labor.
As you complete puzzles which slowly teach you vital elements of constructing tunes you unlock various tools to use in the in-game Studio room. The further into the game you get, the more you’re allowed to add and tweak into the track as you work. It starts off small with only a single loop sequencer and bare minimum controls over the tone of the digital instrument. By the time you’ve completed the entire game, you’re handed an impressively beefy DAW that looks as awesome as the sounds you’re able to make with it. While it is still limited and won’t replace your Reason, ACID or even your old copy of Fruityloops burned to a CD from a decade ago, it serves as an excellent introduction into the world of digital audio production. FRACT OSC is really a musical instruction tool masquerading as a videogame. To make things even better, the game has a built in export function and the dev is totally cool with users making commercial tracks so long as the loop work done with FRACT’s samples were all done in-game. A tutorial to mod in your own beats has been promised as well.
By the time I reached the end of my musical journey my ears were ringing and I felt similar to those nights after a gig. I’d emerged from the 8 hour rave session that I conducted for myself and myself alone, nary another ear to hear what reverberated through the cavernous area but my own. With every box aligned, switch flipped and cogs rotated I had brought life to these dead hills. As though Holy Mountain had been redone as a living Demoscene file, I had seen the secrets of this strange land from the very tip of its highest cliff to the very bottom of its deepest trench. I overlooked all that I had conquered and felt that it wasn’t quite enough. I retreated back to my lair, dark and still, slaving away for hours on what was to be my next song. I’d earned the right to control this giant machine and make it bend to my will. If only because I demonstrated that I understood what it wanted.
It wanted to make you move.

Lightning Returns takes place after storyline of Final Fantasy XIII-2. I have played the entire trilogy and will briefly review them here to give perspective on where Lightning Returns stands.
Final Fantasy XIII:
TL;DR Fun and charming story with some very hateable companions and lacklust gameplay. 60hours worth of run to a yellow dot, hit 2 buttons for autobattle, and watch melodramatic cutscenes.
Final Fantasy XIII-2:
TL;DR Open world FFXIII with pokemons. Forced storyline that made an originally complete and charming fairy tale from FFXIII completely nonsensical.
Final Fantasy Lightning Returns:
TL:DR: Lightning is back with actual player controlled combat and no more pokemons. Doom clock ticking down to 0? Better go plant some more herbs.
Pros:
- GREAT PC port. Perhaps mechanically one of the best PC port of all time.
- You get to play as Lightning again! (Experience may vary.)
- You have direct control of all of your character's moves in real time! It controls well and makes game genuinely fun to play.
- Combat is actually challenging now and you need learn to block.
- With the new clock system, you have an actual sense of urgency to the story line. But not enough urgency to skip the sheep herding or flower planting apparently.
- All the  50 shades of grey monsters are gone. You no longer have 3 different colored behemoth running around for no good reason.
- 4 very different land scapes with diverse biomes to explores.
- Monsters go extinct when you kill enough of them, which is awesome.
- Better music.
- No more annoying whiny ♥♥♥♥♥ companions.
Cons:
- No more pokemons :(
- No more companions (meh)
- Lots of running and you need to min-max the most efficient routes constantly.
- Scope of the game isn't nearly as big as FFXIII.
- Story is rushed and you are tieing loose ends left and right with very unsatisfying final quests.
- Plot line is genuinely uninteresting and poorly paced. Story feels very rushed and poorly polished. It follows up to FFXIII-2 plotline and is genuinely worse.

Salvation Prophecy manages to successfully marry several play styles into one game which makes for an enjoyable excursion into space for fans of shooting and exploration. Whilst the  progression feels a little rigid in places, once the game opens up there's an enjoyable fusion of gameplay elements that keeps the game fresh and worthwhile. The game is very much a budget release, but with so much care and attention placed into this project, it stands as a testament that smaller budget games can be good and don't necessarily need expensive effects or flashy graphics to make them enjoyable. The gameplay and looks are simple compared to triple A games, but if this can be ignored, there's a cool and fun game to play here that's well polished and certainly worth the price of entry.

Salvation Prophecy is a good example of how the whole can be greater than its parts. Or something like that. This is an Indy Game made by a person who wanted to create a space game that explored galactic conflict in a way AAA titles wont. The vastly different types of gameplay mean that none are as detailed as a game would be that concentrates on that one aspect. But every part of the game is enjoyable and together made for a fun package. So while the third person shooter part has been done way better in other games, I will still run to the dropship to support the rest of the Salvation troops in the planetary invasion of a Drone colony. And I will join the rest of the Salvation fleet to defend our space station from the Wyr. And having to navigate hyperjumps and wormholes add that unexpected depth.
Yes the graphics are dated. Then again, we don't play indy games for the graphics but for the innovation.
So while this game isn't for everyone, those who want this game may just realize it is exactly the game they want ;)

I'm in a point in my life where I value games that respect my time. Gorogoa certainly fits the bill.
Let's get this out of the way: Gorogoa is short. I value quality over quantity and thus I don't regret having forked 12 euros for it, but I can see why some people would rather wait for a lower price.
Gorogoa is a puzzle game, although it's not quiet like any other I've ever played. It's a bit like a little hand-crafted clockwork pop-up book. I sort of feels like playing Monument Valley or Fez with their space bending gameplay, but this game is more of a litteral puzzle. Pieces are connected in various ways depending on the context. The relationship between them is surprisingly natural and there are plenty of visual tips scattered around the panels (specially in earlier ones) in order to prevent the player from getting stuck.
The player can peform basically 3 actions over a panel: move it, navigate inside it or undock one of it's layers. Only some panels include navigation hot spots or undockable layers. It's worth mentioning that some pannels include animations and while it's playing some of their actions are unnavailable. Sometimes an hourglass pointer will warn the player about that, but others (particularily on looping ones) it's far from obvious. That's pretty much the worst I can say about the gameplay. Other than that the interface is pretty confortable.
The art and music are great and help setting the mood. The narrative flows in a twisted way, mixing times and places in a rather random way. I think I didn't quiet get what it was trying to convey, but It the end it really didn't matter.
I liked Gorogoa and I definitely recomend it to anyone looking for an original puzzler.

TL;DR -- Fantastic graphics, engaging "out of the box" logic, did not feel disappointed despite the cost and short playtime.
I've played over 100 games and this defies description. The closest I can come is the original Samarost and similar flash games. Call it "3rd-person Surreal artistic manipulator-puzzle game". You get up to four frames, each representing a view on the game world. You solve puzzles by manipulating the frames (zooming, overlaying, or moving). Certain combinations change the game world, and allow you to progress. The puzzles are fairly simple, although I was stumped on a few. But you can solve any of these by trial and error (I think I solved one by accident). An experienced player might make it through in 1-2 hours (it can be speed-run in under 30 min). If you just want to savor the experience and listen to the relaxing mood-music, it might take longer (if you quit your progress is saved, but you have the option of restarting from the chapter beginning). Which brings up the cost/time ratio. The game is about $12 on sale, which seems high for something with only moderate-low replay value. But after playing for a bit I did not feel disappointed. The artwork and animations are great, it is like being part of a surreal animated film that unfolds around you.
If you are stuck or want a little more info before buying, check out the first video on the Steam store page. It's actually a walkthrough for some of the simpler puzzles, and lets you know what to expect.

Gorogoa is beautiful. The puzzles are well represented, not too easy to be obvious but never so difficult as to leave you stumped for long. By manipulating the drawings in a picture book, we change the physical landscape of the world and sometimes the mental landscape of a person. Overlay a different room on a person standing in a doorway and we move them from one to another. The rules of place and time alter in a way that continually delights.
And yet I got through all of it in 1.3 hours according to Steam and I wasn't exactly rushing. So Gorogoa is beautiful, but it's a tasty little dessert of a puzzle game instead of a meal. If the price doesn't bother you and you want < 2 hours of a relaxing puzzle game, I recommend it. Otherwise wait for a sale.

If you're a redneck and love doing the deed with your own offspring, then this game is for you.
Jokes aside, 18 Wheels of Steel: American Long Haul is a truck simulator and not a very good one. There are many 18 Wheels of Steel games in the series, but so far this is the only one I've played, so experiences may be compared to the likes of Euro Truck Simulator 1 & 2.
Honestly... Very lackluster. The controls are absolutely diabolical and feel like you're driving a bathtub on wheels around the road. Finding out where you are going is also a pain too, as there is near-enough, no GPS in the game compared to the other sims.
However, the game is quite old, so you can't fault it for its graphics that have aged very terribly and also the graphical glitches that come with playing the game.
This feels more like Euro Truck Simulator 1, compared to 2 in terms of size. However, you do get the entirety of the USA to explore as well as parts of Canada and Mexico. Locations also feel bland honestly and driving from area to area in the same vicinity as before can feel taxing on the brain.
I have a few things I'd like to say.
1. There are cops in this game. Which was weird so essentially you could get 'pulled over' for running a light, although saying that, the police in this game don't even move an inch from when they sound their sirens. If you stay further away from the cops than what's needed, you can easily not get fined at all on your journey.
2. You can do single journeys. This is great in a sense as you can literally choose where you start and where you end and you can do a delivery like that. Euro Truck Simulator 2 needs to implement a system like this honestly.
3. There is a lack of music. Besides the menu music, there is no music in-game whatsoever. Even the in-game radio only has the menu music listed as an .ogg file. Weird.
This game is pretty bad honestly. I recommend picking up the later truck simulator games like ETS 2 and American Truck Simulator instead. If not, just try picking up the first Euro Truck game instead. That's pretty good.

Darksiders 2 is a semi open world action adventure RPG. It is a sequel to the first darksiders game which was heavily inspired by World of Warcraft lore and its characters(Lich King etc.), just with a different thematic twist to it. However, this game is nothing like the first one. Therefore I would like to outline the key differences between the both games as the community is split between them.
While the first game was aimed towards adults as a love letter for Zelda with its God of War combat. It offered a challenging puzzle design with linear world for story progression as opposed to DS2 simplified puzzles and open world. DS1 did not feature a vast amount of weapons to choose from the way DS2 allows you to. More or less you were given 4 weapons to use at all times, while DS2 has a bigger variety and freedom to choose.
DS2 is a much different game than the previous one. The developers have introduced diablo 3 random loot mechanics and stats into the game. It is also a modern succesor to Prince of Persia parkour traversal along the walls. With the last difference being leveling system.
#Game engine related#
* Graphics - in general they did improve overall texture quality of the original game. In general the game is very pleasing to the eye aesthetically due to its cartoony graphics. This way the game is more authentic when compared to other RPGs that are quite realistic and have a grim and dark color palete. Though I am not surprised about cartoony graphics, as the developers were a long time World of Warcraft players. :)
* 60 FPS - overall gameplay is a lot smoother, as higher framerate allows for quicker reactions/responses in regards to your enemies actions and moves. It is good to see framerate being adressed for PC platform as it is the standard of gaming.
#Game related#
* Open world - first and foremost, it is a good change of pace from the original darksiders. As it feels a lot more pleasant to play and explore.
* The Story - it does have way more depth to it, which is a lot more interesting to follow than darksiders.
* Voice acting - truly some of the voice actors did an outstanding job on this title. Kudos to them.
* Main Character - when you think about main character who's name is Death, you probably picture him as cold-hearted, emotionless, ruthless and what not. However, this is not the case with Death in Darksiders 2. Its surprising to see such a dark character as Death, be portrayed in both good and bad ways. One time you could find him soft, the very next time he would be the guy who never looks back at the explosions.
#Game engine related#
* Low FPS - Certain AMD users might experience major FPS dips in performance. My suggestion would be to try running the game on OpenGL instead of Vulkan. This is a 50/50 solution and depends on your hardware and system configuration. Some people reported it solving the problem.
* Cinematic tearing/crackling/cut off/freeze - Yet another major issue, when sound in animated cartoons begins to crackle. This might be due to my sound card, though I doubt it as I've tested the game on 2 different PC's. Do note that during cinematic's you might experience major FPS drops on AMD GPU's. If you skip the cutscenes, the FPS dips should disappear within a few seconds.
* Sound disappearing - Another issue is the music and combat sounds disappearing after 2 hours into the game.
: Restart your game when this happens, its game engine related.
* Random crashes - This is an issue exclusive to Deathinitive Edition. From time to time you might experience a crash. No potential fix exists.
* Damage number output - From my own impression, the game's engine is surely not coded according to huge crit numbers from your weapons or abilities. This will sometimes crash your game.
: Disable damage numbers from appearing on your screen in options.
* Glitches - This version has not only came out with its own portion of problems, but also managed to incorporate all of the original version's glitches. (Death being unable to move in particular zone's wall moss).
* Light shafts - Certain parts have a horrible or non existent light sources, making the area very dark. Not a major issue, just an oversight.
* DLC's - are far more accessible in this version, however Argul's tomb and the Abyssal Forge are utterly broken. If you experience non-stop crashing on Argu's Tomb, my advise would be to turn off damage numbers in your options. For Abyssal Forge, a ball could glitch out in the secret area. Preventing death from accessing the object to progress further. There is no fix for this issue, only suggestion would be is to keep trying to interact with the object from all the angles.
#Game related#
* Combat gameplay - This might be just me, but I find the combat in DS2 to be very plain and boring. Even playing on the hardest difficulty available, I've mostly spammed the same X button or Y for attacks. R1+X to recharge my wrath and two or more abilities keybinded to my controller. There are no notable combos that are worth combining for greater benefits, all I've noticed is that I had to dodge more on Deathinitive difficulty. Although the same can be said about DS1, where dash strike was king.
* Collectibles - this is my biggest gripe with the game. Collectibles in ds2 are simply not fun to collect as there are too many of them. Plus the whole backtracking of collectibles due to world related blockades being unacesible without tools like death grip, phasewalker and soul splitter that are only obtained by progressing story further. Clearcly the execution of collectibles could of been done better for this game. Well here is hoping for Darksiders 3 having a better system in place.
* No collectible tracker - previous game had an item that let you see all nearby chests. While this game has a similar feature as default for chests. It however does not feature a way to track the missing collectibles. You can end up backtracking hours upon hours to find a power stone or etc.
* Itemization & randomness - Quite frankly I should praise the game for having randomized loot. However I will not. You can end up playing for 30+ hours without having a possesed weapon (strongest weapons in game), or piece of gear that would improve your talent build.
* Legendary items - why are they even in the game? Some of them offer a special ability, however they only drop from story related boss or side quest mini-boss. Yey they are so underpowered in comparison to what you can make of your possesed weapon, that I view them as common trash item that you should just vendor.
* Dependance of crit chance and crit damage % - yes, if you plan on playing on the hardest difficulty, it comes to no surprise that such stats would become your best bet for cookie cutter build. If you have too little of either, some boss might be unkillable or would take insane amount of time to beat while staying alive. It saddens me of how important these two stat sticks are, as it makes it too difficult to finish the Crucible without them.
*Imbalances between the talent trees - for lower difficulties, melee build works just fine. However if you decide to play deathinitive difficulty. You will soon find that the best tree is the necromancer tree. It offers not only great flexibility of drawing aggro from enemies to your ghouls, but with perfect gear pieces and stats. You can pretty much 1-shot anything without being hit once. Even if you would stack 100% crit chance and damage on harbringer, necromancer is just leagues above it.

Since CoD: WWII was recently released, I decided to run through a few of my favorite Call of Duty games and give them a good once over. I'm judging them based on several criteria.
So, now that introductions are over, let the review begin.
There are a lot of aspects of later CoD games that I don't like. They aren't in this one. The controls make a lot of sense, and give the player more freedom than later games, which are simplified, but more restricted. You can make use of Q and E, which allows you to peek around covers, and is useful for slicing the pie on stealthier missions. This is one feature that I sorely miss from games that come after this. There's also less "Yeah, no♥♥♥♥♥♥" moments. The objectives make sense, and the game trusts that you have enough of a brain to follow them and understand what to do. There are no blips on the screen telling you who to follow or where to go, they're limited to the compass.
So, the objective system is a lot simpler, and the controls are better. How about the shooty bits? Well, I can't really explain it, but aiming and shooting just feels a lot better in this game than in say, Modern Warfare 2. The aiming can only be described as crisp and clean, and shooting feels pretty good, as all the guns sound and feel like actual guns. There is noticeable recoil, and muzzle climb, but not to an unmanageable degree. This contrasts between Modern Warfare 2, where the aiming feels a little more spongy and slow.
How about the difficulty? Well, the game has four difficulties. Recruit, Regular, Hardened, and Veteran. Recruit is♥♥♥♥♥♥easy, Regular is a slight challenge, Hardened is a pretty good Challenge, and Veteran is insane. A skilled player playing on recruit will get bored within minutes. It's still very possible to die, but playing it carefully like you would on higher difficulties is just boring. Regular is slightly more exciting, where the enimies target you more often, and bullets do more damage. During harder segments a skilled player might die a few times. Hardened is where things get interesting. A few shots will kill you, and enemies target you more easily, and much more often. Cover is essential. In previous difficulties, you could run around and have fun with the dudes, but hardened brings it to another level. I haven't really played veteran all that much, but It's quite difficult. Enemies have almost human reaction times, targeting you and returning fire. You're damaged like you actually would be, maybe being able to keep going after getting shot in the arm or something, but dying within one shot to center mass.
And that concludes the gameplay portion. Now for:
Well, it definitely doesn't look bad. It's aged very well. The textures look good, fire looks good, everything looks pretty alright. It looks so alright that I didn't really even pay attention to it, and focused on gameplay among other things.
That was quick. how about:
The story revovles around two wars. There is a war in the Middle East (when isn't there?) and a war in Russia. The war in Russia centers around a group called the Ultranationalists. They want Russia to return to the communistic dictatorship of Soviet Russia. The OpFor in the Middle East is supported by the Ultranationalists. The story isn't really focused on characters. It's more about global politics. It played on real actual fears at the time of the games release. What if they had a nuke? What if they used a nuke? In order to appreciate the story you need to keep your ears open and watch the cutscenes between missions, because the situation isnt really described in detail during missions. It is good enough to be quite tense. Near the end of the game a really big bad thing happens, and it acutally made me go like "oh♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; and it was quite a rush. So, story's good.
And finally:
The overall theme of the game is very clear. War is bad. Nukes are bad. The military industrial complex is bad. Whenever you die the game displays a quote. These quotes fall under three categories. Some quotes tell you the price of a common asset to the military. Some quotes are pulled from soldier's journals. Some quotes talk about how we won't survive WWIII. It's all very thought provoking.
Yes.
This game was put out long before the CoD games shot way down in quality. It's actually a very tight and engrossing shooter that will keep you playing for hours. If you have a spare 20 bucks, buy it. If its on sale for half off or whatever for sure buy it.

I was a beta tester for Fract OSC. Getting onto the beta test program was a joy, as I was very interested in the game beforehand; it was lovely seeing the game make strides towards completion, and here it is.
Fract is one of the most original and ambitious indie titles of the last coupla years in my opinion: it marries music and first person puzzle gameplay relatively successfully and it manages to give the player the feeling of being utterly lost in a pulsating, cold yet oddly comforting machine.
Some of the puzzles are slightly fiddly but most of them are decent - nothing too complex, really, though some of them require the player to fully explore an area and take mental notes.
It looks very nice, though I have to say it might not run very well on low-end systems (the devs have done a lot of optimization though); the audio and music fit the atmosphere perfectly, and completing a puzzle feels very rewarding because of the interaction between sound and world.
The studio mode might be slightly simplistic but it's a ton of fun and you can create mighty beats with it - it's a great bonus and I wish the devs will expand on this either with updates or a whole new game.
Recommended if you like toying with music and unconventional games.

The closest thing I can compare FRACT to is the time I showed up in in Kurdish Iraq with barely a month of Arabic lessons (note: Kurds prefer to speak Kurdish, not Arabic). I wanted to venture out from my hotel and explore the city of Erbil. But instead I mostly stuck close to our Peshmerga guards and my friends in our medical service team as we shuttled from location to location. Still, our group braved the communication divide a few times, usually in marketplace situations where Iraqui Dinar could do all the talking. The question lingered in the back of my mind each time we stepped out, “How well are we going to be able to read our environment?” Some navigational anxiety was sated by the fact that I still had familiar objects to read and relate to – things like trees, buildings, cars, and friends. Our group stuck together in this setting, leaning on one another to make sense of our alien surroundings.
In FRACT OSC, I had no language, objects, or friends to relate to. It was just me, exploring an alien world made of abstract shapes and synthesizers.
I needed my music-literate buddy, Max, to help make sense of the world.
FRACT OSC invites me into extreme illiteracy. It’s like landing in a country I’m even less prepared for than Kurdish Iraq. My FRACT illiteracy reminds me of my own privileges. And just how hard it must for people to understand the world with limited access to friends and family. FRACT OSC got rather unpleasant at times, but I also think it’s brilliant. It drew discomfort out of my own inability to read the world. It drew me into reliance on somebody other than myself. And reminded me that understanding often comes from community.
For the record, I haven’t completed the game. But you can be sure I’m saving it for the next time Max comes over.

I honestly wanted to love this game, and it certainly has very high quality aspects to it. But in the end the game is just kinda boring.
So basically in this game you play as Senua who is son a journey to save her husband. The game consists basically of you walking, encountering a puzzle to solve, having to fight a couple enemies and then having to fight a boss after repeating those steps a couple times while learning about Senua's past through flashbacks when you're walking between puzzles and fights. A really cool aspect of this game is that throughout  the entire game voices will whisper you all sorts of things from actual advice, to lies or just telling you that you suck, which is honestly really creative and well implemented.
And while the story is pretty interesting, the gameplay is the problem in my opinion. You'll be walking and hearing about Senua's life, interested in what happened to her, but then you have to fight a couple guys (in a fighting system which is honestly so laughably simple and easy to the point where it's honestly a chore), then you finally hear some more about her story, but no time to solve a puzzle. And while both of these gameplay aspects are fine on its own (even if the fighting is kinda easy) after doing it time and time again without having some real changes added to it, it just becomes boring. It feels like you're reading a book, but everytime you turn the page you have to run three laps around your house. And while the story is pretty good, it's not good enough to have to go through hours of the same boring puzzles and fights.
And you might have heard about the perma death mechanic, this means that if you've died a certain amount of time s your save file will be erased. But this is honestly more of a bluff than an actual threat since I died about twice in the entire game because the game is just that easy and you get an awful lot of deaths before your save file is deleted.
So in the end I personally found the gameplay too boring, simple and with not enough variety for me to want to finish this game. There were parts I enjoyed, but those were between hours of the same boring puzzles and fights, which is honestly a shame because the premise of a character with a mental disorder and the way the voices were implemented was honestly very promising.

This game as a huge amount of positive reviews, which makes me reconsider what I've taken away after playing it though. I'd like to be able to recommend it - there's a lot here to like. The actress who played Senua, Melina Juergens, did an absolutely amazing job; honestly one of the best performances I've seen in a video game. The art direction and assets are similarly spectacular, as is the sound and music design.
The two things I have an issue with are firstly the combat, which is functional, but extremely basic and feels as if it was included to prevent criticism of a "walking simulator". Every combat section feels like filler with zero depth and I found myself completely conflicted; on one hand, more combat would make it feel more like an actual game, on the other the combat is so lack lusture I think it took away from the experience Ninja Theory was trying to present.
The second and most prominent issue I have with the game is that at the end of the game I came away completely confused. I'd just spent 9 or so hours experiencing an extremely bleak Norse world though the eyes of someone with severe mental illness(es) and had no idea what to take away from it, other than to feel slightly ill. This is not a heroes journey, nor a story or redemption. It's ~10 hour journey into a very depressing, albeit pretty, world. Whatever the point of the game was it was completely lost on me.
My only recommendation would be for Melina Juergens to do more motion capture and acting. She's fantastic.

The staggering system, that i think was best on FF XIII, is really annoying and takes away some freedom during battles, since the so called strategy is basically doing what you have to do to stagger that monster and then beat him up. Then you have the fact that most fight are useless, since you don't get any xp, potions, etc... you only get monster items and sometimes attacks or spells.

The side quests are nice, and way more interesting than the main story, and that's kind of sad. When the optional content (here isn't much optional since it's where you'll get upgrades to your stats) is better than the main game you did something wrong.

Following FF13-2 and 13-1, Lightning Returns with a new battle system and an open world concept. It features a day/night cycle that dictate npc interactions and serves as a constant reminder of how much time has been spent. The story was mediocre and aimed too high. However the cinematic story rendering was fantastic and the voice acting was well done (English).
Small gripes I had with this game - Firstly I felt the day/night countdown timer really made players hardpressed to find efficient quest completion routes. If you are a relaxed and slow player like myself, you might not be able to progress far enough into the game to defeat the last boss. My second issue was with the characters and the actual story. I felt the storytelling in Snow's and Noel's storylines were languid. Their motivation in the game weren't realistic and didn't support their original actions against the protagonist. Lumina's behavour was also perplexing, her attitude flip-flopped and you couldn't tell when she was was lying or telling the truth. The story becomes even more unrelatable when you're forced to trust in something she says, given her history of messing with you.
Finally the overarching story aimed too high and simply fell short of my expectations. The final boss and the the wrap-up all felt a little too forced as Lightning, storywise, was shown to be more impressive in comparison to the final boss, a notion that wasn't conveyed properly through the cinematics.
However, despite these gripes, Lightning Returns does conclude the stories of FF13-1&2 in a meaningful satisfactory manner. 8/10. Pick this game up only if you've invested in the first two installments.

Basically a dating sim where instead of dating, you're trying to recruit people to join your club.  People compare it to Persona 3 because it has that "social link" aspect that Persona 3 has, but it's really different in tone.  It's very light-hearted-- not a bad thing, but when the game does try to take a slightly more serious tone, it's just awkward.  That didn't bother me too much, though.  My favorite thing about the game actually was how light-hearted it was, it's very cute.
The main problem is that it's just way too short and simplistic.  The point is to level up your relationship with different characters by talking to them.  You do this by selecting from a pool of conversation topics (like "art", "pets", "music", etc.)-- if the character likes the topic, your relationship improves.  After your relationship improves by a certain amount, it levels up and you get to see a cutscene.
However, there's not much to indicate what topics you should talk about and what you shouldn't.  You can probably figure out maybe one or two of the topics that are good for each person by paying attention to the story, but the rest just seem like random guessing.  It'd be much more enjoyable if there was a logical clue for each topic + character, but I guess they couldn't do that since there were so many topics.  They should've really just had less of them.
The other big issue is that it's just really lame when you try to talk to somebody about a topic, and all the dialogue says is "You talked about X topic with Y.  Y loves to talk about X!"  It would've been more interesting to read if there was actually conversation between the characters about each topic.  The dialogue that's in the game is actually not bad (I played the westernized version), there just needs to be more of it.  As of now, it's too robotic and boring.
If you're a big fan of dating sims and got the game in a bundle, maybe it's worth playing through once just because it's cute.  I wouldn't recommend buying it outside of a bundle, though.

Gravilon is simple, minimalist, and sadly flawed physics game.  The goal is simple: navigate a square from one door to another, using tiny cubes to defy gravity, become gravity-bound, and reach each door.  Even in the first few levels, however, this is somewhat difficult, and can even become repetitive.  Here's why:
1. Remember those tiny cubes I mentioned?  Note the word
, as these cubes can be extremely hard to grab because of their size.  I give the designers credit for planting more than enough cubes across the level (thus welcoming different strategies to reach the door), but it is very frustrating to go toward one and
miss it, over and over and over.  This usually results in death, and could easily be solved by increasing its size.  But the small size, along with being at the mercy of physics as you (most of the time) hurtle yourself towards them, makes switching your gravity much more difficult than it needs to be.
2. Level design.  It is inherently flawed.  Levels have holes that you can get easily stuck in (again, because of being at the mercy of physics), stopping your movement entirely,  and you must start the level over.  These "holes" are in plenty of places, and are simply frustrating; sometimes, you can even fall in badly-placed holes, and die.  You can also get stuck on high slopes, as they are impossible for a cube to travel up; the cube stops, and often you must restart the level.  It can't be attributed to trying to make the game "more difficult"; this is an inherent flaw of the game.
3. Lack of tutorial.  After Level 2 (could have been after Level 1, actually), the game seems to say, "Got the mechanics?  Good, now you can handle a really long level."  They don't really ease the player into it, but throw the player in the moment the mechanics become understandable.
I like the minimalistic look, colors, and gameplay of Gravilon.  But its bad level design, flawed gravity mechanic, and lack of proper tutorial makes it frustrating.  Even so, it has its charm, and I actually like controlling the cube when it comes down to it (though the slow-mo mechanic is fuctionally useless, but kinda neat).  Its sound design is simple, but also very well done.  I recommend it, but keep in mind its flaws.
(p.s.: According to the description, the "story unfolds in the background', and you will "learn about your role in the world" the more you play.  I have yet to see the story, but look forward to it.)
Nice concept

Imagine playing Super Monkey Ball with a cube while being bound and gagged.  That experience is similar to playing Gravilon.
It tries to do new things, but commits a lot of design flaws that contemporary platformers like Super Meat Boy streamlined.  Dying doesn't automatically restart the level, and the animation is a little long.  Inertia is difficult to judge, much less use with precision.  The arrow keys are not mapped for use.  And for God's sake, you're semi-randomly tumbling around as a square.
I did find its level design interesting, but basic movement was just too puzzling to stay fun.  Sometimes, you don't have to reinvent the wheel.

Past Level 1-2 or 1-3, gameplay becomes more frustrating than Super Meat Boy, and Super Meat Boy was more skill-based game (that is if you press exactly the same controls for the same time, the outcome will be identical); I made it up to 1-12 and at least 2 levels were 90% chance-based (the beginning of them to be exact). Using Space for slow-motion sometimes helps though.

Half-Life 2: Update is simply a better version of Half-Life 2 with minor graphical changes, bugfixes and community commentary.
If you have played HL2 only once or twice before, you probably won't notice any changes at all. There are some extra particle effects here and there, lighting and shadows are slightly improved. But it still looks like the game you remember.
The gameplay also flows better in certain areas, especially in the later chapters where all the sieges occur. The turret defenses in Nova Prospekt are now fixed and more challenging. Instead of fighting pathetically small waves with sometimes long pauses between them, you'll now have to deal with a constant stream of soldiers and manhacks. I've also noticed some other small changes like the unique female shotgun rebel in Anticitizen One, who apparently didn't want to join me this time. Another nice detail: The music fades out when you are about to reach the end of a map.
The community commentary provides some interesting tidbits about the development of the game and points out some details that you might have missed the first time through (includes Ross Scott, the voice of Freeman's Mind).
This update is also free, so if you are in the mood for a replay of Half-Life 2, there is no reason not to play this version.

In the begining there were a few guiding principles of game design: logical interfaces, fluent controls, challenging the player and simple multi-player.
Wanderlust: Rebirth however took the short bus to game design school and missed these important principles.
The interface and menu system are morbidly fascinating; even equipping a new item is a small adventure unto itself as you attempt to decipher the arcane menu system. The mouse isn't integrated into the menu system as we can't garuntee that people will have a mouse hooked up to their computer! Instead we'll navigate this menu with the W,A,S,D keys.
Want to use a new spell? You'll have to look it up in your spell book then go to a different window, click and drag invisible lines between runes then do a small pirouette and hope that the you were holding the correct mouse button. Oh didn't we mention? The mouse we're not sure you have is required for spell casting.
Talking with NPC's is initiated with one button (also doubling as your menu button) then progressed with another button.
All of these decisions and more will make you wonder "Why on earth would you design the interface this way?"...because of REASONS!
No matter how you choose to play this game the controls are utterly baffling. They mouse is required to cast spells but moving with it? We'll have none of that! Sure this is a top-down view and it would make more sense to simply click a location to move there but that's too mainstream for Wanderlust.
You're using a controller there? Let me eliminate half the keys and make sure that two of the remaining ones can't be mapped to trigggers, stick push, start or select. Also Let's navigate menu's with the D-pad and move with the Analogue stickbut never shalt their roles be reversible or interchangable!
That modifier key that you had to hold to access your second set of hotkeys on a full keyboard? You don't need it now that you've got less buttons to work with!
All of this could be forgiven however if the core game mechanics held up well. Which, of course, they don't. Playing co-op with a caster proved to be an exercise in futility as the poor melee class was unable to reach enemies with his stumpy little sword before they burst into flames. Inspite of this the combat is laughably easy, particularly with multiple players, as the enemy tends to sit in lovely little clumps and wait for you to attack them.
Progression is handled by way of wandering in whatever direction the game will allow and hoping that you end up on the right path. Luckily there is no open-world, multiple pathways or even competing goals to stop you walking down this long corridor of frankly baffling art choices (Why is the GRASS in this CAVE every colour EXCEPT green for instance).
However this is designed to be a multi-player game, I think, so what it really comes down to is how easily I can play with friends. Well I'm glad to report that private games seem to not work at all. Luckily there were only 3 public games open at the time we played so we added a fourth one. Trying to kick an unwanted player however was an exercise in futility. The menu sequence "Menu -> Players -> [Player Name]" presented me with only one option, Back. Again proving that no one actually bothered to try and design a functioning menu system.
Graphically Wanderlust: Rebirth  wouldn't fly as a DOS era game, let alone today. The graphics don't seem to be retro-styled as much as just poorly drawn, The world consistently shows you oddly coloured and out of place objects that you just can't interact with or even investigate. NPC's are drawn in a painful blend of cartoon and "high-school student who didn't take art class" realistic. The background frequently doesn't give you any clear indication of what is and isn't a walkable path and the colours are just garish.
In all Wanderlust: Rebirth is the kind of fascinatingly, humourously bad game that puts it on par with classic films like "The Room" and "Troll 2" or games like the original "Postal". Worth the admission price only on the suspicion that you'll get joy from mocking it.

Despite the horrible reviews, I actually like this game. The graphics are unique, the music is awesome, and it has a very old-school feel to it. Most RPGs these days are all fancy, and people are biased about games like these, but Wanderlust: Rebirth provides a very entertaining experience for me. 8/10, I recommend it.

Darksiders 2 is a semi open world action adventure RPG. It is a sequel to the first darksiders game which was heavily inspired by World of Warcraft lore and its characters(Lich King etc.), just with a different thematic twist to it. However, this game is nothing like the first one. Therefore I would like to outline the key differences between the both games as the community is split between them.
While the first game was aimed towards adults as a love letter for Zelda with its God of War combat. It offered a challenging puzzle design with linear world for story progression as opposed to DS2 simplified puzzles and open world. DS1 did not feature a vast amount of weapons to choose from the way DS2 allows you to. More or less you were given 4 weapons to use at all times, while DS2 has a bigger variety and freedom to choose.
DS2 is a much different game than the previous one. The developers have introduced diablo 3 random loot mechanics and stats into the game. It is also a modern succesor to Prince of Persia parkour traversal along the walls. With the last difference being leveling system.
#Game engine related#
* Graphics - in general they did improve overall texture quality of the original game. In general the game is very pleasing to the eye aesthetically due to its cartoony graphics. This way the game is more authentic when compared to other RPGs that are quite realistic and have a grim and dark color palete. Though I am not surprised about cartoony graphics, as the developers were a long time World of Warcraft players. :)
* 60 FPS - overall gameplay is a lot smoother, as higher framerate allows for quicker reactions/responses in regards to your enemies actions and moves. It is good to see framerate being adressed for PC platform as it is the standard of gaming.
#Game related#
* Open world - first and foremost, it is a good change of pace from the original darksiders. As it feels a lot more pleasant to play and explore.
* The Story - it does have way more depth to it, which is a lot more interesting to follow than darksiders.
* Voice acting - truly some of the voice actors did an outstanding job on this title. Kudos to them.
* Main Character - when you think about main character who's name is Death, you probably picture him as cold-hearted, emotionless, ruthless and what not. However, this is not the case with Death in Darksiders 2. Its surprising to see such a dark character as Death, be portrayed in both good and bad ways. One time you could find him soft, the very next time he would be the guy who never looks back at the explosions.
#Game engine related#
* Low FPS - Certain AMD users might experience major FPS dips in performance. My suggestion would be to try running the game on OpenGL instead of Vulkan. This is a 50/50 solution and depends on your hardware and system configuration. Some people reported it solving the problem.
* Cinematic tearing/crackling/cut off/freeze - Yet another major issue, when sound in animated cartoons begins to crackle. This might be due to my sound card, though I doubt it as I've tested the game on 2 different PC's. Do note that during cinematic's you might experience major FPS drops on AMD GPU's. If you skip the cutscenes, the FPS dips should disappear within a few seconds.
* Sound disappearing - Another issue is the music and combat sounds disappearing after 2 hours into the game.
: Restart your game when this happens, its game engine related.
* Random crashes - This is an issue exclusive to Deathinitive Edition. From time to time you might experience a crash. No potential fix exists.
* Damage number output - From my own impression, the game's engine is surely not coded according to huge crit numbers from your weapons or abilities. This will sometimes crash your game.
: Disable damage numbers from appearing on your screen in options.
* Glitches - This version has not only came out with its own portion of problems, but also managed to incorporate all of the original version's glitches. (Death being unable to move in particular zone's wall moss).
* Light shafts - Certain parts have a horrible or non existent light sources, making the area very dark. Not a major issue, just an oversight.
* DLC's - are far more accessible in this version, however Argul's tomb and the Abyssal Forge are utterly broken. If you experience non-stop crashing on Argu's Tomb, my advise would be to turn off damage numbers in your options. For Abyssal Forge, a ball could glitch out in the secret area. Preventing death from accessing the object to progress further. There is no fix for this issue, only suggestion would be is to keep trying to interact with the object from all the angles.
#Game related#
* Combat gameplay - This might be just me, but I find the combat in DS2 to be very plain and boring. Even playing on the hardest difficulty available, I've mostly spammed the same X button or Y for attacks. R1+X to recharge my wrath and two or more abilities keybinded to my controller. There are no notable combos that are worth combining for greater benefits, all I've noticed is that I had to dodge more on Deathinitive difficulty. Although the same can be said about DS1, where dash strike was king.
* Collectibles - this is my biggest gripe with the game. Collectibles in ds2 are simply not fun to collect as there are too many of them. Plus the whole backtracking of collectibles due to world related blockades being unacesible without tools like death grip, phasewalker and soul splitter that are only obtained by progressing story further. Clearcly the execution of collectibles could of been done better for this game. Well here is hoping for Darksiders 3 having a better system in place.
* No collectible tracker - previous game had an item that let you see all nearby chests. While this game has a similar feature as default for chests. It however does not feature a way to track the missing collectibles. You can end up backtracking hours upon hours to find a power stone or etc.
* Itemization & randomness - Quite frankly I should praise the game for having randomized loot. However I will not. You can end up playing for 30+ hours without having a possesed weapon (strongest weapons in game), or piece of gear that would improve your talent build.
* Legendary items - why are they even in the game? Some of them offer a special ability, however they only drop from story related boss or side quest mini-boss. Yey they are so underpowered in comparison to what you can make of your possesed weapon, that I view them as common trash item that you should just vendor.
* Dependance of crit chance and crit damage % - yes, if you plan on playing on the hardest difficulty, it comes to no surprise that such stats would become your best bet for cookie cutter build. If you have too little of either, some boss might be unkillable or would take insane amount of time to beat while staying alive. It saddens me of how important these two stat sticks are, as it makes it too difficult to finish the Crucible without them.
*Imbalances between the talent trees - for lower difficulties, melee build works just fine. However if you decide to play deathinitive difficulty. You will soon find that the best tree is the necromancer tree. It offers not only great flexibility of drawing aggro from enemies to your ghouls, but with perfect gear pieces and stats. You can pretty much 1-shot anything without being hit once. Even if you would stack 100% crit chance and damage on harbringer, necromancer is just leagues above it.

A unique take on the Myst-like puzzle-adventure-exploration genre, with a heavy dose of electronic music. The player lands on an alien world, populated only by a flora of luminescent polygons and strange contraptions. Tron comes to mind when thinking about what this whole world looks like, but there isn't a lot of well-known examples that rely heavily on neon lighting and simple geometric shapes. The trailer gives a good idea of what the game looks like.
Similar to Myst's level design, each contraption is located on a seperate section of the map (islands, in Myst's case). So in a sense, it's non-linear. The player gets to choose where he heads out first, and the order in which the contraptions are tackled don't really affect how the game turns out.
What's interesting about this game is that solving the puzzles creates music "tracks". One of the machines spits out a drum loop, another one some chords, and due to the nature of the puzzles, there are usually a few possible solutions for each one. At the end, you get to play around with your creation, remix it, put in some effects... it's actually a lot fun !
There's even a surprisingly apt step-sequencer located at the map's main hub (your spawning spot, basically). Each puzzle solved unlocks a module in the step-sequencer (bass-line, lead synths, pad sounds, etc.), so one you've finished the game, you can give it a go and try to create your very own electronic jingle. Don't get me wrong, it's not a professional studio tool, but it's still a very nice way to finish off the game.
Pros
Very cool visuals
A nice twist on the Myst-genre (if there is such a thing)
Nice soundtrack
Cool synthesizer and step-sequencer at the end that rewards you for your hard work playing the game :P
Cons
Puzzles are a little too simple, would have liked a larger arc that spans accross the entire map
Playthrough is a little short

I ADORED the New Order when I first played it and I really loved the Old Blood even though it felt a bit weaker storywise. Now here we are with Wolfenstein 2: The New Colossus. So I am going to do a good, the bad, and the meh theme of this review.
Good:
-Gunplay is hectic and fun as all get out
-Stealth is a bit more creative this time around
-Brutal melee takedowns
-Creative level design
-Gameplay and movement is really, REALLY fast
-Twists in the story are decent
-Develops each of the characters WAY more
-Come to care about Blazko much more as a character
-The main villain is (pardon my French) ♥♥♥♥ED up
-Added in side missions with the uber commanders
-Graphics are BEAUTIFUL
Bad:
-The health system in the first half of the game makes the game hard to deal with at times
-The new weapon wheel system for dual wield can be a pain to get used to
-The Nazi super soldiers are pushovers this time around unlike the New Order and the Old Blood
-The Panzerhund (big robo-nazi-dog) is WAY to easy when it is supposed to be a challenge
-Some very disapointing things happen in the story
-Game has had trouble loading at times where it would just crash
Meh:
-The Fergus/Wyatt timelines don't feel like they affect gameplay like in the New Order
-Sometimes the detection in stealth can be a little iffy
-Collectables feel a bit less abundant than the other two games
-The ending is to set up another sequal and/or DLC (but it works as a middle installment)
-HUGE exposition dump in the submarine through newspapers and readables
-The enigma codes are used to unlock side missions and farming them can be a chore
All in all, the game is good but is not as good as the first. The action is fun, the story is mostly investing, and the collectables are ok. I say pick it up only after you play the New Order and the Old Blood.

If, like me, you are too impatient to wait for American Truck Simulator to be finished then this game is the best when it comes to driving trucks across the United States from coast to coast.
It is by no means a perfect game but it is one of the best in the 18 Wheels of Steel series. The series includes seven games, but only three of them are on Steam. Most fans prefer the previous "
", but I think that's only because the modding community was more active for that one. Unless you absolutely need replicas of popular trucks then I think it's okay to do without them. Other than that, both games are nearly identical to each other. The only major difference is that American Long Haul has more cities to explore. Not only is the mainland United States traversible (not Hawaii and Alaska), but you can also visit parts of Canada and Mexico. I think that alone makes American Long Haul worth playing over any other trucking simulator.
Like I said, the map is huge; covers all of the country with most major cities being represented. The ony downside to this is that there is no route advisor. A world map and a mini-map on the screen are the only tools that can help you get get around. It's kind of annoying at first having to go back and forth to the map to familiarize yourself with the roads. But then I started liking the challenge because it reminds me of the old days before GPS was available and drivers actually had to use road maps.
One thing I really like about this game and which I think is sorely needed today is the CB radio feature. During your travels you can hear other drivers on the radio asking for weather and traffic reports and you can actually respond to them with a response menu by pressing the "v" key. It doesn't appear to do anything at first except give you a warm feeling inside, but apparently it helps your reputation grow and opens up more drivers for hire later on.
There's no option for using internet radio like you can in other SCS games, but you can import your own music. In that case you must convert your MP3s to the OGG format and there are websites you can use for doing that without downloading anything. I imported a few radio stations from GTA and they sound very nice and natural in this game.
My biggest gripe would have to be the steering. There is a mod somewhere that lets you steer with a mouse, but I prefer using a keyboard for steering. It works for me in other driving games, and until I actually buy a steering wheel that is what I'm going to use. Unfortunately, in this game, the wheel auto-centers itself too quickly so you're having to constantly jam on the "a" and "d" keys when making a sharp turn. It's not a total inconvenience, but it takes some time to get used to. If it bothers you that much then I would suggest a controller.
Hard to believe that SCS made this game so many years ago and there's actually more ground to cover than in any of their recent games. American Truck Simulator was released with only two states and Euro Truck Simulator 2 is being finished by modders. But they have stuck with the same formula over the years and, aside from graphics, their games have remained the same.
American Long Haul is not much different from ETS 2 or American Truck Simulator. You're still a truck driver managing your own company; you take jobs and deliver loads; you hire drivers to work for you; when you get tired you pull off the side of the road and sleep; when you need gas you go to the filling station; police give you a hard time; and when you get money you can buy more trucks. And really, what else do you need? Why not just skip the DLC fest and play this game instead?

While I haven't beaten the game entirely, I have played enough to have a decent feel for it all together. This game, with it's focus on exploration, sounds, and visuals, is a rather breath of fresh care amongst the army of first person puzzle games the indie market has churned out. There's something eerie, yet comfortable about traveling through the dark, neon worlds of Fract OSC. Solving puzzles at your lesure with only a few audiable cues leaves you with a challenge that's not overbearing, but at the same time still asking to be completed. I think the main reason why that is, is because nothing is telling you to complete it. I completed this game in about 11 hours.  I recommend buying the game on sale.
On it's own, the game is quite good, but it stands largely in the shadow of Wolfenstein:  The New Order.
Pros:
+ Fun gameplay.  Dual wielding is especially well-done.  I did a LOT more dual-wielding than in TNO or TOB.
+ Fun story.  I enjoyed seeing the further adventures of Blazkowicz.
+ Varied level design:  u-boat, the ruins of New York, mid-town Roswell (where I was strangely reminded of the funny 1950s sim early in Saints Row IV), the Roswell base, the sky warship, the ruins of New Orleans, Venus.
Overall, the game had enough fun to justify a sale price.
Cons:
- Not as much variety in levels as in TNO.  Also, some of the levels looked like they used virtually the same texture assets.
- Sometimes confusing layouts.  Sometimes I had no idea where I was supposed to go.  While it's nice that it wasn't simply a corridor-shooter, the arena-style layout, while fun to play in, could be confusing if the exit is just a tiny hole in the floor, etc.
- Minor glitches in levels, as both I and enemies sometimes got stuck in the floor.
- Stealth is next to impossible.  While it's more realistic for people to sound the alarm when they find a dead body, most of the levels have two officers, separated by a strong distance, and there are too many armored enemies who can't quietly be taken down.  This means that most levels quickly degenerate into a run to kill the officer before endless waves of enemies start spawning.
- It's quite a bit more difficult than TNO or TOB.  There are far more armored enemies, and many enemies with a "rush" ability that's almost a teleport.  Difficult is not necessarily a bad thing, but I felt the game was quite a bit different from TNO or TOB.
- Many of the characters were unlikable ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
- While I wasn't offended by anything in the game, I did find certain choices puzzling at best, or poorly thought-out.  For example, in a game that tries to pride itself on diversity and acceptance, I was surprised at them falling back on the tired stereotype of the Southern Racist for BJ's father.  Certainly it makes a kind of sense:  BJ has a southern accent, and it was important to the story in a way.  But it's still a stereotype.
I also felt that BJ's taunt "Come and get me you white♥♥♥♥♥Nazi fascist pigs" was out of place.  Why would HE say "white"?  I realize he's actually quoting another character, Super Spesh, but even his comment "Well, you ain't a white♥♥♥♥♥fascist Nazi pig, you either colored or you're a deviant."  is strange, as he's apparently white, although maybe he's a deviant.  The game never specified.  Wouldn't the comment have made more sense if Spesh were black?  Wouldn't it have made more sense if BJ evacs with Spesh, and Grace stays behind to fight off enemies?  Playing momentarily as Grace could have been fun.
- I felt a lot of things were unrealistic to the point of being ridiculous:  Venus isn't just hot.  It's ridiculously corrosive and has crushing pressure (about 90 atmospheres, or the depth of 1km down in the ocean, according to wikipedia).  Not to mention a few outrageous escapes by BJ, Da'at Yichud wizardry or not.
- I felt the final speech should have been 100% Grace.  I saw no reason for them to let Wyatt, who had been largely weak and silent through the whole game, make that speech.  There was nothing to suggest he had stepped up to replace Caroline.  Grace, on the other hand, was an established leader who had pulled the whole team for the whole game.  Sure, it was probably realistic considering the majority of people (white) of 1960s US (even in the real, historical timeline) probably would not have listened very seriously to a chain-smoking, foul-mouthed black woman (or, okay, let's be honest, any black person or pretty-much any woman).  But still, I felt a little let down that "apple pie" wyatt got the last word.
Conclusion:
So it's got some irks, but it's got more good than bad, and even the irks are pretty petty.  So, no, it's nowhere near as good as The New Order, but it's worth the half-price I paid.

I've never really played a "visual novel" style game like this before, but for my first time I really enjoyed the offerings. Cherry Tree High Comedy Club is a feel-good story about Mairu Hibisu, your typical 'I Wanna Be Hokage' type protagonist who dreams of becoming the next big international comedy senstation. Re-opening her school's defunct comedy club is the first stepping stone to her dreams; however, in order to form a club at CTH you need to have at least three members who want to sign up. And this is where the fun comes in!
CTHCC is essentially Persona Social Links The Game, but it puts its own cute little twist on things. You run around town discovering new students to
hopefully recruit, and as you get to know each of the students you meet, you'll begin to level up your social standing with them. Get to know them well enough, and they'll eventually
join up.
One feature I really liked was how by talking to each character on a daily basis, you start picking up clues as to which converational topics they may or may not like. Some are made obvious, and some not so much. You also do better talking to students by increasing what you know about each of the conversation subjects. There are loads of ways to do this, from heading to the cinema or reading magazines in the library, to spending time at the arcade or listening to that weekend's guest speaker at the art gallery. There's genuinely loads to do all over town and many day/time specific events, which I personally enjoyed as it encourages you to get to know and care about the places & people you're interacting with.
I also really loved the variety in each character's story, which starts to unfold as you level up your social standing with them. No story was similar and many were quite serious at times, but the sprites and character art remained adorable throughout, making it pretty hard not to find yourself endeared to everyone by the end. There's also a little re-playability value with the New Game+ mode (where you can start a new game with the stats you built up from the last one), but as CTHCC is just a quick bit of cutesy fun, you probably won't be picking it back up once you're done with it
. Would highly recommend this as a great introductory game to the visual novel genre.
Quick sidenote: if you're looking for pantsu, this really isn't it. There are absolutely zero romantic interactions with any character, which I was more than happy with but I understand would be a turn-off for some.

This is one of those games that comes once in a decade, and then you play it and you realize this level of quality will never be seen again. This is one of those games that I almost wish I paid more for. I waited for a sale, and bought it at $22.50, but that feels dirty have played and beat the game. Notes below.
- It's a short game.
At 7 hours of gameplay (depending on how you play), it's a relatively short game. That will turn a lot of people off, but I think that it's worth every hour and if it had a bunch of filler, it would suffer for it. This isn't the type of game that is meant to be long, and that's a good thing.
- It's an experience.
I didn't play this game, I experienced it. Some people think that the more influence the player has over the storyline the better, but I don't think that's true. I think a linear story has its own perks, and in this case, Hellblade hit on all of those perks and none of the downsides. I felt like this game shouldn't have had any other endings.
- Wow.
This game was so good that I'm afraid to play it again, because if I do, then I'll surely not like it as much. This game is meant to be experienced once. Again, that is a good thing. This is such a good game that I would pay for it at least five more times just so other people could experience it.
That's about it. I hope this review is enough to convince some more people to buy and play the game, which I recommend doing A.S.A.P.! This game will never happen again, so there's no point in not getting it.

In this game you can upgrade your abilities (skills) and completely customize what schema you want to use.  I found that replicating what FF13/13-2 did worked out best for my gaming experience.  You can use three different groups; one as commander (melee), two as ravager (mage), and the third schema as sentinel (tank)/saboteur (debuffs) hybrid.    Following are my final set-ups that beat 99% of the game on normal mode, with the exception of a few switches to battle a couple of the final bosses.
Weapon: Masamune
Shield: Blasphemy
Accessories: Tiger's Emblem, Dawn Gauntlets
Adornment: Killer Shades
Abilities: Shadownbind, Attack, Heavy Slash, Mediguard
Why use this Schema? Leveled up Heavy Slash turns Artemis's Pierce into a one turn killing machine.  Alternatively use Mediguard to life-up.
Weapon: Chaos's Revenge
Shield: Summoner's Shield
Accessories: Falcon Charm, Sniper's Gloves
Adornment: White Mage's Hat
Abilities: Elementa Lv. ★, Mediguard, Magnet, *
Why use this Schema? Elementa Lv. ★ will simply destroy 99% of the game. Alternatively use Mediguard to life-up.  Never found much else to use in the other two slots that was worth ATB Vs. Elementa, besides perhaps magnet and then something like fire or air depending on the enemy.
Weapon: Blazefire Saber
Shield: Noblesse Veronique
Accessories: Preta Hood, Runic Ring
Adornment: Black Mage's Hood
Abilities: Deshell, Deprotect, Imperil, Mediguard
Why use this Schema? Those accessories will make you immune to magic attacks.  This is my default garb, so when the battle starts you can cast Deshell and Imperil onto target then smash them with Elementa.  Cast Deprotect before hitting with Heavy Slash.  Mediguard for life-up.  Alternatively switch to Guard Glove & Ghostly Hood accessories when fighting heavy physical enemies.  Also switch Imperil with Poison for some bosses.
Since the PC version of Lightning returns gives you all DLC for free (turn on DLC in the options and buy them for free in the rewards screen) most of these garbs are already available to you... starting out I did use Cloud's SOLDIER 1st Class in place of the commander's Soldier of Peace garb (along with his weapon/shield.)  The Guardian Corps and Blazefire Saber are unlocked for free also if you have a FF13 save file.

Battleplan: American Civil War offers up a clean and simple, quick and easy series of strategy contest. While it's ostensibly based on the American Civil War, it could just as easily be World War I, The Thirty Years War or Alexander in Persia given the level of abstraction in the game play. This chess board quality is accentuated by the representation of units as slithering lines of tiny cubes and the minimalist landscapes. In fact as I played it, the one game that it reminded me of more than any other was the old Perfect General game from the halcyon days of DOS gaming, only quite a bit simpler. As a ten to twenty minute iOS game, it's cute and fun. As an American Civil War strategy game on the PC, it's not.
