Before i begin i know i have very little playtime on this game but thats only the steam version, i used to play it loads on console and on PC before it required steam.
This is perhaps the single best FPS game of all time, the only other contenders that i can think of are MW2, Black Ops 1, Battlefield 1 and maybe CS:GO.
For a start the campaign is glorious and this is coming from someone who mostly plays strategy games where the campaign can take hundreds of hours depending on the game and most have more than 1 campaign. A lot of FPS games have very poor campaigns and a lot of the newer ones dont have them at all. Look at battlefield 1: excellent multiplayer, great ranking up and unlocking system, mostly balanced, loads of people playing all the time but no one gives 2 steaming ♥♥♥♥s about the campaign.
So you find yourself wondering why this is and why COD4 is any better. Firstly you must remember that this game was made back in the days when multiplayer hadnt really taken off. Sure there were a few games like World of Warcraft but for the most part singleplayer was still the focus of everyones attention and so therefore it was the focus of Infinity Ward's attention. The game was designed so that you would actually get immersed into the campaign, you would actually find yourself caring about the various characters who were on your side and hating the enemy characters. The game actually goes to great lenghts to explain the confilct you find yourself thrown into which by the way is actually a pretty realistic and believable one. Its not like ghosts or infinite warfare where you just get a brief description of some dumbass war that no one can take seriously or even picture.
The campaign missions are a lot tougher than most other FPS games as well. Ever since MW2 there has been a tendency for games to have an increasing number of missions where all you have to do is hold down the trigger until all the enemies are dead. In COD4 the game does not hold your hand at all, you have to actually work to complete the missions, you can die quickly and you cant for the most part just run through the mision like an obstacle course holding down the fire button and expect to come out unscathed. The various difficulty settings add a lot more complexity to the game, they dont just make it so that you take less hits to die but the AI becomes less of a ret4rd and will actually take cover and your allies do a lot less of the work, not that they were overly active in the first place.
Multiplayer
Where do I start? This game has probably the best multiplayer mode of ANY game i have ever played with the exception of maybe MW2. I know a lot of people will disagree with me here but seriously, the game had just the right balance of simplicity and complicity. On the surface it just seems like another generic FPS game where you would maybe clock 20 hours on release week then get bored an go play something else but oh no. This game will draw you in one way or another, why do you think they made a remastered version?
At first you will think that the game is woefully unbalanced with guns like the M16, RPD, M40A3 and Desert Eagle ripping through anyone and anything but after a few hours and a few rank ups you will find class set ups and individual itmes that will counter them in the right situation. Most semi and fully automatic guns in this game are a two shot kill up close and then that 2 shot kill range will decrease over distance so if you come across someone with an M16 at close range then you will have the advantage with something like an MP5 or AK74U because those guns will 2 hit kill someone up close and can shoot faster and have better hip fire accuracy than the M16. However at any kind of range the M16 will have the advantage because its 2 hit kill range is much higher.
This is just one example of how complex the gunplay is in this game. Most newer games dont really seem to make any sense with gunplay, its just seems like whoever has the better connection or the faster fireing gun will win no matter what.
Adding attachments to your weapons will change how they play drastically. For instance the AK74U is and SMG. With no attachments it acts just like an SMG but when you add a silencer or a red dot sight its hipfire accuracy is widened to that of an assault rifle. The red dot sight will imprve your ADS accuracy and the silencer will keep you off the mini map and eliminate muzzle flash but both will severly render hipfire accuracy. Some attachments will also take away your ability to use a perk from the perk 1 catagory. For instance the grebade launcher on assault rifles or the grip on LMGs. This basically means that you cant have a very strong attachment and a very strong perk at the smae time as there are many perks from the first catagory that give you extra equipment such as C4s, RPGs and Clay Mores. Imagine having an underbarrel launcher and 2 RPGs at the same time, it would be like the grenade/launcher spam in MW2 (the game's main flaw)
That brings me onto perks and perk balance. In my opinion this game does it perfectly. In a lot of the later games you too often have the opportunity to bring a selection of perks that when used together are straight up OVERPOWERED AS FCVK. Take MW3 for example: you can use Scavenger, hardline and stalker all at the same time or you can use blind eye, assassin and sitrep all that the same time which makes you invisble on the mini map and to killstreaks, lets you see enemy equipment through walls and hear enemy footsteps really loud. So basiclly you are the terminator. In COD4 a lot of the more powerful perks are kept in the same catagory so you cant use them at the same time. Imagine if you could use Stopping power and juggernaught at the same time, you would never die and could kill everyone faster than everyone NOT using those two perks. Also, as i mentioned earlier, you cant bring certain attachments with certain perks, in the later games you have too much lee-way with custom class selection which is partly why those games suck in comparison to the older ones.
This game only has 3 killstreaks. This may seem a bit limited and boring but in reality it helps to balance the game. The killstreaks are in a 3-5-7 system. First you get the UAV at 3 kills, then the airstrike at 5 and the attack helicopter at 7. Now dont get me wrong, i like the fact that in MOST of the CoD games you can get very powerful killstreaks like the chopper gunner, reaper, predator missile and harriers etc etc but the fact that there are only 3 in COD4 makes it so that you dont have to be really good at the game to get them. On top of that they are not really that powerful, sure they can get a lot of kills but they wont wipe out the whole map. This makes the game a lot more about gunplay and knowing the maps, 2 things the game accomadates to perfectly.
This game has the best maps of any COD game hands down. The only maps that come close are the ones from MW2 and BO1 but only just. A lot of people go on and on about how the maps in those two games allow you to use killstreaks and the more powerful weapons to their full extent but COD4 isnt about that. The game focuses on gunplay and the maps are designed with that in mind. There are big maps and small maps but you can use literally any type of weapon with ease on any map with the exception of shipment, you cant use snipers on that map. Every map is hugely complex, there are long lains of sight for snipers and tight close quarters areas for SMg and shotgun users along with everything in between for assault rifle and LMG players. This means that there are no maps that favour one type of player over another. You can camp, rush or use any weapon you want and still do well and none of the maps make palying a certain way "safe" or OP.
On top of this there are not so many 3 lane maps that seem to be the meta in post MW3 games. In conclusion i rate this game 9/10. its brilliant on Pc with 24 player servers and NO hackers.

Title:No Man's Sky
Status: Released
Developer: Hello Games
Publisher: Hello Games
Genre: Action, Adventure
Release Date: August 12, 2016
No Man's Sky is an action-adventure survival game played from a first person perspective that allows players to engage in four principal activities: exploration, survival, combat, and trading. The player takes the role of a specimen of alien humanoid planetary explorer, known in game as the Traveller, in an uncharted universe. They start on a random planet near a crashed spacecraft at the edge of the galaxy, and are equipped with a survival exosuit with a jetpack, and a "multitool" that can be used to scan, mine and collect resources as well as to attack or defend oneself from creatures and hostile forces. The player can collect, repair, and refuel the craft, allowing them to travel about the planet, between other planets and space stations in the local solar system, engage in space combat with alien factions, or make hyperspace jumps to other star systems. While the game is open ended, the player may follow the guidance of the entity known as the Atlas to head towards the centre of the galaxy.
[+] Nice Visual Style
[+] Immeasurably Huge Universe
[+] No Shortage of Things to Explore and Upgrade
[-] Still Has Some Bugs/Issues
[-] Still lacking in Content that Other Titles Have
[-] Very, Very Repeatitive Gameplay
Points have to be given to Hello Games for sticking in there and continuing to develop the game. That is the sole reason for the positive recommendation. A lot of work has gone into this title, and despite being destroyed by the gaming community, Hello Games continues to plug away at this game.
No Man's Sky is an ambitious game with an unparalleled amount of content in terms of the amount of planets and systems there is to explore. Upon starting the game you are thrown onto a random planet which is fun to explore for a couple of hours before you want to escape into the vast universe that awaits. Planets in No Man's Sky differ in size, shape and colour and all feature 'different, randomly generated' animals and items to discover.
On each planet there are people to meet and places to discover. The people, places and 'the different, randomly generated' animals and items however are always very samey and you will find yourself saying 'I swear I've been here before' or 'I have found this before' despite this the game is still very fun for multiple hours and is still worth playing despite some bad reputation.
Upgrading and finding new ships helps a lot however in my opinion it does take a long time and some farming effort to upgrade and buy ships.
The main campaign in the game is quite short and isn't the most interesting however No Man's Sky in my opinion should be seen as more like Minecraft its an exploration game and if you don't expect the game to give you 500 hours of gameplay in one sitting then can still be a game worth buying and playing.
This game slowly evolves itself. Do not expect it to be the best game but definitely a game to chill and explore

As near as I can tell the game is easier the more divisions (players) you have... and when playing single player you can control up to 4 players.  So, set yourself up with multiple divisions, then really overpower around two lanes in the early game by using all the cards from all the players on just those two lanes.... and leave the other lanes utterly empty.  Your base will take damage in that first round, but you can take it.
Once you have built up your super lanes, then on round 2 you can overload your remaining lanes, and then you just sort of coast through the rest of the game.
It is annoying to play as 4 players solo, however, because each player has it's own hand of cards with interrupts and abilities.... and you will need to either remember what everyone has or cycle through them all every time something important happens.
So, then the game has a simple strategy that makes it not very hard.  You are repeating the same strategy solo.  The interface makes playing this strategy clunky.  You can't play with other people cause there aren't other people playing this.  And then you have to wonder, is this even fun?
Simple but grindy.... was not fun for me.  Sadly I can't recommend.

FRACT OSC is an exploration/puzzle/music buff’s wet dream. It’s hard to articulate how FRACT can make you feel. It’s most certainly an unconventional experience and arguably a one-of-a-kind art form so I’ll try to spoil as little as I can.
FRACT OSC is reminiscent of atmospheric adventure games like Myst. After a very brief introduction to the simple controls, you find yourself immersed in a dark and hauntingly silent underground world. You are given no clue as to where you are or what you’re supposed to do. This may sound overwhelming at first but once you take the first steps you realize there’s a fairly guided and intuitive way of navigating this world.
The Tron-esque and awe-inspiring open-world of FRACT is filled with massive structures, glowing towers and dormant devices you attempt to restore. But despite its mechanical and desolate appearance, the world feels oddly organic. As you approach its objects they react to your presence by expanding themselves and/or giving off delicate melodies.
The exquisite post-processing filters and radiant geometric structures produce a vivid yet dark ambiance. I found the landscape and architecture so jaw-dropping I couldn’t help but taking dozens of screenshots throughout my play-through.
The puzzles are especially appealing because as you interact with them you shape the soundscape around you, the puzzle structures emit different tunes which ultimately burst into a full-blown symphony and explosion of light upon completion. This incredibly cool way of rewarding players makes solving puzzles feel more like a creative process rather than a hassle.
Phosfiend’s work is so remarkable because they managed to create an incredibly rich and immersive experience in a completely unique setting without using a single word or any sort of narrative. It’s just fantastic to see everything gradually come together and rise to a beautiful climax.
On a side note, I recommend using a controller for a more cinematic experience that can only be achieved with subtle movements of the analog sticks; You can still use the mouse for faster puzzle solving.

Play time ~11 hours
Story: There is no real story, but that's the beauty of it. No violence, no worries - totally family friendly. Lots of needing to figure things out on your own and interpreting abstract events as they come.
Gameplay: The game has a very unique and well executed blend of music, puzzles, and exploration. This is not found in any other game I have played. The environment oozes with music and custom tones that are affected by what you do to the environment. The game is not super easy, which is very good, because I like a challenge. The only thing I would have liked to see more is a bit more variance in the puzzle mechanics - many of them are represented as synth / equalizer adjustments to get the right combination. But overall, the game did still boast a good variety of puzzles.
Visuals and Audio: Superb. Game is beautiful in both regards. ESPECIALLY audio (of course!). There are loads of environments and the music and abstract visuals actually blend together in harmony - very nice!
Note: my review doesn't even consider the aspects of the custom synthesizer aspect of the game in which you can compose your own works of music. If you add that, and you enjoy that, this makes the game all the more enjoyable.

I would also suggest you separate your inbound security lines with your outbound passengers.  This will help the flow of passengers coming into the departure hall.
Overall I am truly impressed by the game and hope to see the developer continue patching and making improvements.  I am willing to help if they are interested – so reach out if you are!  I will reserve a full review until a little later once several patches are added.
One note:  Please add a way to adjust the map with buttons on the mouse as well as edge scrolling (which seems to not work as fluid as it could).

Summary: Although NMS peaked my interest initially, I didn’t buy at release because of all the bad press. Reading user reviews after the 1.3x update, however, changed my mind and I purchased the game during the last Steam sale. I’m about 70 hours into the game and still having fun. Unlike Elite Dangerous that has zero story or context, there is an interesting story line to follow if you want. The story is nicely blended with a broad tutorial that teaches you pretty much all you need to know to be a competent explorer. If you like space survival games (e.g., Empyrion) you’ll enjoy NMS at least for a while. With galactic exploration, space combat, base building, farming, Exocraft vehicles and Freighter Capital ships to acquire, there’s quite a bit to do. If you follow the story line to completion (with all the side stuff), you’re probably looking at a 100 hours of gameplay at least (so worth buying on sale for $29).
Other Thoughts:
- This game is based on gathering resources. You gather resources to build things so you can gather more resources and/or make money. It can be tedious and exhausting, and will likely drive me to get bored and quit, but I’m not quite there yet. So if you don’t mind gathering resources or farming A LOT, then you should find the game enjoyable.
- Procedural generation is an interesting concept, but it’s clear it needs some refinement in terms a variability. After about the 10th planet you explore, they all start looking the same with the same terrain features, flora and fauna, and loot, although there are occasional surprises (it’s always fun to find a crashed starship that’s better than the one you own). I find that when I enter a new system, I’ll scan the planets for resources or habitability, and if don’t find anything, then there’s no point landing on the planets and it’s off to the next system.
- The color palette is something you either love or hate. Call me boring, but I like blue skies, green trees, and aqua marine oceans. Orange oceans and hot pink skies I find garish, jarring, and too cartoonish. That’s said, I have come across some stunning landscapes and star-scapes on occasion, but they’re usually few and far between. I find that I’m spending a lot of time trying to find a “lush” earthlike planet that’s not too bizarre (color-wise), but those are difficult to find away from the galactic core. Perhaps as I move closer to the core I will find a better place to call home.

So now that I have dumped about 60 hours into this game I feel that I can accurately write a review on it. The game is good, and worth buying if the following apply:
The game should be on sale. I bought the game when it was drastically reduced, and I can say it is not worth a full price tag by any means. I think I paid $20 for it and that was well worth it at that price point.
You enjoy exploration/survival games. I could play Minecraft for hours. Just zoning out and building bases or exploring dark caves really appeals to me. Much in the same way people like to relax and play Truck Simulator, I can sit down and zone out to the peaceful music of No Man's Sky while exploring planets and gathering materials. If you are looking for a deep and compelling story this is not really the game for you.
You are not looking for an engaging multiplayer experience. This game is not built for multiplayer, despite what people may have thought or may have been advertised. From what I know it is possible to go to other players bases, but I have not done so. In my travels I have never encountered another player and I think that is by game design but I could be wrong.
As long as those three guidlines are in effect I would advise you to grab the game. It is relaxing and fun for me to zip around the universe and discover new planets. After the first 20 hours or so you will begin to see that most of the planets are quite similar to ones previously visited with minor differences, however every once in a while I will make a discovery that makes me want to keep going. Base building is a cool feature for you to store some of your crafting materials and gives you a place of your own in the universe. The developers put out some pretty frequent updates that seem to consistently make improvements to the game which is a good sign to me. I have noticed that the game has occassional glitches that sometimes can be a major problem, but it has not hindered me enough to stop playing. This seems rather reccurent with PC games, so I just try to overlook anything not game breaking.
Moral of the story: for the great deal I got on the game and the amount of exploration and resource gathering available I am happy with my purchase.

Upon finishing the game, I realized how much I got to know about a person I never even met in a matter of 3 hours. The main character Johnny starts off as a completely mysterious person, with little to no information about him, or his life. The thing I really loved about this game is how those mysteries are revealed through out the memory jumps. You get to listen in on two characters having a conversation, and you can only speculate what's actually happening, or why it's happening at all.
A lot of the magic also comes from the soundtrack, which manages to convey the current situation and mood in an amazing manner. As I said in the header of this review, this game made me cry in the very first 20-30 minutes, and that's when Johnny plays a song he wrote for his wife. I knew that I could leave the room at any time, but I just didn't want to. I didn't want to make the melody stop.
Through out the entire game, we get to hear quirky remarks from the main characters, Neil & Eva, who are an amazing comedy duo, and made the game a lot more fun thanks to the jokes they crack all the time. I'm really glad that the creators made sure that there weren't any jokes during the really sad bits, and managed to conserve the atmosphere.
The story is really amazing. I loved every second of it, and wished that it could go on forever.
This game has been an absolutely eye opening experience for anybody with some goal in their life that they want to fulfill.

Sure, it's an improvement but that's like saying $9,834,246.56 is more money than $9,834,246.55. But now I'm at a crossroads. Is it more douchy to give a big fat thumbs down to a free, community made mod, or is it worse to give a thumbs up to something that doesn't deserve it? Well, since the differences this mod makes are trivial, I will grade it over something trivial; the name. Because they named it "Half-Life 2: Update", now Valve will have to spend more time thinking up an appropriate Half-Life 2 subtitle when/if they finally get around to making an HD update.

Wolfenstein 2: The New Colossus is a disappointment. It's not a bad game, but it's certainly nowhere near as good as the the New Order.
The good bits are mired by dreary environments, confusing level design, a terrible map system that only shows the current floor you are on (can't scroll up or down levels, so if your on a staircase, the map will only show that tiny section and nothing else), and many overlong cutscenes, some of them unskippable.
I watched all the cutscenes in my first play through, but upon starting a second game I discovered I can only skip a couple of the first bits of the intro cutscene but I was forced to sit through all of the first person parts which included long, unneeded flashbacks to the player character's backstory.  The intro is very long before you actually get to play the actual game.
Stealth is very hard and not well implemented, and because the developers saw fit to limit the standard health to half of normal (you can overcharge it with pick ups but it slowly drains down to 50) for the first half of the game, the player is very fragile.  Coupled with the bad damage indication, the player can find themselves killed by unseen enemies within seconds if you try to go in gun-ho, or as often the case, are discovered while trying to sneak.
There are a few moments in the game where you are forced into combat arenas - one particular early moment put me immediately into combat in a small, two leveled arena with enemies coming from multiple directions.  Health, armour and ammo is scattered liberally around but trying to pick them up while being shot at from multiple directions (with very little idea where those shots are coming from) and at 50 health in an unfamiliar map layout saw me killed about 20 odd times before got through that section.  And all of this was on medium difficulty in the first couple hours of the game.
There are a few good bits - when the game goes into the more bonkers aspects of Wolfenstein the game gets a lot more fun. There's a story twist at the half way point I didn't see coming.  Gunplay is quite solid but the weapon selection is small and not particularly interesting.  There are a few good and well written characters, particularly Sigrun, and the main villain is very....intense and villainry for the beginning and middle parts of the game (and then promptly disappears until the very end of the game in a short sequence that requires no effort whatso ever).
In summary I can only recommend this game if your a fan of the Wolfenstein series and this game is on at a reduced price. Otherwise I say not to bother with it. Get/play New Order instead.

If you are just here for the story, you will not be disappointed. Wolfenstein II successfully grapples with a lot of powerful themes at once, and it will probably be in my thoughts for weeks or months after I play it.
A lot can be said about the story by people who are much better than myself at these things so I would like to focus on the gameplay aspects for this review. If you are expected DOOM 2016 level combat, you will not find it here. There is something to the combat, but it requires a very particular playstyle. For maximum enjoyment, I have some advice for players who are struggling to enjoy the combat sections of the game:
1. Run and gun. This is not a cover shooter, and if you play it like a cover shooter, you will be frustrated. Enemies have difficulty hitting you when you are moving, so use that to your advantage. Dual-wield the assault rifles, try not to get surrounded, and move.
2. Nose to the ground. The levels are filled to the brim with health and armor. Unfortunately, the radius in which those are automatically collected is small, so you generally have to be on constant lookout for those boosts to top you up. Once you get the feel for things, you will find that health and armor generally show up in the same places, sometimes right next to one another. Remember those places for later in case you need to run back and top yourself up.
3. Nazis are dumb. You knew this already. However, in the game, you can generally get away with shooting a few Nazis in the head (with a supressed weapon) while stealthing around before they will notice you. They will also not notice you if you use alt-lean to peek around corners and pop them in the head.
4. Arms are weak points. Most of the robotic enemies have specific explosive weakpoints in the game, but I found those were pretty hard to see or get to. If you blow up both of their arms, they'll die as soon as the second arm goes. It doesn't take a lot to take them out either, and I had an easier time taking them out just with the assault rifles than any other weapon in the game.
5. The radial menu sucks. Don't use it. The number keys work just as well and you will rarely need to switch between weapons because the assault rifle is the best weapon in the game, if you haven't got that impression from me already.
Have fun killing those nazis.

I really enjoyed this title. It was originally a board game, and is about defending your base from attacks by alien creatures. Each game consists of nine waves, in which you can drop up to four soldiers to reveal and fight four aliens, one by one. Hopefully, you've chosen the right soldiers to defend your base, and equipped them in a way that plays to their strengths. Additionally, there are "instant" cards that can be played in the middle of the wave to bolster your soldiers in the heat of the moment. The game can be played cooperatively with one of many factions, each of which specialize in a particular field. The weapons division can gets it's hands on weapons cheaper and eventually deal more damage, where the armor division can grab armor cheaper and eventually get more defense out of it. I enjoyed trying to win with each faction, and feel that both the NorTec Elite and Hive expansions added a great amount of replayability to the game.  The tense feeling as each card is flipped is very memorable, and good planning is usually rewarded.

Creatives that have difficulty finding an appropriate and productive workspace take note: what if you could make your work from the inside out, literally? Another title for which genre conventions limit descriptive accuracy, Fract OSC is better explained in experiential terms: its somewhat like music composing INSIDE a synthesizer, a DAW that you occupy and traverse. Beginning with a locked studio suite of instruments, you explore this living-synth-world, solving puzzles involving step sequencers and percussion, progressively unlocking elements of that studio, and bobbing your head to the wonderful and reactive soundtrack along the way. Its not only atmospherically engrossing and auditorally engaging, but also makes me hope that someday the creative process of many mediums will be just like this, perhaps further facilitated by VR (I haven't gotten an Oculus Rift yet, but the game does offer VR support as well).

Easily the most creative game I've played since Antichamber. The art style and aesthetic look amazing, you learn exactly what to do without ever being guided, the soundtrack is perfect, and the synthesizers/sequencer are a blast to use.

This is a game that provides more of an experience than a challenge. That isn't to say this game isn't challenging, as some of the puzzles, especially the later ones, will likely have you scratching your head and pushing you closer and closer to the temptation of steam guides. Rather, the puzzles of the game are overshadowed by the overall atmosphere. This is a game that really does deserve to be played with the lights down, the volume up and no distractions. The world and the art style is simply beautiful which, coupled with the superb analog-sounding synths provides both a relaxing and an empowering experience. Each puzzle solved reastores areas of the world back to life, turning a cold, lifeless wasteland into a thing of beauty.
How much you enjoy FRACT OSC will depend on how much you enjoy synthesizers. If you're the kind of person who can tell your VCO from your VCA, use an envelope for things besides posting letters and consider a delay to be a desirable thing, the puzzles will only be part of the attraction. FRACT also provides a feature-rich studio that produces some amazingly warm sounds which will keep you busy for some time. And if you're not a synthesizer fan? Well, perhaps the easy to use interface (which can be toggled between basic, abstract controls to something that wouldn't look out of place in the Death Star's control room) will convince you otherwise.
All in all, it's a great game with a beautiful art style, brilliant sound and a fantastic atmosphere. If you have any interest in synthesizers or music in general, pick this game up.

Of the 3 remasters I've played (Darksiders Warmastered, Skyrim Special Edition, and this), this is the clumsiest remaster I've played. Compared to the normal version, it's very buggy and is prone to crashes from several things, though I do know a few fixes for said crashes. As well, the game stutters like there's no tomorrow until you switch a few things in your graphics driver's control panel.
As a remaster: I give it a 4/10. Before going out of business, the devs failed to manage to fix most of the game's issues, leaving it worse than the original game.
Despite these issues, I still very much enjoyed the game. The game's mechanics still work around the same as the normal game, and don't seemed to be tied to any new bugs associated with them.
The only major bugs I've had are as follows:
1. The audio seems to become more and more broken the more you play, until it eventually gives up. This is fixed by restarting the game.
2. Crashes later in the game that seem to be tied to damage numbers. While I had damage numbers on, the uppercut attack with armblade weapons would out-right crash the game. The fix, of course, is just to turn damage numbers off.
3. Alt-tabbing crashes the game half of the time. This may be fixed by going windowed (possibly), but I hate having a border on my window.
4. Stuttering. As I said earlier: You have to tweak your drivers settings for the game. It mainly comes down to turning on adaptive V-sync for Nvidia users (not sure about AMD).
Other than those issues, the game itself plays highly well. The devs really emphasized the learning of various mechanics in the platforming/puzzles, without invading the integrity of the combat. The story is alright by me, and the addition of a few weapon types for your offhand and the possessed weapons system (comparing to the 1st Darksiders) really adds flavor to the combat.
As a whole: I give the game a solid 8/10. Once you fix the stuttering, you'll find an interesting enough and engaging experience that'll both fill your adrenaline with its combat, and challenge your mental abilities with its platforming/puzzle segments. It may even be worth 2 playthroughs for you, as you can choose whether to be a menacing reaper, or a master of the Necrotic arts.

Gravilon is a minimalistic, jumpless 2D platformer that has you tumbling a square end over end instead of smooth running and jumping. Its a game that requires patience from the player and it does everything it can in its minimalist art style to keep you calm and relaxed. You won't hear music so much as what sounds like rolling dice as your square tumbles end over end. Every level consists of black lines as platforms with a grey background. You'll see the previous level in the foreground and the next level in the background. Getting to the exit will fly you into the background and it makes for a beautiful touch.
The object of each level is simply to make it to the end door a large blue square. The controls are simple,A and D keys will to shift your weight to tumble and the space bar will make slow motion that will give you greater control when you're in the air. Otherwise your momentum can make you easily miss something. Using slow motion drains the meter and it will build back up over time.
Since there's no jump, its all about your momentum, the tumble will make you jump depending on the angle your square hits a surface. To make things interesting there are white anti-gravity cubes that will shift your square's gravity from the bottom to the top of the screen and vise versa. These cubes regenerate in a few seconds.
The game benefits the tumbling with platforms that are on angles to tumble or slide down. Trying to move up any incline is a difficult feat that you'll need to shift your square's weight backward before you can shift it forward to have enough momentum to climb. Any over calculation can send you tumbling back down again.
If you ever get stuck, just hit R to respawn. There are no lives. It doesn't reset the level, but it does put you back at the start. Any time you die from a death pit a hazard or a respawn, it leaves a dead black square. This makes the level feel alive seeing all your dead squares there. You can move them and bump into them. If you hit them hard enough they'll disintegrate.
With the level design, you can make your own way. There's not one clear path to take. Its all about how you take the path you're on. Take one path too slow and you might be stuck. Take another path too fast you might not have the precision it takes to get through it. Levels get more difficult with the inclusion of yellow lines as hazards. One touch and you're dead just like a death pit.
From the moment you start, you're in the game, with a quick hub world that lets you tumble to a doorway with continue, act 1, act 2, act 3, bonus and even quit. There's no main menu and it goes a long way to making you feel in game and keeping you there.
If you're looking for a hand holding experience you won't find it here. Gravilon is a frustrating game almost from the start. The tumbling mechanic ensures that no attempt is exactly the same and a lot of the time it feels like luck rather than skill. Even when you spawn, its at a different angle, causing you to bounce from there. Your tumble could be off and it might send you somewhere completely different. That's why you need to use the slow motion a lot and even then I felt like I would die again and again. There are no checkpoints, every death restarts the level over again. It wouldn't be an issue if you weren't a tumbling square.
To make matters worse your view can get obscured by the previous level. As much as I love the artistic effect it does get annoying. There might not be hand holding, but I don't expect them to cover my eyes either. The game will even turn my level transparent to focus in on the background.
Since you can take your own path, you are allowed to keep trying to make the wrong path work. If you can only get the momentum to tumble up high enough you can make this path work! 15 minutes later, its time for a new path. Yet going back to the game, then you can get the momentum to make it work. Again, it feels like luck and not skill. Doing the same thing 100 times might yield the result you want.
The beginning of the seventh level has a dead square and with that dead square you can make a path to an anti-gravity cube. Hitting that dead square knocks it out of place, preventing you from using it again on your next attempt, unless you set up your living square then kill it with a retry to have it in place as a dead square. That was my path for a while.
The other path I could take is gaining enough momentum, but not too much because you'll knock yourself on a platform or overshoot the needle thin platforms you'll need to slow motion jump to. Then hope you have enough momentum to carry you into the anti-gravity cube or else you'll just have to try again and again. That's just how Gravilon is. You need patience. Your skill will not get you there.
Each level can take under two minutes from start to finish and I'm telling you that to inform you that I'm three hours into the game and I have yet to complete the seventh level. I've never made it through the first act. Perhaps that truth is a testament to how bad I am at this game, or its a testament of a game that's a lot like a roll of the dice.
Sometimes you get lucky, sometimes you don't. Its all in the unique tumble mechanic. While it is an unique game with a great art style, its just not fun. Its painful and frustrating, but there are people out there that will love the steep difficulty and soothing atmosphere.
The game wouldn't as frustrating if it weren't for the tumbling or even if it gave you a reward; some incentive to continue playing and push through the frustration. Your reward is another level. A game should be fun enough to be its own reward. Maybe there are fun, rewarding bonuses, but three hours and seven levels in, I wasn't able to unlock anything from the bonus content.
While I can recommend it for its art style and low price tag, I just can't recommend it as a fun game. Perhaps I found it more frustrating than relaxing. Even if I didn't care for the game, I'd like to thank Fan Wu for giving me the game.

I haven't played much of gravilon yet, but my first impression is that it's beautiful, clever and fun.  The whole game is minimalistic, the visuals, the audio, the controls, the level design.  But from only a handful of game mechanics there is a lot of depth.  The physics-based platforming is very difficult, but it feels so good that you just want to keep doing it and getting better.
This game does not hold your hand.  Some of the paths you need to take are a bit hidden at first, but the level design is clever enough that when you do find the path, you know that you've found it.  It doesn't coddle you, but it sets you up well to figure it out yourself.
So far I'm only up to level 1.7, which has a puzzle right at the start.  Up till that point there was a feature of the game that I'd noticed, but I didn't really understand why it was there.  Then I realised that this little feature I'd been ignoring was the solution to the puzzle, and I was blown away.  gravilon had been teaching me this mechanic for the last few levels and I had hardly noticed it, then it said, "Nope, you're not going any further till you pay attention and notice what's going on here."  I love it when a game teaches me a new way of thinking, and gravilon has done that in the first Act.  I'm seriously looking forward to seeing what else is in store.
I only have a few little complaints, mainly that there is no built in gamepad support.  I can map keys with Xpadder or joy2key, but it would be nice not to have to do this.  If you die you don't automatically restart, you have to hit R, but I can see why that decision was made.  The game isn't hurrying you along to keep trying, it's letting you set the pace.  It's good to be aware of though.  Finally, there is a time slowing mechanic, which I think is just to help with tricky spots, but I don't use it.  It's not really taught to the player, and I haven't needed it so far.  It's entirely possible it will become more relevant later.

Most of my favourite games — the ones I go back to regularly to play time and time again — were released on the Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES). I have favourites on every platform, to be sure, but I have the most on the SNES, and of all of them, if I had to choose just one that I enjoyed more than any other, I'd have to go with Secret of Mana.
Not because it was the best action-RPG title on the console (I'd award that badge to The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past), or because it had the best characters or storytelling (Chrono Trigger, anyone?) — no, it was my favourite, and remains that way to this very day, because of the cooperative multiplayer.
In Secret of Mana, you could play through almost the entire game with a friend, each taking control of one of three characters while the game played the third. It sounds simple enough, I'm sure, but by adding multiplayer to a genre that typically never offered it, Squaresoft had created an experience like no other.
I mention this now because recently I discovered Wanderlust: Rebirth on Steam and for the first time in almost 20 years I feel like I'm playing a SNES RPG with my friends again, only this time it's even better.
LEARNIN' THE ROPES
I was a little afraid of Wanderlust: Rebirth at first; as is typical for me with Steam, I rushed in with no idea what I was going to play. After creating my character and completing the tutorial — which among the basics introduced character point (CP) allocation and crafting — I was thrust into battle almost immediately and lost amidst a sea of colours, characters and combat.
Quickly, I realised that I was one member of a party of 4, the others controlled by the game and each with different abilities. I was an Alchemist who played the role of a rogue, dashing and flinging explosive potions at everything within reach; the others, a Cleric, Fighter and Elementalist all contributing to the carnage in ways I could scarcely comprehend.
Following a series of short battles,  a small mini-boss encounter and some oddly charming dialogue we appeared to have won the tournament, and set out on an adventure to claim our prize.
Everything happened so quickly that I didn't get a chance to process what I'd learned. The end of the chapter brought with it a score screen detailing the awards I'd earned and % completion, which determined the CP I'd earned, and thereby, how much I could enhance my character.
MAKE IT MULTIPLAYER
That's when I was invited to play with a group of friends, and from the very moment we began our quest anew — this time, communicating on Skype and listening to them prepare character 'builds' that would benefit the group/scenario  — I began to fall in love.
Having already completed the game multiple times, some of my companions already had access to every mission on multiple difficulties, alongside an awesome selection of spells, abilities and equipment; though, to keep things fresh they started with new characters and we played from the beginning. It didn't take me long to nail down the basics properly and get a handle on my Alchemist's abilities, and by playing with others I began to see how the other classes worked.
The Cleric wasn't just a healer, but a battle-hardened veteran capable of blocking all incoming damage and increasing our party abilities. The Fighter, an♥♥♥♥♥♥kicker without limits, customisable for every situation. And the Elementalist, another beast entirely, complete with its own spell system and mechanics. On top of it all, each of us had access to a shared 'Soul Charge Pool' that filled as we succeeded in battle. Each of us had a single ability we could use to drain this pool, which effected the entire group, and by utilising these abilities sparingly, saving them until at precisely the right moment, we could topple harder opponents without issue.
The depth was immediately visible, and it only continued to develop as we plunged deeper into a world of ever-growing chaos.
CRAWLIN'
Skip forward half-a-day and I'm a veritable pro, strategically dropping blast potions on large groups of enemies immediately after hitting stealth to maximise my combos and earn more awards. We'd finished a complete play-through and were working our way through Hard Mode attempting to 100% each chapter for more CP.
I'd crafted a blue weapon, too, and using gems switched out some of the lesser enhancements for a massive damage boost. This happened after we'd unlocked a new game mode, The Crawl. Essentially a limitless, randomised dungeon grind, The Crawl served as an easy way to start farming crafting materials alongside honing our group strategy against some crazy enemy and boss combinations.
Better yet, after 5 successful 'crawls', we entered a treasure room. On the left, a blue chest with basic rewards and an instant exit. On the right, a locked orange chest, presumably filled with rarer recipes and equipment. In the centre, a slot machine. Playing the slots is the only way to open the orange chest and win better rewards; however, doing so loads up another, harder crawl, with the chance of boss encounters. Play and win, but risk failure and complete loss of all loot? Or leave now and live, precious crafting materials in tow? This is the heart of The Crawl, and with every successful run from there, you're given the same difficult choice. Ingenious, and incredible. Especially so, on Epic Difficulty.
GET ON MY LEVEL
Eventually, we arrived at Epic Difficulty in the Story Mode and discovered an entire new game to enjoy. New limitations and monster attacks deeply altered our combat strategy, and with death now ending the chapter entirely, the level of difficulty had spiked beyond reason.
It was glorious. Orange-Level gear recipes had now begun to appear, too, with special items required from special hidden boss encounters to craft, and having already completed most chapters 100% on Normal and Hard, we had plenty of CP to spare and an incredible array of new abilities to work with. Almost as though we were playing an MMORPG, end-game had appeared and with it a new host of gameplay to enjoy.
Eventually, we called it a night and continued on the following day. Currently, I'm working on getting every achievement on Steam — a challenge reserved for the greats, it would seem — and I'm getting closer with each passing day. In closing, I've shared with you here my experience with Wanderlust: Rebirth, and why I have enjoyed playing it. To reiterate my opening passage, it takes me back to an era of my life that I've been trying to get back to for years, and does it with grace, style and unique flavour.
Built entirely within GameMaker by two guys, there are some expected issues. Controlling your character is clunky at times, but becomes significantly easier with practice, the lack of multiplayer connection directly through Steam, instead requiring basic port-forwarding is frustrating at times, and there's a learning curve (specifically if playing solo) that's tough to get your head around. Though, rest assured, for fans of the SNES RPG era — specifically fans of cooperative multiplayer and, to a lesser degree, PvP — this is a title that you'll be happy to have gracing the shelves of your virtual collection.

This is the Half Life 2 version of a wine-tasting party. People are going to stand around talking intensely about how they can really notice the woodsy undertones mixed with a slight chocolate after-taste. You're going to sit there sipping wine... and all you taste is wine ... and then another wine ... and another ... and they all taste the same. But, wait.. this one is slightly sweeter then that one, so that's something. And then the wine snobs look at you, roll their eyes after you make that observation, and whisper to their friends that they can't believe you can't tell the differences.
Another example is when my girlfriend's paternal twin nephews come over. I can't tell the apart, but she says "that one has XYZ that is different, it's so easy to tell them apart." It's easy if you've spent a lot of time with them. Not so easy if you haven't.
Essentially that is what this mod makes you feel like ... a clueless idiot that's staring at things intently trying to detect changes. Instead of going "omg, look what they did there! Holy cow, fantastic!" you're going to be going "This looks exactly the same except... is the texture different? No, there's a shader applied to this now? I ...♥♥♥♥♥♥I can't tell."
The things that stood out for me were translucency. The options menu is now slightly translucent. Breen's intro display is slightly transparent ... certain things do stick out. But, they leave you with a "oh... ok, I see what they did there, but ... uh, what about the rest?"
I played this using a GTX760 with all settings maxed, bloom turned on, etc, etc. Unless there's some magical .ini files I need to tweak without realizing it, I just don't see enough visual change and impact from this mod to warrant installing it.
I know they put a lot of time into it, but spending years polishing a piece of silver to get a tiny bit more shine on it is going to be lost on the lay person.
I sound like a complete **** ripping on them like this, but I actually totally understand. I'm in love with the game FUEL to the extent that I went into its HLSL shader files, did a huge overhaul, added in extra effects and polished others. I've spent months fiddling around with things to get them "just right". End result? You can barely notice any changes I've made. So, I never bothered uploading it to the community.
It's "death of a thousand cuts" and while the modders know every single one of the 1000 cuts they made, the lay person only notices like 5 or 6 which means the work spent on the other 900+ is in essence wasted effort to the lay man. But, hey, if it makes you feel better doing it, then more power to you. (That's why I did the FUEL shaders... I liked tweaking the code, even if the end result was minimal at best.)
I think the main reason it's so hard to tell any difference is:
a) the world vertices/polygons are still just as blocky as they were back then, but they did this to keep the original look/feel (IE: no higher-polygon models, no added poly's to environment to smooth out corners and such)
b) the textures look the exact same... I didn't notice any new whiz-bang things like bump-mapping or such to make the environment look more real instead of a flat hollywood movie set. Maybe a texture or two was a tad sharper?
I just don't know ... and that's what's irking me. I don't know really what changed, I don't know what I'm missing, I don't know where to look to go "ah, yeah, see what you did there ... good job, mate!" This mod makes me feel like I'm standing next to someone that sees something special, is trying to point it out to me, and it's flying right over my head making me feel like a clueless idiot.
But I digress...
On the plus-side, the commentary part is really, really good. The player insights are actually really entertaining, and often easy to empathize with (since you may have had a similar experience or feeling playing the game).
As a technical accomplishment, though, since that's what it's primary purpose is, I just have to unfortunately give this a thumbs down. The Cinematic Mode mod provides a far more stark contrast between old and new HL2. (Except that mod goes nuts with character model overhauls that tend to irk purists).
Again, I feel really bad ripping on them like this, but I just don't see any amazing impact this mod does to warrant installing it other then the additional commentary mode.

The New Order was a fun and frantic game that managed to fit MOON NAZIS into a compelling story. The New Colossus keeps that same type of energy and story up, though it’s your call whether it’s to the same degree. My call is that the game is fantastic and much more fun than the first despite the fact that a bunch of the game happens to be an obvious downgrade.
Kill some ♥♥♥♥ing nazis. That's the gameplay and it's fantastic. I'm not talking about stealth though, cause that's just a pile of crap. The weapons all feel fantastic to use. They have a massive kick to them, they sound powerful, look bulky and deadly and they kill Nazis. The way it makes you play is kind of a combo of DOOM '16 and TNO, as you rush around the map to kill quickly (DOOM) while rushing from cover to cover to avoid the
hitscan enemies (TNO). It leans heavier on the DOOM side in my eyes cause of the playstyle, but everything else is very much Wolfenstein. Think of it as, say...DOOM without glory kills. It's just fantastic and satisfying gunplay, and that’s all you really need to know.
Well, maybe not. There's a lot of flaws in it that are indeed a step back from TNO and DOOM. The Laserkraftwerk has had its gimmick removed, the bosses are basically just buffed up enemies, the level design can be a bit frustrating at times, stealth is still crap and unreliable, secrets are practically non-existent, the weapon wheel doesn’t slow down time (yes that’s important), hitscan enemies are still ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, yada yada. There are some QOL improvements such as the auto-pick up items, but good lord is that one unreliable, as are the others. I don’t personally think these are enough to break the experience, but if you’ve played TNO, it’s hard not to notice them.
What can be enough to break the experience is the difficulty, cause this game is unfairly hard. Mainly because your health is low. It's really, really low. Even on lower difficulties, your health and armor will go straight to 0 in a couple of hits from Nazis across the map with hitscan weapons and robots firing giant instakill missiles. It’s not Hotline Miami / Killing Floor hard, where you’re constantly beating yourself up and going “ooooohhhh”, it’s The New Order / PAYDAY 2 One Down hard where the difficulty only comes in how much♥♥♥♥♥♥the game can throw at you and you’re about to smash your monitor in.
While these are some very large negative points, I did have a ♥♥♥♥ing blast playing the game and that was honestly enough for me to overlook these.
TNC’s story is where you’ll notice either a steep decline or a steep uprise in the story. If you loved the fact that it managed to keep itself together and tell a horrifying story about how the world would be under the Third Reich while having MOON NAZIS...you’ll be disappointed. If you just loved that it had Nazi robots on the moon, you’ll enjoy the tone; it’s louder, it’s sillier, it’s dumber and it really shows.
TNO played itself so seriously despite all the crazy♥♥♥♥♥♥happening that it worked and ended up being a serious story within a silly setting, with characters who posed very real threats and had very real conflicts. TNC doesn’t play itself seriously at all, opting for simple, almost one-dimensional personalities. TNO’s story at least felt like each action had a purpose, while TNC feels like you kinda just♥♥♥♥♥♥about America to kill some random bunch of Nazis and find some people to add to your boat.
Honestly, if you want to enjoy this story, just overlook the fact that it’s not as serious as the first. I mean, it’s got giant Nazi robot dogs that breathe fire; that isn’t exactly something most of us would consider serious. Relax a bit, have a good time, and don’t take it too seriously.
The New Colossus in many ways is a step back from The New Order, primarily in the story region where it wanders off into weird places. The gameplay takes some trade offs, though for the better. I don’t really know what you should come into this game expecting. If you come into this expecting The New Order II, you’ll be disappointed. Come into it expecting DOOM: Nazi Edition, and you’ll also be disappointed. I think The New Colossus is a kind of middle-ground between these two, and if you come into it expecting that, then you’ll have a blast shooting, stabbing and killing Nazis.

The amazing movement system with incredibly smooth climbing and jumping has been removed for no reason, it was already in the engine for Wolfenstein: The New Order and DOOM, which were made in the same engine, meaning they took actual effort to remove it, rather than keeping what made aforementioned games so smooth an experience for me personally.  Those two games were speedy in their movement and a joy to play.  Instead in this game, the movement is much slower.  The one thing that benefits from a slower speed is the Hatchet's heaviness in it's animations and weight you can feel just from watching it rip through your enemies.  Unfortunately this is the only area the slower movement of the game works anywhere near as well as the snappy speed did for The New Order and DOOM.
While in the first game I felt inclined to climb everything, and was often rewarded with secrets for doing so (or at the least another angle to attack from) in this game, the climbing is limited to wasit high objects, and the vaulting system is very picky on top of that.  There is one section of the game that takes place on the U-boat, while in this section if you sneak under the floor, rather than climbing over you have to walk up a tiny ramp placed in the most inconvinient location, and letting the player simply climb over it instead would not have broken anything about the experience.  Removing the ability to climb chest, or even head high walls made the movement so much more tedious and less smooth, and considering Machine Games' signiture thing is fast paced action games, this is even more saddening coming from them.  I understand the game was a massive undertaking, but in this one flaw, lies all my problems with this game, it may seem small, but replaying The New Order and then starting The New Colossus back to back, something will feel missing.
In addition, the smooth animations that slowly dragged the camera to the correct position before starting the character animations are gone now, instead hitting 'E' to interact with objects snaps you into place, breaking immersion and really just generally being an eyesore, these small things all coming together are what make a final product of a game so polished, and those small things were at the core of DOOM and The New Order.  They just don't feel as present here.  The whole game feels less verticle (accept once you recieve an upgrade halfway through the game, but even then it's far too sluggish to enjoy properly).  This game in general, all these small details, make me feel like this game needed about another 6 months to cook and be properly polished before it was released, and the lack of bugfix updates since it's release is depressing to say the least.  This game was a massive undertaking, depending on who you save in the first game, you basically get two entirely different experiences.  It's impressive to say the least, but again this came at the cost of the polish that made the previous entry feel so special and unique compared to other modern FPS titles.
In an ideal world, the movement system would not have been changed at all.  As I played through this game, I saw spots I, as a developer, would have wanted to hide secrets in that could easily be accessible to the player if climbing taller walls was still an option.  Some may argue that the "suit" you wear to enable you to walk for the first half of the game is the reason the movement is more sluggish, but in The New Order, Caroline uses it to jump so far and high she's practically flying, meaning this suit would only further enhance B.J.'s mobility.  The movement (or lack of) is the most glaring flaw in this game, but it doesn't ruin it (although you'll certainly wish The New Order's movement was back).  To contrast this I went back and replayed The New Order immediately after beating The New Colossus, and found that something from this game that I loved, was not in The New Order... The Hatchet, the best addition in this entire game, the weight, the feel, the utility.  It feels amazing to throw, and you can feel how heavy it is in B.J.'s hands through the animations alone.  For something so small to break the experience for me, or course something equally small would make me fall in love with it.
But once again this success is undermined by the fact you can now, no longer hold only your melee weapon!  One step forward and two steps back.   But once again The New Colossus makes up for it's shortcomings with an amazing narrative.    The story picks up shortly after the end of the lasts game, and boy is the start action packed.  The characters are amazing, and taking a road trip of the U.S. is refreshing and fun (although a little dry in it's color scheme, consisting of a few too many browns and beiges for my liking).  The graphics are still very good, apart from the laughable thumbs-up B.J. gives to Set after exploring his shooting range, and a few weird first person animations.  The cut-scenes are beautiful, but appear to be stuck in only 1080p, which was dissapointing as someone who owns a 4k monitor.  My only complaint about the visuals is that it leaves behind the first games more cartoony visual style for a more realistic take on the material, which reflects the games darker story.  But on the same level, it did work so well for the first game, I can't help but miss it and downright prefer it, however objectively better looking this entry may be.
The most glaring issue with choosing who to save is the "Signiture Weapon" you get is tied to which character you choose to save.  Fergus remembers to grab your Lazerkraftwerk when you are saved at the end of The New Order/Begining of The New Colossus, but Wyatt leaves it behind and designs a remote-denated grenade launcher.  What if in the story I prefer the Lazerkraftwerk, but want to save Wyatt?  It restricts your story preferences to a gameplay style you might not enjoy as much.  And as a result of having to desgin the game around both weapons, neither of them are used anywhere near as much as in the first game.  In the first game you were constantly cutting holes in things with the laerkraftwerk, and making shooting holes in your cover.  If you ran out of ammo, it's self charging battery would save your♥♥♥♥♥  (The self charging battery isn't even an option if you do save Fergus and keep the Lazerkraftwerk in this game, because of what I assume was balacing issues, but balancing a single-player game isn't exactly a priority for me in a game like this).  It's also sad to see the abliity to cut small holes with the Lazerkraftwerk dissapear, now only letting you vaporize entire sheets of metal, or none at all, albeit from a much farther distance than before.  But I do appreciate the in universe explaination for why it functions differently.  (Set tinkered with it after Fergus suggested some improvements... thanks fergus).
Remember how amazingly satisfying it was to find a new upgrade in The New Order?  The satisfying animations that showed you fiddleing with the new upgrade to your weapons?  Those are gone... instead you upgrade the weapons with weapon upgrade kits you find throughout the levels, meaninig that you could miss a kit, and not ever get all the upgrades.  You always get every upgrade when playing through The New Order, but not here.  Meaning if you want to experience all the weapon types, you'll have to investigate an unreasonable amount, or replay the game and look up a walkthrough.  In addition, despite it's over the top events, everything in The New Order was grounded in some form of reality and at least tried to be explained.  This is where those small details come in again.  So that is why I was genuinely surprised when I found out the "Nail Gun" attatchment used normal bullets to shoot.
I ran out of space to write more here, so if you wanna hear my ramblings through check the commens on this.  The short version is I gave it an 8.9/10.  You should get this game.

The 18 Wheels of Steel series has come a long way since its humble beginnings back in 2002. Tagged as Hard Truck: 18 Wheels of Steel (which was a sequel to Hard Truck 2: King of the Road), it was the first that used the Wheels of Steel tag name as the game play differs completely from racing trucks delivering goods. Since then, there were another four instalments where, besides the graphical enhancements, many changes were made like Mexico being left out then arrived back, sleep timer comes and goes and so on. It seems that every game after the first, developers ValuSoft couldn’t make up their minds what to leave out or to use. Well, the sixth game in the series, 18 Wheels of Steel: American Long Haul, it seems ValuSoft finally made up their minds and just chuck everything in from all the previous series thus making this game the ‘final copy’. And it certainly shows as this simulator will be the closest you ever get other than driving the real thing.
So my real purpose for playing this game is for the love of driving. America / Canada and bits of Mexico has a diverse range of landscapes to discover and thankfully, the game’s visual aspects is quite decent. Nothing ground breaking however still pleasant to look at. In addition to the pretty decent physics, you have a good feel driving around with a massive haul trailing behind. For instance, delivering glass was pretty easy going however when I delivered those oversize tubes through the Rocky Mountains (i.e. from Calgary to Vancouver), with snow smashing on my windscreen, it got my adrenaline running as I need to be very careful dodging traffic as well as ensuring my truck doesn’t tip over. And because you can play your own music using the truck’s radio player, it’s a great experience to have (yet the music needs to be on .ogg format).
So whilst the game’s intent is to build an empire, I felt it failed in that respect as there’s no competition at all. You can sit back, relax and listen to your radio channel whilst having the cash rolling in. Granted, the beginning is quite rough as you need to do some real repetitive jobs (X – Beyond the Frontier anyone?) however once you have the money to buy another truck, trailer and hire additional helpers, the game’s difficulty level gets a lot easier. However, if you, like me, like to drive the open world and seeing vast landscapes, you will enjoy this game as America is a pretty country to see. With its majestic mountain ranges, endless deserts, Great Plains and of course, bustling cities, developers Valusoft chose the correct country to display all of this. However, because it also plays on as a business simulation, it missed the mark.

Cherry Tree is the tale of a girl trying to open a comedy club at school however she needs 5 members to be able to do so and her with her best friend are only 2 people. Recruit 3 more members out of a pool of 6 while finishing all your homework and balancing your fatigue or else you may collapse or fail class!
That's what the advertising blurb said anyway. You get to move left and right on various screens and talk to NPCs but this isn't a platform game and the walking only serves to give the illusion of gameplay or to pick up various objects scattered around. The "homework" just serves to waste days and fatigue can be balanced very easily by just not wasting time working jobs. You see you have 40 days broken down into 3 time slots per day in order to make the potential recruits like you. However the only way to make them like you is to impress them with your various diplomatic actions which are influenced by your diplomatic skills which you increase by choosing a skill to level up, thus also eating into those precious time slots.
This sounds like a game and it sounds like it could be good but the problem is that you can easily increase all your skills very high very quickly and recruit everyone with time to spare. You can also fail miserably if you try to actually engage with people instead of leveling up your skills so it reminds me of 'Long Live the Queen' but without the good writing. Or the fun.
Speaking of writing, this is one of the most boring non-visual novels I have ever read. How do you even mess up a visual novel with a comedy setting? Well it has little jokes relying more on puns and memes and oh ho, before you accuse me of playing the westernized version, I am playing the Japanese translated version.
I didn't enjoy playing the game. The music doesn't create any atmosphere, the story is sweet at its core but lacks any charm and the characters are believable but as soon as they joined I didn't feel any connection or want to engage with them further. Lastly the sound effects are from an open source sound bank so if you reconize some of them from other games (100% Oranage Juice) that would be the reason why.
Really, the graphics are very good and I like the ideas that went into the game but it suffers poor execution
Hopefully the sequel which is a straight up visual novel, will remedy the issues I experienced here.

username: Ghost of Ass-Kickins Yet To Come
text:
Just like the comedy that Mairu (or Miley I believe her name is in the westernized version) loves and aspires to make a career of one day this game is humorous, lifts your spirits, and leaves you wanting more. The only possible complaint I could make was that it felt too short, but then again for a feel-good high school story like this that will happen regardless of how many hours you’d need to put in to finish it off. Cherry Tree High Comedy Club is one of those fun, wacky, lovable, and timeless high school stories like The Breakfast Club and Persona series.
The game takes place over a month and a half; starting you off just before Spring Break with the mission of gathering members for your comedy club. Throughout your quest to recruit members you have 6 potential candidates who all have their own charm and appeal. Even the antagonist (Chitose) isn’t a particularly loathsome individual. She's a waspy preppy girl that you used to be friends with when you were younger and has it out for you now, but you never really feel any animosity toward her, just more of a rivalry. I think this is worth highlighting in my review because in my experience everyone I’d come across was likable in their own way. This casual atmosphere truly gives the game a pleasant and quite laid back feel. I had a successful run on my first playthrough despite my constant concerns that I wasn’t doing as well as I could have. I’m on my 2nd run now (there is a New Game+ feature by the way that I think should be pointed out so even if you do kinda meh on your first run you can come back to the story and do better the next time around) so I can’t wait to see how it turns out on an even better run.
In conclusion/if you felt my review was tl;dr and couldn’t be bothered and skipped to the bottom, this is definitely a great game to get if you’re a fan of comedy, the whole relationship building gameplay from games such as the Persona series, high school tales more interesting than how high school really was/is, or if you’re a fan of visual novels with a bit of a free-roam element. So with that in mind I’m keeping my eye on the developer (773) and highly recommend this game.

To do this you must read magazines and watch telvision to boost your stats, then talk to people about those subjects in order to boost your friendship. Get to level 5, and they join your club. You meet 5/6 of the people over your spring break (and the last one when you get back to school), giving you about 5 weeks to befriend everyone. The days are all split up into 3 portions, two of which you have the chance to really communicate with the people, and then the nighttime where you can call people (Which does very little, to my knowledge), make some cash, or study up on your skills. Homework is also a small annoyance, but easy to overcome if you aren't streamlining friendships.
The story itself is relativly engaging, making it entertaining to converse with everyone you can to get the few snippets out of them. There seems to only be a few that they cycle through, but that's okay. They're often funny, given the whole comedy club point of the game.
There's also a lot of side characters you can converse with with are equally cool and play as much of a role as do the six subjects.
My only quarrel with this game is the wonky controls and the size of the screen. For whatever reason I could not make this game full screen, or could I use my gamepad on it. It only requires the arrow keys and the enter key, but that particular setup is unlike my usual hand placements and felt uncomfortable. The tiny screen also felt unnessisary, but this could be an issue on my end alone so I don't blame it that much.
All in all, a good little game to spend some time on if you haven't anything to do and are interested in basically a dating sim about humor. I'm excited to see what the next part has to offer based on what I did here.

I love that so many board/card games are being given digital versions these days, but this is the kind of release that mars the trend.
To address my low playtime, my issues with this game are not related to the actual game mechanics of XenoShyft, but rather the technical and design choices made for this digital version.
First off, there isn't even an exit button on the main menu (that I could see), so you have to ALT+F4 to exit if you're playing in fullscreen.
The options menu contains no video settings whatsoever, leaving you with no resolution settings. The only thing you can change is whether you want to play in windowed mode or fullscreen, selectable only before you start the game in what appears to be the default Unity popup, Playing in fullscreen results in a square shaped view area with nothing using the left and right sides of your monitor. UI that could be placed in this area is instead crammed in the top and bottom of the screen, which means you have to pan around constantly, even when zoomed out.
Speaking of zooming, it's incredibly slow and requires several full mousewheel turns to get close to the cards. I thought adjusting the zoom sensitivity setting in the options would alleviate this, but it barely made a difference. I have a Logitech mouse with a free-spinning toggle on the wheel that's useful when you're reading documents with many pages. Scrolling up 40 pages or so this way takes a few seconds. It takes about the same amount of time just to zoom in this way in XenoShyft.
When you want to pan, you have to click an area outside of the playing field and drag the view (the way you would do it on a touchscreen with your finger). If you click on some cards this way, it will instead show you a zoomed in view of the card. But it won't do this on some other cards (like generic Militia cards).
I could have dealt with all of that, annoying as it is, but the real dealbreaker is that sometimes pieces of the UI do not respond, breaking the game by not allowing you to advance to the next phase of the game.
The game was clearly ported from a mobile version and it shows all over the product from the nonexistent resolution options, to the unresponsive and cluttered UI, to the awkward panning and zooming controls.
The tutorial does a good job at teaching you the rules of the game, but is done through a slow and annoying "AI" voice that reads to you and cannot be disabled. At least I know how to play if I decide to purchase the physical card game.
It's a shame because the underlying game seems fun. As it currently stands, I can't recommend it until the developers fix a lot of these issues, which really seems like they'd have to redo a large part of the game.
