To get hype for the HD Renovation, I decided to get back into the reviewing spirit and share my thoughts on this wonderful little game. So strap in, folks!
Let's get straight into it with...
The story is that you are an anonymous player, probably self insert, investigating a mansion that no one has ever come out of. You're greeted with the host, Spooky. A cute little ghost girl that owns the mansion. She invites you to delve through a thousand rooms to find what lies at the end...If there's even an end. Legit, she honestly doesn't know. As you delve through the floors, you start to realize just how twisted this seemingly cute mansion is. Obscure, dark places are explored as you find yourself running from unimaginable terrors. At the end...well...spoilers time.
This game looks beautiful, the style works so well with how it changes on you. It goes from a cutesy looking 8 to 16 bit dungeon with an adventure time-like artstyle to a HORRIFYING nightmare with creatures you wish never existed. It impresses me how much this game spooked me. As for gameplay, you walk about in first person through the thousand rooms Spooky has set. Eventually, you will encounter the SPECIMEN. Creatures that want to end your life. There are many kinds of Specimen, so you must know what you're dealing with. They have their own signature sounds...and haunting music whenever they draw near. Most of them guard a specific big room, usually the 10th of every hundred. For example, 310. The appearance of the child-like puppet, Specimen 6. He only comes forth when you do not look at him. And if he takes your life...I hope you didn't mind him taking your eyes. Once you get an Axe in room 555, you can start choppin down Specimen 01 (The harmless cardboard cutout) and other creatures. Just...not the specimens. They're invincible.
This game gets an A+ from me. It does an excellent job at spooking players and getting them hooked with lore. There's also a DLC that's only 1.99 called Kalamari Hospital. More spook, why not? Give it a whirl. I DARE YOU.

I would like to define this game as a “4-Dimension Puzzle Game”.
More than a traditional Puzzle game, which only requires a matching of boundary conditions between 2 pieces,
this game also requires players to find certain relation between 2 pieces in a 3D space and in certain time sequence.
This 4D structure make it possible for developers to put more information into it, like to tell a story with different perspectives (same as others did in BloodBorne). The story maybe simple, but the experience to discover it is just fantastic. And it also requires developers a high narrative Skill, logic ability, spatial imagination ability, and a good taste of art.
That’s not a easy thing, especially for the last one.

This is one of those games that is extremely thrilling and fun, but once you get the mechanics down, it can turn infuriating at times.
The vast majority of the game is utterly fantastic, with the right amount of tension.  Once you start trying to begin special ops in the middle of a conflict area, rather than simply following the orders of your commander directly, the sheer excitement and fear of things going wrong -- which is pretty much "always" in a war zone -- the drama in the game becomes even more palpable.
The main campaign offers plenty of emergent stories, in spite of having absolutely no story to speak of.  The Bawdlerised factions (two of whose real equivalents would have no reason to fight each other in reality anyway) are all fairly well balanced, and the struggles over the battlefield can be positively harrowing at times, never knowing whether you'll manage to maintain a foothold against overwhelming odds, or manage to survive when armour support rolls in.  My favourite moment of the game -- an entirely emergent, unscripted situation -- was when I was caught in the trenches, with Graycollars coming from the northwest, and Brownpants coming from the north and northeast, with our faction fighting a desperate struggle to hold the position against two factions which seemed more keen on attacking us than each other (which they also did, mind you: the A.I. Is Not (Usually) A Cheating ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in this game).  I had to fight in pitched, non-stop combat for over thirty minutes, calling in danger-close artillery support -- an anti-air turret prevented reinforcements -- and afterward my exhalation was incredibly belaboured.
However, the entire experience wasn't perfect.  What frustrated me about the campaign in particular is that they went through the effort of giving you all of the new callouts and squad members to play with, and then removed it all for the first final mission.  A mandatory solo stealth mission as (one of) the final missions in an action game?  Pitched firefights and struggles on the battlefield were far more compelling than having every ability I'd grown accustomed to deliberately removed by an Interface Screw -- where special ops on the battlefield against overwhelming odds with the
of taking a squad along for the mission were thrilling and compelling, the first final mission dialled back the artificial intelligence and made the fight a war of attrition which was boring by comparison... an hour and a half later, it was over, and I was both happy it was over and furious that it didn't get any better as it went.
The second final mission forced me into a kill zone.  No, literally.  Your task is to advance on an enemy position with no other way to go than through waves and waves of defences.  My old school Counter-Strike experience (a long time ago now -- I didn't feel like it was worth competing with those who spent hours and hours a day playing a game that was by all rights not all that great to begin with) paid off well enough in the campaign, but no strategy is possible when repeating the last charge of Tennyson's Brigade.  No matter how brave you are, you will go stupidly to your death.  For a game that was otherwise about emergent tactics and the thrill of outmanoeuvring the enemy, being forced to wade through an enemy force that repeatedly retook their turrets and resumed slaughtering you and your forces (with a jammer near the front lines as yet another Interface Screw), it became an unfair and dissatisfying slog.  Perhaps I'm just too "normal" to appreciate being killed over and over again...
Flawed final mission design aside, the game's fundamental design is otherwise flawless.  Weapons feel appropriately light and manoeuvrable -- like real weapons do -- and allowing yourself to be caught with your pants down is brutally punished while using clever tactics and strategy is generously rewarded.  If they had avoided artificial difficulty in the final missions and simply made it more of the same tactics, but against a stronger force, I would probably have had absolutely nothing unfavourable to say about the game at all.  Totally worth your money!

- Stealth Mechanics : I see people talking about stealth not working right, but I think it's actually been improved. - HUD : I think it looks better.
- Killing Nazis : You can still do this in abundance.
The Cons
- Crouching / Jumping / Ledges : I find myself having to try multiple times just to enter a ventilation shaft. I also have some trouble getting over obstacles or climbing up ledges. It's a weird problem to have in a game like this and also very frustrating.

Aerannis in set in the mysterious future of 2XXX in a world where there are no longer any men and mysterious beings secretly run society. Ceyda is a tough hired gun who prefers to shoot first rather than second guess her orders. The issue of men, and the lack thereof, is questioned by various NPCs and issues of reproduction, femininity, women’s place in society and more are all touched on throughout the game.
The mystery of sinister government plots and the supernatural beings that act as gods is also played up throughout. The scene following most missions shows a prominent political figure addressing a faceless crowd to spin the missions’ happenings, often questionable acts that suggest something larger than Ceyda is willing to pursue is at foot, into digestible bits of just events. The aforementioned creatures haunt Ceyda in dreams and in reality, with their main characteristic being a large single eye and their often fluctuating forms. The omnipresent gaze and ability to appear anywhere and through any form most easily places them as manifestations of the gaze. It’s a fascinating setting, but at times the weightiness of its content gets heavy handed; there is a certain mission where Ceyda is tasked with controlling the leak of dangerous chemical called “testosterone,” which threatens to turn the populace into violent maniacs. Not every bit of text in the game is meant to be lofty though, and there are some clever jabs and nice bits of humor.
The colors, level, and enemy design seem to call back to the older Megaman X games. Even the mission start and end notifications feel like Megaman X style font and transitions. The gelatinous eye monsters in this game also recall a bit of the older Megaman’s Yellow Devil, though the monsters here are much more articulate and insidious. Despite the artistic inspiration, Aerannis very much manages to be striking on its own and the soundtrack does an excellent job of keeping the mood in place. This puts the games form near on par with the content present, but the mechanics of the game could have used some more polishing.
The controls feel unresponsive and awkward on both controller or keyboard and this affects all of the games mechanics. Platforming is a large part of Aerannis, and it delivers a less than stellar performance. Wall jumping slings you out just far enough to not be able to alternate most parallel walls, while at the same time demanding the player to return quickly to the same wall in order to climb vertically: it looks a bit like your character is a confused rabbit trying to stay in the same place but somehow managing to offset itself ever so slightly. The characters regular walk speed is set just above leisurely, and the sprint mechanic arrives late and with a very short use time. Ledge grabbing in the game is untraditional in that the ledge of most platforms isn’t counted as either end, but the center. This is of course more a visual annoyance than an actual flaw once you get the hang of it.
Given the wealth of great 2D games that have used stealth elements recently, Aerannis really seems to have taken a step back. Movement feels slow and controls feel unintuitive: with a button press you can hold up someone to instantly kill, open a door, or use them as shield. Generally the doors enemies can open do not offer much of a shortcut, and they don’t make great shields so you will generally be instantly killing them. The problem is that there were a number of times where Ceyda seems to have a change of heart and let the hostage go, and thus endure a few shots and an alert. The level design overall makes stealth seem disjointed and almost unwelcome. So where other stealth games make a sort of puzzle wherein you use gadgets and skill to figure out the many paths to complete an objective silently, Aerannis is rather stingy with the gadgets (a noisemaker, a boomerang, and a mine), and the linear platform heavy areas make it easier to just ignore large areas, while at the same time not giving you a stealth satisfaction. Similar games with stealth elements often rely on you being able to actually see your enemy: The Metal Gear series started top down to allow you to see enemies, modern incarnations are third person with first person options or gadgets, Mark of the Ninja and Hotline Miami both were zoomed out accordingly and allowed the player to see just a bit further than an enemies field of view for most areas. Aerannis instead has a colored globe that will shrink to red when an enemy is approaching, but beyond that, you are left to guess if taking a step through the door or exiting a hallway is going to earn you a blast in the face or a few quick kill.
The combat, much like the stealth, feels limited. Ceyda’s gun mimics Megaman’s buster gun in that it offers small quick pellets or a larger blast when charged. There was one upgrade that slightly increased rate of fire, but other than that you are stuck with a weapon that encourages you to not engage the enemy directly. The boss fights in Aerannis do attempt to change around the games mechanics: a reflex heavy running sequence, a climbing segment that takes precision mine placement, and then some regular scenarios where you follow a boss’s pattern.
The general rule of thumb for games that want to avoid being linear is that logistics should be quick and easy or traveling should be interesting and it ought to be made clear where important things are. While the first hub area has a few points of interest, a few being less than a handful, every area after that feels like a chore to traverse with no payoff:  no objects to examine, no upgrades, minimal aesthetic variance, and general barren concrete emptiness. On top of this, navigation leaves much to be desired once you leave the first hub area, because some bits of text might tell you a general area or directions, but there are a lot of vertical avenues and buildings of interest to come in clumps. These hub areas only serve to extend the game, which throws off the pacing, as well as highlight the clunky platforming and frame issues, which is overall not fun
Though the mechanics are not the absolute highlight of the game, they are functional for the most part. Aside from the stutters and clunky controls, Aerannis plays fine and is not broken.
Aerannis is less Mark of the Ninja, and more Mega(wo)man with a focus on narrative and light stealth elements. Some have identified Aerannis as a metroidvania, but given the lack of techniques or gadgets that would allow one to explore new paths in old areas, relatively small world area, and minimal recursive structure, little encouragement to explore, and far from easy travel or navigation, I would not shelve this next to Symphony of the Night. Aerannis stumbles a bit in its approach, but the game is certainly interesting enough to overlook its minor flaws.

has proved itself worthy of all of the excellent critical feedback it has received. Ninja Theory took an enormous risk developing and publishing their own AAA title, as it would have been a major disaster for them if it wouldn't have lived up to the hype it created amongst the gaming community. Fortunately for them, they sorted it out and made a fantastic game that, despite not being perfect, has made a large number of players fall in love with it.
We begin our journey arriving at the border of
as Senua, a young woman who lost her beloved Dillion and wants to save his soul from Hela. Her most characteristic feature is her mental illness, which is immediately shown to us by the talking of several voices in her head. These will play an important role both in the story and in the way the future fights and puzzles are going to work, as well as letting the player know how Senua feels about whatever she's experiencing.
As the story progresses, we learn more about Senua's story and her unfortunate past. I would not like to go further in details, so I will only say that I love the way the plot unveils, leaving us with an absolutely awesome ending that lives up to the rest of the story.
I'm sure we can all agree that combat and puzzles are two important elements in the game, so I believe it's fair to dedicate an entire part of the review to their proper analysis.
First of all, I'd want to point out the pretty characteristic camera angle this game uses. Though being a third-person game, we get to see everything from Senua's perspective. This means we can't trust all that we see or hear, since Senua's mind does usually trick us to see or hear things that aren't real. To do this, the camera is set just behind of Senua, matching her height. Some people may find this annoying, but I personally like this a lot. It really helps with the immersion, which is a key element in the game.
While the combat mechanics are fairly good, I have noted the lack of types of enemies we can fight with, being this a bit of a problem when it comes to experiencing fresh experiences when we fight. It's not like it's ridiculously monotonous, but it would probably use more variety, specially when one realizes that combat is going to be very present in the game.
On the other hand, puzzles are my major complain about this game. They are rather simple and can make you waste time, though there are some times that they are actually used to move forward with the story. All in all, I think this is the weakest part of the game.
Visually this game is gorgeous. Ninja Theory put a lot of effort into this and it definitely payed off. We can see beautiful scenery throughout the entirety of the game, and facial expressions and movements are just marvelous. If this is something you were worried about, I can assure you that it will not be disappointing.
Where do I begin? This game easily scores a 10 in sound if you play it with headphones. The voices in Senua's head feel real. It's just as if you were there with them. All of the other SFX have an astounding quality. The music featured in the game fits perfectly with the atmosphere, specially the last part and particularly the ending. I totally fell in love with it.
Hellblade is a game that deserves to be played. Its storytelling, sound and atmosphere make it a unique experience, and as such I think it poses a great success for Ninja Theory.

TL;DR: Fascinating, interesting and beautiful.
It was much more immersive, complex and thought-provoking than I expected.
Since the game has no HUD whatsoever, here's an interesting fact: the voices you hear all the time (auditory hallucinations - the protagonist is psychotic), alongside their main purpose (well... blabbering, as hallucinations do), also serve as game's way of presenting useful information to the player (like introducing a new mechanic, or informing you of danger) in a casual manner, which I found pretty smart.
The graphics are beautiful, I could not stop taking screenshots (and there's an awesome Photo Mode, too!).
The atmosphere is dark and often unsettling, but even I, a person who does not at all dig horror games/movies, gladly delved into it.
The combat system is simple, smooth and enjoyable. And the fights look damn cool.
The puzzles are not too complicated.
P.S. The game comes with a feature video, about 20 min long (available in the main menu), that shows some stages of its development and explains how the game came to be, that was an interesting watch, too.
If you don't care for the plot and the atmosphere, this game is not for you. Otherwise: enjoy, it's quite an experience!

[Spoiler-Free Review]
Wanderlust: Rebirth should come with a disclaimer stating your experience with this game will largely be influenced by the number of people you play with. Although the game is entirely playable in an offline single player environment, I found playing in such a way severely hindered my enjoyment of the game.
Whether or not we care for them, the Action RPG genre has evolved a few staple conventions. When a game largely ignores these, it's noticeable.
Story and Scope: The story is extremely short (around an hour or two to complete the normal difficulty mode), it's unimaginative, and failed to captivate me in any meaningful way. Scenarios felt unimportant as resolution to any situation often devolves into fighting this, that, or the other thing. The world of Wanderlust is barebones, at times lonely, and devoid of life.
Character Development: Characters are one dimensional and expendable, protaganists are mechanical vessels who only strive for the next piece of bait dangled in front of them. Although they're with you from the very beginning, you never grow any attachment to your unnamed NPC comrades and NPC's in towns will rarely, if ever, acknowledge your presence, save for the odd, "Hello". You walk "through" towns not "into" them.
Interesting Gameplay Mechanics: Enter an area, fight, move on, rinse and repeat. Your out-of-battle experience is monotonous and boring. Collecting items and equipment becomes cumbersome as your in-game pouch for holding these things is much too small to quest for extended periods of time without micromanaging your belongings to make room for the next thing.
Exploration/Adventure: There is no sense of discovery because there's nothing to discover (except the odd coin in a breakable barrel or randomly appearing treasure chest). My first instinct when playing a game like this is to scour the areas for chests and barrels, secrets and treasures. There's no point in trying any of that here though, you'll quickly find you're just wasting your time. To top it all off, invisible walls are everywhere, preventing you from walking past even carpets in open hallways (with treasure chests placed on the other side to further remind you of what you can't do in Wanderlust).
Diverse Locales: Ransack location after location, each location serves only as a battleground. In fact, you begin to feel inconvenienced by the discovery of a new area because it just stands between you and the only enjoyable part of the game - the fights.
Intense Battles: You enter an area and fight anything that moves, rinse and repeat. melee enemies employ the same swarm-bumrush strategy upon encountering them (limiting your ability to move), ranged attacks are unobstructed by obstacles leading some battles to feel cheap.
Multiplayer: The best thing about the game. Multiplayer "Crawls" are enjoyable. Story mode levels progress in the same way as in single player, but at least you can develop actual strategies with your teammates. The connection between players is crucial to the formula that makes this mode a success. Without cooperation between actual players, the experience is too rigid.
Replayability: There's enough to keep you coming back for more if you want to improve your character's skills and/or equipment or want to go for achievements.
It's hard to recommend this game. The only redeeming quality besides it's graphical style, is it's multiplayer, but you can get that in many better developed packages. I'll continue playing it to collect equipment and achievements, but I'd encourage people to skip this one unless you've got a group of friends who don't already own something better (like Dungeon Defenders).
Update: A month later...
Thankfully the in-game population has grown a bit more since I wrote this, so finding people to play with isn't such a challenge anymore. I've been playing every day for basically three weeks and have come to the realization this game isn't so bad if you ignore it as a single player experience and only play in multiplayer modes. It's also a lot less like Zelda than the screenshots lead me to believe (part of my initial disappointment). In my experience it's actually a lot closer to Smash TV and Total Carnage (games of that ilk) - especially in Crawls.
I still wish things were a lot more polished, but even as it is, there is fun to be had with this game, it just isn't immediately apparent.

Fract OSC captures the spirit of Myst along with great looking visuals and audio experience to make a good puzzle game. It is not super difficult (it ends up that only need to "learn" a half-dozen some mechanics, then applied in different manners through the rest of the game) but does show great connectivity between the puzzle elements and how these relate to the musical elements. The final product on completing the game also ends up being a fully useable music tracker that can be used to create music of one's own. It's the type of game that is not necessarily groundbreaking but it is a labor of love that shows a lot of effort to be an personal experience.
I will warn that the game does not run smooth on low-end cards or hardware.  It's not unplayable but did experience stuttering graphics, which can be a bit troublesome when traversing areas with narrow ledges. Fortunately death is non-existant and you are simply reset back to a checkpoint, nor does any puzzle require precision timing,
The music is beautiful, the aesthetics are captivating, and the mechanics are absolutely elegant. I absolutely recommend it.

This game will impress you with how scary it is, trust me. Spooky's House of-waitwaitwait♥♥♥♥♥♥ its JUMP SCARE MANSION not House of Jumpscares. Hahaha, what are you talking about? To get hype for the HD Renovation, I decided to get back into the reviewing spirit and share my thoughts on this wonderful little game. So strap in, folks!
Let's get straight into it with...
The story is that you are an anonymous player, probably self insert, investigating a mansion that no one has ever come out of. You're greeted with the host, Spooky. A cute little ghost girl that owns the mansion. She invites you to delve through a thousand rooms to find what lies at the end...If there's even an end. Legit, she honestly doesn't know. As you delve through the floors, you start to realize just how twisted this seemingly cute mansion is. Obscure, dark places are explored as you find yourself running from unimaginable terrors. At the end...well...spoilers time.
This game looks beautiful, the style works so well with how it changes on you. It goes from a cutesy looking 8 to 16 bit dungeon with an adventure time-like artstyle to a HORRIFYING nightmare with creatures you wish never existed. It impresses me how much this game spooked me. As for gameplay, you walk about in first person through the thousand rooms Spooky has set. Eventually, you will encounter the SPECIMEN. Creatures that want to end your life. There are many kinds of Specimen, so you must know what you're dealing with. They have their own signature sounds...and haunting music whenever they draw near. Most of them guard a specific big room, usually the 10th of every hundred. For example, 310. The appearance of the child-like puppet, Specimen 6. He only comes forth when you do not look at him. And if he takes your life...I hope you didn't mind him taking your eyes. Once you get an Axe in room 555, you can start choppin down Specimen 01 (The harmless cardboard cutout) and other creatures. Just...not the specimens. They're invincible.
This game gets an A+ from me. It does an excellent job at spooking players and getting them hooked with lore. There's also a DLC that's only 1.99 called Kalamari Hospital. More spook, why not? Give it a whirl. I DARE YOU.

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is a Dark Fantasy game with a unique pyschological twist. The basic plotline is set in a bleak world involving Norse mythology. You play as Senua, a Celtic warrior who is attempting to save the soul of her lover from the clutches of the Norse Goddess of Death, Hela. While at the same time, having to deal with her own immense psychological issues. I've honestly never played a game that deals with mental illness in this way and I found it very intriguing.
While the overrall story is incredible, I have some minor issues with the gameplay. At the beginning I enjoyed the combat,  the quality of the animations were really impressive, every slice and stab of your sword feels meaty and incredibly satisfying. However, as I continued fighting the same looking enemies just with beefier health bars, I started to find it a bit tedious. The combat only really gets shaken up a bit when you fight one of the games bosses, which are incredible cinematically and even then its just a matter of a slightly changed move set rather than anything really different.
The puzzle sections in this game weren't difficult at all to understand, more incredibly frustrating, I felt like I was about to have an aneurysm at times. They amount to finding letters in the environment to progress through an area. To me, their only real purpose was serving to remove you from an otherwise gripping narrative. I noticed a strange bug as well when it comes to interacting with some objects where Senua will simply refuse to interact with a door, I've seen on the forums that other people encountered this bug as well and it could be potentially game breaking. I'm also not entirely sure if its been patched. Just a friendly warning.
The game's audio is truly outstanding, to get the true experience with this game I highly recommend you play it with a good pair of headphones, trust me, you won't regret it.
Hellblade also has some performance issues, at times you might be running at a smooth 60fps, only to drop down to 30fps seemingly at random. During some scenes for me it can drop to around the mid 40's range. Having said that, these fps drops don't happen that often and generally you can just ignore them, but they can still be jarring when they occur. I've read in some forums that the game runs considerably worse for people with AMD machines. I'll share my system specs so people can compare.
Intel Core i7 7700K
16 GB RAM
Nvidia GTX 1060 with 6 GB VRAM.
Hellblade: Senua's sacrifice was an incredible experience that I greatly enjoyed despite the few minor gripes I mentioned above. You really have to give kudos to the developers, for such a small development team to create a game this good is amazing.
8/10, highly recommended.

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is a great narrative but not a great game. It is a good solid game though and I do recommend it, but it does seem to be slightly overrated.
Pros: The game has an amazing sound design and story. It is very sincere with its depiction of Psychosis and clearly a lot of research was done on the subject matter. The game has beautiful graphics and it also performs very well on PC without any hiccups (it does take a good amount of juice on very high settings). The combat and puzzles which are the major gameplay elements are good for the most part.
Cons: While there are some really cool puzzles and awesome battles (like the darkness boss bottle),  unfortunately a lot of the other puzzles and enemies are boring and dont serve much of a narrative purpose. They feel annoying, repetetive and sometimes even unnecessary. The game might be even shorter without the extra puzzles and battles but I think that would have been fine.  Lastly, the ending for this game was way too open ended. I understand that they want to leave things to the players imagination, but after almost a 10hr journey and soo much build up it felt unfair. There is a secret ending that makes it a bit better but it is a pain in the butt to get.
Conclusion: Hellblade is a good game especially considering its base price is only 30$ (bad name though cuz there aint no hellblade :P). I highly recommend this game to people who love a great story. If you're only in it soley for either the action/combat or solving dem puzzles then you might be disappointed. Again, I recommend this game and if it ever goes on sale it should be a must buy.

This is one of those games that is extremely thrilling and fun, but once you get the mechanics down, it can turn infuriating at times.
The vast majority of the game is utterly fantastic, with the right amount of tension.  Once you start trying to begin special ops in the middle of a conflict area, rather than simply following the orders of your commander directly, the sheer excitement and fear of things going wrong -- which is pretty much "always" in a war zone -- the drama in the game becomes even more palpable.
The main campaign offers plenty of emergent stories, in spite of having absolutely no story to speak of.  The Bawdlerised factions (two of whose real equivalents would have no reason to fight each other in reality anyway) are all fairly well balanced, and the struggles over the battlefield can be positively harrowing at times, never knowing whether you'll manage to maintain a foothold against overwhelming odds, or manage to survive when armour support rolls in.  My favourite moment of the game -- an entirely emergent, unscripted situation -- was when I was caught in the trenches, with Graycollars coming from the northwest, and Brownpants coming from the north and northeast, with our faction fighting a desperate struggle to hold the position against two factions which seemed more keen on attacking us than each other (which they also did, mind you: the A.I. Is Not (Usually) A Cheating ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in this game).  I had to fight in pitched, non-stop combat for over thirty minutes, calling in danger-close artillery support -- an anti-air turret prevented reinforcements -- and afterward my exhalation was incredibly belaboured.
However, the entire experience wasn't perfect.  What frustrated me about the campaign in particular is that they went through the effort of giving you all of the new callouts and squad members to play with, and then removed it all for the first final mission.  A mandatory solo stealth mission as (one of) the final missions in an action game?  Pitched firefights and struggles on the battlefield were far more compelling than having every ability I'd grown accustomed to deliberately removed by an Interface Screw -- where special ops on the battlefield against overwhelming odds with the
of taking a squad along for the mission were thrilling and compelling, the first final mission dialled back the artificial intelligence and made the fight a war of attrition which was boring by comparison... an hour and a half later, it was over, and I was both happy it was over and furious that it didn't get any better as it went.
The second final mission forced me into a kill zone.  No, literally.  Your task is to advance on an enemy position with no other way to go than through waves and waves of defences.  My old school Counter-Strike experience (a long time ago now -- I didn't feel like it was worth competing with those who spent hours and hours a day playing a game that was by all rights not all that great to begin with) paid off well enough in the campaign, but no strategy is possible when repeating the last charge of Tennyson's Brigade.  No matter how brave you are, you will go stupidly to your death.  For a game that was otherwise about emergent tactics and the thrill of outmanoeuvring the enemy, being forced to wade through an enemy force that repeatedly retook their turrets and resumed slaughtering you and your forces (with a jammer near the front lines as yet another Interface Screw), it became an unfair and dissatisfying slog.  Perhaps I'm just too "normal" to appreciate being killed over and over again...
Flawed final mission design aside, the game's fundamental design is otherwise flawless.  Weapons feel appropriately light and manoeuvrable -- like real weapons do -- and allowing yourself to be caught with your pants down is brutally punished while using clever tactics and strategy is generously rewarded.  If they had avoided artificial difficulty in the final missions and simply made it more of the same tactics, but against a stronger force, I would probably have had absolutely nothing unfavourable to say about the game at all.  Totally worth your money!

Far more deep than you'd think an overhead game could be. You're not special, and this ain't CoD. You're just like the man beside you and the only difference is that he's controlled by AI, and your character is controlled by your brain. No buffed health or special treatment here, so dive behind cover and stick with your mates, because this battle is just getting started and it's gonna be long. I'll be dividing this review into Pros, Notes, and Cons. Pros are what most people would consider good for what this game wants to be, Notes are important things about the game that some people may like or dislike based on preference. Cons are things that most people would generally consider to be negative in a game. Let's get right into it!
Pros:
- Includes navigation and coordination mechanics that can take some getting used to like sight, verticality, and even basic movement, but once you get past the learning curve, which isn't too bad, you'll be knowing when to shoot, with what angles, and how/when to move. It'll begin to feel natural quickly.
- Pretty good weapon mechanics. Reloading speed is realistic, and slightly faster to indicate the fast-paced speed of war. Accuracy feels very well scaled and reasonable based on what kind of weapon you're using, and how fast you're firing it.
- Inescapable situations where you can tough it out all you want, but the enemy has you in a position where your death is inevitable.
- Despite its underlying complexity, a noob can come in and play how he wants for awhile without feeling like complete garbage. He'll be average like the men around him; dying once in awhile. But if he decides to observe the flow of battle and the tactics that his enemies employ, he can become more than mediocre and really shine in combat efficiency.
- Many weapons and vehicles to play with.
- I actually found a freaking mod that replaces the war teams with N-Strike Elite, Zombie Strike, and N-Strike mega with the blasters from each of those Nerf sub-brands, and even darts with actual physics that stay where they land. I found a freaking nerf war mod on the Workshop! How sick is that!?!?
- You always feel like there's a playstyle, game mechanic, or tactic you haven't tried yet, and the items dropped by soldiers sometimes hint at it. This makes it replayable.
- You start off as a rank 1 nobody. A scrub. I don't know, well, anything about military ranks, but they seem genuine enough to me. If I'm wrong, correct me in a reply to this review, I guess. Anyway, in the beginning, your fellow men treat you like a rank 1 scrub, sometimes telling you to♥♥♥♥♥♥off if you want to ride with them into battle as well as disrespecting your noob♥♥♥♥♥in other ways, but as you rise in the ranks, you gain access to more weapons (not in a way that feels like CoD either. You really feel like you're becoming a seasoned soldier and you actually deserve it!), and you gain the respect of your fellow men, and can eventually command some of them in a polished squad system!
- Great inventory/armor and armory system. I can't elaborate on the details of it as I have not played enough to comment on this confidently.
- Includes the spontaneity and unpredictable nature of war without being scripted. 1 second, you might see your team driving up to battle in a truck full of troops, and the next, it's been nuked by a rocket launcher, but maybe one or two of your team mates escaped, and a group of enemies is pushing from the west of that truck, causing the survivors of the explosion to have to duck and fight from behind the scorched truck!
- Not all cover is polygonal, and cover can actually be deployed at any angle, likely at any place on land on the maps. This greatly diversifies the combat/cover experience, and serves to, again, increase the longevity of the game. I theorize that if you play this game long enough, you will have a hostile encounter on a line of sight/cover from all 360 degrees around you. The same cannot be said about most modern shooters even from AAA studios. You might shoot or get shot from all angles, but the difference here is you will have a meaningful gunfight on cover that is facing all directions/lines of sight, instead of standing out in the open relying on who saw who first.
- Stable, well-optimized game. I have yet to experience one bug or crash, and it runs well on my productivity laptop with integrated AMD graphics. I salute the developers for their hard work!
- Supported with regular content. Again, I salute the devs!
- Mod support through the Steam Workshop! Thanks devs!
Notes:
- Because of all the toys to play with, the game does have a bit of complexity, and a learning curve, but it can still be picked up and played by a patient noob.
- Matches or battles on each massive map can be long, and control over certain areas can rubber-band between factions like crazy. For example: My longest match on one map was 2 hours long, and my matches average to be about 1 hour long. (EDIT: As of editing this, I've been playing a map for the last 2 days with maybe 4 - 6 hours of gameplay with really slow progress, as there are 2 other factions in this area as opposed to just 1, and I have the game on a custom difficulty higher than the highest.) I personally love this as I've wished for awhile that there were more shooters out there with long, drawn out matches. Others might not like this, so it goes in the Notes section.
- Almost all of the sounds in this game are far from realistic. It gives the game a sort of toybox-like atmosphere. I wish it had realistic sounds, and I hope there's a mod out there for it, but I think others might like it. Also, this is not to say the sounds are bad. They still sound good, but they do not sound like genuine war sounds. I think this was intentional.
- Cartoon style, overhead art. I personally think the art style is great, but others may disagree.
- Man vs. World mode did not really appeal to me, to be honest. It's not bad, and some might like it, but to me it just feels like a tech demo of standard mode if a playerside team wasn't programmed yet. The toybox-like feel of the sounds keeps Man vs. World from feeling as bada** as it should in my opinion.
Cons:
- Not the most popular game in the world, so multiplayer is not exactly thriving, last time I checked. Although you can still find matches if you come at the right time.

Wolfenstein 2 picks up literally right after The New Order, and gives us another adrenaline fueled campaign that is a hell of a ride. If you're familiar with Doom 2016, then you'll feel pretty at home here.
Combat is fast paced, but not as aggressive as Doom, which rewarded you for pushing forward. You'll need to be somewhat strategic when making your move, and what weapons to use for the situation. The differing mechanics you'll be toying with due to story reasons are quite refreshing, but not as creative as Titanfall 2. At it's core, this is a run-of-the-mill shooter. However, I have a gripe with the pickup system. Sometimes, the game will automatically pick up armor and ammo for you, but you'll easily be finding yourself running out of ammo, multiple times in the same firefight. I wish that the ammo-pickup system could be more like Doom, instead of requiring you to keep pressing E to replenish your ammo, which feels very tedious.
Graphics, voice-acting, and facial animation is top notch in this, even in-game. It made me wonder at times why they'd even bother with pre-rendered cutscenes when the animations were amazing. Voice actors are spot-on, especially Brian Bloom, who reprises his role as main character BJ, or Terror Billy.
The story can have its predictable and cliche moments, but then there's other elements that are thrown in that are a welcome change, and kept me interested through my 8 hour playthrough. The villain, Frau Engel, who you contended with in The New Order, keeps flipping back and forth between a great and terrible character. There's times when her actions motivate you to keep pushing forward and killing Nazis, and then there's others when you just want her to go away so you can keep playing the story. Also, why does she repeatedly put her face within inches of BJ when he's slaughtered an entire room of Nazis? This happens multiple times in the story.
----SPOILERS AHEAD----
The elements of BJ dying, and needing to use the power armor at the beginning was a surprise. Unfortunately, when Caroline was killed in the second mission, it felt like something they just glossed over. I liked the elements introduced by the power armor, such as an increased armor capacity, the drop kick, and heightened speed. I also noticed my health only had a maximum of 50, and though that it would increase over time.
Then BJ gets decapitated, gets a new body, and now the health/armor capacities are at the normal 100/100. This entire story piece was fantastic, though they telegraphed the hell out of it by showing off Set's cat-monkey-thing.
However, the story isn't without it's faults. There was no mention of Hitler after the Venus mission. The segment with BJ and his father, though he got his "revenge," it still felt quite rushed, even though that was a stepping stone to BJ's capture. I felt that, after seeing how horrible of a father he was, that BJ's revenge would be a little more meaningful. This same problem also springs up at the very end when you kill Frau Engel, in a set piece that only lasts two seconds and then a cutscene. Yay, she's dead, but I didn't feel like the kill had much more impact than when I decimated hallways full of Nazis with shotguns.
Also, a very brief scene right near the end, what's the deal with pregnant Anya naked, covered in blood, and dual-wielding assault rifles? I wasn't offended, but just felt that it was added for some sort of shock value, which isn't really needed in a game that opens with your father forcing you to shoot your dog, which is a million times more of a mind ♥♥♥♥. It was just unnecessary.
There was also the hanging story thread of BJ's mother, who was said to have died in a concentration camp, and then we get no more reflection after that.
The story, while great, still feel like it had multiple people actually writing it, and each one of them was adding something completely different, while the project lead was high on cocaine and decided to approve all of it. The tone wasn't bad, but just something I couldn't grasp without something else popping up and changing the atmosphere.
---- SPOILER END ----

In Aerannis you play the assassin Ceyda Farhi, who takes on missions from Elsa Wetzer. With tasks ranging from basic assassinations, destroying documents, comfirming/retrieving information as well as tracking down someone kidnapped or freeing a prisoner.
You start out with most of your arsenal and stealth skills, including a chargable gun that can be fired as you jump or move around at three different heights (walking/crouching/sliding) and a pop bomb used to lure patrols away. You can simply shoot most of the critters, but humanoid enemies are often too tough to shoot your way through and stealth missions will actually require you to not get spotted by them or cameras. To take out humanoids quickly you will have to avoid or abuse making sounds to alert them and crawl through vents here and there. If they are not aware of your presence yet you can grab them from behind for an instant kill or push them around as a hostage to open doors and grant you cover.
As the game progresses your skill set will expand, adding wall jumps, ledge hanging, a sprint and a few different bomb types. The whole arsenal is a lot of fun to use. Only the bomb switching mechanic sticks out a little sore, as it has you popping out a wheel of the bombs around you with a button press, select the active bomb type by moving left or right and closing the wheel again with the same button.
Besides health refills enemies will also drop nano machines, which amount to your currency (nm). The only thing you can do with it though is purchase a single defense boost at a certain location in game and otherwise purchase health refills (half or full) directly from the pause menu. Considering the whole game can be played through entirely without buying such a refill it is probably a nice option for anyone having trouble getting past some areas. It does however feel weird if you abuse it to get through the hard mode (there are three difficulty settings which alter the damage from/to enemies and their vision range).
The world mostly consists of several very different city districts and a park, which in turn contain the level entrances (mostly buildings). You cannot enter any of these buildings (or new areas) prior to being directed to them through a mission and the city structure becomes irrelevant about 1/3rd into the game as several save points gain the option of fast travel between them. This however is a welcome feature as the game contains no back tracking and there would be no point in running through the same areas again and again. The game is very linear as all missions seem to happen in a very strict sequence and only the final mission branches out into two different endings.
Besides great platforming, shooting and stealth action the levels throw a huge diversity of music and boss battles at you. Contrary to common convention boss battles don't simply happen at the end of each level, but instead sometimes at the very beginning, upon a mission to revisit a level later on (save point teleport sparing you a rerun though) or even several times in a row. All of which is very refreshing for this kind of game. Not to mention boss battle types range from the traditional damage dealing over survival/escape to stealth.
The story and setting heavily revolves around LGBTQA issues without rubbing it in your face. So even if you have no idea what that means or generally try to steer clear of that topic the writing is so well done that you should be able to enjoy it in any case.
There are some technical issues with the game, most annoyingly text boxes prompting you to hit a key to advance advancing on their own after some time while some other text boxes with a count down cannot be skipped before it reaches 0. Since the game clearly is a work of passion though I expect future updates to iron out such details.

Wanderlust Rebirth is a challenging game that rewards the skillfull use of your character abilities, teamwork, as well as tactics. Failure is punished rather harshly but it does not make the game impossible. It instead forces you to learn from the mistakes made so you can become a better player. The community is great with very active developer support. The game is playable solo albeit more difficult (which is part of the fun!) but it really shines in multiplayer. The story is catching I find and overall rewarding to see all the way through.
The crafting system is where I had some frustrations due to limited carrying/storing space. It is not that bad though once you can move up the tiers of gear you use allowing you to free yourself of lesser materials. The game takes patience and should be expected to be a challenge.
One thing I have not tried a whole lot of is the PVP game mode. It can feature up to 8 players with two teams of 4. It is fun but with my limited experience in this particular mode that is about all I can say on it.
This game is for those who want that challenging arcade style feel with high score leader boards. Those that like to button mash so they can run and gun are probably going to feel lost.

Felt the need to write a review after playing through most of the game and being utterly disappointed. I've seen this touted as a Metroidvania and a stealth-action game, when really it's neither of the two. Rather, the game sends you on purely linear missions and each mission plays either like a level from Megaman X (action missions) or a level from Megaman X where every enemy that sees you insta-kills you ("stealth" missions). While your character does upgrade, the upgrade path thus far is entirely linear and the currency system in the game is rudimentary at best: the only items you can buy are health restores, and you can buy them anywhere, anytime.
The game feels like it has the bones of a much better game, they're just configured wrong. As a Megaman style run and jump shooter it could work, but the poor and unforgiving stealth system make it feel weak and thin. Additionally, the controls are poor on keyboard and not much better on a 360 controller.
Last but not least, the game has a bunch of current internet buzzwords like "special snowflake" and takes place in a world devoid of men, and so far I can't tell if it's supposed to be a shoutout to or a lampoon of tumblr / social justice culture. If you're not into either of those then steer clear.

Aerannis had some pretty interesting gameplay, writing, and art. There were moments where things felt tedious (certain bosses, rooms, finding areas) but overall the larger portion of the game was well done. You can tell the developers cared about their product.
Ultimately, when I think of what I would like a piece of gaming to be, I think Aerannis is a good example-a product that has charm, interesting gameplay, and ultimately feels like there was liberty in making it. Aerannis is the anti-thesis to the modern big box games.

Suprisingly excellent, is all I have to say about Darksiders 2. The Deathinitive Edition has drawn some controversy for having more issues than the base game, but I personally have had very few technical issues. The game consistantly runs above 100 FPS, however I did have to turn VSync on as I had a bug while climbing with an uncapped framerate.
Darksiders is a lot like a Zelda game with God of War style combat. Unlike its predecessor, Darksiders 2 really focuses on the RPG elements, with loot and an open world being added to flesh out the theme. The open world areas seem like a missed oppertunity, but they are a fair bit more interesting than any of the locations in the original game. The combat feels excellent, and much faster than the first game, Death is much more nimble than his brother War, whom you played as in Darksiders 1, and it really comes through in the combat. Rolling around and performing special moves on interesting and difficult enemies is a highlight of the game for me.
Platforming and puzzles is another area where the new movement really shines. Wall running and climbing all feel really polished and make traversing the world quite enjoyable. The puzzles are equally clever and just difficult enough to feel satisfying.
If I have any complaints it is that Darksiders 2 really likes fluffing out the world with side content that isn't of great quality. Nearly every NPC has a "pick up this" or "kill these things" side quest which feels like a way to justify the open world. In truth, I think that Darksiders 2 is neither helped nor hindered by its open world, I didn't feel compelled to explore it, but it rarely if ever felt like it was in the way. As a personal note, I found the ratio of puzzles to combat to lean a bit too far towards the former, but if you enjoy the more Zelda style game that shouldn't be an issue for you.
Despite those issues, Darksiders 2 is an incredibly solid game and a big surprise to me. The Deathinitive edition hasn't given me any problems personally and the base game alone is a killer value, not even counting the DLC included in this bundle. If you're a fan of third person action games, I recommend giving this one a shot.

This is a great game with a lot of potential. However there are a few things that could be significantly improved.
The feeling is of a shooter, fast paced but really strategic and positional at the same time. I have never seen anything like it. You need to keep your eyes opened for immediate threats as well as avoid getting slowly pushed into a corner. The powers available are really strong but they have limited uses and cannot be spammed thus strategic use of powers is essential for success.
You play as a nanobot inside an organism which in itself is already cool. You collect energy and can use that energy to spawn other helper bots. You can keep the bots out and they attack enemies (and you can no longer fire yourself) or you can pull them insisde the main nanobot and then you can fire on your own. The bots are stationary but their fire power is higher than your own. You can pull bots and redeploy them at will for kiting enemies. After a mission you can use energy to buy different helper bots. Advanced helpers come in two flavors, once you buy one helper type, the other type becomes unavailable for that playthrough.
You get three main powers:
-a stationary shield that blocks incoming enemies (except mini bosses and bosses) and projectiles
-a mine that explodes after a while
-a mist that freezes enemies it touches
Powers may interact, for example a mine detonation will break a stationary shield in smaller travelling shields.
The freeze power can freeze a shield altough I dont know how it actually changes the shield.
The game is highly positional which is good but the screen does not always move to keep the player ship in the center which is contradictory to the positional spirit of the game. I mean if you need to stategise you should be able to see what is ahead of you and not be surprized by it.
You have no control over firing. This is really annoying. I mean most bullets you fire have a travel time and you need to fire ahead of the moving enemies but you cannot as there is no fire button. Everyone that can fire, does so at the location of the cursor but they only fire if the cursor is over an enemy and only when the enemy is close to you. This makes it impossiblle to shoot ahead of a moving enemies or even shoot at enemies that you can see but are far away! This coupled with the fact that the screen is not always centered on the player makes for some very frustrating moments.
You can only spawn basic helper bots during figts! This is a major downside. This means that while you may have lots of energy available you cannot use that energy to revive your advanced helpers. This makes a loss of a helper snowball to a major inconvenience. Some helpers are damage dealers and usually losing one is not such a big deal but other helpers are strategic and their loss could mean defeat. For example you may start the level with 6 upgraded attack bots, 1 helper and 1 antimissile bot. The loss of an advanced attack helper can be somewhat replaced by spawing a basic attack helper but if you lose the healer or the antimissile you are basically screwed.
-The game crashes ocasionally with no reason
-I am currently stuck after defeating the freeze boss. It tells me to use the freeze power, I use it for a while and then the game cycles again to tell me that now I can freeze enemies...
-Make the player always be in the center of the screen
-Put in a fire button that the player can control. If the developers dont want players to snipe bosses from afar with no risk of exposing themselves then they could make the bullets dissapear after traveling a certain distance.
-Develop a mechanic to allow for spawing of advanced helper bots (that are already unlocked) - or at least a mechanic to spend energy to regain the bots that the player had at the start of the mission
-Eliminate the bugs that keep crashing the game
-Fix the issue preventing passing the freeze boss for some players
-Nice game idea.
-High potential not fully realised yet.
-Worth a buy but only at a discount. I got it at around 6 EUR but I think it should sell for less in its current state. It could be worth higher but only if the bugs and gameplay issues above are fixed.

This game and generally speaking the XIII series as a whole has divided the Final Fantasy fan base into two opposite groups. You will either love this game or hate it, there's no middle point. The first thing you need to know about the gameplay is the global Time-limit. That's right, you're given 14 in-game days to finish the game in the best case scenario and if you fail to do that (which is quite hard to do unintentionally to be honest), It's an automatic Game Over with an option to keep all your stats and items and restart the game.
But keep in mind that even though there is a time limit, you don't need to rush the game AT ALL. There is MUCH more time than you need to finish everything on your first playthrough. You can also freeze the time by using an in-game ability as well.
If you mostly play video games just for the story (like I do), then you're gonna be hugely disappointed in this game. The whole story revolves around an illogical concept which is pure non-sense. And I mean it in an objective sense. Basically, everything you do until the very end is completely pointless. Honestly, Lightning Returns has one of the worst plot I've seen in a long time and the ending is even worse. I'm not gonna spoil the plot so pet me put it this way. The ending will take everything you've done and throw it out the window, it would also ironically point out the fact that the whole story was intentionally nonsense and why.
On the bright side, Soundtrack is astonishing and gameplay is great. I would highly recommend Lightning Returns solely becuase of its gameplay. If you like to play good games, you should definitely play this. However, if you just want a good story, you would be disappointed.

Absoultely loved this game. Having played the first two entries on console, I missed out on this gem in that time. Glad I waited for this port. The visuals are great, with support for up to 4k displays (upscaled). The story was very easy to follow from the beginning. I felt like the whole 13 day time limit was a bit short and I would have to rush through the game to beat it but, that was hardly the case. The player is given 6* days initially and by completing side quests you essentialy are rewarded with more time, just know that the longer in the story you wait to complete main quests, the harder their respective bosses will become. All-in-all, I loved this game as well as the prior two games in the series. I haven't been so confused and emotional from a final fantasy ending since Final Fantasy 8, and it was a much welcome feeling. If you enjoy this franchise and dont let bad reviews get to you, you'll absolutely love this game. The included DLC is a much welcome bonus and will definitely help you out on at least the first half of your playthrough. Enjoy it!

Hellblade is more of an experience than it is a game.   It is well worth your time to immerse yourself in Senua's world.  Yes, it may be a little slow at times but take that moment to enjoy the fantastic artistry put into this game and what the designers have created.  This is the first title in a long time that actually grabbed me, made me want to work through the story, and see it to completion.  If you go into this thinking about constant action and interaction, you will be disappointed.  Listen to the story, view the harrowing experiences of psychosis, allow yourself to experience the visuals and audio (with headphones!) instead of running around looking for battles and achievement, and lastly, enjoy Hellblade for what it expresses.
The only negative I had with this was during some of the battles the camera swings into a position that makes it difficult to know where you're at, or that you've backed into a viking, ultimately leading to getting hit or even dying.

Heavily recommended. It's an artistic, terrifying, and moving experience with a video game built into it.
I'm quite used to playing horror games, but certain parts of this game were more atmospheric and terrifying than any horror game I've played. The developers really outdid themselves with a lot of the environments, too - especially the Lake of Fire...
The combat is fairly straightforward and becomes easy after a few fights, but you need to experiment a little with the controls while fighting to get the best advantage. There isn't a full tutorial but it's not difficult to master.
9.5/10. Would go through Hell again.

Con (note there's only one, but it was big enough for the thumbs down--I really want to give this game a thumbs up):
The biggest reason for the thumbs down is simply due to the feeling of hopelessness and dependency on a walkthrough just to complete the game.  It felt like a Roberta Williams game in the late 80s.  Bear in mind, I absolutely loved the King's Quest franchise, but I never would have been able to get far without external help and a walkthrough.  The problem is that it's 2017...  It's not that there's anything wrong with this game, but there absolutely will be several times in-game where you're clueless about where to go next for the sake of progression.  Frankly, I got to a point where I was no longer willing to waste my time backtracking for 10 minutes just to figure out a puzzle.  My frustration ultimately yielded impatience where I was YouTub'ng the walkthrough for the puzzle portion of the game as I did it.  That's the con.
Pros:
The voice acting, plot, and protagonist character development is phenomenal.  I absolutely loved the storyline.  If I wasn't distracted with the puzzle solving for 70% of the game, it would be even more so highly immersive (somewhat like Ryse: Son of Rome).  The problem with Hellbade is the jarring breaks from the addictive storyline juxtapose'd to mandatory puzzle-solving.
The combat was simple enough not to be repetitive yet very difficult for some fights to keep any player engaged.  I do wish there was a tad more complexity to the combat, but I'm not going to complain because the game is not a hack-and-slash.  It's more of a story-driven narrative with a hint of action/combat and a lot of problem solving.
I'm a fan of female protagonists, and I love the Celtic roots in the game.  Senua's character has at least one personality trait the player will be able relate to, and that's going to make you attached to her.  There was a great deal of psychology that went into this game.
Speaking of which, one of the unique traits of this game I thoroughly enjoyed was the entire psychosis aspect.  Hearing the abstract inner voices of the protagonist dictating conscious bewilderment, decisveness, argument, or flat out reflecting on what's being seen had a powerful effect on me.  You could hear the temptation of depression sink in along with some other disorders.  It is fun listening to those voices argue amonst themselves over whom is the most dominant Some of those voices change per situation, and it becomes freakishly eerie of foreshadowing in plot development.  Again, it's a great bonus!
Overall, I'm a fan of the game... I wouldn't discourage anybody to try it out at their risk after reading this review; however, I wouldn't recommend it simply to anybody without explaining the above first... If you do decide to go for it, I recommend getting ready to YouTube the puzzle portions of the game straight from the get-go.  Don't allow yourself to get upset or feel like the game was a waste when you can't get past the first puzzle... they're not all intuitive (and in some cases, the acceptance threshold is too low, so you may even walk right past the answer, attempt it, and see it fail thus giving you a false positive).

The elements of mental illness and various mythos is handled well and tastefully. The combat is simple but very strong and rewarding, the boss battles in particular were very enjoyable and challenging in a fair way, with unique mechanics for each encounter.

I'm not really sure how to describe this game. It's a unique experience. Atmospheric and immersive enough so that I went through a range of emotions while playing it. The performance from the voice actors, the innovative animations and directing also contribute to this effect.
This game is like nothing I've played before. It aspires to bring us an insight into the minds of people suffering from severe psychosis. I beat it in almost one sitting, even though I found some of the scenes rather disturbing. I don't know if I would go for a second playthrough at any point, but in any case it was well worth it for me. After all the best games are the ones that leave a lasting impact on us. And this one definitely does.

I normally don't review games, but this one... this one is something special.  Holy crap is it good!!  I'll start with the combat. The combat is a lot of fun. If you time your block correctly, you'll perform a parry and you can go to town on the enemies. You never take on too many enemies at once, but occassionally you'll be surrounded by 3 or so and things get hectic. There are voices in your head doing everything from mocking you to cheering you on and even saying helpful things like "look out behind you!" Between the voices and the enemies ganging up on you, you will feel anxious, but it's a good kind of anxious. It really is exhilerating. I wish there was a horde mode, because the combat is so damn good.  Buttclenching is the best way I can describe it.
In between the combat sequences, there is a lot of walking, but not much to explore.  You'll find some stones that tell you a bit of Norse lore, but other than that, the game funnels you down a set path. You'll encounter small enviornmental puzzles that require you to see patterns in the world around you. It's a really cool concept and I enjoyed finding the solutions.
The voices in your head will keep you company during these more isolated moments. I enjoy listening to each voice and trying to piece together what is happening in the story, why you are venturing down this path, and what happened in Senua's past.  I haven't beaten the game, so I don't know the answer to these questions yet. I'm really enjoying the ride so far.
I had a moment while playing the game where I said, "holy♥♥♥♥♥♥this game is increadible."  Since nobody was around for me to express these feelings, I decided I'd write a review.  There are so many small touches in this game that I didn't cover.  At one point during a boss fight the voices kept repeating a word, and then it clicked that what they were saying would help me to defeat the boss. It is so great that at one point the voices can be your friend, and at another they will encourage you to follow the wrong path.  It creates a constant cycle of causing you to doubt your beliefs and then reassuring them.  I don't have any experience with mental illness, but I can see how this type of disorder can have such am effect on people.

I shed a tear at the end and it had been coming for a while. To The Moon has an amazingly sweet story, with incredibly deep characterisation and a wonderfully woven story. Told over a period of many decades, each point visited or revisited in a non-linear fashion, I sunk into it more and more as the game went on. It features a high number of twists and turns and will keep you constantly guessing as to the next plot point. It hit every emotion I wanted it to hit, and drew laughter, confusion, sadness and joy, and everything in between.
Make no mistake, if you want a rich, beautiful story, play To The Moon. Play it for the story, because the gameplay itself is basic and simple, with no real difficulty as such. This is fine because this is how the developers intended it and it works well. With this in mind, think of To The Moon as an interactive story, which plays best with the mouse.
The plain graphics used are very pretty and paint the scenes well. The world, while often small, but intentionally so, is colourful and sets the mood of the game to a good extent. The music does an even better job of this and, besides the story, is probably the game's strongest point. Piano chords are used most of the time and really boost the atmosphere of the game to help bring out the emotions of the characters and amplify the nature of the setting. The music is very peaceful and helps you relax while you play, which fits well with the beautiful locations.
I would very much recommend To The Moon, especially for the price, and I'm not going to waste a moment in playing the second game.

If you are looking for a game with actual gameplay mechanics... you might want to look elsewhere.  This colorful anime style game is an "adventure lite" and has more in common with dating sims than even adventure games.  You are a high school girl with a little over a month for your last shot at forming a comedy club.  The goal of the game is to recruit at least 3 people for your club (up to 6) before May gets here, and clubs can no longer officially form at the school.  You accomplish this by talking to people and becoming friendly with them.  Starting a chit chat will give you a glimpse at the topics that they like the most so you can engage them in deeper conversations.  But no one wants to talk to someone who has no knowledge or interest of their beloved topics, so you have to level up your knowledge in the things they are most interested in.  You can do this in a variety of ways such as buying magazines to read before bedtime, catching a show at the cinema, watching tv, hanging out at the art museum, or visiting the school library.  Some of these things cost money to do, and usually the more cash it requires, the more skill you will get.  You get money by collecting bottles on the ground, or doing part time work at a few places around town.  Once you have leveled up your skills you can then work on trying to recruit your "comedy targets" so they will sign your paper, join your club and the ending is happy for everyone.  Leveling up with a friend opens up new cutscenes and gives you little insights to their life.
It's a lot of text, reading, guesswork and time management.  Engaging in conversation or working passes the time of the day, which brings you closer to the ending, whether you have recruited anyone or not.  That's where the time management comes in.  Do you try to become closer to a friend by talking to them?  Working at the shrine for money so you can catch that cinema show and level up your romance stat?  Occasionally there's homework to juggle too!
Cherry Tree High Comedy Club has interesting characters and a bite size play through time... I managed four recruits and completed the game around the three and a half hour mark.  Since it is so linear story driven, I can't see myself playing it again for some time, but others will likely want to dive right back in to try for the six recruits "perfect" ending.  If you enjoy dating sims or anime, this game has the tendrils to hook you.  The stories are well written and the translation is at times, quite amusing, being given a very robust translation.  There's controller and big picture support so you can potentially blow through this from the comfort of your couch.  I do wish there had been more variety in the game play, mini games would have broken up the tedium of chatting and time management, and having a wider cast of characters or more inventive ways to get to know them would have been fun.  Instead you are racing for the next conversational topic level... which is entertaining but there was a lot of potential here to be so much more.
Definitely worth checking out, even if just for it's cute quirkiness, if any of the above sounds appealing to you!

Cherry Tree High Comedy Club was a great experience for me. You play as a girl named Miley who's a bit of an oddball among her peers. She's a Senior in high school but still enjoys children's shows such as the "Hero Rangers". The objective of the game is to recruit at least three other people from your school to join your Comedy club by a certain date. I found each character to be pretty fun to get to know. There are plenty of video game references and pop culture, and lots of funny moments (Your trying to set up a comedy club after all) This game left me with a really good feeling, and I enjoyed every minute of the experience. Oh, and the music is great! As well as the 2D art style. You have the ability to move your character around in certain areas too which was nice, not something you get to do in most of the visual novels I've played. I highly recommend this game to somebody who likes slice of life and school themed anime's and wants to play a game with a positive and happy vibe.

The game is not nearly as bad as the vast majority of reviews suggest. I found myself enjoying a great deal of the game. If you have the time and money to invest there is definately some fun to be had.
However, I can't recommend this for several main reasons.
1) Who makes a game about exploration that has no mapping system what-so-ever? This is simply unforgivable. Find something interesting but can't use it at the moment? Too bad you will never be able to find it again. We need a mapping system that shows discovered POIs as well as user assigned waypoints and map notes, as well as a way to tell whether a POI has been explored already.
2) We fly spaceships around the galaxy but apparently no one knows how to make a basic compass. 12th century sea captains had access them, my 21st century cellphone has one. Why is this missing? Everything in the game is visual flight/dead rekoning only.
3) The economy system is horribly broken. The best way to make money by far is to sit in a station and buy arriving ships cargo then run to the trade station and sell their stuff for twice the price.
4) For a game that is all about flying around planets and landing on them - why in the heck can't I easily look DOWN? Didn't any of these spaceship manufactures ever get a request for a landing camera? Moms have these on their minivans so they don't back into the garage door FFS. Find something interesting fly near it and hit the LAND button and hope for the best. You might land where you want or you might fall into a canyon and be stuck. Oh and you use special resources for every take off so forget easily just taking off and moving your ship a little. I've even gotten my ship stuck on top of little elevations where it was difficult to even get back in the ship. Why don't we just have vertical thrusters like every other spaceship game ever made.

There are several bugs that completely destroy the player's ability to enjoy the game. For one, the game crashes regularly. Not only does it crash regularly, but apparently things like screen captures, switching windows, and the steam overlay all have the ability to crash the game and corrupt the user profile. Once corrupted, the game will lock out the user profile from achieving any further in-game perks or achievements.
According to forums, this is a common problem. You can attempt to revert to an earlier save, but many commenters have found that the only reliable solution is to delete all of your user files and to start the game from scratch. Keep in mind, if the game crashes again you may be back where you started. Make no mistake, there are a lot of players who are having this problem.
The game looks beautiful, the action is exciting, the world is interesting. I bet it's a great game, and I bet I would happily recommend it, if only I could get it to run. After my last crash, the game won't even start without crashing again.
--------------------------------
UPDATE
I have since been able to fix my game, but it did require digging into the config files and starting a new game from scratch, twice. I lost about 4 hours of gameplay each time. I am maintaining the thumbs down for two reasons 1) because this issue truly does break the game experience and has happened to a lot of people, and 2) because being forced to replay the first three or four levels of the game showed me that the campaign and story are no where near as deft or as compelling as New Order or even Old Blood. In fact, I would say my experience of playing the game twice instead feels like a chore. The story is (meh?), the side missions are a slog, there are too many cutscenes, and most of the maps are ugly (be prepared to spend the majority of your gameplay in decayed featureless buildings and sewers).
Like any well-made FPS, I will say that despite all of that it is absolutely worth one playthrough, but don't expect wanting to return to it for either the story or the action after you set it down for a while.
