This review contains spoilers.
--
I was browsing Facebook when I saw a friend put up a picture of the entrance to TERF turf, and somehow the game was purchased on my steam library twenty seconds later. It's magic, I tell you! Aerannis is a strange amalgam of extremely familiar elements. It reminds me of nothing so much as Hotline Miami (the frequent checkpoints in levels cause that comparison), and yet there are a lot of metroidvania elements as well.
The controls feel floaty, which can be frustrating. I had a few deaths to them - not too many, but a few. The frequent checkpoints help to mostly mitigate this.
The plot is very science-fictiony and ... underexplained [the other thing that harks back to Hotline: Miami for me]. I felt like there could have been a lot more to the story and world, and a lot more to the main character, who is very ... well, she's what you'd expect from a shooter protagonist outside of her gender. In this story, you're basically just doing the "talk to contact, go through world to do mission, come back to contact, do other mission" loop, and it's very ... apparent that this is happening. Even with the fun touches [e.g.: the first mission is "Figure out why people buy day 1 DLC"], it all seems oddly rote for a story set in a world where there are no men in apocalyptic surroundings. You're forced through a linear path, and that path feels ... incomplete, or at least it did to me.
There are multiple endings, but you can see both of them almost immediately at the end, which I thought was a nice touch. The endings themselves ... are a bit of a lucid dream, as the rest of the plot is. To be honest, I don't think the art style does the game any favors in this area (and goodness, the elevator sprites are almost seizure-inducing), but there could have been more done, just in general, to flesh out the world.
In the end, I would rate this a maybe, but there's just a yes or no option. Upon finishing the game (it took ~6, 7 hours?) ... I didn't love it. It feels serviceable. If you love the subject matter, you won't regret buying it (I don't regret buying it). But I ended the game wanting more from the game than what I got - a character that isn't content to just follow what their handler says forever, a story that's more fleshed-out ... I wasn't really able to connect with the main character in the story. The small throwaway bits are consistent and then the larger bits didn't ... feel that way, to the setting and the story, to me. I felt along for the ride, like my actions weren't doing anything in the story - like I was watching an oddly-paced 8-bit movie about the Illum(inati) and Gods, Devil May Cry-style. And the action isn't good enough to compensate.

The Goods:
+ The best PC port of the trilogy
+ Open world; to be able to explore around is big in RPG
+ Dressing up Lightning for status boosts is actually fun
+ Semi-real time combat; you actually need to time your blocks
+ Some really nice tracks in the OST
The Mehs:
- Bad storytelling; speaking too much in philosophical terms
- Status up relies on completing side-quests that are mostly not related to the story
- Limited character growth; can't really relate to the characters unless you are a Lightning fan
- The concept of a real-time time limit is not really necessary; you have more than enough time to complete almost all of the quests in one playthrough, yet you feel rushed because there are time-restricted areas. But in the end most players will end up with a couple of days with really nothing to do. The concept of doing the quests in any order you like is nice though.

This is a very tough negative review for me to write, because Lightning Returns does so many things right but it also narrowly misses on some very important things.
Lightning Returns succeeds on every technical level.  The graphics are gorgeous, the music is good, and LR has received the best PC port of any Square Enix game to date. It runs flawlessly and even has full Japanese interface available for bilinguals like myself. It is by all means an excellent game on many fronts, and a drastic improvement over its predecessors.
That said, Lightning Returns is direly lacking in both story and gameplay depth. Let's start with the story: It is quite simply eye-rollingly bad. Almost every single line of dialogue is hopelessly contrived at best and laughable at worst. In the interest of avoiding spoilers I'm not going to go too far into details, but my eyes start to glaze over when the major characters are all constantly making melodramatic monologues about how they've been lovesick for 500 years.
To make matters worse, everyone's problems that they've been dealing with for 500(!!) years are MAGICALLY resolved by Lightning Ex Machina because all it takes is a 10 minute chat with Lightning and maybe a fight or two and all 500-year-long issues are instantly resolved. There is no nice way of saying it: it's awful writing that makes Lightning come dangerously close to Mary Sue territory. Which is a real shame because I love Lightning and she has some genuinely great moments.
Another massive issue is that the game is very short. Imagine my surprise when I checked a FAQ to see my progress about 10 hours in and discovered I was over 40% done with the main quest. The main story is astonishingly short and then you're supposed to spend the rest of the time running around doing random side quests before the final boss.
Then there's the battle system. At first blush it seems quite engaging and deep but the problem is that this is actually a massive façade. There is in reality very little strategy or depth to the system at all. I kept waiting for them to introduce new elements that mix it up or keep things interesting but it pretty much stays the same way through the entire game, and that boils down to this:
A) Read stagger conditions/try to stagger the enemy
B) Block when they attack
That's literally it. Stagger conditions and weaknesses vary depending on the enemy but for the massive majority of the game you can get by just spamming whatever and blocking occasionally and you will be fine. I really feel like if the player had been given FULL control of Lightning in battle instead of very limited control that it could have introduced a new dimension of depth to the game that would have kept it feeling fresh.
Overall I have to say though that Lightning Returns is a beautiful game that does so many things right but falls tragically short of being a great game. It may be the right game for someone else, but it just left me wanting more.

The first CoD game I ever played. I originally owned this on PS3, and instantly fell in love with a campaign like no other I'd played so far. The back-to-back missions "All Ghillied Up" & "One Shot, One Kill" are two of the most iconic singeplayer missions in my memory. I had no prior knowledge of Chernobyl, and these levels inspired me to learn more about it.
The entirety of the campaign is a blast, with varied settings and encounters. There's stealth sections, all-out assault sections, ambushes and more. There's also a few collectibles in each level. If you find enough of these, you gain access to cheats, such as a "bullet-time" style slow down ability, unlimited ammo and more; it's not huge, but it's fun feature that brought me back time and time again. The story is interesting, and you'll get a real sense of camaraderie as you work through the levels with the stories characters. All in all, this is worth a buy if only for the singleplayer campaign. The game still has an active community if you're looking to play online too.
The multiplayer offers even more in terms of gameplay and progression. The game has fantastic movement, with none of the wall-running or jet-packs seen in more recent CoD titles. It's a simple acradey shooter, with satisying gunplay and a surprissinlgy deep progression system. There's a good amount of customization in the Create-a-class system with unlocks, various gun camos and guns/perks unlocked via level progression. I logged many hours on this on console, and can't recommend the game enough.

If you're looking for a game that has the linear progression and difficulty from the late 80's - early 90s, this is it. It's a single player, learn through attrition type game. Some stages are top view and some are side scroller.
Pro:
It's difficult. I enjoyed that about the game because a lot of what's out there now tends to just hold your hand through progression without any real threat.
It looks nice. The visuals are nice. It reminds me of Ultratron in color and art style.
Cons:
It's single player. The game does market that and it plays well, but a CO-OP mode would be nice.
Very linear. The only choices you really make are based on which unit you select for each tier. Auto-rockets or sniper? Machine gun or shot gun?
No story at all. Nothing that gives you a purpose or understanding of what you're fighting or doing. Units don't have names, enemies don't have names.
In the end, I say it's a good game. 9.99? not really. I'd rather spend 4.99 for it. It's a good casual game to mess around on but it needs some specific things to go anywhere.
1- Achievements. Seriously how did this not happen?
2- Name the units and add an almanac with unit & enemy info
3- Stage select. Being able to replay some stages would be nice without starting all over.
4- Endless mode. Time Trials. Leaderboards.
5- Some sort of story.

I can't recommend Zigrafk in its current form, but it's a great idea. Why not bring the loot-filled fun of "Torchlight" or "Borderlands" to the space-sim genre? The notion is brilliant, because it can, in theory, speed up the "go on missions, upgrade your ride" loop to a lightning pace. (And it can also create some very zany ship loadouts.)
The problem here is not the lack of a novel idea. No, the problem is the execution of the flying and fighting. Zigfrak delivers a disappointing experience on those fronts, with strange ship handling and uninspired "dogfight" mechanics. There's also the problem of all the HUD displays that pop onto the screen, covering a huge amount of visual real-estate with what amounts to database entries. These elements, as drivers of the wider loot mechanic, have to be a lot of fun...but they aren't yet. They feel like they didn't get very much attention.
What I would love to see Entheogen do would be to mod a game that already has fun combat and flight mechanics. A specialized loot installation, modification, and crafting mechanic could be built for stations and planets, making that part of the game a focused experience all on its own.
The problem with a negative critique is that you're essentially shooting down somebody's hard work. I especially hate to do that with something like this, which tries to go in a bold direction. The developers have come up with an underlying concept that I really want to play - it's just that the actual playing isn't engaging.

Absolutely had to post a review of this game. It's taken me a while post completion to properly digest it. At completion I felt relief, sadness, frustration, elation and confusion. I literally needed a couple days to let it settle.
Firstly the positives.
+The graphics are excellent fot the most part. There are a few odd low res textures here and there, but generally it is visually stunning, Senua has been motion captured from an actress for everything and it is next level beautiful. The scenery and sets are beautifully imagined.
+The sound is the game. Seriously. The music, the sound effects, the voices in your head, the other voices. It's all just mind blowing. I think the fact that I own a great set of AKG headphones really sucked me into the game much more.
+The game plays visual and audible games on you to to transport you to a different reality. Using those tools it makes you feel vulnerable and fearful without any actual real threat at times. It plays on euphoric colourful highs, crushing monochrome depressing lows, clear earthly normality and the depths of hell. It really shows how someone suffering metal illness can change their outlook so quickly.
+Really, when you peel it all away this is just a love story. Anyone that has truely loved someone knows how much you would fight to keep from losing them. Forgetting the mental illness angle, this game is actually about accepting loss,

- Combat is a bit uninspiring at times. Sometimes really easy, sometimes not. Sometimes genius like the boss hiding the shadows that you have to listen for.
- Its quite short. 10 hrs and I don't know if I'll ever play it again. That said at the end of the game I was relieved it was over. The constant voices in your head. The twisted perception of reality. It started to grate at my mind. Those of you out there that suffer from delusions and paranoid schizophrenia, you are tough people to keep it going. Stay strong.
Overall an utterly fantastic game. It really isn't an easy experience but it really an essential one. The emotion and story makes this a definite game of the year for me.

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is a journey.
It's a Journey, not only in a game, but also, through the mind. It takes themes like depression, anxiety and psychosis, and puts it in the centre. It isn't afraid to push emotional boundaries, nor is it afraid to play with your psyche.
It's a psychological thriller that puts the main protagonist literally through hell to get back her lover, after he's dead. Senua is heart-broken, and can't deal with the fact that her lover is dead, so she decides to pay the world of the dead a visit to get him back. Senua's a broken character. She suffer from severe psychosis, and all we see in the game, is from her perspective. There are demons, gods, voices, and illusions, and you have to go through it all alongside her.
The graphics are state of the art, as is the gameplay, but the audio is where this game really shines. Utilizing binaural audio, the game has a tendency of screwing with your brain, always second-guessing whether or not you should go on, and helping/sabotating when the stakes are high.
I'd recommend this game to anyone. Doesn't have to be a gamer. It doesn't take any gaming knowledge to pick this up, as gameplay and combat are fairly straight-forward. It's an experience unlike anything else I've ever had, and I'd love to go at it again blank, having no prior experience with it. It's a mind♥♥♥♥ of an experience, and I'd give it 100/100, or even three-fiddy out of three fiddy.

This is because RUNNING WITH RIFLES is different for quite a few little reasons like it's hardcore gameplay, large environments, xp and currency, loot, smarter than usual AI, and unrestricted playstyle. Yes other top down shooters have these as well, however I have yet to see one put all of these into cohesive action. If some way I have already unintentionally swayed you to get this game please download and play the free demo first, because it is s****y to buy a game, find out you do not like it, and post a negative review to establish some sense of false self-pitying justice. That helps no one, otherwise we are now off to the magical land of greater detail.
I mentioned hardcore gameplay and you have probably wondered (or still wondering) what that meant while I was rambling like a parrot that just snapped about being called pauly and if they want a cracker to go with their subservience... sorry. Here hardcore means you sometimes die from one bullet, and sometimes meaning armor allows you to 'take' more lethal hits and each weapon has a kill probability (mathematics time). Assault rifle1 has a kill probability of 80%, 100-80=20% chance of bulletA not killing you+low tier armor vest=100% chance of bulletA not killing you or 20% chance of bulletA not taking your armor out of the equation. Stick some knives (which ignore armor) in and throw grenades, other explosives, and many other guns and bullets, in there lies the hardcore gameplay. Simple with alot to it when you start thinking dangerously. Speaking of thinking danger the AI thinks about it all the time, when various metals are being tossed about they scramble for all available cover such as boulders, buildings, cars, cars that just blew up, your tank that just blew up, and many other things many of which surprised me about how good the npcs are at taking cover. This is how RUNNING WITH RIFLES hards it's core.
As you play you kill, and as you kill you get xp that ranks you up and allows access to more radio calls and more AI squad followers. You will also get in-game currency (don't panic there are no fee-to-pay dumps here) which you will need for all your equipment (again don't panic standard equipment is very effective and cheap). You can get more via selling loot to armories like cigarettes, portable gaming and music devices, alcohol, gems, and more... and a... sex toy of the for females variety... yeah... this... thissss... was my reaction in a nutty shell... very nutty. Now what else is nutty is how long a battle can last. Most maps must be won by taking bases, to take a base your side needs atleast a two-thirds majority inside the base for a short while (we are looking at seconds yet much can happen in that time). Stalemates will happen, deadlocks over the same base for half of an hour, two hours, five hundred dead bodies... so many dead... ideals are peaceful, history is violent, a whole squad is not worth one guy, you are the man with the gun, Custer was a p****y.

First and foremost:
If your headset is configured for surround sound, TURN IT OFF.
I played through about half the game with 7.1 headphones, and while it was decent, it never felt 'right.'  I turned it off, rebooted the game, and was blown away.  To the point where I may go back and play through again in the near future, just to re-experience the game how it was meant to be.
Hellblade is not a game about leveling up your stats, or getting a better sword, or a bigger gun.
It's a game that's supposed to make you feel like Senua. Batsh*t crazy.  And it does a damned good job of it.  The skeleton of the game (wandering around, finding sigils, fighting enemies) is all well and good. But I really don't think it's the point.
There were times when I found myself talking -back- to the voices in the game.
There were times when I would turn my head because I forgot the voice was in my headphones.
There were (many) times when the game got to me.
And -that- is the point.
There were a few points that were frustrating; mostly when I couldn't line things up just perfectly to unlock the sigil. Or when an unlocked door wouldn't be opened by Senua because I wasn't standing -just so- in front of it.
But, I'll happily take a few minor problems for what this game provides.
10/10 would recommend.
And while this game may be triggering for some, I think it helped me understand some aspects of mental health that I didn't quite understand before.

I jumped into Running With Rifles at the end of it's Early Access period, after playing the demo.
The idea is simple - you are a soldier, on a battlefield, in of one of 3 armies, and your army has to conquer the battlefield by taking all the points. When you die (and you will die, lots), you spawn as a new soldier (but you don't lose any of your XP or stats), and you carry on. There are a variety of weapons at your disposal, and you can drive a range of vehicles, including tanks. In Single Player, you can buy weapons with money and loot you find on the battlefield, and you gain XP and RP to level up the ranks too. The higher your rank, the bigger squad you can manage. Oh and as you get higher in the ranks, you get access to better air drops and air strikes. Multiplayer has a similar system.
On the battlefield, you can do whatever the hell you like. Want to go and support those soldiers over there trying to take that point? go for it. Want to go lone soldier? No problem. Take a tank, drive into the enemy base, running over anyone that get's in your way, including your own squad? Sure thing. Think of it as a "battlefield sandbox".
And that is why I love this game. You will die a lot, sometimes constantly when the heat of battle turns up, but it's a game that doesn't take itself too seriously and allows you to play it how you want to play it.
My experience in multiplayer is generally a positive one, although as a new player my advice would be to stick with the other players and do not drive the spawn truck into the heat of battle. Stick to that rule and you'll be fine.
If you want to try it out, check the demo out - it's the demo that sold it to me and it's a bargain at usual price (even bigger bargain at 50% off).
Highly recommended.

I avoided buying this game when it was first released due to all of the negative news surrounding it.
But I recently got it, and with all the free content updates that the developer has put out, along with all the free mods you can find online, I can honestly say No Man's Sky was worth the money for me. It manages to capture the feeling of wonder when you first land on a planet and explore it for the first time, whether it be a snowy ice planet, or a lush earth like planet, its given me hours upon hours of fun.

The game is not nearly as bad as the vast majority of reviews suggest. I found myself enjoying a great deal of the game. If you have the time and money to invest there is definately some fun to be had.
However, I can't recommend this for several main reasons.
1) Who makes a game about exploration that has no mapping system what-so-ever? This is simply unforgivable. Find something interesting but can't use it at the moment? Too bad you will never be able to find it again. We need a mapping system that shows discovered POIs as well as user assigned waypoints and map notes, as well as a way to tell whether a POI has been explored already.
2) We fly spaceships around the galaxy but apparently no one knows how to make a basic compass. 12th century sea captains had access them, my 21st century cellphone has one. Why is this missing? Everything in the game is visual flight/dead rekoning only.
3) The economy system is horribly broken. The best way to make money by far is to sit in a station and buy arriving ships cargo then run to the trade station and sell their stuff for twice the price.
4) For a game that is all about flying around planets and landing on them - why in the heck can't I easily look DOWN? Didn't any of these spaceship manufactures ever get a request for a landing camera? Moms have these on their minivans so they don't back into the garage door FFS. Find something interesting fly near it and hit the LAND button and hope for the best. You might land where you want or you might fall into a canyon and be stuck. Oh and you use special resources for every take off so forget easily just taking off and moving your ship a little. I've even gotten my ship stuck on top of little elevations where it was difficult to even get back in the ship. Why don't we just have vertical thrusters like every other spaceship game ever made.

Complete a pink puzzle and get access to the lead synth, do another pink and get echo control over said synth. If you're into getting lost in an abstract aesthetic, get FRACT.
If you're into getting lost in a step sequencer for hours at a time, get FRACT.
If you're into puzzles and stuff, get FRACT.
Just...  Get FRACT, yo.

The game, while a fantastic voyage via puzzles does a great job of explaining nothing, it also hits you with so much colour that the next step that you could or should be going isn't always clear. While this is clearly to allow you the freedom to explore wherever you want to go, it is at times more overwhelming instead of the freedom of exploration. I know I'll be playing more of this title, to better understand and uncover more of what FRACT has to offer.

Aerannis is a fun and beautiful story-driven action adventure game that keeps you interested with both story and gameplay.

Aerannis is a short, bittersweet Metroidvania with stealth elements. The control scheme is unintuitive on the keyboard, which is what I played the game using. Glitches are rare, and when they occur they're rarely gamebreaking. Hitboxes for certain actions, like grabbing enemies and ledges, are odd and often difficult to predict.
The story takes place in the Bulgarian city of Plovdiv where men have been eliminated, a revolution somehow forcing all men to undergo hormone replacement therapy, and relegating them to second class citizenship. "Snowflakes" as they're called are reviled by society, treated as little more than potentially violent pretenders only good for reproduction. You play Ceyda Farhi, a Bulgarian Turk who works as an assassin. She was also a transwoman before the revolution occurred, and due to her status as a transwoman only finds illegal work available to her. The story features intense discussions of feminism, particularly factions within feminism, and the place transwomen have in feminism. The game features two endings, one of which feels out of left field and the other more in line with the story we've been told.
A big issue with Aerannis is that it's short, I completed the game in seven and a half hours, and I'm sure a quicker run is possible.
I highly recommend Aerannis based off its story, gameplay, and the setting behind. I feel like Aerannis is a testament to what indie developers can accomplish without the pressure of executive meddling forcing them to make the next AAA title.
A warning: Aerannis features transphobic language and ideas at times, and anyone sensitive to these topics may want to keep this in mind while playing the game.

You alternately sneak, kill, and SneakyKill(tm) your way to the goal while carrying out missions in an oppressive feminist future society. Yes, you read that right.  We need more games like this that actually take risks with the setting instead of having every scifi game basically stealing the universe from Blade Runner.
The social commentary and humor are where the game really shines.  The dialogue is witty, references to other projects and jabs at extremist feminism and the gaming industry are plentiful, and the memes are spicy.
If the game has one shortcoming, it is the palpable lack of wacky waving arm-flailing inflatable tube men.  The devs really should have foreseen this problem and I hope it will be fixed in an upcoming patch or reasonably priced DLC.  Horse armor would also be a good, but less necessary addition.

First of all, I haven't played the other two XIII games on Steam, though I've read that there were various problems with their PC ports. Lightning Returns has run pretty much flawlessly, and I assume Square Enix put more effort into this port.
The game is set roughly 500 years after the events of XIII-2, where Lightning is brought back to save the world. Lightning is the sole character you get to play as, though you get a couple of party members for certain areas during the course of the story. The story mainly revolves around Lightning saving the souls of the people that are left, and using this to lengthen the time the world has left, as well as strengthen herself.
Like the previous games, theres a system quite similar to paradigms, though in this one they're called "Schemata". These schemata are based around different garbs that Lightning collects and wears, each having different stats and giving certain advantages (i.e. giving different values for Strength and Magic, ATB speed etc). You also collect different weapons, shields and tokens which give certain benefits (again, Strength, Magic etc) so you use these to benefit different situations. Unlike paradigms, abilities aren't confined to certain schemata (for example, you could use Fire with Guard or Attack).
Combat has also been changed for this game. Lightning still makes use of an ATB gauge during the battle, though each of her different Schemata has an independant ATB gauge that refills at different rates. Each schemata is limited to four abilities, which the player chooses (though certain garbs come with abilities that can't be changed). Unlike the other games, you don't "lock in" the abilities that you're using and pick which enemy to use them on. If you're using an Xbox 360 controller (which I am), you can use each of your four abilities using either A, X, Y or B, and targets can be changed using the D-Pad. Guard abilities (Mediguard, Heavy Guard etc) play an important part of combat. As well as reducing damage, guarding precisely at the point when Lightning is struck can (most of the time) completely negate damage. Guarding also plays a role in staggering foes (more below). Lightning can also be moved around the battlefield (albeit slowly), though the effect this has on combat is almost negligible in most situations.
Staggering is still important in combat. Most enemies have different conditions for stagger, which can be viewed at any time during the battle if Lightning has either staggered them using this condition, or has bought notes that give her strategies for different enemies. Certain abilities increase an enemy's stagger percentage (like Ravager abilities, Fire etc), and others can maintain the stagger (like Ruin). Certain enemies can also be staggered by guarding their attacks at the precise moment they strike. Personally, I feel that staggering is more strategic in this game, as with many strong enemies they can only be staggered during certain situations (spamming magic abilities won't always work).
So, most importantly, the main storyline and quests in this game are far different than its predecessors. There are four areas, each with their own Main Quests which Lightning must complete to progress through the storyline. These areas are also littered with Side Quests, which, arguably, are just as necessary for completing the game, as every quest completed will increase Lightning's various stats, as well as increase the size of her ATB gauge and recovery item capacity. The quests can range from finding different items, killing enemies or returning to a quest giver on sequential days. The game also features a day/night cycle, where different areas can be accessed at different times, and certain quest givers will only be available during certain times.
So, my personal Pros/Cons:
Pros
- Combat is much more "active" in this game, not that I didn't enjoy it in the previous games
- The Story, for the most part, I enjoyed, though it can get a bit cheesy
- Choosing schemata for combat requires strategy and planning
- A wide range of garbs, weapons and shields are available, which allow plenty of customization for different roles and situations.
- Many, many side quests, which could get tiresome for some people, but I personally enjoyed finding and completing them
- The return of some old friends
Cons
- Some enemies are ridiculously hard if you don't have impeccable timing and planning
- Most enemies can be made "extinct" in the game if they are grinded enough. Once enough of them are killed, a "Last One" variant of an enemy will appear which is more powerful than regular enemies and will drop an item. Grinding these can be very time consuming and boring, and unfortunately killing all of them is required for an achievement, though grinding is not entirely necessary depending on how much time you have by the end.
- Very rare FPS drops
- Some garbs look absolutely awful
EDIT:
I've also read that your computer must be connected to the Internet while playing the game (something to do with cloud saving), which is kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥, but if your computer is always connected like mine is, it shouldn't be a problem.

(I originally played Lightning Returns: Final Fantasy XIII on PS3.)
What an intersting way to end the FFXIII trilogy. I spent most of time this game confused, but never bored. The story reaches critical mass as time has stopped still in the world and everyone is doomed to witness the end of the world. It's Lightning's job to be God's (Bhunivelze's) chosen savior and bring everyone's soul to the Ark to guide them to the new world. In true Final Fantasy fashion, Lightning eventually learns that everything is not as it seems.
Combat is Lightning solo, no companions, but similar to the paradigm shift system, you can customize her with three schemata (costumes) that each contain different abilities and act on their own independent ATB bars. The difficulty on Normal is actually rather challenging, and if you don't strategize effectively even the non-boss encounters may give you grief. It feels like Dark Souls-lite at times.
Voice acting (starring Ali Hillis as Lightning, whose credits also include Liara from Mass Effect!) in this game is well done, the presentation is phenomenal. I loved how I got the sense of how the world was dying and the despair from the people who lived in it. There aren't many locales in this game, but hearing the stories from all of the people in Nova Chrysalia made the world intersting.
I recommend this to anyone that has played the other two games and wants to bring the story to a conclusion.

Compared to the Warmastered edition for the first game, the Deathfinitive edition for this game kinda sucks. First off there isn't an FOV slider, even though Warmastered has this, and I'm guessing it's because most of the dungeons take place in small areas and tight corridors and there's also certain parts with fixed camera angles. Anyways the current FOV is so small that it gives me a headache after a while, especially when there's a stuttering problem that you have to fix outside of the game itself.
They also added in a Diablo/Borderlands style of loot gameplay where you pickup hundreds of different armor pieces and weapons that you have to look through in your inventory constantly so you can decide which ones have the best stats which I personally don't like. Combat is fluid and there's a decent number of combos and spells, but most of the tougher enemies can't be staggered and/or attack very quickly and you can only dodge (no block or parry) so you'll be spamming the spells and doing the dodge attack for most enemies.
There's also a ton of bugs ranging from audio completely turning off for no reason, being stuck in cinematic mode, and the occasional crash. The game dips in frames a few times also.
Aside from those negative points I really do enjoy the soundtrack for this game, especially over the first game, and most of the level designs. Whoever made the Earth level for this game though should REALLY be fired. The puzzles and secrets start out pretty simple as well, but the secrets can get really tricky later on (which is good) and there's minimal back-tracking too.
Death is a great character as well; he's funny, but not completely edgy or super wacky and is still serious.
Buy the bundle when it's $15.

The story is compelling and you'll soon find yourself compassionate for Senua.

But most importantly I feel like I learned something about life itself, it changed my perception of Schizophrenia and I do believe that it helped me understand people suffering from mental illness.
I hope that Hellblade also helps people ease their suffering and let's them realize that they are NOT alone.
But like every piece of art, there will be people who won't understand it or just simply won't care and that is okay.

Long story short, this is probably my second favorite single player experience ever. Only Bioshock (1 and 3, IMO) tops it.
Headphones are truly a must in order to get the full experience of the voices in your head. The best moments of the game, for me, are when you are being overwhelmed by enemies and the voices are right there with you, both mocking and helping you at the same time. The music in some of these sequences, especially towards the end of the game, is masterfully chosen. You might even shed a tear near the end. This game makes you feel what Senhua feels in a way few other games can match. This is one of those games where the title "gaming as art" is appropriate.
For me, the main downside of the game was that some of the puzzle sequences were tedious, too difficult (in a not fun way), or weren't intuitive / seemed like I solved it just based on luck. There were multiple occasions where I just wanted to get past the puzzle I was on so I could get back to the real game / story.
If I had to sum it up in one line, I went back and played the final fight three times. I don't think I can say that about any other game.

I've anticipated this game's release for quite some time now, and I'll start this off by saying "WOW!".
FRACT OSC is a very abstract musical first-person adventure game that engages you in 3-dimensional puzzle solving, with the end goal of being able to unlock various synth engines to play around with and create your own music.
I can say I haven't completed the game, but I've played enough of it by now to get the general jist of it. I will say that while playing this game, you will spend a considerable amount of time scratching your head. It will often fool you into thinking you've solved the puzzle before you realize you're trapped and you have to disassemble the entire thing to escape or move on to the next level. This is good though, because it forces you to rethink everything so that you can separate yourself from the obstacles and move on to the next task.
If you're a "first-person adventure" fan, the first thing that you will find troubling is the fact that you cannot jump. I don't know why they didn't add the feature, but in a world with various shapes and horizontal planes sitting at different levels, you'll find yourself wanting to skip walking around everything and hit spacebar to jump -- only to find it isn't working. I'm kinda hoping they'll include it in a later patch. ;)
There's also various (already obvious) bugs that will probably be fixed later on. You will notice yourself falling through platforms, sometimes at random. Luckily you'll respawn back at the puzzle you were last at or pathway you were last exploring, but I think it has something to do with the mis-interaction with different solid planes. You can also accidentally stumble upon further levels while exploring, but you can't interact with them until you advance far enough with the ones before it.
All in all, it's a stunning addition to the adventure game collection and I can't wait to get further into it, perhaps playing around the the music studio feature more.
It's kinda like Myst and Starseed Pilgrim had a child, who then got into ambient techno when they reached their teens and started hanging out with Fez.

Do you want a cool puzzle game? How about a synthesizer? How about both?
Tron meets Myst (minus the reading) meets electronic music with your own custom synthesizer, much like those boxes featuring a grid of buttons where you can just push a few random ones and end up with a rhythm you can dance to.
The game world itself is lovingly crafted, with puzzle areas corrosponding with the musical tones the puzzles interact with and ultimately unlock in your personal synthesizer.
Many of the pieces of the puzzles correspond to the sounds and music around you, as well as the controls featured on the synthesizer.
Minor performance issues do exist, such as the occasional sudden chugging as it loads an area of the world in the distance, though considering the high system requirements of the synthesizer, I'm surprised it runs smoothly on my ancient Intel Core 2 Duo.

You are seemingly teleported into a Tron-esque world with neon colors amid a gloomy atmosphere.  From here you start an explorative journey into a world where every crystal, rock, and mechanism is generating melodies out of musical pads, synths, and bass. Some of the puzzles can by tricky as there are only context clues to help guide you through, but playing with the mechanics will quickly provide environmental feedback. This game has lots of charm and the completion of each puzzle only makes the journey seem that much more exciting.
I highly recommend this game to anyone especially if you like Myst style games, puzzlers, or just want to immerse in a strange world.

The music is absolutely amazing, I'm not really into music but all of soundtracks are quite enjoyable (I like Paradigm Shift the most)
Customization -
The system is great, being able to change the outfit of your choice as well as having the option to customize most part of it's colors is great, I did spend some time figuring out what color and adornment the outfit would look better with. Not to mention the weapon/shield diversity.
Battle -
I enjoyed every single monster encounter I had in this game, the battle musics are catchy and the ATB system certainly is different for me, at first it was somewhat confusing and yet frustrating, but once you get used to it you just enjoy it. The skill effects look amazing too.
Main Story -
Simple and straightforward. The game is mostly focused on questing than anything else. Unfortunately there's nothing much to mention in this, it IS good though.
Sub-quest -
Even though most of them are quite bland with all the 'kill this' or 'gather this' that most generic RPGs have, the rewards actually make up for it. As an achiever, collecting items and prizes is one of the most rewarding things to me. I even got upset once when I realised that I have missed a quest and I cannot take it any longer.
Challenges:
Bosses are quite challenging, you rather be well prepared or you have to know what you are actually doing in order to take them down. I haven't beaten the superbosses yet and I think I won't, I'm leaving that for the NG+, once I get geared enough.
CONS:
Controls -
I do not own a controller so I had to play on the keyboard and it's upsetting. The game has so many commands that it is impossible to reach all of them with ease during the gameplay, I have totally given up on using the camera movement one, for example.
Overworld -
I really expected the game to be actually bigger. Having only four different zones did not really satiate me.
I have defeated the last boss once however I moved back to my previous save state to finish the remaining quests. I can say that having spent 60 hours over the first playthrough was enough time to enjoy what the game has to offer.
Right now I'm at Medium difficulty and I'm totally salivating over the NG+ Hard difficulty. I'm also interested on getting the previous games as well.
Do I recommend this game? TOTALLY.

The New Order remains one of my favourite games for it's  charm and the depth of it's characters. The New Colossus is dumbed down, sillier and a good way less charming, to the point that I mostly felt disapointment playing it through.

Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus feels less like a good fps and more like a bad stealth game. The difficulty has been increased exponentially by having the player die after only one or two hits. The stealth sections from the New Order have returned and take up the majority of the game leaving little room for the run-and-gun action that the Wolfenstein series is known for. On top of all this the length of the game is painfully short at six to eight hours in length. However, when the game is good it is REALLY good. The graphics are amazing thanks to the Id Tech 6 engine and the music composed by Mick Gordon is incredible. Dispite not living up to expectiations The New Colossus is still a worthwhile experience for any fan of the franchise or old school first person shooters. 7/10

Everyone uses the same menu system these days for the most part, why theres has to be different is anyone's clue.
Now with that being said, I have mixed feelings about the lack of a tutorial.  One part of me likes figuring stuff out on my own.  I remodel houses that way.  Don't show me, I will figure it out, and so far it's paid off, I have done better than the other companies. The graphics are pretty decent so far.  So I kinda like that.  Still on the first planet and it actually feels kinda alien to me.  Which is one of the only issues I have with Empyrion so far.  The first planet your on pretty much is earth.  They need to have more diversity and stuff.  But enought about that game, back to this game.   It did a much better job of making me feel like I was not on Earth.  Sounds are ok, some of the aliens animal sounds reminded me of Spores.  Matter of fact they might have stolen the sounds from that game.  Hope they asked first :)
So why did I buy this game, well it was on sale and I wanted to see how well it held up to Space Engineer and Empyrion.  So far Empyrion with all it's bugs is still my fav space survival game, with Space Engineers and NMS joined together at the hip for 3rd place.  I understand there was allot done to this game to make it better, and that it hasn't reached its potential.  It's kinda still in Alpha if you ask me, there are many basic things that are missing like aliens not giving two seets about you popping in on them.  Just seems kinda odd if you crashed on an alien planet and walk into some guys home he would stay plopped down on his chair and not give you a second thought.  Where's the food, you mean to tell me I need air to breath and a hazmat suite but no food?  I need a damn map, how can I explore without having a good mapping system.
I will play this game a bit more, and I wish Hello Games luck in their endevores but they got a ways to go from what I see to make good on their promises.  I will update my review as I search the starts.  So far.. as many have stated, the game feels incomplete.
EDIT:
Ok even if I give you that, what about defending the rest?  Where is the mapping system.  I mean it's pretty impossible to return to anyplace you have visited.  I found an awesome abandon ship the other night but had to much inventory and not enough cash to repair the extra slots... why or how I can repair everything else on the ship except inventory makes no sense.  So I went and found a place I could sell everything.. well all the extras... so I tried to fly back and find that ship.. yea, I can't figure it out... no map markers and the original mission marker vanished... that ship is lost somewhere.  I mean even my car has GPS, our cell phones have GPS, but I guess in the future there is no GPS anymore and no need for maps.. we will all just endlessly wonder about...  I know your all angry that I dissed your game that you have played 300+ hours on and your probably a fanboy.. but I am allowed my opinion and this game fails to provide simple features that should be there.  And don't tell me use a beacon cause we are allowed only 5... I would need allot more to mark things down.  Thanks...

You're dropped in a barren, alien world with no real idea of what's going on, but as you explore and interact with the strange world around you, you begin to return music and colour to the world and bring it back to life. The soundscape builds around you, taking your own solutions and weaving them into the music of the world.
FRACT is a game that gives you a brief starting tutorial that is completely free of explanatory text. Not only that, the environment is altogether alien and bewildering, and suddenly animated at unpredictable times. Once you've completed the tutorial, the game throws you headfirst into the world without any further hand-holding.
And this is what's so fantastic about FRACT: It's full of secrets and amazing places and things for you to discover. But half the fun of unwrapping a gift is the surprise of opening it, and FRACT doesn't try and unwrap the player's gift for them like an excited younger sibling, it lets you pull every strip apart, revealing the glowing, pulsating melody beneath. It lets you piece together an understanding of how the world comes together and what makes it tick. The puzzles themselves are of increasing difficulty, but they shouldn't pose too much of a challenge once you understand how the game and the world works. And that's where the other half of unwrapping the gift comes in: You get the gift itself.
Solving a puzzle in FRACT after you've worked out the underlying system is satisfying, but it's made even more satisfying by the immediate increase in the layers of sound in the soundscape around you, as the tones you've been making the world make suddenly snap into tune and a swell of harmonies follows right behind. Feeling smart and being rewarded with the music becoming more awesome is a very pleasing reward mechanism, and the game continues it throughout. The world itself is surprisingly large, deliberate, and cohesive. There's a story here, waiting to be told in the silent (and musical) ruins. There are little nooks and corners that seem to serve no good purpose except to be a neat little place for you to find. There are side music puzzles that have no bearing on the game progression, and are merely musical toys for you to discover and play with.
No game is perfect, and FRACT is no different. Some of the puzzles require you to notice and intuit the relationship between things that are not the most obvious even with time and exposure to the puzzle. However, in a game that relies on understanding the subtle environmental clues to solve puzzles, if someone is stuck, it's as likely that in their haste to jump into solving the puzzle they've missed some small but important detail needed to guide themselves towards the solution. A moment's pause and a step back is often the kick that breaks the log jam. Failure in experimentation is inconsequential; at worst, you fall off a platform or have to backtrack slightly, and it's not long before you're right back to where you were, able to progress.
FRACT contains one final gift, even after you've solved the last puzzle, enjoyed the victory spectacle, and seen the credits, and that's the Studio. As you progress through the game, all the way up to the last puzzle, you unlock portions of the very real synthesizers in the player composition facility in a separate, quieter portion of the world. For the impatient, there's the ability to unlock the whole Studio immediately, without needing to finish the game. The synthesizer modulation settings work exactly like they do in-game (not counting the advanced synthesizer options that unlock last), so FRACT in effect teaches the player how to make music.
It's too early to tell still, but FRACT OSC may be my favourite game of 2014. It's going to take something pretty special to beat the high standard FRACT's set.

The soundtrack was an instant classic, combining folk, bluegrass and country, and leaving the player with an urge to recite the lyrics for days after. This was a charming little experience! It could be described as Persona 3/4 without the drama and battling, or as a platonic dating sim, if you're into that sort of thing. Expect some routine anime shenanigans, with characters deep enough to be interesting. It's a very lighthearted, easy-going game, but all the characters feel "real" enough to give it sufficient depth.
My first playthrough took about four hours, and my second around two and a half. It's not a long game, but it's full of characters and personality, like a town from Paper Mario: tTYD, you can keep coming back to people for new looks at them. The game emphasizes making friends and being a well-rounded individual, which I think is as good a moral as you could get. I do wish there had been some forewarning about some aspects of the relationship-building dialogues. For example, you can only discuss a topic once with a "target," for the entire playthrough. Of course, this isn't a huge obstacle, and it only makes the game have stronger replay value.
Don't count on much action, or even multiple dialogue options. All of the gameplay focuses on skill-building, time management, and selecting good topics of conversation. This is simply a great game for those looking for solid characters and friendships in a quirky, somewhat-cliche anime setting. If there's a sequel coming out any time soon, as the end of the game implies, I'm very excited for it!

Such nice graphics, sound, and concept, all wasted on annoying gameplay.
The game could have used more depth: maybe more than just the starting weapon, maybe some level variety, or even some substantial difference in enemies... but the game would have at least been fun in its current state were it not so irritating to play...
One constant annoyance is the radar - it's nearly useless. The gameplay area keeps your ship in the center part of the screen, scrolling the background as you move, wrapping around when you go past the edge. The radar is a fixed view of the level, moving a dot that represents your player... a dot that is identical in size and shape to the other dots for enemies, powerups, etc. Because of this, you can never glance at the radar, you must always stop for a few seconds to:
- scan the hundred dots
- pick out the one that is yellow (you)
- pick out the ones that are white (your goals)
- compare your location to the location of the thing you want to get to
- account for the wrap-around (if something appears to the left of your ship on the radar, you may actually have to go to the right and wrap around to get to it fastest)
- press the .... forget it, you're long dead by now
The most annoying detail is the randomness. Nearly everything is random. It makes the game difficult, but not fun. There are no strategies to devise, challenges to overcome, or satisfaction from succeeding... it's just a roll of the dice. Where will the next enemy appear? You can't tell. How will an enemy move around the screen when you're trying to shoot it? You can't tell. Will a bomb end up near an enemy you want to kill? You can't tell. Gameplay is just floating around a bucket of randomly placed enemies, moving about randomly. Winning is simply replaying a level a dozen times to get a good random sequence; practice can't much past basic shooting and dodging, since there's nothing to learn.

tl;dr: buy if you like space exploration games. This game is not much of a space life simulation game (yet).
A year later and finally I am ready to buy the game. As of this review, I'm 8 hours in and feel like I've just scratched the surface. The game has a certain aire about it where it's full of content but lacking in interaction. The game feels like a snapshot: outside of base building I have found that there is little you can do to meaningfully change a planet or solar system.
The UI choices are strange and frustrating. I'm constantly bombarded with screens that hide the rest of the UI for a single message on screen to appear (it should really be changed to a "toast" message that appears below the nav bar IMO). There are no maps of explored planets (that I have found) for me to look at and enjoy my planetary exploration. The Galaxy map is overwhelmingly vast, but the control scheme for warping is very unconventional (using a controller). Also, holding my mouse button down for a progress bar on every single menu item is tedious and annoying, especially in the pause menu. The inventory is also quite a nuisance: you have essentially three inventories, but you cannot simply drag items from one to the other. Instead you have to press a different key to select an inventory to move the item to.
If you like inventory management and crafting, you might enjoy the crafting. There are plenty of items available for you to craft, although most are not unlocked right away.
The base building mechanics of the game are pretty awesome so far, although admittedly I have yet to dive too far into it.
The space flight can get boring and annoying at times as you're mostly zipping across vast distances at somewhat slow speeds (30 seconds to a minute of flight time from one planet to another) waiting to get to your next destination.
When speaking to other aliens you often have no idea what they are saying unless for some reason they speak your language, until you get far into the neat mechanic where you learn words of their language and they are substituted in for your language words during dialog.
There's also space flight combat, which is simple and sometimes hard but still decently satisfying. From the few space battles I have encountered were somewhat disappointing. I would like a lot more of multi-ship battles and less "oh we're pirates that randomly selected you to blow out of the sky unless you pay us money!!!". I was able to find one actual space battle event that involved a freighter under attack by pirate fighters and that was interesting. The rest I could do with a lot less of.
The new Atlas missions build up the lore of the game and are admittedly way more interesting than most other main missions, so that update was a good success.
Planet exploration is tedious but fun. There's a lot of scrambling to find Plutonium to power your ship's launchers every time you land, which is frustrating. However, the planets themselves are gorgeous to look at. There are impressive mountains, caves, oceans, valleys, cliffs, and the occasional abandoned building. The rocks and plant life are pretty much the same on every planet with few major visual differences between planets. Animal life on the other hand is incredibly diverse but it's a shame that it is hard to appreciate them as they tend to run away (and there's no zoo/data log?). Surviving on the planet long enough to explore away from the ship is hard at the beginning, but I imagine there are suit upgrades that make this much easier.
I have issues where many smaller objects such as animals or rock formations fade into existance as I gaze in the direciton they're supposed to be, and the objects do not render at all even when I can zoom in to look at the position through the scanner when I am still within naked-eye distance. I believe there are mods to change the rendering range for these objects, but it definitely should be a graphics option in the game itself.
There's a game mechanic where I can buy one of those giant freighter ships now and fly that around with a number of my little spaceships docked, which is cool but I have yet to build enough in-game currency to do so.
Overall, I feel like this game appeals to a certain crowd of people who enjoy vast exploration with not as much in the way of meaningful universe changes or empire building. In terms of nostalgia, it's reminiscent of the space stage of Spore with their adventures dlc, except with a huge emphasis on a single captain visiting planets and discovering information rather than controlling galactic civilizations.

Alex Ayers and the crew over at Entheogen have made a great flight sim that works with both mouse and keyboard (personally I use a Nostromo N52, Mouse, and Voice Attack software), and uses slightly modified WASD controls.  With the way loot drops, the variety of loot, and the humor in the references (albeit sans speech), it is a lot like Borderlands 2 in space.  If you know me - or even if you don't - you will know that I love Borderlands 2 (as evidenced by my 1000+ hours gameplay), and I love this game almost as much in just a few short hours. :D
Does it have problems? Yes, but generally they are minor and do not effect gameplay.  Such as accidentally moving a toolbar icon and not knowing where it is stored (there is no ability to lock the toolbar), the huge but unsortable inventory, or flying through another ship.  These minor problems are overshadowed by:
- the sheer joy of blowing enemies to bits using one of the hundreds of weapons,
- watching enemies explode - as the game description says - like loot piñatas,
- a not uninteresting story mode,
- very cool original music
- an RPG element including crafting and gathering (skill trees are coming in a future update),
- a large and easy to use DB on the
site that lists ALL THE THINGS,
- and an awesome price (IT'S ONLY $5 USD!).
Any major problems are often quickly and directly addressed by the developers (as evidenced on their forums), and the forums - both here and on the Zigfrak site - are full of people that are knowledgeable, and information that is helpful.
My only hope is that one day we get co-op. ;)
In short, if you like flight sims or space, and FPS, then this is going to be a fun investment for you.  It will provide several hours of fun and explosions, and that is just in the FREE DEMO. ;)

Darksiders 2 is the beautiful lovechild of Legend of Zelda, God of War and Prince of Persia.  Many games have tried to emulate these franchises, and none, in my experience, have pulled it off so gracefully.  And I love it.  In fact, I loved this game so much, I bought it twice.
Take the thoughtful and mind-stimulating dungeon design of Zelda, the ferocious and fast-paced combat of God of War, the platforming and verticality of Prince of Persia, sprinkle in a Diablo-esque loot system, throw in a intriguing (albeit somewhat confusing) storyline lead by an extremely badass, dry and sarcastic anti-hero protagonist, and you have Darksiders 2.  However, the game is not just retreads of old classics, as it brings plenty of fresh material.  The Darksiders lore, in particular, is fascinating, being a very unique spin on biblical history, with plenty of moral ambiguity and notions of good and evil being challenged in ways you might not expect for such a colourful game.  The writing and voice acting is also top notch, being surprisingly sharp and witty.  And it must be said that both the music and art is in a league of its own.  From the first opening minutes of the game, I was swept off my feet by unbelievable vistas and beautiful music, both of which have their own unique flavour.
It's not perfect.  The camera and lock-on feature could certainly do with some work, especially in larger group engagements, and I feel like keyboard controls suffer somewhat in certain situations as a result.  You'll also ocassionally fall to your death for no apparent reason during platforming sections, but this is almost a non-issue as death by falling is a superficial and almost non-existent setback (and handled appropriately to the lore).  Also I'm not really sure what the Deathinitive Edition brings to the table.  I played the game back on release in 2012, and while I haven't gone back to it since then, nothing is striking me as particularly different.  The same camera/control issues exist, and there appears to be little to no new content, unless it comes much later in the game.  The visuals might be polished up a bit, and I think there's some new loot, but other than that, it seems a bit like a missed opportunity to tighten up the few weaknesses of the game.
Overall, this was one of my favourite games of 2012, and replaying it now confirms that it's held up.  It's actually probably one of my most loved games in my Steam library, and it is, without a doubt in my mind, one of the most criminally underappreciated games of all time.  It's crushing to think we'll probably never get a Darksiders 3, especially when they came so close to perfection of the formula in the second installment.

Think of those old dating sims - you level up various abilities so you can talk to girls (or boys) better. Except instead of dating, you're trying to get them to join your comedy club. It sounds ridiculous, but it works!
Miley's a hyperactive girl frantically trying to get three more members to join her club. The downside is people here actually read before they sign stuff, so she needs to get really friendly with them before they join up.
The game is freakishly difficult for a dating sim the first time around: unless you have a walkthrough or know exactly what you're doing, you will probably fail. This is not a bad thing. But before you can get New Game+, be prepared to really slog it to just succeed.
What kept me hooked was the writing and translation. The dialogue is hilarious; every character has charm and personality, and there are lots of great zingers during conversations. The translators have done a great job bringing this to a Western audience: think of the Samurai Pizza Cats, and you know the way they tackled this.
Things I would change: skipping cutscene dialogue - there's a LOT of talking, which makes replaying the game tedious - and making it clear that if you use a conversation topic, it's only good once.

Quick and fun, but not worth its price tag. They don't really explain the controls to you either. And Capcom's tradition of renaming obviously Japanese characters with American names strikes again. Seriously, Miley? Still, if you like comedy, anime, and visual novels, this is worth a look.
EDIT: With the recent "dewesternized" version, the game is a lot more fun. And now that it's on sale, you need to pick it up.

The game is full of light-hearted humour, references to the real world, fourth wall breaking, and the translation from Japanese to English has been done extremely well (To the point of one of characters asking why there is a Japanese shrine in their village). Each character is pretty unique as far as anime characters go, and I quickly found myself taking a liking to most, if not all of them.
Just like a dating sim, Miley only has a few days to date.. or in this case, recruit friends for her comedy club. While running around as her in the city, you can buy the others gifts, meet them at various places/times for story sequences, and hoping you won't mess it up so they'll actually join you.
I really liked it myself, and I'm not a fan of dating sims at all. If you're ever bored and looking for something outside your usual range of games, this wouldn't be a bad choice!

I first used Expert Rifleman back when it was being Beta tested on the snipers hide forum.
This is not a “game” if you are expecting a game or even a soft core simulator you will be disappointed.
I am not super experienced at shooting long range. As I am limited to a 200 yard range near where I live. I have compared the result from the ballistic calculator in Expert Rifleman to other standalone ballistic calculators and the results where comparable. This is a great program if you want to practice long range shooting or using a Mil-Dot.
I was surprised how much switching from Lapua .338 300 gr SMK to Cheytac .375 helped me engage moving targets. The added velocity really helped even at only a few hundred yards. That kind of info cannot readily be obtained from a traditional ballistics calculator.

This is not a game, but a visual ballistic computer and simulator for shooters.
Not a bad concept, but need polishing.
Pros:
- Adds all the factors that would affect real world in-field shooting. Wind, muzzle velocity discrepancies, bullet weight, coriolis effect, et. etc,
- targets are placeable at various stages, moveable and turnable to various angles
- Pretty easy to get into for anyone who has realoading or real world shooting skills
- Seems pretty accurate as a simulator at first try.
Cons:
- Not a game. Don't expect any bells an whistles, career mode, arcade shooting/sniper challenges...it's a tool
- Graphics need serious polish. I know it's a sim, but still...draw me in. They're too basic
- Scopes reticles are far too few and lack variety. You can customize and add your own, but this should have been released with a lot more already in, so guys can practice holdovers and leads with hunting style scope reticles or whatever.
- Only 3 calibres are in the sim to start with (you can add your own by inputting stats)  as far as I could see - .338, 7.62, and .50 I believe.
- Audio and felt recoil, blast effects could use an overhaul.
- UI needs to be minimized a bit
- You can't walk around in a terrain. you have a panning scope view an that's it.
- Scopes should be able to at least simulate distance haze, and other visual abberations/reflections for a truer "feel". I'd like to be able to add some distortions to my custom scope view to simulate some of the less that awesome scopes on the market.
Conclulsion:
I would have preferred this as a serious rifle range mod for Arma III, where I could choose the landscape, target types, set up a map on a rolling terrain and actually choose what positions to shoot from. All the math is there. Just needs a better body. Still a good buy for those who can't get to the range.

I've never been a shooter (or wanted to be, with a real rifle) but I enjoy games that offer shooting as a sniper. Thus, I expected something significant from "Expert Rifleman - Reloaded". It claims to be the first of its kind for the consumer market, yet offers ZERO instructions or information, but TONS of options to be selected. This should be a plus, but what they mean is largely anyone's guess.
I'm having so much trouble that I've yet to find a target to shoot at, though I'm tried every mode. The movement is horrible, the wind effect in the trees is 20 years out of date. The effect of a bullet hitting is even worse. There is very little good about this game, and this will be my first refund in nearly 600 games (other than "Journey of the Light".)
Consider what is at the bottom of each screen "EXC to exit". Read it again, please.

I love realistic shooting games with bullet drop, etc... that must be taken into consideration when shooting at long distances so I thought this game was a no brainer.
After booting it up I found a very simple starting menu with few options and no descriptions. Before starting a shooting session there are half a dozen pages or so of values and numbers for different weather and shooting variables which have zero descriptions. Unless you are a big time shooter or have military experience none of this makes any sense and there are no descriptions about what they do and how those numbers affect your shots.
The price seems a bit high for the lack of content and unpolished graphics. The actual bullet flight looks almost cartoonish to be honest.
Hopefully the devs can work on adding more content to allow any player who is interested in long distance shooting, regardless of background knowledge to be able to play and enjoy this game without complicated and confusing settings.

Gameplay next.  They did a lot of stuff pretty right, but the bad really over-shadows all the good.  First and most irritating for me was the stupid frigging base of operations. There was a surge of FPS games during the early to mid 2000s. Most of us enjoyed playing but nostalgia can often blind us. Everytime I start this game up I am stunned at how well it aged.
This Call Of Duty game refined the FPS genre for future games. Rewarding players with killstreaks and adding a LV sytem gave FPS lovers a goal to work for. Perks were a new feature added to COD4. Unfortunately Activision does not offer major discounts on their COD games and it'll be hard to find one for a cheap price.  But I can safely say that there's no harm in buying this game for full price. You'll get your money's worth for sure. So strap up solider, pick your loadout and see where it all began.

I'm trying really hard to like No Man's Sky 1.3. Really hard. I'm doing the base building quests. I now have a dune buggy. I rehabilitated an old, crashed hauler. I'm even kinda trying to find Atlas.
But I'm not really enjoying it.
For having an infinite galaxy to explore, there is still very little to see in No Man's Sky, and that's a problem for a game about exploration. The animals and plants that I've found are all pretty samey. The environments look better than they did on the three dozen or so planets that I've explored. Every once in a while you come up on a different kind of space station or a weird new monolith to click at, but there's still very little life to the game. The planets seem to have been previously inhabited, but all of the structures appear to be isolated and expeditionary in nature. No abandoned towns or even inhabited ones.
And then there are the weird limitations. Everything is a brick wall. I wanted to explore an ancient ruin. The game put the structure at the bottom of a sinkhole on a world so cold and windy that I couldn't last 30 seconds outside the cockpit. I found a lush, verdant, temperate world full of sea to explore, but I could not find a shelter to shift my base to. I found new animal and tried to name it. The profanity filter rejected the word "bipedal."
Everything you might want to do is gated with a ridiculous time sink. Want to buy a freighter and collect different spaceships? You're going to need about 100 times the currency you are likely to have on hand. Want to jump from system to system and just explore? Prepare to grind a LOT of resources and craft a lot of fiddly stuff. Want to follow one of the game's two main quests? Fetch time!
Lots of things are deeply affected by the procedural generation of your part of the galaxy. I have tripped over no fewer than three crashed freighters and have been following their log story like is was some kind of regular feature. My friend, who has played this game since launch, has yet to see one. I recently attempted a timed quest given to me by the exocraft engineer to go find a signal 6 minutes across the map. After 5 minutes of driving across rubble and watching the camera shake like a GoPro, I fell into a hidden sinkhole and couldn't get the dune buggy back out. Rage quit.
My kid has become invested in my struggle, though. "Daddy, I hope you find enough iron or whatever."

Zigfrak is basically Elite/Privateer had a baby with DND/Rogue-like partner. Yes, you read that right. This is NOT your typical space game, but is in fact, an RPG set in space. And that's a good thing.
The fact that the game uses WASD to move should tell you this is NOT a turn-and-burn game like Elite/ Privateer / X-series.  Yes, you play this game like a FPS: WASD to strafe. And you can map weapons groups, or just hit "fire wall" (and hold it down if you like) to fire every weapon as soon as they cycle. And the bigger your ship, the more weapon slots it would have. (Reaper-class, the largest ship you can build, has 2P+4S+2D slots)  You have four categories of weapons: primary, secondary, tertiary, and drone. Primary are the rapid-hitting weapons, like energy bolts, or ballistic cannons. Secondary are slower firing like missiles, railguns, and even "flak". Tertiary so far are beam weapons. And drones are basically attack robots that act like little fighters that fight alongside you (almost like pets!)
Just like RPG, you will find bazillion different variations of the same weapon, as well as various secondary effects. A electro weapon can have kinetic secondary effect. In fact, you can find "modifiers" that can be added to some plain weapons to add the secondary effect. (i.e. gems/charms for your weapons!)   And weapons have cycle speed (attack speed!), damage, multi-strike (fires more than one shot per attack), and even reliability (heavy use and damage can destroy the item!)   You have shield, then armor or overshield. Each of which can be generic, or specialized against a particular type of damage (kinetic, thermal, nuclear, electro, strange, etc.)
You jump from sector to sector, and you can do the boring stuff like mine asteroids and whatnot for minerals and energy and such in most places. However, most of the time you'll be fighting. Some enemies can be invading your sector, or you can go to an unfriendly sector. Expect to see a lot of enemies, as there's plenty of humans to fight against, AND there are more than one faction of aliens you will have to contend with.
Fighting is a lot of side-strafing, but also with touch of afterburner to get away from the enemies and retrograde. What's fun about the game is a ton of loot... you'll nab ammo, weapons, other components, as well as powerups that will restore shield, restore health, triples your base damage, and so on. When you blow up a ship, stuff scatter like confetti. If you don't like the mess, disable the other ship, then dock with it to loot it.
So far, this sounds simple, but then you get into templates (blueprints) for building your components, weapons, even ships, and the game makes a different turn, as you realize you can't buy the ship you want... You'll have to build them.
Remember to do all the early missions so you don't miss out a lot of upgrades and such. You'll need the various upgrades.
There are a lot of little features, like trading some special loot for "chests" that can contain surprise goodies, needing some special research to buy super-exotic weapons, finding the stations where such weapons or tempaltes are sold, and so on is a part of the fun. And the galaxy is quite big.
Graphics are surprisingly good, but then drawing "space" and making it look good isn't that difficult During combat the screen can get extremely busy with all your weapons firing with different effects (and other specials like shield-breakers, decoys, holodecoys, and so on all firing off). Add to the flashes caused by weapon hits, and this may be almost epilepsy inducing. Beware.
Sound isn't anything remarkable. There are no voiced dialogs, just text boxes. Music is sort techno-futuro beat electronica.
All in all, this is a fun little game that encourages a lot of replay just for exploration, even if you manage to max out the ship. I have played through this game three times since its earlier days, and I can never get enough of it. I even paid for it twice; 5 bucks for this much fun is just a steal.
What is Zigfrak? Pure unadulterated hilarity in the shape of a space shooter. I mean, it's got "loot piñatas" right in the description.
To say it's got a quirky humour doesn't do it justice; battles are a flashy, dopamine-torrent-inducing show of lights and loot. There is a joke to be found absolutely everywhere, from the purposefully shameless stereotyping (often with a twist!) on some of the characters, missions, and dialogue, to the very names and flavour text of the majority of the equipment you can find: when you get your hands on a nuclear missile launcher called The Freshmaker (with "plutonium cores enhanced with minty flavour crystals") you know this game's a keeper.
It's not a "hard" or "challenging" game by any means. While you are certainly able to roam in-between missions and find yourself in the middle of a bigger badder fleet than you can manage, once you get the hang of the mechanics and controls the answer is most often just getting a few more levels and better gear. The game is pretty streamlined for the sake of fun; and it succeeds, because the humour, the story constantly switching mood from dark to kickass to zany, and the flashy battles WILL keep you entertained for dozens upon dozens of hours.
From a technical aspect, the graphics are not the most realistic hi-poly thing you'll find but it's nevertheless got a unique and beautiful style. The soundtrack is great, and the game is extremely stable and bug-free.
What doesn't it have? Multiplayer, or a truly unforgiving challenge. If you don't really need either of these, then Zigfrak is your game.
There are a lack of sound effects for space combat. I don't get the adrenaline rush of destroying things, or hearing damage occur. This is a huge black mark in my book.

As a game with such a modest price, it is surprising the amount of depth and the end result is a masterpiece easily worth much more.

Darksiders franchise is about the 4 Horsemen of the Apocalypse, loosely based on Judeo-Christian scriptures. These are the guys who aim to help maintain balance and peace from the angels and demons. I got this game for free and decided to once again put on the mantle of Death to review this edition. The Deathinitive Edition has spruced up it's graphics, and all additional content is included with this edition. The story in this video game takes place when War has been with the Charred Council for 100 years. So, this game is actually a prequel to the original Darksiders. Don't let that 2 fool you!
