I found myself listening to this sound track over and over again. It is called, The Guardian. I just kept running around the boss with my horse so that I can keep listening to the theme music of this boss. He is the final boss you meet in the Forge Lands. This edition did make some minor graphic improvements to the original Darskiders II but if you have the original of this game, save your cash. I'd recommend buying this edition when it is on sale.
I must warn you, if you do try and buy Darksiders II: Deathinitive Edition for the PC. This game crashes a lot! And by 'a lot', I mean to the point any normal player would have quit trying to play it. The game really had me hooked so I dealt with it. As far as I can tell it only crashed during combat (No idea why) OR if you ALT +TAB out of the game (No idea why). Also, the patch for Darksiders II has been in beta for about a year already with no communications about fixing this bug. I really do hope they fix it because a lot of people are missing out on a wonderful remastered game. The game is SO good, but I am saddened that they have left their fans in the wings with no remedy.
I keep hoping they'll make a Darksiders 3 with all 4 horsemen available to play and that it could be played in co-op mode up to 4 players. I really do wish the company gets it's act together, but right now THQ has fallen on hard times. I really want to see them rebound so they can expand on this franchise. I spent a good amount of time on this story, and I want to see how it ends.  I hope others will enjoy it, too!

I went into this game with very low expectations, having played Final Fantasy XIII for about 12 hours before giving up on its linear dungeons that simply required me to move from A to B while killing monsters in the process. I was pleasantly surprised to find that Lightning Returns is a far superior experience overall.
To begin with, the world opens up fairly quickly, letting you explore four different hub areas and interact with the NPCs there, from vendors to quest givers, imbuing your character with a sense of freedom that was sorely lacking in XIII. The story is more focused, taking Lightning on a journey to save the souls of mankind before the world comes to an end, but building on that simple premise by adding layers of intrigue through the character of Lumina.
Another positive is how side quests are tied to this story (main is a given), as Lightning will have to undertake personal quests to save souls and learn a little bit more about herself in the process. Nevertheless, I'd be remiss if I didn't mention the Canvas of Prayers' quests that basically have you running around collecting materials for anonymous people.
Since the world is coming to an end it makes sense that there's a ticking clock haunting your every step. At first glance this will undoubtedly come across as a huge negative but the game itself provides you with the means to stall that clock in a variety of ways. First, as you gather souls you collect something called Eradia, what can be used to add more days to the clock. Furthermore, you have an ability in-game called Chronostasis that will let you freeze the clock for thirty in-game minutes. If you're still doubtful, start on easy and you can pretty much forget about that clock. On the plus side, the passage of time allows the game to make the hub areas more dynamic; unlocking areas, vendors, quest givers, and even events, during specific times, building on the illusion that this is a living, breathing, world you're in.
Combat reprises the XIII formula with the ATB system but enhances it via schematas. Schematas are essentially builds you can create comprised of garbs, weapons, accessories, and abilities. During battle you can switch between three different schematas, each with its own ATB bar, what gives you more leeway when dealing with a variety of enemies. Furthermore, both abilities and weapons can be upgraded throughout the game, though the latter only on NG+.
If it helps, I found myself sinking a lot of time into this game without even realizing it. What impressed me the most, personally, was its gripping story and actually interesting and relevant side quests. You also don't need to have played the previous games to enjoy or even understand what's going on in this one as the game does a pretty good job of laying out the background. Ironically, Lightning Returns is, to my mind, a much better entry point than XIII ever was. The ending can be a bit confusing, I'll give you that, and does have a Return of the King-esque feeling to it, but I found it immensely satisfying.
So, if you want to get into Final Fantasy in general, or the Lightning Trilogy in particular, give Lightning Returns a shot. Like me, it could be the game you were looking for.

Gameplay is good. Initially, I preferred the FFXIII-2 combat system, but I will say that in the end I found this system to be gratifying in it's own unique way. And it does a good job at making you feel like Lightning is now capable of combat on an entirely diffent scale than her friends(and herself) were in their previous story lines.  I was not a big fan of the clock countdown in the beginning, as I hate feeling like I'm under a time constraint. However, after having completed the game, I can tell you that there is no real time constraint. In the end, I was sleeping days away at the Inn's, as I had completed all the side quests. So take your time, and enjoy the journey and the atmosphere of the game.
I would recommend this game to all my friends irl, without any reservations.

This game has cute pixel art graphics and nice music, but it is overall very limited.
There are 25 levels but they are all in the exact same underwater setting (only 3 screens wide or so which loop around) with either 1, 2 or 3 spots to defend. There are two broad categories of enemies, the first are a variety of enemies which will go across the level while trying to annoy you by shooting at you, following you or avoiding your fire. The other kind are abductor enemies which will try to capture the kitties mining milk at the spots you need to defend. There are no patterns, the enemies will spawn at random places and go either left or right randomly. This is especially annoying when an abductor enemy spawns right on top of one of your kitties, and makes the successful completion of the later levels luck-based in a large part.
As good ad the music is, there are only two tracks which will get old quickly.
Most frustrating point for me, there are almost no upgrades of any kind for your ship. "Almost" because every time you complete a zone, you get an upgrade which allows you to use your alternate fire mode a little bit longer. But that's it, no fancy weapons for you, you will keep the same pea shooter all game long, and it does not even shoot all the way across the screen. Since enemies get tankier as you go along, completing a level becomes a matter of dodging random configuration of enemies and bullets and slowly killing them with your underpowered gun.
There is however an "arcade mode" which allows you to collect powerups and keep them for the next level, but if you get hit even once you lose one level of all your powerups. You also can't retry, if you do the game is reset.
I can enjoy a game that is frustrating but gives a big reward when you finally overcome the difficulty. This is not that kind of game, the reward is very small so it quickly came to a point when I stopped enjoying the time spent on that game. In the end I wouldn't recommend that game.

The entire premise of this game is basically summed up in its own title; Horror in the Asylum. It's a horror game, and it takes place in the overused setting of a decrepit mental institution. Taking a look at the trailer and screenshots on the store page immediately brings to light that this game is essentially an asset flip; anyone who has played a decent number of these Unity Personal Edition indie cash-grabs will notice that. While that doesn't necessarily indicate that the game itself will be garbage, more often than not, it will be.
In this case, that's exactly what Horror in the Asylum is; cash-grab garbage that tries too hard to be difficult, and offers little to no scare value while creating near impossible situations. You wake up in a dark mental institution, read a couple of notes that talk about taking prescribed medication, pick a few locks, and proceed to solving overly complex puzzles while avoiding medieval skeletons. There's no handholding here, which would be fine if even the basics of the HUD were explained; for instance, what does that "risk" indicator in the top left corner really do? It can be low even when enemies are nearby, and high when no danger is present. It just doesn't make any sense. There's also an annoying dual-control layout shown no matter if you're playing with a KB+M set up, or an Xbox controller.
Be forewarned that there are absolutely no save files or checkpoints here; if you die, you start from the very beginning. This is the "difficulty" factor of Horror in the Asylum, and it makes the entire game one big trial-and-error mission. The only real foes in the game are patrolling skeletons with bad AI, but when they see you they'll chase you down and one-hit kill you if you do not run away quick, or far, enough. In fact, every death is a one-hit kill, and most of them are due events that you have absolutely no way of anticipating, such as a random killer insect hidden in some weird location that you accidentally bump in to; avoidable, though, if you know to have your flashlight off when you get there, but this isn't explained anywhere.
The controls are a beast entirely their own, and they're terrible. The mouse/joystick sensitivity is excruciatingly low, with no way to be changed, and the controller mapping is just god awful. There's no way to rebind the button mapping, whether it be for KB+M or controller layouts. The music is repetitious, the level layouts are boring, there's no real story, the "challenge" is faux and made up by removing any and all save features, and overall the only thing that Horror in the Asylum has going for it is the fact that it does have decent optimization. If you feel like punishing yourself, do so without torturing your wallet and grab this one on sale for a buck or less; otherwise, avoid it entirely.

I've been a big fan of LucasArts adventures since Maniac Mansion though Full Throttle is one I didn't get to play first time around. LA adventures have always been head scratching and in parts infuriating, but FT unfortuantly felt just annoying.
FT suffers from the majority of the misteps adventures started making during the 90's (though fortuantly unlike some Sierra games they didn't go with actually killing the player or making the game unfinishable if you do the wrong thing):
- Objects are hard to identify on screen (even with the "highlight objects" option it's sometimes hard to tell that an object has separate sub-sections that are important)
- Timing challenges (you can happily do exactly the right thing, but at the wrong time, and give up on what is the correct solution because the reason for failure is non obvious)
- Arcade sections (generally unforgivable in an adventure game and, again, you can be failing not because you have the wrong solution, but just because you're bad at a mini game - or a challenge that seems like a mini game, but still needs a specific set of actions)
- Tedious slow character movement
- Artificial extra clicks (e.g. I'm on foot and I want to use an exit from the current location that apparently I must drive through rather than walk. In a sane game you would auto-mount your bike and ride out. In FT Ben just complains he doesn't want to walk, forcing you to explicitly mount your bike and then exit)
I won't even get into the "puzzles" that are essentially randomly clicking on a set of branching options and failing until you slowly pick your way through the correct route.
All this is a shame because the game has a lot in it's favour:
- An incredible cast of voice talent
- Excellent music
- Wonderful graphics (even the originals; but the remaster is stunning)

Darksiders 2, or what I'd like to call it.. Edgy-legend of zelda 2. Makes great improvements upon the first, making the gameplay amazing, fluid and enjoyable. The story is a bit more interesting as well, and the dungeon mechanics/puzzles are decent, although I haven't played through the game entirely, I enjoyed the first games dungeons much more.
Darksiders2 starts with Death, one of the four horsemen going on a journey to redeem one of his brothers(War), for his actions against humanity. Death uses.. scythes, guns, axes and just about anything to decimate his enemies.
TLDR; Darksiders 2 is a hack n'slash game with dungeons and light puzzle elements. Its basically Legend of Zelda but with gear rating, more involved combat and a little less on the puzzles. Its a great game, it just started to get tons of issues for me. I'd play the first one if you want to play this though. That one hasn't aged as well however, but its still a great game. Get ready for a lot of unskippable cutscenes q.q
Positives:
- Great combat
- Great colorful scenery
- Good soundtrack
- Looks fairly good, although its a remaster
- Tons of weapons/equipment to choose from(also a problem I have with it, but its more of a positive)
- Character development of death is great, makes him go from a character you wouldn't like to an understandable guy who really isn't all that bad. I really have to give props to that. Not a lot of games can sell me on their character after the start, but he just grows on you. Shout outs to Michael Wincott(no one probably knows who he is) But great job on voicing death.
- Your generic idea of a nephalem story idea, but I think its done right here. You don't feel too powerful, but you don't feel you're weak either. I just feel like it fits with the rest of the game perfectly.
- Powers: The powers are simply great, it makes you feel like you're getting stronger throughout the journey. every power seems to have its own use, granting replay value if you want to play through again.
- NEW GAME+: YES. THIS IS HOW YOU DO NEW GAME+. New rewards, keep everything you have(like most ofc), but it allows replay value because items are fairly unique.
Negatives: (More so huge complaints/issues than specific points)
- BUGS galore BOIIIIIIIS. If you level up at the archon story area off the quest, the game crashes. The games audio bugs out a lot in the second world which is actually annoying. The games full screen mode causes it to crash if you alt+tab too much woopity doopity so much f-wordities came out at times. Theres a lot, but apparently the developers have talked about fixing these issues. Theres also a whole bunch of community backlogs of problems being fixed, so there is fixes at least.
- A lot of pointless side characters that could've been fleshed out.
NEUTRAL:
- Gear/equips feels overstaying but at the same time it forces you to progress in its gearing. Its nice later on, because it feels rewarding to get a better weapon, or power that helps you greatly.
- Level design is linear early on, but feels much more expansive later on. I think this was done well but slowly at times. I feel like it was more worried of introducing so much at once unlike the first, but it works out alright in the end.
Conclusion:

Easily one of my favorite games of all time, I didn't revisit for a bit, but I'm glad I did. I feel like a lot of my issues were kinda fixed, but at the same time the bugs weren't. I do hope the developers do release that patch they said was in the making. The only big complaint is WHY is The Guardian soundtrack not in the soundtrack thats purchasable. Thats hand down the best piece of music from this game. C'mon man... AND YOU. Whoever is reading this! LOOK IT UP ON YOUTUBE. Even if you won't buy the game, listen to that soundtrack. Its amazing.

You'd think that judging by the comment section of Steam that this game is a bugfest, but I went to check for myself and it's not really. Sure, some people do get issues, but on my end the game runs fine.
I just bought the entire franchise because I didn't own the game on my own personal account and I forgot how phenomenally fun Darksiders 2 was. First of all, I must say I'm quite impressed that not only you get both Darksiders 1 and Darksiders 2 Deathinitive Edition, but you also get Darksiders 1 Warmastered Edition even after it released. A beautiful gesture by the developers.
Anyway, onto the point. Darksiders 2 Deathinitive Edition is in my opinion a lot better than the regular version. There's a lot more features, optimizations and general good tweaks that have been done. The biggest issue I had with Darksiders 2 was that the latest patch caused frame stuttering in combat when using KBM. I didn't experience it here, so that's good. However, don't expect a perfectly optimized game.
I personally am not experiencing any frame drops, although I did get a crash or two, but I quickly solved them by googling the issue. Apparently you can't max out shadows in this game or it causes the game to crash, but the game still looks great.
Another thing is that the game had a few patches in works, but were never officially released. Therefore, I suggest you opt-in for the BETA patch that fix some more stuff for the game.
Other than these minor issues, I honestly fully recommend the Darksiders franchise. I find both games absolutely fun and compelling to play. They're not the most optimized games out there, but they're optimized enough and worth playing!

Call me old fashioned, but I like it when the next in a series don't break off from the established rules from the first one, especially when it comes to basic controls. So while we're on that subject, why is Death running around naked with a pair of pick axes? And why is he modelled like a hunch-backed chimpansee while he's running? War had this slow, steady pace of running, a sort of inevitable doom stride that displayed his unwavering confidence even after being crushed to death for the twelvth time in a row by a glithed spider demon.
Death on the other hand remind me of a paranoid Jumping Spider even in combat, with a Dash that cover twise the distance of War and no apparent delay between them, all of a sudden he cart wheels away from the fight like he's off to join the circus. On second thought, that's probably what he should do, since running up a straight wall is more useful for an acrobat or a chimney sweeper than the Inevitable End embodied.
Gameplay-wise, I felt very confused and costricted. Why are we gathering gold? Why doesn't Death carry some kind of armour? Why isn't he at his peek strenght from the start? Why is he riding a horse that look like it was stolen from the roof of a Vegas casino? Why doesn't he have his own armour? He's dressed like he was in the bath when he realized that War was in trouble, grabbed a pair of pants and his bloody pick axes on the way out. Why on gods-not-so-green-earth-anymore didn't the angels themselves just head off towards that giant On-switch for humanity? Why is Death conversing with everyone like he's mentally challanged?
So many questions, and I'm not even interested in finding out the answer.
The constriction part comes in when moving around outside of combat. There's one road, one way to go there. It's not as much about finding the way as it is being led around by the nose by a flying blue berry.
And so many unintentional humourus situations in combat with War, when a zombie is slowly shuffeling towards you only to get sqashed by the ambulanse you just snagged from a street corner. Or when a massive demon with burning fists are hot on your heels, you see a large piano you want to plant in his face, make a dash for it, with the roaring demon preparing to charge you, it takes off, you reach out... and find youself holding a tiny foot stool that the demon might appreciate as a tooth pick, but not much other use.
With Death, the most fun I had was when... Uhm... Well... I didn't. Which is why it gets a thumbs down from me, now if you excuse me, I'm off to draw more zombies attention to Stop signs, you really have to beat them over the head on that issue.

I have to redo this.
The reason why is because I notice square has almost become godly at recreating systems that have been utter garbage... Save for the ffx style turn based system that in my opinion has been bested by Xenosaga. All other systems made by them that I have tried have been the most fluid and concise of all other systems.
More modern examples can be mentioned towards Final fantasy XII, where micro management systems put absolute shame to the ones used in dragon age. And the current paradigm system that trashes the mechanics in games like xenoblade and White Knight Chronicles I and II.
-The reason why I mention these mechanics is because they are from hit RPGs or RPGs with a strong following Ironically anyone else aside from square seem to not be held by the same standard and while people love the opposing features, they dislike the ones perfected by square. The amount of conveniences they include with very little twitch action or memory required is something those games could have benefitted from. And square aces these tests and moves on never looking back.
Final fantasy XIII Lightning returns is a pretty average game done with enough aesthetic and polish to make you want to play it. Gone are the days where your mythical armor looks like your default gear. And where your best spell marks the end of your search for enlightenment. Lightning returns features armor and accessories that bring the best out of your gear setup, which is essentially your class, proper weapons accessories and skills enrich the role you want to fit into, and the amount of depth involved is enough to make any rpg gamer happy. Normally the inclusion of a plethora of gear would mean that the devs would get lazy and simp on the content or detail. But the amount of detail and polish is mid tier mmo quality which would cost more than the price of a game, or that game would irrefutably be dark souls. Strong spells and skills get stronger provided you find additional skills of the same name or strength if you are feeling lazy, so the journey for the best skills is almost as long as getting max level skills in phantasy star, which is pretty amazing for a single player game.
The concept of the game is of a unique impending doom aspect, where you have a time limit to save as many souls as possible to buy time and figure out and stop what's going on. The idea that you are there to save lives and solve problems that some take more than a few days is the type of thing you normally find people swearing against because it reeks of missable quests and opportunities. However, the game's easy mode treats you with free escapes from lost battles, cheaper time spells, well, basically enough to welcome any fan who hates the concept but loves the game otherwise. I would say it shoots themselves in the feet, but honestly, getting laid out by monsters that aren't supposed to be beaten yet and losing time are things that will eat at your pride for sure, so the fact they took measures to remedy that is nice.
The game is definitely worth a sale buy, and is a nice way to see most of the characters do some growing up, or get some serious saving done for them. It is definitely a must buy for those wishing games had more stress on being a hero with time constraints and obligations that need swift management and tough decisions to properly overcome with great haste.

I've read some reviews that are complaining about the lack of story... well here's the story. The supply of milk is gone, a team was sent out to mine milk from underwater, and you have to protect the miners from robotic fish. That's it. This is one of those games where the story is short and generic as it's not the focus of it, but to give you a general idea of why there's cats mining milk from underwater. As for why there's only milk underwater or why there's robtic fish that want to kidnap miners, who knows, it's not important.
So now that we got that out of the way...
The game is an action, arcade, side-scrolling, shooter with random bullet hell elements (instead of pattern bullet hell). The point of the game is for each level you have to clear a certain number of waves of enemies and make sure the milk miners aren't napped by robo-jellyfish. It starts out easy, but the difficulty steadily increases the more you play.
There are three mods: Easy, Normal and Arcade.
Easy: Start with 5 health
Normal: Start with 3 health, but can have up to 5.
Arcade: Start with 5 health, have one life, have to purchase your upgrades instead of getting them as power-ups, however instead of temporary having them you keep them (till you die of course and have to start over).
Achievements you get in Normal difficulty won't additionally trigger achievements for Easy, you'll have to get them separately.
The controls may feel a bit awkward but eventually you'll get used to them.
It's best to play this in short bursts, as you may eventually find yourself stuck and frustrated. I highly recommend you give Easy a try, get used to the controls at least, before you attempt Normal or Arcade.
The game is fun, challenging, and can become addicting. Sadly there's no online co-op, only local. I am thankful there's no co-op achievements because of this.
The price may be worth it, depending how much time you wish to put into it, but wouldn't hurt to wait for a sale for no lower than $3.

You find yourself locked away in an asylum, and you're going to be the only one who is going to get you out of there. So you will have to explore the asylum, find what hides in the dark, and solve puzzles that present themselves as the asylum doesn't want to let you go easily.
In Horror in the Asylum you will have plenty of puzzles to solve, but there is always just one solution. This of course will come in handy when you die and start the entire game again from scratch. There are no save points in this game, there is no randomizing of the level, and to be honest there's not a whole lot of excitement when you're doing a specific section for the 15th time.
My biggest issue with the game is that there's a good chunk of it that is trial and error, and the error sends you back to the very beginning of the game. Sure this game will keep you wondering what will happen next, but an even bigger thought is, "am I going to have to do all of this over AGAIN???"
Now that's not to say that there aren't some interesting things in the game, but there are more frustrating and boring things that will cause you to want to drop the game after a while. You of course need a flashlight to move around in the dark halls, and I really like the blue light that reveals that which is hidden. I do find it odd, however that when you hide in cover that your light automatically turns on, even if you have it off, or blue. You can then toggle the light all you want without an indication of what position the light will be in once you get out of cover. Speaking of getting into cover, you will have to bend to fit in a spot, or crawl under a bed, however there is no crouch mechanic for items that are basically at knee level so you have to get just the correct camera angle in this first person view to collect items.
I could also mention that this game crashes every time I've exited the game, and look I just did, but that's the least of my worries when it comes to this game. There's something about it that seems like it was rushed. It feels like there's a story here, but there's no polish. The text choice for the notes that you collect while walking through the asylum have a terrible font choice which makes it difficult to read. There's also the lock picking mechanic that doesn't feel right.
I really want to say that this game is worth playing through, but I can't, I really can't, and it really has to do with the forced rinse and repeat actions that are constantly occurring. After so many restarts it's just not worth trying to go through the exact same steps again. This game gets a 4.7 out of 10.

UPDATE: Game completed, see below.
I like to start any review with the positives, so let's get that over with: the game's got two genuinely creepy jumpscare deaths.
The bad: This is one of the most trial-and-error horror games I have ever played. There are no checkpoints, no save points, nothing. You have no health; any enemy that attacks you will defeat you instantly. And any time you die, you are going all the way back to the start of this game. This is obnoxious enough in and of itself, but this gets far worse. Twice I have had the game glitch out and keep me from being able to move. One of these times was, no joke, about 10 seconds from the end of the game.
The story is nonexistent, and there is no proper ending either. The physics are strange. Just try using the numberpads that come up with a 360 controller. I dare you. There's a meter that shows how...in trouble you are, or something, but I have no idea if it actually does anything. It has no effect on the actual monsters, certainly.
The price is out of this world for this game. When you actually know what you're doing, it takes about 10 minutes to finish. That's if you make it past all of the trial-and-error and glitches. I am very disappointed in this game.
UPDATE: I managed to finish the game now. I ended up getting stuck at the elevator literally 4 more times before I figured out the trick to bypass this game-breaking glitch. When you get on board the elevator and it's descending, press yourself right up against the elevator door and keep moving forward against it. You'll hop off the elevator into the morgue room without getting stuck. You have to get on/off the elevator twice more but I was able to do that without my game breaking.
As one can expect, with no checkpoints and a consistent game-breaking glitch so close to the end, I still cannot in good faith recommend this game, especially as it is a consistent issue. I will edit my review if further updates arrive, but having to play around a glitch like that is absolutely ridiculous.

A remarkably deep top-down shooter
It's easy to write of Running With Rifles (RWR) as just another top down shooter. When I first started playing it, I first thought of those old online flash games, Endless War, which I played obsessively as a kid on websites like Miniclip and Newgrounds. But RWR is so much more than that.
First, the scope. The AI admittedly isn't great on a mass scale; close quarters unit tactics are pretty good, with friendlies and enemies alike advancing to flanking positions, calling in support, and doing many of the things you'd expect a soldier to do. But on a meta scale, the engine which controls the games strategic outlook ain't great. For example, sometimes I like playing massive bloodbaths of games; crazy situations in which each side has somewhere in the realm of 800 soldiers each, all fighting it out building by building or trench by trench. The firefights that develop are massive, and I love the game for those. But it's almost like the game doesn't know what to do with larger groups of troops. There's only one 'target' objective at a time. This creates massive killing fields, in which the AI of one team or another will batter itself relentlessly against one enemy strongpoint at the expense of larger strategic objectives and waste hundreds of troops. I'd also frequently respawn at a base only to find it filled with upwards of 100 troops just standing around.
Now you're probably thinking, "of course,♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the game wasn't meant to handle that many guys. It's a game meant to give you the feeling of being one in a mass of ground infantry, throwing you into situations from Stalingrad to Hamburger Hill." And on an individual level, it does that impossibly well for a top-down shooter. For one thing, its bullet physics are remarkably complex compared to what they initially appear to be. Its cover system is as intuitive as it is accurate; taking cover behind a wall, building, vehicle or hedgerow feels as seamless as it should be. Enemies respond to supressing fire. And although taking down vehicles is a challenge, it's about as hard as it should be - which makes it even more satisfying when you do. Hell, even enemy line of sight is handled well; unless they've already seen you or one of your squad, they never just 'know' you or even other AIs on your team are just there, which makes assaulting a base from behind with a full 10-man squad all the more viscerally satisfying.
But this is also where the games weaknesses begin to show. For one thing, you have next to no control over your squad; you can tell them to take ground, or regroup on you, and that's about it. I've also always wanted to be able to form elite squads - say, making everyone in my squad a lieutenant, and therefore has better guns and more likely has armor. Unfortunately, my squads are usually at least half privates or corporals, even when I'm a full-bird colonel. So I guess that's my only complaint about this game - I wish it was easier to get your army to attack a specific location (say, if you've spotted a weak spot) and not just keep throwing themselves into whatever objective the game decideds is important. I also wish I had more control over the men in my squad. But at the end of the day, these small frustrations lend a certain perfection to the game. Because within the confines of the game, you're not the supreme commander; you're likely just be another m-16 toting private with a medpack and a few hand grenades, and that's a frustrating position to be in. Because soldiers in those scenarios don't have control over the strategy of the war; all they can do is choose the best tactical options for the situation some armchair general's strategy has put them in. And this game is very, very good at conveying that sense of helplessness and occasionally screwing you over by chance or whimsy. But it only makes it all the more satisfying when your quick tactical thinking lets you take what looked like a defeat and turn it into a massacre of the enemy foot soldiers who are in many ways just like you who were acting until a second ago that they had you bagged. And it's situations like that, so beautifully thrown into the chaos of combat, that makes me keep coming back to this game.

Short and sweet, Full Throttle Remastered is a solid version of a 90s adventure classic. The game itself holds up well, utilizing the "verb" system of gameplay used in a lot of other LucasArts games in the era (a version of which can also be seen in the much more recent Thimbleweed Park). The world is wildly inventive, the game still looks singularly unique (and in my opinion, really neat), the voice acting is still as terrific and quirky as it ever was, and the addition of achievements gives a great reason to revisit the game and explore more of its world.
I loved Full Throttle back in the day and I'm happy to say that unlike many other adventure games of the era, this one's still worth visiting for the first time for new fans or for a quick nostalgia trip for old ones. It warms my heart to see this game made easily available again.

TLDR Doesn't work well enough as action or puzzle game. Could be an awesome walking simulator, but it's not. Senua as a character is probably reason enough to try it.
Amuzing and frustrating game in about equal parts. I am about 70-80% in (I reckon), took me about a day. And some of its sketchy-er mechanics really start to bug at this point. You will die quite a few times just because the game doesn't bother to explain the rules ("hey, there is actually a strict time limit for this - you're dead", "hey, you're not supposed to move too fast here - you're dead"). Also dark mazes (or more likely - "maze-like experiences", I suspect that the game simply waits while you wander aimlessly for the alotted amount of time and then shows you the exit) - is something I would definitely avoid in any game. I get it that protagonist is lost and confused, which makes a maze seem like a good metaphore, but honestly it's just boring.
In combat it seems hard to keep track of entire battlefield; mostly because the game doesn't allow you to control the camera or switch between targets freely. AI uses this to sneak up on you and attack from behind; feels really cheap. Otherwise it's pretty standard - slow/fast attack, block, dodge; featuring as your opponents: "sword guy", "mace guy", "mace guy with a shield", "two handed sword guy", etc. Occasionally it seems like the game chooses to ignore my input, but not too often. Most of the time it feels good to hit things.
There is an abundance of puzzles where you're supposed to find a specific vantage point, where several objects in the environment align to create a specific shape ("rune"). If you played Batman Arkham series, it's very similar to one of Riddler's puzzles. It's fun for about 2-3 times and then gets repetitive fast.
The game really shines in presentation. Creatures and bosses are sufficiently scary (they are also fun to fight when the game doesn't hinder your efforts). Use of lighting and environment effects to reflect Senua's mood is impressive (although darkness can also be annoying - "it's too dark, how am I supposed to find this freaking ladder/passage/whatever?").  Story so far is somewhat bland, but I haven't seen it all yet. Without spoling too much - it's a (metaphorical) journey of a girl with mental health issues in search of a lost lover. The story is told from the girl's point of view, and is somewhat ambiguous at times.
As it is traditional nowdays, there are also scattered bits of lore that you can find. They are optional and have no influence on the game itself (at least I hope so). I usually can enjoy this, but here it feels somewhat out of place. In a way the game discourages exploration - quite often the protagonist is either chasing something, running from something or just generally freaked out; so stopping to read a short story about Norse Gods doesn't feel quite right.
Basically this leaves Senua herself and her Voices. And she's genuinely interesting and unusual as a protagonist (struggling, vulnerable, scared, often doubting herself, and also a bit of a mistery). Possibly the main reason why I am still planning to finish it.
UPDATE. Finished it, not much to add.
Turns out I was wrong about optional lore; it has _some_ effect.
I also noticed that something weird was going on with "darkness" on Senua's arm. I am pretty sure that I died enough times to fill it up completely; and I was under impression that it was supposed to trigger "Game Over; You Suck" ending, but nothing happened. Instead at some point I noticed that the arm cleared up almost completely and then continued to fill up anew. Not sure why; maybe it just doesn't work that way.
Final battle is a bit of a let down.

Highly recommended. Final Fantasy: Majora's Mask, essentially, but with some cool semi-action combat; this creates a game with far more satisfying combat and depth than MM had, but with that same atmosphere of tension and meaningful time management. The game is reasonably difficult, though at times it can delve into near-unfairness (such as fighting a certain boss after running through a location that slowly drains your HP).
The Lightning Saga naysayers are morons. FFX was far more linear than XIII, and X-2 was just unsatisfying and trapped in the deepest ravine of the Uncanny Valley in terms of its graphics (I understand that it was a different time, but seriously take a good look; that game has NOT aged well in any regard). XIII and XIII-2 were vast improvements over each of the X games, and LR is the first game to truly shove aside the conventions of the series for a (mostly) satisfying ending. Give it a shot.

I won't say I'm much of a fan when it comes to FFXIII in general but Lightning Returns managed to make some changes that made the final installment pretty fun to play. It's nowhere near being a classic in the FF franchise but that's ok.

The voice acting/story/characters are still pretty low points but not much was going to change from the previous games. The gameplay changes were what interested me the most. The time limit mechanic actually being pretty cool and less invasive than one might think.
FPS was also all over the place for me, along with some random crashes in certain areas. Annoying but workable.
Overall I give this game a minor recommendation for those looking to finish off the FXIII series.

AKMMD isn't so much inspired by Williams' 1981 classic as it's an update of -- or perhaps a sequel to -- it.  The gameplay, and even some of the enemy types, are clearly modeled after the originals; this isn't necessarily a bad thing, it's just a description of the situation.  For example, a friend once told me he was lukewarm on Bioshock II (although he loved the original) because it basically felt like an extended mission pack instead of a new game (an assessment I fully agree with, by the way); all I could say was, "and?".  Saying a game recreates another game that you enjoyed is high praise, as far as I'm concerned.  AKMMD isn't a carbon copy of its predecessor, though.  For starters, while it's not a complete walk in the park, don't expect the spine-crushing punishment previously delivered by a game that's topped more "hardest video games of all time" lists than comparatively-easier titles like Dark Souls (that might sound like a joke, since the Dark Souls series is the gold standard of brutal difficulty these days, but I assure you it's not).
Personally, I consider the turndown in difficulty to be a good thing; back then you almost
to make a game crazy hard just to keep it from being boring when you've only got a few kilobytes to hold all your game data...these days our computers have enough storage to hold better gameplay and *gasp* plot.  I played through the full campaign on Easy, and I found it moderately challenging; I'm not very good at bullet hell games, as a general rule, so that's to be expected.  I've played through 10 levels on Normal (1-11, skipping 7 because I was going for the "One Direction" achievement :)) and I have to say I'm surprised at how not-that-much-harder it seems; if the rest of the campaign has a similar difficulty curve, I could probably finish it without too many rage quits.  If anything, I'd say the "Easy" mode should be "Normal" and they should make "Normal" a little harder and call it "Hard" (there is no "Hard" setting, although there is an "Arcade" mode I haven't tried yet which is probably harder judging by the name).  But then, I'm one of those old curmudgeons who thinks that "Easy" should actually mean easy, and not "Well, it's easIER than the other setting".  Be aware of my bias though; for the most part, I gravitate much more toward narrative/story games than action/twitch games.
The one thing that feels arbitrary about the difficulty is the gun: it's pathetic.  I mean, it works consistently and without bugs, so it's "fair" in the sense that Dark Souls players like to use the word, but it just feels like a real jerk move to throw the player into an environment that can get so crowded with enemies (and their projectiles) you can barely see the level background and give them...that (I hope you can hear the word "that" in a disapproving-older-relative voice, 'cause that's what I'm going for).  I can't count how many times I got stuck flying along the bottom of the screen because your guns only fire forward and you literally cannot engage in the activity of vertical movement because there's a traffic jam above you the likes of which would make a Fifth Element taxi driver cringe.  You just have to fly along the bottom ('cause you sure can't stop with all the projectiles) and pray nothing's in the way before you can find a spot to peek up.  The balancing factor is supposed to be your secondary gun (which does mow things down with impressive effectiveness for the 1.2 seconds you can fire it), but that doesn't help you in that situation because it only shoots straight forward as well.
So no, while the game's not 1981-quarter-eating hard, it's not a cakewalk.  That said, Super Meat Boy addicts looking for an extreme challenge may feel like it comes up short.
The basic gameplay here is pretty arcade-simple, and looking at a screenshot will pretty much give you the idea.  That said, a few things do bear discussion with this type of game.  The controls are fluid and responsive, but the movement isn't razor-sharp; if this were a platformer, the word I'd use would be "floaty".  Most of the time it's no big deal, but when you get into one of the aforementioned traffic james it can be frustrating to feel like you just want to get out and push, trying to avoid things (when you get going full speed, it's fine, but it's those little micro-movements when you're trying to dip and dodge that get all muddied up...and you'll be doing that a lot more often than flying across the map on a tear).  As far as upgrades,
.
There's also an "endless" mode which will provide a challenge for anybody eventually (for me, pretty quickly) and an arcade mode which looks like it has slightly different gameplay objectives than the regular campaign and is probably more challenging.
At the end of the day, this isn't what you'd call a deep game...but then, it's not trying to be and it doesn't need to be.  It's a fun action shooter that stops short of being frustratingly-hard, and it's got some cat meow sound effects (note: this is _not_ a lolcat meme game, don't misunderstand...the sound effects are appropriate).  The graphics are exactly what they look like in the screenshots and video; cute and cartoony.  It's relatively rare for me to stick with a bullet hell shooter long enough to be able to even write a reasonable review, much less finish the campaign, so I guess for me personally that's a recommendation right there.

- "Crafting" means combining cards here: 2 Basic cards form a SPECIFIC silver card, two silver cards a SPECIFIC gold card. So in the end it's not crafting in a way "I get the unit that I want to play with", but "those cards aren't avilable directly through booster packs". Which ultimately means that you need 4 times the amount of leveled cards to craft a golden max level card than you'ld need to craft a max level basic card (which would be 4*16.384=65.536 level one cards)
For ONE copy.
Now imagine you actually want to use a certain gold card, but also one of the basic cards which are needed for crafting it... While all basic cards are completely up to booster RNG.

Who could forget levels like the nuke mission or being a sniper in Ukraine! Yes, it is over-the-top a lot of the times but that what made it fun back then. This game spawned a generation of modern shooters (including it's own sequels) that tried to grab the charm of this game. Some were better, a lot of them worse, but this was the first one and so it became a classic. Still plenty of people playing multiplayer for such an old game. Choice of servers is between PunkBuster on or off (don't forget to refresh). Without it you have less of a hassle (no need to go find PB configs) but also can expect cheaters more often. There is a system of ranks and challenges present which can occupy you in multiplayer a bit longer. There are also mods so check some of them out if you want. Overall this is a cool game that aged in graphics but certainly not in how much fun it is. Worth a try for the campaign and if you have the patience/friends also for the multiplayer.

The original Full Throttle came out in 1995. I think that's worth keeping in mind, because Full Throttle Remastered often feels like a very dated adventure game with modern graphics and audio.
Overall, it was alright. Recommended with reservations. I wish I could give it a better recommendation, but I'm honestly torn on it. I enjoyed it overall, but not as much as I expected.
The remade art and audio is lovely, the setting and characters are interesting, the voice acting is great. Playing as the leader of a biker gang in a post-apocalyptic setting is certainly refreshing. While there's the threat of death, particularly towards the end, the game will automatically rewind with a "Hmm, that's now hot it happened". Some of the game sequences were pretty funny, and a couple put a grin on my face.
And yet the game clearly shows it's age in certain regards. Navigating the environment is sometimes difficult as exits are vague. Puzzles - while easy for '95 - had me stumped several times. While the audio sounded great overall, the scene transitions during and around cutscenes were often abrupt with ragged cuts. And worst of all, the action sequences, possibly novel at the time, were clunky and tedious - particularly the lengthy and repetitive Mine Road section, and really brought down the otherwise enjoyable game.  I also encountered a couple bugs during the Mine Road section - at one point a defeat resulted in a black screen rather than restarting the ride, and at another all the enemy motorists disappeared and I was unable to take any exits and had to reload.
If you like point and click adventure games and want to experience a bit of the 90's golden age, it's worth a playthrough. Otherwise, I'd much sooner point you towards Kathy Rain or the many great games by Wadjet Eye (or even Telltale, for a modern take).

Full Throttle is an a story of another remaster done right. Improved visuals and sound bring it up on par with what is to be expected from a game released in 2017. At time of its release the game has received a fair bit of criticism from hadcore adventure gamers' crowd for its relatively shortness, simplistic puzzles and twitchy bike combat. But these very same qualities make it more suitable game for contemporary release than many of the heavy weight re-releases/remasters that have come and gone in recent years.
We are well beyond the times when we stacked hintbooks high enough to serve as furniture, spent countless hours on landline in heated debates with friends on clues as how to crack open that one  fiendishly elusive puzzle,  only to be rewarded a few lines of text after having completed a 40+ hour journey.
Full throttle does not require pixel hunting, running back of forth between multiple screens or juggling 30+ items in your inventory of half are nothing but a dud to satisfy us, hopeless pack-rats.
What Full throttle does offer, is smooth cimatic hog ride filled with fun dialogue, numerous timeless gags, cultural references  and full dose of Schafer (tm) madness we have learned to love. The only aspect of the game that hasn't aged too well is the the rebel assault-esque, stiff  pre-rendered  bike combat which can be an acquired taste at times, but does not detract from the finer things the game has to offer.
While oldtimers may want to purchase it for nostalgia, it's casual nature and excellent writing make a very good entry for those new to the genre, even more so now than back in 1995 when it was first released.

Street Racing Syndicate is crass, sexist, testosterone fuelled filth. And it doesn’t apologize.  It’s like The Fast and the Furious on ecstasy.  Or it could be called a Need For Speed Underground clone. This is a 2005 release.  I didn’t expect any miracles folks.
Sure it can’t even run on full screen, and sure some of the controls are a bit of a nightmare, though for 99 cents, I’m not complaining.  If anything it’s a Sunday drive when compared to the speed and tension of games like Redout and Thumper.
It’s aged horribly. It shows us how far we have come as a culture and how far the racing game genre has evolved. This thing is a dinosaur.  I picked it up for 99 cents. I got my money’s worth.  It’s probably the slowest racing game in existence but it’s still fun.
The customization options, the wagering system, the races, the sheer volume of cars… I mean sure it’s no Midnight Club DUB edition, but it’s got real personality for the price and the value proposition was spot on.  Hot chicks, fast cars and free roam. What’s not to love?
I used to adore burnout revenge and I used to adore Need for Speed Most Wanted. Then something weird happened and both series seemed to merge into a single lane.  Need For Speed Hot Pursuit was the outcome. A compromise that satisfied nobody.
SRS is cheap, dirty nasty fun and it knows it. The keyboard/controller configurations are a little off, the game doesn’t display in full screen, and the graphics are noticeably old. I wouldn’t say its aged well but it doesn’t look terrible.
In spite of being made in the naughties, it really feels like a 90s game.  Seriously who uses live action sequences in video games these days?  The models are sleazy hot, the cars all sound and look very nice.  Buy it for nostalgia. Pull it out on weekends and enjoy it.
If you play it in short bursts it’s a perfectly serviceable arcade racer with some interesting mechanics long overdue and deserving of remake with modern assets and modern cars even though you probably wouldn’t get away with something this racy in this day and age.
Whoever would’ve thought a racing game could be too racy? My only major complaint is that it seems to always crash upon exiting which I can only put down to poor coding. Or it could be Windows 10. I’m sure I could get it to run in full-screen but for 99 cents I’m not too bothered by it.
The shadows can be a bit dark sometimes, the controls can at times be a little unresponsive however thankfully the races are often short so it’s not like you can’t just jump back in and retry the circuit.  Think about a minute per lap, 2-3 laps per race.
You place wagers with fellow racers. If you win the wager you get money in addition to your prize pool money, both of which you can use to upgrade your ride with a reasonable variety of licensed parts to keep your garage and your ride competitive for current and future events.
It lacks a sense of speed though I can only put that down to its age and the fact that I’ve played so many racers. After you’ve played F-Zero GX and Burnout Revenge there’s very little that feels fast in comparison to those classics even to this day.
If you pick it up on sale, then I highly recommend it purely on nostalgia value alone in spite of its numerous small issues it’s a fun title at an insane price.  It’s my Sunday night warm-down for a reason. Because its fun, low intensity and one hell of a ride.
As of the writing of this review the title is still on sale for another 4 days.. For 99 cents, hook in. You won't regret it.  If you like arcade racers you reallly can't miss with this one.  It has cult written all over it and deserves a spot in any racing fans' steam library.   At that price (90% OFF!!), you'd be mad not to!

Cherry Tree High Comedy Club is a rare kind of resource management simulation game seldom seen outside of Japan. In games of this type you have to manage a limited number of turns (time) and resources like stamina and money while trying raise your character's stats up high enough to achieve some goal, usually finding a girlfriend. As such most games of this type in Japan are dating sims, although many Japanese dating sims use a different visual novel (choose-your-own-adventure) style of game play. In this case, while it has the standard dating sim high school setting, the goal of the game is different. You're trying to get enough students to sign up as members so you can start a stand-up comedy club at your school.
While I can very much recommend it to anyone who might like this sort of game, or is looking for something different, it's hard to rank against other similar games since there are so few games like it available in the west. You have to go back all the way to the ancient text game Hamurabi to find something similar in the western canon of games. The only two Japanese games with similar mechanics I know of that have been officially translated are the unreleased English version of Princess Maker 2 and the PlayStation 2 and Wii game Sakura Wars: So Long, My Love. There was one attempt to make an entirely new game of this sort (I think) for the western market, Brooktown High, but I haven't played it. The RPG games Persona 3 and 4 have elements of these sort of games, and as a stretch you could say the Harvest Moon series of games are sort of similar.
(The original Princess Maker, by the way, is the granddaddy of this variety of resource management games. In the Princes Maker series of games you're trying raise a young orphan girl to become a princess, though other good and bad careers are possible. So Cherry Tree High Comedy Club isn't really breaking the mold by not being a dating sim.)
While it has a major publisher in the west, this was independently produced game in Japan and written basically by one guy. So it's not big game, it won't take too long to get through it. I took me 8 hours according to Steam, though some of that might be been while I was away doing other things. The original setting was a small but rapidly growing town in Japan, but this was moved to America for the English localization. That translatation isn't perfect, but changing the locale and cultural references for western audiences was pretty much a necessity. It does produce an odd mashup of American and Japanese culture (why does an American town a have a Shinto shrine complete with shrine maiden?), but a literal translation would've been incomprehensible to anyone who hasn't lived in Japan for sometime.

I'm very torn on how to review this game, since quite frankly, I haven't played enough games similar to this to compare it to. So keep that in mind as I try to jumble through my mixed feelings on this game.
For starters, let's start with what the story is about. You are a senior, named Miley. You love comedy. You want to start a comedy club. Jerk president of the student council or whatever says you need 5 members to establish a club. The conflict comes in here. You only have 2 members. Yourself and your best friend/roommate, who never is a big part of the game.
So you, alone, have a month+ (something like 40 days total?) to convince 3 other people to join your club. You accomplish this by getting their "friend level" up to level 5. They all start out at level 1 when you meet them. There are 6 prospective members you can have join you. You can convince any of them (or none of them) to join your club, through various odds and ends.
One example, and the one I expect most everyone will do on their first (and probably only) run, is the story of a little girl, and her grandfather's candy shop. These stories progress in 5 steps. Step one is the introduction to the character. Step two is the introduction to her story. Step three is the continuation of this story to the point where obvious conflict has arisen. Step four is another continuation of this branch, that usually results in you giving advice, or being helpful to the story's subject. And step five is the conclusion, where the prospective member thanks you for your help in the matter, and then hands you their club signup form, guaranteeing themselves a member of your cult of weirdos.
You need to do this for at least three of the six potential members to "win". If you get all six, you get the "good" ending.
Generally, this is a very easy task requiring absolutely no thought. You wake up in the morning and follow one of two schedules. You have a school schedule, and you have a day off schedule.
On school days, your three blocks of time are as follows... you go to school (and conveniently have most of the characters you wish to recruit in one place, to learn about their likes and dislikes, though this can be uncommon at best), you have a block of time where you can walk around the town and do one special task (whether this is talking to the member you wish to recruit, building your "skills", or spending time eating and doing absolutely nothing), and then finally go home, and sleep/talk to girlfriends on the phone/make beads for money (which is pretty useless honestly.)
On off days, you do roughly the same thing, except instead of going to school, you get an extra block of the free do whatever you want period.
Now, the game sounded compelling in a way, and I'm a fan of anime-style graphics, so this game caught my eye. I went in with the understanding this game is very short (2 1/2 hours per playthrough at best?) and that the characters aren't to be taken seriously, but this feels like a pretty sloppy piece of work, considering how short the game is.
There are various magazines you can purchase, or movies you can watch with the intent of upgrading your skills... but this is mostly pointless, as I barely touched my skills, and managed to beat the game with 4 of 6 characters recruited into my club. I'm sure the books may play a bigger part when you are trying to broaden your horizons and get all 6... but even then, it's pretty simple to get any character into your club, given the stereotypical nature of all the characters (the ones who look like they like sports like sports, and the ones who like smart stuff like smart stuff).
By far the most interesting character in the game is the punk rock girl, Cindy, and her story is so short, that I feel unsatisfied. This is in contrast to Sara's story, which feels long and drawn out, and less interesting.
I don't know, this is more of a synopsis on gameplay than a real review, so I may as well leave my final verdict here. The game is fun for about all of 20 minutes before the repetitive nature gets to you, and you lose interest in the story or what happens to the club. Should you manage to complete the game, (which isn't hard, the game is laughably easy) you can go into a NG+ mode I haven't touched yet (and don't plan to touch.)
When a game offers me more content like that, and I say, "no thank you", it generally doesn't bode well for the overall replayabillity of the game. Unless the characters interests change, and the game gets harder (which I doubt on both accounts) I don't think I'll give this game another look.
If you really must try it, get it during a Summer/Winter Sale when it is wicked cheap, and not at the current price. Paying full price will lead to massive disappointment for all.

I do not review games often, but here I have to make an extremely important exception:
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is a self-proclaimed "AAA Indie game," which is reminiscent of a distant video gaming middle market. This game has proven that in an age of AAA games full of micro-transactions and abritary compromises for the sake of marketability, games like these are still more than welcome and, in fact, arguable necessary.
STORY: (A+)
I do not want to discuss the story beyond that of the description already given but it is the forefront aspect of the game aside from its immersion. I say aside from immersion when really immersion and story are married with each other. The developers have utilised their budget higher than that of a regular indie game in order to elevate the medium to the role of being composed of a story, or supplementary to a story, but being part and parcel with the story. The story is told through the mechanics of the game but maintains both textual as well as subtextual elements. To explore the game is to explore the story, and the exploration is guided through its mechanics embedded into its contexts.
Without giving away exact plot details, the protagonist is an incredibly important and well-crafted one. She is a keen and personal insight into the nature of mental health. While I wish to refrain from imparting my own personal feelings into this representation, I feel it would be dishonest not to mention that it has been humbling and incredibly hopeful to see a subject very rarely touched upon with such excellent and delicate consideration. The rest of the characters, despite not necessarily being present are certainly felt, and their personal connections with Senua are soldered onto you whether you want them to or not.
GAMEPLAY: (A-)
The game is a hack-and-slash/puzzle game but with that way it puts story and presentation into the foreground, the combat and puzzle aspects initially feel like they were less of a focus. That said, as the game progresses, there becomes an intimate construction of the relationship between even these mechanics and the story. The way combat operates is basic and yet somehow the game has a learning curve that is not based on remembering combos but rather one's own level of determination towards the challenges at hand. In other words: The fights start easy, you play to an easy battle. The fights get harder, you fight harder. Any changes or developments are on the part of the player, not the character. That said, there are several moments that these battles feel a bit arbitrary or ill-timed, but this a rare occasion and is a perfectly find trade-off considering the level of investment one will have towwards the end of the game.
PRESENTATION: (A)
This is game that boasts its distinction from a regular contemporary indie game. It has more money, it knows, and it uses it but not to the extent of superflousness but to the point that it has achieved the love and care that the game deserves. The acting, mo-cap, and live-action performances are superb; harrowing, heartfelt, sometimes comforting, and often hear-wrenching. My main gripe is the frequent reoccurence of invisible walls forcing me to re-traverse the level at its relatively slow traveling pace. While I certainly appreciated the chance to slow down and take in the gorgeous sights, sometimes I tried my best to avoid venturing off the beaten path under the assumption I would only be heading towards another invisble wall - this resulted in me missing one of the subtle hidden collectibles. But nonetheless, I digress from my praise. One of the most vital selling points and unique characteristics of this game is the use of immersive binaural sound. When playing this, you MUST wear headphones. With the sounds literally whispering in your ears, you are sutured into the mind of Senua and with wonderfully justified reason. Without giving away too much: Hellbade crafts itself entirely with your occupation as spectator in mind. You are in the world, and you are living in it with all its hellish sensory details.
CONCLUSION:
Hellblade is signficant, if short, phenomenal, but under-marketed. I will happily champion this game. If there's one final nitpick to point out, it is that it is relatively niche in its narrow-scope. Which in a sense is probably also a good thing. It is unapologetic in its diversion from the beaten-path. But it has a budget with which it can lovingly and beatuifully commit to its artistic integrity with the utmost fidelity. This is a must-buy, must-play.
OVERALL: A+

A rather frustrating, but oh-so-rewarding arcade shooter that's best played with a controller(in my experience). The graphics and the music are appropriate and delightful, both fitting very well into the whole retro vibe of the game.
What keeps me going back for more though is the challenging and rewarding gameplay. Basically you have 2 to 3 "milk mines" in each level and you have to defend their operators from evil kidnappers. Things can get very hectic very quick as new waves of enemies complement the remnants of the last one, and since you can only take, in theory, five or so hits before you die, you'll be retrying a level over and over and over and over and over again.
As stated in the beginning, the game can get very frustrating very quick, but the frustration's a good one. The type you get when you feel that a game challenges your skills fairly.
So, if you're up for a retro arcade shooter with some challenge to it, give AKMMD a go. Heck, it's only 7 eurodollars, what do you have to lose?

Despite some quirks, it still stands up pretty damn well.
From a civil war to a nuke to an old enemy, it’s a roller coaster pretty much. Each mission (except in the last section) establishes why they’re there, what to do, and progresses the plot towards the next thing to get at a breakneck speed. The story is not very complex or anything but it’s functional to serve the purpose of the game and the quips by the protagonists do give it some character. It has it’s really good moments but mostly the plot is there in the background.

It’s a first person shooter with regenerating health and two weapon slots. Either you like it or you don’t. But overall, the shooting felt pretty good and it was really easy to slide into the controls. The diversity of the game is fun too. Although you’re always shooting, it presents different situations and goals which do help it reduce the monotony.
There are some negatives as you always need to be the one to push forward which really is a pain when enemies will come charging at you or on your back and you have no support because they’re still catching up. The smoke grenade is literally useless and I wish the frag grenade had a bit of a longer throw back period.
It’s showing it’s age but is in no way bad. There are graphical hiccups but nothing that stops the game in it’s tracks.

It’s a functional competent shooter that I enjoyed playing and liked the roller coaster of a story.

This game can be broken down into 2 parts.
30% Deck Building.

The battles are auto-generated so it's all about hoping for the right cards to come out at the right moment.
It's actually enjoyable to play believe it or not. I surprised myself.
Yes there is a big loss timer, but it just cuts your health by half during this process so you can still play. Just keep mashing the same fight and eventually you'll win (if you got decent cards of course).
Don't get the Platinum Booster. I'd rather 4x Silver packs.
Prices in the game are a bit rough when it comes to paying with gems for extra leveling slots, and unlocking in-game events.
Some of the card combinations you face are unbeatable, but thankfully their deck changes when you take them on again.
The game also gets difficult pretty fast with tons of high level zones. You can still beat them though, just will take some replays. I've been taking on level 50 - 65 decks with a level 40 - 44 decks. It's all in the card types.
If you like addictive brainless gameplay - this is it.

Not sure why this is getting bad reviews, I am guessing its from people that have only played it less than an hour, because it gets fun and challenging the farther you get into it.
The best part about it is the in game purchases are done tastefully and are basically to speed things up if you dont want to wait for timers or dont want to play a lot of hours to buy that special card pack with your next winner :)
I love the single player campaign aspect and how challenging it gets at higher levels.. Also if your into PVP then their is a place for that.

A CCG that is not set in the Might and Magic template that is quite enjoyable. The game has ad much going for it as it does against, below is a list of both but overall the positives outweighed the negatives for me.
Pro:
+ Endless grind. Not gated by energy nor other timers.
+ Auto card battle. Not my number one choice but at least the RNG is screwing both the players.
+ At the moment not PVP orientated. And I hope it never will be.
+ Almost entirely redundant cash shop. See cons for the almost part.
+ Loosing isn’t punishing and isn’t rubbed in by showing a match history.
+ Upgradable cards, really, really upgradable.
Con:
+ The game is full Auto. You build the deck then rnJ will play it for you.
+The progression system is not explain and extremely poorly balanced. What I mean is you can kill 1 campaign mob and it disables lower level “farm” decks from spawning.
+ Lots of noob stomper AI decks e.g. a deck that runs 3 cards in 3 – 5 copy that will stomp on you until you buff up to the point that it can’t scratch you. Lots of these even at the 120+ grade.
+ Since the game is built around time based upgrades and the said upgrades use slots that require premium currency towards the mid/late game you will want to invest some $$ to buy a few extra smithies~. This is not as bad as it sound since the cost are exponential insanely so, thus not many at all would have them, evening out the footing.
+ I’m not sure if the game is Hack proof yet. With 200 players on the ladder at very early pvp I ran into 3 players at lvl 3 running exactly lvl 10 upgrade type 3 (gold) decks. Either that or devs thought it’s funny to populate the PVP ladder with OP botts for such an early period in the game.

There was a time when I had a sudden craving for a space combat simulation game, something to replace my playing of Starfox 64 on an emulator and so when I got a discount coupon for Zigfrak, I figured "Hey, why the hell not, let's try this out".
The product I got in the end however was nothing short of a mess in my opinion. The screen throws so much information at you before you can even handle the basics and so needless to say, the tutorial (if there even is one, I can't quite remember), was obviously lacking.
I expected some pretty enjoyable space action combat but was somehow met instead with a 'stare at your target and press space for 20 minutes' type of combat. Your ship didn't handle like a ship would, it was simply a 3D model in the shape of a ship moving in a 3D environment. Nothing you did in the game felt immersive. The massive and convoluted user interface that took up 40% of your entire screen space also didn't help.
Multiple times have I thought about going back into this game and giving it a second chance but those attempts have always ended up with the game making me feel bored and uninterested.
Who knows, maybe this game just isn't for me but as for my final judgment, I simply think I won't be going back for this game anymore as I have better ways to spend my time and find entertainment.

GET THIS GAME! Unless you're Maverick.
Zigfrak is a pretty awesome game. It's amazingly beautiful, but for reasons I can't begin to fathom it has never overheated my laptop. Not even when I accidentally left it running paused and the temperature in my room was in the mid-80s during the afternoon hours (my room sadly faces west). Even games that are 3D only as window dressing tend to overheat my laptop (RTS games, XCOM Enemy Unknown, and many others). This game I could probably leave running for a week.
This game is what I'd term a casual space RPG. What I mean by "casual" is that it tends to avoid the micromanagement most RPGs entail. Unlike most casual RPGs it IS pretty and there's a very wide variety of enemies and components you can add to your ship. No really, there's TONS of things you can upgrade your guns, shields, armor, missile launchers, whatever to. Going along with the casual game theme, they're often whimsically named. Inconvenient realism tends to get glossed over in this game. You're only allowed to carry so many of each object. Once you hit that amount, it automatically converts those items into the type of credits you spend at a trade station (there's at least three forms of currency, which makes game economics all kinds of interesting).
The author loves puns and references. There's an alien weapon type called "strange." So one of the weapons has an effect called "When you're strange." And given that certain of the higher-end weapon names are prepended with "tweaked" they put in one weapon called "Tweaked Morrison." The references vary between movies/sci-fi (obviously) but you can also find weapon types like Larry, Curly and Moe. I want to hope that Moe is the most effective, with Larry being the less-interesting mid-range model.
It's also a fairly sandboxy game. While there's an arcing storyline, you can freely ignore it if you want, and just go about fighting, looting, crafting or whatever.
The author is AMAZINGLY responsive and non-dickish (even when folks are being critical). Seems willing to take a look at your saved games in order to track down bugs (or just fix your stuck game for you). It's almost unbelievable how responsive he is given that it's a $5 game. I almost feel guilty mentioning that it's fairly easy to come by coupons for this game...
The only reason I mention my friend Maverick up top, it's not his type of game. While I wouldn't call the game overly easy, it rather shamelessly lists as one of its selling points that it's a click, kill and loot game. It even describes the things you kill as "loot pinatas." I like the honesty there, it lets you know that this wasn't done by accident or poor design. This game is for people who like getting loot. It's a nice palate-cleanser for my Shadowclan friends *snickers*. Money is easy enough to come by (and if you putter away a few hours in certain areas you'll be absurdly comfortable). You could also avoid doing as I did to get a "more balanced" experience. It shouldn't be TOO hard to get the things you'd want to buy (in the unlikely event they don't drop as loot somewhere).

I got this for $2.99, and that's what I recommend you buy it at. I'm not saying this is a bad game, but it just shouldn't garner a price any higher.
Now, for the actual game.
If you enjoy simple visual novel-styled games that involve the central mechanic of developing relationships with people based on levels of numerical values, then you will enjoy this. The story is light-hearted, and fairly charming; but there's is very little story to the actual main character herself. In order to get the best ending, you will also need to play through this at least two times, and maybe four times at the most. This is by no means anything on the level of 'Katawa Shoujo', or 'Fate/Stay Night', but is not difficult to enjoy either. The simplicity is really what makes this game fun enough to run through it several times.
You can clear it very quickly, and another playthrough means just getting the rest of the people to join you; and that's where I draw the line with buying it for no more than $2.99: because it's such a short game with little to add during your run of New Game+. It's still good though, and easy to play if you're out somewhere, or waiting for your next class to begin.
*EDIT*
Also, why do they keep pushing the fact that this game clearly takes place in the United States, when I can clearly see how hard they're trying to cover up that this town looks like it's straight out of Japan? Really, who are they trying to fool? Did the developer really think this game would do any better if they attempted to localize it by doing a culture swap?

Why should you buy CTHCC?
Why SHOULDN'T you buy CTHCC is the better question.
It's by far one of the best games on Steam, and if you've EVER read a Visual Novel, you'll like it. It's more of a "classic" Visual Novel in that there's more gameplay than there is reading, relating more closely to a Dating Sim than any other sort of VN.
While, of course, there is no dating, there's lots of numbers that the game tracks, such as various skills attained from investing your time in various activities. Each skill then helps you makes friends interested in the same thing. For example, Cindy likes Music, so the higher my level in Music, the easier it is to increase my "level" as a friend with her.  Upon reaching level 5 friendship with the person, they've joined Cherry Tree High Comedy Club.
Now you can see why I relate it to a dating sim.
I said a little too much. All I need to say is: I love this game buy it now.
