Right off the bat this seems like a typical top-down dual-stick shooter ported for PC. But it's not. If you play it like that you will die, a lot, as I did. Sticking with it for a couple of hours reveals tactics, strategy, and hey- its pretty fun too. The game allows itself to be good an top-down shooter (Ok not  quite top-down but I'm unfamiliar with the eact term) but bear in mind- you are not the end-all be-all hero in this game, and any bullet can potentially one-hit kill you. Using over, crouching, going prone, being wary of your line of sight, and flanking allow you to squeeze out an edge on your opponent (difficulty setting dependant). The inventory system and rp (in-game currency) management are the tiniest bit confusing at first, as with commanding your newly formed squad as you rank up. But as with any good strategy game, practice pays off.
Update: With continued playing, I've since discovered that the game is not rewarding mass quantitative achievements (for example, 1000kills or 200 deaths) despite my game stats being well above those numbers, don't know if this is a bug or something... all other achievements are coming along fine.
Also, I've got a major complaint about the battle commander. I'm playing on a difficult custom setting, and on a map involving all three factions. My faction (Brownpants) conquers the center of the map and drives both to opposing corners. I got the Greycollars down to one base (Greenbelts had three on other end of map). Then the commander decides to attack the Greenbelts, taking away all my reinforcements and all chances of finishing off the Greycollars. Like the commander wants to fight on two fronts? Lost my foothold and my patience now I simply can't finish my halfway-beaten campaign.
There are a couple very frustrating 'features' of this game, I can't wait for an update. Still fun though.

Full Throttle is a simple game, perhaps the easiest of the point-and-click generation of the 90's. Worries about delivering a good story involving the Polecats biker gang who ends up engaging in a "hostile takeover" at Corley Motors. With an excellent gameplay, with motorcycle gang fights on Mine Road and crossing a minefield with toy rabbits, the game also has a great soundtrack and memorable characters such as Maureen and Father Torque.
When I think about the beginning of my passion for video games, one of the images that soon comes to my mind is Ben riding his bike.

So I've played this game for close to 50 hours and just finished it, and I think it deserves my thoughts. I played the previous installments of the Final Fantasy XIII series before playing this too. Overall I'm really happy with this game.
A quick word on the quality of the port:
The port is alright. With an R9 290 I achieve stable 60fps. The only thing that bugs me is the 1080p max resolution with my 1440p monitor. The first FFXIII didn't have this limitation so I'm confused about why this isn't a feature in LR. Regardless, the game is very responsive to your commands and the game looks gorgeous - could do with some better anti aliasing though. I didn't run into any crashes or weird bugs during my playthrough. FInally, controller support is excellent and I would highly recommend using a controller to play this game.
Moving onto the story (no spoilers):
I really like how this game closed out the XIII series. The plot left me satisfied at the end with how everything turned out and the characters in the game are all interesting, with some unimportant NPCs being very well fleshed out While the plots of the previous two were concerned with politics and science/time travel, Lightning Returns tackles the idea of religion being a dominant force in the world. Just a word of warning, though - you will very likely want to play the previous two games of the series before playing Lightning Returns - this game tends to assume you know a lot about the characters in the game already. In addition the story will be a lot more interesting to you and it was really good to see some familiar faces from the XIII world in this plot.
One thing I didn't like about the story was how repetitive it became. Sometimes the same concept would be explained time and time again as if it were being told to a child. All cutscenes are skippable if you're not interested in the story however.
Voice acting across the board was good, but not great. There are the occaisional cheesy lines here and there, but it's Lightning's voice you'll be hearing the most (as well as one other character) and they both do an outstanding job.
Now to the gameplay:
I was actually a fan of FFXIII, depsite the community's resounding hatred for its linearity. However I still really enjoyed the open world nature of Lightning Returns. There are a ton of side quests to complete, some of which give more background on main characters and other NPCs. The main quests are all unique in their completion criteria and are fun to complete if that's all you want to do. I don't recommend just doing the main quests, though.
The time aspect of the game is used really well, even if it got frustrating having to organise where to be at the correct time. I can see it being just possible to complete all quests in a single playthrough - this becomes much easier with new game+ mode, however.
Quick note on the soundtrack:
The game's soundtrack uses some new material, but the majority of it is recycled from the previous two games. While I don't mind it because the music is AMAZING (like literally awesome), it would have been nice to hear some more original material. Music sets the scene brilliantly with a wide variety of beats and songs for every emotion.
The battle system:
I love the new battle system. The ATB of old was pretty good, but the Schemata system in Lightning Returns in miles better. Instead of each ability costing "time" they cost ATB, but you don't have to wait to queue abilities anymore. Instead the "Paradigms" (now called Schemata) have indidual ATB guages that recharge slowly when in use and faster when deselected. The system is very elegant and works brilliantly.
The focus in battle now still remains to stagger your opponent to deal as much damage as possible, but now a new Block mechanic is introduced. You can block enemy attacks (completely mitigating damage if blocked at the correct time). This plays a massive part in combat. There is also a concept called "perfect timing" which involves timing atack inputs correctly to maximise damage. This concept is hard to grasp early, but after the 20 hour mark I was able to flawlessly pull it off.
The number of enemies is far smaller in Lighting Retunrns (just ~31) compared to the previous games. This is not a bad thing, however, as each enemy has unique attack patterns that you must adjust your playstyle and Schemata to. You will be revisiting the same areas often as well so this supports my last point.
In addition to combat there is also a form of levelling through upgrading abilities and completing quests. Abilities are dropped by mosters that can be upgraded and combined at a Sorcery Shop, while your raw stats can be increased by your Garb (clothing), Weapon, Sheild and Accessories, as well as completing quests.
The TL;DR:
Overall, this game is far more in depth compared to the previous installments of the Final Fantasy XIII series. With a rich story, a vastly improved combat system, day/night cycle based quests and your favourite cahracters from the series, Lightning Returns is a brilliant JRPG to close out the trilogy. The only thing that I wish were improved was the storytelling, not the story itself.

Half-Life 2 is a first person shooter and the official sequel to the (basically) universally famous original Half-Life by Valve. The game's story continues right where the previous title ended: Gordon Freeman, a scientist and a witness to the Black Mesa incident, finds himself in a Earth invaded by the Combine alien forces and with the majority of humanity enslaved. Freeman will find himself, willing or not, cooperating with the human resistance just in order to survive.
Half-Life 2 basically took what made the original game a serious hit, high quality scripted events and a lively virtual world you could interact with, and managed to turn it up to eleven. When it comes to level design, the sequel is arguably far better than the first game: while the original title featured mainly the Black Mesa facility and its immediate sourroundings, Half-Life 2 features a pletora of locations, from City 17 to the coast side, from a Combine prison facility to a web of canals. While the game retains the original's linearity, there are some rare instances where losing your way and wondering where you must go or what you must touch to advance can become very confusing. Aside from those, however, most of the time your path is quite obvious.
Another unique feature of Half-Life 2 is the numerous gameplay changes you are tasked to master in the various areas: sometimes you must use a freshly introduced vehicle to navigate several maps and deal with your enemies; some other times you must use the help of a group of NPCs and direct their movement in order to overcome heavy enemy resistance. Each chapter has an unique twist on the formula that always keep you on your toes. Thankfully the new mechanics are pretty quick to master, aside from some vehicles having very shaky controls that make driving them a bit harder than it needs to be.
Regarding the fps elements, Half-Life 2 is your standard fare when it comes to these games: you are given a large number of weapons (some original, others more traditional) to gun down the impressive cast of enemies you are pit against. While there are no bosses to speak of it, some of the larger enemies require some extra strategies to be brought down, which offers a nice change. By far, the most peculiar weapon in Half-Life 2 is the gravity gun: it allows you to get a hold of elements of the scenary and either move them or throw them at high speed to defend yourself.
This Update release is basically a graphic update mod with the aim to fix some issues with the rendering of the original game. While the overall quality of the game doesn't change that much, some will find such changes noticeable.
If you consider Half-Life to be one of the greatest videogames ever made, then you will love Half-Life 2 to no end. If you don't have any experience with the original game, Half-Life 2 will reveal itself as a very entertaining game with plenty of surprises and superb fps action. This is basically the game that began the fps trend of scripted events and sudden gameplay changes, after all

Aqua Kitty: Milk Mine Defender is a side-scrolling shooter modeled after - you guessed it - the classic arcade game Defender. If you're not familiar with Defender at all, the premise is pretty simple: fly left or right in looping stages shooting all in your path while gaining power-ups and occasionally saving the odd human or two. Or in Aqua Kitty's case, cats.
The story is simple and silly, the graphics are bright and vibrant, and the music is amazing. So what about the gameplay? Well, if you like Defender you're set. The controls are responsive, the shooting is satisfying, and the difficlty ramps nicely. There are plenty of different enemies to defeat so the game never becomes repetitive. It's a tad short, but with three difficulty settings and an Endless Mode, there's plenty of replayability.
I thoroughly enjoyed this game. If quirky arcade shooters are your thing, this is the game for you.

In the space year 20XX, the entire world's supply of milk appears to have "ran dry". This would suggest to me that sometime in the future all form of breasts will become either extinct or outlawed and force us to look elsewhere for our creamy goodness. As luck would have it for our kitty chums, though, "deep under the ocean, vast amounts of what appear to be naturally forming full fat milk were discovered". Don't ask me how the milk is now lying under the ocean. Perhaps all the world's mammaries will migrate to below the surface to escape danger or persecution in the future? Either way I guess it's only natural that boobs would eventually start heading downwards with the passage of time. But however they got there, the kitties are determined to get it out and launch an operation to mine it and send the milk gushing back forth into the world once more. But it's not a task without peril for our hungry kitties as they're attacked by unknown enemies who try to kidnap the underwater miners and keep all the lovely, delicious milk for themselves. "OH NOES!", cries the kitty captain. Oh noes, indeed. So out sets a brave pilot to shepherd the miners and destroy the threat, keeping his furry brethren in one piece and saving the world's milk(/boobs?) in the process...
If anybody says the story is dumb then you and me are gonna step outside and have words, alright?! Anyway, on with the review.
In Aqua Kitty - Milk Mine Defender, you'll pilot a small, one-man sub... one-cat sub? Whatever. You'll pilot a sub through stages that loop around on themselves and are no higher than the height of the screen, shooting waves of enemies until all have been wiped out while taking care not to lose all of your miners who walk the surface (as long as one is kept alive you're fine). Additional enemy types are gradually introduced as levels progress and power-ups are occasionally dished out to help your efforts. Its basic formula is simplicity itself, and in that comes so much of its addictive appeal and accessibility as the game sinks its claws into you and doesn't let go.
It isn't exactly laid out this way, but essentially there are three modes in the game. There's the standard style of play (available in easy and normal difficulties) where your progress is saved and failing a level means simply restarting it at any point from a map screen, while power-ups are temporary and don't carry on through stages. There's Arcade Mode, which sets you the challenge of making it through all 25 stages with one life, but with power-up drops being replaced by gems which can be used to purchase upgrades which do carry through stages but are also degraded with each hit you take. And then there's Infinite Espresso mode (also available in easy and normal) where you have to make it through as many waves as possible with one life and very limited power-ups, but at least with no miners to worry about.
There's a slight retro, SNES era style about the look of the game, complete with "chunky" sound effects and some outstanding music that never gets old and even manages to stay lodged in your head long after you've finished playing. Some people have commented about the game being too difficult. I don't really play many side scrolling shooters like this, and wouldn't consider myself especially gifted at them or anything, but I can't say I had all that much trouble with it. There were a few problem stages, sure, and achievement hunters beware, unless you have the twitchy reflexes of a coked-up cat with Tourette's on his fifth can of Red Bull then you're gonna have a ball-achingly hard time getting 100%. But to just complete the game and get most of the experience this has to offer, the rest of us mere mortals should do just fine.
I think it says a lot that even 30 or so hours into this game, no matter how many times I died I still more often than not had a smile on my face and rarely did I ever feel the game was cheap or unfair (maybe aside from the red, grabby b*astards that steal your miners. THEY SHOULDN'T BE ALLOWED TO FIRE! I swear I get nailed by their single, slow shots more than anything else). The hours easily flew by without me noticing and I found I had to stop myself from carrying on anymore trying to beat the harder challenges. If that's not a glowing recommendation for anything then I don't know what is. If I had any complaints it would be that sometimes your sub doesn't feel quite as sharp or responsive as you might like in some of the tighter spots. And while it's perfectly possible to play with a keyboard, I'd strongly advice using a controller. But otherwise, I loved almost everything about this game. Oh, except the fact they had a cat piloting a ship and didn't call him Commander Kitty... I'll never be able to forgive them for that.

I like the presentation and the music, and usually I don't mind difficulty in games, I grew up with games in the 80ies and 90ies and so I thought this game might be enjoyable for me.
In the long run, it was not. At level 10 I had to retry alot, it became tedious and annoying. And it stayed like that till the end... there is little incentive to go on, compared to the tedious retrying that is necessary for most of the later levels.
There is no story, no exploration in the levels or in the world map, no persistent ship powerups worthy of that name (looking at you, turbo cannon). Progression through gradual development of player skill is usually a motivation in many difficult or "oldschool" games, but here it is negligible, the mechanics are too shallow for that, and you constantly feel weak and the powerups are only temporary. Instead of "shoot'em up", this is an "avoid'em and shoot little peas from a safe distance", because in the later levels the enemies take alot of hits to kill.
Eventually I finished the game on easy but apart from the endboss and the achievements, there is NOTHING happening in the game that actually gives you motivation to keep trying.
Another annoyance is the radar: it does not center on your ship. That means when you want to get your bearing in a hectic situation, you will first have to search for your own ship's position on that small radar and that costs precious time when the main screen is full of enemies and their bullets. It forces you to keep your eyes on the radar and off the main screen for longer than necessary. You often loose health because of that, and it always feels frustrating.

- If I find a crashed ship, I still need to invest milions to open up inventory slots - and by the time I'm done, I've spent way more money than I would have just bought that ship. How does that make any sense?
- When I initiate conversation with an alien, my perspective spins around to face the alien - that isn't realistic and the animation is jarring.

Other complaints
- The procedurely created world lacks impact for me because the artstyle and UI doesn't seem to aim for realism. For maximum realism, most UI elements should disappear. If Need for Speed: Underground and Midnight Club were the popular kids in the street racing video game scene, and Juiced/Tokyo Xtreme Racer were the art class nerds, Street Racing Syndicate would be the creepy goth chick standing by herself in the corner. Tortured metaphors aside, this is a pretty awful game. If you're looking for street racing, you have plenty of better options.
Copying the model from every other game like it, SRS drops you in an open world city with a selection of mostly asian production cars like Toyotas, Hondas and Nissans. Everybody's attitude is 'too kull for skul' and the goal is to become 'da best driver'. The grind begins there and it's familiar to any racing gamer. Pick ride, win races, upgrade ride, win harder races, upgrade ride more, win big tournament, pick better ride, repeat. The only new mechanic is the "Girlfriends" you can pick up in the game. There are a number of girls on the streets who will offer challenges. Complete them and you can have them ride along with you. The only bonus this provides is that after a certain number of wins you'll unlock a video of the girl's real life counterpart dancing in progressively less clothing. Some will find this sexist, I just find it hilarious and weird.
So much is wrong with this game. The car controls are too sticky, requiring very little in the way of racing lines. You take realistic damage that must be repaired to keep your car at full performance which constantly drains your funds. Cops are everywhere and the chase system is so hit or miss you'll escape a chase sitting right next to a cop. Applying upgrades to your car is a chore due to multiple categories of the same items and a performance graph that must refresh every time you pick a new part.
Story - 1/5 You're a scrub. Become the best.
Graphics - 3/5 Cities can look really nice some times but the car and npc models are low quality.
Audio - 3/5 Decent soundtrack but the songs repeat too frequently.
Gameplay - 2/5 As long as you know how to drive you can't lose. No variety in races.
Replay - 1/5 You can spend hours accumulating girlfriends for their slighty sensual videos. Or you can use Google.
Overall - 2/5 The bottom barrel of street racing video games. It's competent, playable, but not much else.

You fly a ship. Sort of. Well, you pilot something, you point it vaguely at something which is trying to kill you, there's a lot of flashy graphical effects, things explode. There's loot everywhere. You scramble to collect the loot, it comes in a rainbow of colours and flavours, there's guns, oh dear god there's so many guns. You're spoilt for choice, it's practically like Borderlands all over again.
Zigfrak is a space.. game... sortof.. you fly around and shoot things, lots of things, and collect a lot of loot of various sorts to pimp out your ship with, as you level up and gain experience, the things you can pimp out your ship with get ever more ridiculous until eventually you're shooting drones armed with minature nuclear warheads (which will cause all kinds of hilarious screen glitches, no, do not adjust your monitor, the designer MEANT FOR THAT TO HAPPEN!), and your shield can withstand you being in close proximity to said explosions, mostly...
Over the course of the game you'll obtain a dubstep satellite that explodes with the power of nuclear wubs, an inflatable mini party station that you can dock with and resupply at (which will also pump out some most excellent dance music), you will be exposed to cerulean blue and become addicted to this gorgeous colour. You will hack satellites via minigames. You will encounter Bear Grylls in a worm, and have to construct shoelace traps. You may end up eating shoes as a result. You will work for the space equivalent of the mafia, and for the pirates, and for the police, you will do all these things and yet somehow you'll still be managing to stick to some kind of overarching story which takes place on a very interwoven backdrop.
This game is the product of the mind of one man, and if this game says anything about his mind, it's that this guy probably should be in a room with nice soft padded walls, and his keyboard, monitor, and PC should be securely fastened to solid surfaces, and also coated with drool and chew resistant materials. Insanity does not even come close, yet for all the insanity, there's genius here, a rare diamond of genius that you really ought to try out for yourself.
Beware the refreshing drinks though, I'm pretty sure he laced them with something dangerous. Ditto for the cookies, do not eat the cookies.

Like a lot of people who've reviewed this, I played the absolute hell out of this game back when the original came out.  It's extremely linear, as any point-and-click adventure game is, but the unique setting/plot, wry humor, memorable characters, and phenomenal voicework (especially for the time) kept me coming back to it over and over.
The question, then, is whether the remaster lives up to the legacy.  The answer is "absolutely yes."  The graphics and audio are cleaned up quite well while still maintaining the signature style, allowing the game to look the way I actually remember it, rather than the graphical limits of the mid-90s.  It's stable, it runs well, and the hardware requirements are practically nonexistent.  Couple that with the reasonable price tag, and there's no reason not to give it a go, whether you're a veteran looking for a replay or a newcomer looking at something different.
Well, okay, there is one flaw:  It's short.  Quite short.  Take a look at my playtime, and understand that I finished the game, and even sped halfway through a second time to grab one achievement I missed somehow.  Now, I remember every part of the game by heart, so I knew exactly how to solve every puzzle, but I still took my time interacting with all the characters and objects, seeking the fun flavor text that serves as the meat of the game.  Despite that, though, it's still well worth the money, and I can't recommend this game strongly enough.

Playing this game is honestly kind of stressful with headphones, but i really recommend it so you can get the full experience.
Lastly, the permadeath mechanic isn't what it seems to be and i hope it doesn't drive people away. It really just adds more weight to every enemy encounter. This game isnt really for everyone but if you enjoy a story heavy game and puzzle solving this might be for you.

The purpose of Art is to make us feel and live through someone else's eyes ; someone else's experience.
This immersion, this projection, is often more important than realism. Realism can be very interesting but has it's own limitations : when reality has become common, how do you trasmit the feeling of someone for whom it is not common ?
The answer is : creativity.
That is why Star Wars' AT-AT is probably a better way to make us feel like a soldier of WWI facing his very first tank than a tank in a frame would be. Because for us, tanks are common, but for him, back then, it was a steel and plate invincible monster.
How do you show to a wide audience what is a mental illness without asking them to drop mad or get bored ?
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is the answer to this. Developping techniques that were unique when developped, being backed up by psychologists and groups of people with mental illnesses, with the talent of good creators and artists, this game is make is us feel and live the adventure that is in the mind of it's main character.
Plain and simple, with no detour, with no compromise, with no false promise.
Plain and simple, because everything is thrown at us and we start quickly to think like the main character.
With no detour, because there is a goal, a destination, and nothing else. You have a quest. You promised.
With no compromise, because it was not ment to be bankable, it was ment to feel authentic, if not real. It was ment to make us question our way of thinking and change a bit part of us.
No false promise, because the very first warning screen is telling you : this is about a character with mental illness. And you deduce quickly ; she will have to face her own demons.
You will have to face her own demons.
Your own demons.
Be prepared to help her, and doing so to learn a lot on the way so it can help you later.
Unique, risky and impressive, this game should be bought by anyone having it on his wishlist but hesitating.
You are giving your money to a small dev team who decided to produce itself and risk everything on a game talking about mental illness.
Not very bankable.
But it was way worth it.
On the bad side, I would say that it is not for the hack and slash fan, and it can be hard on you sometimes. The limited number of "lives" (as said by the game, but I never went to the end of the limit) makes it a problem : if you lose all your lives, you will have to restart everything. To be honest, would I have lost the game, I would have stopped there, even if I WANTED to see the end. I would not have had the courage to restart everything from the begining.

No Man’s Sky Review-
This is my first game review! And I choose to review No Man’s Sky.
Games are entertainment right? A lot of games we play are based on this fact. Another fact though is we get excited for games that do more than just entertainment. They immerse us. They challenge our imaginations and take us to other worlds. No Man’s Sky is a game that does this really well for me. I often get hyped for games like open world RPGS, games that dare me to live in a virtual world that corresponds with creativity. When I saw a trailer for No Man’s Sky I was very impressed with its art. Now the gameplay trailer for E3 was gorgeous (and I just re watched it on YouTube to help with this review) and the game comes very close to what I saw in the trailer. Now I haven’t encountered 100 percent of the experience in my 60+ hours (plus another 40 on PS4) it still delivered that scope of space mixed with a Pink Floyd like art style. Sandboxes like these are rare, and this one is also unique. Do I recommend it? I have really got my money’s worth, but I knew what this game was going into it. No Man’s Sky can be boring, or lonely or even not 100 percent what you expect. Games like this are perfect for me, and I encourage you if you like it, take it all in. It’s a special game. Thank you.

Having played through the chapters available as of the time this review was written (seasons 0 through 2), I have to say that Majestic Nights scratches all the itches I expected.
While the graphics are not great (but more than adequate) and the gameplay is a bit sketchy at times (but not aggravating), the theme is great. You are a renegade secret agent (or a detective, depending on the season) that gets knee-deep in the world of conspiracy facts (rather than theory). In short, let's just say that if you grew up in the 80s and experienced the best the Internet had to offer in the early to mid 90s, you'll feel right at home. If you didn't, there are in-game dossiers that will bring you up to speed without being too lengthy.
Speaking about the writing, not only is it great but there are different conversational ways (non-evident most of the time) of accomplishing objectives, which warrants replayability, kind of a big deal for a game that's not too long at the moment.
The music is spot-on for the atmosphere of the game (in the style of 80s synthwave revival) and is included with the game at no extra cost, in MP3 and FLAC - bonus points for a game when so many others sell the OST separately.

You can gun down a swarm of Nyancats, then laugh maniacally until your housemates give you strange looks. That alone is worth the price of entry, I think
But, in all seriousness, this is a fun and fantastic game. The keys are rebindable, which makes it damn easy to fly with mouse and keyboard, so no issues there.
The difficulty ranges from glorious romping 'pwn them all' fights to 'dear gods, will they never stop coming?' - but there are powerups randomly dropped by destroyed foes which help keep you alive even in a drawn out dogfight against an entire fleet.
The AI is decent, for both ally and enemy ships, and sometimes you'll find yourself gritting your teeth and muttering 'That's MY loot, dammit' as you gun down some tractor-beaming scumbag pirate who's trying to zip off with your hard-earned dark matter or rare loot drop. Luckily you can board the sods and steal it back if you can disable them without blowing them into spacedust.
The missions range from basic tutorial fetch quests to humorous shenanigans, all the way up to 'wtf I don't even... what just happened?!'.  There's even a 'Bear Grylls in Space' parody hidden away in there. There's a LOT of laughter to be found in Zigfrak. Did I mention that you can gun down an entire swarm of Nyancats? Sweet vengeance is sweet.
Frankly, for 5 bucks? There is every reason to pick this up, even for a bit of casual play here and there.

This is my first review for a game I have been waiting for over half a year. TLDR at the end.
Good things overall:
- It's a good game.
- It's not perfect, but it's a good port.
- Good price.
- Good cards.
- Achievements are not hard (+100 hours if you want all of them)
- Most DLCs included.
Good ingame mechanics:
- Lightning.
- NG+ system like in Dark Souls II
- Tons of items and garbs to get.
- Tons of quests to do.
- Tons of monsters to exterminate.
- You can switch schemata mid attacks and do A LOT of combos, which makes the game more than just atackattackattack, switch and repeat.
- The days system is not bad, it's just that most FF games are endless. This one is just different.
- You only grind gil, you won't need to slay specific monsters for most missions as you will get the items eventually.
- Missions are only hard if you don't explore (on a sandbox game, duh)
- Game encourages you to go to NG+ to get upgrades and other items.
Not so good ingame mechanics:
- Game is only hard (but enjoyable) during NG on normal mode. It will be REALLY easy on NG+ even if you play on hard mode.
- Enemies don't scale on each playthrough, while you do, The game becomes easier and easier the more you play. I'm on NG+ on hard and only final bosses and last ones are challenging... sometimes.
- Some garbs are better versions of other existing ones, and others are niche and would require a complete garb setup to work.
- Aeronite is a ♥♥♥♥♥.
- Ereshkigal is a ♥♥♥♥♥.
- Most weapons and shields are just enhaced versions of previous ones.
Note: Game tends to crash sometimes in the Dead Dunes laberynths for some reason.
TL;DR: Tons of stuff to do, good replayability potential, but it eventually becomes too easy because monsters don't scale and it starts to get boring. Lightning is love.
I'm seriously waiting for a mod to make enemies scale on each playthrough, it's the only thing keeping me away from wasting 1k hours in this game.

Great remaster of a classic adventure game. You can choose between updated gfx and audio or stick with the originals and there's a nice commentary mode, as well as bonus concept art. There's also an optional updated interface that streamlines interactions a bit. Good stuff all around and props to Double Fine for finding and restoring so many of the source assets.
As for the game itself, it holds up pretty well, though the issues of the original are still present. Some puzzles involve a lot of trial and error and to make matters worse, these particular puzzles usually have hidden time limits. In addition, the game can be completed in 4-6 hours (depending on how good you are at adventure games), which is short even by modern standards. Flaws aside, Full Throttle's writing and style are as strong as ever and definitely worth experiencing today.

I had a blast playing Full Throttle Remastered. It's a short but sweet game and there was a stretch between the early 2000's and 2012 or so when a game like this wouldn't have been made, until the rise of the indies. It offers a fresh milieu in the gaming world and features memorable and funny characters. The voice acting is great and the puzzles are occasionally a little obtuse but as the game's been out a while there is an abundance of help available on the internet.
If you like adventures give this classic a try.

Like many of its genre, To the Moon is an interactive story told through video game as its medium. The game strength rests on its beautifully written story, charming dialogue, and memorable music. It pleasantly introduces the main theme through a clever narrative device - kids playing piano slowly turning up as background music - and you will get easily drawn to the game just from the soothing atmosphere built by the music.
As a game, there isn't much to the gameplay aside from point and click adventure. To the Moon has a brief moment gameplay variation (like the 5 minutes action), mini games, and a few of scattered discoverable trivias, but they are made in such a way that you will discover/play them all along the way, making the game doesn't have much replay value. The control also could've been better.
As an interactive story though, To the Moon captures a lot of attention from its beautiful story, exploring the theme of love and memory. The story takes a few turns that puts me to a bit of surprise, especially towards the heart-breaking end. The plot is structured very nicely and it's paying a good attention to details; as the plot unfolds, the little details you notice along the way helps making sense the story without the characters having to blatantly point it out to you. Comedy (especially pop culture reference) sometimes slips between the bittersweet story, which might get the tone shaky at times, but as the story progresses it gets more consistent with the writing.
A worthy 4,5 hours playtime that is best played in one-sitting.

I've been playing since launch, and have enjoyed this game at every release. I wasn't fazed by the lack of promised features at launch, mainly because I wasn't aware of all of the pre-release marketing - I only saw the initial E3 trailer and didn't know what to make of it at the time. I don't blame those that felt let down - though the echo chamber on the internet got a little out of hand (e.g, fans issuing death threats). This is a review of the game though, not the handling of Hello Games' marketing efforts or the gentle flower that is a hyped gaming community.
The game is completely different now (even since 1.38, a minor release), and I wish I could play the game like this in 2016 before I experienced monotonous gameplay, but its varied and interesting now. The story feels fuller, the gameplay loop richer, and the graphics are much more detailed. There's a missions system, a fourth race, vehicles, bases, some basic co-op support, better planets, and much more. It also hasn't lost its charm as a relaxing exploration game, if you want it to be that.
I'd like to see the fauna have more interesting behavior, and maybe do more interesting things related to them. What if there was a "zoo" of some sort, where you collect creatures and raise them? There's a lot of potential with not only making them a fun part of the gameplay, but also making them more convincing. Currently, aside from the odd frankenstein thing murmuring "kill me", I mostly ignore them.
Hello Games has tried things, and they have made mistakes, but I think they have proven themselves to have much more integrity than what the community's consensus on them was around release. They threw what was probably one of the more interesting viral marketing campaigns in recent memory with the Waking Titan ARG. They've shown they are willing to earn our trust back, and now we should let them.
Get this game, there's really no experience like it, and tune out the noise and baggage following it.

You're a cat piloting an armed submarine and your mission is to protect cat miners from being grabbed and taken away while surviving several waves of enemies: why are there cats under the sea you ask? Well, they ran out of milk but found out there were reserves under the ocean fllor, hence the mining operation.
From the silly premise spawns a simple but decent retro shoot-'em-up with tight controls, fun gameplay and nice art style.
-the cute art style truly fits the silliness of the game
-retro graphics are colorful and done well
-great and catchy chiptune soundtrack
-gameplay, while simple, is quite fun and easily gets frantic as you try to dodge bullets while scrambling to save a grabbed miner
-good progression, as levels advance you're slowly introduced to different enemies that require different tactics
-the three different game modes will provide an adequate challenge whether you're new to the genre or a veteran
-it can be difficult to properly see enemy models and shots once the screen is filled up with them, enemy bullets can easily be overlooked as they don't stand out much and things can get worse if  you've just picked up an upgrade that makes you fire in more directions, adding to the chaos
-the last area really ups the ante difficulty-wise, even on easy you'll be facing several more waves with numerous enemies  and I felt it was the only time progression wasn't as smooth as before
-keyboard controls feel a bit awkward, I absolutely recommend a controller
-sticking to its retro roots means the gameplay is very simple and can get a bit repetitive in the long run
-quite short and, unless you want to hunt achievements or climb the leaderboards, there's little reason to go back once you're done with it
Aqua Kitty - Milk Mine Defender truly feels like a game out of the age it pays homage to, the love that obviously went into recreating the retro graphics, music and gameplay is its greatest strength but also a great weakness. In fact, true to the games of old, it comes out as a very simple and basic game with little in the way or story, upgrades or level variety.
It's a decent, fun game with a very straightforward but enjoyable gameplay and I feel it can be a worthwhile purchase for fans of the genre when on sale (around the 3$ mark): it won't last long but it'll be a nice way to remember the past.

First of all, I am a long time fan of the Final Fantasy series so bear with me here!
This was my first time pleying through the game, I have played through Final Fantasy XIII on the Xbox 360 and PS3, and Final Fantasy XIII-2 on the PS3 and on here. The XIII trilogy might've started off on a bad note for many but it was a great start to what would be a great adventure to look back to. This game made up for any faults the others might have had. It has exploration, tons of quests, "limited" monsters, Postgame/New Game+ content, and more! Sadly the weapon, armor, and accessory enhancement part of the game comes after beating the game in New Game+.
The game follows a sort of Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask timed playthrough, where everything has to be done withing a certain amount of time or doom for all (game over). I was afraid to go into the game knowing this, but I ended up having so much spare time in game that I didn't have much to do. In this game you do not get any sort of XP from killing monsters, but you get a raise in stats after beating quests and saving souls of the remaining people in the Chaos ravaged Nova Chrysalia. I enjoy beating quests and getting the rewards, but this way I thrive even more! Now I gotta admit that I played it on Easy mode so I could escape battles without any penalty, so I did it to have fun, relax, and watch this great story unfold.
The story continues 500 years after the events of Final Fantasy XIII-2, and the world has been, mostly, eaten away by the chaos from Valhalla. Lightning awakens from her crystal sleep after these 500 years by the god of light, Bhunivelze, to help the survivors and save their souls so Bhunivelze could create a new world for mankind. Throughout the story you see some familiar faces (of course), and some familiar names from the FF series (you'll see... maybe). While most of the characters don't help in battle at all, because it is mostly focused on Lightning and her role as savior, they will have great importance in the story and help fill in some o the blanks from the 500 years Light missed.
I'm just going to have to stop there and say that I thoroughly enjoyed every aspect of the game. While I do miss having some companions accompany you through the story, it is a nice way to see the adventure through one person's perspective and get more details from them. The music, while a lot of it sounds like some sort of remix of "Blinded By Light" the battle theme from Final Fantasy XIII, it is put together well to make each track fit in with the environment and situation at hand. Many of the tracks are pulled from the two other FFXIII games, but I loved so many of them that I was glad to hear them in this game, it also has a few songs from other FF games so keep an ear out, and the battle music isn't just one to three songs, but many pulled from the XIII trilogy and played in different maps and times of day.
Continuing from my opinion of the various aspects of the game, the visuals are still easy on the eyes with the same amazing look from the recent games. For you PC snobs (no offense), the freamerate does go up to 60fps so that's a good upgrade, and it has different options for the graphics (look below in the info section to see what exactly). I've seen other reviews complain about the always online DRM, but I haven't gotten knocked offline so I played comfortably, but please Square Enix, don't do that, sometimes we might not be able to connect to the inetrnet, so don't add that kind of thing alright? Anyways, I feel that theer is a high replayability for people who like New Game+ content, achievement hunting, and simply just becoming some kind of overpowered god (out of my Bhunivelze, there's a new god in town) through weapon, armor, and accessory upgrading. Did I mention, the attacks and clothing Lightning wears is customizable? Well, yes it is, each "grab" has it's own stats and some might come with locked in abilities like magic slash and such, but you can change the other abilities to whatever you please.
Now I know I didn't cover everything, I will let you the reader (thanks for taking the time btw) discover everything yourself. I don't mean that in a rude way, but I did mostly have a lack of information purposedly to have that "wow" factor to what new features are in this game. The combat is great too for anyone who felt like they weren't really feeling like there was any strategy to the other combat systems because of its real time live action battle system. I hope you guys enjoy the games itself and ignore the whole "stay online" DRM as this game ends on a high point for this great trilogy.

This game really is something else. It is not a game, it is an experience, no words can describe what is felt throughout this game. Hellblade easily surpasses as one of the best story driven experiences created, and it also has become one of my all time favorites.
The story itself is one of a kind. Psychological horror plays a massive role in Senua's quest. You almost feel for her pain as you play, the obstacles she must overcome, the trek she is trapped within, it is portrayed perfectly and keeps you wanting, in a sense, to help Senua in her fight. Everything is done with consistency. What I mean by that is that the game does an incredible job of allowing the audience to view the world through Senua's eyes, never a flaw in this. You become deeply immersed within the world with Senua. As she becomes stronger, triumphs her challenges, you feel her grow and you feel her fear. You try to help her, but you cannot only having to witness her getting hurt. One of the greatest stories I had the luxury of playing.
Graphics are exceptional, they might very well be the best I have ever witnessed. It is lifelike, it is beautiful, I can point out the details in everything I see. No others can match the beauty in this game. It all felt like a movie, it was cinematic, everything felt screenshot worthy. Ninja Theory hit the nail on the head with this.
Core elements of the game are well polished and executed correctly. Combat is very smooth, simple yet effective, and fun to participate in. Puzzles were fun, easy too, but these two things were not the focal point of the game, as I do not want to focus on this. There were a couple more complex puzzles and enemies but beyond that the game did, with what little it had, well.
Sound, voice acting, facial expressions. Blend with perfection. Nothing more to say, the best of its kind.
Performance was perfect as well, for such a beautiful game I was surprised to run everything on the highest settings with a mid-tier system, without any faults in performance.
The bad.
For a game as perfect as this was, there is still some bad in it, unfortunately.
To my suprised, I did encounter bugs, nothing too serious but this should not be the case for a game as polished as this one.
The combat and puzzles were incredibly repetitive, after fighting each enemy type once and do every puzzle once it was the same throughout the game. There were a few unique ones here and there but that was it. Combat was polished but wonky, not being able to switch enemy to enemy was a hassle when fighting, especially in fights with multiple enemies. As I said before, this is not the premise of the game, therefore I do not chalk this one up as a negative harshly.
Finally, the biggest problem with this game, is the length. I search around reviews and other players and their average playtime is about 7-10 hours give or take. I finished the game within 5 hours, which is a huge letdown to me. I base games on whether they are worth the price by $1/hour method, safe to say this game failed horribly at it. I probably played more around 4.5 hours due to pausing and doing a thing or two. The game itself and the story more than made up for this but if I am being honest, I spent $22 for 5 hours of entertainment, not worth it.
Besides all the negatives, this game is an essential for any gamer. It delivers a one of a kind experience that no other game can. Play this with an open mind and soak it in, cause it really is incredible.

In fact, it was so intense that I was only able to play it in short sessions of an hour or two at a time because more than that was just too much. Part of the intensity comes from the excellent soundscape. There is a message from the developers at the beginning of the game recommending that you play with headphones for the best experience, and I'm very glad that I followed their advice. Senua has a constant chorus of voices in her head, and headphones, combined with great post processing, give those voices an almost overwhelming intimacy. They are in your head as much as they are in hers, which is exactly the point because this game is trying to approximate the experience of having schizophrenia. Not having schizophrenia myself, I can't comment on how successful the game is at recreating that mental health disorder, but it certainly makes for a disturbing experience.
The game aspects include light puzzle solving and combat. The puzzles aren't difficult, which I appreciate because if they had been harder they would have damaged the pacing of the narrative. They are a reasonable difficulty and they fit the narrative very well, by which I mean that they don't feel out of place, it makes sense that they exist in this world. There isn't a lot of combat, it probably comprises less than half of the game time. That being said, what is there is deceptively deep--even hours into the game I was still discovering new combinations. My favorite aspect of the combat is a mechanic where you can be knocked down by an opponent and struggle to your feet to continue the fight. But you are now injured and you aren't as fast, and the voices in your head keep telling you that you're hurt and you can't win. This really ramps up the intensity of the combat encounters, and winning a fight when you're injured is a very satisfying expeerience. There are a couple of frustrating fights in the last hour or so that just go on for too long, but you can change the difficulty at any time. I lowered it to "easy" for the last section so my frustration didn't ruin the game's ending. But that didn't detract from what an excellent and unique experience this game is.

I think i've played it enough to get the general idea of the game but I may or may not update this review in the future. I've also read a few downthumbed comments, and although triggering, everyone is entitled to their own opinions and allowed to share with the world their personal experiences with the game. I will say this though...most of them are thumbing the game down because of the combat and SOLELY because of the combat, which in my personal opinion is nonsense...yes its part of the game, but its not the core focus...if you bought this game thinking "hot damn ninja theory back at it again with another sick flips, trickss, goofs and gaffs combat system" then this is the wrong game for you. There are no powerups, no levels, no new weapons or lootboxes...this is a STORY, a very deep, disturbing story about a very real mental health problem and I think people are giving it a hardtime for all the wrong reasons! That all been said however...I think the combat system is fine, it was easy to understand and not very hard to master, there are even a few short combos you can perform if you switch between light and heavy, and you can even do a strafe attack...the voices..they help you...and so does the mirror...USE IT if you are struggling and switch targets if you are surrounded! Even been locked onto one opponent you can still block the others!
Graphically this is a stunning game, I honestly can't stop looking at Senua's hair, its fantastic! Everything looks so crisp and clean and runs flawlessly at 1080 with maxed graphical settings. The world is dark and menacing, littered with the dead and the many challenges and puzzles that await you.
I honestly don't know much about psychosis or other such mental illnesses, so I don't know what is an illusion and what is reality when im walking around...my only safe bet is that the voices are part of it but its both sickening and sad to know that people suffer from such things..i'd like to think with all the backing the game had though, that they have portrayed an accurate account of what it is like to suffer from psychosis. Knowing very little about the games back story, the lore, other than Senua trying to save the soul of her beloved...its like...is this world filled with magic and gods and only part illusions caused by Senua, or is the ENTIRE journey one big mental trip? Who knows...well, maybe those who have completed it, but I haven't, yet.
I can't tell as of yet how long it actually is, though these days any singleplayer experiences are often relatively short, and i'm going to base my progression on the lorestones I find in the world.
TL;DR honestly, if you want a game thats a little more thought provoking and not just mindlessly bashing buttons to kill everything at high speed, or you are maybe interested in seeing the world through the eyes of someone who suffers from something you may never truly understand or witness firsthand in your lifetime...pick it up, give it a try...I was lucky enough to get this as a christmas present and I have to say, best gift!

I've been playing since launch, and have enjoyed this game at every release. I wasn't fazed by the lack of promised features at launch, mainly because I wasn't aware of all of the pre-release marketing - I only saw the initial E3 trailer and didn't know what to make of it at the time. I don't blame those that felt let down - though the echo chamber on the internet got a little out of hand (e.g, fans issuing death threats). This is a review of the game though, not the handling of Hello Games' marketing efforts or the gentle flower that is a hyped gaming community.
The game is completely different now (even since 1.38, a minor release), and I wish I could play the game like this in 2016 before I experienced monotonous gameplay, but its varied and interesting now. The story feels fuller, the gameplay loop richer, and the graphics are much more detailed. There's a missions system, a fourth race, vehicles, bases, some basic co-op support, better planets, and much more. It also hasn't lost its charm as a relaxing exploration game, if you want it to be that.
I'd like to see the fauna have more interesting behavior, and maybe do more interesting things related to them. What if there was a "zoo" of some sort, where you collect creatures and raise them? There's a lot of potential with not only making them a fun part of the gameplay, but also making them more convincing. Currently, aside from the odd frankenstein thing murmuring "kill me", I mostly ignore them.
Hello Games has tried things, and they have made mistakes, but I think they have proven themselves to have much more integrity than what the community's consensus on them was around release. They threw what was probably one of the more interesting viral marketing campaigns in recent memory with the Waking Titan ARG. They've shown they are willing to earn our trust back, and now we should let them.
Get this game, there's really no experience like it, and tune out the noise and baggage following it.

Overly ambitious game. It looks cool on the surface, but in terms of game design it over reaches and fails to be successful in any one area.
The primary gameplay aspect is inventory management. You'll never have enough space. Even if you find the ressource(s) you want at the moment, you'll use them up immediately. Sometimes it can take hours to find an item you've previously thrown away because it was a waste of space at that moment.
I had to give up on trying to do missions, as they wouldn't always work (non existent objective targets) and they're little more than fetch quests.
While upgrading your ship/suit/multitool should be exciting, it's so rare and so miniscule that it hardly features as a main aspect of the game. For my 30ish hours, I only changed ships 3 times, multitools 3 times, and the only suit upgrades I sought out were inventory space. The ships and multitools I saw were WAAAY out of my price range.
Base building is kind of fun, except that it acts as a tether. Okay, so you build a base on planet A. Then you warp jump 6 times. So now what? You teleport back to your base? meaning all your warping was pointless. Or you start a new base... only to warp further away and need to build another base.
Space is bad. It's not good. There is no solar system navigation. There is no evidence that the planets orbit stars. Would you like to fly into a sun? That would be cool, wouldn't it? HAhahahahaha THERE ARE NO SUNS.
Space battling is bad. Pirates will randomly appear to steal your cargo, chasing you around, inhibiting your ability to warp or even run away to a nearby planet. Fighting them is about as elegant and graceful as a dog chasing it's own tail.
A big issue I have is when you're on the planet surface, in your roamer, and you scan for a destination. It is ENTIRELY IMPRACTICAL TO TRAVEL IN YOUR ROAMER. Destinations are often 20 minutes away. If you really want to go to them, the only reasonable way is to take off in your ship and fly there, which is janky.
The transition from space to planet is janky, so janky. Flying straight towards a point creates an angled approach, which kind of makes sense, except you slow down in the atmosphere, and it creates a problem where you're somehow never going to reach your destination. I nearly always have to approach to generate the planet's surface, then fly back out of the atmosphere and approach from directly above the landing site, flying straight into the ground because there is no physical reason not to nosedive into the ground.
The most fun I had was using a roamer to jump around, and using the terrain manipulator to build ramps and stuff.
Overall, I'd say it's an unsalvagable game because too many of its essential aspects are 2/5.

Aqua Kitty is basically a cute and challenging classic arcade style side-scrolling shooter with a core element of base defense.
If that sounds good to you, I don't have any trouble recommending it.
Pros:
Cute, friendly, self-consistant aesthetic
Variety of enemies with different powers
Responsive controls and good stability
Decent sound and music
Cons:
Limited arsenal
Unfriendly to keyboard users
Honestly when I think about it my biggest complaint is that even if you're using a keyboard, all the game's visible button prompts are for controller buttons, which can be an obstacle in learning the controls. The layout of those buttons also often causes me to turn my ship around instead of firing my big guns, and I haven't found any way to change it.
The gameplay also features a submarine that can only fire forward, and moves more slowly if you are moving "backwards" or attempting to maneuver while firing, which contributes to the game's difficulty. The mechanics work and they certainly make sense for a submarine, but they take some getting used to if you're used to other shooter environments that tend to be more free and loose.
The game is entertaining enough to hold my attention, engaging enough to make me gesture furiously at the air when I lose miners, and though it's not a personal favorite, it's certainly very good at what it does.

A slower, less interesting version of the arcade hit, Defender. I might be an unfair judge,  because Defender is one of my favorite arcade games of all time, but Aqua Kitty adds very little worth mentioning except for a cute aesthetic.
It's not a bad game at all - just don't go in expecting an interesting twist or anything. Just a solid gameplay experience that has been proven fun since the 80's.

The game is worth more than a dollar and it's 60 cents right now so it's worth checking out if you're needing a retro platformer.

Ok About this game.  Its very Space Opera Like.  The story line starts normal and has alot of mysterious things in it.  However everything is presented to you in the old school way of massive text.  Controls for this game are mouse and keyboard.  I suppose you could use xpadder and map some keys to a controller....but you would still have to click on things.  Learning curve for this game isnt too bad but it does take getting used to.  Like not realizing you have to click on things on the right side of the screen and not from your inventory.  They do a fairly good job during the tutorial showing you things.  And you can skip it as it tells you in the text.  Again massive text to read.  Game play wise its ok and takes a bit to get used to.  Other people compare this game to descent or freespace...um no....not even close to that sort of control  This one is more simple and reminds me of games of a few years ago.  In a way this is a very nostalgic game in that way.  Music is not too bad....graphics are not the greatest but they are not too bad either.  You can tell they are hand drawn or hand painted on some.
So let me review...Good things about this game.
Its a Hardcore Space opera
Lots of things to get
Not saddled with stupd things like runing out of fuel or oxygen at least that i have seen.
Simple control scheme
Alot of extras including a plethora of weapons and ammo types
Typical mystery space style
lots of things to find
Now for the bad things
Walls of text..yes alot of text...to find out what to do you must read.
some things not clearly explained so it might take a bit to find what you have to do.
control scheme is mouse and keyboard only
Very nostaligic feel which might not be what gamers want.
Not all loot goes to your ship no matter how close you are...thus you have to click on alot of stuff.
Can only tractor in 1 thing at a time at least what i have found so far.
Its a very long game not going to be completed in 4 or 5 hours so maybe not for the person who wants something mindless
So in the end I recommned this game to people who like Hard Core Space Opera with mysterious alens and are not afraid to read alot of interesting things.  I dont recommond this game for people with a short attention span or people who dont like to read or people who simply want to blast everything and be spoon fed.  I hate to say this but the negative reviews I think are from some people who wanted some "just blast things and get spoon fed" type game with "no effort required" type game.
I will say though....you will know if you like the game in the first few hours or not.

I love this game, sure its not perfect but iv had a lot of fun with it.
Ill start with the bad bits,
Graphics are a bit on the poor side, textures are low quality, there are a few artifacts with the effect.
The missions are all pretty basic, go here, get this, click that, kill them all. though some are dressed up pretty well (the one where you have to kill a station while it dances to dub step was fun :) )
Combat can be a bit too simple at times, especial when taking down larger ships, they mostly just sit there while you circle strife around them till they die or simply sit behind their engines in a blind spot.
There are issues with the UI, from the mouse pointer getting stuck in the center of the screen so you cant click anything to text being cut off due to the small size of the windows, that cant be resized or moved. also the font is VERY small in places making it difficult to read.
The crafting system is too simple, and boils down to getting a few patterns, do a bit of mining and a couple clicks to queue up the crafting, which oddly crafts stuff while the game is paused, even then its also very quick at crafting.
Limited number of pilot able ships, and there isn't much to differentiate them, there are a couple good ones which you can get in order (actually you can craft them), each outright better than the last, you can ignore the others as there isn't much need to get them. it would be nice to have more ships and have more to make them stand out so there would be a need to go back and swap out at different situations.
Limited variation in stations and factions, just seems they are generic no mater where you are with few unique items/stations.
Odd object cleanup/disappearing/appearing mechanic, stations pop into existence slowly after entering the sector, i assume as it loads them, asteroids pop up float for a bit then disappear, you can scan a few asteroids then turn around and there all gone, loot disappears on a timer so you have to be quick to collect it all. overall it gives it an insubstantial dream like feel.
Now the good stuff,
Its FUN, the combat apart from the capital ship issues is hectic and engaging, flying in a dog fight with 20 other enemy ships, missiles, drones and energy weapons firing in all directions, capital ships firing off missile barrages into the fray,   its is insane and sometimes looks very pretty :).
The sheer amount of weapons, ammunition types and add ons is huge, like many loot based games you will spend a lot of time min maxing your load out to fit your situation (which thankfully you can do while paused). some of the weapon and ammo combinations can launch a MASSIVE barrage at the enemy decimating entire squadrons of ships.
The story while linear is quirky, funny and entertaining, completely tong in cheek in places (dub step space station anyone?) but leads you around the galaxy and shows off what this game can do.
Lots of unique and  quirky events they add some spice to the missions and story and some are REALLY off the wall (flying though the gut of an intergalactic monster) .
The music is fantastic, in places the action seems to be linked to the beat too with insane effects pulsing, you will find it hard to to bob along with it while blowing the crap out of the enemy.
The size of the galaxy is impressive, id guess hundreds of planets to visit (iv only seen a small portion at this point).
The sectors are just plain pretty, its obvious a lot of work has been put into it, sectors can look drastically different with unique character and provides a great background to the destruction.
The developer, he/she seems like a good bloke/girl, they respond ont he forums quickly and are always helpful in fixing people issues, i myself had an issue, posted on the forum and got a helpful response the same day that sorted me out.
Overall, if you are looking for some quick and dirt fun, love loot, love blowing stuff up and can overlook the flaws this game is an excellent choice. and at the current price, what are you waiting for?!

I have mixed feelings about this game. First of all it's hardly a game, but more of a visual novel with minor interactive elements. The gameplay feels like an afterthought by the developers; very little effort was put in it. It's mostly just searching for the next trigger that advances the story, and couple of minigames here and there. It's tedious busywork that only gets in the way of enjoying the story. The player has no meaningful choices and there's no way to fail.
The controls are quite clunky. I played through the game using gamepad, which probably was a mistake. There's no way to reconfigure the movement buttons, and by default it uses the analog stick (instead of d-pad), which is awkward. And there are couple features in the game that don't work at all with gamepad, so I occasionally had to switch to mouse + keyboard.
The good thing about the game is its story. It's emotional and touching, and the beautiful soundtrack definitely helps that. There are some moments when the story touches on some pretty heavy subjects.
At the same time the whole thing feels a bit too sentimental. It overloads the player with emotional scenes, and there's always some melancholic music playing on the background. After a while it doesn't have the same impact anymore and by the time you get to the story's climax you just wanna see it all end as soon as possible.

Cherry Tree High Comedy Club. Where do I begin. This is a story very reminiscent of visual novels, and gives you a variety of paths to take each day. This game involves a high school senior by the name of Miley Verisse. She loves comedy, and has for most of her life. She wants to resurrect the Comedy Club at Cherry Tree High School, but needs to find people for her club to start off with. She meets many people along the way, and you make decision, talk to a variety of characters and npcs, and you boost your friendship levels. Once they hit Level 5 in terms of friendship, the character returns a club registration form, getting you closer to resurrecting the comedy club that housed talented comedians in the past. This was a great little game to play, though I recommend it, I would only recommend those who really love the culture of visual novels, eroge, otaku culture and anime, as this might be boring to quite a lot of people, as the demographic is quite a niche. But if the price is right, try it out. I didn't regret it one bit. 6.8/10

It is a charming dating-sim style game. The art is very pretty. The music is nice. The characters and setting are endearing and pleasant. The mechanics do the job. It's short. It's fun. I enjoyed it. Don't expect too much, though.
The localization was bad. For a game/genre this text-heavy, this is almost unforgivable. The game is so Japanese it's painful, but the localization team incompetently felt that they should try to force it into a pigeonhole Americanization. That sort of xenophobic sensitivity is painful and decades out of date. Even ignoring the weak attempts to pretend it was all happening in the US and fit everything into stereotypes thereof, the localization team was in dire need of a fluent English-speaking editor because the English language was abused in many amateurish ways. There/their/they're, to/too, etc. are prevalent errors, and I encountered at least one sentence so broken that it is incomprehensible gibberish. It's a doujin so I let the poor English slide for the most part, but it's something that anyone competent in the language could have spotted in an evening read-through so it makes it feel like they rushed through it.
Mechanically, there are some bugs and design choices I find questionable. At times, the wrong sprites and location lables would show during events and conversations, but it was nothing game-breaking. I found the randomized events and such to be frustrating because attempting to apply strategy in skill-building was ultimately undermined by my inability to predict or control which skills would be leveled by the random events. There are multiple endings and a new game+, and, as it seems unlikely to get the complete ending the first time through, there is a reason to play the ng+, but you'll likely be so over-skilled that you'll finish the recruitment about half-way through, which makes it inconvenient that there are neither text-progression contols nor more effective time-advancing mechanics.
It was alright, but could've been better.

This game is a masterpiece. Its portrayal of a struggle against madness and self-hate hit shockingly close to home. While I was never psychotic, I was driven nearly to suicide at one point in my life by my own failures, and I had to fight my own 'rot' for years to come after. I can well believe it was made with the help of people personally familiar with mental illness, and its portrayal of Senua's battle with hers makes me want to force my friends to play this. I had no objections to the combat, myself. You couldn't make a game entirely around that combat system, but as a vehicle to build tension and to convey the desperate violence of Senua's inner struggle, it's a perfect fit. The voice of Senua's 'shadow' (which I can't talk much more about without spoilers) reminded me so much of my own remorseless, hateful inner voice (who I called Dathien at the time) that it was simultaneously chilling and... cleansing, seeing the manifestation of my own mental damage so closely mirrored. The game is beautiful and immersive and terrifying, and... obviously I can't spoil the ending, but I will say that it is correct. If you've ever been to war with your own mind, or know someone who has... play this. Please.
One of the most impressive singleplayerexperiences i have ever played...and i played a lot....masterpiece.

This is it, the contraversial conclusion to this contraversial trilogy.  And boy is it something.  Those who didn't like the first game didn't like it because of the linear gameplay for most of the game and while this is true, it's pretty much the only aspect of the game that wasn't absolutely brilliant.  The story is fantastic, the characters are awesome, the music and graphics splendid and combat system unbelievable.  Then comes the second game.  It was still sort of linear (or at least as linear as you can make a game about time traveling), but a lot less so.  Despite losing one character in battles, the combat system was still somehow improved.  Story even better, graphics even better, music even better, characters even better.  Even the DLC were brilliant.
Finally, the conclusion.  How could it get any better?  This time they threw linearity out of the window; you can do anything in any order.  Other than that, they again somehow managed to improve the combat despite removing yet another character.  It also manages to answer every question you might have gathered throughout the previous games, and delivers a story that's simply perfect and ends up with an ending that will just... blow your mind.
To recap, the XIII trilogy is a serie that quickly learned from its mistakes and steadily improved at an exponential rate before reaching perfection in its climactic ending.

Aqua Kitty: Milk Mine defender is a good with some inherent flaws.
The basic gameplay consists of a submarine that can move left and right and shoot oncoming robot fishes who try to steal your miner, and each level consists of waves of robots and different layouts. As far as action goes it's good, but doesn't offer much in the way of powerups. There's also a higher powered attack that has a limited meter that rebuilds over time, but I haven't found this to be effective at all.
On the positive, the graphics consist of SNK style sprites, but is pretty simplistic otherwise. This is not to say it's bad though as the graphics and character art is really cute, and there's plenty on screen at time. Additionally, the core gameplay is overall fun and gives variations to the waves of enemies and what type you're facing.
But the one nagging problem that I find is it's difficulty. It's a bit difficult at times, and not for reasons that I feel are based on challenge or skill, which I'm fine with. I think more games need to bring back that traditional challenge.
However, the challenge from this game comes from the interface and level layout. You don't see the entire level on screen at once, including some of your miners that you have to protect. The only way you know if someone's going after your off screen miners when you can't see them is an audiable call from the cat miner and a blinking dot on a map at the top of your screen. However the action is on the bottom half of the screen, meaning that you have to move your eyes off of the level for a moment to see if someone's coming after your miner, which is a distraction that can cause you to be hurt and killed by an enemy fish. This adds a challenge that is hard for you to control, which isn't the good kind of challenge that I like.
Despite this, The amount of levels and variety involved I feel is good and this flaw doesn't hamper it so much as to be truly infuriating. In the end I think on sale it's definitley worth checking out, at full price I might hesitate to recommend but still recommend it.

The premise is straightforward, make it through 1000 rooms while encountering the eponymous jump scares. This starts out like a haunted house attraction, complete with cardboard cutouts, but then when real threats show up, things only get worse from there. The scares are simple, mostly run from monsters, but it can be frightening with certain monsters' abilities. The enemies and their locations you find them in having a bit of variety and styles to them.
In between these bouts of terrors, the game gives enough time to recollect yourself before the next enemy shows up, leaving you to explore the mansion room to room. This can become tedious if you die before the next save point. Especially on later floors when the save points goes from every fifty rooms to every one hundred in the last half.
The graphics are pretty good to look at. The environments range from bright and lively to dark and lifeless. On a personal note, a nice touch I noticed is that staring at torches in a certain range put spots in your vision. The controls are simple and the sound is good and ambience is great.
Finally, it's free, so little harm. But the game can also be fun for horror gamers, especially beginners. It also gives shout-outs to other horror games and series that adds a nice touch to the experience.
