Spooky's Jumpscare Mansion (or "Spooky's House of Jumpscares", as it was originally called. I will always think of this game being called its original name before some German company "Spooky House Studio" put forth a cease and desist against the game's creators because they were attempting to trademark the name "Spooky House". Although irritating, I find the creator's of Spooky's reaction to handling the necessary name change on the game's main menu to be quite amusing even to this day. But for the sake of this review, I will refer to this game by it's current name.) was certainly a game that subverted my expectations in many ways when I first watched YouTube Let's Player "Markiplier"play the game back when the game was still pretty new and slowly getting a name for itself. A friend of mine was curious about the game after seeing it in some video thumbnails, so we decided to check it out and we both found ourselves enjoying the game more than we were expecting. Its only recently that I've finally had a chance to play it for myself, and I've been enjoying it.
In Spooky's Jumpscare Mansion, you take the role of an amateur historian that decides to make a trek up a mountain to learn about a house on a hill that has been at its location for as long as anyone can remember, to the point that its origins have been lost and forgotten. Upon entering the house, you encounter a cute ghost girl who challenges you to make it through all 1000 rooms of the house and see what lies at the end. And that's basically the whole premise. Pretty simple, right?
Spooky's Jumpscare Mansion is basically an affectionate parody of various horror game plots and tropes crammed into a little package that goes from starting out silly and playful to geniunely frightening with very real dangers that you, the player, must overcome as you travel through the various rooms of the house, otherwise they will eat your face (among other things, depending on what exactly you end up encountering). You generally have to move past these face eaters by outrunning them before you are killed, going from room to room and hoping that you'll eventually lose them. You'll also occasionally come across various notes left behind by other people who were in the house before you, which will help flesh out elements of the story, such as some of the rooms you will encounter and the enemies that are trying to kill you. There are also the chance you'll come across some rooms with a few easter eggs scattered about, although I won't go into the detail as to what they are -- that's something that those among you with a curious mind can look into yourselves.
Simple premise, simple gameplay, and the main game is free to play (and I don't mean "free to play" as in the sort of thing you'd typically see in the mobile market of games. The only money you can put into this game is what you decide to buy out of the game's currently available DLC, but I feel that the DLC story "Karamari Hospital" is worth investing into if the main game manages to catch enough of your fancy, because I feel that Karamari Hospital takes numerous elements from the main game, such as atmosphere and how it instills a sense of dread in you, and improves upon it and makes how you encounter some of the dangerous elements less predictable, all the while fleshing out the overall story of the game, although I won't say how -- like with with the easter eggs, figuring out how the Karamari Hospital DLC fleshes out the story of the overall game is something I'll leave entirely up to you. No spoilers from me.
I realize that the idea of simply running away from your adversaries every time you encounter them while going from room to room until you reach the end goal, all the while exploring new elements in the environment as they present themselves, is not for everyone, especially in a horror game, and the game's overall aesthetics may turn some people away at first glance too. But for those who don't mind such a style of gameplay (if not outright enjoy it), and enjoy (or can at least tolerate) games with cartoonish, silly aesthetics just fine, then I'd recommend giving Spooky's Jumpscare Mansion a try. Doubly so if you want to play a game that might make you laugh if you enjoy horror games. The game doesn't mind poking fun at itself and the story elements/tropes it throws at you, and its got plenty of them, so there's bound to be SOME joke or two that will make any horror game enthusiast chuckle.
On a final note, a word of advice to those who decide to try out the game and want a tip to help them get through -- save often. You never know what kind of dangers you may encounter and when, so it's a good idea to save often in case something happens and you don't want to get set back too far. Of course, if you're a skillful player, you'll probably be able to easily afford taking some risks here and there, but if you ever feel unsure of yourself or just want to be cautious, it never hurts to save your game when you can.
Anyway, this is my review of Spooky's Jumpscare Mansion. I don't regret my time with both watching and playing it, and I hope to see the creators of the game go places and make even better games with whatever experience they have gained making this game and it's expansions. Also, to the creators, thanks for making a game that has given me and my friend some fond memories to look back on.

To the Moon tells a very creative, highly emotional story. As for the pixels, actually I think the abstract visuals leave more room for your own imagination and make it easier to relate to what's happening (vs watching a lifelike prerendered video - read "Understanding Comics" by Scott McCloud... he explains what I mean...) - making the experience even more emotional, as in reading a good book.

Lightning Returns: Final Fantasy XIII is the last of the Final Fantasy XIII trilogy; it tries to wrap up the loose ends from XIII-2 in an awkwardly acceptable way.
All of the main cast from Final Fantasy XIII make a return alongside the characters from XIII-2. However, due to the progression of this very convoluted story, many of them are not the way they were from the prior installments. Every character has adopted a darker personality, which fits well when you view the trilogy as a whole. As a standalone, the characters can be somewhat annoying due to the subpar commentary describing these characters right as they're being introduced -- it is a poor attempt to fill-in the newer audiences of who these characters are and what importance they have or had in the trilogy.
The dialogue between these characters can cause people to cringe; they speak to one another in a very uninspiring poetic manner. There are instances when the dialogue between Lightning and Hope can be cute and/or funny, but awkward overall.
Lightning Returns provides the best combat system to a Final Fantasy to date; it runs the Active Time Battle system that is heavily modified to make-up for the lack of party members. It results in a faster paced but still heavily tactical gameplay that keeps the audience active. The change of the battle system also results in change of the enemies. The enemies now have more health and feel alive; they are not stuck or held idle waiting to react to commands. This makes each and every battle dynamic and challenging.
There is no level system in the game. Every statistic boost is either from quest completion or itemization. This results in the in-ability to ever over-level and making the game too easy. Fortunately enough, if the game is too difficult, there is downloadable content in the form of equipment that make the game easier, though it isn't recommended.
Quests are a staple of RPGs and Lightning Returns is no exception. Infact, you want to finish every side-quest possible to make Lightning as strong as possible. There's an intrinsic value of finishing these side-quests, though many of them are unimportant or just poorly fetched out. Many of these side-quests involve locating, defeating, or turning in items and don't prove to be difficult. Most of these side-quests can be done without the need to pro-actively involve yourself with them, which is mostly a good thing.
The scale of the game is massive. Each region has a theme and it is fletched out well; each man-made or natural environment feels alive. There's a ton of interaction with the citizens of each region. As the story progresses and in-game time go by, different people and different enemies will appear, which gives a sense of livelihood.
Lightning Returns reminds me of Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask. In both games, you need to manage your time well to be as efficient as possible and to complete as much quests and missions in one playthrough. The overworld, the cities, and the subcities really make the game feel enormous.
I would definitely recommend this game to RPG fans, as long as they can avoid odd and/or awkward dialogue and like the idea of trying to finish a game against the clock.

To the Moon is an exceptionally emotional story with a unique premise. There's not much gameplay here, as the main goal of the game is the story that unfolds, and that story is bolstered by an outstanding soundtrack. The premise is also interesting enough for other stories within this universe, and there are plenty of twists along the way. It is around a 4 hour experience, and it is one worth playing. The gameplay itself is not that interesting, and there aren't as many interactable objects as one would hope, but what gameplay is there is really only there to keep the player engaged as the mystery of the story unravels. There are interesting gameplay moments that work with the story, and even make fun of certain game genres, but you will not want to play this game for the gameplay. I really feel the gameplay was a missed opportunity as it doesn't seem like much is there to really expand on the story as the story is mostly a linear affair. The dialogue mostly works, but it is not exceptionally well written. It is charming enough, and is often needed due to the depressing nature of the overall narrative. Ultimately, I would recommend this game to anyone who likes a well told story that never overstays its welcome.

The combat system is more flexible than the previous two iterations.  It follows the 'scheme' design, but you ONLY play as Lightning in this version.  She gets three 'schema', which are builds with their own set of ability points that you can switch between on the fly.  You get to choose an outfit and equips for each scheme, and get access to four abilities for each one as well, essentially giving you a rock/paper/scissors style fighting system.
The combat is pretty engaging.  It's more active than the previous two iterations, and less like any other Final Fantasy because of this.
Unfortunately, Lightning doesn't gain experience in this game...combat is optional, minus scripted fights, and only worth doing for items for quests.  Which bites, because the combat is truly that enjoyable that I still find myself going out of the way to do.
The scripted fights are all fairly unique and dynamic.  The bosses are all interesting to go against and it is fun to figure out their weaknesses and defeat them in battle.
Quests are how LIghtning increases her stats.  Every time she completes a quest, she saves a soul and becomes stronger.
This game is essentially 'Errands and Dress-Up Simulator'.  But, it is a nice little wrap up to the trilogy, and provides closure to that cliffhanger ending that is FFXIII-2.
This is the conclusion to literally my favorite VN/story ever created, an amazing murder mystery that I cannot recommend enough.

The murders, mysteries, and intellectual battles continue (and conclude) with the "Answer Arcs" of Umineko (also known as Umineko Chiru) that consists of Chapters 5-8. Let the crazy violence go on! Muahahahahahaha!
Chiru picks up right where we left off at the end of Chapter 4, so obviously you will have wanted to play the first half of the game already before getting into this. The rest of the clues and your ultimate answer to whether or not the story is a "fantasy" or a "mystery" can be found here in the Answer Arcs: Umineko Chiru.

I recently discovered and fell in love with this game. I'm going to explain why Luuthian's negative review wrong:
I'm going to agree with his good points:
|Good:
|- Great pixel art
|- Decent amount of levels/content for an arcade style game and the price.
|- Very easy to learn and control.
and add:
- Excellent music
- Multiple difficulty levels, (but even easy is not casual easy.) on easy mode you have more starting life, less enemies spawn and they shoot less bullets
- Extremely polished gameplay for its genre.
Now to review his bad points:
Bad:
|-Geared heavily towards luck, too little towards skill. The advantage of bullet hell shooters is that there are patterns and expectations. Players can develop skills based on what they learn from patterns. Not so here: enemy positions are randomized which creates a ton of frustration. One game you'll have red jellies congregated in one area, another game you'll be frantically rescuing the cats one after another.
~ He is correct about enemy positions being random, and this is good because it's demands the player to develop skill. Enemy behavior is VERY not random. Meaning, the better you understand you enemies, they faster you can take them down.
|- The player is woefully underequipped to combat the majority of enemies. They absorb a stupid amount of bullets and the power ups, except the two extra cats and the bomb, are faily useless.
~ This is completly false. Half of the enemies take one hit from the blaster, and then strongest enemy takes 5 shots from your missle, which can come out in less than two seconds. While I sort of agree that the powerups seem sort of useless at first, in later stages in the game they are almost essential to be strategically used to reach then next level.
|- Half the nemies are programmed to dive out of the way of your vehicle. This may sound interesting at first, until you realize how much time you're spending chasing enemies that randomly move out of the way of your already underpowered weapons.
~ This is an exaggeration. There are three enemies that dodge you when you approach. And they slightly dodge and then stay put. It's nothing like the green cell mass enemies in geometry wars. OP was just careless.
|- Difficulty essentially equates to dumping increasing amounts of enemies around the screen randomly, often before you've even finished a particular wave of foes.
~ This is true, but not bad, as being able to clear waves quickly give you a clear atvantage.
|- The foreground art will regularily cover enemies and bullets making navigating around the map incredibly annoying and, again, make your survival a lucky happenstance.
~ I personally never noticiced anything like this.
|- Bullet travel length is based on the direction and speed you travel, amking moving forward actual disadvantagous in most situations, despite moving being what you need to do to survive.
~ This is incorrect. From my observation bullet length is a set distance and speed from the player. It just seems slower because it doest accellerate when the player is moving forward.
|- Balancing looking up at the alarm and surviving while doding bullets is way too much to handle. There should have been any easy indicator or red arrow to show a cat is being abducted and the quickest way too them. I can't count how many cats I lost simply because the game expects you to juggle way too much visual information at once with so little direction.
~ Apparently this reviewer just doesn't like arcade game, because the balance of saving the kitties and dodging and fighting a lot of what what makes this game. The game does have an indicator that he mentioned, two actually. One,  with stereo speaker the kitty will cry out when captured from the audio channel left or right that is closest to you. There is also a map on screen showing the player of all ships that capture your crew.
There you have it. That's my criticism of the review. In terms of arcade shooter, I would say that this is one of the most balanced and fair ones made in the last 10 years. There is not an insane amount of bullets and bullet speed is very dodgable. Agility in movement and accuracy in shot is highly rewarded, meaning the better you skill the better you do. They game will keep pusing you to develop new strategies to protecting your operation and taking out the enemy. The game also encourages you when you retry levels, removing frustration.
Maybe the only negative I would say is not having a casual mode for players like Luuthian who can't handle a challenge. For everyone else, this game is EXCELLENT, in it genre.

Well here we are, finally to the second half of Umineko! As someone who has personally read Chiru before anyone even dreamed of it being localized, I must say, this most certainly feels like a dream to me. As a sequel to the original four novels, Chiru shifts from focusing on crazy locked rooms and insane banter between a  witch and a guy who should really learn to get over himself, to focusing on why Beatrice would even create such a bloody tale and what her identity really is. I won't mince words, Umineko Chiru has at times been derided in the VN community as being pretentious, overly convoluted and bit weird at times. And while I won't deny the aspect of Chiru being convoluted at times, I implore readers to have an open mind.
Umineko Chiru is exceptionally unique among VNs, it tackles a lot of the subjects that first four episodes had touched upon but done in a much more sublime way, especially when it tackles the newer subjects-all of which will not only make you think about the meaning of the game as a whole, but also stop to introspect yourself at times
While the murder mystery and logic battles are still here and are all fun and good, expect them to take a bit of backseat for now. You job as a reader and a detective is not to figure out the howdunnit, but also the who and whydunnit. This is not a game between Battler and Beatrice anymore, but between you and the author.
So in that regard, I say you should stay on your toes while reading Chiru as it will not be getting easier
And I guess as a parting note....while I do understand some of the frustrations people have had with Chiru, I can say without a single doubt that Umineko Chiru is the heart and soul of Umineko. Without it, you could say that while Umineko was entertaining in the same way Death Note was, it never reached that level of  lets say....Evangelion did
So to the person who is reading this, I can guarantee that Chiru is outstanding.  Sure its not as solid as the previous four, but Chiru is most certainly a marvel the same way Frankenstein was a marvel despite its numerous flaws-and I say that Chiru's high points are exponentially higher than any of the previous four's or even Higurashi's.
So honestly, enjoy yourself reader. Take it all in. Try and solve the mystery of who Beatrice is and why she created this game. You may not enjoy all of it-but I can say for sure you will at the very least be thinking differently when you finish. But most importantly, you should never loose sight of what's important and never forget the heart.

PREMISE: If you haven't bought/read Umineko When They Cry - Question Arcs, don't go any further.
Go to that game instead, read some reviews (including my own if you want) and then decide whether that interests you. This is the sequel and it requires prior knowledge of what came before. You will be thoroughly confused and will miss a lot of the enjoyment if you start here. Don't do it, Umineko as a whole deserves to be enjoyed properly in my opinion.
That said, if you HAVE read the first four Arcs of Umineko: here is where the fun really starts. You've battled against Beatrice, her demons and servants. You have been taught about the Red Truth and the Blue Truth and how they work, more or less. You've gradually discovered some of the rules that regulate both the Rokkenjima gameboard and the Metaworld itself. It is time to take those foundations and go beyond.
Here is also where the tone starts shifting. The murder mysteries, while still extremely plot-important, are no longer the main "gameplay" element. Rather than howdunnit, Umineko 5-8 deals with the whodunnit and most importantly whydunnit. The Answer Arcs, as the name implies, focuse more on finally resolving some of the mysteries that shroud the Ushiromiya family and the events that led to the Rokkenjima Mass Murder Case (never in a straightforward way, mind, so you'll still be expected to piece together the clues given). They also feature the only examples of "gameplay" and interactivity in all of Umineko, but don't go expecting a whole shift in genre. Umineko is, and remains, a Visual *Novel*. The few instances where player input is required are more slight breaks in the narration than true gaming moments. I thought it was a nice change of pace for a bit, and I really like those moments for a variety of reasons, but if you read the Question Arcs you should already know not to think of Umineko as a "game" in the traditional sense.
If you were intrigued by the mysteries in the previous part, this is for you. Not everyone was satisfied by the ending, but if you liked the first part you owe it to yourself to read this and get some closure.
Umineko holds a special place in my heart. It changed my outlook on some things, and I mostly owe it to these last four Arcs, so for me they are and always will be a worthwhile read.
And remember: "without love, it cannot be seen".

Aqua Kitty is a modern take on the classic coin op game Defender, with endless waves of enemies, some of which try to abduct civilians and take them straight up into the sky (or, in this case, the surface).
The good: It has a very cute, effective graphics, sweet soundtrack, and a humorous concept just bursting with possibilities (cats with a deep sea milk rigging operation under attack by robotic fishes).
The bad: It's just way too tedious, difficult and repetitive to be worth the time. You shoot enemies that are way more powerful than you over and over and rush back and forth between two defenseless cats that keep getting scooped up like week old clumping litter. Every now and then you can get a bomb that destroys all enemies in a small area (and if you got to the bomb without dying the enemies are probably all elsewhere anyway) or extra firepower for a very brief time. It would have been a lot better with more meaningful variety in both enemies, power-ups and level design. It easily could have been so much more than what it is.
It was included in the lowest tier ($1 for three games) of a recent Humble Bundle, so I can't say I wasted my money at roughly 33 cents out of the $4 I paid. (Though I never got the Steam trading card drops. Could have sworn I got them with previous Humble Bundle purchases.) But it's ridiculously overpriced on Steam, even on sale. $2.79? $6.99 normally? Please. It'd be decent as a free online Flash game or maybe $2 tops, as that's probably what I would have put into it in an arcade at 25 cents a play before realizing there are a lot better games out there.

Majestic Nights is a flawed gem.
In terms of issues, the combat and AI are clunky and very easy to take advantage of, once you understand the system. Technically speaking, the graphics look like something that would be home on a tablet rather than your desktop PC.
If you can look past these issues, the game has a lot to offer. The focus on stealth is refreshing. The writing is solid, giving you just enough information to keep you interested, while also keeping you (mostly) in the dark. The references to real world conspiracies and plots are well done, presuming you are at least familiar with the subject material.
The atmosphere is arguably the strong point of Majestic Nights. Stylistically, the visuals are bright and bold and oozing with 80s flair. The soundtrack is phenomenal.
The season pass offers pretty good value. The soundtrack is probably worth the $20 alone. There is also a Pen and Paper RPG on the way, which is not something you see offered everyday.
It's not a game for everyone, but it certainly has its merits.

Full Throttle Remastered is yet another long awaited remaster of a classic LucasArts point and click adventure game. This game has been often brought up as one of the first adventure games to truly attempt to tell the story in a very cinematic way, instead of being a more free-form story told via many puzzles and situations. Due to that, a lot of puzzles often have immediate and simple solutions that require next to no wondering around or item collecting. Game also added some action sequences, which are, thankfully, much easier to handle in the Remaster than they were in the original release.
All of the above meant few bad things too, though. Fans of puzzle-centric adventure games may find themselves disappointed by the blunt approach to solutions, that fits the game and the character. Some might not like that the game can be completed in just about 3-4 hours. And whoever you are, you will definitely hate the action bits, especially the infuriating car-based sequence closer to the end of the game. While some of the action bits at least require some rather intuitive puzzle solving, that car sequence is just pure frustration. But the game is considered a classic for a reason. It's fun, it's stylish, it's pretty unique for the setting and the mood and it's definitely worth a play even today.

Open universe "sandbox", essentially a FPS where your toon is a spaceship instead of a person. Movement is 3 dimensional, with enough predictable arcade-like physics to make the combat easy to navigate. If you are comfortable with a first person shooter Using WASD and a mouse then you should be able to find a mouse/keyboard mapping that makes this work well.
This is a small budget release, so storylines are written, not voiced (but surprisingly in depth). Solar systems follow a few fairly predictable models. Quests are pretty much optional, the story molds like a jigsaw puzzle depending on what you do when, and there are some puzzlers, but the real beauty of this title is that it is designed so that you can enter into the fray feeling overpowered, grabbing loot and more loot, and if you aren't careful suddenly you are toast. The AI sneaks up on you really fast. Lots of hours of gameplay here, and a real 3D space shooter that handles flight well.

If you find space sims, immersive and compelling questing, endless customisation, and a magnificent array of lootable items to be qualities close to your heart in a game, then I'd heartily recommend this title as being worth a try.
Although perhaps unpolished as yet, with load times so long as to be ridiculous and a UI that, were it not for my EVE baptism, I would have a great deal of difficulty in navigating, the game is solid throughout and has so far provided me with several hours of entertainment before I have even reached the game proper: although perhaps an odd decision to continue the tutorial throughout the first few hours of story campaign (I did not learn how to use the toted "Ammo crafting system" until I had already defeated a major boss, although perhaps I simply attempted the quests in the wrong order), the depth provided therein is an ample demonstrator of this game's potential.
The combat system, although a little simplistic (read: select target and press the "fire" button, since the weapons track targets automatically) nevertheless makes for some fairly intense combat scenarios, with victory relying on tactical foreplanning and the correct selection of items for the situation rather than twitch-trigger reactions and the sensitivity of one's mouse. The scenarios the game drops you into early on are ample proof of the ability of the game's engine to handle heavy loads, setting it up for some excellent space-brawls later in the game, and while the effects from laser-blasts and explosions are not enormously fancy, the sound-effects and musical backing more than compensate, making for some intense skirmishes, made all the more entertaining by your ship's fragility: take on more than you can handle, and you'll quickly be shredded, costing you in-game currency to respawn, and adding an element of risk to any confrontation.
In this sense, and also through the game's quest and rewards system, Zigfrak seems to borrow very heavily from the aforementioned EVE MMORPG series, which makes for a welcoming embrace for those who are fans of the series but will perhaps put off those looking for a fast-paced space dogfighter as opposed to EVE's slow, meticulous, cranium-bending micromanagement. I cannot help but return here to the issue of the UI, which, although relatively easy to navigate once the game informs you which panel is for what function, is small, non-draggable, non-resizeable, and written in small, cramped text which overwhelm the player with a great deal of information, which again becomes clear once the game tells you the meaning of every abbreviation and figure, but prior to this is entirely indecipherable. Were this one feature polished slightly, the game would instantly become more useable- a sidebar, perhaps, with each window outlined, would be appropriate.
However, this slight incomprehensibility is what lends Zigfrak a great deal of its charm: the game is unpolished in many senses, and has a skill curve which some may find insurmountable, but this sense of jury-rigged chaos is perhaps very fitting with the space-civil-war-freedom-fighter aesthetic. The madness which ensues in several of the early campaigns, and the endless mystery of the different ports, modules, ammunition types and weapon fittings, give Zigfrak a certain edgyness, a winning smile in the face of the recent deluge of cardboard-cutout space dogfighters (I'm looking at you, X:Rebirth). As it is, the game is compulsively playable, and I look forward to seeing the direction that it takes in the future, and with a few small tweaks, it could be instantly enjoyable by any fan of space combat and exploration.

As with many LucasArts adventure video games, I played the Windows original around the turn of the century on my first home PC and I still have fond memories of it.
:
(+) a high-octane main story set in a gritty near-future alternate-history universe, following Ben, a tough and gruff biker gang leader, as he gets mixed up in murder, corporate and vehicular warfare, and other manly exploits
(+) a motley crew of larger-than-life and memorable supporting characters like the elusive love interest Mo and the fiendish antagonist Adrian Ripburger
(+) relative freedom to explore the game world in each of the greater sections
(+) originally, one of the first games using a radial selection menu to complement the traditional point-and-click controls
(+) occasional bike-riding and/or -fighting sequences that go beyond the routine mouse-based adventuring and kick the gameplay into higher gear
(+) the dry, but witty writing by the dynamic duo of Tim Schafer (lead) and David Grossman (contributing), voiced with gusto by a talented crew including Mark Hamill himself in no less than 3 roles and many other professional voice actors, a feature truly unique back in 1995
(+) the rough-and-tumble, grimy, desolate but vigorous world envisioned in the original hand-drawn art designs by the masters Peter Chan and Larry Ahern redone completely, but respectfully and beautifully in high resolution and with full widescreen support
(+) the full-screen cutscenes are not only more plentiful, but better animated (and explosive) than in most other classic LucasArts titles
(+) the remastered high-powered SFX, licensed music and original tracks composed by Peter McConnell still rock and crank the whole production up to eleven
(+) puzzles with rational solutions that don’t require a PhD in abstract thinking, with the highlightable interactive objects and general objectives often laid out quite clearly in dialogue, but the specifics left for the player to figure out, all of which makes for a perfect starting point for the novices of the genre
(+) the original and the remaster can be switched back and forth at the press of a button
(+) newly introduced Steam achievements encourage exploration, inquisitiveness and sometimes quick reflexes
(+) a vast concept art gallery and extensive developers’ commentary by Schafer, Ahern and McConnell, with the lead sound designer Clint Bajakian, as well as the production manager Casey Acklee and the lead programmer Stephen Shaw
(+) perfectly playable with a mouse and keyboard, but analogue controllers are also supported
(+) expanded language options: full localizations in English, French, Italian and German, but only interface and subtitles in Spanish and Portuguese-Brazilian
(+) all in all, yet another hot rod saved from a scrapyard of gaming history, restored and pimped out by Double Fine
:
(−) noticeably shorter than most other classic LucasArts adventure games
(−) unlike in most similar games of the era, the puzzles are not very challenging and the inventory items can’t be combined, which may disappoint the veterans of the genre
(−) the occasional action sequences can annoy the purists out there
(−) not enough hand holding for novices (many objectives are pretty self-explanatory and the interactive objects can be highlighted, but there’s no hint system to help you out, no journal nor check-lists to keep track of your progress)
(−) an unquashed bug had me stuck on a literal mine field, autosaved in place, forcing me to revert to an older manual save
(−) developers’ commentary automatically plays on top of the on-screen dialogue during some if the cutscenes and the subtitles often can’t keep up with the commentary

The goal of CTHCC is to befriend the game's characters well enough to join the school club. If you've played Persona 4, the gameplay of CTHCC tries very hard to be the town segments of that game. You train certain skills to relate to people better, then talk to them as much as possible in order to become friends with them, see their stories, and finally convice them to join. Oddly, you never actually perform any comedy in the game, because it ends on the club registration deadline.
CTHCC is definitely not anywhere near Persona 4, but most games aren't. Unfortunately, this game has the weaknesses of P4's town gameplay as well. It's very repetitive. The music would be decent for this game if it wasn't repeated over and over ad nauseum. But, this game's strength is the character-driven story. While the characters are not near the level of P4, they were better than I expected them to be, though I wish they had more chit-chat dialogue.
This game has some display issues. Alt+Enter is the only way to make it fullscreen, and even then it doesn't work well. The art is decent otherwise, for being 2D still images. CTHCC controls well enough.
CTHCC is an okay way to kill an hour or two, but I was getting bored by the end of my three hour playthrough. I wouldn't pay much for it, though. Wait for a 75% off sale if this sounds interesting to you. If not, you're not missing too much by choosing to skip this game.

Overall, a cool game and worthwhile experience. It's a short game, and a bit light on actual gameplay; around half your combined time in this game is walking simulator and cut scenes. Fortunately, this game is gorgeous. As for mechanics, the combat is fun, though a bit shallow. The puzzles can be a chore and I never found solutions to be particularly satisfying, but they mesh with one of the game's main themes well.
This one's really about the plot, however. It's definitely a fun experience. This game is truly unique in its visual style and it serves the plot's exploration of schizophrenia and psychosis amazingly. The voice work is also phenomenal in this regard. While fascinating, I do think this game overestimates its meaningfulness regarding contemporary treatment, both medically and socially, of the mentally ill.
**MINOR SPOILERS**
This game runs with the claim that symptoms of mental illness are not necessarily harmful or negative per se, but rather it is the fear-driven treatment of others that is the true cause of suffering of the mentally ill. It even flirts with the idea that hearing voices or seeing hallucinations is virtuous. None of this comes off as unjustified within the context of the narrative, but the game is pretty clearly trying to make broader claims.

Shooting is fun. Usually when I play shooters I feel like all the weapons just feel the same, but these were all very interesting and had their own pros and cons, especially when it got into upgrading them.

I tried one of the loading tips of shooting a silenced round to distract them but even doing that they found me immediately despite hiding in a little tunnel-thing. I thought the music was amazing. Everything was nice to look at. BJ was interesting and I liked the characters overall.
Oh there are side missions and stuff but I totally forgot about them. I ended up not doing any of them. Since I finished the story and everything I doubt I'll go back to it, but if I ever decide to try the game on another difficulty then maybe I'll do it.

Half Life 2: Update is a free mod that enhances the game in very subtle ways. The goal of the re-release was to fix Half Life 2 after Valve very crudely ported the game to the Orange Box engine, while also enhancing the default maps so they can properly take advantage of it.
All of the maps were recompiled to actually use HDR. And in many instances the lighting was completely redone. The biggest aspect of the Update though is all of these changes were extremely subtle. This was done for a variety of reasons but the most logical one being so the game remains familiar while also feeling crisp and new. I like this design decision myself although understandably people would have liked new textures and new models.
Plus the Update also fixes several bugs that remain in the vanilla version, and adds developer commentary featuring many faces in the Half Life fan community. All of which gives you enough incentive to warrant another playthrough of Half Life 2.

This mod supposedly fixes issues created when Valve transitioned HL2 to a newer version of the Source engine and adds more modern lighting effects. I did play through the entire game and I can definitely tell that the lighting is better, the skies were fixed, and the water reflections (is that the 'reflect all' setting?) seemed to actually work; beyond that, I didn't notice anything else, but it did look good.
P.S. I've come to the conclusion that if you want HL3 then you need to take the initiative to get a job at Valve and take it upon yourself to drive the project to completion (don't screw up the story).

The Grand Finale of Umineko has finally arrived on Steam, and oh, what a finale it is; one worth waiting for, perhaps even a thousand years--at least that's what it felt like way back when, waiting for Episode 8 to be translated while dodging spoilers for months on end, like a determined fruitfly teleporting away from your crushing hands.
Have you ever read a book that changed your life? Changed the way you think about the world or certain concepts, influenced you as a person? If you're lucky enough to have had that experience, then you'll understand when I say that such books will always remain close to your heart. This is what Umineko is to me. I first read it almost ten years ago, during a pivotal and difficult time of my life, and it helped me to view certain matters in a different way and fight my way through. Even now, I still remember the things it taught me, and even now, they help me. Before it starts to sound like I'm advertising a bloody self-help book, let me stress that while it helped me to grow as a person, it's also just an absolutely brilliant goddamn series of novels.
While Umineko's Question Arcs certainly weren't lacking in tension and disturbing situations, the Answer Arcs--also known as Chiru--take it to a whole new level. Little is left to the imagination (and when it is, it often makes it worse) and each Episode has roughly a dozen
moments--depending on your tolerance. It shies away from very little, even though some extremely delicate subjects are touched upon, especially in later Episodes.
But let's not pretend Umineko's Answer Arcs are some piece consisting of mere gore and shock value--that couldn't be further from reality. The story gets more complex and layered with every Episode, and emotions are dialed up until the final Episode was enough to bring me to tears--and, once, actual full-on sobbing (I regret nothing)--several times. I strongly advise a tissue box or two for that one.
And ah, The Truth of the Rokkenjima Massacre. In the previous Episodes, this was very much the main focus, only towards the end starting to hint that things might not be so simple--as simple as Umineko ever gets, that is. The Truth is naturally the focus of Chiru as well, only things shift, and it quickly starts to become clear that to get to the very heart of it, you must be willing to look at things from a different perspective.
You will hear these words, more than once. Remember them, and take them to heart. The author strongly encourages, no,
you to read between the lines--to think, and try to solve the mystery for yourself; which I strongly concur with, since as I said in my previous review: answers will not be spoon-fed to you here.
What is truth, and is it always necessary for one to know? 'Yes, obviously,' I might hear you think, and I'd agree with you, on a global scale. However, when we zoom in, and get on a more personal level, would you still give the same answer? Are you certain you would always wish to know your Truth, and is it possible for more than one Truth to exist at the same time? Another version of the Truth? Even now, eight years after the series has ended, fans of the series are still debating said Truth, a testament to both the dedication of the readers and the complexity of the mystery.
Once you have realized your Truth, there's no putting it back in the catbox. Re-reading Umineko in its entirety once you've finished it is almost like reading an entirely different novel, which speaks volumes for Ryukishi's abilities as a writer. When you've recovered from the train you feel you've been hit by when those very last credits rolled, you will almost certainly immediately want to begin anew; I know I did. In many ways re-reading the entire series over again, knowing what I knew, was an even bigger emotional rollercoaster than the first. Ryukishi has always said that it was possible to solve the mystery, even solely with Episode 1; and while this appears to be true in hindsight, you'd need to be a genius of unheard of proportions to be able to have done so with Episode 1 alone. When Chiru comes into play, however, it most certainly is more than feasible to solve the mystery, especially once you've finished Episode 5.
Episode 8, for the first time, actually requires interaction from you, the reader. While it has only one branching choice near the end of the like most VN readers are used to, it also has a host of entertaining features at the beginning that I won't spoil. Let's just say it kept me busy for a good while, and it was an fun diversion from the usual nail-biting tension.
Once more, when it comes to the soundtrack, you can count on songs that will



so beautifully; atmospheric ambient music; haunting tracks that reflect the more
nature of Chiru as opposed to the previous four novels; as well as the electronic music you've come to
and
that will have you moving to the beat before you realise you're doing it, even as you're feverishly reading about fast-paced battles and the potential murder of your
. (I highly recommend you do not read the comments or even descriptions on these videos, as they
spoil you without mercy)
Ahhh, the characters. Chiru throws yet another few handful into the game to give us a grand total of [redacted], but you will not have any trouble differentiating one from the other; so well-written and distinct are their designs, motivations and personalities. Not much more can be said on that front without treading into spoiler territory, and Umineko is far too beautiful an experience to spoil.
Do yourself a favour and treat yourself to the masterpiece that is this magnificent series.

is an easy-to-understand casual game with difficult, yet enjoyable gameplay with plenty of levels and interesting gameplay.
The goal of the game is to paint all geometric shapes as demanded by their border color. You start with a few shapes already colored you can click on them to paint the adjacent shapes with the same color. You need to make sure not to erase some color completely, which is why this game can be so difficult.
There are 60 levels in total and they are divided into 10 level packs. Each pack introduces something new, which makes the gameplay more interesting or even a bit trickier. You are confronted with shapes that vanish once you click them, shapes that can store one color, shapes that can unlock some of their neighbors provided that it is painted with a certain color... It really makes the later levels feel fresh even if the basic mechanic stays the same.
Not all ten packs are unlocked from the beginning: to gain access to them, you have to complete a certain number of previous levels. Doing so shouldn't pose a challenge to most players as the requirements to unlock all the levels are pretty low.
You are free to click any number of times you want as you can only lose if some color is completely gone from the level. However, if you want to "master" the level, you must not exceed a predetermined number of moves. This usually means that you have to can't make any unnecessary moves. Since it's quite unlikely that you'll manage to achieve this in your first try (with the exception of the first few levels), there is some replayability value here. In some levels, it's possible to find an even shorter solution.
I mentioned Adjacency's difficulty a number of times already, which is why I would like to dedicate this paragraph to the difficulty curve. Although there is no tutorial, the initial levels do a very good job at teaching you how to play. Afterwards, the game feels quite difficult all the time, but it reaches your limit very slowly. I wasn't able to complete the last few levels, but I always felt like I was very close.
There are no hints or bonuses in this game and I can't decide if this is bad or not. Although it's sometimes really frustrating when I can't complete a level, this feeling actually motivates me to actually do it myself, not just to click the hint button and be done with it. You have to use all the stubbornness and brain power you have to complete some seemingly-impossible level and that might just be a good thing. Players nowadays are spoiled anyway, especially when it comes to puzzles games (but 10 hints for just $4.99!).
Now that I've finished talking about the gameplay, let's focus on the appearance of the game. The background is, fortunately, dark, which is perfect for night owl gamers like me. The shape border colors are bright, creating a visually appealing contrast with the background. The animations are smooth and fascinating, which is a plus. The sounds are, like the rest of the game, quite minimalistic. Apart from the ongoing atmospheric background noises, your clicks on the shapes result in most of what you'll hear throughout the game.
That's really all there is to talk about. I can't say I've spotted any negative things at all. Nothing except my own incapability to solve some levels was bothering me and although I've mostly experienced frustration during the entire time of me playing the game, I can only recommend the game. The price isn't steep so if you like puzzle games, go for it. You won't regret the purchase.
With love,
BirdCute

Adjacency is a fun, minimalistic puzzler that takes some real thinking to solve - a great way to spend a couple of hours.
The overall goal of the game is easy - match the color inside each shape to the color of its border. To do this, you have to "spread" colors from exisiting tiles to their adjacent tiles. It's a pretty simple mechanic, but good puzzle design along with a few interesting twists / mechanics keeps the game fresh.
Difficulty-wise, it's not too hard, but hard enough that you can't just guess your way through the game. Progression is clear and new mechanics are introduced with some ramp-up. One thing here is that sometimes it was hard to figure out exactly what new mechanics did - there's no textual explanation, so even if you solve the puzzles introducing the mechanic, it might take a while for you to really understand what it's doing.  There's also a perfect score for each function if you want another layer of challenge.
Graphics are nothing to write home about, but the shapes are sharp and the colors make it easy to stare at the screen while trying to figure out the next move. It fits with the type of game this was designed to be.
The music fits well with the aesthetic the game is going for and has some chill and relaxing tracks for puzzle-solving.
Overall, this is an engaging puzzler that's worth your time to spend a few hours with and use some of those dormant brain cells.

Full game review:

Fantastic puzzle game.  It takes a simple concept (spreading colors to adjacent shapes in order to get them to their goal color) and expands upon it in brilliant ways.
This is not a puzzle game that allows for random clicking until you eventually solve it.  It forces you to understand how the mechanics will affect things and to deliberately manipulate things to approach your goal.
The sound is also excellent, (warning: grossly overused buzz words ahead) being an ambient/atmospheric procedurally generated soundscape that responds to your actions.

This game is a ♥♥♥♥ing mess so far. While I like the dialogue (what little there is,) the art style, and the music, the majority of this game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ stealth mechanics, frustrating combat, and bugginess. The AI is alternately dumb as a bag of rocks or clairvoyant - capable of shooting you through walls or thwarted easily by waiting for them to lose interest in the gun wielding, big haired assassin they just saw running past them. Your character can generally only take a few hits before dying in a ten second long slo-mo death animation (which you'll be seeing a lot if you play on hard mode - here's a hint; don't) and your enemies either go down with a single hit or as much as three bullets / katana swipes. When you die, you get to do the whole sequence over again!
I was having fun with this game until the second chapter - Cardholder's story is generally a bit less actiony-shooty, although after a certain point the investigative adventure game aspect of the game is seemingly tossed out the window in favor of horrendous stealth and fighting with Cal's second chapter.
It's also buggy. The AI can often see you through walls and shoot you through them. You will get objectives you've already completed. You will see conversations that have already happened happen again. You will not be able to talk to certain characters despite their being highlighted. Enemies will somehow vanish between loading screens.
What's good? I -sorta- like the story, though I have no ♥♥♥♥ing clue what's going on with it. You're basically thrust into the plot with absolutely zero lead up or introduction, no idea who you're playing as, what their motivations are, what's at stake, who the bad guys are... is this one of those rare games that would benefit from a narrative text dump? Yes, probably. Or, y'know, a cutscene, something to establish what's even happening.
I also like the art. The dialogue is witty and very 80s, which is exactly what you should expect. Music's also fine - I have a softness for techno and electronica. To be honest, I'm disappointed so far in what I've seen. I was really looking forward to playing a game with this sort of concept, but the shortfalls in gameplay and story make it nigh intolerable right now.
However, since Majestic Nights is coming out in installments, I imagine there's plenty of time for the developers to get their♥♥♥♥♥♥together and iron out the terrible aspects of this game. Hopefully.
Right now, it's a waste of 20 bucks - stay the ♥♥♥♥ away from a season pass until they improve on this.

I am very pleased to have the oportunity to replay the Lucas games in remastered form, and apart from a weak first Monkey remaster, all the others are really good, and I find the trend really pleasing. This game remaster is equally good, both the commentary track, the HD graphics and sound, and the gamepad support.
But now, on to the game. This is my first time playing Full Throttle, and after all the praise throughout the years, I am surprised, because I found it pretty weak compared to classics like Monkey 2 or Day of the Tentacle.
+ Artwork, music and aesthetics
+ Some 3D elements, a marvel on release
~ Lucas Arts charm is barely there
~ Cinematic experience, which is something I don't particularly want to find when I play a point and click adventure
- Dumbed down adventure: do you know when you start a new point and click game, and you find yourself in a closed environment with just the necessary stuff to complete a puzzle, serving as a tutorial? The entire game is like that
- It is impossible to get lost
- You only have one objective at a time, and when you sort of have many, you have exactly the same number of locations to visit. You basically can brute-force yourself through-out the game
- Pixel hunting puzzles
- No real inventory puzzles, because the ones where you use the inventory are a given: you just have one object to use, in one location
- The classic insults/dialogue puzzle has one single solution, so if you get it first, the puzzle is non-existant
- A bunch of situational puzzles, where you need to click at the right moment
- Menu puzzles: where you test every option in a menu, watch the outcome, die, and repeat until you find the solution
- Really short: about 3-4 hours max
To be fair, it is like a movie, with some puzzles thrown in. You find some options to chose from, but there is only one that is the correct one. This is not a bad game, by any means, but it is not up to the legacy standards.
If this is your first Lucas Arts point and click adventure, forget/refund this one and do yourself a favor:
And if you want a contemporary homage, that really nails the point and click experience:

Full Throttle Remastered was my first playthrough of the Full Throttle game.
There is not much that I liked about this game.
The story was very linear and short.
The controls and environment were clunky and clumsy, and the puzzles were unintuitive.
The characters are very two-dimensional and do not grow or develop throughout the course of the game.
The highway segments are horrible and feel tacked on.
The positive aspects to this game were all in presentation - graphics, art style, voice acting.
Unfortunately, it does not appear that Full Throttle stood the test of time as well as other titles like Grim Fandango and Day of the Tentacle - but I believe it would still be an admirable visual upgrade for anyone that has nostaglic ties to the original Full Throttle.

I grew up on this game. Even before owning it on Steam, I've probably played through it at dozens of times. The voice acting is great. The animation looks like something out of an animated show. The writing is hilarious. Puzzle solutions usually involve breaking stuff or kicking someone's teeth in. Plus, Gone Jackals' music heavily featured? Heck yes. And this new remastered edition? Fantastic. The animations look better than ever and the character models really pop.
The game has some well-deserved criticisms.  It's a short game. I finished it in 3 hours, but mind you, that's knowing the game like the back of my hand. There are some frustrating arcade portions and a bad pixel hunt puzzle. Playing it back in the day was frustrating and the remastering hasn't changed a thing there.
Despite that, Full Throttle remains one of my all-time favourite games. Its style and humour alone make it worth buying. It's still a classic for all the right reasons.

The re-release of many of the classic point and click games has been a triumph, generally - I've enjoyed re-connecting with Monkey Island, Simon the Sorcerer et al. However, Full Throttle just hasn't stood the test of time. Way too short, no real story to get into, and the puzzles are really, really, really basic, and (in many of the time-sensitive puzzles) flat out illogical with no real satisfaction from solving them. The mini-games are still poor as well.
The game looks as beautiful as ever it did, and the voice acting/soundtrack is still great, but this game just isn't worth going back to. Many disagree, of course, but I was disappointed by this one.
Pains me to give the thumbs-down, as there's a lot to like in here, but your time is better spent elsewhere, IMHO.
Still a good game. There are a few scene set ups that are more challenging to read than others, but you will get there in the end.

"Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice" is an edgy 3rd person tech demo with visual puzzles and mediocre and repetitive combat. You follow the tortured soul Senua as she descends into the Underworld in an attempt to save the forsaken soul of her lover. Dark themes and a theme of darkness abound.
In its technical aspects, the game is a relative success - though the environments are bland, the characters are beatifully designed and rendered. Sound plays an important role in the game, as does speech, of which there is much but little that qualifies as dialogue.
Where the game falls short is in its gameplay - there just isn't much of that. Progress involves the alteration of simple visual puzzles, lengthy cutscenes, and sections of clunky timing-based combat. What you see in the first hour is what you'll be getting for all six.
The story, despite being simple and predictable, works well enough. Though one does occasionally wish for a break in the unrelenting themes of madness and despair.
On the overall, Senua is an impressive technical achievement but a mediocre game. Tech demo rating 10/10, game rating 7/10. The price tag of $30 is almost reasonable given that this is a 6 hour single-player only title with zero replatability. An $15 during a 50% sale would be even more reasonable.

EDIT: Episode One Review
Episode one picks up where Episode Zero left off and has you playing as Cal - a private investigator who has been hired by a shadowy figure called "The Suit". The Suit has tasked you with tracking down Cardholder for him.
Episode One is for all intents and purposes an extension of the prologue and plays very similarly. You'll go to different locations, gather intelligence on your target and wind up in a secret location, hot on their trail.
Some of the issues i mentioned in my previous preview are much more pronounced in episode one, such as janky, aggrivating shooting mechanics and confusing plot. They do make it a chore to play the game at times, but overall things are still enjoyable.
Overall I gave Episode one a 7/10. You can read my full review of Episode One here:
Having just complete the Chapter Zero prologue, I'm impressed...if a little confused. ButI am sure all will make sense in due course.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Episode Zero
Majestic Nights transports you back to an alternate reality 1980s and puts you in the shoes of an enigmatic character called "Cardholder". In Chapter Zero you'll find yourself interrupting your neighbour while he is on the toilet, you'll beat up a bouncer at a nightclub, and gun down lots of secret agents.
I couldn't really make sense of the story, but I think that's intentional. There's lots of talk about faked moon landings, MK Ultra, Illuminati and various other conspiracies. If you are into that kind of thing you'll have a blast.
The game plays out a bit like Shadowrun, except with realtime gun battles instead of turn based. You are given various different dialogue choices for every conversation, and you can choose to play the nice guy or be an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ if you so please.
Gunplay is a little finicky but still rewarding. Holding the RMB brings up your gun with an accompanying laser sight so you can aim accurately. Clicking the LMB fires the gun. Action sequences revolve mostly around cover shooting, and you'll have to brace yourself up against something to stay out of the line of fire.
With Chapter Zero set to release for free, you might as well pick it up and give it a go. It's short at around 1 hour long, but there's lots here for fans of cover shooters, stealth games , or conspiracy theories.

Cute concept, brilliant idea... But it's ruined by extreme difficulty spikes and awkward design decisions. While the first few levels are enjoyable, and all seems well intially, the game quickly divebombs into frustrating and tedious territory.
Good:
- Great pixel art
- Decent amount of levels/content for an arcade style game and the price.
- Very easy to learn and control.
Bad:
-Geared heavily towards luck, too little towards skill. The advantage of bullet hell shooters is that there are patterns and expectations. Players can develop skills based on what they learn from patterns. Not so here: enemy positions are randomized which creates a ton of frustration. One game you'll have red jellies congregated in one area, another game you'll be frantically rescuing the cats one after another.
- The player is woefully underequipped to combat the majority of enemies. They absorb a stupid amount of bullets and the power ups, except the two extra cats and the bomb, are faily useless.
- Half the nemies are programmed to dive out of the way of your vehicle. This may sound interesting at first, until you realize how much time you're spending chasing enemies that randomly move out of the way of your already underpowered weapons.
- Difficulty essentially equates to dumping increasing amounts of enemies around the screen randomly, often before you've even finished a particular wave of foes.
- The foreground art will regularily cover enemies and bullets making navigating around the map incredibly annoying and, again, make your survival a lucky happenstance.
- Bullet travel length is based on the direction and speed you travel, amking moving forward actual disadvantagous in most situations, despite moving being what you need to do to survive.
- Balancing looking up at the alarm and surviving while doding bullets is way too much to handle. Another Double Fine Production. Such a fine Remaster... See what I did there? Nevermind...
Another chance to play again a great classic and amazing Point & Click adventure by the now dead Lucas Arts.
The story is pretty simple, and almost all misteries are revealed in the first half of the game (yet I won't reveal much, just the essential). Ben is the head of the Polecats, a Motorcycle Club. Adrian Ripburger, PR from Corley motors stuns Ben which doesn't want to cooperate and hires the Polecats to escort Mr Corley to a convention for the shareholders, only to kill Mr Corley along the road and frame the Polecats. Great beginning, yet half of the suspance and mistery is gone. But who cares when the point of Lucas Arts' adventures is the humour and puzzles?
As usual there's not much to say, Double Fine did their magic with the usual result, a polished and updated version of the original game. Pleasure for the eyes and the nostalgic mind. Yet seems to me that they did only the "easiest work". The section "on the road" is still rendered to run at about 2/5 FPS, which is definitely a turn down. Unexpected, cheap and disappointing. Good thing it doesn't take long to end it and doesn't require a good frame rate as it's not about the action but it's more about the choice of the items. Yet that section is cancer for eyes...
There's something special in a soundtrack that perfectly reflects the story and the characters, maybe a sitar for a situation in a desert, the Koto for a story in japan, synthetizers for space. Well, hard rock for motorcycle clubs might sound common, but if it's done well it simply is ITS OWN.
There's not much to say about Point & Click mechanics. But I can say something about a small but different section: the road. At some moment in the story you will be able to go along the road and you might meet other rival gangs you need to fight to get some useful weapons (chains, sticks and stuff like that) or some useful item (No need to spoil what is it). The fact that every biker has its weakness makes me feel confused about it, I don't know if it's a clever choice or a cheap one. One thing is sure, this section adds some variation to the game and gives further perspective for the protagonist and his world.
It's short. Not that other adventures are much longer, but this one is quite short. OK, it's short but very intense. I can't leave this section on such a negative tone. Especially thinking of such an intense and unconventional ending (for a Lucas Adventure)

Cherry Tree High School Comedy club is definitely aimed at a distinct subset of people. If you have no interest in anime, ridiculous and exaggerated characters, and playing what more or less amounts to a friendship simulator, I can tell you right now there is nothing for you here. On the other hand if you enjoy quirky Japanese games, Cherry Tree is one of the few of its kind to be found on Steam and that novelty is what lead me to giving it a go. Unfortunately I came away quite disappointed, and am once again left searching for a suitable replacement.
Although there were quite a few things I felt ended up as missed opportunities, the biggest detractor was the lackluster characters and writing. Though it's set in Japan the dialog is decidedly westernized, which led to it feeling less like one of my beloved anime comedies and more like what you might find in a Disney channel show. I never grew fond of any of the characters, and actually became rather annoyed whenever I had to spend an extended period of time interacting with them. This lack of interest also lead to repetition setting in rather quickly, and by the end I was simply going through the motions in order to recruit my required number of members. Given you can beat the game in a short 4-5 hours, how quickly it turned into a grind is very disappointing.
I honestly really wanted to love Cherry Tree. It appeared to have all the ingredients for a game I'd love (anime and pixel graphics, a premise that sounded right up my alley, and gameplay that fell into the realm of the unusual), but it never clicked for me. Interaction felt shallow, the writing and jokes all fell flat, and it's strict time structure left little room for experimentation. There is certainly some semblance of charm to be found here, but for me at least, it didn't wind up amounting to something I enjoyed, or have any real desire to replay.

The items and their descriptions can be hilarious.  For instance, you start out with a "dusty cannon" and it's got "a colony of bunnies live inside."
I also like the ability to thrust and slide in three dimensional space.
That said, I do have a problem with the interface.
For instance, the inventory menu.  I suppose the easiest way to explain it is that It's really compact.  All you have to distinguish the different weapon icons is the border.  Brown/Green/Blue/Purple...etc.  Unlike other rpg games where different items may have different icons, here you find that all cannons look the same.  All pulse cannons look the same.  Etc.  I have to mouse over each item just to see what it is.
That wouldn't be so bad...except the game sorts everything for you.  I'm a messy guy, so I subscribe to the school of controlled chaos.  I'm the type who would store the useful items on one side of the inventory and the junk go on the other.  That way, when I land, I know what leaves and what stays.
Here...The junk and the good stuff are lumped together by category, and it also looks like by level.  Quite frankly, I'm not going to remember what order the cannons are in...so once I hit level 7 and then open up the inventory to equip that cannon that had a level 7 requirement, I end up having to mouse over each item just to find it.
Did I mention that the inventory menu was compact?  Guess what? The item details end up being in a window like 1/5th the required size.  And that's important why?  It means you have to scroll.  And why do you have to scroll?  Because to equip an item, you have to go to the equip options that come AFTER the description.  Right clicking like in other games doesn't work, it just brought up the descriptions.
That reminds me...it looks like there's a fuel and ammo system in this game.  After some poking around, it occurred to me that I can pull that information up by accessing my inventory and then checking the engine and each individual weapon.  I think that's how you do it.  Couldn't there have been some sort of HUD for this?
I'll recommend it, because it truly does seem like an interesting game.  But this user interface could've been streamlined.

Zigfrak is the freshman effort of a single independent developer looking to combine the space sim with the action RPG.  While the game starts out a bit confusing (there is a lot of information to process in a short time span) it quickly becomes clear that you are a stand-out pilot from the Freerunners faction that is traversing the Nautilus galaxy looking for stuff to blow up and loot.
Mixing a fair share of humor and unique sci-fi, Zigfrak offers a stellar RPG experience and plenty of options in the loot department.  While the game lacks the level of ship options that you'd find in other games of the genre, it more than makes up for it in sheer content.
If I had to rate this game among other space-sims, though - Zigfrak does fall a bit short.  As I said, it lacks customization options, and you never really get the feeling like you're a part of anything.  You are a lone pilot, breaking metal loot pinatas. Contributing to the health of the galaxy is not your concern, neither is its politics (save for who to shoot).
Still, for those interested in breaking into the genre for the first time or folks who are fans of ARPGs, you couldn't beat Zigfrak at this price point or any other.

How is this only $2.50? If you see this game on sale, you're getting incredible value for money. Even if it's not on sale, this is a big package for only $5. If you enjoy looting and crafting, and you enjoy space battles, well... you probably already bought this game.

I'm serious. I've never played a single game before in which the sound file compression artifacts would be so noticeable and annoying. You can notice them starting as soon as even in the main menu music, but mostly in some ambient/environmental sounds, voice acting samples and some other sound effects (not all of them). That's quite disappointing for a game which relies so heavily on the overall sound experience - because it hurts this experience pretty badly due to all the perceptible compression...
I really hope that one day the developers will release a patch that increases the audio files' quality (re-export with better quality settings).
One can only imagine how much better would the sound, voice recordings and music in this game sound like if they exported all files with a higher and more proper bitrate. That would be a much, much more pleasant experience in the game, the stereo separation of the binaural recordings would be better, and it would truly prove this game's "Best Audio Design" award.
Developers, Ninja Theory... Why did you do such a thing to the sound quality of your own game - which relies very heavily on sound quality - in the first place...? That's a mystery to me and I would feel much better listening to an explanation that this was just a simple mistake and wasn't done intentionally. Maybe the Ogg Vorbis encoder used was bad?
