TL:DR: This is probably a 6/10. I would probably say this is a very minor step down from The New Order overall, with the gameplay IMO being two steps forward, two steps back, and the story being a very simple two steps back. I'll explain:
-The gameplay is too twitchy (You and your enemies both die very fast, and this is overdone IMO even on Normal difficulty), and the stealth system still sucks. (though it is improved from TNO midway through the game via a certain upgrade that's essentially a buggy Reflex mode from MGSV, which does make it far more forgiving) These are problems that The New Order suffered from as well, they were just issues lurking under the surface Machine Games accidentally amplified, which is what's causing the unrest about these problems now. Normal difficulty feels almost like max difficulty from The New Order (at least in terms of enemy damage). This is probably the biggest overall issue with the gameplay.
-The perk system is... Eeeh. Rather than a tree system they let you get the perks mostly whenever you want, which is a nice step up, and the requirements are FAR less unreasonable this time! However, the bonuses are extremely, extremely boring. You can complete each perk challenge 5 times over for the same boost to get amplified over and over and it feels extremely lazy. No interesting buffs like in the 1st game. The "Contraptions" that you unlock after the 1st act has more interesting bonuses, but it's seperate from the perks system, and 2/3 of the interesting bonuses they provide are just handed to you upon acquiring the Contraption as opposed to needing unlocks.
-The grenade is a significant improvement. I miss the classic visual design but practically speaking it's so much better now, it actually does reasonable damage as opposed to just being a robot stunner.
-The weapons I will say are an overall improvement. The Laserkraftwerk is now essentially a sniper rifle, which is a redesign I like far more- And they just ditched the laser cutting gimmick altogether. My complaints are that the new grenade launcher pistol feels a tad weak especially when compared to your standard, highly upgradable grenades, the SMG feels like it's in an awkward middle, is weak and has little reason to exist, and the assault rifle remains a borderline OP DPS machine that can never run out of ammo, especially when dual wielded. The new heavy weapons are probably the area where gunplay was most improved as they are now more interesting, varied and more fun to use.
-The Contraptions kick♥♥♥♥♥ nothing more to say.
I'll address the story in the form of character critiques because they're the fault points this story falls apart on.
-Grace is the most immediately offensive one. She is essentially the 2nd most stereotypical black woman possible (the fact that she and literally every single one of the many black women who work for her have afros does not help with that), and is an incredible ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Her introductory sequence, like most of this game's 1st act, is very poorly written and serves to establish her as a racist ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who refuses to admit her own ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥gery. When meeting her, she accuses you of being a Nazi, because you're white and not a "deviant", despite her own lover and father of her daughter falling into the same category of people. This would be fine if it was only her first assumption, and hell in TNO multiple Nazis assumed BJ was also a Nazi because of the way he looks, so I could see past it- If she didn't stubbornly stick to that same line of logic for almost the entire scene despite it's blatantly flawed roots. When she later tells BJ that "white America has given up", BJ goes into a passionate speech about how he still intends to fight and still believes the common people have the will to do the same- To which, instead of admitting she was wrong in her borderline racist assertions, proceeds to agree with BJ in such a way that denies her own wrongdoing as if she agreed with him all along (which is pretty much the most annoying possible way you can end an argument). Grace is immediately wholly unlikeable from the moment you meet her and is very easy to hate. HOWEVER! She... Goes through a character arc? Not really as it's very poorly done, but she grows less annoying as she settles into a blander leader role, and she does get a very well-deserved slap + lecture at the end of the game. Unfortunately, she takes it more as "Now you've shown balls ALPHA ALPHA ALPHA GRRRR" rather than "I guess I was wrong, sorry about that", but she nevertheless thankfully stops being a complete♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by this point of the game, despite how poorly handled the transition was.
-Sigrud has some badly written lines, and the fact that nobody mentions that Klaus, a character from TNO, was ALSO a former Nazi and he still got accepted by the Resistance, are serious issues. It's bizarre seeing Klaus almost entirely erased purely for the purpose of artifically creating character conflict with Sigrud and the other resistance member, especially as there are other, more valid reasons to distrust her (eg. She's Frau's mother♥♥♥♥ing daughter!) than just her former Nazism. Still, she actually does go through a character arc, is quite sympathetic and is IMO by far the most likeable new character.
-Super Spesh is a generic alien conspiracy theorist. Very original. I think the most annoying part of his character was actually the way others reacted to him rather than the character himself, as he very clearly mistakes Daat Yichud tech for alien tech ALL THE TIME and BJ makes a half-hearted attempt to correct him once, and then immediately gives up. I THINK he was trying to be the game's comedy relief character, but I wasn't the slightest bit amused by anything he said.
-Frau Engel isn't a new character... But she might as well be. I MUCH preferred her in The New Order. Bubi gave her a good cop, bad cop vibe that actually worked well, she had significantly more personality, she didn't make incredibly awkward lewd jokes (And when she did make remarks of that sort it was directed towards Bubi, which actually made sense and was well-executed), and she was just generally handled better. Hey, isn't it weird that a female is in a position of authority in the highly bigoted Nazi party? Oh wait, Order acknowledges that in a conversation that also clarifies Frau's opinions on the matter, while Colossus just ignores it. Why does Frau have such an obsession with Blazko again? Oh wait, Order has an extremely clear cause and effect with her relationship with him, starting off as fairly neutral and moving towards downright sadistic, while Colossus starts out with her hating Blazko for reasons that new players aren't told about (hell they'd probably assume her jaw scars are likely just birth deformities or something. Her history with Blazko is NEVER brought up!), and she only acts as a figurehead for the Nazi party rather than having her own personality to herself that might allow for some kind of change to happen to her over the course of the game. You get the picture.
-Horton is... Bloody hell, I don't even know what the ♥♥♥♥ he is. An elderly communist hippie moonshiner who channels a bit of Father Grigori for no reason? Whatever the ♥♥♥♥ his incoherent♥♥♥♥♥is, I didn't like him.
The old characters, though, are thankfully their same old selves and still as likeable as ever- It's just a shame they take a backseat to these far less likeable ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. The final scene of the game kinda summed it up: The lovable characters sit in the background, while Grace and Horton ramble completely incoherently about garbage that doesn't make any sense and makes the entire Kriesau Circle look like a bunch of escaped asylum inmates, as opposed to legitimate revolutionaries.
If you enjoyed The New Order, you will likely get enjoyment out of this despite the story's downfalls. A light recommendation overall, but get and beat The New Order first. It's cheaper, and IMO, better.

Major patches are need for all of the FFXIII games.

+ Wonderful Environments in certain areas
+ Fantastic Combat System, this time around you only play as lightning but you have multiple "classes" that you switch bebtween on the fly with their own energy meters keeping the action fast and fluid.
+ LOTS of cutimization, including giving your character silly unique items like hats, tails, cat ears, and the ability to change the colors of all outfits
+ Great Voice Acting
+ Enjoyable characters
+ Plenty of fearsome enemies and bosses
+ Limitations on healing items create the need to conserve and use healing potions wisely, it also creates a need to guard and causes every fight to be worrisome (if you die, it's not gameover you just lose time)
+ Combining Spells to make them more powerful with more potent effects, along with leveling them up
+ Plenty of enjoyable rewarding side quests
+ All quests when completed will improve your base stats along with other rewards. This is a very nice touch, and makes you want to take the time to complete side-quests. (there is no expeirence or leveling system, it's mostly based on your gear and abilities)
- The story is... a bit vague and confusing. You are basically working for a god to save souls to bring to a new world, so that your sister can be reborn. (and apparently everyone seems to be many centuries old....)
- Not a good game to start with, you really want to playthrough FFXIII and FFXIII-2 before you play this one.
- There is this "countdown-timer" that is constantly ticking, it basically warns you only have 6 days before the end of the world, you can extend this to 13 days, but I absolutely can't stand game's with timers, it makes me feel rushed and doesn't allow me to fully explore or set my own pace. *I think they added this for replayability reasons*
- Along with the timer there's a clock, and many quests require you to wait until a certain time a day before starting or finishing a quest. While waiting you are supposed to go around and do side quests, and explore other areas, but it always made me paranoid that I was going to miss something.
- At 6am each day Hope teleports you to the ship no matter what you may doing. He does this so that you can give souls you collected to God to extend the timeframe, but it's really annoying.
- The game is INCREDIBLY DIFFICULT, I'm not using a guide, and the pacing feels VERY OFF, I feel like I'm entering areas with monsters far above my current ability, and doing quests that I probably shouldn't be completing yet. In the video above you can kinda get the sense of this, but there's no indication of what order I should do things in so I end up just choosing things at random, and praying I have the skills to beat the bosses.
- When doing Side Quests you have no indication of where you are supposed to go or what you are supposed to do without a guide, AND most of the time you have to wait for certain times of the day for an NPC to spawn to continue the quest, making the side-quests in this game almost impossible without a guide....
Overall it's a great game in the series, although I HIGHLY suggest you play through FFXIII BEFORE you play this or you may get a bit discouraged.
[Side note: I am a fan of FFXIII, so my view may be a little biased as I know a lot of people did not enjoy that game]

This is the best PC port from the FFXIII series so far. There is some choppiness from loading in some of the larger city areas, but battles and everything else runs fine for the most part. There's no need to worry about technical issues like there has been for FFXIII and FFXIII-2, previously.
The gameplay is action-oriented this time, with a focus on timing your attacks and blocks during battle that is new to the series. The game in general has an emphasis on keeping things moving, rather than taking your time to think and explore. I am an old-school turn-based RPG fan, and it wasn't so action-based that I couldn't enjoy playing. I haven't found a battle so far that required timing skills to succeed, as long as I have setup Lightning's equipment effectively before-hand so that I had enough HP to survive despite my poor hand-eye-coordination, for example.
The story is bonkers, but that's just how FF games are now. It's a good thing the gameplay is fun enough that it doesn't really matter.

Then comes this rainy October eve and I had some free time on my hands and installed it again, lo and behold what a journey it's become.
The beginning is a bit dull as it was, fixing your ship and gather this and that. I also did get a bit stuck when I didn't realize how to build a base, something the wikipedia is quite helpful with. But once I did, oh what a journey it's been. I'll leave out any spoilers, but as I was riding along through the galaxy and getting to know the many individuals better and better with every word I learned. I also stumbled upon a distress beacon which brought forth a wave of emotions. The story is quite rich for being in short doses, in better making my base more habitable. I also grew to know my fellow inhabitants all the while I blazed away in my Exocraft, literally bouncing through the world on every rocky hill there is. Climbing mountains and the occasional drowning in the middle of the planet cause the rendering couldn't keep up so now I die. If you play hardcore, drive safetly. Sure it's a lot of running about and flying here or there, and still a lot of gather but I atleast feel that it's a certain calm to it and a rush to get to the next point of the story.
There's still a lot of love the game can recieve with space battles and all that. There's also a lot of farming, but atleast now it's fun. And I can gladly give it a thumbs up. With the disclaimer that the full price is a tad steep for what you actually get. I'm excited to see what more they bring to the game.

Released in late 2012 and just recently on steam comes Zigfrak. With a name seemingly produced by a name generator, Zigfrak is an action RPG set in space. The game drives the player through a single player story but the player is free to roam off the beaten trail to explore or engage in side-quests.
Zigfrak was a game that I wanted to like as I love space exploration action RPGs ever since Escape Velocity. Unfortunately, in my opinion suffers from some key flaws. Playing this game it's fairly obvious that this game borrows alot from MMOs such as World of Warcraft, which is not something I would necessarily want in a single player game. A lot of quests are tedious and uninteresting "go here and click on this" tasks. There's a lot of loot in the game to collect, which might generate some interest and motivation to play, but this mechanic feel a bit cheap. A lot of sidequests are collection questions that just involve collecting a specified amount of items and cashing them in for a reward.
Since this game is inspiried by MMOs I don't think it really respects the player's time; for example at one point the player must battle a spacestation with a friendly fleet. It took me nearly 45 minutes to deplete half of it's health.
Aside from this, the action is fairly average. The weapons don't have a particularly notable feel and I didn't get a sense that I was actually hitting a target. Instead I just held down the attack buttons until I saw the enemy's health bar lower.
To it's merit, when a 'hacking minigame' came up I was given the option to fight enemies instead. I aprpeciated the option to focus on the game's core gameplay instead of getting pulled off into some minigame.
In terms of production value, the graphics aren't anything to write home about and many things in the game simply don't have any sort of sound effect.
There is no USB controller support for this game.
If you like MMOs and space exploration RPGs and you want a single player game you might find this game fun, otherwise there are better options for you.  I played this game a little over 3 hours, giving it a chance to get me interested but it failed to really inspire me to play.
Score: 5/10

I'm going to keep this short. I've only sunk about 2 hours into Zigfrak, but I've already had more than enough fun with it to justify it's extremely low 5 dollar price tag. The core gameplay is the real star here; it's an A-RPG that wears its title proudly: enemies explode in crazy piles of loot which are easy enough to collect (thankfully flying by loot auto collects it), the writing is fast paced and witty, and the world is huge. It's got all the point-and-click-y fun that comes from diablo as well as slightly strategic gameplay that one might expect from a space shooter. All of which is to say, it's a great twitch gaming experience.
The game itself features a crafting system, mining resources, cloaking, hacking mini-games (which are entirely optional, the game will let you just shoot stuff instead if you prefer), and some slight inventory micro-management (you have a shield for your shield, called an overshield which can take a real beating, but once it goes down, you probably want to equip another one). If you like space games where you get to take control of a ship and use it to blow up other ships while also exploring an expansive universe, check out Zigfrak.
The combats intense the story is gripping and the way the sounds and atmosphere holds your attention, it keeps you locked in through out the whole game.

The game itself is kinda easy going experience you start at point A and go to point B solving some puzzles on the way

someone in your head keeps telling you:
“She will not make it”, “She doesn't know what she's doing”, “She will die”.
Once I got used to the jibba jabba in Senua´s head I started to really bond with this character and to suffer with her.
I struggled a long time if to get the game or not and finally bought it on sale, now after playing I would say it's the full price worth, though.
Does it have any re-play value? Well from my point of view it kinda has, if only to get all trophies done,
I am quite sure that I missed a lot of details in my first play through.
So I strongly recommend this title surely it has some flaws but if you just lean back and let go
you'll have an experience just a few games can give and definitely worth your money.

A gorgeous remaster of a classic mid-90's point-and-click adventure game that never got mainstream attention like LSL or Monkey Island for some reason. You play as Ben, a badass biker who gets unwittingly embroiled in a scheme involving a corporate takeover and murder, and his job is to solve puzzles and kick butt until he unravels the mystery and clears his name.
The game is virtually unchanged from the original aside from hi-definition redrawings of the graphics and remastered audio for the music/voices, although you still have the option of using the "low definition mode" if you want to relive the experience of playing Full Throttle on an old Windows 98 computer.
The fact that Full Throttle Remastered is essentially unchanged from the original works against it in a few ways however, the main issue being the story is too short (it can be beaten in a few hours for a first time player) and the combat/driving is still very clunky. Thankfully the rest of the experience is highly polished and enjoyable, and the puzzles are quite forgiving compared to other games in the genre. This makes it a good first adventure game for those who are not ready for the trickier titles.
Also included is some developer commentary and concept art which can be unlocked by simply playing the game, which is always a nice bonus for the die-hard fans.
I hope the positive reception this game gets can spur the developers into finally making a proper sequel to Full Throttle, as I and many other fans would love to see Ben's story continue!

So considering the amount of enjoyment I've had in the past hour I felt as though I should finally chisel my words unto this slate. Make my mark on this battlefield e call...the steam user reviews section.
I'm going to structure this as a short story.
Deployment
I was called in, a new recruit drafted into this seemingly endless war. My first deployment was fridge valley, when I stepped foot into that frozen hell I was no longer a man, I was a soldier, I was a cog in this gargantuan machine called war. The first mission was to capture a small camp, simple enough eveyone thought and it was, until the greycollars came in full force. Friends I met in the playground, what we called bootcamp, were dissappearing in a haze of gunfire and snow. The sky was grey while the ground was red.
Our second action was to take control of Old Fort creek, nice place save for all the greycollared goons running all over the place, I had gaine some notoriety amongst my allies and enemies, I was in command of a small squad of four we'd been travelling to a nearby textile factory. Supposedly there was an enemy comms truck there and we were going to destroy it. We didn't expect such a large force there I told my squad to hold back until I "light the fuse" or "disturb the hive" We killed them all, after the truck was destroyed we called in eight rounds of Artillery, the sky was falling, the earth was rumbling. When we walked in to see the damage all that was left were the bodies of enemy soldiers strewn about, blood covered the ground, again.
A few hours pass by, I now command a squad of ten. Rattlesnake Crescent, the brownpants were in control of the city. We were travelling in an APC until out of nowhere an RPG hit our rear, they ambushed us. We didn't see them, they were on the roofs and in the alleys. They got six of us at first, we retreated through a small backstreet into a courtyard, another ambush, paratroopers. It all happened in slow motion, like the world was lagging. I saw the men who I reveered as my brothers fall, their blood splattering the gorund like rain.
I ran, for the first time I feared for my life, but, I couldn't move I was hit. The enemy was crowding around me. I was sitting in a well, bleeding out. My short, insignificant life flashed before me. The faces of my allies, the faces of my enemies were all I could see. I only remembered the time I spent Running with Rifles.
*God like voice*

Just to start off and make a quick TL;DR.. This game is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing. It's ArmA but with simple graphics and top-down.
I know I only have five hours in this so far.. which is a single campaign match, basically. This game is surprisingly tactical and realistic, despite the first glance impression I got. I went in, got through a tedious and barely helpful tutorial, then instantly started following the attack markers. I jumped into a trench with my trusty rifle, saw four grenades getting lobbed into the trench.. and died.
I respawn with a shotgun and medicpack, and start running towards the screams of fire and the whizzling bullets. Yet again, grenades and bullets fly all over. A grenade lands right next to me, and I instantly dive into prone, barely avoiding the shrapnel. I crawl towards some of my mates that got hit, and patch one of them up. He thanks me and runs towards the bullets again.. only to get shot in the face by an APC.
This game is so addictive. There's a wide variety of different maps, three different factions, and a bunch of side-objectives, though you barely understand what they mean, for most of the time. You can go all in with the rest of the army, and win through brute force, or take a jeep around to the back of a base, and sabotage them, meaning lower spawn rate and loss of equipment, giving your faction a drastic advantage.
There's a bunch of different vehicles to use, and they're all equally fun. You slowly gain ranks, and with it, more members to your personal squad.
You can call in arty, weapon drops and much more.
Hijack a hostile ammo truck and deliver it to your base, and you'll get even more weapons throughout the rest of the campaign. Weapons are a bit dull at first, but find hidden crates and trucks, and you'll get some exciting things.
Definitely a must-buy for people that enjoy a tactical shooter, despite the camera view, and enjoy killing your friends with jeeps!
Remember, you're a soldier like everyone else. It's okay to cry.
(NOTE: The devs are incredible people at releasing patches, fixing underpowered and overpowered items, and giving out free content for the game. The recently released workshop patch is already working out great. There's multiple overhauls out, making it a zombie survival game, a WW1 game, a WW2 game, a Warhammer 40K game or even Mass Effect. Great devs, great community.)

Okay, it was hard and I have mixed feelings about this game.
Usually, when you review anything you start with the pros but it's not the case here, so here we go.
Cons:
- Controlls and gameplay. All Japanese games have something in common: awful controls. But this game, it is something else. It is pretty simple, all you have to do is to point you mouse at some object/place and press LMB in order to interact/move (or use arrows to move, it's up to you). Problem is the sensetivity is way to high and there is no way you can adjust it, so you you will probably end up pointing the cursor in all the places but not the one you need to. Also when the character(s) is moving it is crucial to click on the exact place you want go. Otherwise, you won't be able to interact with something you wanted to.
Also, every animation is slooooow and it is really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off right from the start.
- Levels architecture. Seriously, it's disgusting. There lots of situations when you need to interact with two object which are located nearby, but you have to make a long way in order to do it.
Pros:
- Story. It is simple and yet it is perfect. It has quit a few twists. Also, the are a lot of stories (not only in games) which are told by the following system: slow intriguing start and fastly-paced ending. In this game storry is narrated smoothly and evenly. This type of story-telling really suits such kind of plots and it is implemented just perfect.
-Music. If "To the Moon" required a lot of money it's because of the OST. Actually, it is the only reason I haven't dropped the game after first 30 minutes.
"To the Moon" is a small game and there is not much to say about it. Also I do not know if I would recommend it. If you are a fan of interesting stories and you are okay with awful gameplay, then you should buy it, if not: run away and never look back.

As an user that has bought this game for 90% discount recently this year, and that finished the game legitimately, and soon onwards to 100% rating, I can safety say, this game is possible to beat, but it almost cockblocks you at the end, just saying.
Most of us bought this back in the day including me, for the PS2. the PC re-release is both good and bad for a few reasons. It's good because more people will get this mediocre gem once more, bad because, GameSpy servers are, well, very much dead. However, you can still have LAN Parties, or if you cannot be arsed, use Evolve to play with other people, friends mostly.
SRS is your usual cheesing street racing racing game, with not much story. You start out driving Ken's Skyline, only to get your cut and start off the game with a new car and race crews. But something people didn't care so much including me, were the girlfriends, they don't add much to the game, and a few of them challenges, can be pretty harsh.
But the way of progression is most definitely odd and ineresting. You don't just race for the ANTE or wagers. No points here like championships, but you gotta earn RESPECT points. That's right, if you have no respect, you don't own the streets, and no one will respect ya! You do that by doing, crazy tricks. Near misses, drifts, clean laps, sounds familiar right? Only that you'll be required to get respect points, if you wanna be with the big boys. And that's the kinda unfun part of the game, it gets to a point, you need to get good.
The game also features the arcade mode, such as time trials, quick race, and two other main features of the game, for bonus cars, that are not just arcade mode - they...go towards the street mode of the game. Dope, isn't it? Either way...
The physics and customization of this game aren't all that impressive, but you can actually flip cars, if you're risky enough. In freee roam, you also have to worry about cops, if they see you commiting illegal actions, and do hefty fines, that might hurt your financial doings at the garage or showroom. The soundtrack is okay and in other moments, cheesy enough to fit in with the game.
Overall, if you have friends that are willing to play the game and try the lan mode for multiplayer, the full price while questionable, might be worth it. Or if you're here for the cards and to finish the game, get it dead cheap. Also for nostalgia, any price does it.

Cute, humorous game that's has elements of a VN crossed with an RPG/Princess Maker game.  Basically you work to gain money, use said money to build on conversation peices (stats), and use that to raise relationship levels with the girls. Get said levels high enough they'll join your club.  Ending depends upon how many of them you end up geting to join by the time limit, it is possible to get them all, if you play it right.

It's kinda difficult how to describe this game exactly.  It's basically Persona 3 without Tartaris.
You go through each day, (morning, noon, and evening) and try to recruit fellow students to join your school club.  To do so, you have to talk to them (like building social links) but in order to make interesting conversation, you must build your rank in various and sundry topics one might converse about (just like leveling personal attributes in Personas 3 and 4).  As you can imagine, this all takes time and the clock is ticking down.  That being said, at it's core, CTHCC is really a time management sim, but you get to experience some nice character development and funny dialoge along the way.  One could make an argument that this game might even fall into the Visual Novel genre in a round about way.
A minor gripe with this game is that the translation tries to portray the story as if it were taking place in America even though there is a shrine at the edge of town complete with its resident shrine maiden as well as numerous other aspects of the game that simply smack of Japanese culture.  For those who aren't familiar with the U.S., we don't have shrines... like... AT ALL.   It doesn't have any kind of action/platforming what so ever and is so absurdly riddled with typo's, you begin not even to question if the translator speaks English natively so much but rather, if they are even fluent in it.  Regardless, the writing gets the job done and the characters are all unique and interesting.
All things taken into consideration, the "slice of life" aura CTHCC brings to the table is a breath of fresh air in a market flooded with violence, zombies, and post apocolyptic environs.  Personally, for eight bux, I'm certainly getting my moneys worth out of this title.  For a nice distraction from the drudgery of the waking world or even other games, I whole heartedly reccomend this off beat title.

As most of the other reviews have mentioned, this port is pretty good in terms of performance compared to the previous two games in the series. It runs better and looks better, and though people with higher-end monitors might be disappointed with the 1080p/60fps limit (I personally have a 144hz monitor so it's a bit of a downer), it's nothing worth complaining about in my opinion. I am, however, disappointed by the fact that there are no mouse controls, at all. Why they waited for the third game to remove them is beyond me, but the game is a mess to play unless you have a gamepad to the point that if you don't have a gamepad you may as well stop reading here. The game also requires you to activate the Steam Cloud in order to play, which doubles as more-or-less of an always online requirement, which may bother some people. I found this annoying because I really don't like using the half-baked feature that is the Steam Cloud, but not enough to prevent me from playing.
In terms of gameplay, Lightning Returns is a pretty dramatically different game from its predecessors in a lot of ways, with the big one being that the world is ending in 13 days. Rather than just being a plot point, this is an actual timer in the game, similar to Dead Rising. The actual timer itself only counts down six days, and you have to extend the clock by doing side quests and helping others pass on into the next world until the full 13 days have passed. The timer isn't enough of a threat for me to imagine anyone being turned off by it, and if you manage your time well you'll still have plenty of exploration time, but it does add a nice pressure to it that gives the game a unique feeling. If you don't manage to do everything the first time, there is a New Game+ option, which gives the slower or more thorough players a chance to see everything the game has to offer as well. The game is full of quests, both main ones and side ones, and even the main quests can be tackled in any order due to the game being a fully open world from the start, with the only limitation being the tougher monsters in certain areas. Monsters can be killed to the point of extinction, discouraging farming and encouraging you to fight for your right to have a peaceful nature hike through the Jagd Woods or even just kill every monster on the planet if you're feeling particularly full of determination. The overall frame of the game sort of feels like a less forgiving Majora's Mask, and while a lot of people seem to be against it I really like this system.
The other big difference is the combat. The combat is now far more action-oriented; you don't move around much, but there are no turns, and instead of controlling a party you control Lightning alone and swap between 3 outfits, each with 4 attacks you can assign. The new system feels both smoother and faster, and you get in and out of small fights a lot faster due to the lack of unnecessarily long intros and outros. The same tactics from the previous games are all here, but now they feel more active, with many things requiring timing and strategy to do instead of just choosing the same attack order every turn. This is all aided by the fact that there's no longer a leveling system, removing the urge to grind entirely and allowing you to actually fight because you want to fight something instead of fighting everything because you need the experience. You upgrade your equipment instead, through various methods such as combining spells to increase their power or changing outfits with different stats.
The story is where Lightning Returns falters somewhat. The game only introduces one new character, and the returning characters get painfully little time to do much of anything except for Hope, who serves as your guide. The main quest itself is pretty shallow, and instead the game focuses primarily on the content of the side quests, which isn't necessarily a bad thing since a fair amount of them are pretty interesting in their own right, but it's a shame that the characters they spent two games buildling up get more or less sidelined for the grand finale, with some of my favorites being outright benched and getting less than a minute or two of total screentime. The overall plotline isn't bad by any means, but I just didn't find it as interesting as XIII-2, and I felt like they could've done more with the returning cast to make the end of this series more exciting.
Overall, Lightning Returns is a pretty great game and mechanically my favorite in the series by far, and even though there's plenty of room for improvement it's already worth playing in its own right. If the port woes don't scare you away, there's no reason not to finish the series if you're already this deep into the XIII trilogy.

Played this game on console prior to the Steam release. This was a decent enough port. It ran smoothly for me and even had English voices included, since XIII and XIII-2 only had Japanese VO for me due to regional restrictions for whatever reason. But overall it was a good port and it felt nice to finally play LR at 1080p 60 fps and have shorter load times. Really made a difference.
As for the game itself, my opinion stands that gameplay-wise it's superior to the previous XIII games, because of the brand new combat system that's reminiscent FF X-2's dressphere system, even though sometimes it may seem like the game is basically Lightning Dressup Simulator 2013. There are a WIDE range of garbs you can choose from, and you can customize the skills and weapon types that they use. They usually have one or two skills that are locked to that specific garb, so each garb can be unique in their own way.
You get skills like Attack, Fire, etc as drops from enemies and their levels vary. You can upgrade these skills by way of synthesis and later on in the game boost their levels. There's an encouragement to do New Game + with this game as well, because there are a few new features available to you that you can only get in NG+, such as upgrading weapons and shields. I was a little disappointed at first that you couldn't do that from the start, but if you think of your first playthrough as a stepping stone, it's fine.
The game pretty much drops you into its world and lets you go about the various main quests and side quests however you like, so I wouldn't say it's COMPLETELY linear. But I wouldn't say that it's open world, either. It also has a time limit with an in-game clock that can be a hassle if you don't know how to manage it and use it efficiently. I highly suggest following a guide, because certain quests in the game have very specific requirements, and their availability very much depends on the time of day and your progress in the main questline of that area. The reason I recommend guides is because the game doesn't really tell you much about these things when it comes to finding or completing these quests, and since the world of the game is a literal ticking timebomb, having a guide handy will help you complete as many quests as possible, as fast as possible, if you're the completionist type like myself.
The story is, quite frankly, abysmal nonsense. Granted, the XIII series' story in general wasn't that strong in the first place, but I liked the simplicity of it and thought it ended nicely. However, starting from XIII-2 it just went downhill from there when it started to introduce time travel and alternate universes. LR expanded on that and made the story even more nonsensical and not even worth your time investing in, in my honest opinion. Since I'd already experienced the story in my first playthrough on console, and was completely baffled at the time, this time around I skipped through the cutscenes and dialogue. I just couldn't be bothered with it anymore.
I'd recommend this game based on the gameplay alone and suggest that you tune out the story if you liked the story in XIII, because this game pretty much ruins it all with unnecessary convolutedness and turning all the characters into hollowed-out shells.

But this is not about Bethesda, no not those greedy, back-stabbing ♥♥♥♥s. No, this is about Hello Games, and, more specifically, No Man's Sky.
What is No Man's Sky? Well, at it's core, it's an exploration game. A space exploration game. Oh, and, it's multiplayer too. Yes, right now you cannot "customize" your "character" (although to call the little orb thing that respresents you a character is an insult to most), however I have faith that Hello Games will implement something of the sort soon enough.
Wow, can't believe I just said that. Hello Games? Faith? Ridiculous! And to be honest, a year ago I'd have agreed. But this isn't a year ago. And holy (excuse my french)♥♥♥♥♥♥how much has changed.
To give you a bit of backstory, I was one of those people that didn't really buy into the hype. I saw one of the trailers and went, "Hey, this looks interesting. I think I'll get it." Yes, I was one of those suckers who pre-ordered, and yes I was let down. I can't imagine the betrayal people who were on the hype train felt when they got a glitchy, unoptimized, empty, boring game, and I can't blame any of them for either refunding, or uninstalling the game and never thinking/touching it again. I was one of them.
But then... I got an upgrade to my PC, an upgrade which allowed me to play more graphics-intensive games (think DOOM 2016, Assassin's Creed: Syndicate, ESO, etc.). I discovered that No Man's SKy was on PC (I had had it on console .-.) aaaaaaaand went ♥♥♥♥ you.
Yet, here I am, with only 10 or so hours in the (PC version of) the game, leaving a positive review and (apparently) my life story (sorry). I bought NMS thinking I'd try it and then refund it, but then actually found myself enjoying it. It's gone from a kind-of nice looking walking/flying simulator (and a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ simulator at that), to a living, breathing, enjoyable game. Its 30-minute story has changed to nearly 10+ hours (which, for a multiplayer sandbox, is pretty good), tons of the previous annoying glitches have been ironed out, there are Quality of Life improvements everywhere, new features such as base building, faction wars, and yes, multiplayer have been added, and more. I'm impressed, to say the least. It's changed into the game we were promised a year ago, and to that I say... better late than never.
Think about it, Hello Games coulda taken our money and run. They coulda dissappeared from the radar and we'd have never heard from them again. But they stayed. They worked, and made a good game. They fullfilled their promises, and show no signs of slowing down, something that most AAA publishers nowadays don't even consider. Bravo, Hello. Bravo.
In conclusion, this game is worth the buy. However, if you can wait, I'd reccommend getting it on sale. Less money that way. It's a fun little thing to hop into if you're tired and just want to relax, or if you're looking for a satisfying progression system in the form of mining/selling/buying that keeps you engaged for hours. It's fun if you're looking for a relatively short, kind of complex storyline that'll make you "What?" on the odd occaision. It's also a lot of fun when you're high (seriously, smoke a blunt then hit the Hyperdrive, you'll go to space. Literally.).
Get it. Play it. Become a part of our little community. We're always looking for more. :)

The core gameplay is good, but the campaign is just flat out broken. The allied AI is completely useless, so no matter how well you play, you often end up in a stalemate that can last for hours. If you capture an area, there's no way of knowing if your AI is going to try to hold it. You don't even know if and when your allies will spawn. Sometimes there seems to be dozens of soldiers fighting by your side and you completely steamroll the enemy. Then they dwindle down and don't seem to respawn for a long time. The enemy then recaptures their areas and you're back where you're started. The allied general and your troops also doesn't seem to have a clear goal. They just mill around, camp your base, occasionally attack the enemy target, but ultimately there's no cohesion or plan of attack. This results in a complete inability to execute attacks or defend areas.
The enemies also seem to instantly respawn, so you never really feel like you're gaining ground, and killing enemies feels pointless. You can defeat an entire enemy squad, but 20 seconds later, they'll return. It's just a grind where you try to hold an area long enough to capture it, then hoping that the terrible AI will reinforce you and help you defend the area.
The game is so full of potential, but the tactical side is just stripped out of the game due to the poor AI and gameplay mechanics that boil down to mowing down a constant stream of respawning enemies. It's just a frustrating grind.

Where can I begin? Lightning Returns is an amazing game, but you can probably already see that from the videos and screenshots at the top of the page. Instead of being lured into flashy videos, you're probably wondering if this game is worth the bang for your buck. Not only do I say a resounding yes, but I am also going to break down the pros and cons of the game:
Pros:
- A great story-line -- Lightning Returns: Final Fantasy picks up the story where Final Fantasy XIII-2 left off. Lightning wakes up after the events of XIII-2, a few years into the future. Things have changed in the world, with many people having souls that need to be saved, As God's personal savior, it's Lightning's job to save the souls of the inhabitants. There's a brand new antagonist as well, who has such an amazing character, that they have quickly become my favourite Final Fantasy character of all time.
- A functional day/night cycle with timed quests! Hearkening back to epic games such as Dead Rising and Zelda: Majora's Mask, Lightning Returns essentially works on a time cycle. The game will naturally progress through time, with you automatically returning to the Ark at the start of each day. As time changes, the sky will get lighter/darker, you will encounter different characters and even different monsters depending on the time of the day. An excellent concept that was well executed!
- Regions. Again, quite similar to Majora's Mask, the game is essentially divided into four regions. Each region in Lightning Returns has the soul of an important character who needs to be saved, with one region containing two souls due to its shear size. Each region is completely isolated, with different appearances, characters and quests. The game does an excellent job of making each region feel like its own independent story.
- An interesting change in level progression. Long gone is the Final Fantasy classic level progression of defeating monsters and earning experience points. Instead, you must save the souls of the inhabitants of the world. If you can successfully complete a quest for an inhabitant to save their soul, you will be awarded with bonuses to your health, strength and magic ability. Saving the souls of more significant people will award far more bonuses, as will the more difficult souls to rescue.
- Replay-ability. There are numerous timed quests. On your first playthrough, you could easily miss some of the quests, as the quest-givers only show up at certain times. Along with this, there are diametrically opposed quests; you can complete one *or* the other. In order to see both stories, you will need to start a new game. In addition to collecting health, magic and strength bonuses from completing quests, quests also award unique adornments -- making for another reason to complete both sides of a quest.
- Scaled bosses. Similar to Final Fantasy VIII, bosses will get stronger the longer you leave them. Unlike Final Fantasy VIII, where they scale based on your level, in Lightning Returns they scale based on the day. While saving souls throughout the world, make sure to complete the main quests as quickly as possible, or you might find yourself with quite a challenge on your hands! Then again, if you tackle them too quickly, you probably won't be strong enough to defeat them ;)
- The hardest boss in any Final Fantasy game. Ever. I'm not going to spoil it, but there is a boss in Lightning Returns with more HP than in any other Final Fantasy game. Although arguably Yiazmat from Final Fantasy XII is harder, this boss is certainly no pushover! There are methods to make him easier, but you will still almost definitely need to wait until your second playthrough to take down this beast!
Cons:
- Online-only. You heard me right. Lightning Returns requires an active and constant online connection to play, despite the fact that they took out every single online element of the game. You won't get to use the main online features like Outerworld Services to post updates to Facebook, so there's really no need for an online element at all. Heck, it's a single-player game!
- A game-breaking bug. It may be because I bought this game on release day, but there is a game-breaking bug that will affect a lot of players. Many antiviruses pick up a very small amount of this game as malicious, and refuse to download them. As such, you may be unable to progress far past the initial loading screens and cutscenes. If this occurs, disable your antivirus (temporarily) and verify the integrity of the game cache. There will be 80.4mb missing. After downloading the missing data, remember to re-enable your antivirus and enjoy the game proper!
- This game is heavily religious. Every second sentence will have a mention of God. I'm not here to sway you one way or another regarding religion, but if you're not religious, this can really put a dampener on the game's appeal. The sad thing is, it's completely out of place, with many characters who previously never made any religious reference suddenly becoming extremely religious (especially Lightning and Hope).
- Poor porting. Lightning Returns has been out for a long time on the consoles now, and there's been a lot of time for Square Enix to make the PC port run as smoothly as possible. If that's what you're looking for, prepare to be disappointed. Instead of adding an in-game 'quit' menu, there is a poorly-tacked-on menu bar that hides at the top of the game window with some basic options. These allow for a few more graphical improvements (that don't seem to be visible in any noticeable way), the ability to change default controller mapping, and the option to quit playing. On top of all that, the menu *feels* tacked on, looking like something from a retro Mac system.
- No mouse camera controls. Many of the older PC releases of Final Fantasy games had the abiltiy to control your camera with your mouse. Because you now need to be 'able' to use your mouse to access the pointless menu that was added to the game, it means you won't be able to use it to control the camera. At all. It seems like an incredibly poor trade-off.
- Continuing on the poor port and the terrible menu, there's no free roam over controller mapping. This is a bit of a stickler, as there are two in-built controller maps. One of the inbuilt maps perfectly mirrors the original XBOX 360 mapping, which is great. But what if I want to switch up my action button to my controller's Y button? It can't be done. The controls are intuitive, but it would have been nice to allow me to modify them, like many previous Final Fantasy games did.
All in all, Lightning Returns is an excellent game. If you enjoyed the previous two Final Fantasy XIII games, you'll definitely enjoy this one!

But this is not about Bethesda, no not those greedy, back-stabbing ♥♥♥♥s. No, this is about Hello Games, and, more specifically, No Man's Sky.
What is No Man's Sky? Well, at it's core, it's an exploration game. A space exploration game. Oh, and, it's multiplayer too. Yes, right now you cannot "customize" your "character" (although to call the little orb thing that respresents you a character is an insult to most), however I have faith that Hello Games will implement something of the sort soon enough.
Wow, can't believe I just said that. Hello Games? Faith? Ridiculous! And to be honest, a year ago I'd have agreed. But this isn't a year ago. And holy (excuse my french)♥♥♥♥♥♥how much has changed.
To give you a bit of backstory, I was one of those people that didn't really buy into the hype. I saw one of the trailers and went, "Hey, this looks interesting. I think I'll get it." Yes, I was one of those suckers who pre-ordered, and yes I was let down. I can't imagine the betrayal people who were on the hype train felt when they got a glitchy, unoptimized, empty, boring game, and I can't blame any of them for either refunding, or uninstalling the game and never thinking/touching it again. I was one of them.
But then... I got an upgrade to my PC, an upgrade which allowed me to play more graphics-intensive games (think DOOM 2016, Assassin's Creed: Syndicate, ESO, etc.). I discovered that No Man's SKy was on PC (I had had it on console .-.) aaaaaaaand went ♥♥♥♥ you.
Yet, here I am, with only 10 or so hours in the (PC version of) the game, leaving a positive review and (apparently) my life story (sorry). I bought NMS thinking I'd try it and then refund it, but then actually found myself enjoying it. It's gone from a kind-of nice looking walking/flying simulator (and a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ simulator at that), to a living, breathing, enjoyable game. Its 30-minute story has changed to nearly 10+ hours (which, for a multiplayer sandbox, is pretty good), tons of the previous annoying glitches have been ironed out, there are Quality of Life improvements everywhere, new features such as base building, faction wars, and yes, multiplayer have been added, and more. I'm impressed, to say the least. It's changed into the game we were promised a year ago, and to that I say... better late than never.
Think about it, Hello Games coulda taken our money and run. They coulda dissappeared from the radar and we'd have never heard from them again. But they stayed. They worked, and made a good game. They fullfilled their promises, and show no signs of slowing down, something that most AAA publishers nowadays don't even consider. Bravo, Hello. Bravo.
In conclusion, this game is worth the buy. However, if you can wait, I'd reccommend getting it on sale. Less money that way. It's a fun little thing to hop into if you're tired and just want to relax, or if you're looking for a satisfying progression system in the form of mining/selling/buying that keeps you engaged for hours. It's fun if you're looking for a relatively short, kind of complex storyline that'll make you "What?" on the odd occaision. It's also a lot of fun when you're high (seriously, smoke a blunt then hit the Hyperdrive, you'll go to space. Literally.).
Get it. Play it. Become a part of our little community. We're always looking for more. :)
Oh, the optimization is still♥♥♥♥♥♥though. It sucks but... they're working on it. :/

Perhaps four hours isn't enough time to give this game. Perhaps the AI isn't designed around the concept of playing alone. Perhaps I'm not as good at video games as I thought.
But I've been trying to capture this "Eastern District" sector for FOUR ♥♥♥♥ING HOURS. I read in some thread from a few years back that the AI values defense more than offense. Quite frankly, though, that sort of turtling up is what turns RTS's into unnecessarily long slogs. And since this game isn't an RTS, I can't tell my own team not to turtle up.
The game has its fair share of pros and cons, and I approached this game like I do any other game. I boot up the game, start a campaign at the game's default difficulty setting or harder, and try to beat the campaign. On one hand, this game really makes you feel like an expendable soldier in a massive war. When the massive array of weaponry and armor ISN'T locked behind the ridiculous level requirements, it's actually really impressive. On the other hand, the controls are a bit wonky (The player characters seem to have a hard time discerning between cover and empty space), the AI is unusually asinine (That SPAS makes a better sniper than the sniper in the hands of this game's aimbots). The game is played at this weird perspective that makes it unusually hard to get used to the fact that there are things behind the terrain.
Worst of all, the default experience and resource gain is actually really stupid. Why do I have to kill 150+ men without dying (It's even more since you seem to spontaneously combust occasionally) just to reach PFC? Also, I see all these medals and achievements flying around about how this low-ranking sergeant has killed the population of entire towns. If I'm so great, why do I feel like my entire faction doesn't listen to me?
I saw a dev say how their faction auto-captures a region after an hour or so. Since starting this review, I left the game on in the background and prayed that my mass murders of the enemy were miraculously the reason why my army refused to move up.
We're about to lose East Beach.
I think the worst part is, I started up another campaign, but rigged everything in my favor, just to see what capturing the whole map was like. It was actually a lot more interesting solely because the tide of battle was actually moving. When I captured the whole region, I found out the campaign wanted me to slog through NINE DIFFERENT REGIONS. I don't want to do that on the base difficulty.
If I can fine-tune the difficulty to something that isn't full of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ while still remaining challenging, I'll let you know. But as a forewarning, I don't like the thought of it, because it makes me feel that I have to rig the game in my favor just to win.
EDIT: We finally took Eastern District. Then immediately lost it. I'm not even mad. I've moved past that towards a sort of Zen state. I took the district. Even though my general is a total idiot, and my comrades will never move past Grade 2, I have won my own personal victory. And with that, I uninstall, content that I have finally moved passed the obstacle that so long perterbed me, even if it was for less than a minute.

Addictive.  The return of 16 bit gaming that seems pretty unabrasive.  These devs did a nice job capturing that retro pixel art and arcade style gameplay and brought it to an underwater environment that keeps you more than busy.
This game is a 2D continual side scrolling shooter that is underwater.  Continual... meaning; you leave one side of the screen and you come in from the other.  The entire underwater environment is a bit long so you kind of don't go off screen until you've traveled a few screen lengths.  Once you've got this navigation down, the game will come better to you.  Sometimes you need to calculate the quickest route to save your miner and sometimes the quickest route is to simply go off the screen to the other side. You don't want to get in the habit of chasing enemies when you can simply turn around and get another and wait for that enemy you were chasing to go off the screen and come in from the other side and now he's headed toward you.  Watching your mini-map is key here.
You play as a kitty in a submarine protecting your milk miners on the bottom of the ocean.  There are various power ups and enemies to deal with while you're protecting your miners on the bottom of the ocean from being taken.  You fight your enemies in waves that get progressively harder with progressively different enemies to fight. Three game modes; 'easy', 'normal', and 'arcade'.  I prolly would have went with 'norma'l and 'hard' so players don't feel like they're wimping out by playing the 'easy' mode.  Normal is pretty hard in the upper levels so I don't know why they didn't but maybe they intend on releasing some DLC that has a new game mode for 'hard'core players or something (*hint *hint devs)
My only real criticism of the game would be that I'd like to see better contrast coloring with the stuff you can avoid colliding with and the stuff you don't have to worry about colliding with.  They do a good job with the power ups because they almost flash glow but when you're watching everything on the screen at the same time... and you have to avoid enemy fire and enemy ships but not worry about colliding with any explosions, your milk mine or the miners.  Then sometimes there are extra 'helper' subs in the area and they move up and down.  These subs block your fire hindering you from saving your miner but mysteriously you can't collide with these subs.  The background has some foreground objects to give the game some 3D feel but you can't collide with this stuff either.  It just adds confusion as to what you can avoid and what you have to watch out for in a game you're just learning.  It's not a problem on lower levels but as you progress it gets hectic and it would help if it were a bit more obvious as to what you can move through and what will kill you.  I know as I play I'll get used to what's there and what I don't have to worry about... but it's a learning curve for a game where everything is moving and I think it could be fixed with different coloring.
I had no problems playing the game with my gamepad.  Nice enjoyable game.  Buy on sale.

Okay, I'll make this short and sweet so I can get back to the game.... Wolfenstein II is a mash-up of DOOM, Fallout and The Man In the High Castle. If you know what all those things are and you like them, you'll probably like this game. If you don't know what all those things are, Google is your friend.
I like all those things a lot, and I LOVE THIS GAME!
A few other things to note:
I am not a hardcore gamer or a FPS fan. I'm mostly playing this for the story (and it is EXTREMELY story/cutscene heavy). Luckily, the game has a difficulty level to accommodate many types of players and skill levels. That said, there are a few times when the difficulty level  spikes and, if you're like me, YOU WILL DIE many, many times. My advice is to accept this (avoid the urge to rage-quit) and use your first few lives to recon the level and figure out where all the armor, weapons, and power-ups are stashed. Once you figure out where everything is, it's actually fairly simple (if not easy) to clear the level--not to mention a lot of fun! Shooting robo-Nazis and Klansmen in the face is a hoot!
Some people might find the games shifting tone a bit jarring. The game goes from heartbreakingly brutal (really, I mean it) to hilariously goofy. Personally, I liked it, but it's a fair point of criticism that puts some players off.
Finally, and this is my biggest beef with the game, we need to discuss Wolfenstein II's depiction of Nazis...
As I mentioned before, you'll fight a lot of robo-Nazis in the game. Since this IS an alternative history/sci-fi setting I can deal with that. HOWEVER, there is not a single Nazi with a Tiki Torch to be found in the game and none of them cry either! Suspension of disbelief has its limits, and this was just too unbelievable for me.... It really threw me out of the game. IF you can look past this glaring mis-characterization of Nazis, you might just have an extremely good time with this game! I know I did...

Finished it last night after playing it on and off. I thought the game was fun with interesting characters and over the top violence.
There really isn't much of a story because the main villain is barely in the game and underused. It more of an exploratory sequel where we get to delve further into BJ's psyche and his relations with others. The ending isn't all that satisfying either as the face-off with the villain isn't as good as that from The New Order.
I think The New Order was more varied in terms of locations and action pieces. This sequel feels very repetitive and can get boring. One major gripe i had was that the game doesn't take advantage of its setting and relies too much on pushing you down one industrial corridoor after another. For example, the Venus sequence was just dull save for the Adolf Hitler cameo. There's a unique Roswell sequence which starts off well but then just becomes more of the same mechanized industrial violence. Don't get me wrong because there were some stellar story moments (BJ visiting his father, the court room), but more variety in locations would have been appreciated.
I also hate the lack of music in large sections. The action is very fast paced with some very destructive weapons (double shotgun is unstoppable), but its pace doesn't let you appreciate the killing and violence. Graphics are on point but I had a few issues at the start with 4K (fixed in patches).
Overall, it's a serviceable sequel that's fun and has some fantastic moments in story telling and action, but I won't be replaying it. I much prefer The New Order which still feels fresh and original.

I decided to check this game out after playing the remastered version of Grim Fandango which was an excellent game though the puzzles were a little confusing but the writing and story was very great. Especially the performaces by Roy Conrad (R.I.P.) as Ben and Mark Hamill as Ripburger which are the games highlights. Kath Souice and everyone were excellent too in their respective roles.
In comparison to Grim Fandango were they only thing that was remastered were the sprites but not the backgrounds. Making me feel like I'm playing a Playstation game. Full Throttle has updated art and sprites and they look gorgeous to look at when you switch it to the original art for the game which still looks good. The remaster makes the game look even better. Every rock beat was just porn for my ears.

You and your gang have been framed for murder and you're trying to put a stop to the murderer's plan of taking over his murdered victim's company. The controls for the motorcycle combat sections are infuratating and very short lived. You can use either your mouse or arrow keys to move your bike. The controls are very frustrating and you're better off using the arrow keys. Because the mouse is also used to control your bike it makes the combat sections a little annoying but you can skip them. Most of the time I was just spamming my fist to take down a biker to acquire some of there weapons. Aside from the chainsaw lady and the Cavefish biker which I had to use a different weapon. These sections in my opinion require minimal effort honestly and they're not hard to do.
The puzzles in the game aren't half bad to solve thanks to the SHIFT key. Which allows you to highlight the areas that are interactive. I solved a few and did got a little stuck on some of them. Resulting in guide consulting. One of my favorite puzzles is were you're trying to go into a biker's hideout and it's suddenly rigged with explosive mines. To solve this you have to use these wind up toy bunnies to blow the mines up and it's just hilarious. Probably, one of my favorite moments in the game. Another moment I like is constantly alarming the cops while refilling oil for my bike which engages in some pretty funny dialogue.
This game is definitely worthy of a check out. It's a badass game albeit very short with some really good production value and a lot of heart too it.

Now that the always online requirement has been fixed I'm repurchasing the game and changing my review to reflect my new opinions. Although my play time at the moment is very short I spent upwards of 80 hours on the Xbox 360 version.
The story is pretty good, I felt that it was a satisfying end to the trilogy. If you haven't played the other games or haven't paid attention to the story so far then it will be pretty hard to follow, so I recommend playing them first. Some of the dialogue is a little cheesy, but no more so than in the first two.
The combat system is very different in this installment. It is much more intense and fast paced and will probably appeal a lot more to those that had a problem with the combat system of the first two. The open world aspect offers a lot more to do and explore as well. You can do many parts of the story in whatever order you want, so the game feels a lot less restricted and linear.
Many people are also wary of the clock aspect of this game, and I don't blame them. I generally hate being timed in games, the most notable exception for me being the clock in Majora's Mask. But after 80 hours I can safely add this game to the list. Its presence encourages you to plan out your quests, and the availability of certain events at certain times adds a fun layer of complexity. Part of the reason it works so well is that there really isn't a huge penalty for running out of time. Unlike Majora's Mask, the only thing you lose is your progress on the story. All quest completion will reset, but you get to keep all your items and abilities and whatnot. Plus it's pretty easy to beat all the main quests without running out of time. Completing quests also increases how much time you have left before the end of the world, and you can get up to 13 total in-game days. Don't let the presence of the clock be the factor that keeps you from trying out this game.
Overall, I really loved this game. I spent a ton of time on it and even got all of the achievements. I haven't spent a ton of time on this particular port, but from what I've seen it's a significant improvement over the console versions and it has a ton of graphics options. More than likely if you didn't like the first two 13's then you probably won't like this one either, but this is also the one you are the most likely to enjoy out of the three. Take from that what you will.

A rated "E for Everyone" Visual Novel Title about a silly girl who wants to make a club before the deadline. While you hear silly lines, there are no dating options. Once you explore and conquer all six kids while finding easter eggs, along with plainy New Game +, this is about it.

It's easily worth 5 bucks if you're into Visual Novels (or have a younger sister who likes cheesy things. It seems to be a perfect "Get together with Onii-chan" game). I wouldn't recommend it to anyone else otherwise.

I have always been a sucker for history, a story so full of weird characters, odd occurrences and unlikely coincidences that any fiction writer would be laughed at if he made it into a script. I admit to being unfamiliar with the history of Ptolemy III and Ptolemy IV before playing Choice of Alexandria. But playing through the game like I did had the feeling of history in the making, complete with all the qualities I noted. I particularly appreciate that the game is perfunctory in its descriptions of places and people. There is just enough detail to set the scene and you go from there. Only truly professional writers know how to perform the trick of sketching enough of the story to let the mind fill in the rest.
The best Choice of Games adventures put you in situations with equally rewarding choices where the outcomes are anything but clear. I had a definite goal in mind to change history to the point where our universe's version of Alexandra never came to pass. As it happened, I failed in achieving that goal through a series of unwise choices...and yet I succeeded in changing history in a very unexpected way. I might add that the goal I did achieve came completely by accident, focusing on the individual lives I was affecting rather than the big picture. It all comes to a head in the epilogue, where certain events enshrined by one William Shakespeare can be completely rewritten due to a final set of choices made.
While I can acknowledge that such CYOA games are not for everyone, anyone who enjoys such entertainment should definitely check this one out.

This is an amusing, if sometimes tricky, little choose-your-own-adventure novel. I bought it to try out the idea of it... considering they seem to have a habit of showing up in my discovery queue. Anyway, this being the cheapest, it felt like a good first choice...

Definitely recommended.

This is one of the absolute best, most thought-provoking choose-your-own adventure style text-based games I have ever read/played. Its emphasis on philosophy and the potential long-term consequences of your choices (and the potential endings which result) are extremely interesting and fairly well written. The characters are more complex and the various messages and themes are far deeper than much of the intellectual content found in most graphically intense games which have yet been created. The ethical dilemmas this game presents can be extremely difficult and the results of your actions, while not always easy to predict, make perfect sense in hindsight.
Unlike Champion of the Gods, the genre of this story is not fantasy but alternate history (a somewhat unusual form of sci-fi). This story/game attempts to answer questions of what might have been had people made different decisions to bring about alternate events. What if the great library of Alexandria had not burnt down or fallen into disrepair? What if wisdom from the ancient world had not been largely lost? What if the Alexandrian Empire had been successful in competing against Rome and had lasted for much, much longer? The choices you make in this game will help setup (or destroy) these potential alternate histories. This game explains how the petty or selfless actions of someone in a position of authority can, in a tenuous situation, help cause the vast potential of the future to be destroyed or created.
This game will also more obviously delve into how your decisions as a tutor to a royal heir may cause him to either become a great ruler or a vain despot or perhaps, something in between. Moreover, this game also attempts to answer the question as to exactly why providing people with a good education and access to knowledge is important to the longevity and survival of a civilization combined with the vital role that certain, sometimes seemingly minor technological inventions and scientific discoveries can play in the shaping of the unknown future. Seamlessly integrated into all this are important messages about the absolute necessity of maintaining balance and fairness among the people, even the very poor and those of another race, (messages which some of us, in our modern civilization seem to actively refuse to comprehend) if a civilization is to have a chance of thriving.
Unfortunately, Choice of Alexandria suffers from the same basic failings as most other games of this type. Unlike in a real book, there is no Back button to go back to a previous page or to undue a previous decision so you can easily see an alternate plot. This is extremely frustrating if you want to easily or quickly see the full potential which this game has to offer and track multiple potential timelines simultaneously. In essence, the interface lacks flexibility. While the descriptions and writing is at least adequate for the most part it does tend to be a bit dry and tends to be lacking the visceral detail which many actual novels would possess. You get to read very little of your character's personal life nor do you get a clear idea of what it was like to actually live in the distant past. You almost never get to read about what your character's living arrangements are like for example. You don't get to hear how he/she bathes, how he/she eats how he/she sleeps etc. There's so little written on your character's quality of life that your character seems like a lifeless, 2-dimensional, cardboard mask for you to wear while you make occasional menu choices. He/She doesn't hardly seem to live, or breathe or sweat or ache.
So, In short:
+Great choices, meaningful endings, philosophically deep, interesting alternate histories, good character motivations, reasonably logical results due to your choices. Important messages and themes. Socially and intellectual important content throughout. Thought provoking. Deals with issues relevant to the real world. Far more intellectually involved and deep than most high-graphics games which have ever existed.
-Inflexible interface doesn't let you go back to a previous page or to a previous decision to easily see what else might have happened if you chose differently causing you to have to play the whole game over again if you want to see the differences caused by choosing any other choice. Somewhat dry writing style featuring little visceral or sensory detail and next to no information about what it might be like to live, from day to day as an Alexandrian royal tutor. Sometimes, seems like less of a true novel and more like pages and pages of interlocking introductions to various menu choices which makes main character seem like a mere interface through which you can make decisions rather than a living, breathing person. The first play through provides the most emotional involvement if you decide to try to seriously make the choices you think you would make in the same situation. Emotional involvement with the story tends to decrease during subsequent play throughs.
