Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare is a first-person shooter video game developed by Infinity Ward and published by Activision. The fourth installment in the Call of Duty series, it was released in 2007 for the PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, and Microsoft Windows. The game breaks away from the World War II setting of previous entries in the series and is instead set in modern times. Developed for over two years, the game uses a proprietary game engine.
The story takes place in the year 2011, where a radical leader has executed the president of an unnamed country in the Middle East, and an ultranationalist movement ignites a civil war in Russia. The conflicts are seen from the perspectives of a U.S. Force Reconnaissance Marine and a British SAS commando, and are set in various locales, such as the United Kingdom, the Middle East, Azerbaijan, Russia, and Ukraine. The multiplayer portion of the game features various game modes, and contains a leveling system that allows the player to unlock additional weapons, weapon attachments, and camouflage schemes as they advance.
Critically acclaimed, the game received an aggregated score of 94% from both GameRankings and Metacritic. The gameplay and story received particular praise, while criticism targeted the failure of the game to substantially innovate the first-person shooter genre. The game won numerous awards from gaming websites, including IGN's Best Xbox 360 Game. It was the top-selling game worldwide for 2007, selling around seven million copies by January 2008 and almost sixteen million by November 2013.
A remastered version of the game, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare Remastered, was released on PlayStation 4, Xbox One and PC alongside the Legacy and Deluxe Editions of Call of Duty: Infinite Warfare on November 4, 2016.[3]
As opposed to earlier games in the Call of Duty series, the game features modern equipment and new features, many exclusive to the multiplayer part of the game, such as "killstreaks"; killing a number of enemies without the player dying in between kills allows access to various assets including airstrikes and helicopter support. A character can be positioned in one of three stances: standing, crouching, or prone, each affecting the character's rate of movement, accuracy, and stealth. Using cover helps the player avoid enemy fire or recover health after taking significant damage. As such, there are no armor or health power ups. When the character has taken damage, the edges of the screen glow red and the character's heartbeat increases. If the character stays out of fire, the character can recover. When the character is within the blast radius of a live grenade, a marker indicates the direction of the grenade, helping the player to either flee or toss it back to the enemy.
The player takes on the role of various characters during a single-player campaign. The characters' involvement in the plot occurs simultaneously and overlaps the events in the game. As such, the player's perspective changes from one character to another between missions. Each mission features a series of objectives; the player is led to each objective with the heads up display, which marks its direction and distance. Some objectives require that the player arrives at a checkpoint, while other objectives require the player to eliminate enemies in a specified location, stand their ground to defend an objective, or plant explosive charges on an enemy installation. After the credits, a special epilogue mission is unlocked for play, featuring a four-man squad retrieving a VIP from terrorists who have hijacked an airliner. The SAS rescue the VIP and escape before the plane is destroyed.
Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare features team-based and deathmatch-based multiplayer modes on various maps. Each mode has an objective that requires unique strategies to complete. Players can call in UAV reconnaissance scans, air strikes, and attack helicopters, when they achieve three-, five-, and seven-enemy kill streaks respectively. A game ends when either a team or player has reached a predefined number of points, or the allotted time expires in which case the team or player with the most points wins. If the points are even when the time expires, Sudden Death mode is activated in which there is no re-spawning and the team who either has the last man standing, or achieves the objective first are the winners. If the player is in either of the two matches, then there is an Overtime match, in which the next team to win is rewarded the victory.
The player's performance in the multiplayer mode is tracked with experience points, which can be earned by killing opposing players, completing challenges, completing objectives, or by completing a round or match. As the player gains experience, they advance in level, unlocking new weapons, perks, challenges, and gameplay modes. The highest obtainable level is 55, but on the console versions of the game, the player has the option to enter "Prestige" mode, which returns their level to one and removes all accumulated unlockables. This process can be repeated up to 10 times with a different insignia being given each time.
Completing a challenge grants experience points and may unlock weapon attachments. As a player's level increases by gaining experience points within online games, it unlocks new weapons, perks, or challenges. As the player advances in levels, they earn the ability to customize their classes; this includes selecting their main weapon, side arm and special grenade type. Additionally, the player can select 3 perks, one from each of the three "Tiers", that can customize their character further. Perk effects include, but are not limited to, extra ammunition, increasing bullet damage by the player, or dropping a live grenade when the player is killed. The player is also given the choice to complete challenges in order to receive even more experience points; challenges include achieving a certain number of kills with a specific weapon, shooting down a helicopter or performing a number of head shots. Additionally, when the player attains a certain amount of headshots with a specific weapon, excluding sidearms, the player unlocks extra weapon "camos", or camouflage, to use for that specific weapon.

Ok now that is out of the way this is what I think of this game. So "The New Order" is a pretty darn good game. Sure it had some issues like the difficulty scaling was off in certain areas and the level design you would sometimes get lost. No big reasons though becuase it was a good game. You would think the designers would overcome those flaws for the sequel right? This game takes a LARGE step backwards in the franchise history and lore.
1) Gameplay
Gameplay consists of you getting lost in a German sub. As you go through the sub you come across side missions and some incredible mocap work on NPC's. In fact I estimate a good chunk of development time went into this area which essentially is non-gameplay. They have a shooting range area like COD, an area to replay missions (nobody likes to replay missions for a faster time and screams laziness), a porthole that shows some bubbles float. Essentially I got very strong reminders of the game "Rage". It's as if the influx of new designers and fresh talent was developing the new Doom (from ZeniMax and ID employees) and the old thinking and stale designers was developing this game. Two very different games with 2 very different design philisophies with one stuck in the early 00's and 90's and the other with a more modern approach. Some missions like the Saturn missions were clearly inspired from the success of Doom I felt. The gameplay really is just using 1-2 weapons, AI is very poor, very poor level design as you get lost, very poor damage indication to the player. Most of the times on even easy you will die and you had no idea how you died or where it came from. For some reason the game wants you to take out Ubercommanders silently and THEN have fun and kill everything. A complete backtrack from the entire series as Wolfenstein is essentially Doom with Nazi's. The Ubercommanders are hilariously bad as when you get to them they usually don't notice you and when they do, they have pea shooters that fire once ever 3 seconds or so.
2) Graphics
Graphics at times look good and at other times look terrible. The textures really look poor in certain areas. As crazy as this may sound the game rivals Doom 3 in being a dark game. The game though doesn't even give you a flashlight. Often you will be trying to find your way to the next section in dimly lit crevices.
3)Story
The story is pretty attrocious. Around a 1/4 of the way through the game it quickly became apparent to me this was a BAD game with some really bad bugs. I tried returning it but became stonewalled from Steam because I had gone simply an hour over the limit. So I begrudgingly played it. Around halfway through the game a very big event happens and should have never happened. Instead they found a comical and terrible gameplay/story aspect that both shames and abuses the franchise of Wolfenstein. Before this big event though there is a scene and it's just great. I mean you are blasting Nazi's like the Matrix and it's just great. In fact the game went from a 4/10 for me to a full 6/10! A full 2 points just because of this scene. It built momentum and gravitas to an otherwise ♥♥♥♥♥♥ game! Then they just take it away and say it was all just a dream! Literally that is just saying a big ♥♥♥♥ you to the fans and player. The way they portray African Americans, females, Jewish people, German "language/culture" (everything is German if we just put uber in front of it), the strange obsession with milk shakes in the game, the strong amounts of politically correct stuff. In fact let me take a moment on that point because you can write a novel on the amount of audio logs and text logs that literally offer no true fun or meaning to the game. It's also to the point of way too much territory. The political correct stuff is insane too. They certainly saw their target audience as a young gamer who hates Donald Trump and bought this game to "punch Nazi's". Like gameplay and story be damned just punch Donny the Dump!
3) Bugs
Numerous bugs plague this game. Games always have bugs but they get fixed sometimes. I know I never will buy another Bethesda game due to their buggy games for example. This game has issues though that I have never experienced in a game. It has issues with overlays such as the Steam overlay. It has issues with NVIDIA cards I suspect which of course it does because ID Software is with AMD but even then Doom runs and looks great on even a toaster (again having RAGE nostalgia). It frequently crashes the video card drivers, can't write crash reports, pops up blue boxes in DOS in a form of crash reports.

While remaining faithful to the original style and graphics--the community made some minor changes that made major impacts on the game. This is an amazing mod for those who are Half-Life fans who just can't get enough. Good work guys!
Now you can get high-definition jumpscares in Ravenholm.

For me the most notable changes were as follows:
--- rooms were generally lit better (a good example would be the train station waiting hall)
--- in some cases the sunlight coming through the rooftop was visible and beautiful
--- shadows looked much, much better; it's worth looking at one of your followers (e.g. Alyx) with the flashlight turned on and moving it in a circular fashion - it looks amazing how the shadows keep changing
--- the sky generally looked better - most notable was Ravenholm which now has a much darker, much horror-like tone
--- fire sprinkler system was added to many rooms - I liked the water effects a lot
--- blurred vision under water, finally!
You should also turn on the commentaries to hear feedback not only from some of the developers but also the people behind the community mod. The game is ten years old but is still worth a playthrough!

While improvements are always welcome to what I consider one of the greatest games of all time, there's something to be said for leaving well enough alone.
Most changes to the lighting were for the worse, making many parts of the game that were once easy to navigate, only navigable with the flashlight, or with the brightness cranked. Other parts of the game, for example the bridge sequence, are overexposed, meaning it was difficult to pick out enemies from the background sky bloom.
Changes to the fog in certain levels looked good, but they are really the only graphical change worth noting, and they cost me a whopping 7 gb of hardrive space.
The changes made with this update would go unnoticed by all but the biggest of HL2 fans, and a lot of the lighting changes are for the worse. While I very much appreciate the hard work that the developer put into this update, especially considering he did it for free, I still can't give the thumbs up.

A thought-provoking variation on the usual game.  Normally you're a decisionmaker (starship captain, US Marshal, or at least a loner), managing various relationships but bound by none.  In this game most of your ultimate goals can be achieved only by influencing young prince Ptolemy IV, or sometimes king Ptolemy III.  Rupture that relationship, and much of the game falls out of reach.  But, of course, protecting the relationship has a price - including the fact that keeping your young charge happy is not always the best teaching strategy, and failing as a teacher has its own consequences.
So this is basically a game about teaching and child-rearing.  As a parent, I enjoyed that novelty.  And the various choices lead to alternate histories that are amusing, even intriguing (despite one terrible Fight Club joke).

I've always had a soft spot for alternate history, and the Library of Alexandria is one of my favourite topics, so this game fits into my interests.
I would say that Choice of Alexandria does have issues with characters, in that I find it hard to get as emotionally attached to the characters compared to other Choice Of games. They are well written and devloped, but harder to get connected to for me. That said, the writing is excellent and immersive, and I've really enjoyed just seeing the different endings I can produce.
As usual, I do wish that Choice Of Games allowed for colour customisation. While there are ways to edit the colour scheme manually, not having options in game is the one constant bone I have to pick with them.
This is a fantastic game, with a great deal of narrative depth.  As noted in other reviews, there are several forces at work within the story, and seeing them interact is fascinating.

It's locked into fairly standard anime tropes and character archetypes, and for a game about a girl that wants to start a comedy club, lacks even one moment of genuine humor.
The localization is fairly offensive too in how it tries to portray the game as taking place in America, even though all of the world's locations (the high school, the shrine) are clearly Japanese. This is 4-kids level, straight out of the 1990s localization that isn't even so bad it's good.

Plot's simple, you're Death trying to save your brother, War, by reaching a certain area where Death can save War. To do that Death does a lot of favors for people via main quests until eventually he reaches the area where Death can save War.
Practically everything in the game's excessively huge, even Death himself but compared to what's around Death he's puny.
It's an open-world game with its fair share of side dungeons usually with side quests to go along with 'em. The maps are generally huge but the outside roaming areas can feel very empty since there's not usually a whole lot to do in the open areas aside maybe from finding generally well-hidden collectibles. You can at least fast travel from one dungeon to another key location but you can't fast travel to the different world hubs you'll be able to unlock.
Every dungeon generally has the same keep-solving-puzzles-to-reach-dungeon-boss thing and not much else. The puzzles aren't really challenging themselves either.
There's loads of Prince-of-Persia-esque wall running and climbing that you can do on conveniently marked walls and wooden posts/ledges but they don't really offer much gameplay value as in there's no challenge to go along with 'em aside from a few areas. They only exist as a means of being a slightly more interactive way to move from one place to another. Pitfalls don't kill you either and even if you do fall you don't take much damage from 'em if at all.
They decided to go the loot-based route here where you'll find equipment with varying stats that you can make use of or sell to to NPCs, with which whom you can buy equipment off of as well.
If your inventory gets full in the middle of a dungeon, so long as you're in idle mode of sorts as in there's no enemy currently bothering you or something, then you can fast travel out of the dungeon, sell your unwanteds to an NPC, and then fast travel back to the last checkpoint you reached in the dungeon you were just in.
The hack-and-slash gameplay is pretty well done here. You've got your dual scythes as your primary weapons and various other kinds of weapons of your choice as a secondary.
You've got a relatively small list of combat moves & upgrades you can acquire, with one more useful than the other, though the only real useful ones I think are the buyable combos.
Since you can't block like in the first game you're to rely on i-frame dodge rolling for damage negation. They made it so you can't dodge no more than 3 times in succession as the third dodge apparently has a longer recovery time before you can do anything else again. I can't remember whether or not you buy or acquire it via leveling but at some point you can acquire a dodge-counter type of thing where if you dodge in a certain way at the right time you automatically do a counter attack that doesn't stop your dodge.
The game's a speedy hack-and-slash so you'll usually be up against groups of enemies and every now and again larger groups. Because of that it can get a bit tough to make use of some combos since they'll often be grouping up on you in attempts to not give you much chance for attacks. Thankfully many of Death's attacks were made specifically for large mobs. Some enemies don't flinch as easily so some timing would still be required when using certain combos to avoid unneccessary interruptions against yourself.
Most of the enemies are actually unique from one another in terms of their moveset and design. Even a couple of recycled enemies at least have one different attack from their other variations.
There's a skill tree you can spend skill points on, which you usually get via leveling. The skills are split into the Harbringer and Necromancer trees. Harbringer is meant for the more physical builds which the Strength stat governs. Necromancer is a mage-like build for temporary summons which in this game the Arcane stat governs. Just so long as you meet the level requirements you can put skill points to either skill trees.
For both controller & keyboard you can use skills via that rotation wheel thing that console games usually have that pauses the game to give you time to select whatever. On a controller you can assign skills to LB + X/Y/B/A by default for quick access & use. On a keyboard I think you can do something similar but I could never find out how to do it. However you can assign skills from the key rebinding menu to whatever key you want though that's much more of a hassle due to how bothersome key rebinding can be.
The level cap is 22 and if you want to hit level 30 you have to start New Game +. Your equipment and stats carry over. All quest items and quests are reset.
There's a game with decent combat mechanics here but unfortunately the downsides that come with it are potentially overwhelming.
The game itself isn't too bad but this "remaster's" worse graphics & even more bugs that can be  gamebreaking doesn't do it good.

All and all, for one dollar it's an okay game to pick up try for an evening, I guess, but save your money if it's not on sale.

Another gem from Kevin Gold, the author of Choice of Robots.  If you enjoyed CoR, I definitely recommend Choice of Alexandria.  If you haven't played CoR, I recommend Choice of Alexandria if you're interested in alternate history stories, because this is a good one.
CoA has many endings, many paths to those endings, and provides interesting choices (and consequences) along the way.  You also don't need to be a history major to understand the story either, which was my only real concern before I tried the demo.

Choice of Alexandria is at the time of writing one of the newest text based games on Steam and a slightly different one than the others. Instead of pure fiction, supplemented by bits of history, it uses history as a base and fiction to walk the what if paths. Some blanks, like Euclid's gender, have been filled in though.
So what to make of this game? As the nameable scholar protagonist you can focus on many different things, some in combination. Your choices do make a difference in how things play out. But there's the sense that in the background things are afoot too, historic occurrances taking place and so forth, that may or may not come back to haunt you.
Ultimately though, I think you'd best experience this game for yourself. It is good, within its genre, and for its price something you'll not regret picking up. If you like it, consider Choice of Robots by the same author as well.

Choice of Games brings us another entry from Kevin Gold, the man behind Choice of Robots.
I've done two playthroughts of Alexandria so far and I'm fairly impressed. In short, this game provides a wide range of choices about how you wield your influence in and around the city of Alexandria. As someone who has taught Egyptian history, I've found it really quite fascinating.
However, the game is not as strong as Choice of Robots. This is not a bad thing! Robots is, maybe, the best choicescript game released. With Robots, I felt very attached my little creation and the cast of supporting characters. Alexandria just doesn't quite reach that same level of attachment with the young Prince you help raise.
Much like Robots, however, Alexandria truly succeeds at making you feel like you're altering the course of history.
Still, this is definitely one of the better Choice Of games around. If you like history, philosophy and so on, pick it up. If you liked Robots, pick it up.

Just like Choice of Robots, the other interactive novel by Kevin Gold, Choice of Alexandria is a bit short; but it more than makes up for it with impactful decisions and a few emotional moments. A "choose your own adventure" type game, Choice of Alexandria heavily revolves around your decisions, and, just like Choice of Robots, your decisions have a massive impact on the game, even changing the final chapter completely.
As a philosopher in ancient Alexandria, you are tasked with raising the future ruler of Egypt. How you teach him is up to you, and you do feel connected to the young prince, at least in my experience. I became very dissappointed when the prince did not turn out how I wanted him to. Additionally, the setting of ancient Egypt is very unique when compared to many other Choice of Games titles, which are usually either a low-fantasy world or superhero-themed. At the very least, very few, if any, are set in ancient times, and have the player take the role of a primitive scientist.
Despite it's brevity, Choice of Alexandria is still a memorable interactive novel, and while I still prefer Choice of Robots, people who enjoyed that title are likely going to love Choice of Alexandria due to them having the same author and having impactful decisions in each of the titles. Overall, 8/10.

Much like when the remastered ‘Day of the Tentacle’ came out, I bought the game and played it to completion in a few days. Sometimes remembering the puzzle, sometimes not, sometimes I even forgot whole parts of the game. These were the games I played and loved the most. Adventure games were big once, and this one, being made by Lucasarts was one of the best. Because that is what Lucasarts did, they made the best adventure games. They knew everything that was wrong with all the others and improved it with great stories, crazy situations and hilarious jokes. Full Throttle is most of these, but also breaks some of these rules.
It has horrible action sequences (which luckily you can keep trying without really dying), timed events and trail-and-error sections. You won’t find any of these in MI or DotT (they were present in the Indiana Jones adventures, though) which is why those games rate higher for me then FT does.
It’s also very short and the puzzles are easier and more logical, so normally you should be able to figure out things fairly quick, locations are also limited so you don’t spend too much time walking around a huge map trying to figure out what you missed before. It probable was, in it’s day, the most accessible adventure game for most people.
After more then 20 years the game is still great, if you like adventure games and haven’t played this one before, you should. If you played it when the original was released you should also play it.
Why? Because it’s gives you the same feeling as watching that great movie you haven’t seen for a long time and wonder why they don’t make them like they used to anymore. Even though, with upgraded graphics and all, it doesn’t feel modern and aged a bit.
The remastered graphics are great, I love that they just upgraded the original art, just as they did with DotT. The remastering of MI was a let-down for me, as it was too different from the original artwork. That is not the case here, it’s just as you remember. It’s also around this time that pre-rendered gfx was started to being used in Lucasarts adventures and, well, they don’t really age well, even in remastered form I prefer the hand drawn pixelwork any day.
One thing I find funny now, is that Tim Shafer kinda looks like Ben Throttle. I also saw the making-off video on youtube and he didn’t really look like that in the 90’s.

I am not enjoying this game enough to do a "proper" review, so here's what I'm not liking about the game:
You have separate sliders for music and ambient sound, but no slider for the narrator, and no subtitles.  This means that the game is obnoxiously loud except when the narrator is speaking, but you HAVE to have the sound turned up or you will miss important information! >_<

On sale for $2, it seemed like even a game with less than stellar reviews would be worth a shot, and how do you go wrong with Tesla?
God how I was wrong. Right off the bat, the game has no intuitive feel to it. Most of the few levels I could deal with was fighting zombies, but the way you do so is that you effectively grab one zombie in your gun, then shoot that zombie at another. There's a whole realm of issues with that. First of all, there's a long animation of the zombies coming out of the ground before they can be interacted with. Then there's that when you do use this, the zombies bounce straight back at you so if you're remotely close to the zombie you're shooting, you end up getting hurt by your own shot. "That can easily be avoided by not being close to the zombie" you say. Well, the field of view is so small, and so much of this involves narrow platforms, that that is an incredibly difficult thing to pull off. Plus, there's a max range for the gun, so it limits you to relatively close quarters combat with something that is distinctly not close quarters suitable.
The view is also a huge issue because it means it is extremely difficult to see where you're trying to go, especially leaping from ledges, as a large part of the time, there are jumps that one makes just presuming there will be something to land on when you get there. This could be forgivable if not for the fact that it seems like the terrain is semi-randomly generated, and so each time you die, you end up in a new landscape so you face the same issues time and time again, rather than at least being able to learn the particulars of the level.
The game has, theoretically, checkpoints, but with how poor the level design is, it feels like there should be more checkpoints. It also should correspond much more to events, as, for example, you find a pigeon to help you, but that's in the middle of a long stretch with no checkpoints, so finding that, going on a ways, then dying meant having to go get the pigeon over and over again, rather than having a checkpoint where one finds the pigeon in what I'd consider a more reasonable manner.
If this game is on sale at it's full price, don't buy it. If it's on sale, don't buy it. If someone offers it to you for free, decline.

This isn't the kind of game that you can pour hundreds of hours into. No collectibles, no microtransactions, no online mode and little (if any) replayability either. If those things are importrant to you when looking at the price of this game, you may want to give it a miss.
There are, however, other things that (to me anyway) make it more than worth the price of admission if you're into them. For example, it has a very highly polished, lovingly-crafted singleplayer campaign. The story tackles themes not often seen in games outside of an early Quantic Dream game or obscure games that only play on a single element of what this game covers. The controls, while basic, are easy to learn and gradually get used throughout the campaign in different ways to keep them interesting. The sound is great and is utilized fully in the game's environment (definitely an experience best played on headphones. My 5.1 speakers just don't do it justice).
I've always enjoyed single-player experiences that leave you thinking about the narrative and themes inside its story. This is definitely one of those games.

Simply put, Running With Rifles is fantastic.
After a few hours of play it has brought back that nostalgic feel of playing Battlefield 1942 in a friend's basement, trading off every round, replaying the same map endlessly because each battle was different. Running With Rifles captures this classic, comic-book style of gameplay perfectly, and can be played in such a manner as well, not to mention the online capabilities.
The game functions on a game mode similar to Battlefield's "Conquest" mode, where players fight over a control point until they caputure it, forcing the enemy back to another controlled point. The large maps and huge number of NPC's make the battles chaotic and interesting. Ocassionally battles with certain settings will end up bottlenecking at certain points, but this forces you to try new tactics. From vehicles to airstrikes, and not to mention a pretty cool selection of mods, this game has a lot of replay, and I can see myself sinking a lot of time into this one when I'm looking for a quick action game. The arcade style and quick match setups let you play a fast match or an epic battle, and you won't even realize how long you've been gaming.

Cons:

-Not for gamers looking for a story or a profoundly "deep" game - it is classic run-and-gun.

No Man's Sky is an amazingly fun game... But only for some hours. With a game where you can explore the whole universe you'd expect that each planet will be different, but quickly enough you realise it isn't so. After visiting some planets, you will find out they all look alike, sure they all offer different items depending on their biome, but structures, landscapes and even size of the planets are all the same. I love this game, and I would love if the developers would add more things to the game that make you want to visit the planet even more.
Space combat, great concept, but the handling of the ships is so annoying, the enemy ships are overpowered.
Structures, all generally the same, why not add more different structures, structures where you have to solve some puzzles in order to access them, structures where you have to do some parkour to enter them, tempels, maybe?
Wildlife, great job on that, but still could be so much better, why aren't there rivers or waterfalls, why aren't there huge forests with plenty of secrets to be discovered? Why are all the caves the same on every single planet out there?
Why aren't there villages on planets? Villages that are abandoned or villages that host life, with NPCs that can give you quests on that planet?
Why can't we have unlimited storage containers, or at least, more of them? Why can't we make a map of certain area's of a planet, to find truly navigate? This game is in space, why can't we fly to the sun of a system? Why are all planets the same size? Why don't planets have rings?
Also, let's talk about that annoying 'timer' that says in how much time you'll arrive somewhere... Why is it there? I don't want a game to tell me how long I will have to play it to reach a certain place and I definitely don't want to know how much time of my day I'm wasting playing videogames instead of doing something productive. why can't it show the distance instead?
There is unlimited possibilities to improve this game, but the developers aren't taking advantage of it. These were just a few of the ideas that crossed my mind when writing my review, I could list so much more things that would make this game a real pleasure to play, and I hope that one day I will truly be able to play this game again and have all the fun I had in the beginning of it. For what the game has to offer, I think the price tag is way too high. Way too high.

Unresponsive controls, poorly designed boss fights, unnecessarily long dungeons, and enemies that cannot be interrupted while attacking make this game a miserable experience. I loved the first Darksiders game and was expecting its sequel to imrpove on its original. No such luck. Stay as far away as possible from this one.
Often the character would not react to my commands. In a game where you rely on evading enemy attacks, when you're surrounded by enemies and evade doesn't work every time, it becomes annoying really fast.
This is the reason I couldn't interrupt many attack of even the weaker enemies. Some combinations (like Shift + LMB) wouldn't work for me every time, opening myself to enemy attacks without having time to evade.
I also never got used to delays in enemy attacks. The enemy would begin his attack animation, I would jump out of the way, and only after that he would attack and hit me as a result.
I don't think dungeons are fun in Darksiders II. Optional dungeons aren't too long, but they can be skipped completely. The dungeons you have to complete to advance the game are terribly long and boring.
For example, many dungeons require you to complete a set of objectives to get to the boss, and often you'd have to do three identical tasks in three different parts of the dungeon. Why have three? Why not only one? Why do I have to find three magic stones to activate a guardian, solving the same kinds of puzzles three times? Doesn't serve any purpose other than making the game longer than it could've been without filler content.
Anyway, I understand that some people like this kind of thing. I don't.

I played the original ff13 way back in release and understand why some might think the original game sucked... It was too linear, and there was no freedom to explore the world. Like most games that were made after 2010, the developers seemed to have put in too much time and money on graphics, and not much else for their story writers.
ff13-2 promised; and admittedly did its best, to fix all the aforementioned "problems" in the original game. I played it when it was released as well. As the original game poorly reviewed, you'd think that nobody (outside of japan at least) had the taste for a sequel. The time traveling aspect of 13-2 was too complicated for some people, and many couldn't stick through with it despite the many improvements from the original game. As much as I didn't enjoy the story in 13-2, knowing about it is important in order to understand some parts of the story in this game.
After 3 years of not touching ff13, Lightning Returns actually brings an unexpectedly good closing to the original game, and fills in many of the holes left behind after the arguably complicated mess that was 13-2. The PC port is actually rather decent for a PS3 game; FPS drops are rare except in towns, although the controls could definitely be better. For one, there is no option for mouse use at all, it's basically a direct traslation of the console controller buttons onto the keyboard. For a more fulfilling and immersive experience, I suggest the use of a gaming controller. Combat is fun and challenging, and the multitudes of sidequests are really fun to do. The story does justice to the characters and I think they are given the "ending they deserve" with this final sequel.
For those who have yet to play final fantasy 13 at all, I suggest doing the following if you wanna give it a shot:
Play the original ff13 (or watch if you can't stand the linear gameplay), watch ff13-2 (or play if you don't mind sidequests and alternate timelines/endings), definitely buy and play lightning returns once you've seen the first 2.
Oh and as with all JRPGs, the japanese dub is way better and you should always play in jp with eng subs if you want to play the better narrative.

This is one of the better "Choice of" games. The decisions you make actually impact what happens next as oppose to some of the others. This is great for people who are interested in the history of Alexandria and scholarly choice making. You can invent stuff, raise a prince, and as guide a kingdom to glory or ruin among things. You can even hang out with Archimedes, so if you're into the pre-electric era machines you'll enjoy that (I know I did, he's written as a total bro too).
Kevin Gold did a great job writing the story and taking the time to create a ton of different paths to take. I think there are 7 unique endings and a bunch of achievements giving this game a lot of replay value. If you dig this game you'll really like Kevin Gold's other "Choice of" game called "Choice of Robots". I personally like "Choice of Robots" better because I'm more into sci-fi than historical books, but of all the "Choice of" authors Kevin Gold is easily the best.

As the author's follow up to Choice of Robots, which was one of the better productions from Choice of Games, I have been anticipating playing this game for some time.  After playing it multiple times, I can say that I was not disappointed.  It is a very accurate representation of the Hellenistic era, which is sadly an era of world history that tends to be largely glossed over.  You play as a philospher who comes to Alexandria to advance their own studies and to serve as a tutor to the future heir to the Ptolemy dynasty.  With another advisor who intends to raise the heir to be hedonistic and pliable, so that they can control them for their own personal gain, you have to decide whether to focus mostly on your own research or to slow down your own career in order to focus on tutoring the heir and being a good counterbalancing influence (Or so they will be pliable to you instead of the other advisor).  As for your personal research, you have the choice between developing, and potentially excelling, at the skills of rhetoric, medicine, or techne (Technology).  The choices between your own skills, accomplishments, and service to the dynasty (With potentially serious effects on how Egypt is ruled) are the main focus of the game, and finding a good balance is what drives the story.
I only have two complaints about the game.  The first is that it feels a bit short, but that might be because Choice of Robots was fairly long and I expected this game to be similar.  The second was the ending where you can invent the steam engine.  It is one of three different choices at the end where you can create a significant lasting work.  Two of them are an epic literary work and the germ theory of disease.  In these endings, your work has an effect on world history, but it is not an overwhelming one.  However, the steam engine ending has a very major effect that does not feel realistic to me.  Based on the level of technology at the time, it is extremely unlikely that a practical and economic steam engine could be developed.  Personally, I felt that maybe the option should have been that you develop a philosphy that the universe is a clockwork mechanism, similar to the devices that you have focused on studying and developing, leading to an earlier development of the scietific method and empericism by subsequent generations.

Being both a mild layman to philosophy as well as deeply interested in it, I was very pleased with the premise of this game and was not disappointed in it.
As short as it is, there's a large variety of different things you can focus on, from the genius focused on doing what's best for everyone to a conniving manipulator looking for power. So far I've found tutoring the prince to be the wisest and most selfless ruler possible to be the most interesting, but I'm undoubtedly going to explore the other avenues of this game on future plays.
This is probably the best example of "a thinking gamer's" interactive novel from Choice of Games, and it bears the distinction of being just as cerebral as it is entertaining. I've gone on three different runs now (offline and online, explaining my short time on it) second-guessing myself on how I could get what I believed to be the "best ending", and each time I find new pieces of the puzzle I hadn't even considered before.
Highly recommended, especially for the incredibly low price it's being discounted at in it's early release.

Let me start off by saying that I truly wanted to like Tesla Breaks The World, I really do, but it just doesn’t do a whole lot of things right. Which is absolutely a shame, because you can tell it has its heart in the right place.
Okay, I’m just joking. Fooled you, didn’t I ?
Actually, that wasn’t a joke. The problem is that the game breaks with vsync on. Controls become too unresponsive at 30fps and for the life of me I couldn’t get past the second level. The second level ! It was infuriating !
So I randomly decided to try it without vsync on to see if that would change anything. I was looking for just about anything to make this more playable and I had already decided that if the game wouldn’t perform better after that I would just stop playing it altogether. Fortunately for the friendly developers of Achetype Global this worked. The game now runs at 60fps which is a world of difference. I strongly suggest that the developer removes the vsync option, or at least fixes it properly.
Tesla Breaks The World is a platformer with puzzle elements. You control Nikola Tesla who finds his electricity gun in the beginning of the game, after a huge incident caused by Thomas Edison. With this gun you can zap zombies that now randomly spawn all over the space and even teleport them with it, or if you want to give it a more useful purpose you can use it to teleport items (and do things like dropping boxes on them). Further into the game you’ll find even more weaponry and gadgets and you’ll be able to get (and control) a pet pigeon that you can send anywhere you want it to go. The pigeon is useful for flipping switches or hard to get items;.collecting these items will add to your score. Until you lose all of your lives, that is. And this will be pretty frequent if I had to take a guess.
The levels are randomly generated (which is pretty cool) and halfway through there’s always a checkpoint where you can continue if you should ever die. You start with 3 lives and 3 vitality and if all lives are lost you have to restart the level from the beginning.
The game was terrible to play at 30fps but even at 60fps the controls are sometimes too unresponsive. This game needs tighter controls for walking and jumping because right now this all feels very floaty.
Technically it’s a bit of mess. The collision detection is pretty poor; I’ve had several times that a bullet hit my body even though it was still at least a digital meter away. The electric trampolines are unreliable; one time they’re working fine, other times I have to recalculate my jump more than a few times because it doesn’t give me enough velocity. It makes the game more frustrating than it should be and things like this should’ve been tested properly. I don’t care if you call it a part of the difficulty because I find that completely unbelievable. Games are about having fun, and this just isn’t.
One thing I am positive about is the graphics. The developers have chosen a unique style with cartoony characters and a semi-realistic world with fantasy elements in them. And more than a few electrical devices. The cutscenes should remind you of the silent movies from the 30s, which unsurprisingly adds to the game's atmosphere.
The voiceover/narrator does a good job at telling you what’s happening and the music is also quite alright. Nothing to complain about here.
But, as you can see, I’m not a big fan of Tesla Breaks The World. Like I already said, I tried to like the game. But the game just didn’t give me a proper chance by continually trying to test my limits. I'm still stuck at level 3...
I’m sure there’s a group who will still appreciate this game for what it is, but I can guarantee you that I'm not one of them and that this is not for me. I play games to be entertained and this did not meet my requirements. My apologies, developers !

They are gameplay in this case. They have to be good, meat shouldn't be rotten, buns shouldn't be moldy etc. Then there comes extra ingredients like sauce, lettuce, tomatoes blah blah you name it. They also have to be good. If you go to Burger King and eat a burger, it will probably taste generic, artificial, like plastic. Or if you go to some another place that no one really heard or give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about, that place could have amazing burgers right? Sometimes at least.
Now as we all of know, world is not just black or white. In fact, there is more gray than black and white. So sometimes Burger King can make good burgers or that underground place would make actually ♥♥♥♥♥♥ burgers. Soo, what all of these have anything to do with Hellblade?
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice doesn't have the most quality bun and meat. They are generic, mediocre, average. A bit better than Burger King's burgers in this case. You do some puzzles, then enter combat with some guys. You kill them, you do puzzles, enter combat, repeat this until the end of the game. Now, combat is okay. There is some kind of an item that slows time and heal you to full health, so you don't die. I played it on hardest difficulty and given the game's unforgiving condition which deletes your save if you die quite a lot, this item is kind of useful. But also caused me act like a careless idiot because I knew I was safe. There are no combos, some enemies require fast attack to be killed, some require slow attack, sometimes you have to bring down their shield with button combinations. Not much to tell. It could've been executed better though.
Now puzzles. They are repetetive. Way more repetetive than combat. Until you lose your sword during the middle of the game, these puzzles are tedious, unfun, boring. I haven't enjoyed most of them because they are literally the same thing. Even after you lose your sword, these puzzles are still same. There will be some extra things added to these puzzles and for me, they are added because they thought they will add more diversity. Could be true. Not for me though. If you try to add some sparkles to a poop, it is still a poop. Yeah, puzzles in this game are poop.
Hellblade's gameplay doesn't bring anything to table. It is just there, to keep story going forward and I think that's a really big mistake and it is a trap that many developers are falling to. I am really mixed up on gameplay.
Now for story and atmosphere, I don't want to give any spoilers though. They are fine. They are carrying this game from the seas of mediocrity. In fact if this was a TV series, it would've been way better. I really have don't much comment on story or atmosphere. I was impressed about the story after I finished the game and it lasted for at least two or three days but that's about it.
I started to play it at some afternoon and finished it before midnight. Roughly 8-9 hours storyline. Alright.
Yeah well, this game doesn't have exceptional good quality bun and meat, it has some good extra ingredients but you don't even remember them because well, they are not that really important. Of course I would want them, but without good backbone, only thing they can do is carrying the burger above mediocrity. That's Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice.
And yes, I know developer is a small studio with limited resources. So kudos to them, it seems like they actually tried, even what they did wasn't the best thing. Still, it is good to see that at least they have tried.
Also writing a review to Steam ♥♥♥♥ing sucks. "Do you recommend this game? Yes or No". Well ♥♥♥♥ this. I even said on the second paragraph, world is not binary, it is not just black and white. There is a lot of gray. What the ♥♥♥♥ is this borderline review system? How about a score system so it would've been more accurate? ♥♥♥♥ you too.

No Man's Sky is an amazingly fun game... But only for some hours. With a game where you can explore the whole universe you'd expect that each planet will be different, but quickly enough you realise it isn't so. After visiting some planets, you will find out they all look alike, sure they all offer different items depending on their biome, but structures, landscapes and even size of the planets are all the same. I love this game, and I would love if the developers would add more things to the game that make you want to visit the planet even more.
Space combat, great concept, but the handling of the ships is so annoying, the enemy ships are overpowered.
Structures, all generally the same, why not add more different structures, structures where you have to solve some puzzles in order to access them, structures where you have to do some parkour to enter them, tempels, maybe?
Wildlife, great job on that, but still could be so much better, why aren't there rivers or waterfalls, why aren't there huge forests with plenty of secrets to be discovered? Why are all the caves the same on every single planet out there?
Why aren't there villages on planets? Villages that are abandoned or villages that host life, with NPCs that can give you quests on that planet?
Why can't we have unlimited storage containers, or at least, more of them? Why can't we make a map of certain area's of a planet, to find truly navigate? This game is in space, why can't we fly to the sun of a system? Why are all planets the same size? Why don't planets have rings?
Also, let's talk about that annoying 'timer' that says in how much time you'll arrive somewhere... Why is it there? I don't want a game to tell me how long I will have to play it to reach a certain place and I definitely don't want to know how much time of my day I'm wasting playing videogames instead of doing something productive. why can't it show the distance instead?
There is unlimited possibilities to improve this game, but the developers aren't taking advantage of it. These were just a few of the ideas that crossed my mind when writing my review, I could list so much more things that would make this game a real pleasure to play, and I hope that one day I will truly be able to play this game again and have all the fun I had in the beginning of it. For what the game has to offer, I think the price tag is way too high. Way too high.

As a PC Port, this is definitely the best of the lot. PC players will remember the multitude of crashes that pestered XIII and XIII-2. I played this game on the PS3 and loved it, clocking over 200 hours on it.
All core gameplay remains the same, and Square Enix has rather generously given access to all DLC except the Aerith set. You're really not losing out on anything special. Outerworld has been disabled on the Steam port, making it potentially more difficult for PC players as they can't get Turbo Ethers and Ethers off random NPCs. As mentioned before, DLC does make up for this by providing fairly overpowered equipment. If you want to experience the game with some challenge, try not to use Yuna's Summoner Garb and Cloud's Soldier 1st Class.
I hate the fact that you can't truly customize your key assignments. This port forces you to bind keys to the PS3/Xbox configuration, such that Jump/O/A. Full customization of FFXIII and XIII-2 was possible. Why not here? This is arguably more important for LR, where button preses are even more important than past games. If you don't have a Numpad, you're going to find it difficult to find space to bind keys into a comfortable configuration.
First, some background. Lightning has awoken from crystal stasis 500 years after Chaos flooded the world. When Chaos flooded the world, it had the side effect of stopping humans from aging. Humans did not age, and thus no longer died of old age. They could, however, still be killed by monsters, or die of disease. Lightning was awoken by God, Bhunivelze, to be the saviour. Her duty is to save souls from the remnants of the world so that they can be reborn in the new world that Bhunivelze is creating. Lightning has 13 Days to fulfill her duty before the world ends.
Now let's address the content. Lightning Returns is completely unchanged from the PS3/Xbox version. So let's look at some of the graphics: The NPCs don't look great, the dogs look horrendous. However, the environments bring across each individual theme well. Lightning, however, is of course well animated, although there's some visible tearing in her hair when Lightning touches the crest on her chest where her L'cie mark used to be.
Story: One of the main issues with this particular installment of Lightning Returns is the terrible English translation which ends up contradicting itself. The English localisation does not differentiate between 'Heart' (Kokoro) and 'Soul' (Tamashi). This is a key point of contention within the mythos, and has to be cleared up. As a result, I highly recommend having audio in Japanese and reading the English subtitles. However, always keep an ear out for the above two Japanese terms, 'Kokoro' and 'Tamashi', as the English translation makes no distinction between the two.
Characters: One of the most obvious problems since XIII has been the bland, one dimensional characters. While we may be tempted to continue the bashing, there actually is justification for a one-dimensional character this time around. Imagine if you've lived for 500 years with no true end in sight. No new lives are being born, and death is common. Nothing changes. You'd be depressed too. Each character has their own motivations, but they all end up the same. "I'm in despair, Lightning, save me whether I like it or not." It is bland, and this time, understandably so.
Gameplay: I'm going to be breaking the gameplay down into 3 parts, Adventure, Time Limit, and Combat.
Adventure: Lightning Returns gives you four fairly large regions to explore. In each region, you'll need to clear a Main Quest, and do a fetch quest for the 5th Main Quest. The rest of the Side Quests are fairly simple fetch quests, which tends to be boring more often than not. The mythos is well fleshed out, however, and you'll finally understand what the hell is going on when you clear Main Quest 4. But as with non-linear stories, depending on the order in which you choose to clear the Main Quests, you may find yourself confused at one point because you may not have the context of XIII or XIII-2 to back up your knowledge.
Monsters are in limited quantity, as befitting a game where the world is ending. Large scale enemies like Zaltys and Zomok have a population of 30, meaning there are only 30 of them in the game. Monsters do NOT give experience upon defeating them. Instead, stats are given as quest rewards. Basically, the more souls you save, the stronger Lightning becomes.
Time Limit: Take it from a player who has over 200 hours into the PS3 version of this, there's more than enough time to do everything. The clock DOES dictate some actions. Some NPCs require you to report to them at a certain time of the day to advance a quest, and some quests are time-sensitive, meaning if you don't fulfill the requirement about visiting them the 'next' day, you fail the quest. You are going to have to keep track of things, so it is recommended to clear Side Quests city by city. As the days pass, monsters also get stronger and drop better abilities. Thus, please don't hunt them to extinction within the first few days. Take your time.
You start with 7 days, and you extend time as you complete the five main quests to a maximum of 12 days before the Final Day arrives. If you complete enough side quests, you unlock a bonus dungeon and a bonus day for a grand total of 14 days.
Personally, I like the time limit. XIII and XIII-2 had themes about time. The party of six in XIII were counting down the days till they turned into C'ieth. Serah was counting down time as well. Lightning Returns makes it literal, forcing it into your face, "TIME IS PRECIOUS", and you only have THIRTEEN DAYS to save the world.
Combat: This is where Lightning Returns shines. Unlike XIII and XIII-2, where Auto-Battle was your main option, Lightning Returns has a very immersive combat system, and is extremely customizable. Think of Lightning Returns as more of an Action JRPG than the traditional turn based JRPG. The Stagger system makes a return, although it's not as necessary as it was before in XIII and XIII-2 for normal encounters. Do note that for Boss encounters, you are expected to know how to Stagger the enemy, so build up your knowledge on normal encounters, and check the Bestiary regularly.
You control Lightning; ;her equipment, every movement, every Guard, every attack. Both your strategy in setting up Lightning's loadout and your execution of your strategy is extremely important, and this is what makes combat in Lightning Returns so satisfying when you are successful. However, inversely, every failed fight is also the fault of the player. Not Guarding, or not reading the Bestiary to find out stagger conditions is a recipe for failure. There is good news, though. Tons of players before you have beaten this game, so if you need an active demonstration, Youtube is an excellent teacher. Unlike old Final Fantasy games, stat grinding doesn't win fights. Execution of your strategy does. Keep that in mind.
Summary: While the characters are justifiably one dimensional, the story itself is actually fairly decent as the mythos of this series of worlds is finally explained in greater detail. This is, however, let down by a bad English translation (I'm running on the assumption that most people speak English here...), which makes the story seem self-contradictory. As mentioned above, it is recommended to play with Japanese audio and whatever language you prefer.
The combat system shines. I would really love to see a combat system similar to this in the future, but with hopefully more customization of Locked Abilities. However, for new players, the learning curve might be fairly steep especially if you run into an encounter you're not prepared for. All I can say is, keep at it.
While I do recommend this, I can't give this game a really high score because of the HUGE GLARING FLAW in translation, which is integral to storytelling. 7/10.

There are bugs, glitches and horrible camera angles in the game that makes it very hard to enjoy. I died many times because the camera FOV is not large enough. The combat and puzzles can be frustrating too, because there is a lack of context in regards to the mechanics.
While the game ran fine for me, I crashed a few times. The game doesn't support ultra widescreen either very well as the mini-map suddenly had icons appearing outside of it.
Music starts off strong, but become annoying quickly and rather lackluster. Only the song at the very start really pulled me in. The rest was either okay or downright forgettable.
Sound is also all over the place, I found some sound design to be spot on and some not well thought out. I am not a fan of games that adds in mechanics of having to use your ears to determine if you are close to hidden stuff and then throw in a lot of garbage prop sounds that sounds similar making the feature pointless and frustrating.
Side-quests are the typical "Kill this." or "Collect that." A very lifeless addition to the game that doesn't help carry any strong narrative outside of the main campaign.
I will say the strongest thing for me, personally, is the mythos of the world. I would read a book in this world.
If they intend to make a Darksiders 3, they really need to adjust a lot of things or remove the RPG element all together.

Aqua Kitty is a great, well-polished shmup with a really cute cat aesthetic. That being said, don't let the kitty theme lull you into a false sense of security; this game is quite hard.
The game's graphics and gameplay are extremely crisp and enjoyable, and the music is definitely not something to put aside either. The scoring system works quite well too, as it offers more points to players who are able to perform the most efficiently, giving Aqua Kitty's online highscore competition a lot of relevance. Because of this, there's a fair bit of replay value to be enjoyed, but it can get a bit repetitive and stale after you've fought the same groups enemies over and over.
As I mentioned above, Aqua Kitty is
. While there is an easy mode for those who might not be up for the challenge, the normal and arcade modes are quite difficult and will tax even a shmup veteran's skill. Most of the difficulty is justified, but in some cases (such as the Infinite Espresso mode - the game's endless level), the screen will end up being filled with more high-health enemies than you have firepower to deal with. This is to be expected at some point because of the scaling difficulty, but it often happens relatively early in Espresso runs, which boils down to a slight problem with enemy balancing.
Overall, if you're a shmup fan or you enjoy the gameplay similar to the 1980 arcade classic, Defender, Aqua Kitty is certainly worth picking up. Just don't delude yourself into thinking the game's going to take it easy on you.

The above line is basically for TLDR.
In the beginning, fps had no story, there was only gameplay. Then came half life, which added narrative to its game. Many games of similar design followed, and one of them was Medal of Honor. The team that made it later created Call of Duty. After 5 years of making WW2 themed shooters, the next logical step was to move on to a more modern setting.
Personally, i would like to think of call of duty games as a pinnacle of cinematic action games, or at least held 1st place for that title for many years. You have entertaining cinematographic setpieces, amazing score, and story that keeps you on the edge of your seat. Also, what older call of duty games had compared to the newer ones is plausibility of the plot. They tried to stay within the spectrum of possibilities.
ps: even though the ww2 era CODs didn't really have a story or characters, they did have those setpieces and the score, which made they stand out so much from the competition.
Now, onto the multiplayer. Personally, i had my fun days in COD4's multiplayer. I was a big COD fan back in the day. The perks, killstreaks, and all that. I found it very appealing. You could say that i was into COD's multiplayer for about 4 more years, playing every iteration of their game.
That said, the current state of COD4's multiplayer is very different. It's not dead. It has mutated. It's not a very popular opinion, but currently, the game is filled by 64 player servers with hardcore on, and i hate that. It's just not very enjoyable or fun to play on such servers, and that's 90% of the servers right now. You have to cherry pick to find the traditional ones.
And that's the reason why i really like what MW2 did, when it restricted mod support and limited the max player count to 12/18 players.
That said, ironically, in both cases, the game dies. In video games with open mod support, vanilla is just outright forgotten, and in games without them, the game just dies. It's sad really.
Anyway, moral of the story is to play games at the right time.

Seems like a solid game, could use some more ways of progression, since currently all I could do to "upgrade" my weapons was to pick up the bonuses that spawn every wave, and all they seemed to do was either increase the amount of projectiles fired from one of the 4 weapons, increase the size of the projectiles or just give the weapon a damage boost, which didn't really seem to affect the guns performance much.
Now, there are 4 weapons as I mentioned before, your standard blaster, which from upgrades receives extra projectiles.
The second weapon I'd best describe as a curved (banana shaped) projectile, that at higher levels grows bigger, and passes through a few enemies.
The third weapon seems like a rocket launcher of sorts, but the explosion barely deals any AoE, even at level 9.
The fourth weapon was one of my favorites, along with the 2nd weapon, this one shoots sort of like, mini rockets, that deal no AoE, but with levels you get more projectiles. The reason I'd describe the projectiles as mini rockets, is because they're angular & slower than the other projectiles.
after wave 20, you get a boss fight, and after beating the boss, you get to choose between four (presumably) random perks.
after choosing your perk, you're thrown back in to the arena where you started, just now there's more enemies spawning & the walls have moved a bit.
after reaching wave 36 or so, I got killed.
That's about as far as I've made it as of now, I do intend to play the game some more, just to see what the other characters do & if they have any differences.
To unlock a second character you need 15.. let's just call them crystals.. I've got no idea on what criteria I'm awarded crystals, but after three runs of the game, I've gained 8 of them.
The game claims to have controller support, but it didn't seem to recognize my xbox one controller, nor does it have rebindable keys.
I had no issues with the keyboard layout that the game uses, except for the odd choice of putting a specific perk (bomb I believe it was called) seemed to be bound to z and 5.. you change your weapons by pressing Q,E,1-4 or right clicking, or scrolling your mouse wheel.. but using a perk (that you might get after wave 20) is bound awkwardly to 2 buttons that aren't easily reachable, especially when your left hand is already stuck on WASD.
all in all, a very good game for its pricepoint, hope they add more content in the future & fix the keybindings & controller support.
p.s. who binds shooting to the bumpers and toggling weapons to the triggers?

What a journey. Bought this game for £40 on PS4, played it for a few weeks and loved it. Then my denial wore off. I had received a fraction of what I was promised and even the things I did get were washed down. I finally realised I had been lied to. In it's defence, No Man's Sky is a decent game, but it should cost a max of £15.
Exploring planets gets tedious unless you find a nice pretty planet and even then its the same old "walk here, discover this, walk there discover that" thing. The game got boring and eventually I stopped playing it.
Then one day, while realising I had nothing to play but money to spare, I purchased this again on PC for £14.99 on a sale. And boy did I like that price. After so much time I finally got to experience the first few hours again, exploring and having fun making new discoveries. Then the same thing happened. Got bored of the grind, uninstalled the game and never looked at it again.
And now. Oh boy now. I reinstalled this game after finding out they had added vehicles and the Atlas Rising Update was out and base building was a thing. Ho-lee-f***. I have 36 hours total as of playing this, 20 of those from the last week alone. I love it. The story is intriguing, the new exotic planets mean I have something else to look out for, the base building is fun, and I just enjoy playing it a lot more now.
Honestly, if you can get this game for any less than £20, get it. Don't pay more as you will be dissapointed. The game is a time filler, you hop on and explore a few planets before moving on to something else, still not worth the price but man is it getting there,

A cautious recommendation as the port is passable.
Its not the "great" or "perfect" port everyone says it is, people are just excited that its the first game in the 13-series that isnt unplayable on PC. The bizarre framepacing thing is gone and for the most part it runs just fine.
The resolution is limited to 1080p which is a problem even if you do not own a higher resolution screen. If a game lacks proper anti-aliasing which this game really does lack, downsampling from greater resolutions often solves the issue, but because of the limit it cannot be done right now. Forcing FXAA from the control panel helped, but as we know it makes the image just a bit blurry in some ways. Nothing bad, looks passable, but I wish they would add some proper AA.
The framerates do♥♥♥♥♥♥themselves in certain areas where the game loads in the next "sector" of the map. It has nothing to do with anyones hardware, doesnt matter if its installed on an SSD, doesnt matter if you are running it on the most powerful rig possible, there are some sudden stutters that only last for a brief moment, mostly in cities. My guess is that its some terrible loading system that was left over from the console version. It makes one of the bigger cities of the town really unpleasant to play in as your framerate seemingly goes ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in certain areas.
Its definitely a step up from the previous shoddy ports that frankly they shouldnt be even selling as they are so ♥♥♥♥ing bad, but theres lots to improve. I know they wont though, they left the earlier ones in a bad state, left them screaming in a puddle of their own puke "GOD LEFT ME UNFINISHED!" and didnt even look back.
TL;DR
If you dont mind the ocasional hickup in cities and other zone changing areas, its passable, but you have a bunch of (extremely poorly written) story to catch up on so you will have some idea on what the heck is going on in the game if you havent played the previous games.

This Final Fantasy XIII title is a far better port than it's previous two releases. But when you look closely you might realize the game is an emulated PS3 title, as it clearly says in the tips to not "Turn off the Playstation 3" when saving. It could have been an easily missed thing during transition. But who knows for sure.
Either way, they did a good job bringing this to PC and it looks great. The game is actually pretty fun and has many interesting elements, for example it's possible to make monster species extinct by getting in combat enough times with them. Doing so helps you gain massive stat bonuses once you get the missions to make these creatures extinct.
While the game looks and runs better than it's PS3 version. Some of the graphics of the "extras" in the game are laughable at times. Including a cat they show a close up of in one mission that looks like he walked out of a Nintendo 64 game. The main cast, monsters, and environments look graphically amazing, but the extras look awful and downright laughable at times.
Protip: Use the Cloud outfit as soon as it becomes available for you. It's ability can easily help you do 5-digit damage early on to staggered enemies. Also spam the ability to stop time as often as you can. I did this and managed to complete every mission with two full days left on the clock.
Minor note about the ending without spoiling anything....
The ending of this game feels like the true ending to Final Fantasy XIII, almost as if the original Final Fantasy XIII had it's ending ripped away from it and placed at the end of this one. Characters come back to say goodbye you wouldn't know unless you played Final Fantasy XIII and even old characters like Snow are suddenly wearing their original garb at the end... They even show them using summons you also haven't seen since Final Fantasy XIII. It's a weird thing.
Infantile behavior from developers aside, this was an impulse purchase that I regret.  I still have the original, it still works fine, and the new art only takes the gritty edge away from the game.

Flashback to Bad to the Bone 90s with some Full Throttle Remastered!
LucasArts Monkey Island fans rejoice with another long-awaited revival!

Full Throttle is a game originally developed and published by the gods of adventure games; LucasArts and has been faithfully remastered by Double Fine Productions, the same people who did Grim Fandango Remastered and Day of the Tentacle Remastered
Full Throttle's story is brilliant. From its quirky characters to its lovable cutscenes and quirky comedy. The music (especially in the remastered edition) is absolutely brilliant! The cutscenes are lovable and fun to watch, overall the game is brilliant!
The puzzles and game progression, although when I was young and I played Full Throttle for the very first time I did not have any walkthroughs or guides, hell I didn't even have internet back in 2003 (just after playing Grim Fandango for the first time), so the puzzles were a bit challenging and can be a bit too awkward for modern-day players or even newcomers to the genre. The game does not help you at all when progressing through and does not hold your hand when your stuck on a puzzle for too long, so be prepared to get stuck here and there, thankfully I remembered most of the stuff! Lucky guys with internet nowadays, you can simply type in walkthroughs for the game!
The remastered version, Double Fine have really done a job well done for remastering this classic. The music is spot-on and digitally remastered. The cutscenes, although not fully converted to HD are very watchable, and the new HUD system they implemented has made it easier for players to play the game (honestly, the game's original controls were clunky and very awkward, surprisingly you can still play with the old controls!). The addition of HD graphics and shadow textures, etc... made the game more stunning than it originally was (and if you want some nostalgia, you can play the game in its original graphics!)
The thing that put me off slightly was the aspect ratio, this game is not tailored for 16:9 monitors and it seems that Double Fine did not optimize the game for 16:9 monitors but kept it at 4:3 aspect ratio, you can still change the aspect ratio from its original 4:3 to 16:9, but you might have to play the game stretched out.
Overall, Full Throttle and its remastered version are simply brilliant and if you are a fan of LucasArts (like me!) or you like adventure games or you want to try something new, then I would highly recommend playing Full Throttle and I hope that Double Fine will continue to remaster these old LucasArts classics!

If you consider this game as buying a 8 track chiptune music album with an arcade shooter as a bonus then it's probably worth a purchase, especially during a sale.

Full review:
Aqua Kitty is a retro submarine shooter. You're in charge of defending kitties that are mining milk from the ocean floor.
You're in charge of a submarine, which is equipped with a basic gun, allowing you to take out incoming enemies. These enemies either serve to destroy the submarine or capture the mining kittens. All of these enemies are some sort of robotic sealife. For example, robotic jellyfish will attempt to pick up your mining kittens and bring them above the surface of the water, where they'll be lost forever.
The game's levels are spread out over a rather small world map, quite disappointing seeing the small amount of levels available, wish there were more. The game gets progressively more difficult, as one might expect. The game gets really intense around the 10th or so level and I found it really difficult to progress around this time.
The game does have some rather lovely pixelated graphics and an amazing soundtrack going for it, but the price is $7, which seems a bit high for the low amount of content offered. Maybe $4 might have been better?
I can recommend the game purely from its gameplay and soundtrack, but the lack of graphical options is a bit of a pain for me, especially considering the fact that the game maxes out at 1280x720, which is not acceptable in 2014.

This game was recommended to me by one of my friends. It was his favorite game of 2017.
I was really impressed by this game. The immersion level is great. The graphics are superb if your computer can run them (I had to play the game mostly on low settings). Combat is fun, and the puzzles aren't too difficult.

As an avid, long time gamer there are very few games that actually keep my interest anymore. Most just seem like rehashes of the same thing over and over again and I usually finish them in a short amount of time and really never think of them much afterwards. This one is different. Very, very different. It's as though the creators were able to see things from my perspective; finding patterns in the world and using them to help shape the way others see things with me. Although trying to explain it to others always leaves them confused, it was very nice to be able to play a game that sees things the way I do. The biggest problem I had was the voices. I would have to stop after about 30 minutes of game play because I found myself talking to them and at one point, when they were gone, I became genuinely upset. All in all this game has gripped me tightly and I can see myself getting lost in it for a long time to come. Story telling was a 9/10, combat a 9/10 and the intellectual involvement was a solid 10/10. I absolutely do not regret buying this for PC AND PS4.

Despite some bugs that can pull out of the immersion, it's a fantastic game. Atmosphere, sound design, visuals - it's all great. Highly recommended; hope there will be more games in the future that take on risks to be different.

Graphically this game was amazing.  Breathtakingly beautiful at points.  I found myself taking frequent screenshots it was that pretty.  However, the overall vast majority of the game was simple rune puzzles and environment exploration.  Combat was infrequent and after long bursts of exploring meaning that you never built up a good rhythm to combat controls.  By the time you do it’s much easier but comes a bit too late in the game.  Personally I found combat to be slow for a hack and slack, with frequent periods where responses to buttons didn’t occur meaning you got frustrated at your helplessness to actually respond effectively.  The story is where the game shines out.  A simulation on psychosis in the underworld with a grim back story.  The story leaves you feeling hollow and depressed meaning that whilst some complain at the games length I personally wouldn’t have wanted to play it more than I did for fear of slitting my wrists!  On that front I feel the games length was about right.  Given the story, like others, I wouldn’t suggest there is much in terms of replay value.  Highly recommended for a first run through, enjoy, digest, move on to a more cheerful game.
