I think this game has a great premise.  I love the graphical style and the variety of load-outs available to the player.  My central issue with the game was its ability to provide meaningful information and feedback.  In a game where you have so little health to work with, it becomes vital that you have as much information as possible to make good decisions.  For instance, am I in cover? Is this enemy below me or above me? From which directions are we currently being attacked?  The player is forced to spend a large amount of time panning the camera to try and ensure that enemies aren't approaching from an odd direction, and "feeling out" elevation - the latter might take the form of shooting a 'test shot" to see if you are on the same elevation as your enemy when climbing a hill, or shooting the roof with the few shots while attempting to take position on the top of a building.  Although it's in a different genre, I would point to Mark of the Ninja as a game in which the player has very little health but is given the information to make good decisions.  Otherwise, many of your deaths feel cheap or silly.

I was going to start off by comparing this to other series', but when I got to the Zelda comparison it  stopped me short when I realized how ridiculous that particular one was. It would be like saying God of War ''is like Marlow Briggs''. One series is irrelevant and outdated whereas the other is superior and more complex in practically every department. I'm not gonna compare Darksiders to a game series that has been pumping out the same game since 1996 since it's insulting to the work the developers put behind DS2.
So let's ditch the Zelda comparison and get to more appropriate ones: Darksiders II is a quarter Prince of Persia platforming, 50% God of War combat, and one quarter overworld exploration with dungeons strewn about the land that are completed through a mix of combat and puzzle elements.
The simplicity out of the way first: the Prince of Persia platforming consists of wall running, wall climbing, and pillar jumping. You're not going to have difficulty navigating the levels since this isn't primarily a platformer, it's more of a way to get around rather than a challenge itself. Some parts are tricky and integrated into the puzzles themselves, but otherwise there's nothing complex here.
The God of War part is simple, but provides enough options to make combat fluid and varied. Rather than being a system comprised of memorizing long strings of different inputs for X and Y for different moves, DS2 has roughly around 8 or so different combos to memorize that each have their place. The variety comes in the options afforded to the player in other venues; each level increase nets you increased stats like any RPG, but also upgrade points that can be used to unlock abilities. 8 abilities total with three tiers each (for increased damage and effectiveness) as well as upgrades for said abilities to add additional properties to them. The weapons themselves have their own attributes and properties that vary massively, with possessed weapons allowing you to upgrade them however you see fit and to combine different attributes for a really powerful piece. The RPG elements, in essence, carry variety into combat itself without actually requiring route memorization of long combo strings like other games with this type of fighting system (God of War, DmC, MGR); it's a huge plus because you wind up being complex without me having to look at the menu to remember what the 30 different button press combinations do.
As for exploration itself; its exploration. The game isn't a huge quest-a-thon, but there are enough to have you exploring the overworlds beyond main storyline matters. Of note is that this game has 4 overworlds; granted they get progressively smaller due to size constraints, but the change in art direction and music almost makes it feel like a different game. It's fantastic and definitely feels better than one large overworld; combining these areas to place them in one map wouldn't have fit the story anyway.
Music's also worth mentioning. Jesper Kyd is fantastic and made an OST worth giving a dl; don't know why it isn't up for sale or a downloadable. DS1's OST was forgettable but this here's a work of art; it's like Jesper took the overworlds with all their art direction and somehow made them into audio format. He's that good at ''capturing'' the visual and making it auditory.
I guess for the negatives:
-There's some stuttering that can be fixed easily, but I shouldn't have to fix it myself
-Some areas have funky lighting that goes on and off on the walls, don't know what that's about
-There will never be a Darksiders III and this franchise will never be finished off

To the Moon looks like an RPG; but, with perhaps the exception of one sequence, there are no fights or encounters like you’d find in a normal RPG. The game started off with a strong story, filling the reader/player with questions, and it held my attention throughout. There were little mini-games to complete at the end of each section of the game, but I didn't have to think so hard about any part of the game that it took me out of the story.  Your reward for exploring the world is discovering details. Each chapter has particulars relating to the story that have to be found before you can move on to the next chapter, and throughout it all you are learning about John and River and what happened in their lives. You experience the agonies of having to make choices for John via Dr. Rosalene and Dr. Watts, as they travel through his memories trying to fulfill his dying wish.
If you want an RPG in the traditional sense of the word, this game isn’t for you.
If reading through a story-centric game is a problem, you’ll want to skip this one.
If it bothers you to cry over characters in a game, don’t bother with To the Moon.
But if you’re looking for a thought-provoking, love story involving all the twists and turns that are reality in many people’s lives, you will more than enjoy this offering. I cried as River’s life was revealed, John’s secrets made plain, and ultimately, as they found resolution in a way that neither of them could have imagined at the beginning.
My only complaint about this game was the amount of swearing that it contained. No, it wasn’t what you’d call “excessive” and, yes, I know the arguments that can be made for it being there (being in real life situations, stress, etc.). But it was the one negative for me - the only thing that was distracting (jarring me out of the game, so to speak) as I played, and I would have preferred that it was left out. JMO.
To the Moon is supposed to be released in 5 installments, and I am literally on the edge of my seat waiting for the next. Can Freebird Games involve me as completely in the next adventure they offer, as they did in To the Moon?
Oh, and the soundtrack is just as compelling as the game itself.  Don't get one without the other.

Easily one of my most favorite games of 2017. I won't go much into detail about the story but this game is phoenomal. I only have finished the main story and haven't really dived into the side missions (Yet)
Gameplay wise, if you have played the The New Order, You'll feel right at home. Apart from some minor changes, combat remains the same for the most part. You got guns, theres Nazis. You kill said Nazis, Its simple but super fun.
Storywise too, this game is amazing. Everyone is on point, the game has it's badass moments, as well as moments that would have me burst out laughing on how absurd and awesome they were. Though of course, the story isn't flawless, but it's pretty great. My main issues with the story isn't much about how it goes, but the ending. Which from what I hear is a common complaint. It feels very abrupt, in a "to be continued" sense, but regardless it is great.
Now, graphics wise I can't say much as my rig is a bit too old to run this game on it's highest settings. But from what I've see. Even on the medium graphics preset this game looks visually stunning, for anyone wondering. My setup is as follows: CPU is a Intel i5 4690K running at 4.2Ghz, GPU is a AMD Radeon R9-280X, RAM is 24GB DDR3 memeory running at 1866mhz, In most parts of the game I've been seeing the game run at around 30-60 fps, though in some areas the framerate has dropped to even as low as 15. forcing me to run the game at 720p to make it playable. The game has even perfect 21:9 ratio support. I played the game at 2560x1080 and everything works perfectly. Hud elements scale properly and aren't awkardly stuck in a 16:9 window. FOV wise, the game defaults to 90, but allows you to go up to 120, though without first warning you that the game is was made with 90 FOV in mind. Though that is not bad at all! Since a lot of other games are made with console level FOVs for their cutscenes, causing some weird problems if you try to use a normal FOV like 90. (Looking at you, Battlefield 4) Speaking of cutscenes, the pre-rendered cutscenes are in a letterbox 21:9 format. With black bars on top and bottom to make it more "cinematic", and the great thing about the is that they scale properly for 21:9 screens. As in the black bars are removed and the cutscene fills your whole screen. I absolutely applaud MachineGames for their wonderful support of 21:9.
Though, I do have my cons with this game. Not major ones, but they were a bit annoying. For the most part, the game relies too much on pre-rendered cutscenes, sometimes awkwardly switched between the two formats, making it look rather odd and out of place, other is really minor. but the weapon selection wheel is really annoying to use. A lot of the time the cursor that appears for you to select the weapon doesn't follow it fully, and has been the reason why I have died so many times trying to select the proper weapon. If you want to switch weapons, just use the top row numberkeys instead and save yourself the headache.
Oh and one more thing, THE SOUNDTRACK, Mick Gordon has done it again, making a wonderful and fitting soundtrack for the game, It doesn't have the same music system that DOOM 2016 had, but it still is wonderful and makes combat a lot more intense.
Overall, Wolfenstein II is everything that I hoped it would be. I loved The New Order, and I love this game as well, and I highly reccomend picking it up and playing it. As of this review being written the game is currently off for 30 USD, I highly suggest picking it up if you got the computer to run it.

It's a relatively realistic racing game - very forgiving, but you do have to brake for turns - and features mostly a sandbox style play. You get a car, you drive around LA and do several types of races, from organized street races, to pick-up races against roaming cars. In most cases, you bet money, it doesn't come out of nowhere like in a lot of games, except the prizes at sanctioned races.
As a side thing, you can do challenges to pick up girls. It's a bit silly, but it provides an extra interesting touch. You can pick one to ride with you and they will be the starter for street races.
The car modding is also fairly realistic, but somewhat limited. It's not Gran Turismo with 100s of options, basically a few for each part of the engine.  And the car selection is also relatively limited to imports (mostly Japan, but also VW for some reason)
To a certain extent, you make your own challenge, it's very easy to soup up your first car and completley annihilate 90% of the competition.
As an older game, it has some technical quirks. It doesn't run at a high resolution (though there are hacked exes that will do this, the rear view mirror ends up being in the wrong place). It's somewhat finicky, it takes about 2 minutes for it to start after hitting run...just nothing, then eventually it pops up. The interface was designed for a controller, so is a bit quirky. Probably not worth $10, but it goes on sale frequently for 99 cents and is easily worth that.

update 11.25.2017: I hit a little over 400 hours on this game before taking a break.  Still lots left to do.  My favorite game this year.  Really glad the devs stuck with this one.
Original review from Sept below: ========================
For me the game can probably best be summed up as "Wow, this is just a cool exploration experience."  It's amazing to me that a proceedurally generated world this vast can exist.  I've explored many star systems and worlds and have yet to find a system that has been visited by any other player.
This is a fun, imaginative, exploration game with crafting and light survival elements in normal mode, and there is permadeath if you prefer.  I'm just a little over 200 hrs in and have had a great time so far.  I've enjoyed exploring each new planet, seeing the animals, plants, learning the story of the different races, fixing up my ship, building my base, doing a few missions, and making money.  If you're the kind of player that likes exploring levels just to find the odd things that are there, you'll understand the appeal of this game.  Many times I'll just see a scenic view while driving my buggy over a desert landscape and stop to take a picture.  It has that kind of wandering feel to it. If you prefer well defined goals or to rush through the game to reach the end this may not be your game as it has a slower pace.
At it's core No Mans Sky is an exploration game.  If you need constant action this game is probably not for you as there's far less action than exploration.  There are some gun fights, and there are some space battles, but it's not the focus of the game.  You can do more fighting - it's very open world - but the design clearly lends itself more to exploration than fighting.
If I had state a couple of main cons:
- The game is a little bit grindy in places.  Early on mining ore to make money to repair my ship got dull, but I found I probably would've been better off to just start a base sooner and leave mining behind, or not spend so much effort trying to repair a wrecked ship I found.
- Inventory system is more cumbersome that I'd like, but they're working on it.
There are a few bugs here and there, but nothing that has bothered me too much.  Probably falling through map a couple times, and getting stuck or shot out of my ship are the biggest issues I've had.  The game is undergoing regular updates/patches addressing these, so it's still a game in flux and improving at a steady pace.  Substantial new ideas are still being added.
TLDR - an imaginative game for explorers.

This is not a review for the emulator, but for the game Ecco the Dolphin.
There are some things wrong with this emulator:
1.	You can’t review the games. I would have put this for Ecco's page specifically, but there’s no option to do so anymore. The couple old reviews left on steam are relics of the past. This is just dumb.
2.	Lag. The emulator is really badly optimized. That being said, the games are cheap. I wouldn’t spend more than a few bucks on a game or two, but I don’t regret giving $ for the best (and only, really) dolphin in gaming.
On to
.
This game is a rather fast-paced level based adventure that takes you through various parts of the big ocean and toward much, much stranger tides. Ecco is probably most famous for its atmosphere and mood conveyed through graphics, music, and sound effects, and it really does live up to that fame. The ocean is a beautiful and ominous, lonely place for a dolphin. Although the visuals are old by now they are colorful and sharp and make everything interesting to look at.
The music is incredible in both this genesis version and the updated sega cd version -
atmospheric, whimsical, eerie, and distinctly aquatic. Several tracks have become iconic to me just on this first playthrough, so excellent work by the composer Spencer Nilsen. Overall this game’s atmosphere could be comparable to Super Metroid in quality, and certainly up there with the best in 16-bit games.
Gameplay and design. These are the parts that haven’t aged as well.
Once you get used to it, Ecco controls decently, and it’s extremely fun to leap in and out of the water and dash around at high speeds. But he really does turn like a tank, and has the hitbox of one too. Movement can become frustrating at some of the very tight maneuvers you have to perform with this giant hunk of fusiform flesh who loses hp at the slightest touch on the fluke.
As a mammal, Ecco has to breathe air, so one of the other challenges is having a time limit underwater. I found myself dying several times not because I ran out of air, but because I was rushing to get to the surface and ran straight into an enemy, so you need to be careful
underwater and don’t go too far down before you know the layout of the depths. Ecco’s dash move damages most enemies, but sometimes it just refuses to activate if you are too close to a solid wall/obstacle. Still, this dash is very fun to build up speed with in addition to the ‘speed button’, which increases Ecco’s tail oscillation as you mash the button. The combination of the two adds some speedrunning possibility and a high risk high reward playstyle.
The last button with a function is echolocation. Ecco shoots out a visible sound wave
from his big ol’ melon. With this you can talk to other creatures
and interact with glyphs, and with optional upgrades you can also stun and kill enemies.
If you hold the button, the wave bounces back and functions as a minimap.
I love the addition of this and the sound effect it makes is mighty satisfying.
The UI of this game is clean.
All you get are two meters: 1 for air and 1 for health - and that’s all you need.
An important thing to note is that damage to your health scales exponentially. I don’t really see the porpoise of designing it this way, but it’s easy to get used to.
The first Ecco game has become somewhat infamous for its difficulty. It is inconsistent: one stage can be a breeze and the next is torture. However, one of the best features is how quickly Ecco respawns. There’s no drawn out death animation, the game sends you right back to the level’s title card in a heartbeat.
This takes away a surprising amount of the frustration from dying, or it may be I just love the music and playing as a dolphin enough that I never got too annoyed. Some of the really difficult levels (like Dark Water) were more fulfilling than frustrating to finally beat.
The one exception to this enjoyment was the last level and final boss - the only time I believe the difficulty went too far.
The last level The Machine, is an autoscrolling maze with enemies that go through walls.
If that doesn’t sound bad enough, it’s because the final boss in this North American version is the real problem.
This game runs on a password system – there are no checkpoints in levels, ever. If you die at any point - it's back to the start.
But with the final boss if you die you get sent all the way back to the beginning of The Machine – the
.
The
thought this was too difficult, so in their version they toned it down, letting you respawn back at the final boss if you die.
She also has a 1 hit kill move (in every version), but in the Japanese release this sends you
to a unique, short level The Stomach which spits you back out at the boss when you beat it.
I almost quit by this point. This was the only time I had to use a savestate to keep my sanity, and it killed a lot of the hype I had from getting this far all on my own. I wouldn’t say this last part is undoable, but it is too much for a first playthrough and thank Delphinus later versions gave you a checkpoint before the final boss.
Despite this hype-killing end I loved most of the game.
The mood/atmosphere is fantastic, the gameplay is fast and punishing but forgiving too, heck the story is even memorable and has some interesting text, especially in the secret glyphs:
(ECCO, IF WE BREATHE AIR WHY DO WE LIVE BENEATH THE WAVES?)
I have high hopes for the sequel Tides of Time, which I'll be playing next. It’s a shame this franchise is dead - the last game was all the way back on PS2 I believe (cetacean needed for that fact). I’d recommend Ecco for anyone that likes atmospheric open-level adventure games, and/or dolphins.
Because dolphins.
Alright, I finished
. To sum it up, this sequal is similar to the first but overall a better experience. It still has some of the original's problems, running on the same engine, but the final areas are a huge improvement and not unbalanced like The Machine was (there's a checkpoint before the final boss this time!) The graphics are a step up and look solid even in 2017, but I think the music was not as memorable as the first game. I didn't like the 3D sections much either, but there are only a few of them. There are a few crystals throughout the game that function as checkpoints, which is generous, but the series still doesn't explain some important objects like these at all to the player.
The settings of ToT are a lot stranger than the original, and with time travel they change often, giving the game an odd lack of the 'oceanic' feeling and more 'alien'. As such I don't think the atmosphere works as a standalone dolphin game, but it does work as a follow up to the original game.
Some stages I loved and some I hated. Lunar Bay and Skylands were unique and great, Sea of Darkness and Sky Tides were good too. The only level I actively hated was Globe Holder - I never want to do that tedious headache of a boss again.
So yeah, ToT I would recommend playing
after the original, but if you liked the first, this one is better, especially in terms of gameplay, and very doable without any savestates.
Next I'll be playing Ecco. Jr. because I'm a completionist. I'm ready for a real easy, relaxing change of pace.

This is not a racing game. This is a puzzle game.
The car follows the track, and you can click to rotate each of the track pieces. Randomly, one piece will mutate into another one. And that's the entire gameplay.
Why am I giving a negative review? Because...
* The camera angle is terrible.
* It would have been better if this game was a 2D game instead. Instead, by making it a 3D game with a fixed camera angle, the game gets artificially more difficult and more confusing. (actually, you can slightly change the camera height by clicking on a button at the left side of the screen, but the angle is still terrible)
* The extraneous graphic elements, such as trees and even clouds, serve no purpose other than trying to look good and instead obscuring your view.
* There is no animation for the track rotation. It just instantly rotates 90 degrees.
* You can only click with the left mouse button. So, you can only rotate tracks in one direction.
* There are no options. It runs in a window with a fixed size.
* It has built-in coins to implement some kind of
grinding. For what? For more cars! And for paint jobs!
* It has some kind of Facebook integration, but it does not work.
* The music gets annoying pretty fast.
* It looks like a mobile game that was quickly ported to PC without much thought. Heck, even as a mobile game it is not good.
* The game progress is saved at the Windows Registry.
* It is boring.
The PC Gaming Wiki lists some command-line options to change the resolution.
I like the core gameplay concept, but I dislike this implementation. Avoid this game.

There are so many design flaws in this game that I don't know where to start. By far the worst part of this game is the characters. The cast in TNO (The New Order) were excellent, but the hard work that went into their writing has been butched by the changes in TNC (The New Colossus).
The once caring and supportive Anya is now running into gunfights with Nazis whilst heavily pregnant. Nothing in her actions has any substance this time around, her personality feels like it has been erased so she can simply be BJ's baby making machine. She also keeps getting naked but I can't figure out why.
In TNO Frau Engel was successfully portrayed as a perceptive but creepy power-mad opponent. TNC tries and fails to replicate this with long, overdone, in-your-face close ups and some really weird lines that just don't fit with her character. Oh, and she's also the mother of six or seven children for some reason, including a plot device character who adds no real value to the story.
Like Anya, Wyatt's personality has also been wiped clean. Now he's constantly tripping on acid. I don't know if this is supposed to be comic relief, but it ends up being another plot device and culminates in a truly awful speech at the end of the campaign. I didn't replay the game to see what they did with Fergus Reid - I don't think I could take that much disappointment from one sequel.
Max Hass hardly does anything... except beat Set Roth (now a bumbling old man defeated by the simplest of problems) at a game of chess. And don't get me started with Caroline: her role was the most powerful one in the game, but you only have to play through the demo to understand why that is not an applaud to the plot. Caroline's struggle with Frau Engel at the begining of the game could have been mirrored by BJ's showdown with Engel at the end, but the opportunity to form a good plot was missed completely.
The new characters are all one-dimensional. Suddenly we're taking orders from an overly-aggressive Grace Walker whose sole job is to boss people around and find new verbal insults for the Nazis you're sent to kill. Then we're introduced to a moonshiner who... well I'm still wondering what exactly we needed him for. He just cusses and talks about killing Nazis, so he could have been anyone. His philosophical conflict with BJ lasts about sixty seconds, after which he becomes the same as all the others - homogenous and structureless. There's nothing specific about any of these characters that really make them stand out.
Without comparing it to TNO there is some fairly good gameplay, but there are some areas that lack a lot of polish. The art direction is obsessed with gloomy levels pierced by bright lights that blind you to anything near or behind them. Enemies blend into the grainy scenery, not because of good camoflauge, but because there is nothing to make them 'pop' out from the backdrop. The three "contraptions" that you can choose from are simply three different methods of getting from one section of a level to the next; the level design is far too restrictive to promote creativity in the way you play.
The game's setting might be trying to ride some kind of 'MERICUH! hype train but it felt extremely trite. BJ's backstory, told by flashbacks, felt tacked-on, whereas in TNO it was delivered subtly by the protagonist's tortured inner monologue. The previous game's atmosphere was that of a doomed protagonist determined to fight to the end. This game doesn't have anything like that. I don't think it has an atmosphere at all. If you replaced the Nazis with aliens or killer robots the plot would barely change.
In summary: the narrative felt forced and amateurish. The gameplay was not improved and the versatile laserkraftwerk has been replaced by a simple grenade launcher. Every single situation can be covered by the upgraded assault rifle - unless you need a supressor there is never a need to change weapons. The level design is underwhelming, failing to meet the bar of the previous game.

I recommend this game under the scrutiny that the developers will fix some issues. At this current point, wait for it to go on sale, around 25 to 30 bucks. After the issues are fixed, Absolutely worth the 60 dollar tag. My issues with the game are as follows...
1. Too, damn, hard. I finished the game (minor miracle, honestly) on the second to easiest difficulty setting. Everyone I know who has played this game put it on the easiest, because it was too hard. There were more than a few times I was frustrated to the point of quitting. Again, I was on level 2 of 7 on the difficulty settings. Keep that in mind if you play this.
2. Physics tearing was getting ridiculous by the end of the game. It really seemed like the farther I got into the campaign, the worse it got. Near the end of the game, there were three weapons I just couldn't use because the tearing was so bad. That definetly added to the challenge.
3. The console/devmode issue after the November update is a joke. Around the middle of the campaign, the game updated, and the next time I launched it, this issue was present, my first Autosave file was corrupt, and I couldn't gain anymore achievements. That was honestly the point where I almost gave up. It wasn't the achievements, per se, it was the fact that there was no option to disable the devmode/console in the game itself. I had to look online, and those who didn't just give up, figured out that changing a launch option with +devMode_enable 0 and a few other tweaks fixed that issue. By the time I found this out, I was almost done, and just wanted to finish the game at that point.
Those issues aside, it is a beautiful game with a storyline that doesn't pull any punches. That I really appreciated. Dealing with the racism of the 60s, romance during war, drugs, Nazis, etc. I was impressed. So, great storyline, and the ending was... ok. Not really the best they could have done, but good nonetheless.
The gameplay is great. The weapons are pretty varied, some are unique, and the combat in general is good. Again, tough at times, I can't stress that enough, but good. The stealth is... eh. Not the best, and at times infuriating, but stealth really isn't the way to go here. Keep moving, shooting, and don't try anything fancy in the way of melee kills. Melee kills during a firefight aren't fast, and open you to lots of damage, so just don't. Granted the stealth melee kills are great, but you can break stealth so easily in the game, just don't sweat it when you get found out.
All that being said, on a 1-10, I'd give it a 7. It's a great game, and with a few fixes, it could be a 9 or 10.

NOTE:  I bought this game at the onset of Atlas Rises Update.
I was told about this game from a friend of mine who also plays open world survival games.  I have a deep love for the genre and its provided me countless hours of enjoyment in virtual worlds.  When the release date actually arrived, I found myself caught in a dilemna because it became readily apparent just how much of a stir Hello Games prompted but didn't deliver.  I felt that the community reacted very poorly to it.  I didn't purchase it.
If there is one thing that life has taught me in all my years is that is best to wait and let things cook for a little while longer.  In the age of Pre-alpha and beta games (I refuse to buy into them) I've really noticed a hot trend of garbage games coming into their own over time.  That is usually when I'll buy into them.  This also allows me to skip and fast forward past the Content Zergs who overload servers and then leave and go whine on the forums why things didn't work out for them.  I just can't be a part of that anymore.  Coincidentally I also never see movies on opening night either.  lol.
I'm so glad I waited.  While I do notice that large groups of vocal folk will pass this game over because of its procedural generation (a common complaint is how random but formulaic procedural generation is, and they'd be correct to say so.) the real reward in my humble opinion is on the strange and rare occasions where things just fall into place.  That's the real gold and often the food for some of the most wonderful screenshots that players conjure.  Sure you'll run into a droning system of odd analogues but then there's always that one memorable system that totally jumps at you.   Those are fun feels for creative people, and I consider that my meat and drink in No Man's Sky.
The Good is that many difficulties and goals are now overcome, and the developers (Sean Murray included) continue to press on and make their game better.  In a year if I look back, I wonder how far have the changes gone?  Will I even recognize old haunts anymore?  There are already reviews in play that already say so from a year back from players that bought in at launch.  Multiplayer as of now (Atlas Rises 1.35 update) is still shaky, but there are changes coming down the pipe and I even heard a rumour about global chat.  I'm excited for that change.  I love tradeskilling, and I want more of it.
The Bad is that there are still some bugs that really impact the little things.   Collision and hit box sizes can be janky but mostly not harmful unless you find yourself slipping through the terrain into the netherworld.  Procedural generation often finds a way to make common things even more common, and thus less special.   Ships are not entirely customizable nor can they be built.   You can't upgrade unless you get an entirely new ship.  I find that the empty slots between equipment, cause me to loose a lot of valuable time ship hunting because I'll find just the RIGHT aesthetic but then what's under the hood is disappointing.  I'll find ships that are well configured in slots, but will be very weak in terms of stats.
No matter how much cash you have, its never enough.   Nanites eventually loose their value over time, due to owning all the blueprints.   You can quickly go from tutorial to end game if you're smart enough to take advantage of both trading and tradeskilling.  By the time you own a Freighter, any freighter, most of your problems are already going away in normal mode.   Much of the game has been polished to the degree they proposed back in the beginning, but that path is fraught with little problems that still need some attention.
The Ugly is when the new and the old community clash.   That's really the only thing that goes beyond reason for me.  Listening to the complaints of the first buyers and the overly whiny negativity gets old really fast.   Many of those folks just haven't gotten over their own disappointment.  Troll Culture is en vogue and critique with thoughtlessness brings everything down; even things you may normally enjoy.   Negativity is viral.  Wait for a sale if you are skeptical.  Never, ever read the comments.
At the time of this review, im over 340 hours with this game, and I've completed all the main and side quests.  I'm not filthy rich, but im comfortable enough to spend most of my time tweaking my basebuilding skills, or just exploring.  I'm an avid shiphunter.  The theme and the story are very much couched in existentialism.  You're an explorer in a vast universe.  Why are you there?  What are you doing?  If those are not questions you are willing to wrestle with in No Man's Sky, then the game might not be for you.
But to re-iterate, the vastness is compelling when it does come together.   Warping over to the next galaxy hoping to see and interact with something unique?   Suddenly, a violent storm or attack sends you on a spiral?  The best times in the game for me are when I'm struggling.  If that has any appeal to you, then No Man's Sky is definitely for you.

I really, really love this one. The original Darksiders was fantastic, and reminded me of an open-world Zelda game with God of War style combat, and this improves on that in every way. A really good upgrade/leveling system, nice crafting mechanic, & impoved combat, combined with an even better story and an INCREDIBLE soundtrack equals a strong thumbs up from me. There are also 2 major "worlds," each with a good sized map and plenty of variety in the areas, along with 2 more minor "worlds" that are pretty much just dungeons but are set apart due to the story. I've seen an insane amount of whining about this remaster, mainly because they didn't get it for free (upon release, the devs gave it away to those who had bought the franchise pack, and heavily discounted it for owners of the original, resulting in people losing their minds they had to pay a few bucks for it, even though they already had the orginal game and all the DLC), but don't listen to them, the developers did a great job here, albeit with a couple of hiccups. The dialog and/or background music occasionally cuts out when interacting with an NPC, but that's about it. The visuals got a nice little upgrade (nothing major), and all the DLC is included. The DLC weapons are pretty much trash that might be good for a level or 2, but it doesn't take long for you to be able to craft your own weapons and gear (that quite frankly can be really OP). The DLC dungeons are fun if you're craving more content, and you can pick up some nice gear and such that can be broken down via the crafting system. On top of all this, the main character is pretty likable for an apocalyptic horseman named Death.
Just a really, really FUN game, that I recommend very much. Can't wait for Darksiders 3.

Even after all these years, this game is amazing. Sure, Punkbuster doesn't work, you have to rely on server admins banning potential cheaters, but man this game is so good. On discount for 10 euros it can provide hundred times more fun than any free to play game, it's graphics did age really well and gameplay itself is really solid too. And that's just rating the multiplayer part of the game as SP campaign is definitely one of my favorite in CoD series too.
Best part about this game is that it's multiplayer is completely open to custom servers and modding.
Because of modding, you can get all maps from other CoD games, including newer titles such as MW2, MW3 or Black Ops series (yes, entire series!), guns from other CoD's ranging from WW2 style of CoD2 to futuristic stuff of Black Ops 2. And that's not even the end of it as there is also good Star Wars mod, which provides some nice CoD gameplay with Star Wars skin on top of it.
Generally speaking I didn't encounter many sketchy cheaters as I actually expected, it's still very playable. There are loads of populated servers even when not playing in primetime and community overall seems rather nice.
So in nutshell you get:
- Maps from CoD2 to Black Ops 2 (+ Star Wars mod)
- Guns from CoD2 to Black Ops 2 (+ Star Wars mod) including customisation support
- Game that still looks decent and runs on pretty much everything (I have very stable 60fps on Macbook Air)
This game aged well, I was really skeptical when buying it (although on sale), but damn I had a really good time with it so far. If there is one Call of Duty you should definitely buy on PC, it's this one. One of the best FPS games of all time, and trust me, I can be very critical of Call of Duty franchise.
If Counter Strike is too hardcore for you, and your PC can't run newer CoD with decent FPS, this is probably the best shooter out there to get, even after all these years. Just turn off your brain, run and shoot - that's the best part about CoD online gameplay. Definitely worth the 10,- € price tage on sale, especially when compared to free to play games, which will eventually force you to spend way more on them.
If you love FPS games, buy this.

This is my first review, so please bear with me.
I'll start by saying that the game was a 14.3 GB download, and the size on the disk for me is 20.6 GB. The version I purchased here in North America included both English and Japanese voice options. The game also came packaged with a fairly decent amount of graphical options compared to the two previous installments.
The graphics options are as follows:
Display Format (Choose between Windowed or Borderless fullscreen)
Display Resolution (1920 x 1080, 1600 x 900, 1440 x 810, 1366 x 768, 1280 x 720)
Scale Display Area
Colour Correction
Glare Adjustment
Depth of Field Adjustment
Shadowing
Lighting
Texture Filtering
Frame Rate (Choose between fixed 30, or Dynamic 60)
The included DLC is very nice, but quite overpowered. It makes the boss battles super easy, so I advise using normal equipment if it's your first playthrough to avoid ruining the enjoyment of the game. I believe most of the DLC is included in the game as well, minus the Aerith garb.
Finally, the performance of the game is pretty good on my end. I'm running a mostly smooth 60fps on the highest possible graphical settings. The framerate never drops below 60 in battles, and seemingly only drops in the open world when you're loading in a new area, or many new NPC at once. Even then, it only lasts for 1-2 seconds for me.
All in all, this game is a really good port. It's quite a step up from the previous two games in the series. Square Enix taking the extra time to release it made a large difference in the quality. It's an even larger step up from the console versions, and I would highly recommend any fans of the series to give this a go. It's easily worth the $17.99

This is one of the most solid remasters I've ever played. Like many on here, I grew up with this game and I consider this specific one as one LucasArts' crown jewels in their adventure game library. Those that are fans of the game, know the game. If you like adventure games, this one is essential playing. The remaster itself is so well done that it's apparent a lot of TLC went into its making. Switching between the original and remastered artwork is seamless and additional interface features have been added. Among those is a highlight feature that illuminates interactable objects and environment elements. Another is gamepad integration that works fairly well if you want to kick back and play on the living room TV. The audio is crisp and punchier than the original due to original tape access by the dev team. Everything has been redrawn and animated and everything is done with surgical care. The game is now 16:9 and seeing this game fill my HDTV was gaming nirvana. This remaster commands a second play through just for the developer commentary.

Full Throttle.  If I had to name 10 games from my childhood, Full Throttle would definitely be on the top 10, if not the first or second game mentioned. As for cons, the only things I can think of is there are the odd bugs here and there (eg. audio slightly off by a millisecond when changing scenes sometimes, credits didn't display for some reason, etc), some of the puzzles do show their age, and the game is rather short at around 3 hours (if you remember the puzzles)...but that said, if you enjoyed this game back in 1995, then buying the remaster is a no-brainer.  Looking forward to them adding cards (in future I guess?), and will likely replay it at that time with commentary on to get the full experience.

Pro cycling manager receives a few improvements each year, but also a few setbacks. This year is no exception.
What I dislike:
I miss the old way of setting up the schedule for each rider, and PLEASE bring back music while riding! I understand a lot of players turn it off, but I don't understand why music at the very least cannot be an option. Though, these are minor flaws in my opinion. At times, the breakaways can be almost inhumanely strong, and the peloton waaay too passive. I feel like I have to do all the work in order to ride them back in, the other teams are just passively riding along. The game is still poorly optimized, so you will experience lag even on high end PCs. The water bottle fetching is still a bit of a hassle.
What I like:
I love the new method of setting up trains by dragging and dropping a rider onto another. This was a huge improvement from earlier versions where you had to click "protect" on every rider in the exact order you wanted, and you couldn't switch positions between two because this would ruin the whole setup. This improvement alone is a reason to buy the game this year. Graphics has improved slightly, and the new songs are pretty cool. Quick simulations seem a bit more fair, and winning stages is always a huge rush!

Party Hard Tycoon is a wild ride, but does it live up to the hype? Or are you the person that has to inject it with HYPE!
Let's just start right off comparing the original Party Hard to Tycoon. Is it the same? How are they different? Tiny Build shows off its cleverness with this new release in a few unique ways. Right off the bat with the glaring obvious is the re-using of the entire Party Hard universe and engine. Looking back at the first game, it becomes apparent that it would be an absolute travesty to throw away all those sprites and levels, which are pretty darn magnificent in all their pixel glory. Tycoon recycles this all for a completely new game--stressing the fact that it IS a brand new game, even if old characters pop their head in for a visit.
In Tycoon, you play a party promoter, starting from the bottom and working your way to the top. It's like a coke-fueled, neon Cinderella story of sorts. You throw trash parties in the beginning, working with a meager budget, earning little by little. The success of your parties lands you new jobs from a very peculiar cast of characters. The dialog is appropriately channeled through texting--the authenticity of it all being pushed further by things like typos and text-language. The characters are bold, loud and completely unapologetic, as is the person you play. It's all very interesting and instead of being a nuisance, the story ends up being a welcomed side track to it all (not to mention how you progress via rewards!).
You work on a calendar, which is marked for better or for worse on buffs for certain days, days that aren't good for your parties, and a colouring system. Since you work at a low level and climb up a ladder, there's different clientele to impress at every corner. The poor and the rich have their own flavour of a good time, and it's up to you to tailor accordingly. It's a smart game, and a lot of it is rooted in the tracking of your money and resources. You have to build a fan base, simulating word of mouth. You gain rewards for 'likes', and lose fans when you don't fulfill them. If you can't keep your 'hype' going, the party ends. It's addicting to say in the least--each party you throw having to be better than the last. Seeing the screen light up like a Christmas tree with either attendance, likes, hype or money is more than enough to keep me playing.
You're dropped in at the deep end. There's no tutorial level or much in terms of live help, except the occasional mouseover suggesting if a piece of decor might be good or bad for a certain vibe. The mechanics of losing and gaining fans, followers, aren't clear either. To me, this obfuscation adds a good dimension of gut feeling, and trial and error. Still haven't quite figured it out but it's a heck of a lot of fun getting there.
Despite a few bugs (some of the text messages were unavailable, when notification was showing, and it seems perhaps some placeholder text is still left in there), it seems like Tiny Build is on its A game pre-releasing in early access. I can't find much to say that's wrong about this game if it's your type of play--it's fun to get invested, fun to throw the parties themselves, and fun to live the life of a party planner.

For the most part, Tycoon games do not interest me.  Management sim mechanics are a good compliment to games like State of Decay and the recent XCOM installments, but it isn’t really my cup of tea when it is the main focus of a game.  There has to be something special to make me want to play a game in this genre.  Luckily, Tiny Build’s Party Hard Tycoon has an interesting premise and aesthetic that intrigues and encourages you to keep playing to see all the shenanigans that can unfold, despite many rough edges.
“When it’s time to Party…”
Party Hard Tycoon tasks you, a nameless protagonist with a high amount of starting capital, to throw the best parties in town and attract a following of socialites of various backgrounds.  These range from the haughty aristocrats who will only attend the fanciest of gatherings, to people who enjoy getting drunk and fighting in a field out in the sticks, college kids looking for weeknight thrills, and a few others in between.
To make these parties happen you must plan the theme, location, and for the day of the week accordingly. For example:  A Drum n’ Bass party might be best hosted at a suburban house with young people in the area on Wednesday, but it might not go over so well with a tough-guy or sophisticated crowd.  After picking a theme you then place equipment like speakers, lights, kegs, and bars.  The latter two generate revenue that you can use to throw more expensive shindigs.  The key to this is placing revenue items near speakers and lights so your partygoers will be led to purchase more food & beverages.  You can also enlist personnel that will help generate hype around a specific area so if the party is dying down, you can revive the vibes and GET HYPE!  The more Hype you generate, the more fans you will receive at the end of the party.  Fans will invite friends to their parties, and you will gain more money from the buzz.
You will start at a map screen that shows color-coordinated pips denoting the social group of potential new fans in the area.  These pips indicate which demographic of people are near certain venues.  You are only allowed access to two venues and themes at the start so it can get confusing as to how the player will appease these other groups.  The tutorial takes the form of conversations sent to your phone with a few dialogue options. You are instructed on how to generate hype, revenue, and how to gain more fans by using the right theme for the right location.
Unfortunately, the game only gives you this information once.  Then it is entirely dependent on you to have absorbed all this information as you plan more parties.  As you can imagine, it was frustrating to try and remember everything in that initial info dump.  A glossary or help index would’ve really improved my experience, it seems almost insane that there isn’t one.
In fact, there seems to be a LOT of information the game withholds from the player.  Item descriptions are missing for many items in the décor section, Food/Beverage items are vague on costs for refilling stocks, and some prompts only appear sporadically.  The version I played of this game was an Early Access edition though, so hopefully refinements have been made for the retail version.
“Okay, Nobody Parties but Me!”
As you gain revenue from charging cover and selling refreshments at your parties, you gain access to more lavish options to furnish new venues. Oddly the same equipment from the lower-tier venues costs more, but the hijinks that can unfold is even more fun to witness.
You can hire sumo wrestlers to encourage guests to buy food, kung fu masters to liven up the dance floor, and literally The Joker to steal money from guests to add to your revenue.  The personnel all use these abilities on command and have a cooldown so it is wise to have them near speakers and lights for maximum effect.  You also want to have security guards for certain parties because a couple themes can lead to fights breaking out.  Waiters, especially “Vampire Waiters,” are a necessity for almost every party as you will need them to quickly refill the refreshments and keep guests from leaving.  As stated before though these refill prompts sporadically appear and not being able to dictate which tables get served is super frustrating. The wacky cast of personnel is one of the main highlights of this game and I kept enjoyed figuring out who might be best suited to what kind of party I was trying to throw.
The difficulty ramps up in a big way when you have to cater to the highest class of people and you have not leveled up enough to get a variety personnel, themes, or venues to cater to these high society types.  There are sometimes whole weeks where you can only throw these parties and if you haven’t focused on appealing to this demographic, it can be tough to turn a profit.  But the game is still zany enough to entertain up until this cliff.  I was constantly asking myself if this was a game I wanted to see through to completion, but couldn’t come up with a compelling reason to keep going past this point.
Will We Always Party Hard?
Party Hard Tycoon is a fun but flawed experience.  I enjoyed the aesthetic of this game so much, but felt a huge disconnect with how many mechanics go under-explained and how little variety there really is under the hood.  The music thumps and the cast of characters is fun, but I found myself getting really bored towards the halfway point when the difficulty outweighed my actual enjoyment of the whole package.  It’s kind of like a party at college where you some friends invite you; there’s a good turnout, but the kegs are dry and everyone seems to be moving on to the house down the street full of booze.

Unfortunately, Party Hard Tycoon doesn't quite make the cut.
At it's core, the music is great, the animation and art is fitting, but the gameplay is shallow and empty.  You are tasked with running a party each night in one of many different venues, after you provide investments to them such as decor, speakers, lighting and vendors.  At the start, the tutorial is expectant of the player to achieve the goal with very little instruction - once said goal is achieved (though what one may consider a 'miracle'), only then does the tutorial offer up *additional* information that really should have been provided up front (such as what each type of fan is, or how much you should charge at a venue and its impacts - but by now you've probably figured it out.  In my case, it took seven parties before I achieved the first tutorial goal - in other words: the game is poor at explaining its own mechanics; icons are unlabelled and many tool tips do not function).
Party Hard Tycoon falls shorts in that it's barely a tycoon at all.  Outside of unlocking new venues and types of parties (each party type is matched with a venue for 'maximum hype' effect), or other staff members, the game is pretty much completly seen.  Run a few parties and all the games mechanics have been revealed.  You're expected to continuously repeat parties until funds exist to move to another venue and invest, only to rince and repeat to yet another venue in an endless loop, unlocking nothing more to the game itself then new art to see.
There are many interesting factors presented to the player, such as "themes" to a party (VIP only, Ladies Night, etc.) that modify party-goers or entry fees, or types of people that visit your party to disrupt it (where a Cop would be handy), but otherwise the gameplay is very bland and uncaptivating.
A lot of the problems of the game stem from just lack of explaination (Why does that character have a thumbs down?  Why is there not enough hype?  How do I get more people here?) or what is explained is confusing (the tutorial jokingly tells you that speakers in a bathroom are a bad idea, yet, the AI characters will enter a bathroom and exclaim 'Where is the music?!').
Ultimately, I did not find Party Hard Tycoon enjoyable.  I will give it another opportunity after substantial updates, but for right now, it's more like a demo than a game with how empty it is.

I bought this game because I thought it would improve upon its predecessor. What I disliked mainly about the original Darksiders was the mediocre voice acting, flat and predictable character archetypes (e.g., the warrior angel obsessed with purity, the no nonsense protagonist, demons that wanna wipe out humanity, etc.), and choppy animations.
Sadly, this has all of the same problems, and only improves on the first one slightly. The voice actor for Death is well matched to the character he plays. He really does sound like the embodiment of death, a little bit of purr, but with the tiniest bit of medium-high whine, to give it what would probably be likened to a 'cunning' voice. But, like most games in 'Ye Olde' settings, his voice acting is exaggerated and not believable. So, while it's better than the first game, Darksiders II still falls victim to that shortcoming.
The character Death, just like War, is boring and undeveloped. He has no personality beyond 'I must kill whatever obstacle stands in my way, and sound very grim about it'. In fact, he plays the same way War did. One would think that Death would have a different fighting style than the other Horseman, but in reality the only difference is the main weapon being a pair of scythes rather than a sword. To that end there have been no improvements made to the characters or the mechanics, meaning that again, the game falls short here.
Last and ugliest, the animations are jittery. While to most this seems trivial, it's a big deal to me. Growing up, the games I played most were Super Mario Sunshine, Mario vs. Donkey Kong, and Wind Waker. Those games were made at a time when fewer technologies were available, but yet have smoother animations than this more modern game does. For this I mean to point out how the character turns. In the previous three games, when a character runs in one direction and turns around, it takes a split second to stop their forward momentum and move backwards. The same goes for any change in direction. But in Darksiders when you stop pressing the forward arrow and press the right arrow instead, Death is instantly facing to the right and moving at full speed in that direction. They made a small effort when he does a 180, but skipped out on doing the work for the other directions. The momentum on horseback is fine, so it begs the question why the animators got lazy when it came to on foot movement.
The meat of this game is hack 'n' slash. It does that. It's got a lot of flashy combos and you feel cool when you can actually pull them off. You can spin your scythes, throw them, and even bring out a ghost of your 'reaper' form in one of the longer ones. So if you want a little bit of extra 'God of War' fun, it should satisfy yet. It's not well done at all, but can satisfy that urge if you aren't the type to notice or care about the rest.

Besides that the game runs smooth at 60 FPS on the 980TI (Not really required to max the game) with all settings set to "Advanced" which I am guessing is the highest setting of the two options for each category (lighting textures etc).
The game doesn't have a launcher anymore, it simply launches straight into the game in windowed mode and from there you can use the drop down menus to adjust the options to your liking. The resolutions for now are quite limited, especially for someone with a higher resolution than 1080p, thankfully I only have a 1080p monitor, so that's not currently a problem for me.
You can pick from two options in each category such as lighting and textures, Advanced and standard, advanced being the "Ultra" option.
You can go into full screen after selecting your resolution by either pressing LALT+ENTER or selecting the "Full Screen" option from the drop down. Note that the full screen is not an actual fullscreen, but rather a borderless fullscreen, so don't have any apps running that have a tendancy to be "always on top" since they will get in the way. You can change the settings in game by taking your mouse pointer to the top of the screen which will bring up the drop down menus again but in fullscreen.
I would reccomend playing the game with a controller, since that is what the game is catering more towards and you can change whether the game shows Keyboard controls or gamepad controls, as this is not done automatically, but is an option in the settings menu of the game which I personally don't mind doing, since I only have to do it once as I am using a controller to play the game.

Okay, new review, new computor. Ill put my current specs at the bottom of this one but above the old review.
First off... game runs terribly, and I mean this. Dont expect to get a flawless 60fps even on an SSD, GTX1080 or a Titan card, i7 and all that. This game was MADE for consoles that were limited to 256mb (megabytes) and 512mb (yes, half a gig) of ram. the ps3 and xbox 360 respectively.
In fact, I seen a very modest improvement switching OFF of my SSD to a mechanical drive. The reason seems to be the way this game deals with culling. Everything is unloaded and loaded in a furious pace to stay within the 256 or 512 megabytes of ram and on an SSD, this happens so fast and so often it actually kills the graphics engine which is the crystal works engine that ff13, 13-2 and FF14 (before realm reborn) used.
Do not.. under any circumstance buy this game expecting it to run well.. it just wont.. it actively CANT run well on new hardware.
In fact, I suggest building a new old pc for this game, under 4 gigs of ram and a radeon 4800 equivelent graphics card with a slow mechanical drive. Basically try to emulate the speed of an xbox 360 or ps3 and the game will run better.
Also this game runs in windowed or borderless mode, no actual fullscreen support.
All graphics options are basically a TOGGLE, you get normal.. and advanced. And there are only about 7 or so. This is more bare bones than about any PC game ever released in the past 20 years. So other than resolution you dont have really any control of the graphics of this game.
Controller for 360 is supported but not ps3 at least not prompts, supposedly there is a mod to add that in but it has mixed results. Also you need a mod to get you all the outerworld costumes and the siegfried garb you get for completing the demo which I think doesnt exist on pc.
This game comes with almost all the DLC besides the Aeris (flower girl) garb so this version will always be incomplete compared to my xbox 360 savefile which has ever dlc (i bought the flower girl off of ebay for 15$.. not proud of that but I have a perfect dlc collection on it)
The game runs around 15fps to 60fps in luxerion on SSD, around 50-60fps on a sata mechanical hdd (see what I mean) The sand dunes on both ssd and mechanical ran fine, yusenaan got down to almost single digits on ssd, and gets to 30fps on mechanical and stays around 50fps.

NOTE:  I bought this game at the onset of Atlas Rises Update.
I was told about this game from a friend of mine who also plays open world survival games.  I have a deep love for the genre and its provided me countless hours of enjoyment in virtual worlds.  When the release date actually arrived, I found myself caught in a dilemna because it became readily apparent just how much of a stir Hello Games prompted but didn't deliver.  I felt that the community reacted very poorly to it.  I didn't purchase it.
If there is one thing that life has taught me in all my years is that is best to wait and let things cook for a little while longer.  In the age of Pre-alpha and beta games (I refuse to buy into them) I've really noticed a hot trend of garbage games coming into their own over time.  That is usually when I'll buy into them.  This also allows me to skip and fast forward past the Content Zergs who overload servers and then leave and go whine on the forums why things didn't work out for them.  I just can't be a part of that anymore.  Coincidentally I also never see movies on opening night either.  lol.
I'm so glad I waited.  While I do notice that large groups of vocal folk will pass this game over because of its procedural generation (a common complaint is how random but formulaic procedural generation is, and they'd be correct to say so.) the real reward in my humble opinion is on the strange and rare occasions where things just fall into place.  That's the real gold and often the food for some of the most wonderful screenshots that players conjure.  Sure you'll run into a droning system of odd analogues but then there's always that one memorable system that totally jumps at you.   Those are fun feels for creative people, and I consider that my meat and drink in No Man's Sky.
The Good is that many difficulties and goals are now overcome, and the developers (Sean Murray included) continue to press on and make their game better.  In a year if I look back, I wonder how far have the changes gone?  Will I even recognize old haunts anymore?  There are already reviews in play that already say so from a year back from players that bought in at launch.  Multiplayer as of now (Atlas Rises 1.35 update) is still shaky, but there are changes coming down the pipe and I even heard a rumour about global chat.  I'm excited for that change.  I love tradeskilling, and I want more of it.
The Bad is that there are still some bugs that really impact the little things.   Collision and hit box sizes can be janky but mostly not harmful unless you find yourself slipping through the terrain into the netherworld.  Procedural generation often finds a way to make common things even more common, and thus less special.   Ships are not entirely customizable nor can they be built.   You can't upgrade unless you get an entirely new ship.  I find that the empty slots between equipment, cause me to loose a lot of valuable time ship hunting because I'll find just the RIGHT aesthetic but then what's under the hood is disappointing.  I'll find ships that are well configured in slots, but will be very weak in terms of stats.
No matter how much cash you have, its never enough.   Nanites eventually loose their value over time, due to owning all the blueprints.   You can quickly go from tutorial to end game if you're smart enough to take advantage of both trading and tradeskilling.  By the time you own a Freighter, any freighter, most of your problems are already going away in normal mode.   Much of the game has been polished to the degree they proposed back in the beginning, but that path is fraught with little problems that still need some attention.
The Ugly is when the new and the old community clash.   That's really the only thing that goes beyond reason for me.  Listening to the complaints of the first buyers and the overly whiny negativity gets old really fast.   Many of those folks just haven't gotten over their own disappointment.  Troll Culture is en vogue and critique with thoughtlessness brings everything down; even things you may normally enjoy.   Negativity is viral.  Wait for a sale if you are skeptical.  Never, ever read the comments.
At the time of this review, im over 340 hours with this game, and I've completed all the main and side quests.  I'm not filthy rich, but im comfortable enough to spend most of my time tweaking my basebuilding skills, or just exploring.  I'm an avid shiphunter.  The theme and the story are very much couched in existentialism.  You're an explorer in a vast universe.  Why are you there?  What are you doing?  If those are not questions you are willing to wrestle with in No Man's Sky, then the game might not be for you.
But to re-iterate, the vastness is compelling when it does come together.   Warping over to the next galaxy hoping to see and interact with something unique?   Suddenly, a violent storm or attack sends you on a spiral?  The best times in the game for me are when I'm struggling.  If that has any appeal to you, then No Man's Sky is definitely for you.

At launch, this game really was not worth it even at 80% discount - now, at 50% discount this was a pleasant buy, the story is engaging, the controls despite their console feel work well, and overal the game is very smooth.
Of course, this game is still far from perfect, there is very little variation from one world to the next, missions start to feel repetitive really fast, and the whole exocraft mechanic feels tacked on, introducing 2 unique crafting ingredients that even within exocrafts are barely used at all, and despite the effort required to unlock these ingredients they are almost without value in the market place.
The money system is perhaps my next complaint, the way it is currently setup means you spend 90% of the early game grinding for 10 minutes to fill your inventory, spend another 10 minutes going to a space station and selling your loot, then repeating this a dozen times until you finally have the millions of credits needed to perform a single ship or multitool upgrade that is actually worth making.
The economy needs major work, as most non-grindy credit sources are from exploration, giving at best some 5000 credits, a mere drop in the bucket of your average 1.5 million credits needed to upgrade your ship to next the level - not even considering the hundreds of millions needed to get yourself a freighter.
Another complaint is the base system, what is there is incredibly well designed, but there is honestly very little to actually do.
Once more a situation that feels like exocraft happens, in that a whole bunch of ingredients are needed for the base building process, but those ingredients are not balanced into the rest of the game properly, causing a heavy dissonance that breaks immersion.
All in all, if you enjoy space, exploration and a compelling story supported by a good PC-friendly control scheme, then go and buy this game at 50% off, but I cannot recommend this game, even now, at the full price tag, not until helloGames gets around to really integrating all the separate parts of this game into a proper whole.

Wolfenstein 2 the new colossus builds up on everything that made Wolfenstein the New Order and improves the formula. Even though the game makes a good job at summarizing what happened in the New Order, not playing Wolftenstein the New Order when starting Wolfenstein the New Colossus would be missing a great story, because ultimately it's what makes the Wolfenstein Reboot the masterpiece they are :  A great story. Both games (even the three of them if you play the Old Blood, which I would recommend) piece themselves together perfectly, and eventually you're playing a great Action FPS, but you're also enjoying a great story. This is a tough story, one that doesn't shy away from showing the true nature of the Nazi reich, but it does so in a perfectly built dystopia, mixing real and dystopian elements, genuine and caricatural facets so it never really makes you face an horror story just to face an horror story. It is thus a perfect distraction for grown up people. White Supremacist will have to face the cold hard reality of their hatred, which would help explain some people disagreeing with the game. After all, the world has changed very much since The New Order released.
In terms of content, The New Colossus has changed the formula slightly, and you end up with a more tactical game. This is best seen while fighting heavily armored enemies, or trying to sneak your way into ennemy territory. The New Order was letting you sneak quite easily when you could sneak. The New Colossus still lets you try, but it requires more patience and skills to achieve the same, and the commanders you need to dispatch are more often than not entranched in hard to reach areas. On the other side, heavily armored enemies are easier to dispatch thanks to a stronger firepower and a more tactical approach to those fights (you can either empty your entire magazine on an enemy, or identity its weakness and dispatch it quickly). The way perks work have been changed and it will be a matter of taste whether you prefer this way or not. I struggled at first but had loads of fun playing with those perks.
The game has a great duration, and given you're doing the side activities, is likely to take about 30 hours to finish. Less if you shy away from side activities and treasure hunts, more if you do the challenges. It has also 2 distinct timeline, and even though they don't change much, they at least change your signature weapon on top of changing the story a bit. So if you're completionist, double that.
Overall, I'd say this is the best single player FPS of the year. Way better than Titanfall 2 in my opinion. Hard to compare it to Doom as both games are very different but I couldn't name one my favourite over the other.
Last but not least, this game looks absolutely gorgeous. It runs way better than the New Order thanks to the use of Id Engine 6, far better than Id Engine 5. If you played Doom, you know what you're getting. Performance wise, it never broke a sweat playing at 5160 x 2160 Maxxed (Ultra wide 4K) on a Titan Xp. I'd expect a 1080 to deliver proper 4K performance at near max, and a 1070 to do 4K at very high, 1440p without sweating, and 1080p in the > 120 fps.

Party Hard Tycoon is a party management game that uses the Party Hard universe (and a lot of its assets) to bring life to parties, rather than the death the original game has you create.
The aim of the game is to create the best parties possible and make enough of a profit to ensure your next one is even better. You start with a reasonable budget but dear lord don't make the same mistake I did and spend it all on one party (leave the damn DJ table alone!) because this is your overall budget and not on a party-by-party basis. As with Party Hard the music is excellent and the graphics are easy on the eyes. It's a great concept and I can see having a lot of fun with it as the game moves through Early Access.
I've encountered two problems thus far that limit the potential of the game though. First of all, the graphics don't really scale with the resolution you choose. If you have a big monitor the text becomes at best a little blurry and at worst borderline unreadable, the map suffers a similar issue. This doesn't have much of an effect on in-party graphics, but I would expect the text to be crisp, clear and readable on all resolutions. Secondly, you need to place speakers literally EVERYWHERE if you want to avoid guests exclaiming "where is music?" every few seconds and this really eats up a big portion of your budget. I had guests stand directly behind a speaker and say this on more than one occasion, the radius in which music is audible to guests needs to be more realistic.
As I said earlier, it's a fun concept and it's one I'm very much interested in, but at the moment some real work needs to be done to the mechanics in order to make this more enjoyable, including a more in-depth tutorial. I'd still recommend picking it up though since it's very reasonably priced and, despite its current shortcomings, it's an enjoyable game that has real promise.

Party Hard Tycoon is a party management and simulation game based on the 2015 hit game, Party Hard which slashed all the other games (based on the Party Hard universe). At the time of this review, it has been 1 week previous to the game release (Friday 13th October). PHT offers around 20 - 30 hours of gameplay all around.
You start as a completely new party host / hostess with 2 places for parties. One is completely and entirely free while the other one is $1000. You start with a certain budget of around $25,000. The main objective of the game is to be able to create the best parties ever where you can make a lot of profit as well as trying to keep a stable fanbase and budget. When you start, you only have enough for certain stuff. Try not to spend too much at once on like a DJ table for $15,000. If the party backfires and not many people come, You’ll lose a lot of money and potentially go bankrupt unless you come up with a master plan.
The best way to maintain cash flow at the beginning is keep your budget at around $5,000. That is enough for enough stereo speakers for a lot of music, beer deposits, and a few tables for people to sit at and get food service. Maintaining profit and fan-base is a good way to get throughout the game to the point you can afford the most beautiful attractions and devices. Ingame, there is also an XP upgrade. You get XP by having likes from each party. At the summary of the party, all likes are put into your XP bar. Everytime you level up, you get to choose to upgrade either; Locations, Themes or Personnels (Employees for hire like entertainment or cops). It is pretty fun to be able to upgrade locations so you don’t always have to party in one environment for the rest of the game.
The graphics are really cool, same entities used in Party Hard {2015}. The graphic design for the main menu is more special as we haven’t seen that kind of graphic style in Party Hard {2015} and Party Hard 2 {2018}. Seeing a main menu that looks hand drawn looks unique unlike most games these days when all main menus are fancy and designed using animations and models from ingame. I think it is a unique addition to the game and I hope that they make a rough game one day using that design. The performance and optimisation is also very smooth and great compared to Party Hard 2 (which some may have experienced during the early alpha of level 1 and 2.) It runs very smoothly on my graphics card which is an AMD R7 250 and on my processor which is an Intel i3 - 6100 3.7GHz Dual processor all at 1080p HD quality.
The audio is what you expect from a Party Hard franchise sequel. Awesome and original! The developers made the audio from their own team and may I say that it is funky and sounds like you’re in a real party. I love the sounds and effects from music, people paying etc. It lightens up the aspect of the game and adds more enjoyment when you’re playing it. I have loved the music since Party Hard and the sequel. It would be more nice to make some new music tracks instead of using some that are over 2 years old. Still fun though to listen to.
The replay value is enormously awesome as you end up with the same result every game. Some games the AI can be aggressive and hate your party, sometimes they’ll love it and let you upgrade. Not to mention that the upgrade choices are random every time and game.
Original and Fun Music
Great escapism from reality
Menu is well designed

Greatly optimised
XP is a good mechanic
Needs a bit more extra and brand new music to our ears
In conclusion, I recommend this game for lovers of Party Hard and Party Hard 2. You will be expecting to see me in the Party Hard 2 store page of reviews when that is written. In conclusion, this game is a 9.5/10.

EDIT:  After the developer reaching out to me, I've changed my opinions somewhat.
Basically, this is HL2 with an engine upgrade. Half life 2: update is to Half Life 2 what Half life: Source was to Half life.  At the moment, I can't really recommend a regular playthrough: the guns feel exactly the same, look exactly the same, and the levels are exactly the same.  But the real gem here is the commentary mode:  voiced by great voice actors in the HL community, such as Ross Scott, this mode shows insight into the development of both this mod, and HL2 itself.
The issue that I have with this is that no textures, models, or sounds were updated.  This means the levels look the same except for lighting changes, the guns feel the same as a decade ago, and the can you pick up is the same can as it was in 2004.  I was hoping for more out of this.  Half life 2: update is to Half Life 2 what Half life: Source was to Half life.
BUT THERE IS STILL HOPE FOR MY DREAMS:
The lead developer is open to community made DLC that could change all of things that haven't been updated in HL2: Update.  If you are a texture artist, animator, or modeler, be aware that your input can shape the future of this mod, and the legacy of HL2.

It's HL2 but with better fog, better particles, some better textures here and there, better cubemap (basic) reflections and more realtime reflections, some lighting tweaks that look a fair bit more natural, bugfixes (bunnyhopping still lives thank god), and colour tweaks that overall improve the feel of the game.
If it's been a while since you've played through HL2 then this is the way you should do it.
