I have both iterations of Darksiders II, the original and this "Deathinitive Edition" and I can say that as far as I'm concerned the graphics look much better.  But that's an improvement over the original edition, so why do I not recommend this game?
Tl;dr
It's a terrible console port, nothing more.  Yes, the grahpics have been upgraded so they look prettier on a PC, but the controls suck, the menus aren't navigable using the scroll wheel, causing you to click and drag to scroll through things, the combat doesn't feel fluid at all and the story is a complete joke.  Do yourself a favor, save your money and just read the wiki page that sums up the game.  You'll save money and time.
Longer version
The controls are terrible, the first ability you gain is "Teleport Slash" and is the number 6 key, so if your fingers are on the common WASD keys, then you have to stretch to reach the number 6.  Logically you would simply reassign the keys, which is perfect... except you can't unassign another key.  Example: the letter 'Q' is used to aim, but I would prefer to have the "Teleport Slash" ability on that key, there's no way to unbind 'Q' from aim.  So... good luck finding a close-by alternative for your buttons.  Playing with a controller may solve this, but I don't want to do that if I'm playing PC, maybe this makes me jaded but that's how I roll.
The menu screens are awful, there is literally no scroll support, you have to click and drag on every icon to read further down a list.  When reading the abilities or whatever, you have to click and drag.  This game was put out in 2015, I've been using a scroll wheel since 1993, get with the times.
The skill tree page is meant to be navigated with the keyboard, or a controller, not a mouse.  If you click on a new ability to read about it, the system thinks you are trying to "buy" that ability and will prompt the text to "purchase" it.  If you're not paying attention then congrats, you just inadvertently bought the ability when you were probably just trying to read about it.
The combat SUCKS.  This is partially because the controls are so poorly laid out, but when trying to hack n' slash an enemy and you wind up hack n' slashing empty air because you moved the mouse slightly too much, you'll be aggravated.  The game DOES try to solve this by letting you push (and hold) shift to focus on a target, but have fun holding shift down while cliking like crazy AND trying to press that '6' key.
I got about 2-3 hours into the game and simply gave up out of frustration, if the above problems were solved then maybe I'd try it again, but the story is still horribly stupid.  Imagine what your 6 year old self would have comic book characters do, and imagine how crazy, disjointed and silly that story would be.  That's Darksiders II, or as I like to call it "Bad Console Port, Definitive Edition".

While Darksiders 1 was an amazing game in it's own right, Darksiders 2 improves upon it in almost every conceivable way.  I will say that I felt some of the bosses were inconsistent as you progress through the game with some of the earlier bosses being much harder than later ones, but that's probably one of the only gripes I have.  The tones of the game are more consistent than the previous one, the story is longer, and the weapons, abilities, and upgrades are altogether more entertaining and rewarding.
If you enjoyed the first Darksiders or really any hack n' slash kind of game, I highly recommend this game.

I don't play multi-player, so this review strictly pertains to the single player and technical side.
To keep it short, any potato of a PC should be able to run this game. For the time CoD:MW looked fantastic, it still holds up to some extent, but it's liver spots are showing. Otherwise, you shouldn't have any trouble running this game unless your PC is at least eight or nine years out of date.
As for the campaign, I've played through several times on my Xbox-360 and only once so far on PC. I ended up getting the Modern Warfare games in a package bundle, it was worth the price for a good old shooter. Nothing particular special other than typical linear levels with plenty of baddies and a handful of situations where you take on vehicles on both the ground and air, but each are very short lived sequences. But, CoD:MW was something of a landmark for the CoD franchise and anyone who likes a good shooter should give CoD:MW a shot. It's a great game, though for any seasoned gamer, you'll be able to slam your way through this game in a matter of hours on normal, or hard if you have your wits about you.
I will say, in retrospect, many of the levels are particular short, but crammed full of great setpieces and action sequences. The story isn't anything amazing with a few likeable characters and draws heavily on the influence of older war action movies, some scenes practically drawn straight from them. Though the same could be said for any CoD game really. As for difficulty, you'd have to be brain dead to some extent to have any real trouble here. Enemies are incredible predictable and most areas are cakewalks on hard difficulty unless you forgot how to use a mouse.
But did I have fun? I sure did. Gotta enjoy a nice shoot 'em up.

Continuing its trend of remasters, Double Fine has injected new life into the cult favorite Full Throttle. Over the past couple of years, Double Fine has been putting a lot of love and care into some of the classic Lucasarts games of yore including Grim Fandango and Day of the Tentacle. Now some remasters come across as superfluous and lazy but in the case of this Lucasarts trio, it was quite the necessity seeing as how these games don’t really play nice with modern operating systems. As someone who missed these games the first time around, I’m quite glad to see that Double Fine is making them available for modern machines.
Although I had never played any of these classics when they originally released, I have been following their release quite closely as I’ve always heard them put in such high regard. And despite the critical acclaim of both Grim Fandango and Day of the Tentacle, Full Throttle seemed to be the one that fans seemed to be frothing at the mouth for the most, at least anecdotally. After finishing Full Throttle, I can see why. The game excels in a number of categories but presentation is the first that comes to mind. Set in a pseudo-Mad Max world, the world of Full Throttle creates an excellent sense of place. The dinginess and music all lend itself to the lawless world that the game tries to create. The voice acting is also exceptional, with the incomparable Mark Hamill making an appearance as well. One thing that did stand out for me that separates Full Throttle from its Lucasarts brethren is that the game is very filmic. It presents its shots and framing in a way that neither of the other two did and helps to create a wonderful sense of adventure. I can definitely see why this was such a big hit when it released in 1995.
As far as the gameplay goes, well, it’s still an adventure game from 1995. I have a certain love-hate relationship with classic point and click adventure games – I love their comedic aspects and stories but I find the puzzle solving to be overly obtuse and sometimes nonsensical. Full throttle was no different in this regard. I greatly enjoyed the story but found myself relying on a walkthrough to get me through much of the game. Purists may cry heresy over this but that’s the way I played the game and I still enjoyed it. I think it’s important to know what kind of puzzle solving you’re getting into here. There’s a reason games like these aren’t really made anymore.
When it comes to the state of the remaster, I found it to be pretty excellent. Like its predecessors, you can swap between the classic graphics and the remastered one. I did find myself constantly flipping between the two to see the changes that were made and see what the original was like. Overall, I’d say I enjoyed the classic graphics the most. The pixel art, especially in close ups, is still phenomenal. The characters have distinct silhouettes and strike some wonderful poses. During larger scale scenes though, I did find it better to switch to the new graphics if not for anything else than to make things a bit more legible and easier to navigate. The audio is also noticeably crisper if you have the remastered graphics on.
No matter which setting you prefer, Full Throttle Remastered is the definitive way to play the game. It’s still a terrific experience from a different time in gaming and one that I’m glad old and new gamers alike can experience. While the puzzles are still not all that great, I’d say don’t be afraid to use a guide if you want to experience this classic for first time or the fiftieth.

This is the poorest made of the remakes/remasters that I've played in the genre. The graphical update is often underwhelming and, in a sense, too faithful to the original and all its artistic flaws. There are also a couple of bizarre graphical glitches as well as a lack of detail in the remaster, which caused me to play most of the game in its original incarnation -- you can choose between original and remastered graphics and audio as you play these remastered adventure games.
Aside from how lacklustre the remaster is on a technical level, the game itself is very interesting in many ways, with an intriguing plot of deceit and murder over big business and future ambition of the Corley Motors company and its owning partners, who share (or do they?) a passion for legacy motorbikes. Unfortunately, the game suffers from readability issues and isn't terribly intuitive in allowing you to really get a feel of what exists on the screen, which can lead to some frustrating misses of objects that need to be interacted with. It also feels a tad bit on the short side and overall it's marred with a lot of small problems which do detract from the overall experience of what is still a good game. All in all, the game lacks the cogency of most other LucasArts adventures.

I really enjoyed the first 2/3s of Hellblade. I found it very gripping, suspenseful, immersive, and masterfully told and crafted. The animation for all characters was sublime, and the level of detail (and attention to detail) were and are breathtaking. This game is a feast for the senses in every respect. Likewise the story and voice acting are absolutely stellar. Hellblade drew me in with a novel story set in what I assume are Viking times, with primitive structures and weapons, and a world ruled by myth and legends of dark gods. It was just badass, and really captivating. I haven't played anything like Hellblade before, and it's doubtful I will again.
That's where things fall apart unfortunately. If you play through the game with an open mind like I did, you will get sucked in to Senua's plight, and really want to see her story through. The momentum of the first 2/3s of the game starts to drop off 5 or 6 hours in, and I felt a real drive just to see things finished. The puzzle mechanic became tedious and repetitive, and the combat had lost its flashiness and exposed its barebones design. The narrator began to just repeat the same old lines about darkness and loss, but without the weighty effect it had in the beginning. Then the ending came and went, and the story I thought I had been experiencing revealed its true form.
It was a very disappointing denoument, and reminded me of other Indie games like Firewatch, Ethan Carter, etc. Instead of letting the players completely lose themselves in a fascinating fantasy world, they suck you right back to reality and try to make a statement about how normal our lives really are. Any thought of paranormal involvement, or supernatural struggle is gone, and you realize it's just a game about a normal person with completely normal powers and weaknesses. Maybe some players will enjoy that, and be able to relate more to Senua because of how ordinary her story ends up being, but I really wanted it to be more than what it was. The final confrontation was so fantastic, that it made up for all the lulls before it in my eyes, only to end with a complete whimper. A true letdown for me

A pretty simple match-3 game that requires very fast and precise mouse movements and reactions.
Since I don't have that level of mouse mechanics (I don't play FPS well, etc.), the game felt frustrating because I'd become overwhelmed and couldn't pull off any nice chains or combos. It would end up where I would just make single attacks, trying to clear the board of enemy attacks and hexes. And when you lose a character, it just goes snowballs from there because you lose attack/ability options and need to clear the dead hero's chargers to move things around. I wish there were lower difficulty settings to slow the pace down a little so someone of my skill level could execute plans a little easier. Right now, I just try to clear everything bad with 1-2 attack strikers at a time and hope that the upcoming gem sequence isn't impossible for me to clear. And I only use abilities to clear the board when I'm overwhelmed instead of offensively. It's like being only able to play Tetris or Tetris Attack/Puzzle League on a hard difficulty- things go by too fast to really have fun chaining and comboing things unless you're already good at it.
Eventually, if you grind it out, you can unlock upgrades that make the game easier. However, I cleared 24 levels (beating the final boss) and only got 24 xp. There are about 9 upgrades for each character, scaling from 20xp to 110 xp (adding up to ~2095xp total). You'll need to clear many levels to unlock everything.
You'll need to clear many levels to unlock much of anything.
I would have liked your attack strikers to automatically fire when they reach the end of the screen (instead of disappear and be wasted).
Maybe it would be easier to control with touch screen or keyboard/controller controls? The former would probably be better, the latter would probably still be too slow for the game.
If you have high mouse dexterity (required) and rapid thinking (more instinct than movand enjoy challenges, this might be for you. If you aren't at that level, prepare for a frustrating experience where you can't do what you know needs to be done in time.

I think it is time that I pay my respect to this game.
For almost forever I have wanted to play a game where I am on the field as a soldier, yet I am able to make tactical decisions changing what the AI focuses on, and RUNNING WITH RIFLES has given me almost exactly that.
In my library this is my second most played game and with good reason. The gameplay is good, the graphics are clean, and the controls well thought out.
First of all the gameplay and AI are something that you will see in the reviews of this game a lot as they really are special and unique. The game is top down at an angle so 3D elements are visible creating an interesting tactical view allowing the player to analyze situations and choose where to move and what to do. Secondly, the cover mechanic in the game is well planned out and doesn't allow players to play like the "heroes" they normally play as in call of duty because they will die. Accuracy is another thing as it adds another tactical layer to gaming as shooting while running is very ineffective when compared to crouching giving the positioning of the player (crouching, standing, or prone) great importance. In RWR, there is no hitpoint system, instead there is a chance for each bullet to kill depending on the weapon (although one could consider the vests which absorb a few "kill bullets" as hitpoints) meaning that everything needs to be tactical with the risks understood. Based upon all of that, objectives are given out by the commander AI and a set distribution of AI are sent there to try and capture zones. The player can get a set amount of AI in their squad if they have a high enough rank and can control and set movement objectives for these AI in order to help push the objective or take down buildings that reduce the enemies capabilites. The stealth mechanic is really fun and it feels really rewarding once you finally run away and detonate the C4 to destroy an objective.
Moreover, the AI in the game have amazing discipline. They find cover, dive a away from grenades, and will punish you for making bad decisions. It is great as they fight in a tactical way that players should learn from.
Also, the gameplay works well in multiplayer, where players can either work together in co-op versus the AI in dominance mode, or to fight against each other in a vs mode. I had a great time where I joined a squad and took down buildings behind enemy lines.
Vehicles are another part of the game, that when used properly can turn the tide of battle. Vehicles are powerful but can be shredded apart easily by well coordinated attacks making teamwork even more important in the game.
All in all, the gameplay really makes the player feel as if they are but just a cog in the machine of war. It makes the player realize the mistake they made that caused them to die. It makes them realize they are someone who can die with some power to make decisions but in the end only enough to make a difference if done right. But even then, at times a player can win through using skill, reflexes, and fast decisions in even the toughest of situations.
Secondly, the graphics in the game are fun and voxel based, along with the weapons. To solve the proble of the angled top down view, buildings are translucent and the silhouettes of enemies can be seen through them. The graphics will not blwo you away but allow you to see what is going on clearly, at least until an arty 8 comes along...
Finally, the sounds are fun. It's not really anything special, but just something that isn't bad in my opinion.
All in all RUNNING WITH RIFLES is one of my favorite games of all time and I would reccommend it to anyone who likes a strategical shooter with action-packed moments relying on skill, patience, and strategy.

A fantastic game incorporating many long missed horror elements. What I first thought to be a monotonous randomly generated dungeon crawler quickly proved me wrong. This tension and atmosphere never gets too much either, being interrupted by various jumpscares. They range from cute and kawaii to scary and unnerving with threatening warnings. They also each come with various bits of audio, making their arrival unpredictable and feeling unique, rather than a cope out in the place of atmosphere. They've done so much right in both atmosphere and mechanics I can hardly fault them for themostly incoherent plot and "Eh" ending. The trip, rather than the destination, is what makes this game great.

The game overall is good, a solid contiuation on previous editions, but new features are limited other than the fundamental changes to planning a riders training program. I do however, have a few areas of criticism.
1. Sprint finishes are much worse than they have been in previous editions. The sprinters energy levels go down way too slowly. For example, in Milan-San Remo my sprinter can sprint for the entire 3km the game allows you to sprint. This is obviously ridiculous, as in reality a sprinter can only max out their sprint for around 200m. This means having a solid lead out train is pretty pointless. You just make sure your rider is at the front at 3km to go and then its near impossible to be beaten irrespective of your riders stats (provided they are a sprinter). I don't even bother with flat stages in stage races anymore, but it does ruin the classics that often end in a sprint such as Milan-San Remo, Tour of Flanders, Paris-Roubaix etc a bit.
2. There is a lack of diversity in career mode due to having the same parcourse for each race year after year. After the first season in career mode is complete, none of the routes change and therefore the game becomes somewhat predictable. In one of the previous editions of the game the Tour de France route alternated between 2 differing routes. The game would be substantially improved if there was different routes every year, at least in the grand tours. Even if it was just the route models used by the devs in previous editions of game. For example, in the first year of career mode the Tour route was the 2017 route, in the second year it could be the 2014 route, the next the 2016 route and so on. This would make it much more difficult to acheive dominant runs of victories and give the game a much more realistic feel.
3. Its far too easy for a rider to be 'blocked'. I appreciate it is not easy to move around a peloton, but sometimes it is ridiculous in the game. You can be in a small group of 4 or 5 riders, on wide roads, and one of the group attacks. You try to follow the attack and another rider directly in front of you doesn't, so your rider just sits their like a melon while the rest of the group disapear 2 or 3 minutes up the road and the race is over for you. Its infuriating. It is the same at the start of races with breakaways. You plan on sending a certain rider in the break, but by pure luck the rider you planned on sending has been positioned at the rear of the peloton when the stage generates. Sometimes it can take 40-50km for the rider to work his way to the front and by that time the breakaway is well and truely gone. There should be a neutralised roll out for a few km, as there is in real races, before each race where riders can 'ghost' through other riders to get to near the front. Also there should perhaps be a rider stat for 'positioning' which dictates how easy a rider can move though the peloton or hold a wheel.
4. In career mode, rider contracts can only be negotiated after the 21st of July on the year the riders contract expires. I understand in reality teams cant announce new rider transfers before a certain period, but they can renegotiate their existing riders contracts at anytime and not only in the final 6 months of their existing deal. It makes it possible to lose over half you team with little notice. The contract negotations are simplistic at best. You basically negotiate the salary and duration. It would be better if you could offer bonuses or a signing fee to make up for a smaller salary and perhaps having the riders demand you sign a teammate etc. Also riders make demands, such as they want £70k p/m over 2 years, you then offer them that exact terms, they reject them saying they need a better offer and then when you renegotiate the offer they are still asking for £70k p/m over 2 years. Makes no sense. This can go one for months, you offer them much better than they are asking for and they reject it. This is annoying considering, as i said earlier, you have limited time to negotiate.
5. The sponsorship parameters are very poor. Again, everything is left until the last minute, which i accept is a possibilty but it is not standard practice. You can sign a multi-year deal with a sponsor for a certain amount a year, but depending on how you perform in relation to your sponsors objectives they can raise or lower how much they pay you without warning. Whats the point in having a contract if they can just change the terms at will without consultation? This means you literally have no idea about your teams budget from year to year. You also have very little input into the sponsors objectives. They can demand you win in all disciplines of cycling, the cobbled classics, Ardennes classics, stage races and grand tours and sprints. In reality, most teams are predominatly focused on one or perhaps 2 aspect of cycling. You often don't find out who is sponsor you until late in the year and you literally dont find out what their objectives for you are until 1st of January. By this time you can sign new riders to help you fullfill these objectives. Sponsors should give you a flat and unchangeable rate for the term of the contract with bonuses for fullfilling objectives. Also being able to negotiate objectives at the before signing the contract would be an improvement.
6. The TT stats are worthless. In the 40km slightly hilly Giro TT i had Tom Dumoulin (TT stat of 83) and he beat Davide Formolo (TT stat of 66) by only 28 seconds. Both were rated 78 for hills. You would expect Dumoulin to take a minimum of 2 minutes, probably closed to 4 minutes here. Non TT specialists doing extremely well against TT specialists seems to happen every TT i have done, irrespective whether i quick simulate or 3D race the stage.

I have both iterations of Darksiders II, the original and this "Deathinitive Edition" and I can say that as far as I'm concerned the graphics look much better.  But that's an improvement over the original edition, so why do I not recommend this game?
Tl;dr
It's a terrible console port, nothing more.  Yes, the grahpics have been upgraded so they look prettier on a PC, but the controls suck, the menus aren't navigable using the scroll wheel, causing you to click and drag to scroll through things, the combat doesn't feel fluid at all and the story is a complete joke.  Do yourself a favor, save your money and just read the wiki page that sums up the game.  You'll save money and time.
Longer version
The controls are terrible, the first ability you gain is "Teleport Slash" and is the number 6 key, so if your fingers are on the common WASD keys, then you have to stretch to reach the number 6.  Logically you would simply reassign the keys, which is perfect... except you can't unassign another key.  Example: the letter 'Q' is used to aim, but I would prefer to have the "Teleport Slash" ability on that key, there's no way to unbind 'Q' from aim.  So... good luck finding a close-by alternative for your buttons.  Playing with a controller may solve this, but I don't want to do that if I'm playing PC, maybe this makes me jaded but that's how I roll.
The menu screens are awful, there is literally no scroll support, you have to click and drag on every icon to read further down a list.  When reading the abilities or whatever, you have to click and drag.  This game was put out in 2015, I've been using a scroll wheel since 1993, get with the times.
The skill tree page is meant to be navigated with the keyboard, or a controller, not a mouse.  If you click on a new ability to read about it, the system thinks you are trying to "buy" that ability and will prompt the text to "purchase" it.  If you're not paying attention then congrats, you just inadvertently bought the ability when you were probably just trying to read about it.
The combat SUCKS.  This is partially because the controls are so poorly laid out, but when trying to hack n' slash an enemy and you wind up hack n' slashing empty air because you moved the mouse slightly too much, you'll be aggravated.  The game DOES try to solve this by letting you push (and hold) shift to focus on a target, but have fun holding shift down while cliking like crazy AND trying to press that '6' key.
I got about 2-3 hours into the game and simply gave up out of frustration, if the above problems were solved then maybe I'd try it again, but the story is still horribly stupid.  Imagine what your 6 year old self would have comic book characters do, and imagine how crazy, disjointed and silly that story would be.  That's Darksiders II, or as I like to call it "Bad Console Port, Definitive Edition".

While Darksiders 1 was an amazing game in it's own right, Darksiders 2 improves upon it in almost every conceivable way.  I will say that I felt some of the bosses were inconsistent as you progress through the game with some of the earlier bosses being much harder than later ones, but that's probably one of the only gripes I have.  The tones of the game are more consistent than the previous one, the story is longer, and the weapons, abilities, and upgrades are altogether more entertaining and rewarding.
If you enjoyed the first Darksiders or really any hack n' slash kind of game, I highly recommend this game.

There are a lotta reviews on this page that say Darksiders 2 isn't original, that it feels like a mashup of Zelda, God of War, and some others. True as that may be, I don't necessarily think that it's a bad thing.
This game certainly has its flaws - I've had it crash on me a few times, and in some places explanation is lacking (for instance, when I'm in my inventory screen I can compare detailed stats like DPS between my currently equipped weapon, and those in storage, but if I try to buy a weapon from a shop, I can ONLY view the basic damage & added stats of the weapon on display, but can no longer compare).
The controls, with the exception of a slight feeling of input delay during some of the platforming (namely running up walls and jumping off them), feel responsive. But it's worth mentioning that Death is somehow incapable of climbing the smallest of ledges unless they have a wooden ledge for him to grab. This leads to some irritating moments where small jumps that you 'feel' like you should be able to make result in Death doing the obnoxiously slow wallclimb ending animation, and either 'falling' the 2ft to the floor or leaping in the opposite direction.  OH YEAH, AIMING. Aiming the pistol in this game, or any of the explosives you need to throw to complete puzzles/kill a boss, is MISERABLE. The aim assist is WAY too generous - to a fault. Sometimes it won't even lock your crosshair on the key target, just somewhere near it. Thankfully to use your pistol or throw explosives in combat you can simply hold the target lock button and avoid the aiming interface entirely, Zelda style. Ultimately if you can get past the inconveniences this game might throw your way now and then, you'll find an enjoyable action RPG with platforming and puzzle elements throughout.
The story is... Well, it's a story. If you could get behind an angry Spartan murdering the gods of Olympus I think you'll at the very least tolerate this one. I haven't finished the game yet, but the word 'Corruption' is used so often in dialogue you'd think you're in Peewee's Playhouse and it's the word of the day.
Full disclosure, I have only played this game using a Steam Controller - I cannot speak to how well/poorly this controls with Mouse+Keyboard or other input devices. I'd imagine aiming would likely feel smoother with a mouse, but that the rest of the control scheme might feel underwhelming (there are no rebind options). I have never played another game whose aiming mechanics feel this horrible on a Steam Controller, however.
I picked up my copy on the summer sale that just recently ended, and I'd say it's worth it at the discount.

Initially I was pulled in by the graphics - they've probably been bettered elsewhere, but I'd not seen facial animation this good in a PC game before. As I played I found so much more to this game than a slick appearance.
I found the combat *incredibly* stressful! I appreciate that most people are game-savvy enough not to need tutorials any more and it helped with the immersion aspect... but I only found out about "Heavy Strike" and "Kick" very near the end of the game and these would have been useful earlier on.
That doesn't matter though - this game pulled me into its reality. The puzzles and combat weren't groundbreaking but it built an emotional connection with Senua's story. When it came to it, I actually wanted to watch the cut scenes without picking up my phone which is a huge rarity these days.
The production feature was fascinating too. To realise that the distorted reality effects were based on people's experiences was horrifying.
The only downer - there's a song over the end credits and the lyrics were too on-the-nose for me. We've had Senua's story and narration, then having someone else come and sing over the credits felt as though the story was being taken away from her. Still, I was crying by this point!
So much effort and heart has gone into this game. I wish I could express more eloquently how beautiful and affecting it was.

I was on the fence about getting this game, given its past history and the controversy that ensued from the moment it was released. However, after watching the latest major patch it was starting to look like a real game and I wanted to give it a chance. I bit the bullet and purchased it at full price. As the world loaded before me I was incredibly excited. I began following the tutorial to fix my gear and my ship, even exploring far enough to discover an abandoned location that provided me with anicent relics of a civilization. By then I had understood the basics: look up what is needed to craft, scour the world in hopes of finding the item while spamming the scan button, burn through your laser multi-tool while simultaneously making sure to don't die because your radioactivity or life support drains rapidly, then craft the item to go onto the next tutorial piece that does the exact same thing.
At this point I was low on inventory space and was forced to either start dropping them into my ship or drop ESSENTIAL crafting parts, all the while making sure I kept inventory space to craft energy recharge items for my life support and sustain my mining laser. But then, flight! I fixed my space ship and was ready to hit the skies!... right after I figure out how to take off... bam! Wait, one of my ship pieces takes 25% damage every time I take off? So I have to make sure I keep that resources on my ship at all times so I can continually fix it? Ok fine, I'll deal with that as long as I can fly over to that cool new planet! Which upon entering its atmosphere and onto land, was pretty much a different looking version of my first world, with some terrain changes and a stegosaurus looking creature (by far my now favorite part of my 3 hour experience), and the same resources as the first one with no difference in primary abundance compared to the first one (more or less same amount of iron, Thaium9, carbon, etc.).
Fast forward, I make it to the trade station and realize it's looking like this is my life: find the next mission, identify parts needed for crafting, fly down to planets to gather resources with my pathetic mining multitool, throw away things I want because my inventory is too small, get frustrated because I figured by now I'd be able to expand my inventory, mine faster, or at least use my ship to identify resources and then fly to them, and then suck it up and hope that the next mission gives me access to one of those things. I don't know if I quit too early but after three straight hours of playing I got to the anti-matter recipe and realized I was more frustrated with the game than I was having fun. I can see this game being worth purchasing if it was maybe $30 USD, but I wasn't going to pay the full $60 and force myself to MAYBE get to a point where I was having more fun than I was getting irritated. If you are interested in getting the game, I highly advise you wait until some level of sale is going on for this game; it's just not worth the full price tag.
TL;DR version - Decided to give it a chance, game appeared fun upon starting, turned into frustration and giving up due to lack of inventory space, repetitive running-simulator resource gathering quests, and constantly breaking/recharge needs for multitool and ship.
It is a good game now. Wait for a sale and try it out.

If I told you that Dungeon Hearts was a match-3 puzzle game, RPG hybrid, would you dismiss it as another Puzzle Quest clone? Well, it is, but you shouldn't, because it isn't. Let me explain...Dungeon Hearts puts you in control of a party of four adventurers who rush headlong from one battle to the next in an unquenchable thirst for glory that doesn't end until they're all dead. As the adventures race in place and the world scrolls past them, monsters appear in a steady stream from the other side of the screen. Defeat one, the next appears, and the battle begins anew.
During battles, which account for about 99% of the gameplay, four lines are drawn horizontally across the screen, each aligned with one of the adventurers. Colored stones scroll along these lines, fate lines as the game calls them, from the right edge of the screen and make their way to the adventurers on the left. Using the mouse you need to drag these stones to place three of them of the same color together either horizontally or vertically. When you do they combine to form a gem that will damage the monster when double-clicked. The gem will also trigger other gems aligned with it either horizontally or vertically to explode, and the more gems in the chain reaction, the more damage is done to the monster. Include gems of different colors in the chain and you'll score even more bonus damage. The gems are also used to trigger the other types of icons that travel down the fate lines. Skulls represent the monster's attacks, and if they're not eliminated before they reach the end of a line they'll damage the adventurer that they hit. Spell and buff icons, for both the party and the monster, are also triggered or destroyed by the gems. If an adventurer dies during a battle, the corresponding colored stones become grayed over and can no longer be used to build gems. This gives you fewer opportunities to make gems, takes away some combos, and puts more obstacles on the fate lines. If you manage to win the battle, the adventurer will be revived for the next. If you lose all four in a battle, then it's game over. Defeat a monster and you'll get to play a fast-paced version of the game in which a tightly packed run of colored stars make their way down the fate lines. Matching three of the same color will level-up the corresponding adventurer, one level per every three stars matched. The game's fantasy theme and level-up bonus levels are the extent of its tie to RPGs, and it's far more of a puzzle game than it is an RPG. The background graphics are colorful and evoke memories of JRPGs of a console generation gone by, but you have to stay so focused on the fast-moving fate lines that you won't really be able to enjoy them. There's no persistence between games, so after your party is all dead you'll begin the next game from the beginning with a group of level one adventurers. And if there was any doubt left about the game's primary nature, at the end of a game you're given a score.
So it's not much of an RPG - no big deal as long as the puzzle part's fun, right? Well, Dungeon Hearts is a fun puzzle game, but also one that's more geared to those with quick reflexes than those who want to carefully setup and execute their gem combos. The game is fast moving and will keep you so focused that you won't be aware that a game can last twenty minutes or more unless you check a clock (luckily, the game will let you pick up where you left off if you need to leave early). My biggest complaint with the game comes from the controls, specifically that the mouse has a tendency to drop a stone as you try to move it around another stone, particular when you 're trying to turn a corner around another stone.
Dungeon Hearts is a fun and challenging puzzle game, but I can see it disappointing gamers looking for more of an RPG element in the game or those who will find that the fate lines move too fast for their tastes. It's certainly the kind of puzzle game you'll come back to now and again. Since it's an indie title and can be had for a relatively low price, it's easy to recommend adding this to your game library.

Street Racing Syndicate is an arcade racing game, created on the wave of astonishing success of the Need for Speed Underground. There were plenty of them back in the days, but only a few deserves our attention after all those years passed. If you need comparisons, I'd say that SRS is more realistic than NFS Underground 1 & 2, and have some unique features to hold player's interest - the most noticeable, the down-to-earth system of upgrades, and, of course, girls. Girls who encouraging the player with the original driving quests, and awards with private go-go dances, once you achieve something on the streets.
As of downsides, the game is quite dated at moment (released in 2005), and it is not a "living classic", like NFS games. Sadly, even being more fair with player than NFS, Street Racing Syndicate is not possessing the fleur of the "legend in flash". Which is more, it lacks the drive that raised NFS Underground so high. The driving in the open world could be the pain in the back, as the map is not just slightly informative... and gosh, how many coppers there on patrol?! It's really hard to speed there, staying under the radar.
Overall, I can't hardly recommend it. Get it on sale, or bundled, if you're up to some arcade racing with open world, where cars not bouncing from the border lines, maintaining speed. Where you have to pay for repairs, which urges you to drive a bit more carefully. Where you have your own club of long-legged female venerators... however low it may sound, it feels alright, try it sometimes.
My personal mark will be 6.9/10. It's on the level with Juiced or just slightly not even with NFS Underground 2. But yeah, it's been about 12 years now, and there are plenty of newer open-world racing games, starting with TDU 2 or the Crew. None of them holds so much go-go dancing girls, of course, but I wouldn't buy the game just to look at dancing cuties. Would you?

Set in a somewhat dystopian future in the year 2040, Full Throttle takes place in a world where hover-vehicles are slowly erasing their old fashioned, motorised counterparts from existence, and the few people to cling to the old ways are Ben Throttle and his gang, the Polecats.
Framed for the murder of Malcolm Corley, the CEO of Corley Motors, the last company to build motorized vehicles, Ben works to unveil the truth of the murder and clear his and his gang's name. After finding Maureen, the estranged daughter of Malcolm, he sets out to help her claim her rightful place.
For a game that is now 22 years old, Full Throttle's original graphics still look amazing and the original audio holds up, albeit a bit fuzzy. I opted to go for the remastered graphics and audio for the true remastered experience, despite this being my first play ever.
To be honest I just wanted to make full use of my monitor and not deal with those pesky black bars.
You can tell a lot of work was put into this overhaul, as switching seamlessly between rendering modes will show how much has changed, the colours are crisper and cleaner, there's more to the backgrounds too and the characters just look better overall.
There's no wall of text when it comes to choices like the stellar Day of the Tentacle or Secret of Monkey Island which gave you a multitude of ways to interact with people. In Full Throttle however, you play a biker so of course you think like a biker and so you either punch, kick, or talk to people or use objects in that manner.
While its neat that they simplified the UI in this, it also feels extremely simplified compared to previous LucasArts games.
Full Throttle has some truly stellar voice actors, I mean they had Mark Hammil voice the damn villain and he is superb as ever, he just emanates pure evilness as Ripburger. Roy Conrad's deep, gravelly voice suits Ben so perfectly that its a shame he didn't do much voice work after this. Kath Soucie voices Maureen and she's great, as a child I adored her as Phil and Lil from Rugrats. Can't forget her as Lola Bunny in Space Jam too but uh... thats a different thing altogether.
There was this one section in Mine Road where you have to acquire an item to get another one which in turn opens up the area you need to access. The worst part is that the enemies randomly spawn, so you have to either keep knocking out enemies or skipping the fights to get what you needed. This took way longer than it should have, and considering that the combat is also clunky as hell with the mouse controls, I failed a bunch before I finally succeeded, this was one area I was definitely glad to be done with.
Even playing for the first time, I didn't struggle with the puzzles, for the most part they had incredibly easy solutions or required some precise mouse positioning. They could be annoying but at least they weren't overcomplicated or required absurd solutions.
Overall the game took less than 5 hours for me to complete, even with me taking my time and exploring, but despite the short playtime I really enjoyed this game and it reminded me of how great LucasArts was during the 90's.
The characters are interesting but with the short playtime, their storylines feel rushed
Great music
Humour is on point
Extras such as concept art and commentary
Oh there was one small thing that bugged me, which is that you can only see the end credits in the original version and not the remastered. Not sure why but, there ya go.

Full Throttle was one of the first games I ever played when I was a kid, and while I probably wouldn't have remembered the title off the top of my head prior to the Remastered announcement, those memories of the game remained and I often have flashbacks to playing it. As soon as I saw the Remaster, I knew it was a definite purchase. Its artwork and animations have stuck in my mind for all of these years (I turn 30 this year), yet the second I started the game, all of those many memories came back to me.
The execution of this game has, so far, been flawless. The art has stayed true to the original while giving everything a modern visual upgrade; animations look fantastic, and the colours stand out beautifully. Switching between the remaster and original on-the-fly really drives home how magnificent both versions are; each respective of their eras.
Double Fine have done it, once again. This is a testament to the quality of the game, and they have delivered a superb remaster. Highly recommended for both past, and new, players alike.

Having played almost all of Tim Schafer's games, I can safely say that Full Throttle is the weakest and shortest of his games that I've played. I played the game once, years ago, and with only a vague remembrance of certain puzzle's solutions from that playthrough, I was able to beat the game this time in under four hours.
I feel that in comparison to other Schafer games I've played, Full Throttle still remains the weakest in various fields, such as puzzles, length, humour, characters, and story.
It may seem strange then that I'm recommending the game, but it's simple: Even Schafer's weakest work is still great.
For the €15 asking price, you are getting great material here. Double Fine don't half♥♥♥♥♥their remasters. A lot of blood, sweat and tears go in to these remasters, beyond just making the game look nicer. There are some great bonus features that we've come to expect from these remasters. You are getting value for your money, even if you've played the game before.
The game, as it originally came out, tried some new features, and they pretty much fail. Anything outside of the pre-established point-and-click gameplay just doesn't work. This includes the game's infamous motorcycle fight sections (which really aren't that big a staple of the game) and the motor derby section. These are still included, and it may suck some fun out of the experience, but they are presented as they originally were, and, what's the point of claiming to play a game if you're not going to play it, warts and all? I seem to remember a cheat code in the original version that just won the motorcycle fights automatically. I can't comment on whether or not they're in this version. I couldn't remember the code off hand, and I didn't bother looking it up to test it.
I was hesitant with other remasters from Double Fine after buying Grim Fandango Remastered, only for the game to crash constitanty. The only solution, at least at the time, was to put the settings from remastered to original. It worked, but it kind of sucked that I couldn't experience the remaster of the game. Then I played Day of the Tentacle Remastered and it ran beautifully. So I had no concerns with Full Throttle Remastered, only for the game to crash on the first cutscene. Thankfully, this was the only bug I encountered in the game.
I think for seasoned vets of point-and-click adventure games, Full Throttle may be too simple for you. Actually, I think there's a tendency of seasoned vets of point-and-click adventure games to overcompensate for the often convoluted steps required to solve a puzzle, therefore the almost laughably simple solutions to puzzles in this game may prove a challenge after all!
I feel with its short length and simple puzzles, Full Throttle may be a good intermediary for people who haven't played point-and-click adventure games before. (If I recall correctly, that was the intent of the game when it was originally in development in the early '90s, to bring new people to the adventure game genre. Adventure games were a niche market, and had a hard time breaking beyond the 200,000 or so sales, and it worked, as Full Throttle sold over 1,000,000 copies.)
Oh, and the artwork and soundtrack were then, and are now, awesome!

I knew I would like this game after watching the trailer made me weep... I felt entirely compelled to see if the game experience would replicate that feeling of despair and darkness streaked with a nearly imperceptible ray of hope.
It did not disappoint. After drying my eyes and putting on my headphones, I was met with an aural experience that was truly haunting. All of the voice actors, audio engineers, and editors that were part of the sound development truly created a piece of art with Hellblade. It constantly drew me in, and felt so real that for a time I could not even play the game because I was so rattled by the experience.
The visuals were also nothing short of amazing. There are many ways to conceptualize fear, anxiety, pain... rage... and the environments truly draw out the overwhelming experience playing out for Senua at every turn.
Truly beautiful and sometimes terrifying are Senua's facial expressions as she goes through her trials. Melina did such an amazing job with Senua...A better choice could not have been made.
The battle sequences take a bit of a backseat to the overall story and are fairly simple, requiring only a basic understanding of timing to be successful. I feel that this was intentionally forgiving as a default setting to make the game accessible. Simple is good in this regard, creating a combat experience that is fluid and responsive. Again, the aural experience enhances this, having your internal voices contribute to your self-preservation (and, indeed, their own) by alerting you to potentially unseen danger.
The puzzles and tests of perception in the game are challenging enough to be fun, and not frustrating. Taking note of odd angles and shapes in the environment can sometimes lead to hints to progress, or it could in fact be nothing at all.
Of course, the psychosis that Senua endures plays with all of these facets in interesting ways...and watching the Making-of video after completing the game was eye opening. I really wish more developers would put more thought into the process, instead of just churning out big budget games with ZERO depth, emotion, or purpose.
I would buy this game again. It shook me to the core and was difficult to play at times, but it was very rewarding. I will recommend it to everyone I know.

The voices in your head making you second guess yourself. The flashbacks telling you the back story of Senua. The monsters and bosses are very well made for a studio of 10+ people. Obisouly not on par of AAA games like Dark Souls or the Witcher 3 but this isn't a AAA deveopler and I beileve they did an outstanding job at making this experice for all of us.
I just want to say thank you Ninja Theory for the expierence and for opening my eyes to the mental disabiltys that people have out there.

First off, this game certainly isn't for everyone. A lot of people have found it boring and bland, but I've been with it since it was a 100 MB ZIP file on IndieDB (aka the very beginning) and I think it's come a long way since then.
But moving onto the actual review, the game's main sense of horror is the fact that it lulls you into a false sense of security then scares the crap out of you. And despite the title, there really aren't many jump scares (Specimen 1 is pretty much the only exception), just a lot of monsters.
Another great aspect about this game is how much it parodies other horror games. You'll see animatronics, something that looks like it came straight of The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask (and more related to the Ben Drowned creepypasta), dead Japanese schoolgirls, and a whole section of the game that's just a big nod to Clock Tower. It's awesome.
But this game really starts to shine once you start digging deeper (metaphorically and literally). It gets scarier as it progresses. Much scarier. And then you get even deeper to the biggest scare. Well, it's really more of an Easter Egg, but it has to do with Spooky's death. If you're a parent, and you find out what happened to Spooky, this game WILL scare you. I guarantee it.
And one more note before I go: "Spooky's Jump Scare Mansion." Ugh. If you've been reading reviews, you've probably come across more than five complaints about the name change. The full story can be read here since I don't want to go into too much detail:

Dungeon Hearts is a fun and face paced spin on the match 3. Where your 3 characters will fight against enemies in battles dictated by your ability to match gems. The game itself is simplistic, albeit not intuitively straightforward, as such even after playing the tutorial you will still struggle with some of the mechanics. The core concept is simple however, match up gems to initiate attacks of your characters (based on color) and counter enemy attacks/disarms etc. The game is visually stunning and although the gameplay starts off slow, it becomes horribly complex and fast paced shortly. The casual appeal of this game is great however it doesn't have much more long term value than all match 3 style games. Despite this I fully recommend this as a fun casual game to pickup and play. (Review was given an update at 4/9-2017 9th of September)
As a quick reference, I am talking about this game from a Co-Op standpoint, NOT a PvP one.
Running with rifles is a game that seems very interesting and seems to cater to your love for the old DOS game named Cannon Fodder.
It doesn't play exactly like Cannon Fodder did, seeing as you do not have a squad trailing you that you have as lives.
You are basically controlling a single infantry man fighting others, and you keep respawning when you die.
That is fair enough, however the core of the game is flawed, in Cannon Fodder there was always a sense of progress, but in this game that is missing.
What do I mean? For an example you get the feeling that you can unlock weapons by bringing them back to the armory, but that is just temporary and gives you only 4 hours, before the gun poofs and you have to redo the process.
It wouldn't be that bad if this was the only mechanic, but this game has more crap in store for you...
Imagine fighting battles where enemies can SPAWN ANYWHERE around you while you are focusing off your character?
Because in this game, you have to constantly be looking at the enemy because you get no feedback from the game if your bullets are making contact, so you are spotting for bullet impacts and blood.
And while you are doing this, and trying to get that line of sight to make sure the bullet can get there, a guy can SPAWN and move in on you from your rear, left or right flank and kill you.
Enemies will also keep spawning in areas where you are fighting, making you feel like you aren't making any progress except killing tons of soldiers.
And then there is the "AI Commander" that decides which sectors you are to attack, if there are two opposing factors, he will keep cycling you between attacking faction A and B, essentially you are capturing territory A, and losing B.
You then move to attack B and lose A and this cycle keeps repeating, forcing you to fight over the same territory for HOURS.
The developers take away all sense of progress with this game, and it will quickly frustrate you as a player.
And when the progress disappears it becomes tiring and you eventually lose the fun factor after  1-2 hours of playing.
Once the fun factor is gone, the game turns into a thumbs down experience...
So as a Coop game? Stay away from it, as tempting as it may seem, it needs a massive overhaul and should still be Very Early Access.
UPDATE: I have given this game another run through since the initial review, and it pains me to say this...
The conclusion still stands, a lot of the annoyances are still there, even after the period of patches it has gone through, which is a shame.
So pro tip... Just get and play this game for 1 hour, then you need to stop, I don't care how much fun you have.
The reason is that past that one hour, the flaws in the game will start to get to you, and you will really start to get annoyed at it... Longer stints will ruin the future fun this game can provide you.

Lightning Returns: Final Fantasy XIII is a port that completely blows its predecessors out the water. Performance-wise, Lightning Returns is pretty much superior in every single way compared to its predecessors. Gone are the 30 fps limiters, controller-seeking microstuttering and just terrible optimization in general. With any decent modern day GPU/CPU, you can typically expect a rock solid 60 fps gameplay in battles with only occasional drops to 40-50 fps in the Open World. Due to 60 fps being most important in battles, this port sells itself as a pretty darn optimized port.
Specs that I'm running:
i7-4710HQ @ 3.4 GHz Turbo
8 GB RAM
GTX 860M 4 GB GDDR5
Note that the 860M is the laptop equivalent to the 750 Ti, a mid end gpu that most people use in modern day budget builds. Even so, with everything on max settings (except Scaling - as I'm running a display of 1920x1080 on my laptop), the game holds a 60 fps in battles effortlessly while having occasional dips to 40+ fps in the Open World. Considering the fact that the game had such terrible performance even on consoles, the performance of the PC version is not just a small step-up; it's a huge one.
Despite having such a stellar performance compared to its predecessors on Steam, it takes a few frustrating steps back - steps that which are easily rectifiable and would have made it a perfect port. For one, as this is a first day review, the game only supports a resolution up till 1080p. Hence, everyone who runs higher resolution monitors would not find this too pleasing. There is a very very good chance that some workarounds will be here very soon though, and perhaps, just maybe, a patch from Square Enix themselves.
Other than that, the game still has no option for True Fullscreen to be enabled. True Fullscreen would give quite a big performance boost to everyone, but alas, its not present. The game's "fullscreen" is a borderless window.
The biggest gripe to all non-controller users though, would be that the mouse is not integrated into the game. As such, the mouse holds no significance/level of control whatsoever in the game. The cursor is visible too. For non-controller users, you'd have to be playing this game with both hands on your keyboard. The plus side is that all keyboard controls are rebindable, unlike its predecessors, although its predecessors had mouse integration into the game. At this point, I'm not quite sure which is preferable if you could only choose one of them to be integrated...
The Final Fantasy XIII trilogy is a very controversial series due to its nature of making its players either absolutely detest it or love it. Admittedly, if you've gone through the first 2 games, the 3rd won't be a disappointment. The combat system of the game is quite different from its predecessors and just about every other main title Final Fantasy. It uses a very heavily modified ATB system that functions more of like an "energy" system of sorts for your real-time actions. You also only control Lightning in this game as opposed to other entries in the series.
The game is widely known as a Dress Up Simulator for various endearing reasons. Lightning pretty much has to swap "schemes" (formally known as
) that features her in different garbs (read: clothes) with different equipment customized to the garbs themselves. The entire bundle forms a
. As one would expect, every garb/piece of equipment has its own intended job, and as such, can be viewed as something like a paradigm/mode by itself. Lightning is able to battle with 3 schemata at any one moment, and this is pretty much where the common FF strategy part lies.
Since the game is already 2 years old, there is really no better way to describe the game than to simply watch some video(s) of it and form your own opinion around it. Unlike the initial entry into the XIII trilogy, Lightning Returns stays true to an Open World scenario too, and is where you do everything that isn't a battle.
While the port is certainly incredibly impressive in terms of its performance, it startlingly lacks some really tiny yet important features that its predecessors had. Frustratingly, it serves to show that it
a perfect port if only it paid attention to some smaller yet integral fine details. Regardless, especially if you're a controller-user, the port is pretty damn solid and is very satisfactory, especially when compared to its predecessors.
As this is a first day review, it will be updated, should any fixes/patches get rolled out. I definitely want to believe that Square Enix would deliver some proper love to M+KB users as they did in Final Fantasy Type-0 HD. If they do, that would definitely make me not hold back on going on some 700 hour crazy spree or anything of that sort. As it is now, it's just not so comfortable playing this game unless I buy a controller, which is a shame too, since this is definitely the game that I've been waiting for since... well since it was announced back in 2012.
At the very least, in a lot of ways, I can honestly say:
Well done Square Enix. Now, just at least patch in mouse integration like you did with Final Fantasy Type-0 HD along with more resolution options and I'm sure many of us will be eternally grateful.

While Ancient Times is a direct sequel to Masked Intent, it is a nice enough hidden object game on its own. Sure, it really likes to use point ‘n’ click gameplay over anything else, but if you don’t mind that, you have a solid HOG on your hands.
The Secret Order 3: Ancient Times didn’t take any chances: it uses the most common hidden object game elements and almost entirely forgets that it is supposed to be in the same series where the first game was about a heroine using a future tablet computer to battle time-travelling mobsters.
Here, we get a typical fantasy kingdom instead, with all the cute fantasy fairy tale creatures to save and/or defeat in order to stop two power-hungry wizards before they destroy said kingdom. As usual, the main motivation is to save the heroine’s father, although this little fact gets a bit lost after the intro…
Like story design, gameplay stays as much on familiar waters as possible. So don’t expect anything new or creative, expect a lot of familiar puzzle types. Thankfully, their design is good enough to be enjoyable from start to finish, adding a nice enough piece into Artifex Mundi’s published portfolio.

This game has potential but severely lacks features.
It is your typical darwin pond game.
Who likes these games knows that it is not so much about constant interaction, but more about watching an ecosystem slowly evolve.
Sadly, because of a lack of complexity, all those games fall short in this regard. Sooner or later you get a stable / stagnant mono-culture and no matter which mass-extinction events you introduce, it stays that way.
With Evolution, this moment comes very early, sometimes even before the 10th generation.
While there is some complexity in the bots behaviour, the game lacks in any other regard.
You can't even save creatures in your pond to lett the "winners" compete against each other.
There is absolutely no environmental diversity.
Important evolutionary features like mating for example are missing as well.
Also, other than in the laboratory, you don't have a quick way to play intelligent designer and tweak a creature on the go.
Other than the most basic stats like health and hunger, you have nothing. No save or load, import or export functions, nothing.
I'd like to have a so-so thumb for this. As said, if you look into the quite complex neuronal workings of the bots, this could become a good evolution game but as of now, it just isn't.

This game is probably the only game in my steam library that is literally unplayable. There is no way to progress in this game at all. When you run out of matches, candles, and light sources, which if you have even a cursory interest in exploring the levels you will, and very fast, the game is effectively over.
Your options are to either memorize where the candles/matches/lamps are, or stumble around watching an entirely black screen. There is no way to see in this game without a light source, at all, so running out of light is effectively the end of the game. Turning up the brightness on your monitor does nothing, as the game's darkness is just a flat black screen with no detail whatsoever for the brightness to accentuate.
The game's titular house is HUGE, so even if you do find all the light sources through sheer trial and error and memorization, you will be forced to backtrack through areas without any new light sources and will, guaranteed, run out of light and the game will be essentially over.
I have yet to get to a part with any combat, though the screenshots make it seem like there is some. I wouldn't know, I've only made it half an hour in before I simply could not find a single other light source in the whole house. And again, the game is absolutely 100% over once you run out of light, as you can see absolutely nothing but what might as well be a flat black .jpg in front of your screen.
Light sources drain at around a percentage point a second, and the light pickups you find will never give you more than a handful of percentage points of increase anyways. Lighting the ambient stationary lamps, sort of like what Amnesia has with tinderboxes, is glitched and broken. Even though the lamps do turn on, they don't actually cast any light on anything, making them totally useless for actually being able to see and get around.
The opening cutscene is a laggy mess with typos galore, you can't re-bind key settings, there's no story from what I can tell, and the jump-scares may well be horrifying, but you'll never find out, as you'll never be able to see them.
This game is, no exaggeration, a black screen simulator. Don't buy this, don't even buy this as a gift. For that get Bad Rats, Desert Gunner, if you can find it Air Control. Those are bad in a funny way. This isn't funny, it isn't even a mess, it's simply rendered impossible by the developer forgetting that not everyone that plays the game is him, and as such won't be able to make a beeline for every single light source.
This game needs some manner of night vision, or at least some way to make out small details in the dark, or simply making your light sources dim once you run out of light. But it doesn't, and it probably won't, so as such, it's unplayable garbage and a total waste of what little money it costs.

Wolfenstin 2: The New Colossus is something that i enjoyed but also had it's fair share of annoyances, most of which sit on the story and certian aspects of the gameplay that have changed.
The Story is a noticable mark down. I could not care less about the new characters introduced and  lot of the older characters are shunted to the side in favor or less developed and less liked characters.
The bad guys also don't feel as well developed and seem a lot more cartoonish now compared to the first game. BJ's father for example stands out as evil for the sake of evil. Abuses his wife, his sun, hates jews, hates blacks, openely states that the only reason he married was to get his wife's buisness connections via BJ's grandfather and even kicks dogs (not even kidding). I was wishing for more parts like the train scene from TNO but instead we have way to much jumpping the shark with tiny bits of greatness smooshed inbetween oneupmanship.
The gameplay works and the gunplay is nice. Everything sounds great, the effects are awesome, everything has a punch to it but it all feels like needless complexity has been stacked on top while not actally going anywhere new. We get weapon upgrades but the weapons are now less interesing vs the first game, we get dual wielding of 2 different weapons but it makes switching less smooth, we get more perks but a lot of them boil down to "+ x damage/damage resistance" and take a lot longer to unlock. The actual shooting is fun but everything around it leaves a bit of a sour taste in my mouth. Not to metnion the choice to make you super weak in the first half makes sense story wise but is not fun to play.
The real prblem i have with the gameplay as well as the content gating that goes into the side missions. In the game the major side mission is to kill off the Nazi Oberkommandos that are running the US. In order to do this you need to first find enigma codes, decode their location (which is a place you already played through), go to the location, do the level in reverse from the first time and then kill them at the end. The frustrating part is that the commender you need to kill in question has a rocket pistol that can 1 shot you from full health and the only checkpoint in the level is at the beginning. This doesn't sound to bad but it quickly became tedious when you realize that you don't have enough enigma codes to unlock the next commander and it's back to grinding. Why make us sove a puzzle first can't any of the 30-40 people on the boat do it? Why not give people enough codes on the first playthough to unlock the side missions? WHY NOT JUST LET US PLAY THE SIDE MISSION AFTER FINISHING THE MAIN ONE INSTEAD OF LOCKING IT BEHIND BUSY WORK?! The kicker is that it really has no tangable in game benefit unless you missed an upgrade the first time around or it's one of the 3 locations that has a contraption. It's just more of the same levels, this time with shaken up enemy layouts and types.
The contraptions are interesting but 2 are clearly more useful than the other. One is a charge that can kill enemies when you sprint though them, one is a pair of extendable legs that allows you to get to high positions and peak over cover, another is a vest that lets you squeeze into tight places. The first 2 are useful both in and out of combat, the last one had very limited use. I suspect that i was supposed to be able to use it in some spots but it was very glitchy and often wouldn't activate no matter which way i approached it.
The Art took a major hit going from TNO to TNC. Where in each level every enemy had different uniforms, distinguishing looks and were easy to tell different enemy types apart. Now most levels contain the same copy pasted gray black enemies and robots with the exception of 1 or 2 varients based off of enviroment.
The level design seems to have followed suit for the art department, most levels being made up of fairly bland gray corridors and brown-gray ruins. Nothing really stands out compared to the first game. In the first game you had the moonbase, the giant bridge, a prison complex in the middle of berlin, a research base, invading a nazi u-boat. Now we have mostly boring ruins. I was hoping to see more of the nazi americana but really it's boild down to one short section on a city street, yay.
The music is the one posotive thing i can say that 100% got better from the first game. It has a mix of slowly pased ambient sound, a haunting orchestra soundtrack, and doom speed metal. Not to metnion they still have the alternate history popular music of the time which helps contribute to the atmosphear.
Overall the game still has it's fun moments but it has a fair number of flaws and doesn't live up to the greatness of the first game. The spark is still there, it's just not as bright piled under a bunch of useless junk. I recommend that if you want to pick it up wait for it to go 50% off or lower.

Whilst I enjoyed playing the campaign, the game is riddled with bugs. Broken AI that can see you through several layers of walls when trying to do stealth. The melee/throw hatchet is the same button without the ability to have seperate options which means when I try to stab someone sometimes he throws a hatchet across the room and alerts everyone. The side quests are boring and just repeats of the maps you have already done. The plot shows promise with the ideas of his backstory but is so over the top in other parts with no character development with the other characters it doesn't work. Then the ending where the game finishes on what feels like the halfway mark. The combat is repetitive and clunky and usually frustrating. Not to mention having autosaves half a second before being killed which is great. Also when you explore a district and die you have to restart from beginning no matter if it was the last soldier that killed you. Overall I would wait for it to be on sale theres no way the game is worth 80 Australian dollars for a 10 hour campaign without the DLC (which is generous given it can be done in far less). I would pay maybe 20 bucks for what it is, I'd wait for a sale.

DISCLAIMER:
This review is purely foccused on the title as an experience.
For any in-depth review on fps and as such go elsewhere.
So you're thinking about getting this game but still not sure, right?
Hopefully this will give you a better perspective about what you can expect.
Let me start by saying that playing the other games is not required at all, with that out of the way let's get into it.
This is the story of William Blazkowicz, a little boy who grew up surrounded by violence and racism.
The little boy turned a veteran who like many others is sick and tired of bowing down on damn Nazi's.
To ensure that his beliefs are met, he puts his trust with "the resistence" as the last effort to stop the future generation's of being raised in Hitler's paradise.
Do not think for a second that this is your typical title where the creators were shy to stand up for what is right, to stand up for an experience carefully curated with violence, love and self justice.
Wolfenstein is at its core a movie, the cutscenes are filled with nazi gore, the treath of violence is constantly present in which would other wise seem like a perfectly normal situation given this new society and this is portrated beautifuly.
At times, you can see yourself in the characters virtual but yet so humanised eyes, just like us they show fear, yet they are the brave ones.
Throughout this wonderful yet peculiar experience, you are gifted with grotesque scenes that reafirm the setting and tone for what's to come, yet again reafirming the threath of violence.
Character's personalities are tied to the visual elements before you while they yet again display their emotions strongly, almost as if showing emotions is tied to a consequence.
Patriotism at heart, unaconted actions are taken, violence happens, Anya's tears are dropped while bullets get closer to Hitler and general Irene Engel, the risk of death is constant but a future free of the threat of violence is from the upmost importance.
The music played while politics are discussed in the room, bullets are shot from the window and drinks are poured, this...this is the humanity in you, this is the life, the risk and what must be done.
The gameplay is good, but the level design can be repetitive, however this is quickly erased from perspective when the light shines on the bigger picture, as an experience this is a master piece, only flawed by our own expectations of having more, bigger and louder.
We are not gonna take it, no we are not gonna take it!
tl;dr Taking what's ours back.
You play as a guy who wants to free america from Nazi's with his group of new found lovers.

Original review, 6/26/16:
I love this game. HOWEVER, I played it on 360... but I recently joined Steam and this pack (this and DS1) was one of my first purchases.
Now, out of the various games I've played, via Steam or other means, this is the ONLY game I've tried that really suffers on PC; there is something about the graphical engine that destroys its framerate. I've tried every fix I could find via Steam and Google to no avail... even with minimal settings, the framerate still suffers noticeably. And, ultimately, no matter what problem you have with it, the company will insist the problem is you and your machine.
The game is good (although I've recently started to dislike SP games with extensive random loot generation... 99% of results are garbage, but the farming is a big time sink), but the version of the game for PC will have you scrambling for solutions. Some people find easy fixes, some never get that lucky.
Buy it if it's cheap, because it's a good game, but watch out... there's a chance you may never be able to finish the tutorial level for the buggy graphical engine. Because of this issue alone, I technically have to give it a thumbs-down.
Update, 6/2/17:
Almost a year later, I've never  found a suggestion that actually made this game playable. And it's still the only game I have that has this problem. It's a bug-riddled nightmare port of an excellent game. Play it on console and save yourself the gamble of possibly buying a completely unplayable port.

So right off the bat, I have to say this... If you're not a massive cycling fan, then I probably can't really recomend this game. All the fun for me comes in the form of assembling a top team from some of the hottest up and coming riders in cycling and so if you don't have that level of investment in the sport then I can't imagine that the gameplay is strong enough the tip the balance here.
I mean don't get me wrong, the actual gameplay is fairly solid, you can now perform most of the actions that you would want to as a cycling manager, (I'm especially grateful for this years addition of the abilities to form rider trains and to set a rider to try and reduce the gap to a breakaway rider) however there's nothing magical about the gameplay of this management game that makes it better than any of the other sports management games out there.
So just to sort of sum it up. If you are just a fan of simulation of management games then probably turn somewhere else for a more accessable game, however if you following road cycling on the TV, then this game can definitely scratch an itch for you!
p.s. Also there is a 'Be a pro' mode and thats pretty good I guess

The combat system makes the game harder than just to move your mouse and click on someone's head as it is more chance based rather than just shooting and getting E-Z kills. Easy to learn, Hard to master. servers used to be low populated but as of now the game got a huge increase in players. My suggestion? Buy it. Don't hesitate. Would be nice to see a few new players on the battlefield!
