I like my racing games and I enjoy my puzzle games. Racer 8 is a budget shifting tile puzzle game where you must ensure that your racer makes it safely through a checkpoint and to the finish line. Each course is a mix of different tiles, curved tiles, three way turn tiles and a few crossroads. Think of a train on a track that can only go forward and rather than being the engineer, you're the one that ensures the track is laid out properly. If there's no track ahead, then you crash and need to restart the course again.
I'll start off with the good. The game has pleasing, cute, simple almost cartoon in a way graphics. Everything looks sleek and uniform. You can purchase more cars and different paint jobs for them with the points you earn for racing. Each vehicle has its own stats for acceleration, deceleration and whatever 100% scr is. The game's help system could be a lot more informative than telling me what all of the menu icons are. Its all nice stuff that adds to the longevity of a game with at least fifty courses. Its sad that once a course is done, its done. There's no going back.
Before you get to challenge those courses, you face a practice map that's like the others. You do this before anything else in the game. Its best to jump in head first and there's nothing difficult at the start. Once you're done with that, you get to go into the main menu.
Since Racer 8 has a rally car theme, its a race and that consists of fuel, speed, a checkpoint, a finish and what amounts to jewels to collect on your way. Once you've been on the track for a while, the checkpoint will spawn and you'll need to rotate tiles to get the vehicle through the gate. With that done, after a few more seconds, the finish line will appear. You'll need to mind your fuel though.
While I enjoy puzzle games, these tile puzzle games are among my least favorite, but it takes more than a bad genre to make a bad game. Its the glitches here and there. Things as simple as using the menu. I can click on leader boards, settings and stats to see them, but the problem is, there's no way out of them without closing the game. There are interfaces that look like they should slide up or down. They have arrows indicating it, but there is no mouse wheel support, but more surprising than that, clicking the up or down arrows does nothing as well. Trying to purchase a new vehicle for 200 points when I had 200 points told me that I did not have enough to make the purchase.
Then there's playing the game, you click a tile to rotate it left, your right click to make it rotate right. That's simple enough, but to make things more challenging, certain tiles go under construction, making them a wildcard, because they can turn into any different tile. I'm fine with that, its part of the challenge to avoid them, but there are other tiles that shift without me telling them to. There's no warning that they will shift, it just happens. Worse than that, there are a few times when the vehicle has been on the road, about to leave the tile to a road that's connected and it just crashes as if it was driving down a highway with no turns, no cars and then slams into an invisible wall.
There are no hot keys and to pause the game, you'll need to mouse click it. To control the racer's throttle, you'll need to click and drag it left to go slower or right to go faster. While faster might get you where you're going, it just takes your mouse away from the tiles it needs to be at. Tapping with a finger would be much better, but even then, you risk a tile rotating when you're busy messing with the speed. The further you drive, the faster the racer seems to go.
Trees can obscure your vision of the course and tiles. Could you imagine if Tetris blocked out part of your screen? The game's camera is cumbersome. You need to click the camera icon and mess with a slider. The slider raises or lowers the camera and you can click and drag the camera around. It will always continue to look down on the map like its a chess board. Racer 8 is a touch screen for sure. A top down perspective would have been advantageous, but it would have taken away from the style the game has.
Everything culminates in a bad game. A budget title with menus that force you to close the game, a less preferred genre in general with a problematic camera. Its difficult to recommend this game to anyone but tile puzzle lovers on touch screen devices. Even then, there are still issues to contend with.

Dungeon Hearts has a lot of game potential but some of the design choices suck the fun out of the game.
There's no control on Dungeon Hearts. Unlike like other match three games like the incredible PuzzleQuest I never felt incontrol of the action. Instead I felt like I SHOULD be in control of the action. The scrolling speed is too fast for one thing. Moveing the gems is maps to the mouse click and drag style and that's horribly inaccurate. By the time I've seen how to make a match the gems are half way across the screen. And this in a game where the gems are basically free form.
I'm still under an hour and a good chunk of that was spend trying to understand the tutorial which doesn't actually tell you that you can drag the gems by the way. I sat there trying to figure out how to make a match for seconds before i realized the thing wanted me to drag and just didn't say so. Yet still I feel no progression. There's no level end, there's no tally up. Just a temporary detour between enemies where I'm supposed to do what looks like a bonus round but is instead just more of the same tension and frustration of trying to see gems and then move them and then click them.
I'm not a fan of the double click either. Part of the reason the game feels too fast is that you can't just match three gems and then fire them off. That oly generates the actual attack gem you need. Which you can then drag and drop and THEN click to perform an attack in the background you never notice and in the foreground that you can never care about because you're too busy trying to find your next trio.
It's late I'm going to bed and I Dungeon Hearts was a terrible choice for a good night game. I have no idea where I'm supposed to stop. It isn't as if I had to run through X more enemies to complete the level. As far as I can tell there are no levels. You just run and run and run each time adding new gems to the mix. The double hit gems are bad enough. I can't make combos i can barely hit the single baddies. Unfortunately I just can't say I had any fun with the game. It looks fantastic, It runs smooth, I'm sure the soundtrack is banging but at the end of the day.. the game is something I don't want to go back to. I don't WANT to see if there is an end to the level because I don't feel my characters getting better I don't feel anything but annoyance that the gems won't go where i want them to go as fast as I need them to go without getting it and it feels unfair.

My PC gamer buds know that, once in a while, if I'm terrifically impressed by a game I'll rave about it. Here's another one I've started up recently: "Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice."
A fantastic story involving Norse legends and gods and a young girl who is coming to terms with psychosis due to awful events in her life. Deserves to be played with a good pair of headphones and a PC that handles frame rates well. The sound is incredible, the story pulse-pounding; harrowing, in fact, there's actually a warning at the game head stating that if one has experienced psychosis...I guess in this case voices in one's head...one should NOT attempt to play the game (because it will F===. You. Up).
Graphics are running on Unreal 4 engine. Not as "clean" as, say, Witcher 3, but you are immersed just the same. The psychotic visual effects (ranging from minor to unnerving) make it one of the most unusual-looking games I've ever played. Beautifully deranged, in a way, and despite that the burning villages, mountains and forest,waterfalls still take seem real enough to me. Their weaving of real actors (through CGI) into the story makes it even MORE immersive. Your character looks real because she IS real.
Everything about this game says you cannot stop playing, despite inherent frustrations (finding paths through fire to survive,for example) and dying often. The battles are not terribly inventive, but they're almost a welcome respite from all the sudden survival attempts to get from point A to point B.
Lots of mouse button mashing, in my case. But the heroine is wonderfully presented and her "spirit guide" weaves some great tales along the way. Voice acting is superb.
Be warned...the voices in her head contradict often. It may drive you batty, but damn if it doesn't make for a great game.
...one more note: there is a hoax, actually presented by the developers when the game came out, that if you die too often, the game wipes your save file (no spoilers from me revealing why) and you must start over. This actually slowed their sales from what I've read. I've died countless times but haven't had to start over,thankfully.

Full Throttle is a point and click adventure title that was originally released in 1995 by LucasArts, a company better known for their Indiana Jones, Sam & Max, and Monkey Island series'. Don't feel bad if you've never heard of this game, as it's one of the more obscure LucasArts titles. Despite the fact that it sold over a million copies, it's still considered a cult classic, one that faded into obscurity until now. Back in the day, two sequels were planned but both ended up being scrapped.
Within the world of Full Throttle, the player will take on the role of Ben Throttle, the leader of a bike gang known as The Polecats. The year is 2040, and motorized vehicles are being replaced by anti-gravitational cars instead, meaning that motorcycles in general are about to go extinct. The last domestic manufacturer of these beloved two-wheeled beasts is Corley Motors, and Ben, along with his gang, end up running into the company's CEO, Malcolm Corley. Some things go down, and Ben realizes that the entire company is in jeopardy, which eventually leads to him attempting to solve a murder that he ends up getting pinned for. I can't go into too much detail here, as doing so would spoil a good chunk of the game.
The updated graphics are excellent, as always Double Fine have done an outstanding job of sticking to the original game, all the while giving Full Throttle a fresh coat of paint; one can even change between the new and old graphics seamlessly at any time with the press of a button. The voice-overs and soundtrack have also been given a dynamic boost, leading to all of this title's elements feeling brand new. There's also a good chunk of extra content included, such as concept art, developer commentary and the like, some of which is unlocked throughout your playthrough.
The soundtrack and voice acting here are phenomenal. Many gamers who are in the age bracket of 25-35 will probably be more prone to recognizing many of the voices from various 90's cartoon shows and movies, such as Kath Soucie from Rugrats, Maurice LaMarche from Pinky and the Brain, and Tress MacNeille from Animaniacs; let's also not forget Mark Hamill who's the voice for Adrian Ripburger, the main antagonist. Needless to say, for its time it was an All Star line-up. As for the music, every song is performed by The Gone Jackals, and while the game doesn't feature any "hits", it's still a decent rock n' roll soundtrack.
Unfortunately, that's pretty much where the good side of Full Throttle ends, the remainder is just a pile of mediocre mush that ended up getting this revival thanks to the cult following that the game amassed. Do you like motorcycles? Explosions? Heavy Metal? A generic biker protagonist? Then this game still probably isn't for you. Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus is a great shooter with a great story but doesn't really do much to differentiate itself from other games in genre.
I clocked in at 7 hours on the easiest difficulty (I don't really like shooters that much, just wanted to play the story) but I still felt like there was a lot of filler. The sections at the home base make the game slow down to a crawl as you're forced to complete tasks that add nothing to the story. All you do is fumble around a U-boat that feels like a maze and talk to people until the game feels like you've done enough ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t to keep playing the fun stuff.
Speaking of the fun stuff, killing Nazis, that's what you do in this game and it does this well. The shooting feels good enough, but I would give the edge to Doom in this regard. I'd say the game has too many weapons, but that's a minor gripe. I only really ever used the machine gun, shotgun and the heavy weapons that you can pick up. That may also be because I played on easy, so take it with a grain of salt.
In terms of level design, it's pretty lack luster. The majority of the game is set in very similar locals and you often get lost trying to find your way to the next objective. The game does not have any kind of waypoint system, which is a good thing to me, but it's only a good thing when the levels are designed in such a way that you can find your way forward and not fumble around the same corridors for 5 minutes. Great examples of good linear level design can be found in games like Uncharted or The Last of Us. Those games give you a sense of exploration and discovery even though you know the game is linear.
As for the acting, sound design and music, it's all superb. The actors do a great job in playing their characters. My only gripe is with B.J. not being able to talk while you play. Characters will talk to him and he'll just stay quiet, it would make sense in games where you have a silent protagonist but B.J. talks all the time in cutscenes and inner monologues, so it just comes off as very incoherent. And as I said, sound and music is great. Was a while since I played The New Order, but this game felt more Doom in it's music than what I remember from TNO, however, may just be talking out of my♥♥♥♥♥on that one.
In conclusion, if you like shooters, play it. If you like cool alternate universe storytelling, play it. If you're tired of playing the same game over and over again even though the story is different, you could find something else to play.
I would recommend it though.

takes place directly after the events of the second game in the series, however, it isn’t necessary to play previous installments to understand the story in this selection. This game is a colorful point-and-click adventure filled with hidden item scenes, plenty of puzzles and an enthralling story that follows Sara through many mystical lands.
When you begin the game you get a brief overview of what happened in the second game to bring players up to speed. The main thing to know is there were two artifacts collected filled with immense power that now pose a danger to everyone.
with the goal of going to where the artifacts were created, the Kingdom of Aeronhart, and destroy them to stop present-day events. While at first you travel to London’s past, most of the game is spent in a mystical land called Aeronhart so there isn’t much time travel to be had actually. Once there the game turns more to high fantasy as you fly on griffins and battle against magical powers. Sara must help the people of Aeronhart to forward the story and gain access to the artifacts she’s searching for before time runs out.
Everything is point and click, using your mouse to move from each area of the map and to click on items and people for interactions. You collect items that are used elsewhere, like a rope or crystal that join your inventory. You also have two very useful aids in the game, the first a baby griffin who can help you reach items that are higher up since it can fly. It’s utterly adorable and rests on the lower right side of your screen. The second is a golem’s heart which has magic that can control stone statues. You can power it up more and more throughout the game and use it to control different stone things.
Puzzles come in a good bit of variety; there are slide puzzles, matching games, pipe puzzles and a host of other ones. There are two different types of hidden object scenes in the game, the traditional list of words and a scene to find said items in and another type where you have the items at the bottom in a scene.
All parts of the game come to life with beautiful colors and well drawn scenes. The game does not disappoint visually, except the people themselves. While they’re drawn well, the animation when they talk is a bit odd, their eyes are lifeless and their mouths move unnaturally. That being said, it’s the only visual issue I found in the game and not a major one. The art is good, the hidden object scenes are well done and the items are not blurry or too hard to find if you have bad eyes.
, the score helps set the mood of the narrative.
This game is a great addition to the library of any hidden object fan or anyone who is looking to get into the genre. I found some of the puzzles a little easy as well as some of the hidden object scenes however but this may help with those after the achievements. No achievements are based on what difficulty you play under or if you complete everything without hints or skips so it’s not hard to gain all of them. The game also
and a bonus level that continues Sara’s story a little bit more. While the game may be on the short side -I finished in four hours- it was time well-spent and a satisfying experience.
is a great example of strong storytelling mixed with a fun gaming experience.

Before reading my review, I want to make it known that my hours clocked in as recorded by steam is about 40 hours short of my actual play time, since I was playing in offline mode for most of the game. As proof, look at my achievements and youll see ive compelted the game.
Lightning returns, but not with a bang but with the liquid ♥♥♥♥♥.
Honestly, this game is terrible. Not in terms of optimization and configuration, because lets be honest here if you playing a port of a game a year or more older and from japan most of you probably dont expect much better than what the console release did. In that form it is surpisingly better, being able to give 60 fps during cutscenes and battles, higher resolutions than just 720 and 1080, and other settings for a better experience, however the frames take a marked hit while in the overworld. Apparently this was an issue even in the ps3 release since it was rushed out the door before the 8th gen consoles came around.
The gameplay however is just a complete, confused mess. The game has a doomsday clock feature where you have to complete objectives with in 13 days before the world ends. A minute in the doom clock is 3 seconds in real time, and by extension an hour goes by after 2 minutes. I didnt think this was a problem at first, but make no mistake, unless youre gifted with luck, you NEED a guide to be able to get everything done with in that time frame. Some quests are hidden, some are failable if not completed quick enough, others are missable and while in other rpg's it would normally just mean the loss of a weapon or item of some sort, in this game it means your weaker before the end game. This game does not have a level or exp system, instead growth is given from quests you do in the game, meaning that any quests you miss means your weaker when fighting a boss, or worse, the end game boss.
The doomsday clock also takes away from one of the bigger elements that rpg games usually have, that being exploration. Normally in other rpg's youd be able to explore areas, discover secrets, talk to npcs and discover things as you go along, however the clock makes the beautiful visuals impossible to take in, to the point that I have to read what npc's are saying as i run to the next objective. This relates to my earlier point about quests, since the limited time frame you have to complete objectives, yet are still expected to talk to npc's to start quests makes you have to plan out ever move you make before you begin each day in the game. Granted the one thing the game has to make completing quests easier is a feature called chronostasis, which pauses the clock for about 1 minue real time. This can be done so long as you have enough eradia points, which can be refilled by killing monsters.
About fighting monsters however, that is where the game is the most dim. The battles use an active time battle (here on our called atb) system similar to the previous final fantasy 13 games where actions take up atb points, though the typical action such as guard or attack take up very little points. Its complicated by the fact that you have 3 atb guages. Each guage is linked to a schemata, that being a set up of 4 abilites, a garb, weapon and shield. A garb is the clothing lightning wears that also grants auto abilites but also locks one or two abilites, in practice similar to the job systems of previous final fantasy games. You switch between garbs in battle to have access to abilties you have set, such as an attack, a guard, a magic attack, etc. Though this could have been a fun way to shake things up, it only adds another layer of confusion to the gameplay. The atb guages fill rather slowly while in battle and at times you will standing waiting for the guages to to fill before making another move, that is unless you plan ahead and manage every action you take. When the enemies in this game are tanks that at times can take for ever to kill, it adds a pointless way of wasting time to a game that could otherwise move at a faster pace. Dont be surprised when a chunk of your hp was just taken when you meant to switch garbs and press the command button for guard, but accidentally switched to a different garb instead and used an abiltiy you would have otherwise wanted to save for later. Locked garb abilites for that matter means that abilites assigned to a button cannot be placed elsewhere on your list of commands, just to make it more difficulty for you muscle memory.
The game is further complicated by an ability system that makes it highly difficult to have a proper set up. Abilites come in different types, such as different attack abilites like heavy slash, elemental atacks, blitz attacks and the like, but also come in levels, from 1 to 5. Dont be surprised if later your ability list is swamped with loads of abilities that you dont know what to do with. The ui for the list is terible as well, even by sorting, it says alot that couldnt add a ui to sort by ability type. The ability system which could have been interesting like that used in kingdom hearts birth by sleep is made pointlessly difficult to understand and honestly quite a chore if not for the level system, since youre also expected to synthesize abilities, which require in game currency as well as a limited pool of items you get from killing enemies. For that matter, the garbs i mentioned earlier have locked abilities.
As for enemies, there are very few unique enemies in the game, There is less than 50 actually, including bosses, if you dont count last ones. Last ones are much stronger versions of 31 of the enemies in the game which appear after killing a certain number of that monster. After its killed, thats it, that monster will never appear again during your current playthrough. My biggest gripe with this is that such a complicated battle system, with an even more complicated ability system, seems wasted on such limited content.
And to make matters worse, later enemies you fight can do hefty damage. In rpgs this is normally not an issue, just heal up and keep going. Actually scratch that, there is no cure spell other than curaga which uses your limited eradia points, and the only other two ways are using mediguard, an ability thay blocks attacks and reocovers hp at a snails pace, or by using recovery items which you have a very limited number of which you can hold at one time. Your supposed to be able to trade blows and do damage to tanky enemies through out the game yet some how still guard, which isnt perfect since residual damage will go through and slowly chip you bit by bit, and are expected to do this over the course of multiple battles as you complete quests or main objectives. For that matter i was at a loss at what to do when fighting the first boss. The first boss does way to damage, I did way to little and my guard ability didnt exactly do a good job of guarding. At this point I should mention perfect guarding, which a function of using the guard ability in which if I used the guard command right before the enemy attack connects, much more damage will be blocked while also possibly staggering the enemey. Staggering means the enemy will be be idle for a short amount of time and take more damage. The problem with this is that even on normal, the window for perfect blocking is small. VERY small. If youre a guarding master in dark souls, then this game will be a piece of cake for you. How ever for first time players new to the battle system, being expected to know how to perfect gaurd when im barely on the first boss its just to extreme. Perhaps if the window was bigger on normal difficulty and made smaller in hard, then i could appreciate it as a mechanic for people who want a challenge, but for now, if I wanted to play a clunkier dark souls, then ill just ♥♥♥♥ing play dark souls.

Wow, what can I say about Hellblade, what a pleasent surprise.
The game is incredible, graphically, naratively and gameplay-wise.
The game is essentially an over-the-shoulder adventure with walking segments, puzzle segments, and combat segments.
It is a linear title, so walking is pretty straight-forward, however, the graphics are so impressive that it doesn't feel like a chore.  Everything is always very good to look at and the scale of some areas is just incredible.  Looking off in the distance at a tower, or the far-end of the beach is just a sight.
As far as puzzles, this is the weakest point for me.  Most of the puzzles consist of focusing on a nordic character, or symbol, and trying to identify a similar shape of the character in the real world. Hellblade is a third person action game where the player controls a Celtic woman called Senua, who is fighting through Hell to rescue the soul of her dead lover from the Norse gods.
The melee combat system is really enjoyable. You’re armed with a sword, and you’ve got four basic moves – quick attack, strong attack, dodge and parry. You can also charge up a focus mode, where time slows down but you still attack at normal speed. There are a few different enemies to fight including one armed with a sword, one with a mace, another with a mace and shield, one who dual wields small axes, and a big dude with a massive two handed axe. And of course there are a few unique bosses.
The key to success is to watch your opponent’s movements to anticipate their attacks (there are no flashing icons above their heads here), dodge or parry, and then follow up with your own attacks while their guard is down. The quality of the character animations allows you to really feel the weight behind every hit, especially when Senua gets knocked down, and when she blocks an attack, causing the enemy to stumble backwards.
Hellblade has a kind of permadeath mechanic in place. You’ve got an unspecified amount of lives, and each time you die, a dark black “rot” grows up Senua’s right arm. If it reaches her brain, she dies permanently and your save will be deleted. This adds an intensity to the combat, and makes you want to play cautiously instead of just rushing in and button mashing. However, its not something that you need to be scared of, or a reason to avoid playing the game. I beat Hellblade in one playthrough, and I’d guess I died around ten times. Even the later fights, where you’ll be up against multiple enemies (at one point I was simultaneously fighting eight enemies on a narrow bridge), aren’t too hard if you make intelligent use of focus.
The other primary gameplay mechanic is puzzle solving, but the quality of these is a bit of a mixed bag. The most common type of puzzle requires you to find “runes” to unlock doors. These runes are hidden somewhere in the environment. For example, a letter N might be formed by two tree trunks and a tree branch. You need to stand in the correct spot and then focus your vision on the shape of the rune. Its not a particularly interesting mechanic, and the game solves 90% of the puzzle for you anyway, because you’ll see a bunch of red runes floating in the general area where you need to stand.
The better kind of puzzles involves interacting with objects to change the layout of the environment. For example, your path might be blocked by the illusion of a wall, until you look through an archway which dispels the illusion. In another area, you’ll look through masks to switch back and forth between day and night, to bypass obstacles that are blocking your path.
Throughout the game, you’ll frequently hear several whispered voices, which seem to be a representation of Senua’s internal hopes, doubts and fears. These voices are sometimes helpful or supportive, but mostly they taunt you and try to make you doubt yourself. During combat, when an enemy gets behind you they’ll warn you to “watch out”, but when you take damage they’ll say “she’s going to die”. As you’re wandering around the environment, they’ll claim “she’s going the wrong way, she’s lost”. These voices sound really cool and I can’t remember this being done by any other game that I’ve played.
Senua’s facial expressions might be the best I’ve ever seen in a game. I felt like I could understand her emotional state, especially pain, fear and sadness, just by looking at her face. The way her eyes move makes her seem alive, especially when she looks directly at the camera, and lip syncing is a perfect match to the dialogue. If every game was like this, we could forget about the uncanny valley. Senua’s voice actress, Melina Juergens, also gives a phenomenal performance.
The environments are absolutely gorgeous. Generally I don’t really care about graphical quality, I’m more focused on gameplay and story. But there were times when even I had to stop for a moment and say “wow”. Occasionally you’ll be outside in bright sunlight, looking at a colourful field of flowers. But mostly you’ll be surrounded by ruined buildings full of burnt corpses, or in dark caves, the floor covered in bones, with only a small torch to light the way ahead.
However, I think the area layouts could be better. Many modern games design levels in a kind of circle. When you reach the end of a section, they’ll find an elegant way to quickly get you back to the start, for example through a previously locked door, or by dropping down from a higher platform. In Hellblade, particularly after defeating a boss, you just have to spend about 5 minutes backtracking through the areas you’ve just cleared, with absolutely nothing happening. There’s not much space to explore, and the only reason to do this anyway is to find stone markers that tell you small pieces of stories which are not at all related to Senua, and mostly fall into the category of “a long time ago, this guy you’ve never met and don’t care about did a thing to this other guy you’ve never met and don’t care about”.
I easily maintained a constant 60 fps with all settings maxed at 1080p, and I didn’t suffer from any bugs or crashes. However, you can’t fully rebind controls on a keyboard. In particular, you can’t rebind movement to arrow keys, which is my preferred setup. Instead, I played with my 360 gamepad which worked great.
Overall, while I’m not quite as in love with this game as most of the critics, I did find alot to enjoy, so I’d recommend Hellblade to any fan of action games. As it only took me 8.5 hours to complete the game, I’d suggest waiting for a sale of around 25-33%.

Fun game, with rather confusing, maybe misleading concept.
Let me just state first, that I do enjoy the gameplay, and I do think this is a decent game. Nevertheless, it does have a rather awfully frustrating asepct. When it comes to the details of overall design in gameplay, it does raise some questions.
This game 'indirectly' encourages stealth play, rather forefully, by making non-stealth approach quite difficult and frustrating. Your ammunition supply is somewhat limited, enemies will appear from everywhere and evetually surround you, whilst it takes about a whole magazine of assualt rifle to kill a single enemy.
There is no real cover-and-shoot mechanics within this game - yes you can utilise the 'lean' actions, however it is clear that the applications are limited. Moreover, anyhow, cover-and-shoot style is not really opitmal anyway, as there will be numerous enemies coming from every angle.
Furthermore, your health is capped at 50, with additional health slowly decreasing to 50. Yes, there is armor which bascially functions as additional health, however the problem is that the enemies do considerable amount of damage, with outstanding accuracy. So, whilst you need like a whole magazine to kill a single enemy, and there are swarms of enemies rushing at you from every angle with high damage and excellent accuracy.
So at this point, as a player, I am not really sure what to do other than following the stealth apporach. I would not mind a challenging difficulty, however this just feels unfair - it is simply discouraging and frustrating.
Summary and conclusion? If you enjoy a rather difficult stealth FPS game, then yea give it ago. Otherwise, you might want to think over it again, as it turns out, this game is not really what it is presented as; a hardcore rush-and-shoot adrenaline-boosting game. This is a stealth game with optional all-out fighting approach.

*This review doesn't mean that Wolfenstein 2 is bad, just that I cannot honestly recommend it. I played the game on the third hardest difficulty level out of seven.*
Wolfenstein 2 is a linear storybased shooter that is quite fast paced when there is action. This game has lengthy cutscenes in between every level, which are pretty entertaining I have to admit. The characters and story are all goofy and the game doesn't take itself seriously at all, much like some recent mainstream Hollywood films, but the humour here is much better and the acting never really annoy you or anything like that.
As a game though, Wolfenstein 2 is first of all short and a bit rushed I'd say. The levels could use more refining, like something else than a recurrent airvent between every room where there is a fight. There is loot absolutely every where you look at, so running out of ammo will not happen and the enemies die from very few bullets anyway. This game has some more satisfying battles towards the end of the main story, but most of the battles are just short and uninspiring. The enemies are not like in Doom titles, where they are all very different and have variable damage and health values. In Wolfenstein 2 enemies are always deadly from close and easy to kill from far, so you tend to fight them from far away. It's anticlimatic that the game ends in endorsement of USA and just leaves it there without any revelations or uncovering of events.
Wolfenstein 2 is good when you have those arena like shooting scenarios going, but otherwise it is meaningless and mindless. The graphics and music are good though and the game is very well optimized, but who can I recommend this game for? I can't think of any, since it won't satisfy a fan of a good shooter or a fan of a thrilling story either.

However, with the psychotic short times of the light sources, and even with what lamps I could get lit before I ran out of the very and I am not exaggerating, major very short matches, even the candles lasted only about oh, 7 or 8 steps, there was not enough light to do anything. (running only seemed to make them go out faster (if that is possible!) )
I looked at the forums for inspiration as to how to possibly get over my initial put the game down and never pick it up again reaction due to the almost entirely unplayability and found that an update to the game was done July 3rd  to increase the light source burn times. Now.... If there was an increase prior to my playing this game, then dear goodness, how anyone could play at all astounds me. Litterally the light sources right now, with my system, I blink and they're out, I cannot imagine if what I experienced is a "longer burn time" what the old burn time could have been.  I understand the short burn times are to have the sound effects, the jumpscares and such affect the player more as they stumble around in the dark, however, let me propose this, allow a gamma slider. Even pitch black, the eyes adjust and some light even if everything is grey/shades of black are seen with the naked eye (Without roadrunner fast matches and such illuminating for a second), so perhaps instead of having it pitch black, allow it so that folk whom are without resources of light can see at least loosely what's infront of them in order to try and find more light, to continue the game. Also, like another commenter I read suggested, when a lamp on the wall is lit, make the light it casts longer than the immediate vicinity of where it is on the wall, especially in rooms where there are more than one lamp lit. When I've lit more than one lamp in a room, the light combines and the room is brighter as each lamp collectively contributes to the light in the room, the lamps in the rooms barely make it worth lighting them at all.
As I said, this is perhaps early to write a review with only 25 min play time (don't know why this review logger isn't showing it), but these are my initial impressions that quite frankly due to the sheer aggrivation in attempting to play my first time starting it up. I bought this game for less than 1€ in Humble Store, but I can’t recommend it even for this price.
The idea is really good if you if you like “matching gems” games and specially if you really enjoyed Puzzle Quest, with the Rpg factor involved. You basically have 4 different heroes with different skills and you gather experience after every combat. Gems appear from the right side of the screen and disappear through the left after a few seconds, and by matching them you attack the enemy or avoid his attacks, so all what you do is click or drag gems all the time in order to perform different actions. The idea is really good, what a pity that is so poorly executed.
I can forgive the extreme lack of detail of the enemies because for this kind of games graphics are not really important, but the lack of detail is embarrassing some times. Obviously they could have worked a few days more to improve it, but they didn’t. We are talking about enemies that almost don’t move and stay still on the screen all the time, it would have been nice if they had the same detail than the heroes or if they just didn’t appear at all in the screen (I rather have a picture of them like in PQ than having a big non detailed grey mass on the screen).
I can even forgive the terrible controls. As I said the only thing that you do is click or drag, and you must be fast. As other players complained about, a lot of times you click but the game detects that you are dragging, and vice versa. That can be really annoying sometimes, especially in difficult combats.
What I can’t forgive is the lack of a story mode. There is absolutely no story, no map, anything to encourage you to continue playing. Every time that you play you start from 0, facing one enemy after another one until you die, with nothing in between. Considering that I enjoyed 10,000,000 to a fair degree, I had reasonably high expectations when I heard Dungeon Hearts was a mixture of puzzle and role playing games as well. Much to my disappointment, I instead found myself bored to death within 20 minutes of starting.
My biggest gripe with Dungeon Hearts overall is that the RPG elements feel very tacked-on and unnecessary. Character skills are poorly explained and feel clumsy to use due to generally poor interface design. Above all, there's very little feeling of actual progression and very little done to break the general monotony of the gameplay. Every enemy is fought in more or less the exact same manner - form attacks by combining 3 of the same color piece, move the attack gem onto a line that contains an enemy attack gem, and click. Repeat ad infinitum. Combined with the total lack of story,  the "epic journey" feels like little more than a slight occasional change in backdrop scenery.
When you strip away the façade of supposed RPG gameplay in Dungeon Hearts, what remains is the puzzle game aspects. Unfortunately, as stated before, the puzzle game core is incredibly repetitive and comes with a click-and-drag system that feels incredibly choppy and awkward to use. In the end, the only redeeming factor to be found is the surprisingly solid soundtrack.
In summary, Dungeon Hearts pretends to be a unique blend of the classic "match-3" puzzle type game and an RPG, but at the end of the day, the RPG aspects are little more than a shallow veneer coating an even shallower game.

Dungeon Hearts is a continuous stream of match three, with some spells and frantic shuffling. Easy to pick up, hard to get through all of the levels without dying. Abilities that you wind up to can help, and certainly if you play through the game enough times you can unlock various abilities with a store where you spend experience points to make your life a little easier. All in all a fairly fun, casual game.

Dungeon Hearts is a match 3 puzzle game.  Dungeons hearts adds some enjoyable elements to make this millionth iteration of match 3 games a bit more fun.  There are blocks that are sent by the enemy to slow you down.  Your goal is to crush the enemy while stopping his attacks.  As you progress through the game you get certain skills that fall outside simple block movements that can get you out of a pickle.  You also gain experience which gives your characters different abilities.  This gives the player a chance to feel like they can actually beat the game even if their skills aren't up to snuff to make it to the last boss.  There is an incentive to keep playing and boost your skills so that those final levels don't seem to tough.  If you are into puzzle games and don't mind staring at moving blocks all day, you will probably enjoy this game.  If you are sick of the million different iterations of puzzle games, I would probably pick up something else.

Sara Pennington thought she could breathe a little after defeating the traitor in the Order of Griffins. However, the artefacts she retrieved are unstable and cause damage, eventually killing her father. In order to prevent that fate, she has to go back in time and find the kingdom of King Amedon, Aeronheart...
While you didn't really need to play the first game, which isn't on Steam, to understand The Secret Order 2: Masked Intent, I think that it's better to play the sequel before Ancient Times.  But even without the previous knowledge, the game in itself is very understandable. The storyline is also well-done, as many twists are also present and given how the game ended, you know that there will be a fourth game (already released elsewhere). I just hope that Artifex Mundi got also the rights to publish New Horizon (the first game) and Beyond Time (the fourth) so that we will have the whole saga on Steam.
The gameplay hasn't really changed from the last game: you're still picking items, solving puzzles, clearing list of hidden objects (whether it's a written list or a pictured one). You have also a little helper, a little baby Griffin that can fly and take things for you when you can't access them (unless the game is requiring you to use a ladder...).
The game is now more oriented towards fantasy, as the famous kindgom, existing towards 3500 ACN, is based on a medevial society with champions and on fantasy as you have dragons and griffins in it. Anyway, you don't know if you're in another world or if you're really in the past. Besides, Cyrus and Zerina, the brother and sister turned evil, are also two sides of a coin: one is living in a palace in the desert and the other was more attracted to an icy landscape. King Amedon was somewhat in the middle...
The graphics were nice: I loved the mythical realm but you didn't get in it immediately, as you begin first at the HQ of the secret order before visiting London in the 19th century. After that, you're stuck in Aeronheart and the bonus chapter is telling you a tale set directly after your adventure, where, again, the fantasy is the main theme: dwarves, elves and fairies will be in the center of it.
I loved the soundtrack too, even if it was always the same tune whether you were in the desert or in the ice land.
In other words, The Secret Order 3 is a nice sequel, very well constructed and leaving you with a cliffhanger of some sorts. As usual, Artifex Mundi chose well and I'll be happy if I see in the Upcoming List the fourth game. I don't know if it's an hint from Artifex or if it was already inside when the game was released before Artfiex but there is a banner with Beyond Time inside the game. So, yeah, I do hope that it will arrive in 2016 on Steam.

The bonus chapter seems a bit rushed though with a lot of 'find x similar items to use in the next minigame' puzzles. Still the artwork and also the story make it worth at least one playthrough.
Overall another fun casual adventure game that you can sink a couple of hours in.

Mi opinión va al respecto de la remasterización, no del juego en si. Full Throttle me lo pasé en su día y me lo he pasado varias veces a lo largo de los años. Me parece una buena aventura de LucasArts, lo cual ya lo situaría entre las mejores aventuras de la historia, pero ni de lejos me parece una de sus mejores aventuras. Es un juego simple, el resideño del SCUMM fue muy mejorable, es muy corto y la sección de la autopista, una buena parte del juego, sobra bastante.
La remasterización, sin embargo, es la típica holgazanería de Tim Schafer cuyos últimos años parecen más enfocados a su canal de Youtube que a hacer juegos con una calidad acorde a su importancia en la industria.
Ciertos gráficos han sido creados desde cero con un buen grado de detalle y gran calidad artística, como los personajes y algunos objetos, pero a los fondos sencillamente se les ha añadido un filtrado horrible (estilo xBRZ), lo cual hace que vayan desde lo aceptable hasta lo más chabacano que te puedas imaginar. Hay fondos concretos, como la choza del tío Pete o la guarida del avión Jumbo, que son una desgracia visual. Al menos crearon nuevo contenido para rellenar hasta los 16:9 y no hicieron el recorte de pantalla de Grim Fandango, algo es algo..
Pero su mayor problema es que el juego no tiene un solo frame de animación nuevo con lo que sigue yendo a los clásicos 10-15 frames de animación por segundo, exceptuando algunas animaciones de la autopista, lo que con los nuevos gráficos hace que quede aún más tosco de lo que quedaba en su día.
Obviamente todo esto es al respecto de los nuevos gráficos. Siempre se puede elegir el pixel-art original a 4:3 y disfrutar de los gráficos originales. En cuyo caso, en mi opinión, sigue no recomendando el juego porque no ofrece absolutamente nada sobre ScummVM + el juego original que algunos ya tenemos.
12€ por una ejecución nativa en Windows 10 me parece demasiado dinero y por eso no recomiendo esta obra como remasterización. Como juego desde luego sí lo recomiendo, aunque recomendaría antes algunos otros juegos de LucasArts.
En Steam no me lo he pasado porque tardó un par de días más en aparecer respecto a GOG, quién sabe porqué. A lo que habría que sumar las 5-10 veces que me lo he pasado en su versión original antes que esta remasterización.
Si ponéis Full Throttle Remake en Google Imágenes, la primera de ellas es un impresionante artwork creado por un tal luisimage hace siglos. Eso, concretamente, es lo que hubiera esperado de una remasterización actualizada.

Years ago a played a demo for the the Darkness II. It was ok but not my type of game so I passed. I think this was around the time Darksiders II came out. I had never looked into the first in the series and I confused the second installment with what I had just played... Darkness II. I thought they were the same game. So I missed Darksiders II. Years later, I was on the verge of purchasing DS2 when I read about the upcoming Deathfinitive Edition. So I waited longer. Finally bought the Deathfinitive Edition and it played horribly on PC. Poor port. I got a refund. Fast forward even more and it is on sale via Steam for around $3. I checked the forums and it seemed all issued had been resolved so I bought it again. Played it for 25 hours. Enjoyed it. It was like Diablo made a 3rd person ARPG and mixed it with Zelda and God of War. Now I'm reviewing it and moving on with my life.
Pros
- Excellent action combat. Placing the beatdown on mobs always felt great. Primary weapon and secondary weapon working together seemlessly. Combos, weight to the attacks. It all felt really good.
- Boss battles were fun and always something to look forward to.
- The writing was well done and the cast of characters were colorful and entertaining. Voice acting was also good.
- I enjoyed the art style. A gritty, yet colorful comic book brought to life.
- the small RPG elements were a nice touch. Building Death was not overly complicated and added some variation.
Cons
- puzzles became a bit tedious.
- the game seemed to wear out its welcome a little after 20 hours. Once I made it to Voidwalker and Phasewalker I was over it. They seemed to pile the puzzles on after that to extend the game to make it more epic perhaps. I felt like they could have trimmed the fat a little and shaved off a few hours and ended the game with me wanting a little more rather than relieved it was done. Like going out to eat. A great meal leaves you wanting one more bite when it is done. On the flipside, a good meal can leave you feeling like crap by the time you are done if the chef just piles 5 pounds of it on your plate.
Overall I really enjoyed the game and hope to see a 3rd installment one day :)

Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare is considered by some as the game that put fps games into the modern era and others consider it as the game that ruined the fps genre for the modern era. I personally believe that it set a fundation that many fps games followed, (warmode maps are based off cod 4, sniper ghost warrior 2 is an attempt of recreating a mission from the campaign). Cod 4 was released in the November of 2007 and the last cod game with free dlc, the game was remastered late last year.
*Campaign review is first and the multiplayer review is lower*
(I had issues with the multiplayer so I played it a while after the campaign)
Positives
Great graphics for time period
Amazing frame rate (no frame rate drops)
Good voice acting
This game puts you in a scenario to determine the best difficulty for your skill level
Great variety of missions
Great variety of weapons
RPGs, rocket launchers, bombs and any other explosions are done perfectly
'good guys' don't aways succeed
The game puts you in the perspective of multiple people
Story and missions are set in multiple time periods
Allie characters have interesting and varied personalities
My teammates actually shot the enemies and actually kill some enemies
Negatives:
Way to short about 5 hours long
AI positioning and spawning areas and timing is lazy and dumb (game showing its age)
All enemies look the same (again game showing its age)
My teammates always cut me off or bump into me in the first mission or prologue
Overall cod 4 is one of my favourites games and is a nice breath of fresh compared to modern games. This game had so much potential and only lived up to some of it. If they could of made the campaign 10-20 hours long then fixed AI spawning issues in the remaster and obviously update graphics we'd have two out of this world games. I rate the campaign a 8.5/10. I got it for $13 AU on a humblebundle sale and it sits around the same price on♥♥♥♥♥or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ so your definitely getting your moneys worth so why not buy it?
Cod4 multiplayer is much different then modern cod, there aren't any supplydrops, map packs, skins, dlc or any other way activision try to rip people off. Furthermore it isn't packed full of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gamemodes. However the movement is quiet slow as well as the scoping or aiming animation and hitboxes are laughable at times. Many of those things we take for granted in modern fps games. One of the best features of cod4 is the amazing community made mods some of which fix slow timings. There is even an impresive bo2 mod. Some of the maps in this game are great structurally with only spawning position faults but many maps are the same couple types of building scattered around the map at random with enemies spawning right behind.
Positives:
Server browser
mods
not many hackers (that I came across)
some great maps (bog, killhouse, overgrown, backlot, district)
mounted machineguns on some maps (they are extremely overpowered but are even more satisfying)
great variety of guns
only classic gamemodes (ffa,dm, headquarters and search and destroy)
no in app purchases
multiplayer maps come from missions in campaign
kill streaks are basic but satisfying
Negatives:
Activision don't give two ♥♥♥♥♥ about pc
poor map design
spawning positions
hitboxes (especially around the head)
most rifles aren't one shot headshot
slow movement
player base averages around 200-600 people
Overall Cod 4 multiplayer is amazing and most of its floors are because of its age. Activison hasn't bothered to update or patch the pc version. Without the pc community cod 4 wouldn't exist but they continue to ignore the pc community. I suggest starting with this game if you would like to play through the cod series or if your sick of modern multiplayer and want to play a less in your face simple fps game.
In conclusion, the multiplayer and campaign definitely hold up great 10 years after the game's initial release. Every fps fan needs to play this game to see firstly how amazing the game is and to see how many modern games have completely copied parts, missions or aspects of cod 4. So do yourself a favour and buy this game. Buy it from♥♥♥♥♥ humble bundle or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Please don't buy it from the steam market. It's a bloody 10 year old game and their charging $45 USD for it!

I've owned No Man's Sky from launch, and played it for around 25 hours then before losing interest. It was slow, it was repetitive, and it lacked depth.  There was very little to actually DO- I didn't much care for all the drama around the hype; it was disappointing yes, but my main issues were the lack of things to do.
Now that there've been some updates, the game is much, much better! It's still slow, and it's still repeptitive. But if you enjoy a solo experience where you do the grind and get the rewards, it's a good game. It still has some major flaws in my opinion, mostly lost opportunities- all the bases, and space stations look the same with only exceedingly minor differences. There's still only like, 3 people in a space station, and the conversations and interactions are just as shallow as before. The pilots of the ships that dock at trade ports and space stations never get out of their ships- overall, the universe is a lonely feeling place, with just the barest of hints at the life and cultures around you. The overhyped 'random creatures' you find on planets are all still very, very samey, as is all the planets plant life. Supposedly that's been updated as well, but I haven't really traveled very far in the 40 hours I've played since the latest update, and haven't seen anything I hadn't seen the first time around. That's not to say you don't find neat things, and I have for sure, but MOST of the fauna I've encountered have all looked much the same across the planets I've visited.
All around though, it's a better experience. There are minor quests you can do to earn some money and items. There's a new and improved main quest chain to work on, probably the best addition I've noticed, which leads you through building a base, and getting your land rover thingy, as well as upgrades and craftables. There's much more of a goal in mind than 'fly around between planets'. Flying the ships feels good, and every ship feels different in it's maneuverability; space combat feels better as well, provided you've outfitted your ship with weapons and upgrades and own one with decent manueverability. You can also buy the enormous Freighters that warp in near space stations, and keep multiple ships on them, though they're exceedingly expensive and it's a late game prospect. The graphics are great, though there are some stylistic choices that some people don't like. I think they're fine.  I'm personally not a huge fan of the menus and UI, but it does the job. Some things are still frustratingly random, like finding upgrades you want, or new multitools, or decent ships.
It's nice that the developers have continued to work on the game- there's still a LOT they could do, and I hope they continue, but they've made a good effort so far and persisted despite the hate train around their game, which is commendable. They've done enough now that I could happily recommend this game to the right person.
So yeah, I'd recommend this game for sure-IF you do proper research and know what you're getting. Don't go into it expecting it to be something that it isn't and get upset about it. Watch some videos and read the RECENT in depth reviews. Know that it's a very time consuming game, that's focused around exploration, and it's slow to play. It rewards time and effort, and you need to know if those rewards are going to be enough payoff for you. It's a gorgeous game and a great experience, but only for the right person!

You race against the clock trying to save everyone's souls which actually ties into the "levelling" mechanics of the game. The more people you save, the better chance you have to unlock a secret dungeon before the end.
Plus side of the PC version is you get all the DLC (minus Aerith... For now) and even the choice between English & Japanese voices for cheaper than their console counterparts. The game doesn't use a launcher this time round which is a plus side for changing settings on the go (although some options such as voices and enabling DLC still require reboots).

TL;DR: if you have played The new order you will be dissapointed sometimes. If not,
the game does a reasonable job of being ok and should be a short lasting blast.
STORY:
I don't really like the story personally. Caroline being killed, the eh, dark invasion with the alpha afro taking over the u-boat. Thoughout the game it's revealed that you (B.J.) is a half-jew litterally teaming up with commies. The story of this game is way too political unlike TNO. Not much depth in details unlike the previous installment too. Also, unlike the first one, there is too much unneccecairy toilet humor in it and over-the-top stuff just to make the game appear more edgy. the serious tone is mostly lost :/ That's just my opinion though..
The antagonist (general Engel) barely gets any screentime. Except for the posters she´s almost never present. With General Deathshead it was the same but his presence was everywhere! You could often hear him though speakers too. It was awesome to kill him. Engel however, i didn´t really care whether she died or not.
In addition, The ending is a big pig pile of dog poo. The story is really short in comparison to TNO. After the fight on the Ausmerzer i thought i was around 50% of the story, turned out to be the end.. And i'm someone that explores slowly. There are too many and too long cutscenes. If you're a player that doesn't care about collectibles and rushes though the game, it will feel like an interactive movie. You will complete the game in a few hours tops. The Order 1866 is the only game that has a worse cutscene-to-gameplay ratio. To top it off, the whole 'revolution' element is missing while the ending basically behaves like sequel-bait.
CHARACTERS:
Only the main cast does well obviously. But most of the new ones lack any depth or character progression unlike in The New Order. Many are stereotyped slitghly too much and feel forced and a bit out of place. Anya barely said a word. But overall the performances are good enough and the voice actors did a good job!
WEAPONS/SKILLS:
The weapons are ok but meh. dual wielding is a huge mess. Maybe great for controllers but for pc it's cluncky. The shooting sounds feel too light. The Laserkraftwerk is now a glorified sniper. TNO did it better. The only awesome weapons are the big gewehr's.
SETTING/LEVELS:
The level designs are reasonably ok. Manhattan and New Orleans are boring and feel like Fallout however. But some are great! I expected more from Roswell though. You only walk around the corner there before going underground. There are too many underground levels anyway and many of them feel narrow and meh. TNO was much more open with many nice views. The enemy's are more boring this time and the focus is often on the commanders. The 'stealth' element is pretty much gone this time too. The locations of health/armor/weapons proof that. The retro future 60's style is fantastic but feels a bit too modern because of many robots you fight.
END:
The game is ok-ish but way too expensive for what you get. At the very least the seasonpass chronicles should be included. I actually pirated the first one but decided to buy The New Colossus. After playing it i wish i had done it the other way around.. This one is cracked too btw. If you're not into pirating then buy this on a big sale. The game is worth €30,- at max in my opinion.
Any good stuff too? well yeah. The game has its moments. Some area's are really well done Like the base on Venus and Roswell. Also the music is stunning at times and fits every moment. Graphics and performance are excellent. For reference i got a FX6300, 16GB ram, GTX970 and 1080p screen running win7 64bit. Got everything on max except image streaming which is on high. Sometimes the atmosphere can really drag you in the game. The concept stuff and minor end game stuff after the story are a cool minor addition.
Overall, I rate this game 4 / 10. I hope the sequel, The New Frontier will be better.

Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice isn’t Ninja Theory’s biggest game, but it might be one of its best. The game takes you on a journey into a savage viking heartland with Senua, a Celtic warrior struggling with trauma & psychosis. It focuses on psychological character study, following the quest to enter hell and reclaim a loved one’s soul. It’s driven by fantastic acting, both from the voice actors and by Senua's character model. Hellblade is brave for tackling psychosis so directly, and braver still for pouring so much of its efforts into its narrative. It’s unlike anything else you have played, and for that reason it deserves a slice of your time.
The game triumphs equally as an action/hack & slash, mythical quest and psychological character study, bringing together some amazing visuals, great performances, beautiful sound and ingenious design. It’s short-lived, but perfectly paced with a blend of action and puzzles that grows in richness and complexity as the game goes on.
Pros:
Incredible visuals, design and audio
Clever perspective-based puzzles
Immersive storytelling
Cons:
Smaller variability of enemies
Repetitive combat

Without a doubt my favourite game from my childhood. Being able to relive my old memories from the game and to be able to change between old and remastered graphics as well as sound was amazing. -Able to switch between original pixelated and newly remastered graphics as well as sound with the click of a button
-Great story
-Easy to use controls
-Newly added main menu, allows you to save, load saves, has a bonus menu and more
-Selective dialogues
-Skippable cutscenes
-Skippable Dialogue
-You are able to interact with certain objects in the game and as you progress further, you will need to find certain objects along the way.
-Able to interact with other characters, this being talking to or fighting other bikers on the road with your fists, feet, or weapons that you find along the way
-Short game, can be finished in under 3 hours (The original game was released in 1995 which is understandable)
-Can seem 'too easy', requiring simple thinking to continue further through the story
Overall I would rate this game 9/10. The game may be short but it is worth replaying to get 100% completion. The game allows for overall great interaction with the other characters, being fighting other bikers, using objects scattered around the world to progress further into the game and the dialogue with other characters. Easy at times, certain parts will leave you thinking or send you off to Google to find out how to pass it. Other than that, I cannot find more fault in the game, it remains my favourite game from my childhood.

You only have a limited time to make matchs (before they hit the end) and it gets very hectic very quickly.  Mouse controls just don't work very well for this, and I think a touch device would work better.
Anyway, the gameplay is cool and the ideas are unique enough that although they don't really work that well in practice, I recommend checking out Dungeon Hearts just to see this gameplay.  I really want to get good at it but it's god damned hard, and I think the difficulty comes largely from the limited means by which we can play it.
Oh, the basic idea is to order colors together before they reach the end.  You want to stop enemy attacks from getting off while building up your own combos via hitting multiples of s color. Years ago a played a demo for the the Darkness II. It was ok but not my type of game so I passed. I think this was around the time Darksiders II came out. I had never looked into the first in the series and I confused the second installment with what I had just played... Darkness II. I thought they were the same game. So I missed Darksiders II. Years later, I was on the verge of purchasing DS2 when I read about the upcoming Deathfinitive Edition. So I waited longer. Finally bought the Deathfinitive Edition and it played horribly on PC. Poor port. I got a refund. Fast forward even more and it is on sale via Steam for around $3. I checked the forums and it seemed all issued had been resolved so I bought it again. Played it for 25 hours. Enjoyed it. It was like Diablo made a 3rd person ARPG and mixed it with Zelda and God of War. Now I'm reviewing it and moving on with my life.
Pros
- Excellent action combat. Placing the beatdown on mobs always felt great. Primary weapon and secondary weapon working together seemlessly. Combos, weight to the attacks. It all felt really good.
- Boss battles were fun and always something to look forward to.
- The writing was well done and the cast of characters were colorful and entertaining. Voice acting was also good.
- I enjoyed the art style. A gritty, yet colorful comic book brought to life.
- the small RPG elements were a nice touch. Building Death was not overly complicated and added some variation.
Cons
- puzzles became a bit tedious.
- the game seemed to wear out its welcome a little after 20 hours. Once I made it to Voidwalker and Phasewalker I was over it. They seemed to pile the puzzles on after that to extend the game to make it more epic perhaps. I felt like they could have trimmed the fat a little and shaved off a few hours and ended the game with me wanting a little more rather than relieved it was done. Like going out to eat. A great meal leaves you wanting one more bite when it is done. On the flipside, a good meal can leave you feeling like crap by the time you are done if the chef just piles 5 pounds of it on your plate.
Overall I really enjoyed the game and hope to see a 3rd installment one day :)

I wouldn't necesarily say I recomend this game fully. The gameplay is very basic, progression from going room to room gets old, and it's not the most terrifying game to hardened horror fanatics. But, if you got some time to kill, it's a fun distraction in short bursts.
The game is very emersive. The ambience is very well done, the sound design alone really makes you feel like you're trapped miles below ground in a endless maze. The humor is very entertaining and quirky, which is probably the strongest point of the game. The "jumpscares" in the name sake aren't the main point of horror. Instead, they're really kind of the joke of the game. When a real threat shows up, it actually doesn't resort to jumpscares. And the monsters are varried enough to keep it suspensful when you're locked in a chase.
The only downside, once again, is that it can get old really fast. Basically you just walk room to room. Every now and then you'll read some notes that parody the ones in other cliche horror games. And the jumpscares get more and more sillier. But, sometimes it can feel like a real chore to play this game during long periods. And I have no real interest to go back and find out how to get the good ending, nor do I really want to spend any money for the DLC. But, all in all, it's kind of fun to switch on every now and then when I want something spooky, but not too spooky.
Forget about MW:R, this is the real deal. Not to mention it changed the series into something different.

A bit of DOOM here, and the nazis are fun to kill as always! Dual wielding returns, and you can mix and match this time around. Introduces a weapon upgrade mechanic. Gunplay is solid. Slick weapons, but the variety is lacking. Stealth is as bad as the last one. If your cover is blown, the entire batallion in the area comes after you. The perks system return. Quality, and quantity-wise, not as exhilarating on the boss fights department like the New Order was, which is disappointing.
Quality and variety of the locales not as good as the New Order...it is mostly corridor shooting. Thankfully, there are a couple of levels like the New Order that shine. New to this game are the contraptions, and they can be chosen to suit your playstyle. They take you to the same objective in different ways, but end up feeling like a missed opportunity. The waypoint system sucks, and there was a couple of instances, where I kept running around not knowing what to do next. This is despite the game telling me vaguely where to go, and with the level's map for reference.
Peaks at the beginning, and a bit in the middle, and then ends up becoming a normal fare with several plotholes.
Pulling back no punches, there was so much more potential here. Instead, we have shallow plot, unanswered questions, and plenty of things happen just for shock value.
The new supporting characters are decent, but they are not as developed as in the New Order.
You set out to spark a revolution in this game, and but it does not feel as satisfying as the New order did, once it ended. Did I mention that there are hours of cutscenes? They are well done, but I would rather spend most of that time blasting nazis in the face.
Did not have performance issues/slowdowns on my machine with an Nvidia card. I have been playing since it was released. Game ran smoother after the second patch though. No hard crashes.
This game is worth checking out if you are a Wolfenstein fan and/or if these apply to you:
- Like a mature story-rich single player game, with 10-12 hour campaign on average
- Like fast-paced challenging gameplay with old school mechanics
- Dislike tacked-on multiplayer on your FPS
Is it worth full price? Depends. This is a challenging game, even on normal difficulty. I got over 19 hours out of the game on normal difficulty. This is despite dying a few times, doing a couple of assassination missions, and scouting all levels for supplies. If you do all side missions (lazily done; they take place in the levels you already played before), you get more mileage. If you are a completionist, you get even more with the amount of collectibles and upgrades. On top of this, you are encouraged to play twice since you then get to experience the Fergus/Wyatt timeline properly. If you are going to play on easier difficulty as a straight-up shooter, and not exploring much, you would be better off picking this up during a sale.
I do appreciate Bethesda for not adding microtransactions, but it feels like they cut content. We are talking about starting a revolution here, and I would've wanted the game to have at least 4 more fleshed-out levels. DLCs appear to be shorter also.
Overall, this pales in comparison to the New Order. Although enjoyable, not as much of an immersive and epic experience. On the line, but I will recommend.

Most enemies can and will kill you in just a second or two, so you have no choice but to be faster and more accurate than they are. Even on a stealth playthrough, there are multiple times the game forces you to get into a big firefight; which I enjoyed. Overall, the gameplay is a significant improvement over the first installment.

I really liked "The New Order", and did want to like this game, but there's a lot going against it, which led me to stop playing off and on, and which lead to an overall recommendation against it. I experienced some issues that make this game less than - amusing.  I had latest drivers, and experienced no technical problems at all.
The story and cutscenes make up too much of the game, the lead characters are TSTL parodies (explained in "spoilers" later).
The game tries to pad out it's time by throwing up sidequests that just have you revisit maps that have already been explored without any great incentive to do them. You get little for doing them, and it's just a poor way to stretch overall game time.
The weapons' effectiveness is not handled well, where a handgun can kill better than an assault weapon, and where there is no silencer option for the assault weapon.  Upgrades to weapons don't seem to make combat easier - are compensated for immediately by "upgrades" to enemies.
The game introduces many named characters of no discernible importance, and little value.
*Spoilers:
In this game, Blaskovitz is a cliche-spouting moron, who starts off as a paraplegic, then is angst ridden in Caroline's warsuit (she is killed messily and uselessly), then later has a head transplant onto a different body after THE (mid-game) boss fight.  He seemed punch drunk throughout.
THE mid-game hard-to-win boss fight, which must be completed to proceed, literally turns out after all that work and strife to have nothing to do with the story.
Grace, the Resistance leader and boss-of-all, is a ghetto originating, jive talking (1961?) black who insults everyone who is supposed to want to follow her, and who is married to an ineffective, alien-fixated space cadet supposedly caring and a genius at something.  Caroline was much smarter, and was likeable. Grace is unlikeable, and acts stupid.  Blaskovitz is unlikeable in this Wolfenstein edition.  I consider the story line disjointed, and pieces of the story were sort of cut in without value except to portray Blaskovitz clumsily as not a racist (even though he is against all Nazis).   "The New Order" provided a much better progression.
None of the characters were admirable, the writers have handled diversity very strangely, and I was astounded to see a very pregnant Anya suddenly appear in the midst of many bullets, energy pulses, rockets and everything else.  No pregnant female would have been allowed unnecessarily on the "front lines" had Blaskovitz or the fake non-leadership any sort of common sense.
I concluded that this game needed an adult proofreader and editor.

This is a mid-level game with mid-level, albeit solid, gameplay.  It looks spectacular... but the story is outstanding.  The vast majority of triple-A titles haven't put this much thought into forming a cohesive and impactful narrative.
Every bit of this game was obviously designed with passion.  The developers have created a beautiful world, powerful characters and a compelling narrative in order to explore themes that are not only important for them but for us as a society. Don't come to this expecting Dark Souls. Don't come to it expecting the Witcher. Come to it as a thing all of its own and you'll come away from it with one of the most powerful gaming experiences you'll ever have.
The story is wonderful, told mostly through the voices in Senua's head and past trauma relived as parts of her quest to rescue her lover's soul from the gods of the Norsemen. The graphics and environments are incredibly immersive - you can practically smell the wet, rotting wood, feel the sleet and rain on bitter winds, and in the rare moments of sunshine, you share the relief and joy that Senua feels.
If you let the story and the character take you with them, the puzzles make sense. Finding patterns in the environment, walking between different versions of Senua's reality and finding your way through dark areas by sense alone, all feel like a visceral part of Senua's experience.
The combat isn't massively difficult, but it is fluid and responsive. There are relatively few enemy types, each with their own tactics to beat, and the challenge comes when you get them in waves of different combinations, switching tactics and targets on the fly.
But really it's Senua herself that's the main feature. Perfectly rendered, perfectly acted and perfectly animated every step of the way, you come to genuinely care about this damaged, vulnerable slip of a girl as she advances through her hallucinatory, metaphorical quest against odds that she cannot possibly beat. By turns she goes from determined to frightened to fierce to doubtful to angry to despondent and implacable, and as her moods change so does the world, all of it narrated by the voices in her head which become voices in your own head.
It's an incredible experience that is far greater than the sum of its parts. It is intelligent, respectful of its subject matter and doesn't treat the player as an idiot. It's a game that will stay with you for a long time after you've finished it, and it'll make you think about a lot more than solving its puzzles and working out its tactics. It's a heart-wrenching and heart-breaking experience.
A genuine work of art, both visually and as a piece of digital literature. I know how that sounds, but if you take Senua's Sacrifice for what it is you'll know exactly what I mean. There really is nothing else like it.
