I don't recommend supporting Sega. Even buying their good games supports bad practices.
If you don't care whether you support DRM that may repeatedly force you online for re-validation; or make games that use it eventually cease to work for all legitimate owners; or you only care about this particular piece of software then it's safe to ignore the preamble & "score" of this review. I believe the rest of its contents are fair criticism.
Buying any of Sega's products, even older ones that lack that DRM like this one does, will support the inclusion of said DRM in future products. As someone who does a lot of gaming offline I can't support a company which does that.
If that doesn't bother you, again, feel free to ignore my preamble and "score".
---
Though there are good games available for this hub they're lumbered with a garbage emulator with ludicrous system requirements.
There's no reason it should make a PC that can comfortably run Blast Em, Exodus or Higan set its fans constantly on full blast and still suffer from stuttering.
Even when it does run at full speed, audio emulation is woeful and the version of Alien Soldier that's included is inexplicably the European one being forced to run at NTSC 60hz even though Sega already created an optimised 60hz version of the ROM for the Wii Virtual Console.
Further showing Sega's inconsistent practices, the version of Revenge of Shinobi included in this hub is the very revision introduced by the Virtual Console; this time to the game's detriment.
There's at least a good dozen SMD/Genesis games that have been sold under license from Sega on other platforms which aren't available here such as Monster World 4, OutRun 2019 and Arrow Flash.
It's also missing third party games which Sega seem to have obtained the rights to since launching this "collection", such as the much-loved Thunder Force games.
Sega abandoned patching the emulator after a couple of attempts to fix its issues. The fact that "Sega Forever" continued to use a revision of the same emulator combined with a poorly optimised Unity frontend at launch on far less powerful ARM devices shows how little attention Sega pay to their mistakes on PC.
You do have the option to switch to the "old" version of the emulator which will run on any potato at full speed but is just as inaccurate and lacks the upsides of this newer version: a nice looking CRT effect; "mod" support and any ROMs you own being included, DRM-free, for use in significantly less terrible emulators.
Not that you have a choice which version of Sega's emulator you download since both are included.
Since the most desirable bit of the emulator is already DRM-free, why couldn't the games be released on GoG or have a DRM-free option on the Humble Store?
The minimum system requirements on the store page only reflect the old emulator while the recommended requirements are optimistic at best for running the new hub.

The screenshots and trailers made this game look pretty cool, like something similar to Amnesia The Dark Descent. When I saw the price, I had my doubts on its quality, and those doubts ended up being correct.
First of all, the opening screen (eg when you press "New Game") is bugged if you have a higher resolution than 1024x768. Text disappears off the side into two black boxes. Then when the game finally started I couldn't do anything; I had to alt-tab out of the window and click back into the game for it to work properly. There are no transitions from the title menu to the game, nor from one level to another; so when the game swapped levels I thought for a minute the game had crashed. Transitions are so so so important.
The controls are not clearly explained; it took me a minute or two to realize that I had to equip my lighter before I could start using it, since I was under the assumption it would be assigned a key like "F". Even when you pull the lighter out from your inventory you still have to click a few times for it to "light". I found that to be particularly annoying. It also looks like you should be able to light up things like the lamps on the walls and the fireplace, but I've tried pressing all the controls while my lighter was out and nothing seems to work. If I'm not supposed to use my lighter on them, why does text pop up in front of them?
The game is also nonprogressible after your lighter runs out of oil if you can't find more of it. I don't know if you're supposed to find oil, but I couldn't find any from the start of the game and within five minutes I was unable to see anything. In real life, even when the lights are out in a house, your eyes will adjust to the darkness at least a little bit, so that you can make out shapes. It shouldn't be pitch black.
As for the scare factor, it definitely has an atmosphere, I'll give it that. The three jumpscares I ran into were kind of cheesy but they did startle me a little bit. But it was ruined by my frustration with the game mechanics and inability to see anything after my lighter ran out.
If you are looking for a good, short, horror game, this is not it. I would not recommend this game to anyone unless the developers address some of these issues first. It seems to me that it was really rushed and could've used a month's more worth of tuning up.

Puzzle Hearts is a very good game. Don't dismiss it thinking that low price means it is some junk. What may appear like a rhythm rpg is actualky a match three puzzle, which feels almost like something entirely different. As you start playing and pass some easy levels you will begin seeing different shapes, new types of blocks, and ability blocks. All of this is happening with the playfield moving to the right quicker and quicker. Gameplay becomes even more fun because of the shorter time available to move your blocks, and having to decide which blocks to match. Based on that last decision you may perform any of the number special powers each of your character has. As can be seen in screenshots, each character has 3 powers fo ra total of 12 when you have all 4. Basically the premise and the gameplay are excellent.
In regards to graphics and art direction, Dungeon Hearts does not impress too much. Character models are 3d cartoonish characters with large heads. They are not very impressive. Their animations are very basic and sometimes repetitive. It could be annoying or irritating. The models of enemies and their animations are much more interesting. I am not sure how many there are, but they are pretty well designed, diverse, and since they circulate and you see new ones a lot, it maintains interest. Backgrounds are great. Pretty good on the eyes, but they don't mean much contextually.
there areBut all of that depends on importance you give to those things. Different for everybody.
Sound is alright, and I do not have much to comment about it. Maybe one area that deserves commenting is the music. It doesn't play a big role in the game, and you do not hear a bunch of unique soundtracks. It may give that impression perhaps because the playing field looks like the screen of a sideways Guitar Hero screen. It is just techno action, somewhat generic tracks.
I recommend the game if you want a very cool battle match three game, which involves rpg elements and to a lesser degree strategy. If you want to be impressed by music and fancy graphics, this game appears to never have aimed to impress us with those features.

Where to begin. If I wanted to treat this game punitively, I'd say it takes the standard Final Fantasy team line-up (warrior, black mage, white mage, archer) and they've thrown in a puzzle game). I can't be that punitive. This game has complexity, and depth you'd struggle to find in some of puzzle games you'd immediately think of.
You have four lines across the screen, gems will slide towards you, if they reach the end, they disappear. If you move 3 of the same colour in any pattern except diagonally, you can make an attack gem. Which, when clicked, will attack the enemy you are fighting. The enemy has their own gems too, if you can't move them quick enough, or can't use your attacks to remove them from the bar, they will attack your characters and drain their health.
And I'm only getting starting. Characters level up between runs, learn abilities, monsters, mini-bosses, runes that make the game move faster, or randomly freeze different runes, or make you take more damage.
Oh, one thing I didn't mention. This game is tough. It starts deceptively simple, but it works through it's mechanics like Neil DeGrasse Tyson blows your mind.
It has different modes of play, an easy to grasp tutorial level, and a very FF-esque art style (think DS remake FF games).
The only thing I can even think to ping this game for, is the soundtrack is incredbily repetitive. You might do better to listen to your own tracks and turn the music off entirely.
The best part? This game costs under a dollar. Seriously, less than a small fries from McDonalds. If you've been looking for a rich, deep, and challenging puzzle game. I implore you, pick this up. You will have an absolute blast.

For a long time, whenever I have seen this game, I thought it must be utterly dull and boring. Than one day, I had nothing really to do, so I decided to play through something that takes only a few hours. I picked To The Moon... and realized how wrong my initial impression was...
The game actually contains two stories. One is John's. For me it was the driving force to keep on playing, as it is told backwards, and so my curiosity was constantly fed, wanting to know what events led to certain situations. After I finished the game, his story was complete. And it made me thinking. About many things. It had an impact on me, that I did not anticipate. Apparently, it had a strong impact on almost everyone who finished the game, and I think that fact on its own should tell a lot.
The other story belongs to Eva and Neil, the doctors, who fulfill John's wish. Now, that one is a difficult case. It is hard to talk about it without spoilers... What I can tell however, is that it will make you think too. Not the same way as John's story, no. But you will think about it, especially after you played through the minisodes as well (they come free with the game and play after the main story). And once you are there, you will likely understand why do I recommend it...
More of an interactive movie than a game. But an extremely good movie.

This game is repetitive, and I mean absolutely repetitive to a point where you question everything in your life, your entire existence and why you are even alive. The theme for the entire Darksiders franchise is the number 3. Every single boss is cookie cutter, meaning each time you go to enter a "dungeon" or chapter, you have a basic structure to follow. The puzzles are repetitive and boring, sometimes ridiculous, and often don't leave you satisfied. Basically, when you enter a dungeon, you usually meet an NPC. You are given directions on what to do and then you enter a main chamber. There are usually 3 doors aside from the one you entered, and at least one or two of those doors will be locked, forcing you to go in a very repetitive pattern. Go in one door, find a shard, a piece of some equipment, anything really, and you collect up to 3. Unlock the other door by triggering some event from the previous door, and then repeat the process in the second door to unlock the third, while collecting another item of some sort. When you advance to the next area you will most certainly find another challenge, a way to get to the actual dungeon boss. You will probably be tasked in finding another piece to finish a broken item, or you will be needing to flip switches, step on pressure plates or rotate statues in order to trigger an elevator or unlock a door. Then you go to the boss fight, and it's relatively simple. Another similar structure in the game is collecting 3 of an item again, fighting mini bosses in each collectable area with little puzzles in between. I just described the entire game to you in this short  account of my experience. The game may be cheap - there's a reason for that. I would NOT recommend playing this game, not even if you have a few extra dollars to throw around. Pass on this "opportunity", you will find zero satisfaction in the completion of the game and the DLCs are basically just added dungeons with no depth. It took me about 16 hours of gameplay to beat the game + DLCs. This game is in no way fun to any extent.

Years passed and we have Deathfinitive Edition in our hands, and since I could pick it up on a nice discount for roughly 3€, I gave it another shot, half year after DE's relase and after it's tremendous amount of bugs are likely fixed according to the developer diaries on the Commmunity Hub.

1. Shadows became huge blocky things. Let's search for a fix - there is none, devs abandoned the game.
2. The previous version had stable 60 fps, this does not. Let's search for a fix, try to reduce graphics (on a PC way above the recommended hardware requirement) - there is none, the lack of graphic options really tells you this is a low effort PC port.
3. It doesn't recognize my keyboard outside the menus at all if I had a 360 controller plugged in before, you have to restart the game. Is there a fix? Didn't bother, oh and developers abandoned the game did I mention that?
4. Okay. I'll swallow it, let's enjoy the game itself, at least it doesn't crash anym... oh it crashed. Good thing it was after a cinematic so the checkpoint is right there. Progressing. Another crash half an hour later. Another 2 hours later, right at the end of a hard bossfight (I played on Apocaliptic difficulty from start), when it had 2 hits HP left. Like you think this happens in jokes, but it's actually a thing with DS2DE.
5. Okay let's swallow it. Playing... playing... hey half the sounds are suddenly gone? Music entirely, most of the weapon hits and stone ball sounds too? Let's look it up on the internet. The only thing I found? The developers admitting this is a problem that can occur if you play more than 4 hours of the game at once. FOR THE ORIGINAL GAME. NOT EVEN THE NEW EDITION. YEARS PASSED, THEY ARE RESELLING THE GAME AND YEARS OLD CRITICAL BUGS ARE STILL PRESENT.
3 hours didn't pass since I installed it, by the way.
Overall, there are way more technical issues, fps drops, flashing textures on distance rendering, shadow problems, crashes, sound problems, game breaking bugs (such as if competing a certain main mission grants you enough exp to level up, the game crashes no matter what, so you have to grind sh.t so you level up first, then complete the mission), than the original edition. And not only literally all the problems the old version had which the developers abandoned and never fixed (instead re-relased the game for full price again with slight graphical updates because X1/PS4 came out during this time) are still present, but all new crashing, fps dropping, visual cluttering issues came with the new "improved" version, that the developers abandoned on PC AGAIN!

EDIT: I realize now why this has so many dislikes, turns out I had 60 fps on the brain considering this ports never hit it that so I wrote I was getting 60 fps instead of 30 fps. Welp, too late now.
TL;DR at the bottom.
So, Lightning Returns, the third installment of the notorious FFXIII trilogy. Well, first things first, the all-important question for us PC users. Does it run well? Well, yes, yes it does. Unlike the previous two titles, I'm able to get 30 fps for the most part..... I say for the most part because I find when I'm in menus it definitely dips here and there, but really, it's the menus. Also, there's the occasional spike here and there but it's not a real problem. There's no more launcher, if you run your mouse up the to the top of the screen, there's a unimmersive drop-down menu which has all the settings you desire. Well, not really. There's a bunch more options, but you choose between standard and advanced as far as I know. But regardless, it looks and plays better than it did on consoles. Some things to point out though, IT'S NEARLY IMPOSSIBLE TO PLAY WITHOUT A CONTROLLER. This time around, the nature of the gameplay means you'll need more buttons, and square obviously doesn't know how to make a keyboard button layout that actually makes any logical sense. It'd be much simpler if there was mouse support, but I think it may have occured to you something was up when I said you get the drop-down menu when you drag the mouse up to the top edge in-game. Yeah, there's no actual mouse support here, making it even more impractical to play with a keyboard. It's not even KB+M anymore, it's just KB. Oh, missed an important point, you need online connectivity to play. Yeah, that's brutal. Anyways, on the to the review.
-----------
Uhhh, so basically a bunch of nonsense happens and the story of FFXIII-2 which overwrote the story in FFXIII, is overwritten again by the story in Lightning Returns FFXIII here. Welp, sure, whatever, no one's really expecting anything at this point. Anyway, bad stuff has happened various circumstances have made everyone still alive immortal. However, the world will end in 13 days and you, Lightning, obviously, have been chosen by the god Bhunivelze to save the souls of the worthy within the 13 days. And you know all the other characters show up, blah, blah, you defy fate because when do you not do that in these games. Bottom line, who really cares. I like the ending scenes though. The characters are still dull sacks of potatoes. Snow, whose was the energetic meathead, is kind of a dull sack of potatoes now. Hope, lmao whatever. Lumina, a new character, mysterious....mysterious and generic. Yes. So on and so forth. The characters are boring, that won't change no matter how many games you put out.
-----------
Let's talk about something more interesting. The combat system has been redesigned yet again and so we go from having a party of 3 in FFXIII, to a party of 2 in FFXIII-2 with 1 monster ally, to a party of 1 tsundere and her various costumes, er, schematas. You can now move in battles, albeit it's not that useful, and basically you switch between 3 schemata, each with it's own abilities and action bar. Essentially you play all 3 party members combined into one. There's realtime blocking now though. Now that all sounds great, real-time combat, moving and blocking, etc. But really, it's still arguably turn-based. You unload on the enemy with all your skills, then you save some points to dodge and block the enemies attacks. By that time some of your bars on your schematas will have refilled, signalling it's your turn again and you proceed to spam once more. It's TBS, without actually telling you it's TBS. Staggering is back of course, that's the name of the game no matter what enemy you happen to come across. Get a monster's stagger up, stagger it,unload spells, rinse and repeat. It's still fun though. This version comes with all the DLC schemata, except the Aeris one which I think is now available nowhere. So you can enjoy dressing up your Lightning for better combat efficiency or simply because you have waifu 4 laifu syndrome. Perfectly acceptable reasons.
------------
The gameplay. So while FFXIII had linear everything until Gran Pulse opened up to you, which was essentially a never-ending bland field of shortgrass and rocks filled with more floating rocks that provided you with generic kill quests, FFXIII-2 had more open zones filled with gates for you to open, and places to throw your mog at for pointless collectables, LR decides to combine all those together, yay! Well, what you get are 4 open areas, some being linear city streets and other being more open plains and deserts. There's side quests and stuff to do everywhere, but the trick is, they don't appear all the time. Remember when I said 13 days, well it's really 13 days to play in these zones. Some things only appear on certain days, certain times per day, etc. Think Persona. But with 13 longer days (optional 14, hint hint). What to do when you missed something? New Game + (beating the game also unlocks hard mode) unlocked by clearing the game or getting a game over, meaning you wasted 13 days chasing chocobos...yeah, you can actually game over if you screw up the days. All the typical JRPG content is here, dungeon-type things, battle arena-type things, questing, talking to people, talking to people at different times, walking, running, yep, yep, yep. The 13 day system may feel a bit restrictive, which to some extent it is. Heck, if you flee a fight (unless you're on easy), you lose an hour of that day. But they attempted to balance it out with the multiple playthroughs. Why get it all in one long playthrough, when you could do it in multiple shorter playthroughs? I don't know, design choice, hit or miss. Some things are only obtainable on the unlockable hard mode, so multiple playthrough was encouraged by the devs for sure.
-------------
TL;DR = Fans and critics call this is the weakest of the series, but there's some bias considering the fact they even decided to make it is an automatic -2 points to a lot of people. Everyone believes milking the boring cow too many times only yields (insert witty phrase to make point). But this is a solid title without a doubt. It's not better, but it's not that much worse. What it is, is different. Slightly refreshing combat, larger areas with more content in each to mess with, collecting items, etc, it's got it all. Games like this, you used to be able to get them all the time. Like every week there'd be one. But now, not so much. LR:FFXIII is a little bit nostalgic, a little bit cringe-worthy here and there to be honest, but it's a content-packed JRPG with pretty aesthetics, an eargasmic soundtrack, and lots of potential for great gameplay.

I'm a big fan of the Final Fantasy franchise, but hated XIII.
I went into this game without expectations, and if I don't compare it to other Final Fantasies then it's great.
The combat system is really unique and the amount of equipment available is incredible.
The story isn't as needlessly complicated as FFXIII and easy enough to understand for people who haven't played it.
If you think you'll like it or even just want to try something new, then go for it! It's really cheap compared to most games.
As a heads-up though: the controls can be pretty awkward. You won't be using the mouse at all, so I rebound all the keys around WASD like a MOBA, and then my right-hand is strictly reserved for camera and menu control. I found it much easier after making that small change.

Lightning is back, and you play with her, instant recommend. Now you can see the third terrible port, but at least Lightning is back! Figuring the new keybindings will be harder than monsters for your first hour, but by the time you start changing her clothing you will forget about that. Game starts about 500 years after the ending of the second game.
I will consider you came from the previous ports so will only comment on what changed.
Before you want to kill yourself, hint: "." to access datalog etc (no longer TAB). You jump with "<= backspace"... don't ask me why, but you can change it.
PROS
+ Did I mention you play as Lightning? ok.
+ Few more visual options, far from enough.
+ A lot more RPG-like with more "free roaming" and side quests that actuall change someting
+ There is a pressing time limit that ACTUALLY MATTERS (time passes as you play, you have to do stuff withing real time-frames, not like those games that say "hurry" and then you can walk around and sit because time doesn't really moves until you "trigger" the quest ... here, you can't idle, in fact there are skills to stop or slow down time so you can move/do stuff faster)
+ You can dress her up, change her whole wear and customize colours. After you reach the Ark, go "buy" all the downloadable content (they are included free - alas they cost 0gil, but later you can sell them at huge amounds, kind of cheating if you ask me). You can even change her panties colour on some garbs if you are perv enough... over 80 garbs according ingame data. Also, weapons and shields are plentyful in both appearance and function.
+ Lots of NPC's to talk to/with, and quests to succeed/fail
+ ESC no longer freeze the game out of windows, but is an actual in-game pause/menu option, which is good (though at main menu, you need to alt-f4 to quit). Alt+Enter works like a charm to switch to fullscreen and back.
+ You can save at any moment
+ You can actually move Lightning around during battle with ASDW. No more watching your character die because randomly stood on the way of a massive attack like the other two games.
+ You move the camera with IJKL. At first I thought it was weird and unplayable, but just sit your left hand on ASDW and the right at IJKL and every other shortcut come together. Specially good when you get how to use "u" (preemptive attack).
+ Partial (see cons) KEYBINDING OPTIONS, change anything at your heart content (settings > keyboard settings").
+ HP carries on between battles, so you have to take potions/avoid enemies if you win but are left with low HP.
+ (if you like it) more action, less turn based
CONS
- Some "advanced" visual effects actually make the game look worst, might be due to video card/drivers but the other games looked nicer IMHO (most options I toggled back to "standard" because there was a noticiable FPS impact but very faint visual change)
- Some FPS quick drops when the camera changes, specially when talking to NPC (mind you, I run the game from a SSD and my video card has 1Gb, shouldn't be texture loading ...)
- Mouse camera movement is gone, only keyboard! Mouse is now totally useless.
- This make fighting multiple enemies a annoying because you must also select target (arrow keys) and move the camera to see what they are doing. Best way to "mitigate" this is to keep zoomed out ("," key, you can default to zoomed out at the settings).
- Limited potions (you start only able to carry 6)
- Paradigm shift now is called schematas and is changed with E or U, which is very weird until you get used with the new keyboard layout, other than that, makes it more action based (no pausing)
- While you can change keybindings, the use of some keys is the same and you can't change, for instance, "M" is the map while not in battle, and guard in battle ... changing the key binding changes both -_- ... even worse: Jump, Cancel and Attack are all the same "<= backspace" ... get used to jump with "<= backspace" or rebind to space and get used to cancel with ... space? wtf
- If you accidentaly make the terrible choice to "Control Button Assignment Type 2", which makes confirmation the "<= backspace" instead of "enter", just move back to Type 1 ... yes, I don't get why they did this.
- Screensaver is not turned off on fullscreen, be warned it will start during long cinematics -.-
- Cannot reuse same garb/weapon/shield on different schematas
- The REAL time constrain can make you rush when you wanted to explore sometimes ... not sure if a pro or con...
- (if you don't like it) less turn based, more action
- THE TERRIBLE AWFUL ENGLISH TRANSLATION IS BACK, if you know any shred of Japanese you will benefit a lot from using Japanese audio and english subs, so you actually get the slang or exclamations right. I will never understand why the english translation is so bad.
Tips:
* To quickly back up from the enemy, use a magic skill
* When you start and have no clue how to play, just hit "<= backspace" until the enemy dies, start learning from there ... most early enemies will die before you use all your ATB. When the ATB ends, like the other games, you can't attack or defend until it reloads, so just switch to another schemata ("E" or "U") and slash and hack again ... yes, as mentioned, more action, less turn based
* Don't loose your time trying to control the camera in battle, just zoom out (set it as default), so you can forget the IJKL buttons and focus on the useful buttons
* Stop staring at her panties, perv

I picked it up for £25 with the season pass yesterday and finished it the same day as it was only 7 hours long which surprised me. I still have the side missions and DLC to do but the campaign is done. I really enjoyed the first 2-3 hours, it started very strong but definitely got weaker and weaker as it went on, and frankly just bizarre. The characters definitely carried if for me, I loved them all and they're were voiced really well, there was also a great mix of sadness and genuinely funny moments. The gameplay was fun but nothing special, I felt there was a lack of weapons and I didn't get anywhere near enough upgrade kits to modify even half of my weapons and I never felt particularly strong? Especially when getting instakilled by a headshot on normal difficulty, I just never felt like a Nazi slaying badass. I did like the inclusion of melee kills but in general the gameplay felt like Doom 2016 just not quite as good, and that feeling also extended to performance, while Wolfenstein 2 ran perfectly fine for the most part there were multiple areas that ran terribly for no notable reason (going from an average of 100fps to 30-40fps, one example being the courthouse which was a choppy mess). One of the cooler set pieces was also ruined by performance issues due to the game having issues with fire apparently. The game also crashed every time I tried to alt+tab out. I was expecting much better on this front considering Doom 2016 ran maxed out at 100 - 144fps and felt so crisp throughout.
Overall I was a little disappointed, especially as it started so well, it's not a bad game by any means, I'd probably still give it a 7 or 8 but I expected more, and I definitely expected it to run better than it did. I do wish I had waited for a deeper sale now, £25 for 7 hours (maybe another hour from the side missions) just isn't worth it to me, and we all know it'll hit £15 at some point, and at that price point it would be good value.

Dungeon Hearts is one of the most fun, addicting, puzzle/RPG mashup games I've ever played. It's gameplay style is simple, but can quickly turn from being easy to making very quick thinking. You need to match up 3 of the same color circles in order to create a diamond to attack. It gives you something to think about, and strategize as you go further in.
The graphics have a nice style to it, but nothing outstanding. One of my favorite parts about this game is the music, ranging from 5 different soundtracks entirely. (Pop, Jazz, Metal, ect)
Now the gameplay. These color ruins represent each character, and the grey ruins represents the enemy's attack, or debuff abilities. They travel from the right side of the screen to the left side of the screen. If the color ruins hit the end of left side, any of your ruins will dissappear as well as grey ruins. If an enemy's diamond ruin, or debuff ruin, hits the left end, then it takes effect on which ever character it was heading for.
I can go on forever on the gameplay, but it's somewhat simple. I do have a few problems with the game. The difficulty can spike, even on Normal mode. I got half way through the game before I couldn't do anything. It felt like the enemies would take more than 10-15 minutes to defeat if you don't stack the damage. Another thing is that the enemy's don't have a clear health bar. The only way you can tell that an enemy is near defeat is when their ruins begin to crack which can be somewhat annoying. One last thing is the level up system. It is a minor nickpick, but I don't consider it all that bad. You must match 3 color star ruins in order to level up. Fail to do so will result in low level characters, and some challenging enemies.
Overall I think this game is fantastic with amazing music, and quick thinking puzzling, RPG, gameplay. It's just very nice to play this game and it puts me in a relaxed mood in the beginning to becoming intense in the later part of the game. I give it an 8/10.

Dungeon Hearts is a match-3/RPG crossover that fails under its own ambitions of trying to recreate the wheel. It's bursting at the seams with original mechanics and a fresh take on match-3 games, but seemingly forgot to test if any of the ideas it presents actually add anything to the experience or makes for a game that's worth playing. It continually tries too hard to insert itself as something unique in a broad spectrum of derivative peers, that it forgets that the reason those games bare such a resemblance to each other is because the formula works, leaving it standing awkwardly on the sidelines like an odd kid who has been ostracized at his own party.
Broken down into its simplest elements, Dungeon Hearts plays like a combination of Collapse and Guitar Hero. Colored gems come horizontally across the screen toward your characters, and you must combine three like colored gems to form a power gem that allows you to clear away skulls which hurt your character if they make it all the way across. This basic system is continually and rapidly expanded as you play, with unique levels for your four characters, blocks that can't be moved, skulls that take multiple hits to clear away, and so on and so forth. It all combines to make for a game that starts out simply enough but quickly becomes entirely and utterly overwhelming. There begins to be so much constantly happening on screen, that it's nigh impossible to begin to keep up.
I kept hoping that maybe if I just played another round or two Dungeon Hearts would finally click for me, but the longer I stuck with it the more annoyed I became at its cumbersome controls and incessant need to constantly throw more at you than you can handle. There are undoubtedly some really neat ideas hidden in Dungeon Hearts that could potentially be spun out into a better game, but what Cube Roots has done with them feels more like they threw everything at the wall hoping something would stick, than careful and deliberate design. And even then it almost works, which makes the colossal waste of a game that it turned out to be all the more disappointing.

The so called "RPG element" is pretty much totally pointless, and I would say that it's not a puzzle game at all, since the only difficulty in the game is that you will be stressed out and not be able to make your moves in time - the moves themselves are more or less obvious.
So, this is more of a reaction game. Which I guess could be fun if you're into that, but they just keep upping the speed AND throw in more and more blocks that are in the way of your moves. That is the only way they are "controlling" the difficulty. Combine this with controls that don't always understand that you want to drag the thing you are click-and-dragging (I'm guessing it's a sub-optimal touchscreen port) and you have a game that is all about frustration and not at all about having a good time.
Buy this game if you like to be stressed out without having fun, if you love being pointlessly frustrated, or if you would like to try how it feels to get a cramp in your hand. Everybody else, stay away if you value your sanity.

Overall there are some little flaws that just scream bad design, but there is one horribly designed mechanic that kept me from having any shred of enjoyment. For added difficulty the board you have to work with is constatly changing one spot at the time, which in itself is not a bad idea, but because of flaw in the design the game very often tries to change the spot that you are currently on, which results in automatic failure.
Because of that the game forced me to restart the very first level (not counting the tutorial) at least ten times, for no other reason than "♥♥♥♥ you, do it again."
If this game is not going to be, at the very least, fair with me, then I have no intention to waste any more of my time on it.

The SEGA Genesis/Mega Drive is arguably SEGAs best console and 'SEGA Mega Drive and Genesis Classics' is a compilation of two HUBs to play your games on, a 'simple launcher' and the much better 'room' hub. As well as that you have a huge range of different, retro games to buy, taking the title of DLC's. Many of these games are timeless classics like the Sonic The Hedgehog, Phantasy Star, Streets Of Rage and many more.
Pro's
> Wide selection of fan-favourite genesis games that can run on weaker systems.
> Very easy to pick up and play.
> Works with most if not all controllers.
> Mod support - seriously, ROM hacks make buying some games so much more worth it, props to SEGA for allowing Steam Workshop support.
> The HUB room is very well made, featuring various items of the 90s, a CRT Television and the console itself with your game library.
> Sonic 3 & Knuckles. Need i say much else? :D
Con's
> Games can be quite pricey for their age, i'd just wait for a Steam sale to invest in titles you can wait for.
> Could have more emulation features
> You can pick this game up for much cheaper used on the consoles. (PS3 & XBOX 360)
Overall, with mod support and a wide array of 16-bit awesomness to play, why not pick it up? Maybe when it is on the cheap though.
Overall Rating: 70/100

If you are considering buying this game, I highly recommend buying "Arcana Heart 3 LOVEMAX SIXSTARS!!!!!!" instead of this version. Six Stars is essentially an extension of this game with every single character and arcana from this game plus new ones.
Arcana Heart 3 LOVE MAX!!!!! is an excellent 2D fighter with massive replay value depending on how much you appreciate well designed 2D fighters. There are 23 unique characters and 23 different arcana to select, making over 500 combinations of the two. It plays a lot like Blazblue, and even uses similar light, medium, and heavy attacks, but with the addition of one button just used for dashing directly to your opponent, as well as an extra button just for your arcana. It's fast paced and there is no tutorial, but if you have played any 2D fighter before, you shouldn't have too much trouble learning how to play this one!
Overall this is a very well made game, combos feel very satisfying, the learning curve is pretty fair if you are willing to spend more than an hour in the game. The final bosses are pretty challenging but that's the whole point of them being "final bosses", so don't be discouraged. Highly recommend to those who enjoy other 2D fighters such as Blazblue, Guilty Gear, Skullgirls, and even Street Fighter.

This game is more of an experience than a game.
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice takes you into what it feels like to endure through psychosis and really takes the cake when it comes to presentation. You NEED to play this with headphones and preferably alone and undisturbed. The headphones permit you to experience the binaural audio that the developers have worked so hard on, permitting you to experience the voices in your head like no other. The background music, sound cues, sound effects and voice acting are masterfully executed, really sucking you into its atmosphere and allowing you to fully experience the game's design. All of this mixed with the interesting plot that absorbs you into the wonderfully bizarre world of norse mythology makes for one of the best video game experiences I've ever had.
The gameplay is fairly simple, explore, focus, think and fight. The game gives you no tutorial because no tutorial is needed. The puzzles are ridiculously easy considering how many hints the game gives you, however some people might find the pace to be slow considering how slowly Senua runs. The controls are there for you when you pause the game, and the fighting flows rather well for a game that is supposed to be more about the experience than the action. The combat system is very linear, the enemies you encounter all have simple mechanics and patterns, the voices in your head give you advice on your fight and the immunity/blocking frames of your dodging/blocking are HUGE.
All in all, you shouldn't have any trouble popping this game into the hardest difficulty for a bit of action to match the intensity of the story. If you're more of a cinematic player then put it in easy and let the show begin.

This is a FPS set in a reality where the nazi's won World War 2, and now control America. You once again play as William 'BJ' Blazkowicz, who is soon to be a father and wants a nice non nazi America for his kids to grow up in.
Having killed his main nemesis, it falls on General Engel (BJ disfigured her in the first game) to be the villain this time around. Though sadly it is fair of the negative reviews to point out she isn't as twisted as the previous villain.
Uh...I guess after the first "new" Wolfenstein this was never going to be a sensible game, and sure enough - it's just as nuts as that, if not more so. If you really couldn't get along with the previous game, then this won't persuade you otherwise.
If you did like the kooky mix of weird philosophizing, cartoony characters and bat poop crazy plotting - this doubles down on that, though it can veer from ludicrously amusing to just ludicrous.
Gameplay wise - its tight action, and decently designed. Nothing spectacular, and doesn't have quite the impact of the first game, but no more or less exciting than every other other FPS out there these days (the very few there are, anyway)
To be fair to this title - you can cut and paste that  sentiment for pretty much every AAA game you care to mention. Since none of them are doing anything new or amazing, then any game that passes the time nicely is a good game. It just won't knock your socks off.....

I bought this game on PS4 when it first came out, I splurged on the CE after having my eye on it for nearly a year. The first rotation I had with it, I found it an enjoyable, albeit repetitive, experience. I was excited for a sandbox universe, somewhere I could ease the tensions of being a final semester college student who heavily enjoyed bands like 65daysofstatic (who did a stellar job on the soundtrack, pun intended). But eventually, it got shelved away in favor of games with more replay value and things that sucked me in more.
Fast forward to August 2017. I bought a new gaming PC and decided to pick the game up after hearing about how big Atlas Rises was. I was not disappointed.
This game has sucked me in and I have been all over it as of late. There's so much more content, so much more to chase after, and purpose for it all. I'm in the middle of trying to buy a freighter (saw a beta for patch 1.36 where the prices went down to affordable range for me, I've got 1million units banked as of now) and it's all I've ever wanted in a game. I feel like it's a universe that finally has substance to it. It sates the drive within me to be the greatest explorer the universe has ever known. It's a game the allows me to pour the infinite motion of my mind onto a blank canvas and create something greater than myself. And I love it for that.
Breakdown as of Patch 1.35 (Atlas Rises Update 5)
-Content: Plenty to chase with new story and vendor missions and the accompanying rewards.
-Gameplay: Plays great. New flight controls take some getting used to, but overall very intuitive and enjoyable.
-Visuals: Dynamic, powerful, though the framerate gets choppy on some planets with my GTX1050TI and ASUS ROG ZSeries motherboard. Great color palate and visual design.
-Sounds: Beautiful ambient work done by 65daysofstatic and great sound effects as well.
Overall Score: 9 out of 10. Needs some polishing with framerate and minor visual glitches, as well as decreasing costs for major purchases like freighters and some later starships.
If you get it on sale like I did ($23 USD was a value), INVEST. The Sky is the limit. Well, maybe not anymore...

There are some positives.   It was enjoyable for about 300 hours of game play.  After exploring about 7 solar systems, you realize there are only about a dozen different planet types, about 14 different creatures and about 20 different flora, and everything else is a randomly generated variant on those basics.  The main quests don't pay off very well, and the side quests are very limited and monotonous.  Each planet has the same half a dozen types of things to find, and you quickly max out your ship, suit and weapon and then it becomes pointless.  It is nicely seamless, but a bit buggy (ie, right now my base has grass suddenly growing up through the floor and although it is on a "paradise" planet, suddenly I have toxic rain?).  From what I understand some of the upgrades like Atlas and Pathfinder improved it...can't imagine what it was like before them.  If they would keep adding planet/flora/fauna/ship/weapon/etc. types and add cities and civilizations (even abandoned ones) it would keep me going on it, but at the moment, I'm done.  If that kind of time is all you want, its fine, but being billed as a limitless game with a quintillion different planets is kind of a half truth.

I never write reviews, but I am compelled to do so with NMS.
The moment this game hooked me was during the following scenario:
I'm visiting random planets, and all of the sudden, my ship crashes for no reason.  I awake to a 15 minute walk from my ship, and stirpped of most resources.  I then had to survive random weather anomolies and creature attacks while making my way back to my starship.  I arrive at my vessel to find it is damaged, and unable to fly.  I then had to find more resources to craft the proper repair materials.  Once repaired, I'm given a message that the crash was due to a poorly installed component.  However, it allowed me to learn the blueprint for the component and reinstall it.  All of this seeminly random.
This is a great game for one particular reason.  It is a great "shut your brain off" type of experience.  I enjoy puting on a podcast or movie, and flying around doing all sorts of stuff:
- Discovering new animal/plant species
- Spacestation missions
- Building bases
- Hunting pirates
- Being a pirate
- Crafting unique recipies
- Driving around my home planet on my rover
- Much more...
I think the initial negative reviews during the launch of NMS were well deserved.  It launched well undercooked.  However, I think the dev has done a great job redeeming themselves.  I was hesitant to buy the game seeing that it was still $60.  However, I feel I'm getting my money's worth.  I've not looked back on the pricetag since I began.
Great game.  Highly recommended.

Full Throttle has finally gotten the same treatment that Day of the Tentacle got in its remastered version. When releasing old classics on modern platforms such as Steam, there's the issue of whether to stay true to the original or to improve on the graphics & sound to provide a fresh experience that is more palatable to modern expectations. Fortunately, Tim Schafer & Co. have found the compromise in being able to seamlessly switch back & forth between the original version & the modern reinterpretation. The graphics line up perfectly with the original, and yet are of a much higher quality. Even the soundtrack & voicelines are a higher definition, since the original was released on CD-ROM, which didn't have enough space to handle the high def versions.
As to the game itself, the plot flows incredibly well with the puzzles. It seamlessly tells the story as you progress through the game, giving it a rather cinematic feeling. All the atmosphere & characters are incredibly well-written. There are a few downsides that should be noted: The most common complaint is that the game is a bit short, which is true. The upside of that is that the game never drags. The other negative is that there are a few arcade sequences (one of which can be skipped), and while I don't mind arcade sequences, they're almost never well written in adventure games. The bike fights are certainly playable, and even enjoyable on some level, but the novelty wears off quickly.
Obviously, it's hard to talk about the quality of the puzzles in an adventure game without spoilers. So I will sum it up by saying that I find the puzzles to be well written, never so difficult that you get stuck, but also not so obvious that there's no challenge. Overall, I highly recommend Full Throttle as an adventure game, and the effort put into the remastered version really gives the game the tribute that it deserves.
Oh, and the soundtrack blows me away. The Gone Jackals CD is worth getting if you can find it.

Think of it as a top-down Battlefield, with mechanics that affect your aim based on how much equipment you're carrying, and what stance you're in. Also add in a slight rogue-like element, which means that once a character dies, they're gone for good and you lose small amounts of XP and RP (the game's currency for buying new gear). Since, I referred to this game as a "top-down Battlefield", you're probably expecting a few key staples of that series, e.g.
Wide-open, expansive maps that allow you to approach objectives from different angles? Check.
Nice variety of weaponry and secondary gear, e.g. RPGs, medikits etc? Check.
Huge battles featuring numerous soldiers and vehicles? Check.
In terms of gameplay value; you have singleplayer (custom games, campaigns and skirmishes), and multiplayer (either PvP or PvE). Singular levels in the campaign, seem to be appropriately lengthy (though I dont know if it's normal for a battle to go on for a couple of hours and still not see a victor). Multiplayer can be 64 player battles or co-op against the AI, though I haven't sampled the multiplayer extensively as of yet.
Overall, I'd say that this game is incredible for an indie title, especially at that price point, and would reccomend that everyone buy it immediately!
Note that I haven't even mentioned mods in my review, which can easily add many more hours of playtime to your record, and feature total conversions to zombie survival, reskins set in different time periods, and even a ME themed reskin!
Final verdict: 9/10

Anyone who leaves a negative review on this is failing to understand what this is about. It's not a game as much as it is an interactive narrative experience that tries to convey thoughts and feelings in a way that transcends mere literary techniques, at which it succeeds absolutely fantastically; which is especially relevant when it comes to quite a touchy subject matter that needs a LOT of nuance and care to come across in the way that it was intended, which I think Ninja Theory have succeeded in more so than anyone I can think of to date.

I read about this game some time ago. It was supposed to be one of the best games ever and I thought, well I just read another markting sponsored editorial. Then I saw this game at the autumn sale at thought, let's give it a go. I bought it, but then it almost slipped into my "Pile of Shame" (games you buy, but never play). Last night I thought, let's give it a go. I have half an hour and if it sucks, it will definitly go into my "Pile of shame". So I pressed play.
And I was amazed. First of all, the sound is exeptional. I use a Steelseries 9H, coupled with a Soundblaster X-Fi Pro, so I'm used to good quality sound. But now I was really amazed. The voices make you feel like you're inside an schizofrenics head. The background sounds help you to suck you into the game world. Then there is are movement visuals of Senua (main character) which is great. It's almost like there is an actual girl walking. The face is as lifelike as I've ever seen. The Unreal4 engine does begin to show its age, but overall it still looks amazing.
When you start the game, you really don't have any clue about how to use the character. Not that it's that difficult, but you feel sort of lost. I imagine the creators intended it to be that way, because Senua is also lost. There is no HUD, so you have no clue on "health", "ammo", "compass", "map" or any of that. This even adds more to the confusion. Later on it is explained there is a sort of "health system" (No spoilers) but not as you expect it. And I think this new system is one of the best and original ways to implement it. Certainly into a game as this one, where there is a sense of lost, hope and persistance. It makes you feel there is an urgency which I haven't felt in a game in a long time. Bit of a minor point is that it is mostly scripted, even parts of the fights. No free roaming through hellblade. But I sort of accepted that. I just wanted to hear more of the story filled with Norse mythhology and a girl looking to find the love of her live.
They really, really put a huge effort into this game to make it one of the best games I have seen in some time. There is an  huge amount of attention to detail, in sound, display, story and overall gaming experience. Buy it. Play it during the christmas, in a dark room, with a good headset on and you won't be disappointed.

This is the stealth game of the year. I don't think I'll ever play anything quite like it. Forgetting about the beautiful graphics (and it is a stunning game, visually speaking) what really drives this game home is it's representation of scizophenia. I have never had a game make me panic like this one did. I've always been able to brush off survival/horror games, but this one actually made my heart race. Everything is layered in such a way to increase your sense of panic, and to keep you from thinking "Oh, I'm just playing a video game". If you lose too much, your save is deleted. The voices you hear come from all angles and both hurt and help you. Your enemies are often an ambigous and oppressive threat rather than just something to beat up (although, those are around too) It is masterfully done.
As far as faults go, I'd say that the game isn't really in the habit of helping you figure out how to play it. A lot of people mentioned the combat being kinda bland, which is how I felt until I discovered you could parry around halfway through the game. After that, I really enjoyed the combat, it felt dynamic while still being grounded, and you only being able to focus on one enemy at a time really forces you to be aware of your surroundings while not looking at them, while building on a sense that threats could come from anywhere.
My second complaint is that some of the puzzles can feel a little repetative. Sometimes they do some really cool stuff with the main characters altered perception of reality, but sometimes I just want to open a door without being instakilled by some screaming fire.
Other than that, it's a beautiful game, and an experience like nothing else, and I can't recommend it enough.

It's extremely difficult to decide what rating this game gets and whether I recommend it to others. I think it caters to a very specific audience as you'll either love it or hate it. The story is wonderful, probably the best of 2017. It's a tale of psychosis, the game gets in your head by forcing you to empathize with Senua. The graphics and environment are beautiful and mesmorizing, but unfortunately the gameplay is lacking. The combat is quite decent in the beginning as there's a slight learning curve, but it quickly becomes stale and causes quite a few minor glitches. A large part of this game is solving what some may call "puzzles"; but they were frustrating rather than difficult, and it was more time consuming than rewarding. I understood the angle they were going for with these puzzles with Senua's psychosis, but I don't think it worked well. The voice acting is superb and definitely worth noting. Senua's voices certainly drove me a little mad at some points, and even got me emotional at some points in the game. The overall audio design in the game is some of the best I've ever heard, you're gonna want to play this with headphones.
It's an interesting game to look back upon, it's difficult to decide whether you loved it or hated it. I think it was quite brave of Ninja Theory to create a game with mental illness being at it's centerpiece. The story, audio, and visuals makes this game worth picking up in my personal opinion. You should buy this game if you're interested in experiencing both a unique and accurate representation of psychosis, otherwise you'll be disappointed.

Hellblade seems more concerned with making a great visual experience than it is making a good game. There is a movie in here fed to you piecemeal after puzzle/platforming sections which long overstay their welcome. The story itself – lets be honest here – will be unintelligible to most without watching the accompanying documentary, and a narrative breakdown. There is very little to thread the story together as its foundations are unsettled. You are made aware earlier that you cannot really trust what it is you (Senua) are seeing or hearing. The voices themselves are as unreliable, borrowing much from anxiety disorders about intrusive thoughts (as I understand it). Those little voices in your head will voice multiple opinions about what it is that is happening, even during combat. You will find a dozen or so totems/altars that initiate a narration about norse mythology, that you will more or less already be familiar with. Taken as a whole, you won't feel as if you have had a grasp of the narrative by the end of the game.
While playing this game, there was a lingering frustration over the movement system that was so persistent it ruined my enjoyment for much of the playtime. You see, this game, although fashioned within its marketing as a third person action game, is actually a puzzle/platformer (less platformer). Mobility in puzzle/platformer games is important. If you cannot move quickly, then reattempting or experimenting with the mechanics becomes very frustrating. Senua moves very slowly. Her default movement is a slow walk, her quick movement is a nauseatingly brisk jog. This makes testing out the different puzzles, whether they be phantasm gates, glass-like fractal constructions of the landscape, lighting or portals, a frustrating experience. You’ll find yourself stumbling about a level negotiating whether you should backtrack, explore a staircase for fear it will take a needlessly long amount time, but nonetheless you must so as to marshal all your potential solutions to the problem the game has set you. What becomes even more grating, is that the game arbitrarily decides the speed of Senua at certain junctures in the game. One particularly egregious example of this is when Senua is running through chest high muck at a faster speed that she would exploring the normal landscape.
You will occasionally engage in combat, ‘occasionally’ being the operative word. Combat, more or less is given to you as a treat at the end of frustrating puzzle. This makes mastering the mechanics of combat an annoying venture because you do so little of it. You will find yourself, as I did, discovering certain combat moves e.g. charging, blocking, flourishing while counterattacking, during these exchanges. This is not to come off as an accomplishment, that the game ingeniously teaches you its own mechanics through some type of repetitive experiential learning. The experiential learning is necessitated by the player because of a lack of combat tutorials, which is exacerbated by the lack of a tangible UI/HUD system. I understand the desire to not want Arkham styled prompts flashing on the screen. This game styles itself very much as an authentic experience. There’s a type of cleanliness in this game's visual design. You aren’t bothered with mini maps, button prompts, navigation points, skill meters etc. Nonetheless, don’t expect an engrossing combat system.
This is all to say nothing of the fact that combat ultimately feels just as contrived as the rest of the game. The game gives you no real control of the camera during combat. The purpose of this I suppose is to engender a sense of anxiety and claustrophobia about the demons that may appear behind you instantaneously. It forces you to kite your enemies into an observable line of site. I can’t help but feel as if they could have achieved this another way. There is a sense of satisfaction and determination when you have a bearing on where your enemies are within combat. It allows you to systematically plan which ones to take down first, where to use your time slowing function, or flourishes/counterattacks. And there is time to do this as combat is slow, with very little opportunity to cleave multiple enemies at once. This game wants you to defeat the demons one by one – albeit with the camera contrivance. Enemies do vary. How much? It is difficult to say. Some enemies will look different but have the same attack set. Some enemies will vary in both, i.e. sword and shield, two handed wielder tanks, dual wielding teleporting chargers – not including a handful of unique boss fights. Again, this is a small portion of the game, so your familiarity with all these enemy types will be wanting throughout the game.

Played this back in the mid 90s. It took me a while to get Full Throttle compared to the other LucasArts games I've played but I got what it was able to do. Point and click games could be rough and gritty. They didn't always need to be slapstick and light. A tale closer to reality can be woven in that genre.
Full Throttle comes across somewhat differently to most of the LucasArts catalogue. It isn't as complex in figuring out certain puzzles like Monkey Island or Day of the Tentacle was. It's not as story-rich as The Dig or as detailed as Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis. But what it does have is attitude, a protagonist unlike those of other LucasArts titles in a very good way, a belting soundtrack by The Gone Jackals and mixes in some of the usual zany LucasArts humour with a gritty tale and setting.
Ben is a badass. The context to give a damn about him is established quickly. Maureen is capable of handling herself overall and has her own axe to grind. It's their tale to tell. If the rest of the cast don't seem detailed/utilised enough, it's because of the lone wolf mentality that encapsulates Ben. Just keep on riding, punch whatever's in the way and do whatever it takes to survive. Ben is more than capable of carrying this tale and Maureen adds some depth to it when required.
Brief summation on the various ramblings I've seen about whether the remaster was worth it. Overall, yes. Some moments/cutscenes had very awkward looking facial expressions/character designs in the original. They're very clear here and don't lose the style of the original. There was the odd moment the game froze and the odd moment in a couple of cut scenes did drop in frame rate. But it was still a smooth experience overall.
All in all, it was one heck of an experience to be able to play Full Throttle again. It still goes well compared to how most of the genre plays out today and is worth remembering. Appropriately priced, as well.

This game feels like it was designed and intended for a touchscreen interface.  And probably with that setup it's a fast-paced, fun, and engaging game.  But I played it with keyboard and mouse on a desktop computer, and in that more traditional situation it felt like playing the worst level of Bejeweled quest mode imaginable.  Everything has a short and punishing time constraint, including collecting XP to level up after a level (or failing to do so!).  The basic gameplay is simplistic and boring -- yet actions that should be the simplest, easiest, and most basic fundamentals of the game are awkward.  Difficulty comes from bad ergonomics, not from a true skill requirement.  There is a lot of interesting complexity to explore, but it's set up to remove rewards for actions several steps from good play, so even the best parts of the game design make the experience less compelling.

Game is a lot worse than I remember, must have been wearing those rose tinted glasses
Positives
+ Fighting in a tank at the same time as commanding the force is a fun concept
+ Campaign gives a sense of progression
+ Interesting time period and combatants
+ Reasonable depth (unit variety and off map support for example)
Negatives
- Fighting from your tank is a lot less fun than you might think given the tiny screen. You'll be shot across the map without seeing what killed you.
- Interface is bad (want to cancel an ongoing artillery barrage to save your suicidal tanks? Nope)
- Interface is bad (want to know how long until your artillery barrage is ready again? Nope. You're not allowed to know that)
- Interface is horrible (want to see a company's waypoints? You have to hit the company info button on the toolbar, navigate to the company with the left and right arrows, then hit waypoints, then hunt around the platoon map for the lines because they don't appear on the strategic map)
- Interface is really horrible (want to give your army a simple move order? How about setting your army's starting orders from the same screen you deploy them? Nope, you have to give each company individual orders, and you have to quickly cancel the automatic starting orders if you want control over how the engagement proceeds from the start)
- The AI of your units is completely unpredictable. Will the "assault" order make your company chase the enemy across the map, turn around and flee, drive in circles, or scatter in every direction? Roll a dice! It could be any of these!
- Combat is completely unpredictable. There're no indications as to which units can see the enemy or even what the range of their weapons is. Foot infantry can defeat medium tanks.
- The pathfinding is almost braindead. Your units often head in the opposite direction to the waypoint you gave them. They will rush into enemy units when you told them to stay still. They will move around a forest when you told them to take the road going through it.

let me preface this review by saying that i *really* did not like darksiders. i thought it was badly designed, the dungeons and bosses were medicore at best and infuriating at worst and the controls were a nightmare to navigate, especially when anything needed to be manually targeted. because of this, i avoided DS2 like the plague, thinking it would be more of the same.
however, i was very pleasently surprised to find that darksiders 2 is far more tightly designed, open, and fun to play then it's predecessor. the RPG elements and loot systems are satisfying to engage with and tickles the part of the brain that likes to see the numbers go up. the dungeons are far better designed, with interesting puzzles and fun traversal sections that are clear, but just obfuscated enough to still be a puzzle. i never felt like the game was tricking me or like i was battling some badly implemented part of it like i was in DS1. even the voidwalker (see: portal gun) is far more interesting in DS2 then it was in DS1, where it felt gimmicky and tedious to use.
however, there are still elements that are less then ideal in DS2. without spoiling story beats, there are sections where the game becomes akin to a third-person shooter with an over-the-shoulder camera, which feels clunky even when everything is working well. the controls and gameplay systems simply aren't setup for this kind of play style, and the parts where these gameplay elements surface are very much weak links in the strong chain that makes up most of the play time.
the story and art design can be very hit or miss for a lot of people, but i found the goofy mismash of Every Mythology Ever sprinkled with more then a little bit of comic book logic was pretty entertaining, and Death is a pretty entertaining character. Joe Mad's art may sometimes look like a self-replicating WoW character that succumbs to greeble, but i feel like it fits the big, dumb world of darksiders.
i encountered a few crashing issues when alt-tabbing after the first world, which was strange, as well as a progression issue during the second DLC campaign in a side-dungeon, but nothing major. the touted graphical upgrade for the Deathinitive edition wasen't really noticable in a huge way, but it was very much welcome, though i wish the shadows were better, because they often fall prone to super bad striping in close-up character scenes. i played for 70 hours on a GTX 970 and a 3.4ghz i5 4670k with 8gb of ram at 1920x1200 and only had a few stutters when loading due to the game being installed on a mechnical external drive instead of my SSD
in conclusion, i was super happy to play this game and was ashamed for avoiding it for so long. sadly, we might never get a DS3 because this was very much THQ's swan song, but Nordic Games (who now owns the rights to darksiders) says it might happen someday. next time, i'll keep my eye on it.

The original Darksiders 2 was an absolute gem of a game, and The Deathinitive Edition is basically the original game with all of the DLC gear integrated into the game proper. The various pieces of DLC gear are appropriately leveled for when you find them, and a few of them actually level with you. This is in contrast to the original Darksiders 2 in which the player received all of the DLC gear up front as level 5 or level 10 gear that did not level with the player.
The graphics were updated / remastered to compete with current generation console titles, but you will need a High End 2015 Gaming PC or better to run the game with all the new bells and whistles. The game can still be run on older / less powerful machines on lower graphical settings, but you'll basically be getting the 2012 original Darksiders 2 graphics. This isn't necessarily a bad thing. The art and character designs have a 'graphic novel' feel to them, so even at lower resolutions the visuals look pretty decent.
The combat and exploration mechanics are still the highlights of this game. The controls are intuitive, and the game makes you feel like a badass ninja during exploration and combat. The exploration is similar to the Prince of Persia 'Sands of Time' games. The combat is similar to the original (i.e. pre-reboot) Devil May Cry games. There is one small portion of the game where you're forced to play from an over-the-shoulder 3rd Person Shooter perspective, but that part of the game is (thankfully) fairly short. If you've never played Darksiders 2, the Deathinitive Edition is a solid purchase.
Disclosure: I received Darksiders 2 Deathinitive Edition as a free download because I purchased the "Darksiders Franchise Pack" (which included DS 1 & DS 2 & All DLCs for both games) in 2014. The Deathinitive Edition was released in 2015.

Darksiders II takes a similar approach to story telling as the original but with faster fight sequences (Death is MUCH more agile than War), a much improved loot system (akin to Diablo), several fully explorable (and returnable) worlds, and a variety of side quests to compliment the main story.
The DLC, while not as in depth or detailed as the main game, still adds plenty of value and gameplay to an already great game.
Yes there are a few bugs with sound cutting out, the damage indicator crashing the game, a few movement glitches, and very rare visual artifacts but the overall quality and finish is AAA worthy; nothing dibilitating or experience ruining. The only missing element is more replayability: a harder difficulty, multiple New Game+, more level progression (current cap is 22 & 30)...just...more!

Wolfenstein II is a fitting sequel to the franchise, and it delivers on all its promises: kill Nazis by the truckloads. This is not an open world game. It's a linear, story driven FPS that sets up set-piece battle after set-piece battle with a wide, but limited, range of adversaries. The AI is passable, as the enemies swarm to your location relentlessly once you've made yourself known. The key to game is to keep moving in a firefight, because if you camp in any one spot, they will come at you from differnt positions. Once in a while, you find a decent choke point and, if you're a good shot, you can turn it into a Nazi kill box.
PROS:
The aforementioned gameplay is solid. The story is as over the top as its premise.Your allies look like they were ripped from one of those 70's blaxploitation era films. I was waitign to hear them say "jive turkey" at any moment. The message is pretty straightforward - racists and Nazis are BAD. The End. That may make some of you uncomfortable, that is, if you're a racist or a Nazi sympathizer. Otherwise, it's all in good Nazi hating fun. The graphics are not a leap beyond the previous game, but they are very good.
CONS:
You don't get to interact with the characters in any meaningful way except to move the story forward. This is a sad waste, as the characters seem very intriguing, and you want to get to know them better. If you hover over them, they will speak dialogue, but you don't get  to say anything back, and all your missions are solo.
VERDICT:
Thisis a great game! It's worth the sale price - meaning, get it while its on sale.

About the gameplay itself the game it's fantastic, very engaging, like The New Order, with improvements, a fast paced shooter, smooth and incredible satisfactory. The level design are good (with one level with reminiscences of Fallout 4). You can go there as an agent of mayhem and chaos, or you can approach it in a more stealthy way. Its campaign is extensive, and with many collectibles and replayability. Numerous difficulty options, with some really challenging. The optimization is magnificent and graphically it looks incredible. And of course, the soundtrack by Mick Gordon, as always, outstanding. The game is a sensational achievement, one of the best of the year.

Okay, so, after reaching floor 500, I felt I could write a little review on this.
This game is a free horror game, and unlike most of those, it actually has some cleverness and creativity behind it, instead of just having you walk through a badly written narrative with a Slender-brand flashlight, collecting something while avoiding a generic monster.
Instead, you're in a 'creepy', zany cartoon/chibi-esque mansion, progressing from room to room, and floor to floor. Each floor has a hundred rooms. The cartoony look of thing persists through the entire game, but instead of staying cutesy, it actually gets quite twisted along the way. The first 100 rooms or so, the only 'monster' you meet are cardboard cutouts that jumpscare you occasionally. This is actually my favorite monster in the game, because despite being a parody of generic jumpscares, they still kind of work, especially when you get farther in the game.
Speaking of which, somewhere in the 200s of rooms, you actually will be getting stalked by an entity. It's slow, it takes some health from your regenerating healthbar when it touches you, and it's still somewhat cartoony-looking, but it can startle you the first time. This is where you're introduced to the whole 'pursuit' mechanic. Every 100 floors, a different monster will join the pursuit. You'll go through rooms randomly that introduce you to it at first (a creepy lab, a creepy school, a creepy Silent Hill-esque industrial area, etc.). As long as there's an entity stalking you, you will hear its theme, and different kinds of warning sounds, until you lose it. As far as I've seen, the entities have different speeds and strengths, and gameplay mechanics change depending on what's chasing you (the Silent Hill monster thing can mess up room textures, which might lead to difficulties finding the exit door, for example).
This all is quite interesting, but you'll still end up walking through a lot of the same randomly generated/repeating rooms over and over. They only get some variety when something's after you. So, in that way, the game has ups and downs between making you really nervous and just boring you, because you kind of know what's coming on each floor, after a while. Still, you do encounter some special computer rooms where all the monster are somewhat neatly categorized, which is sort of like a preview of coming attractions.
So, do I recommend it? I would say, yes, especially if you've played a number of Indie horror games. There's really good ones, and ones so horrible that you can only laugh at them, and 'Spooky's Mansion/House of Jumpscares' (or whatever the title is this week) references both kinds, and plays with the associated tropes. Even the fact that some of them seem to be made only so some particular Youtuber can scream and freak out at them.
And even if this is the only game of this kind you'll play, it's fine, because it has more variety than others. So, all in all, worth it! If this developer made another game like this, I would probably pay for it, even ;)

Half-Life 2: Update is a mod that improves lighting and shadows, as well as some other minor graphical aspects of the game.  Its subtle enough that you probably wont notice it unless you are looking for it, because its doing its job. It doesnt seem like much, but if you look at the lighting side by side its definitely noticeable.
The Update mod also comes with community commentary, so thats a plus.  This mod is not as game changing as many other graphical mods, and is subtle enough that it refines and improves the base gae, instead of changing and trying to enhance things.  Overall its good to download if you are actualyl interested in the community commentary, or want to play the game again with better lighting.
I myself downloaded it and played through the intro,  jumped a few maps to see the different improvements without having to replay the whole game, and I have got to say, in some places its really noticeable, but in others you cant tell anything has changed.

Along with enhancing the graphics and adding more overall detail, the bug fixes is what i REALLY love. I dont recomend using this update though if your computer isnt mid-high end, however even toning the settings down, it can still be a glorious time exploring.
But in general, Half-Life 2 somewhat needed this; fixes and graphic increased, as normaly... It still looked stunning at the time but after sometime playing, this recent Update mod is the overall king.
..Oh, and those few who nit-picked about the separate data.. Get used to it, think of it as a new, fresh start.
