The Shorts
To be fair I mainly recommend this game because the devs actually continued developing the game after the ♥♥♥♥♥torm they received. Imho that wasn't entirely fair. There are many games that are way worse and did not get the same treatment. However, many of the negative reviews that actually have some depth are not necessarily wrong.
The Wuts
So what I'm saying is the game isn't that bad. With the base building expansion the game has a bit more purpose to it. The exocraft are a nice touch, but since you start out with a spaceship they don't add that much to the game other then having some shiny stuff on your lawn.
The best way to define this game would be "THE GRIND IS REAL". You actually have to grind to be able to grind (recharging thrusters, mining lasers). Even the "quests" are grind X amount of material Y. There are only a few materials on each planet, forcing you to "explore" the galaxy. Now this isn't necessarily bad, and you'll probably have a good time for a while.
The Buts
As it is procedurally generated, RNG is a factor. In my first system a lot of critters on different planets actually looked the same. The big misconception about procedurally generated content is that is delivers a huge amount of different content. While this can be technically correct, you'll have to remember it just means the existing content is reshuffled. It does not create new content, it just adds or subtracts a wing from a critter you already know or paints it blue instead of red. Hurray!
The game seems to be riddled with strange design flaws. They might get to you as they got to me in the end or you might not care. You don't just click a button, you have to hold it for a while. The waypoints you find will hijack the camera and float for a while. Movement is excruciatingly slow outside your craft, however your craft handles like a truck that is made out of bouncing ball material and some things will not load fast enough while you're skimming the surface (critters and such). You can only build 1 base and the size is highly limited in basic settings. You can only own one starship until you get a freighter (which is horribly expensive). All these things make the exploring/building/gathering far from a smooth experience.
So is it as bad as the first reviews, no. Is it as good as the first trailer, certainly not. It's a mediocre sandbox game which is fun for a while and can look quite fancypancy.

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is truly a work of art. I've never been a big fan of walking simulators, but Ninja Theory really knocked it out of the park with this one. The game is incredibly captivating and visually stunning. My sole criticism is that the combat is not particularly enjoyable. You have a very limited move set, and particularly in the larger battles it feels like the true enemy is the camera angle. That being said, the game is still definitely worth picking up.

Waifu Wars: the Game.
Characters:
All of the characters here are female and represent many typical anime archetypes, which people will basically either love or hate. I'm a little neutral when it comes to that. The mood here is fairly light-hearted, so that's mainly what you can expect from the characters. There are a few more serious ones here and there and they are usually my personal favorites. The cast is pretty diverse in terms of what they can do in the game, many traditional archetypes are present here. Shoto-style characters, charge characters, grapplers, zoners, everything is more or less here though they can be adjusted depending on arcana choice which I'll get to later.
Gameplay:
Inputs are (mostly) smooth, even if you have a janky controller like I do at the moment you can usually get what you want to come out pretty reliably. Inputs are pretty much character dependent, with arcana inputs mainly being typical rolling inputs like quarter-circles, half circles, etc. Gameplay is fairly fast and fluid, though the character movement may feel clunky until you get used to the homing dash movement. Then it suddenly feels like you're completely free as you're flying around. Movement controls feel awkward in general at first, but putting some time into getting used to them can pay off. It is an anime style (if it wasn't obvious) fighting game with double jumps and even jump cancels, special cancels, super cancels, and other types of cancels so the combos can get pretty crazy at times. If you're looking to play the game competitively, be aware of that, but if you just want to play casually it's quite fun even without all of that.
Arcanas:
These things are actually extremely important. They are like additional moves you can gain depending on which one you choose, and can alter your character quite a bit. Some of them can give you projectiles, some can act as assists, some can even alter your character's movement! They really bring a lot of depth to this game and can create all kinds of matchups. Competitively this could be an issue, because there's so much to try to remember. But casually it's freaking awesome. It feels like there are limitless possibilites for the character and arcana combinations which adds tons of value for people wanting to have fun and play casually with friends.
Music:
Nothing super incredible here, but it's not really bad. There's a few tracks I like more than others, but I don't think anything will stand out too much to most players, especially compared to many other fighting games out there. Still it does its job and fits the mood of the game, which as I said is fairly light-hearted.
Story mode and extras:
The story mode itself isn't anything too special. Mainly just an arcade mode with character endings. I think there's a bit of dialogue here and there before the endings but it's been a while since I've played this mode. The after story mode has a lot more to offer in terms of actual story, but it still doesn't get really crazy or anything. Just a goofy little extra bit to get to know the characters more. It's got more of a VN (visual novel) style to it, if you're into that sort of thing. There are also things you can unlock in the gallery called "memories" which are like even more VN style tidbits. There are no battles in these that I can remember. Time Attack is what you would expect, with a special boss at the end. Survival Score Attack (I think that's the name) is basically a mode where you fight all the characters, then fight another special boss at the end. Unlike most survival style modes, you can continue in this. Finally in trials you can choose a character and try to complete various challenges which will be reflected on a score card type thing that you can display online to show off if you wish. The final challenge here is quite the doozy though, as it requires defeating one of the most difficult bosses in Arcana Heart's (and many other fighting games) history. There's a training mode of course and a gallery which lets you view various things you unlock during the game. There are a LOT of images and things called link animations which are kind of cool things that show (optionally) in the side bars while you're fighting. I guess people will have mixed feelings about them but I really like them personally.
Oh yeah, I suppose I should mention that while I only have 2.3 hours logged into this game at the time of this review, I have countless more in the PS Vita and PS3 versions of this game and have seen most of what it has to offer, which really is quite a lot.
So, in summary, for people looking for a lot of content and a fighting game to enjoy casually, this game definitely fits the bill. Just be aware it has heavy anime influneces and has the cutesy light-hearted theme. Competitive players may be turned off by the sheer amount of variability that the character and arcana combinations can create.

long story short:
Hellblade is a fun game with good gameplay and an intriguing storyline. Well worth the money if you like games that make you think, but maybe not if you're looking for a game to sink some long hours into. (Note: I only spent ~$24 on this when it was on sale around Halloween)
long story not-as-short, but not long:
it's hard to objectively measure if this is a "good game" because there's a lot of factors that some will like and others won't. A quick list:
+ Compelling storyline. Despite getting stuck on a few of the puzzles, I never felt like I needed to take a break, I wanted to keep playing through the end. This may have also been, in part, because I knew the game was fairly short.
+ Great animation. Especially after watching some behind the scenes footage, I've really grown to appreciate the facial expressions of the characters and the other visual effects.
+ Good puzzles. I thoroughly enjoyed some of the puzzles this game threw at me. I did not include that under a blanket "good gameplay" tag though; I'll get to why in a minute.
+ Innovative. No part of the game in and of itself was a new concept (except maybe the binaural delusion-voices; I don't think I've seen that anywhere before), but it created a unique experience when they were all put together to explore the complicated mental illness of psychosis.
- Short. If you are someone who follows the "1-hour-for-1-dollar" rule, that may be an instant turn off. I'm typically slow at this sort of game, and it only took me about 11 hours to finish the game and get all of the lorestones. Expect 8-10 hours, depending on how fast you play.
- Boring battle mechanics. Once you get the timing down for individual enemies' attacks, they get very predictable. This is why I didn't say the gameplay as a whole was good. I only lost against 1 of the bosses, and the only time I died in normal battles was because I was an idiot and got myself surrounded. It's worth noting, though, that the battles aren't a very significant part of the game so that doesn't detract too much from it as a whole.
Overall, a strong 8/10 to light 9/10 imo. Frankly I've not played many games that just came out this year, but Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is my GOTY so far. Feel free to make a decision on whether to purchase this for yourself based on the above points, but for my personal preferences I thought it did well just about everything that was important for this game, and the few things that were sub-par weren't so awful that I couldn't mostly look past them. The main detractors were price vs playtime and the combat system.

Sadly the fact that the game looks like it's made for middle-school kids will make people pass this by without second glance which is sad considring how enjoyable this fighter is.

* A slew of modes to add some replay value for single player
* Tons of Visual Novel to keep you interested
* Learning curve for Arc finishing and new homing button mechanic
* Beautiful, colorful sprites and Marvel vs Capcom-esque movement

The game's combat is super fun even though not as polished, tight or smooth as Melty Blood's in my opinion but there's alot to do to keep you come back for more. The Anime Link is nice feature for me, some people find it distracted but I dig the funny animations in the side-bar as characters duke it out.
Unfortunately the game suffers from what alot of ASW games suffer from, bad netcode and not a very big player base if you're looking to play online alot there is still some issues you may experience time to time.

This game is simply what redefines the term 'FUN' in 2D fighters. Just when most people thought 2D fighting games were long superceded by their next gen 3D counterparts, AQ interactive blasts on to the scene to resurrect the genre and bring back the fun and flair of old school 2D fighters.
Now a simple analysis of the cast leads us to realise that the game's selectable characters all have one thing in common~ they are all female, yes, whether AQ was specifically targeting a female audience by using an all female cast or simply smartly tickling the senses of the SHIM. They have managed to put together an interest line-up of all female characters.
The character designs are very original to say the least in the sense that there is a little bit for everyone to enjoy in this game. The games version of a 'Grappler' (Zangief type from Street Fighter) is a 12 year old girl, who uses a water sprite in which she rides to fight for her. Beware, innocence does not Piledrive you into the cement pavement :)
To add to the creativity of the characters are the colorful sonic effects generated by the characters performing their special unique abilities, the animations and sprites really bring this game to life, and needless to say the battle arenas and environments are generously colored and detailed to keep you engrosses in this 2D fight-fest. The environments are large and tall, that give the players the chance to launch their opponents skyward and perform devastating air combos mid-flight to further lay the smackdown to your unsuspecting FOE.
Interestingly enough, Arcana Hearts plays similar to most other 2D fighters, most players will reflect with games like Capcom Vs Marvel and the like. However, to add to the ferocity of an all out smackfest, they smartly introduced the DASH system. Hitting 'X' on the controller will allow the players to perform DASHES to intercept, cancel combat moves that would otherwise leave your butt open for a full-scale combo assault. In addition, to act as a cancel/combo starter. The DASH gauge consists of three bars that depletes when you use the DASH command. TO those anticipating, fear not, for when your character is not utilising this ability, the gauge will replenish itself so you may use it again and again. The best part of this mechanic is that it adds more strategy and intensity to the already fast paced battles you will partake in Arcana Heart.
The other aspect that turns heads in Arcana Heart, is the ability to customise your characters 'SUMMON' ability, each character is able to choose a 'SUMMON' ability that can be performed once per round in a battle, that acts as a super ability in addition to the characters individual special attacks. Each 'SUMMON' also has their own variety of special moves, so if your opponent is frying with pestering lightning attacks, or rooting you with the PLANT summon, there is no excuse for you not to select the same ability summon and join the fight with tide-turning abilities of your own. This game system further adds depth and customisability to what some may consider a limited cast of characters. You are likely to spend hours tailoring your characters play style with restrospective as its supporting ability, this adds really great replayability to an already enjoyable game.
The game itself has the same features as most 2D fighters, an Arcade mode, STORY mode, VS mode, Special features and Training mode. One of the few drawbacks to Arcana Heart is its lack of secrets to unlock and no unlockable characters, for those who loved the challenge of unlocking multiple characters like in the Tekken series, this aspect of the game may disappoint. However, rest assured the characters are likeable and more than well-thought of to deem the game very much complete.
The sound effects are more than decent and majority are 'OH so cute' the musical score is also enticing and plays very well with the majority of colorfully themed stages. All in all, Arcana Heart is a 'MUST' buy for FANS of the 2D fighting genre... Heck, even if your not a FAN its just so whacky and fun that most people will enjoy something about the game's overall flair for surprises. Definitely an IMPORT title, to watch for those 2D girl crazy fighting fanatics and those who do not shun or cry at the defeat of a 10 year old girl played by your middle-aged neighbor :P

RUNNING WITH RIFLES is a top-down isometric tactical shooter with open-world RPG elements. In RWR, you join the ranks of an army as a common soldier, in one of the three factions, the greenbelts (United States), Brownpants (Russia/China), Greycollars (Germany/Fourth German Reich), among thousands of other soldiers of your faction. You start off as nothing more than a common soldier having access to nothing more than the most basic weapons, the M16, AK47, and the G36. You slowly progress through the ranks unlocking more weapons and armor as well as grenades. These will save your life multiple times and will take many people's lives doing so. You gain access to sniper rifles, rocket launchers, artillery(support), shotguns, and silenced SMGs. There is a loadout to suit every player's style, whether you like striking out as a lone wolf weilding a sniper and a PDW, or you decide to become a heavy weapons specialist carrying a machine gun as well as a rocket launcher or a dozen, or even if you want to be a common solfier sacraficing his life for the glory of their country. However, one of the few cons of this game is the seemingly impossible online connections in which it is extraordinarily difficult to connect. This game offers something for everyone, so I come to my conclusion, I HIGHLY recommend this game to anyone who happens to stumble upon this.

If you're a fan of match 3 games and is looking for a little twist in your usual gameplay, this game might seem appealing to you. It'll probably be fun for the first couple of minutes, while you still think there's more to the game than it seems, but then you'll soon find out that there isn't.
You have 4 heroes on the left side of the screen, and colored runes come scrolling towards them (with each color representing a hero or the enemy). If an enemy rune hits the end of the line, the hero on that line gets damaged. If all your heroes die, it's game over.
At this point you'll think that each level will have something different besides an increasingly rune-cluttered group of lines that scrolls faster and faster, but nope, that's it. And while it's fun for a bit, the lack of variation gradually becomes very boring. There is no story, no interesting quests or goals, just few very "meh" achievements.
To make matters worse, the thing is incredibly buggy, specially on level transitions. Pausing is a dangerous choice as chances are that the game will bug instead of really pausing, leaving you stuck in a weird limbo in which you can't do anything but see your heroes dying, which can be very frustrating if you've been playing for a while. You'll then have to start from 0, and hope not to get caught in a bug again.
The controls are at times a little wobbly, giving the impression that the game was designed for a touch screen and poorly ported to the PC. So at times things won't scroll as they should, and you'll fail to drag runes around, very often leading to death.
If you're looking for a fast and mindlessly repetitive buggy match 3 game, however, you've found it.

For the purposes of this review, im am going to ignore the fallout the gaming community went through as whole regarding the hype of and release of No Man's Sky. At the time of reviewing this game, the basic multiplayer functionality had been implemented.
This game is about exploring a galaxy full of procedurally generated planets full of procedurally generated animals and plants. Starting out you have a small tool set and no way to travel between planets or solar systems. The purpose of this is to introduce you as the player to the tools and mechanics of the game. Personally i had a good experience with this introduction to the game as it prevents you from getting overwhelmed by putting up barriers to the next feature. Being able to name creatures i discover and having that shared out across all other players is fun. With that said, anything you can name isn't worth naming as the monkeys on alpha, alpha, one look like the monkeys on beezwax wartwrangle 20.
After you get through the game’s introduction in the first solar system. You quickly realize that you are now greeted with ever increasing walls of progression. To go farther you need fuel. To store extra fuel you need cargo space. Cargo space that is precious as you might want to put equipment upgrades for your ship in those slots instead. Valuable upgrades as they let you go farther or upgrade your ships weapons. The same goes for your multi tool and space suit.
I enjoy base building in this game to a degree. It felt though as if it was plopped into the game though for a game built around exploring the galaxy. Base building gives you planetary vehicles and additional storage options. As well as a level a output of creativity as you get to create “your space in space”. Everything involved with upgrading your base just felt like wading through a swamp. “Oh you want to farm” the annoying frog man said “bring mean radioactive poop please” and i'll give you the blueprints. So you spend 30 minutes tracking down the correct radioactive only to find out you didn't have the right tool to harvest it. YOu then find out that someone else at your base give you the blueprints for that tool but first you have to fight 20 or floating light bulbs for him, then tell him his wife his dead.
Stargates! The recent addition to this game. At first i thought this would be really fun as i could leap across the galaxy to some actually unique planets to explore but the game gives you more resources to grind in order to activate the thing only for you to not to be given any direction on where to look for gate addresses.
I can't say that this game is bad. There is plenty of content to unlock and do in this game. Content that i want to play. It is just locked behind hours of grinding and doing what i just feel amounts to nothing. The game’s overall quality is good though. There are landscapes that I enjoyed stopping and looking. I would jump from a solar system with nothing but a ice moon into a system in a green nebula that was bountiful. If the developer treats this game well with future content patches i hope they will better flesh things out.

The original Darksiders 2 was an absolute gem of a game, and The Deathinitive Edition is basically the original game with all of the DLC gear integrated into the game proper. The various pieces of DLC gear are appropriately leveled for when you find them, and a few of them actually level with you. This is in contrast to the original Darksiders 2 in which the player received all of the DLC gear up front as level 5 or level 10 gear that did not level with the player.
The graphics were updated / remastered to compete with current generation console titles, but you will need a High End 2015 Gaming PC or better to run the game with all the new bells and whistles. The game can still be run on older / less powerful machines on lower graphical settings, but you'll basically be getting the 2012 original Darksiders 2 graphics. This isn't necessarily a bad thing. The art and character designs have a 'graphic novel' feel to them, so even at lower resolutions the visuals look pretty decent.
The combat and exploration mechanics are still the highlights of this game. The controls are intuitive, and the game makes you feel like a badass ninja during exploration and combat. The exploration is similar to the Prince of Persia 'Sands of Time' games. The combat is similar to the original (i.e. pre-reboot) Devil May Cry games. There is one small portion of the game where you're forced to play from an over-the-shoulder 3rd Person Shooter perspective, but that part of the game is (thankfully) fairly short. If you've never played Darksiders 2, the Deathinitive Edition is a solid purchase.
Disclosure: I received Darksiders 2 Deathinitive Edition as a free download because I purchased the "Darksiders Franchise Pack" (which included DS 1 & DS 2 & All DLCs for both games) in 2014. The Deathinitive Edition was released in 2015.

Darksiders II takes a similar approach to story telling as the original but with faster fight sequences (Death is MUCH more agile than War), a much improved loot system (akin to Diablo), several fully explorable (and returnable) worlds, and a variety of side quests to compliment the main story.
The DLC, while not as in depth or detailed as the main game, still adds plenty of value and gameplay to an already great game.
Yes there are a few bugs with sound cutting out, the damage indicator crashing the game, a few movement glitches, and very rare visual artifacts but the overall quality and finish is AAA worthy; nothing dibilitating or experience ruining. The only missing element is more replayability: a harder difficulty, multiple New Game+, more level progression (current cap is 22 & 30)...just...more!
A game worthy of two playthroughs and 100% achievements. 4.5 / 5

RUNNING WITH RIFLES is a top-down isometric tactical shooter with open-world RPG elements. In RWR, you join the ranks of an army as a common soldier, in one of the three factions, the greenbelts (United States), Brownpants (Russia/China), Greycollars (Germany/Fourth German Reich), among thousands of other soldiers of your faction. You start off as nothing more than a common soldier having access to nothing more than the most basic weapons, the M16, AK47, and the G36. You slowly progress through the ranks unlocking more weapons and armor as well as grenades. These will save your life multiple times and will take many people's lives doing so. You gain access to sniper rifles, rocket launchers, artillery(support), shotguns, and silenced SMGs. There is a loadout to suit every player's style, whether you like striking out as a lone wolf weilding a sniper and a PDW, or you decide to become a heavy weapons specialist carrying a machine gun as well as a rocket launcher or a dozen, or even if you want to be a common solfier sacraficing his life for the glory of their country. However, one of the few cons of this game is the seemingly impossible online connections in which it is extraordinarily difficult to connect. This game offers something for everyone, so I come to my conclusion, I HIGHLY recommend this game to anyone who happens to stumble upon this.

Clash (sorry, CLASH) is a third-person, multiplayer shooter with a leveling scheme. Unfortunately, there aren't a ton of active users, so the game depends on bot competition. Fights with bots tend to be a matter of deciding whether to stand facing each other and chip away at their shields or run away if your own shields are failing. This doesn't seem like the right way to play, but I'm having a hard time figuring out the skill system. For some reason, I can only use each skill once. I must be missing something.
The maps are more interesting than they first appear. It took awhile to figure it out, but holding the jump button (spacebar) activates a limited rocket jump ability. So the key to many of the maps is learning to jump up buildings or rock formations. That will let you attack from above and avoid being ambushed yourself. I'm guessing there are skills to be learned to improve jump height, but I haven't figured them out. More jumping would be great!
I'm recommending this on the strength of being a free game that's still actively being developed. Would be improved with more players and less confusing leveling interface.

They forgot to paint a nut in one of the puzzles, so if you havn't played the game before you may be really confused if you're in "remastered mode" and not "regular mode" where the nut is still painted in.

I bought this game after the first Atlas Rises update, so I don't know what kind of glaring issues this game had when it first released, but I urge anyone who already owns this game to give it a second chance. The game gets updated a few times per month with pretty significant quality-of-life improvements and bug fixes, and I'd say the current state of the game is pretty enjoyable. It still has a list of issues that need resolving (storage containers behaving oddly and tanking framerate comes to mind), but with the rate the devs are updating the game, I expect most of these to be resolved in the near future.
For those who have never played the game, it's mostly a sandbox / exploration game with a loose storyline that you can choose to follow or ignore. I'm not sure I can recommend this game at its full price tag, but if it ever goes on sale, it's worth checking out.

One of the most immersive games I've ever played. You're thrown into the story of a young lady, who's suffered the most tragic of misfortunes, and endured incredible cruelty from nearly everyone around her. As you help Senua to conquer her inner demons, among the lies and deception, the truth unfolds with truly horrifying precision.
The game manages to depict Senua's illness as a logical and rational consequence of her experiences. So, prepare to delve into the darkest corners of your soul. I am amazed any game even dares to touch upon such taboo subjects. And Hellblade does it masterly.
The gameplay is well paced, with a balance between exploration, puzzle solving (most of which are reasonable, some are quite hard), and boss fighting (you can adapt the level of difficulty, I'm not so much into combat combo's and so on, but the game is finishable with not too much skill, and only one of the boss fights felt really too long). Occasionally there are sequences where you have to run from various horrors, these are truly terrifying.
Be wary that this is a very, very dark game, with plenty of disturbing depictions. I'd go as far as saying that you probably shouldn't play this game if you are easily disturbed.
With that disclaimer out of the way, I very strongly recommend this game to anyone who looks for games that entail deep emotional experiences.

Not gonna lie, I only do the offline DLC, but it's quite fun. The bots are usually stupid out of combat, but once in combat they get themselves back together and act well. Just a heads up, [H] Bots will dodge bullets and you'll have a very hard time dodging theirs. This game can somewhat be played casually, but each match can be a challenge, depending on how you approach it.
The game is basically a third-person shooter, but in an arena with abilities, so it's also a MOBA. Before you start, it's not like Overwatch at all. Teamwork can be used, but it's actually optional, which I think is the best part. You CAN go Rambo and ballistic and carry the match, since the leveling system allows it. You start off with 3 abilities and get more as you level up during the match. There are 3 class trees: Proficiency, Accuracy, and Survivability. Proficiency is all about doing damage over time, and being constant with it, so it tends to have lower cooldowns, lower damage, and DoT. Accuracy is about bursting hardcore, so higher damage, but higher cooldowns. Survivability has low damage and high cooldowns, but you set traps, heal yourself, and what not, so you die a lot less with this class. The leveling up is a bit strange, because you level up branches, not skills, so when you upgrade proficiency, all skills under proficiency get upgraded.
You have 4 constant DPS abilities, which are photon shot, energy shot, regenerative shot, and fight for survival. Starting off a match without one of these four abilities will guarantee you pain, unless you play it off super well. Each is the first ability of each tree, with the exception of energy shot, which is, also, under proficiency. Getting photon shot and energy shot feels super awkward, so I'm not really sure how you would use both.
I mentioned bot AI before, but I should also mention that bots on your team will be dumb. Horribly dumb. They'll aim well, but their IQ is far below the number of genders (2). You usually can follow them around for a solid clean-up crew type game, just remember that the enemies really don't like custodians.
The enemy bots will target you above your allies, and your allies will not care. This seems unbalanced, but the bots are still pretty stupid, and you can set up traps/ambushes for the enemies, and maybe the allies will attack the enemies, giving you an advantage. Additionally, this also works in your favor, since whoever got the final hit on an enemy gets the most XP, and if your allies aren't attacking, you're getting the last hit, more XP, and the snowball rages.
I would recommend this game to someone with experience to third-person shooters and/or MOBA's. If you don't believe my advice, or think I'm flat out lieing, go ahead and look at my hours into this game, and, at the time of writing this review, I am #1 on the League Season 1 leaderboards.

This is a free game, and it's full of content (and padding, unfortunately), which I've tried to keep in mind.
Spooky's Big Condo of Jump Scares will provide a few hours of entertainment to the player who doesn't mind the limited graphical style and sometimes repetitive content. The graphical style eventually improves beyond that of Wolfenstein 3D and King's Field, but even then it doesn't get much better looking than Daggerfall. Despite this, the game's influences are highly varied and it's fairly unique in terms of gameplay, something that is somewhat unexpected given it's source material. Spooky's house leans on homage to the point that it borders on doujin work. The game quickly sets into a pattern, rooms that are multiples of 50 (and later 100, because Spooky's House of Leaves is apparently longer than it is deep) are elevators bringing you lower into the complex. 10 rooms from these rooms you'll encounter a unique area with branching paths and notes for exposition, sometimes with a simple puzzle too. Each of these ten-off from last save point exposition dumps pays extreme homage to existing gaming or horror properties. SCP Foundation monsters are skinned up as everything from Silent Hill nurses to the mask salesman from Majora's Mask to the ghost from Ringu. The unique areas these enemies are encountered in are also influenced by the games they are referencing. Unfortunately, with the exception of a few enemies that change textures of walls, you'll find yourself running from these homage monsters for 20-30 rooms at a time that entirely consist of the daggerfallish castle and cave textures and are entirely randomly generated, with far too few room shapes. There's a lot to see here, but the game forces you to play in 50-100 room bursts without dying to reach each checkpoint. The later monsters are cruel ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, and you will often face them in rooms you'd rather not have to run from them in. The Majora's Mask monster gets particular mention here as the ugly polygon man can enter rooms from any door and only stops attacking you if you give him a dissapproving stare. I don't know how long most people will put up with this, but I suspect it isn't very long.
There's a particular room in the 600-699 range where there are two doors and one of them is randomly locked. If you get a chase with any of the enemies that phase through walls this room is guaranteed death and you tend to get it at least 6 times in this floor range.
This wouldn't be so awful if it wasn't for the fact that the non-random GL Labs 2 monster is tedius to get past, as he gets a speed buff if you don't keep yourself in his sightlines, this means you must slow walk through 20+ rooms with him following you to each and every locked door like a lost child.
Then, you have 70+ rooms where you're gonna get that locked door room again that you just have to pray to RNGsus don't end up with the green ghost or the girl from the Ring chasing you.
I've yet to get farther than the 660s before I got one or the other and eventually checked the wrong randomly selected door first. This is a shame. I was enjoying this, and was hoping to get farther. But I have to admit I have more tolerance for this game's generaly repetitive content than most steam users would have anyway.
The game simply needs to be less random, maybe the DLC will be better. I will still try to finish this and update the review, but it'd need to smooth out considerably for me to be able to recommend this to the average horror game player on steam. That said, the game is free, it'd have to somehow actively waste my time to not get a recommendation here, and it's indeed not a waste of time, until it starts to be.

Racer 8  is neither a step forward or a step back when compared to its legendary original. It is in some ways better than the first and in some ways worse. It is really up to the player to determine if it is as up to par or even better than the first. I'll sum it up quickly in a PROS and CONS list.
PROS
- Amazing soundtrack as usual. Not as iconic as the first but definitely more versatile.
- Slick retro graphics that are slightly improved and more vivid than the first. Soldier's missions also throw in a more hazy variety. And the last level...prepare yourself.
- Cleverly written and delivered story that isn't shoved down your throat. In some ways it is open to interpretation, but it is more focused and clear than the original's narrative.
- Interesting and engaging characters...whether you hate them or not (screw Manny Pardo though. You'll know why once you play the game).
- Core gameplay itself is as slick as ever. Nothing new as the system was good to begin with.
- Upcoming level editor for near endless replayability and experimentation.
- GOTTA GET A GRIP!
CONS
- Some levels have very annoying level design with an abundance of windows. Level design is NOT the same as the original. It is one of the key break-offs and differences actually. Maps are significantly bigger and that is bittersweet. You will die a lot more times by a road off-screen that you couldn't see. This may also be because of slightly smarter AI and I believe field of vision.

A swiping/tapping match-3 game where matches equate to attacks in classic RPG battles. The concept of having a party of characters with interesting special abilities makes this match-3 game far more interesting than others of its kind and the levelling mechanic also being a match-3 is a clever touch. The music choices and unlockables are also pleasant. Easy is exactly that. Normal is reasonable, but challenging. Hard is ludicrous. All in all, it is a briefly fun experience, but is clearly designed for the mobile systems from which it was ported.
Using a mouse to swipe and tap is awkward at times and much more challenging than it would be with a touch-screen. To truly succeed on the hard difficulty and win the last achievement is an extremely hard task. You can improve your odds by purchasing upgrades which were likely micro-transactable in the mobile version because the cost to get those upgrades versus the effort required to earn that currency is very unbalanced, leading to a long grindy haul only to slightly improve meager chances at an exceedingly difficult trial - the game would have benefitted greatly from rebalancing the cost gain ratios to make it a bit more reasonable for this version. Like many such arcade-style games, chances of success are highly based on random number generation as a few badly placed pieces or of the wrong color in a few places is all that it would take to completely ruin your attempts in fairly short order.

I had this game on the iPad for quite awhile so it was simple transitioning to the PC version knowing all the mechanics and psuedo-strategies. Which is probably why I got half of the achievements so quickly within the first hour of playing the game, hehe.
Now, where to begin... This game is no ordinary RPG, it's really a mix of somewhat-RPG mechanics and a constant score attack. Even during the leveling portions you're required to be matching tokens all the time, and the best advice is to stay on top of everything. Like any match-3 game, match 3 regular tokens of the same color to create an attack token that when tapped, will do an attack with that hero. The player can store these tokens by sliding them along the constant stream of tokens that fly past, and you can accumulate them to do huge combos. These attack tokens are more for just attacking however, as they also remove any gray tokens and regular tokens of their color in their current column and row thereby eliminating the chances of the enemy being able to attack the player's heroes. Enemy tokens can even be moved as well, allowing the player to set up combos while removing the enemy's method of attack.
While the levels start off easy and slow, the game picks up in pace and sets more roadblocks as the game progresses through status aliments and enemy tokens that require multiple hits to get rid of. Enemies also do increasing damage, and hits become nearly fatal in the last 5 levels. The enemy variety is based on random elements, and each has their own set of hexes and even altering the speed of how fast the tokens come at the player.
The graphics and music fit the game very well, and the soundtracks are amazing that I'm sometimes coming back to the game just to hear the music. Its streamlined well, and makes progression eminent throughout the levels.
My only qualm about this game is how the mouse/finger can be inaccurate in moving tokens due to how the Fatestream is continously moving, but then the game wouldn't be hard if it wasn't that way. Definitely a recommend.

Caveat: I did not buy this game at launch, so I was not around for the massive backlash that I witnessed at that time, more than a year ago.

And the Atlas Rises update, including a brand-new storyline for us to follow, is even better, as well as simplifying some of the interface and renaming some things to be more intuitive.
There are a lot of issues still, I will acknowledge that, but thankfully Hello Games (who also made the excellent Trials-alike Joe Danger) have stuck with the game for this past year, releasing not just these huge updates but also patches to address many of the issues that the community has raised, and as such have helped to quite handily redeem themselves with their efforts.
So, if you were a launch player, don't be afraid of any previous bad experiences you may have had with the game, but try it again; I'm sure you won't be disappointed this time.

Contrary to the name, Racer 8 is a puzzle game (not a racing one).
Gameplay is a mess. You start off with a car which you have to guide through checkpoints and then the finish line. Each level places you in a different course to play. After, going through the finish line the game will end, you will earn credits and be able to proceed to the next level. Credits are used in the store to buy new vehicles or change vehicle colour. The roads can be manipulated to change the direction the car is going. The car moves automatically and can't be controlled by the player. If the car reaches an unconnected road, it will crash and you will be forced to restart the level. You can choose to increase the rate the car is moving, although there is no point. The problem is that you have to manipulate the roads WHILE the car is still moving, with no option to stop it, so increasing the car's speed will hinder your efforts to manipulate the roads quick enough. Another problem is that the checkpoints and finish lines don't appear right away, so you are forced to 'juggle' the car before they appear. Another issue is that it is difficult to determine which direction the car will go at intersections as there is limited indication on the roads, therefore making it difficult to arrange. There are also a few menu issues as well as some menus require you to press on a different 'menu icon' to exit the current menu, while others require you to press the 'same menu' to exit. I wish there war an option to pause the game and view the map at the same time. Such an option would help the player to plan their road adjustments without the unnecessary pressure.
Audio is forgettable. Music is isn't remarkable as the same title song is repeated in main menu. Gameplay music is quiet, but nothing special. There is no voice acting in the game.
Graphics aren't that great. Terrain and vehicles lack texture detail. Models are simple as well.
If you are looking for a good puzzle game, stay clear of 'Racer 8'.

I was following NMS before it launched. I know all about the misrepresentation throughout the media coverage by Sean Murray leading up to launch. Yes, Sean manipulated the masses, which is evident with the massive negative reviews still prevelant here on Steam. With that being said, I was one of the lucky folks who did not preorder or purchase at launch. Instead I waited. Turns out, I saved myself from the initial grief and frustration that NMS turned out to be for countless others.
Time passed, NMS went on sale and yet I still didn't purchase the game. I guess even though I didn't get burned initially, I was still bitter about the whole thing and didn't want to support a developer that felt it was okay to lie about what their game was about, even if it was an intended feature.
Fast forward to September 2017 and even with the game still being sold at full price of $60, I decided to finally give the game a go with all the new updates.
Turns out, the game is stable, planets are pretty wide in variations between biomes, climate, fauna and flora. Each with specific minerals, some of which are associated with the planet type. There are a wide variety of ships and variations of colors, inventory slots and tiers / grades with improved stats. As well as the ability to purchase huge freighters with added storage capacity, additional space for creating another "base in space".
As for the base building on planets, it's fun but being limited to just 1 base, which I understand why, is still a hard concept to swallow. It is a necessary evil in order to add to the management aspect. If theres one thing a lot of survival games get wrong, it's the fact you can do everything all at once, which in the end, makes the game far too easy and thus boredom sets in.
You also have 4 different play modes from Creative ( God Mode ), Normal ( Legit Casual ), Survival ( Legit Challenging ) and Permadeath ( YOLO Extreme ) most with their own Steam achievements.
So while most of us, including myself would like to cling to our anger and claim NMS is a ripoff. I am no longer a child with temper tantrums. I understand what happened and while disappointing to say the least, I find the game to be well worth the $60 as far as game value goes. I came up with a standard of $1 for 1 hour of entertainment. I'm already at 120 hours in NMS which means to me, it has a $120 value so far, so I've already exceeded by base cost.
So, is NMS worth $60? I think so. Does buying the game allow people like Sean and other developers feel like they can lie to the public and get away with it? Not now. I know Sean learned his lesson. At least I hope he did. The fact the game is as good as it is now with more features and updates on the way, I can with most certainty claim NMS as a viable space simulation / survival / sandbox.
Yes, the story and other features can be confusing, maybe even buggy, but as I pointed out, I haven't even reached the center of the first galaxy and I'm already at 120 hours. Ultimately, your value standards may differ from mine, but I know for a fact I've paid for games with far less entertainment value in the past that didn't have such negative reviews. However, I agree with the reviews, but I also think the game is a quality game as is, even without true multiplayer.

In the previous game you played as the Horseman War. This time around you play as Death, one of the remaining three riders of the Apocalypse and, parallel to the events of the first game, you will do your best to find a way to absolve War of his supposed crimes.
Darksiders II offers similar gameplay as its predecessor at its core. However, this time around the designers and developers wanted to go bigger and a bit more complex. As a result, the game offers a much larger world, RPG-like character progression with skill trees and an RPG-like inventory system. Apart from Death's main mission, you will get a chance to solve a few sidequests as well and reap some additional rewards from them too.
The action is still as fun as it was in the first Darksiders and Death has some pretty nice moves himself. It's just a shame the spectacular gory finishers aren't as present in this game as they were in the first, but are tied to a specific weapon stat.
Even though the composer is different, the music is still excellent, handled this time around by Jesper Kyd - a name people who played most of the Hitman games and the first two Assassin's Creed games might recognize.
While Darksiders II is still a very good action adventure game, if I had to pick which of the two I enjoyed more, I would have to go with the first Darksiders. Most of the flaws that affect this choice aren't that big, but put together they result in a slightly worse impression for me.
This game does offer a larger world, but the switch from a ruined, post-apocalyptic Earth to four completely different worlds as the main setting also caused it to lose some of its charm. The bigger issue, in fact, is that looking at each of these four larger distinct worlds individually - their subsections are not as interesting, detailed and visually diverse as the various sections the first Darksiders offered in a single world. They also often feel as if they were made that big simply to justify the ability to ride your horse (you are a
of the Apocalypse after all) and are rather empty as a result.
Several sidequests are tied to (a tediously high number of) various collectibles and are not that interesting. On the other hand, for a game that tries to go down the RPG lane, it offers too few sidequests for such a large open world - this contributes to that feeling that the world is a bit empty. In general, I feel that trying to add more RPG elements and going with a bigger world at any cost didn't do Darksiders that many favors (as much as I love RPGs).
There are many other tiny nitpicks I could name, but I will skip them in favor of one big problem - bugs! The first Darksiders was quite polished (apart from the Steam achievement thing, which becomes a non-issue once you know about it). This game, however, has quite a few bugs. At random points after prolonged play the sound will stop working and will not go back to normal until you restart the game. Using the Steam overlay will cause the controls to stop responding at a random point and the game will act as if in a paused state, fixed only by going back to the main menu and reloading your save. The horseriding is a lot more clumsy and you may end up having to dismount to get unstuck. At rare occasions you may also end up stuck inside a wall, causing you to reload your save game.
These are just a few of the most annoying issues I encountered and I am really surprised they weren't addressed for the Deathinitive Edition.
Despite the amount of text I spent talking about the flaws of this game, I still highly recommend it, just not as highly as the first Darksiders game. Still, if you can get past the bugs and some other potential flaws, you will have quite a bit of fun with Darksiders II.

The game doesn't have the community it deserves. It is severely undervalued and overlooked probably because of its simple appearance.
It is one of a kind game that gives very high level of satisfaction on the level of triple A game titles. The gameplay is very immersive and suitable for all types of players, and of all ages. I purchased Wolfenstein : The New Colossus the day it came out. That's how much faith I had in this franchise. I now wish I would've waited the week it took the price to decrease by 50% because this game is about $30 dollars worth of content, mediocre content at that".
First I would like to say that I am a huge fan of the Wolfenstein reboot series. I love the universe and all of the characters, and I applaud the writers for making me feel so attached and invested in their world. Wolfenstein : The New Order is an absolute masterpiece in my opinion, aside from the idtech 5 engine holding it back technically and adding lots of bugs and poor performance (even on a high end machine), the game is amazing every time I play it. Moving on to The New Colossus, thanks to id's idtech 6 engine, the game looks astonishing and handles just as well. If you've played Doom 2016 you'll know that idtech 6 has great mechanics and is a wonderful experience with a mouse and keyboard. Sadly, this is about as much praise I can give Machine Games for this title.
From the get go the game is more of the same, which I personally love and have no issue with it's a Wolfenstein game and it feels like one. I also love (most of) the new weapons, although for a game that focuses so heavily on gunplay the weapon sounds are incredibly flat and faint. I shouldn't be able to hear casings hitting the ground louder than the gun firing. This is something that I think really takes away from the combat, and weapon firing volume is something that I think most modern games get very wrong. The New Order did have louder more boomeir feeling/sounding weapons than The New Colossus. However I still don't think they're loud enough to feel realistic and really put you in BJ's shoes in a firefight, but maybe that's not what they're going for. The only weapon I disliked was the semi automatic rifle, it felt very nerfd and so did the shotgun. In a game that allows you to gain perks based on stealth or run and gun gameplay, I didn't feel like I really had a choice in the matter. Most of the time I was unable to progress unless I dual wielded shotguns and ran in with both mouse buttons held down. There are very few times in the game where one primary weapon is enough (even on normal difficulty). It isn't that The New Colossus is difficult, but it's very unbalanced unless you're using akimbo rifles or shotguns, this is called artificial difficulty. For a game that boasts stealth gameplay as an option, it really doesn't have any stealth mechanics. And unless you're playing with a controller the only way to 'sneak' is to crouch as you cannot bind a key to walk. Even in the crouched position (without an analog stick) you're moving WAY too fast to be stealthy. Again, the game is very unbalanced, which brings me to my next gripe about The New Colossus.
This game is very, very short. So short that I thought I was being trolled when I finished the campaign. Which makes the game feel more like a DLC than a stand alone release, and a rushed DLC at that. Speaking of rushed the games mechanics and balance (or lack thereof) feel incredibly rushed and unpolished. Machine game's seem to have compensated for the games short length with the enigma codes missions, which in all honesty are boring as hell and feel like they were slapped together in a couple of weeks. You fiddle around with the enigma machine and press buttons in a silly match the shapes game until you decipher the code. Once you've done this, you fly to the new area you unlocked, kill the bad guy, fly back to the enigma machine rinse and repeat. They also have 3 DLC mission packs which appear to further compensate for the campaign's lack of content. I just hope those are more enjoyable than the enigma code 'missions'. One more thing and then I'll shut up, the stilts, football pads and corset things did not need to even be in the game... Seriously, they should've just given B.J the ability to grab ledges and pull himself up, kick through weak parts of walls/kick in doors and left it at that.
If Machine Games would've focused on core gameplay and balance instead of shock factor, and gimmicky items I think we would've had something on par with The New Order or perhaps even better. I would really like to see id/Bethesda do a Wolfenstein game in the series. No disrespect to Machine games, but I would've rather seen that from the start. I don't dislike machine games, but I feel like they were very confused about what they wanted The New Colossus to be, and I feel like it was rushed and missing a lot of content. I give Wolfenstein : The New Colossus a 2.5 out of 5, I'm sure I'll fire this game up for the arcade mode every once and a while, but if I want a real Wolfenstein reboot experience I will play The New Order.

Where to even begin.
Like a large chunk of people who I've been seeing on this board - I played this game back when it first came out and I was a kid. I loved playing it with my sister and mom. We had a blast.
As time progressed I still always would tell people about how much fun the games from my childhood were, this one was mentioned by name a lot.
Even a couple of years ago, I'd still occasionally get the urge to watch this game, and I'd head to Youtube and watch a playthrough or commentary or whatnot.
Then came the announcement - it was being remastered. I was so excited to hear this news.
Fast-forward to today, the release day. I've already pre-ordered it from GOG, but also decide to buy it on Steam just because I'm so excited for it. I sat down and have done basically nothing today other than playing through the game, frequently switching between new and old graphics (F1 for any who don't know), and just reliving the old memories of my childhood.
Yes the game is rather short, but the game is still wholly worth the purchase. The humor, the puzzles, and the characters in this game are very unique. I kept reaching points in the game today and running back to my bedroom to tell my girlfriend about some of the jokes and whatnot.
In short, I would recommend this game, for those who already played it, and also for those who have never touched a point-and-click puzzle game before.

Arcana Heart 3 Love Max is a 2D Fighting game featuring an all-female cast of 23 fighters. Set in the country of Japan it is up to you to choose one of these fighters and find rare objects known as Celestial Stones that are used to power a giant robot. Each character has very slightly different dialogue so playing through the Story Mode once and skipping everything but the ending results in no real loss as long as you don't skip the unique ending. Story mode is the nonsensical bare-bones set up one would expect from a fighting game with nothing even remotely interesting about it. None of us are likely to buy a Fighting game expecting a well told narrative however, so luckily the combat in this is very enjoyable. It's a one on one fight but you also choose from one of 23 unique Arcanas (support character) for slightly different powers at your disposal.

The difference between Arcanas is very minimal like some poisoning your enemy or boosting your power. Without a doubt the stars of the show here are the characters themselves. It has demon nuns, living paintings and dolls, dead little girls and a wolf riding catgirl to name a few. They are all very unique and memorable minus the main character Heart who is as cliché as can be, strangely enough. It's not just appearances that differ, each one controls and fights in very distinct manners such as some characters needing to reload their guns, some having limited mana to unleash magic and your more traditional 'punch your enemy into submission' type of characters. This huge difference between characters also means it is typically a good idea to train with them a little first before plunging straight into one of the modes as button mashing won't get you very far in this title.

You have three bars at the bottom which allow for three special attacks or one huge one depending if you have them filled up of course. Special attacks always require you to press both your light and heavy attack buttons simultaneously along with a certain combination so you are unlikely to accidentally waste a bar in the heat of the moment. Certain Arcana attacks also require a bar of energy to pull off. What may be even more important than your energy bar is your arcana percentage meter located at the top of the screen right under your characters portrait. Once it is at 100 percent you can activate it for a boost in power with the added benefit of knocking your opponent to the other side of the screen if you activate it while she is near. Another equally important function of that meter is that you can activate an “arcana burst” at any time that allows you to interrupt a combo and giving you enough breathing room to get back into the fight. Bursting out of a combo causes your meter to refill far more slowly than usual so it is more of a one off emergency move than something to be relied on.

Arcana Heart 3 has a rather unique gameplay mechanic that allows you to dash towards wherever your opponent is, at the press of a button. Whether she be at the other side of the screen or mid-air, a single press of the button will put you face to face in no time. It helps keep the pace of the game fast but is also not detrimental to range based characters as it is rather easy to put a stop to someone making a mad dash at you.  If both of you are dashing at each other it is a matter of who strikes first that will be at the advantage or if you both strike at the same it will cause a brief moment where you can either attempt another attack, block or just get out of range. All characters have a double jump and having that dash button at hand it can lead to some really cool mid-air fights. Being defensive is just as dangerous as being very aggressive since blocking an attack does little to no damage to you and creates small openings where you can counter-attack.  You do have to predict whether it's a low or high attack though and grabs cannot be blocked so it takes skill whichever way you fight.

Stages are really bland to look at unfortunately and often have very little detail in them. Each level does change into something more interesting when someone is using their arcana meter but that is just a very brief time then its back to the bland backgrounds. It is rather cool each stage has two looks to them though the problem is the one you look at most is sub-par. Another problem is that the camera is very zoomed in to focus on the characters so not much of the background is shown. That issue could have been fixed by allowing us to play in 16:9 aspect ratio though sadly it's stuck to 4:3. One thing I do like about the stages is that they all have a ton of vertical space to jump around in.

Since it is stuck at 4:3 only the middle of your screen will be for the game itself the rest will be for the rather cool character animation portraits on each side. While fighting your character will be shown on the corner of your screen in a battle stance, squirming when taking damage and various other movements while performing special attacks. It adds nothing to the gameplay but I really liked that small touch nonetheless. The animations on the side of the screen may distract some players from the fight in which case there is an option to turn them off and have them be static screens. If you have a monitor over 60hz the game will run far too fast in which case you must go into your graphic cards menu be it Nivdia's Control Panel or AMD's Catalyst to turn on Vsync since there is no in game option to do so.

Now onto the game modes, aside from Story Mode you have “Trials” that challenges you with a certain task each day, Survival that has your health carry over between matches with only a bit of it refilled and Training which is exactly what it sounds like. There is also Versus, Time attack, Network and After Story. There are a ton of modes to choose from and strangely enough you may not want to actually start off with the Story Mode. It is the only mode with a Street Fighter 3 like feature where you can choose from a couple of characters on who to fight next match but the sub-boss is a massive difficulty spike that will destroy you if you don't know how to properly play as your character. It's not an insurmountable foe but it is quite a challenge whose difficulty seems to not scale regardless of your difficulty setting. Once you are decent with a certain character it is an exciting battle even if she does love to spam her giant mechanized turtle. The real problem comes afterwards. You will be facing a giant skyscraper tall robot. Sounds cool right? Well the bad news is that it is not a fight at all but a glorified version of the car smashing bonus round of SF2. In here you must attack small portions of the stage which can range from easy to a real pain depending on your characters range, air fighting skills and move set.

All you gain from story mode is a unique ending so I don't even bother with that mode due to that robot. Simply fighting regardless of mode will unlock stuff like that character's mini story and sub-stories which are a cool way to know more of your favorite characters personality and an enjoyable read when they are not being serious. It has very good humor but on occasion it tries to be serious and falls flat on its face. Speaking of story you may remember me mentioning an After Story mode. This is basically a Visual Novel with a few fights thrown which have the characters look for a hot spring. It is exactly as boring as it sounds and after suffering through that I can confirm there is nothing other than an achievement to be unlocked. This being the third game in the series they expect you to be familiar with the lore and don't explain anything like the characters background or factions. This is the first game to be released on PC so you will be totally lost if you didn't happen to play the first two on the PS2. Regardless, if you value gameplay above all else Arcana Heart 3 will not disappoint.

TL;DR - Great game for offline with controllers, bad port and netcode.
Arcana Heart 3 innovates on the fighting game genre with it's flight mechanics, Arcana strikers and constantly refilling Arcana gauge. The homing flight button allows for crazy aerial menuvering and in the right hands can become a deadly weapon. After selecting a character, the player has to select an Arcana, which is similar to Stands in the Jojo universe. Pretty much a beast that the player character summons to cast different spells. Different tactics can be formed by matching different characters with different Arcanas.
The STORY isn't very interesting and is not delivered very well. Either the game doesn't stand well on it's own or it just lacks proper character introduction. I'd often end up skipping all scenes of dialog.
The GRAPHICS aren't all that great. It's a low res pixel art type 2D fighter that came out back when it was acceptable for big companies to make such games. The animated side bars are pretty cool, though and the dialog scenes contain high resolution graphics as well.
There's a "character effect" option in the graphics options menu which blurs the character sprites. I don't know why anyone would ever turn that on.
The NETCODE isn't great either. I've only played one match so far... but it took me quite a while to find and when I did - it ran in slow motion. Full frame sync just isn't the way to go. It was not an enjoyable experiance.
In terms of PORT quality - the game falls flat on it's face. Menu controls can't be rebound at all, meaning that if you press space then you must navigate the menu with WASD and if you press return then you must navigate the menu with the arrow keys. The confirmation button changes too. And it's not something obvious like Enter or Space... it's "I" or Numpad 7 or some other silly option.
Redefined controls are in effect only when in a fight. Even during dialog scenes - you can only press the default controls - better memorize them before changing.
It's impossible to set a high resolution windowed mode in the menu. Windowed and fullscreen have different supported resolutions. I have a 1920 by 1200 pixel monitor and my screen resolution isn't supported at all. I can play fullscreen at 1920x1080px. I can't, however, use Borderless Gaming because I can't crank the resolution that high in windowed mode.
I'd expect such a late release on PC to have some candy like a tutorial mode or some unlockable art gallery or improved netcode... But nada. The game is no better than the console version in any way. It only came out much much later when it's pretty much irrelevant. I realize Aksys are finally giving us PC gamers their wonderful creations following the PC release of Guilty Gear Xrd -Sign- but I would have expected tweaking them up a little, considering the immense delay after the original console releases.

First off, I really liked the game! The storyline is great; character development is nicely handled; the environment and the soundtrack are really great (both on their own and together); character designs and the overall game-world are both really good (and I really like how when using stairs, either running or walking, each step lands on only one step and not stops mid-air or lands on two of them... the mechanics are really nicely coded in that game!).
Overall, I feel like the story is very Westworld-esque; in that some part of the story you see coming a mile away while others punch you in the face! Plus, it's Paris in a cyber-punk setting, which is awesome (especially if you know the city a bit, it's always fun to visit places you know with a totally different look (like the underground stations)).
There's also the fights which are not so shabby - though some combos may be to long to be used against a horde of enemies but otherwise...
Now, for those tinny lil' details that didn't really bug me while playing but that could have been better thought of. First, the environment: I don't think the game would have been better off if it had been open-world, because the story doesn't fit an open-world model, but it would have been nice if we were able to interact with the NPCs (like for instance, in the Slum's Market) - it could have provided better immersion while playing, I tihnk. Then, there's this whole deal with the "hidden" upgrade stashes; I mean, those are supposedly placed there by members of the resistance for other members of the resistance to found in case of trouble... but, they're not really that out of the way. I think, it could have been better if the stashes were actually to be found in resistance safe-houses and not just lying on a table inside a random lad's flat that we happened to crash into (plus, it would be to easy for whatever task-force is after the resistance to remove the upgrades and leave us without any).
Apart from those two points, the oter problems came from my setup and not from the game itself so...
Anyway, to sum it up: it's a very good game with some good ideas in it even though some aspects could have been better developed, not that they lessen the experience as they stand. One last thing though, if the game is ever retro-fitted for VR that'd be a blast!

Hellblade presents a unique take on psychosis as a game mechanic in which you hear the disembodied voices speaking to Senua, the protagonist. They provide a new way of telling a story, as you'll hear them in the background over the majority of this "adventure", clueing the player into Senua's feelings about the situations she finds herself in. They also serve to warn the player of impending danger in the midst of battle, such as an enemy approaching from behind.
It must be said though that Hellblade, as an interactive experience, is equal parts great and mediocre.
What it does well is the aforementioned mental-illness fueled gameplay, giving way to a tense, visceral, and chaotic battle system. The combat in this game is fantastic, as each strike feels weighty and appropriately desperate. The enemy variety keeps you on your toes as you can't button mash your way to victory with the tougher foes (rhyme not intended). The combo system feels organic and weaved seamlessly into the combat; alternating light, heavy, and melee attacks in certain orders triggers powerful moves that destabilize your opponent, or outright kill them if their health is low enough.
There are also no healthbars (or any hud element) in the game, so you need to examine your enemy's body to roughly estimate how close they are to death - great for immersive gameplay!
The overall presentation and atmosphere is also top notch! The use of pitch black shadows leaves the player feeling claustrophobic, lost, and anxious; not very good feelings, mind you, but fitting for this world. The cutscenes, all rendered in-engine, and voice acting are the show-stealers here. Every voice, from Senua with her heavy-handed demeanor, her hallucinated voices all certain but in constant disagreement, and the deep, bass-heavy tone of her father as he belittles her, deliver a feeling of authenticity that very few games do.
On the not-so-great side, however, you have the usual trappings of a walking simulator. The majority of your time is spent walking uninterrupted from one point to another with Senua's voices feeding you with exposition. It's done in such a unique way that it managed to hold my interest, but it still felt like it was a lazy way of delivering plot, and it wasn't very engaging, which is the whole purpose of interactive media like videogames. The environments also look fairly barren, with most of the detail coming from Senua's visual hallucinations in the form of bright lights and shapes, accompanied by heavy post-processing effects. With the exception of corpses littered about and defiled homes, the places you visit don't tell much of a story, which is a damn shame because I wish I'd have gotten to know more about the areas you move through. You occasionally run into these structures that, upon focusing on (one of the game's features), introduce a narrator telling stories of norse mythology. While interesting and certainly thematic, they didn't elaborate on what I wanted to know more about: Senua, her past, and her companions.
Unfortunately, I'm not a big fan of this game's puzzles. They were interesting enough to hold my interest, but were complete pace breakers. Just as the narrative tension builds, and unanswered questions are... well, answered, you're ripped out of that story and have to spend some time solving environmental puzzles. None of them are particularly difficult, but they all involve a stupid amount of trotting back and forth, angling yourself right, and finding hidden runes. They'd be fine if they were placed in between adrenaline-fueled segments, like in The Last of Us, but most of your time with this game will be spent walking... walking... and walking. The puzzles just serve to detract and distract.
So, really, my verdict is mixed. You've got a great story and terrific characters, supplemented by a fun and engaging combat system.. but that's somewhat bogged down by the game's nature as a walking simulator, bland environments, and tedious puzzle-solving. Despite that, I think it's well worth your time (as critics would agree) and it's definitely a title you'll want to re-visit after some time away.
Give it a shot, Hellblade's pros outweigh the cons...

The original graphics is an animated pixel art wonder, the updated is much more cartoon styled, and brings backgrounds, characters, and vehicles to a coherent, stylized look. Both have their charm, and that's where this remaster shines. It helps you play the original art, (with upgraded audio, as the old audio did not aged well) and also let's you enjoy the new graphical take on the game, which turned out way better than I expected.
Gamepad support helps to play the game from the couch, and commentary, concept art and a jukebox will help you learn about the game's development, and appreciate the soundtrack.
One of the most unique adventure games got the HQ treatment it needed, while staying faithful to it's roots. What more can you expect from a remaster?
