Running With Rifles is a top-down, tactical shooter developed by Modulatio Games. In RWR you play as a soldier for one of the game’s three factions: Greenbelts (America), Brownpants (Russia) and the Greycollars (Germany). Most of the game’s maps see all three factions fighting each other though some of the small maps are just one on one battles.
The game’s cartoon-esque graphics are fantastic and fit really well with the game itself. They give the game the feeling that you’re playing with little toys in a sandbox. The UI is minimal, it’s big enough for you to see it and there’s all the information you need but it stays out of your way so that you can see everything on screen and effectively aim at enemies. What you see on screen also isn’t the limit of your view, if you stand still and aim off screen your view will move out slightly so you can see further (though your soldier probably won’t be on screen).
What makes RWR so special is the fact that you play as a regular soldier. Sure, once you’ve ranked up you become a little more important, you’ll even have your own squad, but you die a lot and when you die you become a new soldier (though you keep your XP). You’re going to die a lot. Even if you’re really good at the game there’ll be time where there’s a sniper on a roof you didn’t see or a tank that somehow managed to creep up on you. Dying without the ability to put up a fight in this game can be frustrating but it’s made up for by the awesome, intense firefights or the moments where you’re behind enemy lines, picking them off one by one without them figuring out where you are.
Weapons, vehicles and other equipment, while not the main focus of the game, have enough variation to remain interesting. Each faction has their own weapons and while you can unlock the weapons of the other factions by selling the weapon you want five times (enemy soldiers drop their weapons and equipment when they die) you’re going to spend most of your time using your own faction’s weapons, bought with RP (Resource Points) providing you’re a high enough rank for certain equipment. As you’d expect the factions have an assault rifle, sniper rifle, LMG etc. as well as silenced pistols and small submachine guns. Equipment ranges from frag grenades to ghillie suits as well as less exciting things such as deployable cover. Other than some small boats for specific maps, the vehicles in RWR are land vehicles. These range from common jeeps to armoured transport vehicles and tanks as well as a few others. What vehicles you’ll find (and what quantity you’ll find them in) depends on the size and location of the map. For example a small island map will have far less tanks than a large landlocked map will have.
Weapons and equipment aren’t the only thing to spend your faction’s resource points on. Above a certain rank you’ll be given a radio to use and, again depending on your rank, you’ll be able to make certain requests. Low ranking soldiers can call in small airstrikes and paratroopers while those who are higher ranking can call in more advanced support units such as tank units. While I didn’t find support units overly helpful (paratroopers are usually killed while they parachute in if there are any enemies around) I did find the airstrikes particularly useful for situations where I was pinned down by enemy forces who were a safe distance away.
Going back to basics, the game has a campaign mode as well as a quick match mode, both of which are available for multiplayer. For singleplayer, both modes allow you to fully customise the difficulty as well as choose what rank you start at, something that’s particularly good if you want to play a campaign as another faction but don’t want to start with the most basic equipment again. The campaign sees you fight on several different maps (some of which only feature one enemy faction depending on the map’s size) and once you take complete control of a map you’ll have to move on to another one by driving to an extraction point that will take you to the next location. The one thing that bothered me about this portion of the game is that, at least from the Greenbelt campaign (I haven’t played the others yet), the maps split off and some maps are only connected to one other map. What this means is that you have to backtrack through a map you already control which gets rather tedious, especially if you accidentally extract to the wrong zone. It’s not a huge issue but it certainly bothered me.
Lastly, I’ll briefly talk about controls/gunplay. There’s not much that’s noteworthy about controls since they’re very good but there is one part of the game’s controls/gunplay which manages to be a great feature and a not so great feature at the same time. You see, in RWR you have two reticles. One large one which is shows where you’re pointing with your mouse and one tiny one which shows where your bullet will actually go when you fire. The reason you have the second one is because the maps aren’t flat and there’s also lots of cover so you need to know if you’re actually going to hit. In theory, having both reticles is fantastic. The problem with this is, the second reticle is so small (it’s also a very faint white) that it’s rather difficult to see and I died a fair few times because I was straining to see the little reticle and an enemy came up and took advantage of my distraction.
Running with Rifles is a truly awesome tactical shooter that's great for singleplayer and multiplayer despite its minor issues. Whether you’re looking for quick skirmishes or long battles, RWR has a hell of a lot to offer players.

This one is hard.
The game has so much potential. And doesnt use almost any of it.
1. Gameplay
You can choose between different classes, Samurai, Knight, Magician, Archer and maybe some more, i didnt look through every class. I chose the Warrior.
Fighting is simple, click the left mouse button and you shoot your arrow. But you can only shoot right or left. That does feel very bad. Its just clunky and sometimes annoying. The rest is pretty good, you can dodge attacks, move acceptable fast enough.
2. Graphics
The graphics is in a sort of Pixel Art, and it looks really good. I've seen too much games with Pixel Art and trying to be Retro and look like garbage. This game looks good. And it runs almost constantly smooth with 60 fps. I had some Framedrops here and then, but that could be my fault, because I often ALT+Tabed out.
3. Story
I did not get much story, basically because i skip textboxes (i hate those most of the time), so i just now that there are demon thingies and the villagers and soldiers have tough time to defend themselves and you as a warrior is welcome to help them out. Pretty basic i would say, but not a bad thing. It is good enough to get you some motivation.
4. Quests
The Quests are quite poor. Take this to this place. Kill 3 of those. Kill 30 of those. Collect this. And that was it. At least this is how far I can tell, the reason I`ll explain at the end.
5. Items/Crafting
It is annoying. In order to get the first Item for boosting health and attack you need 20 wood, some iron ingots and green slimy stuff I think and gold. Or dollar, the game can't decide what it calls the currency. And the symbol for gold coins isn't helping either. So yeah, you are collecting wood and stuff to get the first item done. And then you see, if you want to craft the 2nd Item you need 3 of the first plus extra 25 wood and Iron and Dollars. And to craft the 3rd Item you need the 2nd 3 times, which meens 9 times the first one PLUS 3 Times Wood and Stuff PLUS other Stuff. And then there is a 4th Item... You get the Idea. I only made it to 2 times the 3rd Item. Alone the collecting of wood is a mess. Only Wooden fences and Wagons give you randomly wood. Why is there even a forest around you??
Then there is a "build" feature which I didnt use yet, because I dont know if it will be useful for me at this time. Basically you can build houses, Mines and bunkers. I built a house and it was destroyed immediately by suddenly upcoming Centaurs...
6. Enemies
The standard mob is a orc-zombie-like thingie. Dumb, not strong, close-combatant. Pretty easy to kill even in the beginning. Then there is an archer, sometimes annoying that he can hit you when you clearly can't (his arrow flies a little bit more up or down than yours). After that there are some types of strong enemies, like a giant swordsman, a giant taurus with an axe, some crabs, Centaurs and Ghost-like Siren women who can teleport. They have different patterns of attacking, so this is pretty good. But also annoying when you have the quest to kill them and you dont stand them any chance because you are too low-leveled. Its hardly balanced.
The biggest flaw of the game, despite of several bugs and the annoying grinding for wood (I have soooo much of the other items), is that you have the map and you see the world and you cannot visit half of the map. There is a huge barrier, like some sort of magic, like in gothic or whatever. And you can't pass it. I dont know how to get this away. I did all the quests I could found (visited every location at least twice) and I cannot play any further. Along with the grinding I dont have any motivation left.
This game still feels like Early Access and it is definetly not finished. So I will not recommend it. Not even for the ridiciously low price I paid. (The game was in a bundle)
It is not really bad (especially for the price i got it in a bundle) but sometimes feels like an Early Access title that needs quite some polishing.

Do you dream of rolling out of bed at eleven at night to join the world of illegal street racing in Los Angeles while betting against competitors and having more than a dozen generic girlfriends to start each race? Street Racing Syndicate has all the fun of a solid, easy to play street racing game with a lot of open world frills to keep it interesting. Its a deep game full of customization, unlockables and still everything feels like an earned reward from winning a bet to unlocking cars, girlfriends and videos of them.
You have an open world Los Angeles at night. A big broad area that strays from details like side streets and allies. There is plenty to do here and I'll start with some of the side missions before I go into detail about everything else. You can find street challenges from cars that just sit waiting for you to offer cash in an open circuit challenge one-on-one. On the road there are other vehicles looking for a race. Get up behind them, flash your high beams and its on. Outside of racing there is a garage, a dealership, the warehouse where all of the women are stored and even three cruises that let you soak up the city as your car drives for you. Its a good use of the game's city.
For anyone that wants to get to the event rather than drive to it, the game lets you have that option with the map. The sad thing is nothing is on your mini map. You need to hop in the big map and select your next location in a menu and whether you want to jump to it or drive.
Since this is an open world, there are cops here and there. Police never interfere with races, but when you're outside a race and you speed by, they'll chase you. These chases have a meter how close you are to escaping or being busted and I say this meter and the game itself is glitched here. I've been in front of police cars and hear over the radio that they can't find me. Other times I've been busted with the cops far behind me. Its a toss up whether this is bad or good, but just take it easy around police. The game will warn you when they're in the area.
The bulk of the game is in crew meets where you race in a series of three different races on three tiers. Each race and tier takes place in the same area, so it modifies the course a bit each time. It makes for thirty-two races in four areas from the start. Before each race of the series, you can select to place a side bet with one of the three competitors. If you beat them, you get the money and if you lose, then it costs you.
A nice touch is being able to see the stats of the vehicles you can bet against. I say just bet the one offering the most money. As they win or lose through betting, their cash will increase or decrease, so it turns into an issue of beating the same person means others will have more money by the final race. Its incentive to bet against others.
To unlock the next tier, you need cars with a minimum horsepower and you need enough respect. This respect is earned by winning races and you can get some bonus respect here and there for slides, near misses, overtaking competition and some air off of a bump. If you knock into anything before your respect is calculated you lose it, but its no big loss since winning races gives far more respect.
Women and racing have always gone together, but wow does Street Racing Syndicate plaster them all over the game, its menus and on its streets. It makes the game different in a laughable, offensive or great way depending on your perspective. The women offer a variety of challenges. Everything from checkpoint rallies and big air competition to chasing them in their own street rides. Once they become your girlfriend they then hang out at the warehouse. Your own harem of women that you select one to roll with who will drop the go signal at each race. For those out there into videos there are provocative videos of the real women these girlfriends are based after. Someone had to chose to put these videos into the game. It goes a step beyond and an extra frill to keep you in game.
Street Racing Syndicate blurs the line for me between an easy to play arcade game and more of a realistic game. Your car takes damage and after enough damage your car starts to drag a little. You can either instantly repair it at any event or you can take a drive to the only garage in the city. These repairs cost money, so try to stay away from obstacles.
Nitrous is a luxury instead of a given, because you need to buy it at the garage. Using the nitro boost is still a challenge, you need to hold it down to see any significant momentum, because when you use it, your opponents will too. Its easy to just forget about it until the top tier races at the crew meets.
On the mid tier races, your competitors are like jackals that hang around you, waiting for the proper moment to overtake you either with a mistake or a wide straightaway. This pushes the pace and depends you to avoid making major mistakes. The intelligence of the others feels top notch. They can avoid my reckless driving and compensate for a lot of different factors. Its very subtle and you need to go to great lengths to reveal it.
I need to speak up about one crew meet that drives on an abandon racetrack at dusk where the sun is right in your eyes. The flare is giant and as a human I have a difficult time seeing through it. To the game's credit, there's nothing to bump into as you stare at the sun, but you can miss a hairpin turn and slam into a wall. Another thing that the game loves to do is put civilian vehicles in front of you going into turns. I've lost the final few seconds of mid tier races thanks to a well timed taxi.
The customization goes to the furthest depths of the deep end. You can get lost looking at all of the ways to customize the look of your car. Spoilers, stickers, paint jobs, body kits, electronics, lights and so on. That's just the look though, you can upgrade each of your fifty unlockable cars with engines, mufflers, exhaust, and everything else that I will never fully understand. All I know is that each thing costs money and tweaks the stats ever so slight.y
With all of these upgrades and even purchasing vehicles, the worst part is the navigation to do so. You look at manufacturers and then you look at the parts. Switching between parts creates a load image so you need to remember which part had what stats. I wish there was just an easy way to see what I needed or even to compare them.
On the plus side there are a lot of real world vehicles and companies. So many get stuffed into this game that it almost feels like an advertisement complete with billboards.
Outside of the real game is an arcade with a few different modes and races. These are one off events that take place in Miami, Los Angeles and Philadelphia. I'm happy to have Miami, because its the only city that yous race in the daytime. It makes the city feel far different than the other two and lets you see its beauty rather than darkness. You can unlock plenty of new vehicles in the arcade. I'd love to unlock new cities, but with four hours in, I've seen no hint of such a thing.
The game allows for controllers and controls easy with them, but the menus are still listed as keys so you need to remember what you have them set as.
Street Racing Syndicate is a fun, engaging, immersive and well comical game with its overuse of certain things. Well worth the cheap asking price.

Finished the game on Easy, because I can't be arsed to finish an action RPG on any other difficulty.
Pros:
- Combat is fun. Combos are very fluid, the variety of weapons is fantastic, and enemy types are varied enough and mostly fun to fight (although you can breeze through most of the game with Exhume, like seriously, you can neutralize most of the game's difficulty with a fully boosted Exhume, but granted I was playing on Easy). I think The Lich stands out as a really well-designed enemy - it summons numerous but weak undead mooks to fight you, nothing special for a necromancer enemy. Of course you logically jump to the conclusion that killing the necromancer will dispel the mooks, right? Well, you're correct! The solution for that is the Deathgrip, your trusty tractor beam, which should pull The Lich for a blade dance, except it smartly counters such a strategy, where every time you Deathgrip the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, he will groundpound with his totem, dealing significant damage and knocking you backwards several meters, making the Deathgrip a very risky tool to close the gap. That's pretty genius, I'd say.
- Art direction. This game is ♥♥♥♥ing well-designed. Enemies look amazing, Death looks amazing, NPCs look amazing, the equipment looks amazing, and the world is stunning. The scale of the first two main boss battles are jaw-droppingly impressive, and the levels are well-designed. Everything looks beautiful, and I /love/ good visuals!
- Sound. The music is great, and the voice acting is stellar. Listening to Drenchfort's music really imprinted wonder and scale, for instance, while the soundtrack for the Kingdom of the Dead is haunting and desolate.
- Puzzle difficulty. The Soul Splitter puzzles greatly magnified the difficulty of the game, at least for me. I like the puzzle breaks in between the mindless Exhuming and claw-wailing.
- Character vanity. God, I love character vanity. Death looking different with each piece of equipment is a fantastic selling point.
- Replayability. There's just so much you can do in this game, although I'd have to say some of it is painfully tedious, like the Mystic Stonebite quest.
Cons:
- PORT ISSUES. Game is a ♥♥♥♥ing mess on PC (no controller). The radial menu is a pain to navigate, the map is super unwieldy (I can't overstate this, it's so annoying to Fast Travel around), and God knows what's happening with the control scheme. Assigning hotkeys for skills require you to go to the key bindings menu. The CapsLock menu is bugged. And while I love good visuals, the lack of advanced graphics configuration = can't turn off dynamic shadows = ♥♥♥♥♥♥ framerate.
- Camera issues. Lots of issues with the camera, particularly elevators. In combat it gets pretty ♥♥♥♥ed occasionally; even just fighting 3 enemies at the same time will give you visual troubles (if you're locked on). Feels like the field of view in combat is too narrow, making it harder to manage multiple enemies.
- Story. You keep getting bossed around the entire game, so it feels like everything's a fetch quest. I don't get the ending at all. Plot in the Shadow's Edge opened a lot of questions and left nearly all unanswered. Basically an unfulfilling end to an interesting start.
Overall, it's a fun, beautiful game full of good platforming puzzles and adventure elements. The terrible state of the port ruins some of the fun, and the quest structure makes the story a little duller than it should be. I'd be sold on the art and sound direction on their own, but the substantial action alone makes it a worthwhile pick-up for anyone remotely interested in an action RPG.

A very interesting game… It’s gameplay mechanics are kind of like Mirror’s Edge, but 3rd person. I did enjoy Mirror’s Edge more than this game, but that doesn’t mean this game is bad. It certainly has a better story than Mirror’s Edge. And I did enjoy it. The parkour was a bit meh, but I enjoyed the fist fighting. However I do want to address the problems I did have with the game.
The first problem is whenever you start the game you get a loud, unskippable Nvidia ad that annoyed me to no end everytime I started the game and had to hear it blast through my headset. There are no skippable cutscenes in this game. I assume they weren’t added because this game is more story focused, but when the game does crash, and I will list those in a second, I don’t want to listen to an annoyingly loud Nvidia ad than re-watch a cutscene to get back to where I was. Glitches I encountered were a cutscene where the audio bugged out and it sounded like it was being said in a tin can, a glitch where the screen was stuck with a red tint and restarting from a checkpoint to try to fix it crashed the game, and a glitch where I was remixing a memory and mid way through the game crashed. Character leveling feels a bit… lacking in this game. The parkour seems very liniar, even more so than Mirror’s Edge. And lastly the upgrades you need to collect to upgrade your health and special are very easy to find and I feel they should have just added them to the leveling system.
Overall I liked the game. I can see why some people may not like it. And looking back at it, I noticed I played with the DLC… I’m not sure what the game is like without the dlc and customization to your moves, but it sounds like it would be even more bare bones. This game isn’t for everyone and I would say go play Mirror’s Edge and come back to this if you enjoyed that game.

Remember Me (re)mixes Matrix, Portal and Blade Runner in a polished cinematic experience with a top-notch art direction and a coherent, immersive cyberpunk narative. Combat and action/puzzle/platforming phases are weaker than the rest of the game and could have done with more fleshing out, but remain smooth enough to keep the player going to the end of an engrossing story.
Heavily recommended for players enjoying cinematic games.
Mileage may vary with players favoring action over narration.
+ Fantastic art direction
+ Voice acting par for the course
+ Immersive
+ Impeccable narration
+ Overall smooth experience
= Somewhat under exploited mechanics
- Disparity between platforming and combat difficulty
- No replay value (only one storyline)
------------
Full Review
------------
Remember Me is an action/platform game set-up in a dystopian future where memories have become an addictive commodity. You play as Nilin, a memory hunter who can break into the head of anyone and remix its content to make them remember whatever is necessary to achieve your goals.
Nilin is also somewhat of a Dastan (Prince Of Persia) and has a knack for bashing opponents after a little parkour without shedding much of a sweat.
She will use her skills for light action/puzzle platforming, combat, and memory remixing. The latter is most innovative: Nilin navigates key NPC memories, rewinds at will, and introduces little changes which will greatly alter the whole picture, as well as the NPC's behavior.
These phases are weaved together through a solid narrative, which is the most impactful aspect of the game. Regardless of the plot, DONTNOD has managed to semlessly merge disparate environments into a credible, immersive universe with flawless visuals, scoring, and good voice acting for a cross-breed of Matrix, Portal and Blade Runner in a true cyberpunk style.
The end result is a coherent and engrossing story which players might end up consumming like a good book (I did finish the game a single, continuous run).
That said, Remember Me isn't flawless. While the memory remixes are polished and well thought out, they don't happen often enough and leave us begging for more. There is also a real disparity in difficulty between visually attractive but effortless platforming/action phases, and combat sequences which can at times feel jittery and dragged-out. The combat system with editable combos is indeed interesting, but it feels like it would have benefited from some fine tuning before release.
The linearity of the story, making it impossible to really make any choice and granting the title almost no replay value, might also deter some players looking for a longer time investment, especially since the game is already pretty short (7 to 9 hours without looking for all achievements).
While it's regretable that the game didn't go full Prince of Persia, with better fleshed-out platforming and shorter, more intense combat, the experience remains smooth enough to avoid breaking immersion and will only become a problem for players seeking a full fledged action title.
As for the linear aspect, it all boils down to taste. I personally feel that the effort gone into production more than justifies the relatively short length of the game.
Ultimately, Remember Me Delivers a polished cinematic narrative supported by a top-notch art direction and, while not perfect, is well worth the full price and a steal on sales.
Heavily recommended.

Mental illness is not discussed in many mediums, especially video games. There are not many games with a female protagonist, and even less where she is not sexed up or romanticized. Hellblade is the story of Senua, a Celtic female warrior fully clothed in era appropriate armor and warpaint, and she has Psychosis.
Senua is a Celtic barbarian whose lover is killed by the "Northmen" (Vikings). She makes it her quest to travel into Helheim to recover his soul. But from the onset of the game, it is clear her suffering is not only the trials ahead of her. She suffers from a severe form of Psychosis, experienced by 3D Binaural sound of voices surrounding the player throughout the majority of the game. They warn you, laugh at you, mutter foreshadowing, berate, scream at, and constantly tempt Senua to turn back. Senua's mental illness is referred to in many ways, mainly as "The Darkness".
This game has had a massive impression on me. It deals with mental illness, abuse, suicide, and loss. This game deals with so many tangible, painful, and real things in an emotional, testing, gritty way. I've never cried because of a video game. But this story told so painfully, cinematically, and realistically portrayed changed that.
This game is definitely not for everyone; it is violent, has horror elements, and is frightening. But I believe everyone in our culture benefits from more discussion and awareness about mental illness, and games as a medium provide a powerful way to create that discussion.

With the proper input method, Dungeon Hearts might not be a bad experience. The game is played by matching three like-colored objects to build attacks that are used against a random selection of monsters. Sliding objects around the playing field is cumbersome and often unresponsive with mouse controls. I can’t play more than a few rounds before my wrist starts begging for relief. Chaining together attacks is especially difficult. I was constantly scrambling to clear out poison blocks with no time to consider any sort of strategy. It is rather rewarding to pull off a massive combo, but all of mine were complete accidents. The RPG elements in Dungeon Hearts are all fluff. I like the idea of incorporating an upgrade system into this type of puzzle game, but it wasn’t implemented in a very effective or interesting manner. You gain experience points by playing a mini game between battles, and your characters automatically level up to be stronger and have more special moves. I would have felt like I had greater influence over the game if there had been a simple skills tree. Dungeon Hearts isn’t terrible, it just doesn’t seem to belong on PC.

Full Throttle Remastered looks decent and plays just as it used to, bugs and all.  The audio quality is vastly improved, including dev commentary that alongside the retrovision toggle makes this a self-contained piece of history, much like the other Double Fine remasters.  It’s short but inexpensive and as a point and click adventure hits all of the expected notes.  However, because of how faithful it is to the source material, there’s a good chance that modern gamers without an element of nostalgia for the game could be turned off by having to deal with gameplay elements that we used to put up with simply because they were normal for all games at the time.  On that basis, I will tentatively recommend it to those gamers who already know they won’t be scared off by retro point and click idiosyncrasies.  Everyone else can probably avoid or wait for a sale.

I've been looking forward to this since I found out about it, although I was really just happy that I could buy Full Throttle again.

Now that I have, when I sit back down with this later, I'll be sticking to classic. While Double Fine does a great job, I still find myself wanting to see the artwork in its original style, not a reinterpretation and extrapolation.
What I have been really enjoying is the commentary. It's great to hear the team that created this discuss it in-length. Considering I've loved this title for, gosh, 22 years now, that was exactly the type of material around it I wanted. I also appreciate that the soundtrack is available in-game.
So, if you liked Full Throttle, buy this, hands-down. If you never played it, I can't say my review is for you, but I'd recommend it anyway if you have even the slightest inclintation to buy it. It's a great point-and-click adventure from Lucas Arts.

Another great Lucasarts remaster! After Lucasarts released the two Monkey Island "remasters", Double Fine produced the Grim Fandango and Day of the Tentacle "remasters" and Ron Gilbert made Thimbleweed Park it's a great time to be alive for a Lucasarts Graphic Adventure fan. But now that my favorite has been "remastered", Full Throttle, I'm super excited.
I've finished the remaster, and it just feels awesome. I must have finished the original version at least 20 times (at least once a year since my Pentium 133 in 1996), and it never becomes boring. And with the new visuals and the audio commentary it's a real pleasure.
For the original release it was amazing to see these full-screen animations. They even hold up really well today. It really felt like an interactive cartoon. Way better than a lot of FMV adventure games before it. But it was still a full Lucasarts adventure.
The improved graphics are a real treat. Sometimes it seems there was more effort in the animation in the original, but only on the details. Which are more clear now anyway, so I guess that evens it out. The quality of the audio is much improved as well. You can switch between the original and new graphics and audio on the fly, and through the options-menu you can also mix-and-match the original and new graphics and audio. There seem to be some odd transitions, but those feel like they're going to be fixed in the first patch or so.
If you have enjoyed it in the past, it's a must-buy. If you've never experienced Full Throttle in the past, it's also a must-buy! And with the new controller support it's a blast to play on the couch (on screen prompts are for a PS4 controller, but an Xbox 360 and One controller also work fine out-of-the-box). Even my girlfriend loves to watch!
And as extra's you can look at a bunch of concept art, listen to original music (the Gone Jackals tracks are not here unfortunately. They're still in the game though.), and re-listen the commentary.
For me the perfect game just got better!

The game is not perfect, but it is constantly being supported and cared for by the developers. The gameplay always keeps you on your toes, weither it is the AI trying to flank your position, or a sudden push from the oppisition. With only one bullet needed to end your life, cover is vital and required to make something out of it. But if you happen to catch an unlucky bullet (regardless of it was the first bullet fired upon you or the whole enemy team unloading their whole mag on you), you will find yourself at the nearest base in a new body, ready to keep pushing, or think of another tactic to approach the enemy.
The game doesn't usually have too many people on sadly. PvP is more dry than a desert, except for a sunday event or a few people screwing around on there. The main attraction is obviously the PvE, in singleplayer or multiplayer. You'll find around 36 people at max at times in invasion servers (PvE),though I heard reports of more. The community is small, but there are some people on there that are so friendly, that they will die to save your loot.
Single player provides plenty of customization for quick battles such as AI accuracy, how many bots total, or even what rank you start as. There is also a customizable campaign you can do,featuring most of the maps and allows you to stick with a save through out the campaign until the very end.
There is a variety of weapons, both ones that you can simply buy at the armory, and rarer ones you might find laying on the corpses on the higher ranking AI, or secret crates containing these weapons. Loot can also be found these ways, from things such as cigars to sunglasses to gems to even unreleased CD's!
Plenty of thought was put into the game, but confusingly, it has a small community. If everyone not only bought this and persuaded their friend to not only buy the game, but to convince their friends to get the game and so on, the community would thrive with more players to play with!

I may be a little nostalgic for this game, but it is pretty damn solid for what a racer.  Its a little like the poor man's Need For Speed.  It doesn't demand much out of your PC, and the AI does have a little skill behind it, so you find yourself actually having to work for first place late game.
The police system is a bit wonky, but is surprisingly competant.  If you get put into a pursuit, it actually requires a lot more than a fast car alone to get away from the cops.  If they remain in pursuit of you for too long, you get busted and lose your ingame cash.  You also get a sort of "beep" that goes off faster the closer you are to a cop, and if you're going too fast, you get one warning before they engage in pursuit.  If you're paranoid like me, however, you'll find yourself doing 25 mph anytime you're near a cop.
However, this game hasn't aged too well over the years, so the graphics do look a bit dated.  The game's feel also isn't spot on, so you find that 140 feels more like 60.  Frankly, that is a small price to pay.  If you enjoy an open-world(ish) racing game with some customization thrown in the mix, then this game is worth a try.

One of my favorite parts of the game is the use of notes to set the tone. The varying authors either build tension or shift the mood while giving story relevant information. The lore is fairly well developed for what it is while including popular references from (mostly) horror games.
The artistic direction seen early in the game gives the illusion of a cute game that changes into a more gritty and detailed style as the game progresses. The music is fantastic and always fits the tone of the monster the player is dealing with. The monster that happily approaches the player has a simple, upbeat tune, while the monster that forces the player to hallucinate has a harsh and dreary theme. The music is also helpful with gameplay due to the repetitive nature of the game.
One of the benefits of a game with few monsters and pre-designed rooms is the low burden of knowledge. Approaching each monster gives a general idea of their strengths and methods that will be used throughout the game. The game has very few ways to kill the player without the player making a mistake. The downside of this being that the game is fairly easy. Each room will eventually become well known to the player as they progress throughout the mansion, and each sound will let the player know exactly how to react. This usually comes down to, "get to the door as quickly as possible", but not always. Regardless, it gives the player a feeling of power and control of a situation as the game progresses.
Funnily enough, the cute jumpscares were the scariest part of the game, but not in a bad way. The game eventually reaches a point where they aren't on the player's mind, then they appear at the worst times. Then there's Howard, a legitimately terrifying jumpscare.
All in all, it's a 7/10 game. Pretty short and tedious, but very fun and rewarding. Well worth the free download.

Pretty great fighter, although it will take some time to get used to it. If you can put aside the theme (take my word for it, it's tolerable in game), you are in for a treat.
There are three main reasons the game sticks out as a 2D fighter:
- Homing button
You can use it to jet yourself towards the opponent, delay your attack, fly around projectiles, extend your combo, dodge attacks. No other fighter allows you to be this mobile in the air. It's something that you will keep finding ways to exploit, it's pretty great.
- Huge hand drawn stages
The stages are massive, especially vertically, and its incredibly enjoyable as you and your opponent fight it out practically everywhere in the air. It just feels massive.
- Arcanas
An Arcana gives you a bonus to your character and you can summon them to do an attack (like MVC assists).  The bonuses are quite different, like allowing you to float in the air to giving your attacks superarmor to making your character fall faster and less vulnerable combos. You can combine any arcana with any character which gives you a lot of options to try out.
Balance wise its pretty good. While there are a couple of really strong characters, they don't feel unbeatable. Everyone has an arcana they can use to keep them in the fight.
The netcode is pretty nice. It starts off quite laggy, but it should smooth out by the time the match starts. Overall, haven't had issues with playing people from completely different regions (EAST/West/Europe). It's still not great as it's not using rollback like GGPO, but overall quite playable.
My main complaint is that the game doesn't have high-res character sprites. This is largely unnoticeable in the match because you are moving around so quickly, but it makes a bad impression in the beginning. Also the single player is quite lackluster although you do have a story mode, time trial etc.
Aside from that, this is a great game. You might need to grab a friend though, the online playerbase is quite small.

You're in for a treat with this game. With 23 fighters and 23 Arcanas to choose from, the latter further customizing and adding depth to your chosen fighter, you will have a lot of fun experimenting and finding your own fighting style.
This game's mechanics share some similarities with those of other air dashers, such as Blazblue or Melty Blood, with a unique twist to it: the homing mechanic, which allows you to home in on your opponent with the press of a button, which in turn allows for extra defensive and offensive options, along with fast-paced mind games.
The game launched with a few bugs, but most of them were quickly addressed with a couple of patches. I won't say it's perfect now, but personally my experience hasn't been negatively impacted since then.
I highly recommend this if you're into fighting games but haven't yet tried Arcana Heart. Veterans of the series will already know this game is awesome :)

This game is quick to dismiss for its price tag and its initial presentation of anime-heavy content but it's actually fun to pick up as a fighting game and let's be honest we could all use some extra cuteness brighten a bad day.
-PROS-
Mechanics are what you will enjoy here because everyone is capable of dashing/canceling very easily. It's not as "on-point" demanding like in Guilty Gear or others that require (Roman) canceling to be done only with certain moves with very specific frames of attack.
The clash system will also keep you on your feet and help give you a fighting chance in times you'd least expect it. Clashing is when two characters hit each other in their hitboxes and their attacks stop in their tracks. You are then given the option to try and get another attack in before your opponent does during the clash animation.
The supers in this game are fun to abuse. Heck the Arcana Eclipses are basically a free super attack. You have to go into Extend Force to use one but extend force refreshes very quickly. (Like a few seconds) and also your character's own super meter recharges fast too. Remember the effort it takes to get a level of super in other games like street fighter and when you lose that level it takes a lot of effort to get it back? In this game you can just turtle for a couple of seconds and you can get it back. With 23 characters all completely different from each other and 23 Arcanas to choose from you can mix things up and have fun working around seeing what works and what's just plain gimmicky. (Brawlers that zone with long range pink lazors? WTF....surprisingly it's highly effective.)
There are some other things to do:
Survival(which really needs to be changed to Score Attack. That's what it is. You're still allowed to keep trying on the same fight you lose so it's not really survival which you must defeat as many as you can while given only one chance.) Time Attack, and Trials for the characters.
The trials pit you against CPU opponents that ENCOURAGE you to use the game's mechanics. Like teching/jump cancels/etc.  It helps give players that don't have much experience in fighting games to actually try some of the more advanced stuff instead of just giving them a dummy to pound and a command list of the special moves and leaving the players with no clue how survival in games like this works.
However this game isn't without some really bad serious flaws.
-CONS-
Obviously fighting games never offer much in the realm of rewards. Your best reward is defeating tough opponents online, I'd imagine.
The unlockables are just anime artwork/visual stuff and the after story is just some anime episode shoehorned into this game that has nothing to do with what is really happening in the main plot. There isn't even much fighting in it it's just a lot of dialog. It's almost as if it feels the girls' main life outside of conflict is more important the catastrophic events that took place beforehand. Pretty stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥but it has those warm cute moments.
When you're doing stuff outside of story mode, you're going to hit stuff that is scaled incorrectly with respect to difficulty curve.
I know that sounds greek so I'll spell it out.
When you're doing the Time Attack/Survival/10th trial gold medals  you're going to hit broken CPU opponents that are going to pit you against odds that are impractically doable or just downright borderline impossible to combat. Some of which is said to even be tougher than King of Fighters bosses, or so I've been told. If you're already more than familiar with this game...you know who I'm talking about. The primary reason this is horrible is because these are your final bosses that you must beat to place your score. You could clean sweep your way to the end and have to fight something horribly broken compared to everything else you had to fend off to get to the near end. It's not so bad in the 10th trial because that's a purely optional thing to do but for Survival and Time Attack that was an awful idea to put stuff like that at the very end.
Summary
Overall the game is fast paced and fun and gives players many options to combat with so whether you want to play on your own with a friend and goof around seeing what does what it's great. If you want to go competitive the adrenaline from the insanity is worthwhile. I do recommend it but 20$ would've been a better price. I felt like I was paying 15$ for a nice fighting game and another 10$ for some anime stuff as an feature buying this on it's prerelease discount of 10%(or whatever it was.)

Total load of horse♥♥♥♥♥♥20% of the time, which really hurts an otherwise alright game.
First, do not use a mouse/keyboard setup to play. The Quicktime events will ♥♥♥♥ you - I learned this at the very first boss fight where he seemingly became unbeatable because no matter how I moved my mouse to simulate rotating a joystick, it didn't trigger the right action and I had to keep repeating the event. Not entirely the game's fault, but it's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ oversight for a port. Luckily, I have a controller, but the time wasted is a problem.
Second, glitches/bugs exist where enemies can get stuck inside walls/floors depending on the combat situation. This is extremely frustrating because the game uses a kill order mechanic for several fights. Specifically, the little mobs make the big mob more powerful, or the little mobs are necessary fodder to power up your ultimate attacks, some of which are the only way to reveal invisible mobs. More than twice this has happened, thereby making a battle all but unwinnable.
Third, there's no way to avoid some of the very lengthy cutscenes involved in this game, which means that if you die in a fight then you may need to sit through about 45 seconds/1 minute of cgi nonsense before you can actually go back to playing.
The first item can be overcome (just start with a controller instead of keyboard/mouse), but the other two persist throughout the entirety of the game. While there's plenty of fun to be had here, I found myself turning the damn thing off periodically to go play something more accessible. Just a damn shame, really.

It's been a few years since I originally played this, and it was recently brought to mind again, so I thought I'd write a quick review.
The basic premise is simple enough, and the graphics for the most part look like your typical RPG Maker fare, so I wasn't expecting much. I certainly wasn't expective to be turned into a bawling pile of mush too embarrassed to leave his room for a half hour or so after the game had been completed. I was wrong on both counts.
If you're looking for innovative gameplay or amazing grahics, you're not going to find them here. You walk around, interact with objects, and "talk" to "people," and that's it. You have two characters, and sometimes you can choose which of them performs a certain task, but it makes no difference to the overall narrative. You will get from point A to poin B, and that's that.
Where this game really shines is in its storytelling. Items that you interact with early on will take on new significance as the game progresses, often in surprising ways. And even when the reveals are predictable, the writing is so good that they are still touching. As you learn more abou the man whose mind you're invading and the people of significance in his life, you can't help but be drawn in. I only expected to try this out for an hour or two, and I ended up binging them entire thing in an afternoon.
This also touches on moral dilemmas that can arise from this sort of technology. In the game, you're invading memories in order to grant someone a wish before he dies, but in the process you learn just what rewriting memories could cause him to give up. Is it alright to do this even when he's asked for it? Is there a way to grant him the memories he wants while retaining other, incredibly imporrtant memories he already possesses? Do you have an obligation to at least try even though it's not required by your contract?
Without too many spoilers, it's sometimes predictable, sometimes suprising, always touching, and it left me a quivering mess when it was all over, but in a good way, you know. The soundtrack is also superb. It's very atmospheric, and there's one song in particular that'll stick with you for a long time to come. Just hearing a tiny bit of it on the Store page brought back so many memories and convinced me that it was time to finally leave a review.
I'd say try it out. I'm hesitant to even call it a game in the proper sense, but it's awesome nonetheless. Hopefully you'll find it just as touching.

This game was personal to me. The main character suffers from metal illnesses, bipolar and ptsd. I, myself am bipolar type 2. These are themes that are presented in a very intelligent, accurate but sensitve way, from the perspective of someone living in the celtic age. The sound design was brilliantly done, almost too well. I actually had to stop my playthrough at times because the sound was disturbing me too much, causing my own hallucinations to happen ( you will understand what I mean when you play).
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is a VERY story driven game. This is something, I feel has been lacking from games that have come out in recent times. It is a game with emphasis on adventure over combat. Don't expect a hack n slash beat'em up. The combat is fluid and simplistic but intuitive. It has a Dark Souls type feel with an element of rock/paper/sissors mechanic splashed in with how attacking is handled. Ninja Theory did put some effort into making combat exciting. Button mashing will not work. While this is a short game (averaging about 8-9 hours of gameplay) it is very polished and is priced appropriately at half the cost of a AAA title. Ninja Theory did not have to turn to any AAA publishers to get their vision made. No forced, last minute tacked on multiplayer or day one DLC BS. Just a single, complete story driven game that knocks it out of the park. As of writting this, Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice has won Best Audio Design, Games for Impact and Pest Performance (Melina Juergens) at The Game Awards.
Hellblade isn't a perfect game but for what Ninja Theory set out to prove, they have MORE than sent a clear message to the entire gaming industry that there is a space between indie title and AAA game. Buy this game, you won't regret it.

This is the first game I've bought that I've actually requested a refund for, out of almost a hundred games (though some were in bundles that I haven't tried).  The straw that broke the camel's back was finding out that armor simply does not work.  Both display-wise and testing actual damage taken, the gear you equip shows that it has an armor stat when you look at its stats individually, but your armor perpetually displays as 1 (or 3 or 5 or whatever is the base amount for your class, that varies), and does not change when you put on the gear.  Once I noticed this, I let a couple of different mobs hit me with and without gear equipped, and sure enough, the damage did not change.
As for the rest of the game:
- It looks like an unpolished flash game, the text and interface are clunky and unappealing, and have no artistic background.  I'm not big on graphics and don't mind "retro" or heavily pixelated games but this just looks like no effort has been put into it.
- There's next to no plot.  Demons are invading, each quest mob has about one sentence that amounts to "It would be gr8 if you killed some of these".
- Each class has a default attack and four long cooldown skills, of which three can be equipped.  Leveling up increases your attack by 1 and gives some hp.  There is no variation or choice whatsoever.
- "Survival" consists of killing random deer and chickens for food drops and remembering to eat occasionally.  It doesn't add anything to the game.
- Construction looked interesting, but is completely unnecessary and also adds little to the game.  You can build houses, mines, and bunkers in one area of the map.  Houses yield gold, mines yield metal, and bunkers are defensive to protect the other two.  However, copious amounts of both of these can be gotten from mob drops.  Gold is useful, but the limiting resource is wood, which despite the map being a giant forest, can only be obtained by blowing up fences and wagons, and it takes a while to farm enough to craft better gear.  Unless I overlooked something, there's no buildable structure that yields wood.  If there was, then construction would be more worthwhile.  Even so, construction feels like an extra thing tacked onto the game rather than a central feature of it.
- Whenever you die, stats gained from gear disappear until you unequip and reequip your armor.  As mentioned above, the actual armor value does not work regardless.
- If you make more than one character, all share the same gear and inventory, but also the same quests, meaning once you do quests on one character, you can't do them on another character.  Quests give a ton of xp and gear is level restricted, so this basically forces you to grind a lot more to level up any other character.  I haven't played through the entire game so I'm not sure what effect it has on the main quest if there even is one (so far I've just seen single quest mobs that give out quests unrelated to each other, no overarching quest chain.)
+ Combat is so far the only positive aspect of this game for me.  Most mobs except the basic zombies and archers are tough and have a  specific attack pattern that needs to be dodged or you will die or take a lot of damage.  Though it is still a bit odd as you can only attack left and right, not up and down (or north or south), which does not translate well for a 3rd person isometric game, but regardless, the controls are quick and fighting the bigger mobs is fun.
Overall, between the way it looks, armor not working, and constructing being mostly useless (at least until they add a lumber mill), this is basically a simplistic and semi-broken flash game.  It needs the bugs mentioned fixed, lumber mills added to construction, a much more detailed character development system and some polish in order to be decent.
Edit - though to avoid being a total buzzkill I would add that it has good potential if some of these things are fixed.

Short Review:
Pros: 1. Still "Half-life 2".
2. Better lighting, shadow, fog and water effects.
3. Gaming Youtubers (Not let's-players) doing commentary.
4. Ross Scott.
5. It's free.
Cons: 1. Could have made more changes with better looking textures, fire effects and NPC's.
2. Loading times are longer (not much, but just a few seconds longer).
Verdict - It's "Half-Life 2" with few graphical tweaks. Love it ? Then play it.
Longer Review:
"Half-Life 2: Update" is the same game as the vanilla version only with better lighting, shadow, fog and water effects, everything else is the same. If you are expecting a next-gen looking "Half-Life 2", then you might be dissapointed a bit. I know they tried to keep the same fell of "Half Life 2" unlike Cinematic Mod, but they could have some changes more noticeable, like better fire effects, sharper textures and better looking NPC's.
I don't know about the "bug fixes" part, since I haven't encountered much of them in the original product, but I heard from other players, that the mod has some of it's own bugs and crashes, but they should be patched out soon.
The most interesting part is the commentary itself. Rather than having only mod Devs talk about the game(the development, Source engine, choices that Valve made and why the game was special), they decided to hire some famous gaming youtubers to do most of the commentary, such as: "caddicarus", "projared", "ricepirate", "brutalmoose", "balrog the master" and "Ross Scott", so it kinda feels like a interactive "Did You Know Gaming" episode.
Verdict - It's still "Half-Life 2" only slightly better looking than the vanilla version. If you loved it before and want to experience it again with youtubers and devs presenting the game, then go for it. If not, then you'll know my answer.

Little Walker is an overlooked gem. The game is a hodgepodge of bells and whistles that keep the player stimulated and constantly surprised. The sheer variety of enemies and obstacles encountered kept me on my feet throughout. The many friendly NPCs also supplied a fair few laughs. The dialog is as charming as the excellent updated visuals are adorable. Every little detail in the game oozes character, adding to the fun-loving tone of the game. The way Walker emotes depending on his health is perhaps the most compelling incentive to actually avoid damage. The game is certainly forgiving, making the game more about enjoying the journey than overcoming a challenge, aside from a few more difficult sections. Still, the world is so delightful and the gameplay so charming that the difficulty is hardly missed. Having a character that can't stop walking keeps the pace moving at a breakneck speed, and challenges hardly overstay their welcome. The game may be short, clocking in at just 80 minutes for me, but it feels satisfyingly complete.
I do have two main criticisms for the game. First of all is the text. The text is very blurry, in contrast to the rest of the crisp pixel art. This makes the menu incredibly difficult to navigate. After looking at some old game footage, this problem is either only happening to me or is specific to the new art update. Either way, I hope that this problem is resolved soon. My other key criticism of the game is that it suffers from Sonic 1 syndrome, in that the first level is so much fun that the rest of the game has a difficult time stacking up. The first few levels are full of so many different paths, mechanics, secrets, and other bits and bobs, while the middle of the game takes a bit of a dip in terms of pacing. While this certainly serves as a good hook, the middle of the game really needs some more stand out moments to keep the game on a healthy interest curve.
Despite any shortcomings, the game is still a blast to play and I would certainly recommend it to anyone considering picking it up, especially at such a low price.

Darksiders 2 Deathinitive Edition is the continuation of the hidden gem Darksiders: Wrath of War, after THQ went bankrupt, Nordic Games bought the franchise and re-released the game with all DLC’s included and improved graphics, maybe necessary or not, the fact is that many, including myself, want this franchise to get a third game, for the sake of the story and lore. I originally had the normal version of Darksiders 2 so I got this new edition for free.
On this episode, we play as Death, War’s oldest brother, his mission is clear, to save his brother War of an unfair trial, blamed for the destruction of the Third Kingdom, because of this War has been imprisoned by the Charred Council. The storyline develops during the time Death’s brother is captive and whose soul is taken away as punishment. On this new adventure Death travels to many different worlds seeking the truth of what really happened on Earth and for this he meets new characters such as the Makers, who are old as creation itself, the crow father, keeper of secrets and many other demonic and angelic beings alike, some of them will stop you at any cost, some others will bargain to help you, whichever the case, Death’s path will be filled with powerful enemies, traps and many puzzles to solve, for in his journey he will have to face something more, Corruption has spread throughout the worlds hiding a more dangerous enemy well-known to the horseman, following the same formula as the original game, but this time with many more RPG elements and looting system, the search for the Well of Souls begins.
The game itself introduces a new system and mechanics, on the original game, the looting system did not exist, instead of that we collected artifacts and power ups that would help us gain more power. Now on DS2, a looting system has been created, a welcome addition if you ask me, as we struggle to get the perfect set of armor with many more capabilities and characteristics, we also have the addition of a whole new variety of weapons, scythes, hammers, axes, gauntlets and armblades, among others, which make the game much richer regarding content, we can also find possessed weapons, which can be upgraded by sacrificing other non-possessed weapons that will give them especial characteristics that will generate more damage, resistance or arcane abilities.
The worlds we travel through are bigger and filled with more puzzles that follow the same pattern as in the original DS, some of them are simply easier, and some others require especial tools to be solved with, which again will make you come and go from time to time to find unreachable chests or secrets that are far-off, all of this, enriched by the different worlds we will visit and enemies we will beat. Also, we count with a set of new skills and powers that will help us beat enemies easier and a level up system that will let us use much more powerful weapons and armor sets, always looking for a balance among them. Not great changes but still they are welcomed to get a better experience.
When playing DS2 Deathinitive Edition I could not noticed the differences between the original version of 2012 and this new one, but as I got it for free, I thought I could give it a try expecting maybe the addition of the DLC’s in a different way (which I will address on another topic of this review) Nevertheless, the game still looks beautiful and follows the same comic-like patterns as the previous title, but this time it looks shinier and much more polished, and less rough around the edges, there are still some muddy textures here and there, but you forget about them instantly as you advanced on the storyline, considering the game has many different worlds, each of these worlds with diverse environments and vivid colors, from the more natural world of the Forge Lands to the gloomy and grim Kingdom of the Dead, the aesthetics of DS2 shows a variety in graphics, always highlighted by the details of every and unique world, beautiful art and design.
The original Darksiders had a great soundtrack filled with more operatic and orchestral characteristics, here the music has changed, it was developed to what I believe a more atmospheric/ambient music, it really fits the game if we think about the world we visit, some of them require a different approach regarding the musical aesthetics, this makes travelling and dungeon/puzzle solving more appealing to the ear, it instantly hooks you to the mood of the mission, especially the Kingdom of the Dead, the music highlights the decadence of the kingdom and the gloomy atmosphere, the soundtrack has a lot of merit.
As for sound effects, they are equally good, you can feel the cracking of bones, the flesh being cut and scythes hacking and slashing the many enemies, demons still growl fearsome, angels still have that deep voice that make them feel righteous and fearless. As for the voice acting, I must say it is superb, on the occasion we have two famous actors doing voices, for Death we have Michael Wincott, who has done an outstanding job, it can’t be better, he fits the bill perfectly as for one the Makers, we have James Cosmo, broadly known for Game of Thrones and also the priest for one of the game’s trailers, just two actors to show how impressive the voice acting is here, they are believable and deliver powerful lines and flawless attitude for both characters. Just superb sounds and voices.
When I got this edition of the game and heard that all DLC’s would be part of it, I was expecting for them to be included as major side quests, for the normal version of DS2 had the DLC’s as extra content, but outside the main maps we visit. I was disappointed when I saw the same content was added the same way as before, it would have been much better to have these extra missions as part of the main story, making it easier and more comfortable to travel at any time during main missions, that is not the case and to do these extra quests, you must leave the main game and look for this extra content, a great addition but flawed by not being added differently.
As for technical issues, the game suffers from crashes from time to time, in the middle of battles or just randomly, annoying at times, but it doesn’t happen that often, what affects the game more I would say is the bug where every time you go to your map and come back to the main mission, every single key stops working, the only solution we have is to restart the game or just go back to the menu option screen and be lucky not to have it anymore, sometimes this helps sometimes it doesn’t, an annoyance when you want to continue playing.
Also, there are sound issues, when playing some sound effects and some voices will stop working, or sometimes all of them at the same time, I noticed that this happens when there are many sound effects working at the same, this produces some other to start malfunctioning or don’t emit any sound at all, again, restarting the game will solve this problem for some time, not knowing of course it will happen again anytime soon. For a deathinitive edition this is not game breaking at all, but it weakens the definition they use for a game that has been re-released.
As stated on my DS review, the franchise has been compared to other similar games that dominate this genre and what not, but I insist that DS has the lore and world to make a greater franchise of its own, they have the tools, they have a rich world full of factions, characters to make of Darksiders 3 the game we have been waiting for since Nordic Games bought the series.

Arcana Heart 3 Love Max!!! does the job in the Fighting genre even 7 years after its initial release, with variations in the combat that fighting game players have come to know and love, but without going too far off the rails. The cast of characters and arcana is diverse enough to have a lot of different strategies and tactics, and the smart use of the arcana gauge and how it builds tweaks the formula enough for it to feel fresh. It's a shame that it falls into the same trap as other rereleases of this type do for a new platform: not having a player base to work off of, which limits network play despite what seems to be strong net-code overall. It could have used some HD visuals and polish for the game, because despite good character design and artwork, the sprites have shown their age at this point. In the end, a great fighting system and fun and quirky story mode helps bring the game worth a look despite the multiplayer downfalls, and was something that was fun throughout my experience, all be it a bit frustrating at times.

While the aesthetic may not be the most appealing, this game more than makes up for it in the mechanics. In particular, the use of a guard cancel instead of near-frame-perfect blocking to turn defense into offense is something I wish more airdashers had, as this does. It also doesn't require long combo strings to do well, though learning them will secure victory 2 or 3 touches sooner.
The Arcana system is interesting, but as a fair warning, while every character seems viable, and nearly every arcana seems to be viable, not every character/Arcana pair is equally useful. However, most characters have a few Arcanas they will work well with, and each Arcana seems to have it's place with at least a character or two.
Netcode also feels solid, at least as far as input delay netcode can take a game. Part of this is the actual code, and part of it is the lack of timing sensitive mechanics (such as instant blocking or FRCs) frustrating one's practice time. The only issue I've found so far is that the game will slow down a bit when connections are poor, which I'm guessing is more due to packet loss. As always, try to play from a computer wired into the internet. If you want to find games, look up the associated groups, since there are still regular tournaments run.
Overall, as fighting games go, it's an enjoyable airdasher with a deep movement system, and without the reliance on strict timing on the defensive and long combos on the offensive.

I've had this game in my library for a couple years but have just finally gotten around to playing it. I'm sure I got it on sale as I was interested in it and wanted to come back to it at some point. Anyway, several months ago I discovered the game "Life Is Strange," and it turns out it was the second game made by this developer, Dontnod Entertainment. I absolutely loved Life Is Strange, and it's actually one of my all time favorite games now; needless to say, I was very excited when their logo came up in Remember Me. It's an entirely different style of game and very action focused, but it still has what I found to be a moving story and a unique experience.
I thought the challenge level was just right at the normal difficulty setting, and I finished the game over a few days (11 hours total). It's unusual for me to play a game of this length all the way through in such a short time, but I was completely hooked once I started playing.
I particularly enjoyed the combat with its customizable combos, but I was also glad that the system didn't ever become overly complex. It also included some nice puzzles, and probably my favorite aspect of the game were the memory remix sections that involve trying to change people's memories; I will say that I thought this aspect of the game was somewhat underused, and I'd have loved to see some more of these scenarios.
After having played both of Dontnod's games, I can say that they are fast becoming one of my favorite developers. I can't wait to play their next two games, Vampyr and Life is Strange 2. I have great faith in this team to release solid work, and I highly recommend Remember Me!

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is an excellent game if you enjoy a game which primarily works through its atmosphere and story. It is relativly short and as a result the gameplay mechanics cannot become particularly complex, so if you are looking for $/h value and deep mechanics than this game will likely not appeal to you.
However, if you can get into this game, then you will get a truly unique experience. It explores the struggle of celtic warrior, struggling with her inner demons and psychosis. A subject matter rarely explored in any medium, let alone video games. Every mechanic in the game, every dialogue line, and every piece of visual and audio is finely crafted to serve the purpose of this story.
As a result the game is short but extremly powerful, as the story and its implications stick with you quite some after playing it. Personally I also found it eye-opening to experience the game world like someone who actually has a mental disorde. Some of the setpieces of the game are actually constructed from reports of people, who do have psychosis with all their wonder and all their terror.
If you are the kind of player who can even remotly get into those kinds of game I wholeheartedly recommend Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice. It offers a fresh and unique perspective, which is something rarely seen in todays gaming market. A final piece of advie: Use headphones if possible. It enhances the experience considerably.

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice can be best described as a rather unusual action-adventure game developed by Ninja Theory. The videogames is about the titular Senua, a young Celtic warrior woman who embarks on a dangerous quest into Hel itself (the Northern mythology equivalent of Hell) in order to find a way to bring her beloved Dillion back to life. The protagonist's journey is made all the more dangerous and frightening by the fact Senua has been plagued by dark visions, mysterious ghosts and confusing voices, some sort of "Darkness", as the characters like to call it, for a very long time.
Hellblade's core gameplay is very hard to describe to an average player.
The game's advertisement and promotional materials would lead you to believe that Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is mostly an hack-and-slash videogame very reminiscent of the Soulborne series: you face multiple enemies by focusing on one of them at a time and dodge, parry and strike as needed, and sometimes activate a power mode of some sort (your focus) in order to make special enemies vulnerable or cut to pieces common enemies with impunity. Truth be told, the game's combat department is deeply enjoyable: parrying or evading your enemies' strikes becomes increasingly fun, there's a good enemy variety (along with a handful of unique bosses for you to face) and you having to focus on a single enemy at any given time isn't much of an issue (Senua's "voices" will inform you if someone is attacking you off-screen, and thus need to either parry or dodge, and your focus will always swift to the enemy who just attacked you/you defended yourself from).
On the other hand however Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is also a videogame which can be best described as a modern walking simulator, with an heavy emphasis on plot and character development. The other half of the game is indeed spent walking or running around the various environments and collecting (or focusing on) environmental clues in order to solve the "puzzles" barring your way and advance. This core gameplay is also often accompanied by strange voices apparently speaking to Senua as the events unfold and interrupted by story-advancing cutscenes where you can't do anything but watch and experience Senua's struggle. This gameplay formula is helped immensely by the fact Hellblade's virtual world is simply put too detailed and gorgeous to look at, with well-crafted environments, masterful use of lights and shadows and vibrant colors and effect which make everything and everyone really look alive. The only optional element in all the exploring you are tasked to do is in the form of lore stones scattered around the game's world which offer very interesting bits about the major events of Northern mythology.
Luckly enough these two main cores of Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice mesh incredibly well together and balance themselves over magnificently: every time exploring starts boring you the game is savvy enough to splice things up a bit vy throwing some enemies to fight at you, while bosses and harder fights are usually followed by peaceful strolls through the gorgeous environments). The main gameplay structure was carefully planned by the developers to achieve the main goal of the game: portray the innter struggles and issues in adjusting oneself with reality a person suffering from a deep form of psychosis like Senua goes through on a daily basis and the general feeling of loneliness this may cause in such people.
In this regard Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice is not only a very entertaining and gorgeous game, but also a successfull and interesting experiment in videogame storytelling technique I'd suggest to anyone, really

This game is as wide as the Pacific Ocean, but not even close to being deep enough to drown in...
Review:
God damn I regret getting this. Even with the most recent updates that everyone hails as being the best thing ever, I cannot help but think "This is the most boring, repetative crap ever!". Sorry, but this is my honest opinion...
You might say: "Yeah, but, you only got 7 hours in and haven't unlocked the majority of the game!...." Hm yes, this is true and a very valid point.. But I'm on discord playing alongside a friend who has over a 100 hours into this game since the latest 'fixes everything' patch, and he continuously talks about upgrading to a better X (where X is ship or tool). That. Is. It. And that's where I'm at after 5 minutes! So 7 hours in, I have a few million and upgraded my ship once and tool twice... And the cycle goes on.
Yes there is building/farming, which is nice! No negative points here really... Although, it would be nice to actually be able to build where I want, rather than a pre-set location with a radius I can build in.. But still, it's better than nothing.
But... That's about it... "Finally, an upgrade for my tool! YAAAAY IT'S WAY BETTER!!.. Okay, now to upgrade my tool...." <---- This is not the thought process I want for over 100 hours.
There's something about this infinity (in the sense you cannot visit everwhere) that leaves the 'in the moment' relatively detail-less. A cave! Yaaay let's explore.. Okay, what's within... Just... Ongoing paths with a bit of fauna, MAYBE an animal that does the same as every other animal (nothing)... Kind'a pointless feeling and it does not give you that feeling of excitement and adventure.
Spore is far better a game than this, that's for sure! And I mean this in terms of value for what you get.. Yes Spore is technically not as good, but it's basically free and has a LOT more game-variation.
Anyway, 2/10 from me. Shame really.

I'm five hours in and the game just isn't fun.
Pros:
+It's pretty.
Cons:
-Level design is atrocious; the levels are like someone chucked spaghetti into the map editor and shipped it.  There will be situations where I have to hunt for minutes to find the way forward, and even scenarios where I can hear the enemies running and shouting but cannot find them.  I can't emphasize how bad the level design is; this game feels like an expensive chore.
-The default enemy encounter involves a bunch of soldiers/robots/dogs and a commander who can trigger endlessly spawning enemies.  But ANY enemy spotting you triggers the alarm, even if said commander is sixteen rooms over.  So you can either attempt stealth or dash for the commander and pray that enough shots miss you that you don't have to reload.  Sadly, stealth in this game is not functional or fun.  So grab that rosary and get ready to reload often!
-You can double-fist any weapon in the game, but the interface for switching weapons is BEYOND AWFUL.  Let's say that you're dual wielding silenced pistols and see an enemy that requires more firepower.  Switching to your machine guns should be fluid, right? WRONG!  You select the machine gun, but that leaves you with one machine gun and one pistol.  So you press the machine gun key again, and you put away the pistol and fold out the stock on one machine gun.  The THIRD press finally allows you to dual wield machine guns.  But each of these transitions takes several seconds, and this is not a game where enemies will give you a chance to leisurely swap out weapons for ten seconds every time.
-I'm not sure if it's the weapons bob, but movement in this game feels off and is slightly unsettling to my brain.
-Plot and characters is really stupid.  You're basically taking on all of occupied America with about twelve people, including old men and pregnant women.
-The tone of the game is schizophrenic.  You spend half the time moaning about dead friends and a broken body and the other half mowing down legions of Nazis with ease.
Skip this game and play Doom 2016 again.
