Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus, is a frustrating game. The New Order had an interesting mix of stealth and combat that worked well and a bold portrayal of a horrible world where Nazism truimphed during the Second World War. The sequel does not know what it wants to be and is a mess plagued by gameplay issues and an interesting setting that is underused.
In terms of gameplay, the game does neither stealth nor shooting very well. Stealth has been made more difficult by introducing the ability for enemies to find bodies that raise a heightened state of alarm. The problem with this system is that you do not have the ability to hide bodies and often enemies on the other side of the area you are sneaking through might find a body and alert the entire garrison of enemies in the map. When you are spotted you are forced into combat, and while in the New Order combat was fun and you could easily fight yourself out of a difficult situation even on the harder difficulty levels, combat in the New Colossus is a frustrating mess. There are less interesting weapons, less enemy variety, and to make matters worse, you can die with only one or two hits on the higher difficulty. One enemy soldier flanking around you could be fatal. Enemies also seem to have pinpoint accuracy and are bullet sponges on the higher difficulty, while the player’s accuracy with weapons seems to be a lot lower. This forces you to play the game as a cover shooter when it is quite clear that the maps were not designed to be played this way with many item-pickups lying around combat arenas. It gets even worse when there are certain scripted areas where stealth is not an option and you have to fight against wave after wave of enemies. The worst example of this is the courthouse scene, which is supposed to be an exciting sequence where you shoot your way out of a courthouse using the heavy weapons that are placed around the courtroom. Instead most of the time will be spend hiding behind a desk or bench in the courtroom popping out every few seconds to shoot at enemies. The final boss battle just consists of fighting two large robots that have an obvious weak point. This is quite a disappointment compared to the multi-stage boss battle from the New Order. There is also new side content that can be unlocked by using enigma codes, but this is just a rehash of levels previously visited. The earlier side missions feature new voice acting but it is obvious that the developers either ran out of time or went over budget because later side missions have no new voice acting. There is also a hidden bonus side mission in a new map, that is only unlocked when you complete all the other side missions. Which is the only mission to feature the Statue of Liberty, which is strange since the title the New Colossus is a reference to a nineteenth-century American sonnet about the statue as the mother of exiles that welcomes the displaced from the old world to America to start a new life. While the symbolism is there, with the u-boat that serves as the main base being the mother of exiles for the resistance, I found it strange that such an iconic landmark was hidden in a secret side-mission. Frustratingly all the side missions are unlocked by collecting enigma cards from enemy officers and there are not enough officers in either the main content or the side content to unlock the hidden mission without replaying content to grind these cards. This is just artificial padding to make the game last longer without having to create any meaningful new content.
The story is a mess too. During the opening of the game it seems that one of the main conflicts throughout the game will be between Blazkowicz and his father, who has obvious Nazi sympathies. I thought that his character would be used to show how Americans have adapted to their new overlords and that the theme of collaboration would feature heavily, especially considering the marketing campaign for this game which focussed heavily on American collaborating with the Nazis. Sadly, the storyline with Blazkowicz’s father is resolved abruptly about one third into the game without an interesting pay-off, even though the game hints at him being more than a one-dimensional villain in a flashback just before encountering him. This is a huge waste of potential that could have been an interesting aspect of the story. The theme of collaboration is also wasted in the rest of the game. You don’t really get to see what life is like in the United States under Nazi rule except for the Roswell level which is quite short. The KKK is apparently in charge of the southern states but only three members are encountered throughout the game, one in an optional side mission. You really don’t get to see what the Nazis have done to life in the United States. This is such a waste because there have been obvious flirts with Nazi ideas like racial purity throughout American history by people such as Charles Lindbergh, movements such as American First, and even earlier with the harsh treatment of ethnic minorities. It would have been interesting to see this dark aspect of American history explored in the fictional setting of a mainstream video game. Sadly, this potential is wasted and even the Nazis, except for a certain scene later in the game involving Hitler, aren’t really the embodiment of Nazism like they were in the New Order. The new characters that are introduced are just exaggerated American stereotypes and a lot less interesting than the characters in the New Order.
There are some good parts to the game though, the sequence that happens about half-way through the game is amazing, but feels a little out of place, like it should have been later. The game looks amazing, runs smooth and has very few bugs or glitches. Technically, it is a well made game with great artwork, good voice acting, a great soundtrack, and smooth animations.
I really wanted to like this game since I was very impressed with the original and the way it boldly combined great gameplay with an interesting and ‘realistic’ portrayal of Nazism rarely seen in video games. The sequel is just an average game without a sense of direction that does not do anything new or interesting compared to the New Order and even does some aspects, like the combat, worse compared to its predecessor. I really felt let down by this game and therefore do not recommend it. Let’s hope Machine Games gets its act together and focusses and expands on what made the original game great in the inevitable Wolfenstein III.

A prime example is being on a sub and told to go somewhere but where it might be is not shown and none of the many NPCs you encounter will respond. Lots of failures - you have to fight to kill the baddies and unhook your house, a situation which will persist until it is done, and it makes no difference. You have to fight to free yourself in another setting and, after numerous attempts, it turns out it was all for nothing. You go to blow up an enemy HQ, do, but they've all left and you fail again. And on and on. The social-political commentary is jarring in the context of a cartoon shooter. There are some excellent shooting sequences but trying to get close to the real world horror of Hitler, and failing, just comes off as something done by a committee of dillitantes. I think the structural problems with the game (mapping, achievements that are distracting, etc.) and the attempt to be edgy falls flat and, at least for someone familiar with history, makes the game an endurance contest.

Dungeon Hearts is what it was set out to be; a different match-three puzzle game with intensely strategic elements added in with the mix. For $3, I definitely can't complain, and anyone with decent hand-eye coordination and a durable trigger finger probably won't either, since the game does require both of these, especially on the higher difficulties and further in to the story mode.
There are only two things I can possibly make a negative remark about. The "XP rewards," which one uses to buy rudimentary upgrades for each of the 4 individual characters, are very stingy (there are tens of upgrades in the shop, and they all cost between 20-110 XP, while a full story-mode completion, which takes usually around 50 minutes, only gives you 11, 22, or 33 xp on average when finishing on easy, medium, or hard difficulty, respectively). There is also the fact that if you do the entire story without a break (saving and resuming later is possible, however), you'll probably feel like you have carpal tunnel in whichever hand you hold the mouse in for several minutes afterwards, as playing the game does require many precise clicks and rapid mouse movements.
However, neither of the negatives impact the actual gameplay, which is fun, intense, and both simple and complex at the same time. Not to mention the game comes with up to five soundtracks, which are all absolutely amazing and go perfectly with the theme of the game. I personally can already tell that I'm going to get more hours of entertainment out of this than some of the games I've spent $10-20 on simply because of my love for intensive and strategic puzzle games, and anyone else with similar interests in gaming genres will probably be able to say the same. $3 well spent!

warning:
- personaly, I think this game is awesome, like REALLY awesome, its quite literally my favourite game, why? i dunno, probably a lot of reasons for it. that's just my subjective thought thoe. I'll try to make this review as objective as i can, but I cant promise you it'll be that way. Oh and also this is mostly a review of the original game, not the deathinitive edition and because the original doesnt exist anymore, I'm gonna write this review here.
In this game you play as death, as THE Death, you know, the guy with a big a** scythe (two in this case) and he's here to undo his brother's crime, which he unintenionally commited (I dont quite understand how you ACCIDENTLY end the entire human race, but ok you can dive into the game's lore once you play it). And because of this he has to travel to all these different realms, trying to unlock the well of souls, so that he can restore humanity and save his brother's a**.
The games main storyline is driven by a quest system along with a couple of side-quests for some extra lore/loot. The plot is quite interesting, the characters are pretty average thoe (the main evil guy, the guy who looks like gandalf and dies... like gandalf, the stronk independant female blacksmith, that one bulky guy who never talks  and that other bulky guy who always talks but has the intelectual capabilities of a peanut and a few others, but you get what im sayin', dont want to spoil anything for you), there are many awesome sights and you are gonna want to take a screenshot every 15 minutes or so to savour the moment later, the level layout is pretty neatly done (and the devs actually made sure you wouldnt have to marathon around the entire place, so they placed a few shortcuts, which show up once you're done with a certain part of the level), the puzzles are pretty cool (not too easy, it takes time, but at the same moment not hard enough to force you to look up walkthroughs on the web) and there are also a few extra things to keep you with the game for a bit longer such as the crucible, labyrinth and a few mini dungeons/bosses.
As for the combat system, it's made pretty well, you can definetly tell that the devs were influenced by DMC and God of War (and thos game were awesome). It's pretty much a hack and slash game most of the time with some elements from both, above mentioned, games, although, there is this one moment when the game just turns into a 3rd person shooter (don't unerstand why they did that). Combos and attack animations are pretty well done, you can learn "some of dem sick moves" from 2 trainers within the game. There is also a skill tree, which gives you a few fun abilities, but needs polishing.
Now for the bad part. First of all, the RNG equipment drop system, Why? I honestly think this game could have been a lot better without it, the game is so exploitable because of that. An upgrade system (like the one for possesed weapons) could have done the job a lot better. Then there are the last 2 realms, those were clearly rushed, although what was done was great, they were really short (~3 quests),  I really wanted it to be a bit longer. And the last thing that I disliked about the game is the nightmare creatures, they are seriously unbalanced compared to the others. That is all.
Darksiders II is a very under-rated game, I think it deserves a bit more attention and luv. Definetly recommend buying it, I mean I bought the whole franchise for 3$, I dont think i should complain about anything. This edition also features all of the DLC for the game, although it has it's own bugs which were not present in the original. On the awesome games'o'meter i would give it 8.5/10.

Started playing this again recenty after having bought it some years ago. Started over from the beginning too.
PROS:
- Fantastic, compelling storyline to follow. In some ways, the game feels like an interactive movie.
- Has scalable difficulty from casual gamer to extreme. More on that in Con listing.
- Graphics are great, to the point of gorgeous at times. Plenty of lighting, shading, blur effects, etc. If you play on dynamic contrast then that will only enhance the feel as you explore the darker, more forboding areas.
- Has a good dose of story, mixed with manual action and fight scenes. Seems pretty balanced for the most part in that realm. You're not constantly fighting, but you are also not constantly being a viewer either.
- Game seems pretty forgiving for the most part if you screw up or make a mistake, die, etc. However, see CONS for rest on that.
- Plenty of near-future science fiction and cyberpunk throughout.
- Great characters you can interact with, good voice acting by their real ilfe counterparts, great character development on the central character in the story, Nilin. Initially when I first started playing I was skepticle it would be that good seeing as you are starting with a character who has no memory of either who they are or how they got into that situation. However, it's not long before the story and memories start coming back. Or do they all come back? The one scene in the game is truly unexpected and mindblowing. And at one key moment, you don't just find out something mindblowing, but also reveals more of the backstory and sense of self. No spoilers, but when you get to that point you're gonna get hooked good.
CONS:
- For aging gamers like myself even the easiest setting that is supposed to let you focus more on the story and less on fighting can be incredibly difficult. Perhaps delevopers can take that into account? Geritol mode! Seriously though, as a lifelong middle-aged gamer whose muscles and tendons have been wrecked from life, car wrecks, falls, too many all-night gaming sessions, etc. to the point of feeling like I'm an 80 year old on a good day, some of these boss fights will make you take a break. At one point I feel I'm putting in 50,000 clicks an hour on some waves of bosses that really do take you a while to complete.
- Yes, some bosses will keep you literally fighting for an hour if you so much as make one wrong mouse click. Most of the game allows you to pick up from where you left off if you happen to make a serious mistake like falling off a building, dying, etc. However, some bosses that come in waves... no such luck. You spend 15 minutes of non-stop fighting to beat 3 waves, make a mistake, you have to start all over from the very first wave. In that respect the game can become too punitive in its punishment. Not all of the boss fights are like that, mind you, but the further into the game you get the less forgiving it seems to become. So make sure you bring equipment that take the key pressing and mouse clicking abuse. Also, make you got the bottle of aspirin handy too if you're athritic like myself, lol.
SUMMARY:
All in all I really like this game a lot despite the fact that I have to take breaks and can only go for 1 to 3 hours at any given time. Stellar game, but did see the occasional bug. Nothing game breaking, just simply reload from last checkpoint and you're good to go. Game auto-saves constantly as you make your way through the story which is nice since you can focus on the game rather than constantly worry about saving at key moment. So don't worry so much about making a mistake. Chances are it's saved just 5 seconds before. I would put this game into the same genre as stuff like the Tomb Raider series. Similar kind of feeling game, though completely different setting with sci-fi and cyberpunk theme throughout.

I don't often write reviews, but this game is one of the few that I think genuinely deserve it and highlight what gaming can be; a completely immersive and thought provoking medium that can rival (and beat) cinema and literature on that front. As opposed to what some developers want it to become (cough): shallow lootboxes and lacklustre content.
First things first this is clearly a passion project from Ninja Theory, and that shows, the graphics, acting and overall narrative are some of the best I've seen on any gaming device and the facial tracking software is a huge advance for the industry. I'd hold this title up to classics like Bioshock, The Witcher series and KOTOR for sheer impact.
I terms of positives:
+Sound - The voice acting and video acting from the entire cast was outstanding and should set a standard for other titles to follow. Melina Juergens, as Senua, stole the show in her first role! Nicholas Boulton (brought witty comic relief and horror as a Gaelic advisor) and Steven Hartley (Eredin from the Witcher 3) was cool as **** and menacing as ever.
Headphones are 100% a must to properly enjoy the game, as the music and sfx give clues and add to the overall experience.
+Immersion - Has to be seen and (more importantly heard) to be believed, it's an experience that can't be relayed adequately in words. The Furies and other cast aid so much to this sense that you are Senua and the sense of dread that flows from area to area; as well as being a brilliant tool to show you the way/push you on. You really want to prove the goad's and mock cheering wrong.
+Narrative and Story: A Pictish trek from Viking Midgard to Hellheim, story is at the forefront of the game and this shows, characters are well developed and you're pushed on and pushed on constantly to finish. Lore is really interesting and well thought out/organised. You become really immersed in Senua's story from start to finish.
+Graphics: Visually striking in every department, each new landscape that Senua ventures or stumbles into is as equally breath takingly goregous as it is melancoly, lonely and filled with menace. The art style is fantatistic, a gritty supernatural reality that makes you stop to take it all in (particularly with photo mode it's photo realistic at points).
+Subject Matter: Ninja Theory naturally took a gamble on taking on such a sensitive subject that is mental illness. To their credit they have done their research and haven't shied away from showing both the darker and lighter sides of the subject matter.  It offers an insight into mental illness that would be difficult to pull off in other mediums.
The voices, angst, searing colours, random symbols and fragmented screens with live video performances mixed into live gameplay all combine to make the average person finish the game very reflectively on what remains, to this day, a very taboo subject. I felt it enduced a lot more understanding and empathy for my part.
+Combat - Combat was really good in this game, it felt like it should feel fighting with a broadsword: impactful and weighty. As new enemy types entered the frey you had to think tactically and pull off a greater selection of moves to beat them and the controls were responsive, fluid and simple to learn.
Good job to Melina Juergens and the fight choreography team/animators, it was like Witcher 3 style combat - I felt cool kicking Vikings off bridges with a Senua highkick.
+Puzzles: Puzzles were unique, embracing the vision and creative aspects of the subject matter.
+Enemies: Good selection of enemie types, art style and concept of the various Vikings etc.. was very imaginative. Spot on.
In terms of cons: mostly minor points
-New Game mode:  Would be good to get a 'level' or load system in place as I'd like to go back and show certain bits to friends/retry certain areas again without starting a new game each time. Or to show certain scenes.
-Photo editor: Photo editor is a great idea, but it doesn't have an option to actually take a photo in game with it, can only print screen. Adding the ability to take a photo in game seems a bit missed. Given how gorgeous the game is and how otherwise intuitive the editor is (with filters and depth/roll options). Up/down button similarly, didn't seem to work for me.
- Puzzle introduction: Only got stuck once or twice on the puzzles, as there's literally no hand holding in the game (which is good). The first real symbol I was walking around confused as to what to do, as I misconstrued that the game suggested her focusing eyes closing/glowing red was the key when it was just the symbols lights blinding her like a laser pen seemingly.
Overall rating: 10/10 - would gladly go through Hell and back again with you Senua.
(Sequel please- Senua: Ragnarok)

So, I pretty much ridiculed this game when it came out - not the people that bought it, but the game.  The game was enjoyable for some, but as the ratings showed, it was too barebones for most - or more accurately, what was released was not what people expected...  What people were led to believe the game would be.
Here we are now at 1.3 and so much has changed.  Sure, there are still bugs, still features that people wish were implemented, and various things that people simply hate, still, about the game - space combat for one.  However, with the introduction of bases, a storyline, better flight mechanics on planets, etc., they have taken the game in several steps in the right direction.
I'll be honest, the base building was a big draw for me.  Apparently I wasn't alone in this respect.  The fact that it was implemented in a way that no matter how far you travel away from it, the base can still be useful - bonus.  Still, not the best base building out there, but pretty darn good.
The game went from a very disheartening, "Mostly Negative," from early buyers to the very optimistic, "Very Positive," from recent reviews.  It doesn't mean the game doesn't have issues or that the game is now a success.  It means that the dev team actually carried through on what should have been done closer to launch - whether you blame Sony for that, meh.  The updates have moved the game in the right direction and it will be more of these updates that determine the final fate of this game.
I hate to make the comparison, but it is almost like a pure space version of Minecraft minus some of the more technical things available in that game - redstone circuits, logic gates, etc.  However, it does have a loose story - you don't have to follow - base building, various mobs, better graphics, and the one thing that has always been the main appeal of Minecraft - the ability to forge your own story.  This last was something that fans of this game have always crowed about, right from the very start, but it wasn't until this update (and the sale price cut) that I was willing to find out for myself.
I'll give it a thumb up and hope that Hello Games continues to surprise those of us who doubted.

Like it a lot!
Absolutely worth a look if you like puzzle games, and maybe even rythm games like Rockband, DDR etc.  TL;DR- I find it to be fun and addictive, in the good way.  Buy it; it's like $3.
It's a fusion of your match-3 type puzzle games (Columns, Bejeweld, Candy Crush etc) with a timer aspect like the rhythm games have, mixed in special moves and an RPG aesthetic- something like an RPG version of Super Puzzle Fighter II Turbo.
As with many puzzle games, the things speed up during the course of the game/match, which ups the level of excecution required- unlike just using a keyboard to move directions and a button to rearrange like your classic puzzle games (Tetris, Columns, Puyo Puyo etc), you use your mouse to move around tiles of the same color together to form gems (chargers), which allow you to destroy the tiles/runes of enemy monsters.  This gives you more freedom, but also allows for a challenge, since you have to figure out what to move where, before things scroll offscreen, resulting in either the loss of assets, or taking damage from an enemy rune which was not destroyed or moved.
From a design standpoint, there are a lot of good touches here- aesthetically it looks pretty good, (simple is good), and there are actually an additional three soundtracks, each of which you unlock by beating the game.  When a character is low on health, their color of tiles in the timeline (fatestream) will show cracks, indicating that they are on the verge of death.  The RPG aesthetic works very well.  It took me a while to realize that the various monsters seem to have different styles and skills, which was a nice thought.
From a gameplay perspective, I like that there is some element of excecution allowed in the special attacks- to poison an enemy with the archer, you have to swipe your mouse in the direction of the enemy monster and hit a target.  Healing spells heal more the more frequently you click the appropriate color after choosing to use that skill, etc.  If you want to level up to gain access to skills, there's a bonus stage between battles- but this is also timed, and your ability to level up is dependant on your ability to match special star tiles before they scroll offscreen.  These things help keep players, or at least me, more actively engaged, and I dig it.
If I were playing this game using my hands/fingers? Maybe. If you play this game all the way through using a mouse, you are asking for carpal tunnel. Gameplay is a horizontal match-3 variant.

The Sega Mega Drive Collection is basically an emulator with a small selection of Sega’s best games, However games are bought and added to your library through DLC essentially. It’s not a bad system and you can choose to buy individual games rather than buy them in bulk for a high price. Although cheesy to me, the Sega Mega Drive launches through steam and in the application you are brought to a bedroom with a CRT TV and a shelf full of the games you bought for the Mega Drive.
The point of this is to recreate the environment of someone who played these games back in the day if you hadn't already. Alongside this there is a day-night cycle while being in the room. The way you play games in this application is to essentially select the game you want to play on your shelf of purchased games and watch the animations of the game being taken off the shelf and put into the Sega console below the TV. When you start the game you also have the ability to play the game with a fishbowl effect on the screen and glare like there would be on a regular CRT monitor.
Again Cheesy to me, but I appreciate the effort that went into it. If you want to avoid all of this you can simply by selecting the simple launcher when launching the Sega Mega Drive game in your Steam Library and thankfully so, because there are some options and menus that are hard to find in this bedroom setup that the developers’ have you start all of your games in. Aside from that you are playing all of your old Sega games that you bought prior to launching the Mega Drive.
Like I said before this is basically a glorified emulator that you can purchase games for and they work as they should, but I swear that I get these frame rate drops occasionally when I'm playing the sonic games and it’s likely because the application is forgetting to dump files and free up space or something. It’s nothing that ruins the experience but just something to keep in mind. Overall it’s a decent way to sell you some old Sega games that you maybe don't have a way to play and something that I would recommend if you want to play some old Sega games.

Overall I will give this game a 5/10. It was on sale for $3.00 when I bought it on a Steam sale. If you look at buying this game at all, I reccomend waiting until it goes on sale. While the game was fun and kept my attention, I am still rating this with a thumbs down because of the many down sides to the game. The game crashed on me several times throughout my playthrough, probably once every 2-3 hours worth of gameplay at various points in the game. While there are a few sidequests you can pick up pretty late into the game, the main storyline is quite linear. And while Darksiders 1 was a very pure game at heart with it's combat and puzzle solving, Darksiders 2 attempted to give more of an RPG feel to it's game. Unfortunately, I don't think it did much to add to the game at all. The leveling is nothing more than arbitrary, and  the random loot drops are needless and excessive in most cases.
The puzzle solving was fun for the first half of the game, however, at a certain point the game just felt like it kept dragging on and on. You meet a new NPC, and he needs you to go run an errand for him, and then after spending an hour going to collect a few things for the NPC, you go meet another NPC and it's just rinse and repeat, even 15-20 hours later.
The biggest negative for me was about 19 hours into the game, I ran into a very serious crash bug during a cutscene at Archon's citadel. Restarting the game didn't help, the crash occured in the same place. Skipping the cutscene didn't help, would crash immediately. Checked the forums, and the devs said that they found an issue and would patch it asap, however, that was a post from 3 years ago, and clearly the game was never patched to fix it. Many people reported that leveling up, or talking to a few different NPC's fixed the issue for them, but I had no such luck. So I am done with this game. This is even the new shiny Deathinitive edition, and it still had many crash issues. Disappointing.
However, I got my money's worth from the game. All said, if you are looking for a cool puzzle solving game like Zelda with the combat of God of War, perhaps this is a game for you. But if you hate games that make you feel like "I've been here and done this a hundred times before", then pass this one on by.

I've only skipped through this so far,
That being said, I would like to point out that this mod
, especially when it comes to overall color/lighting of a space or even an entire map. The more heavily stylized turquoise sky/fog in Ravenholm stands out as the most obtrusive artistic change to me, and while some may argue it looks better, it's a fairly drastic departure from the nostalgic Ravenholm ingrained in my mind. The “more realistic” indoor lighting changes will unfortunately sometimes change the color temp as well and eliminates the cold, industrial, fluorescent lighting feel in some scenes that was part and parcel with the Half-Life series. And while addressing the stark nature of map boundaries with extra foliage or details seems appropriate, completely changing landmarks with new styles of buildings not previously seen seems like a bold choice. (In a small way, that's changing the HL universe.)
Other small items: G-Man's glowing eyes during the intro comes off as a bug rather than an improvement. And while adding small wave patterns to the shore line was direly needed, the random 16 foot sprays crashing against rocks don't seem plausible at all given the tame water and come off as extremely odd. At first I didn't even recognize what they were and thought it was some sort of explosion/glitch. Just bring them down to about 20% of their current size and I'm sure it would be a nice addition.
For every negative, there's a dozen positives though. I was always a proponent of Valve going back and fixing visuals and bugs in HL2, both those that were there from the beginning and those caused by subsequent updates. (I still think they should!) But I'm glad Filip has taken the time over the years to do this and a few other items while retaining HL2's vision and not going crazy with extras.
This is about as good as you're going to get if you want to get a more polished HL2 and don't want all that FakeFactory junk. Great job Filip, and THANK YOU SO MUCH for being a giant fanboi... we are all reaping the benefits!!! :)

It's...okay, but there's just not enough there to keep me interested. The concept is interesting, but the story, dialogue, and overall execution is lacking. An interesting mix of Arkham-esque brawling, environment traversal, and, while not nearly as prevalent in your average title - mind-rewinding ♥♥♥♥ery.
The combat is comprised of your standard light and heavy attacks, with a long-distance roll as an evade. What makes the game much more interesting, however, is the custom combo-mechanic in place, which allows for different "pressens", which are each individual element of the combo, which offer everything from increased damage, to healing, to the faster regeneration of the plethora of powers (shield break, stun, extra power, etc) on offer.
As interesting as entertaining as the combo mechanic is, however, you will quickly build a standard deck of 3 or so essential combos that will serve you throughout the vast majority of the game. The mechanic is fun at first, but becomes almost pointless not far into the game.
On a visual level, the game impresses. Purely adequate texture work aside, the game shines through in its use of color, art design, and highly detailed, if linear world.
Not technically impressive by any means, but a great showpiece of overall art design that keeps itself interesting and entertaining to the eyes throughout it's moderately varied world.
The game clocks in around 8 or so hours on the medium difficulty, though I recommend playing on the hardest setting for any sort of real challenge. Only a few deaths were to be had throughout the entire experience, so anyone looking for an even somewhat hardcore playthrough should try their hand at the title.
Solid voicework hold up a rather middling, tame story that, while interesting, felt a bit scattered. With a couple plotholes and logical falacies put in place for good measure. There are a few strong characters to be had here, but most are offered very little screen time, with the protagonist, Nilin, serving most of the narrative-driven expression on your journey. Luckily she holds up very well as a character, and is most definitely a driving force in an only moderately entertaining story.
All in all, I enjoyed my time with this title. The gameplay is, for the most part, fluid. The story, for the most part, is worth experiencing. And the production value, for the most part, is properly on show.
If you find the game for $10 or cheaper, I definitely say it's worth the time spent.

a lot more like a visual novel / walking simulator throughout most of the game. You solve puzzles, take in the environment, let the story take you away to another world. And then the game kicks you over the shin with sudden, intense combat (which feels a lot like the combat in Dark Souls 3, in my opinion).
The game tells a sad and painful, yet honestly beautiful story of a woman, who all of her life has struggled with inner darkness and heartbreaking loss, sprinkled lightly with norse mythology. It tells an, albeit imperfect, tale of life with psychosis, struggling with your inner demons. I had to take several breaks to clear my head of the mental state the game put me in. The blurred lines between reality and fantasy, and the struggle of self-hate hit closer to home than expected.
That said, however, I utterly loved this game. The narrative, the graphics,
the sound (the music during the final battle is incredible). I feel that I learned a few things about myself throughout this experience.
Easily one of my favorite games of 2017.

Senua's Sacrifice was easily one of the better games I have ever played. Ninja Theory did a outstanding job at creating an engrossing story and a character you can empathize with and care about. Mental illness is still heavily stigmatized in modern society but games such as this help to start to bring attention to the issue rather ignore it. The voices and other aspects of mental illness are handled very tastefully and respectfully - there was a great deal of care taken in crafting Senua's character to make her feel like a real person.
Senua's journey takes her in search of the soul of her lover into the realm of the Northmen. There is a lot of exploration through absolutely stunning environments, intersparsed with puzzles. Combat is brief and usually quite brutal but still feels quite fair. There are some parts in the game that err on the side of unsettling but there are no jump scares which is always a plus.
I only ran into one small bug which was easily fixed by going back to the title screen and reloading my game but otherwise I had no issues at all. The length of the game is adequate for the price - roughly 8 hours but you may want to get it on sale (I got it for about 22 instead of 30).
I recommend this game to anyone that wants a one a kind experience. Please make sure to play with headphones for an even more immersive experience.

Following on from the successful Call of Duty 2, developer Infinity Ward moves to modern warfare with Call of Duty 4.
Story: Modern Warfare starts off normally enough, with the opening mission guiding the player through a training session involving firearm use as well as general movement of the character. However, once we hit the second mission things start to get interesting. It involves a SAS soldier by the name of John "Soap" MacTavish who is after a package on a Estonian Freighter. This mission is tense, exciting and memorable and sets the tone for the rest of the missions in the game. The pacing of the story is superb and never do you feel at any point that the campaign is boring to play through or lacks variety. Each mission is designed expertly and contains memorable characters, level design and scenarios. The story was easy to follow and is the start of the Modern Warfare storyline.
Graphics: The game has started to show its age and rightfully so, as it was released a full decade ago. Textures look muddy by today's standards and there is not much detail in the character models, vehicles and weapons. They all look pretty basic. As a result, it would be difficult for this generation of gamers to completely immerse into the experience and they may not enjoy the game as much.
Sound: Gunfire, soldier's screams and the whir of vehicles are captured accurately and sound authentic. You really do feel like you are in the midst of a battlefield when these sounds effects go off and credit to Infinity Ward for having excellent sound designers. The voice acting is also superb. Each voice actor brings an authentic performance to the table which allows the personalities of the characters such as Captain Price to shine as well as depicting emotion well.
Gameplay: The gameplay of Call of Duty 4 has set the benchmark for all other FPS games to follow. It is fast, frenetic and highly addictive. Controls are tight and it feels very smooth to move your character around the level and aiming is easy to accomplish and highly accurate. It often feels very satisfying to land a kill may it be in the single-player campaign or multiplayer. In regards to multiplayer, it is still active to this day and at any given hour you should be able to enter a server filled with people and play.
In summary, Call of Duty 4 - Modern Warfare is an outstanding first-person shooter game. It has redefined the modern FPS and its formula of having blockbuster action set-pieces and zippy gameplay has been copied over and over again. It is a must-play for any gamer.

Not a bad street racing game. Gameplay is solid, perhaps a notch ahead of what the NFS games from this era gave us. The handling model is a bit grippy but the car behaves well, paying for repairs or a new bottle of NOS are nice touches. Even though winning Arcade Mode, something doable if you're not uttery useless at driving, will give you a slightly overpowered car
But overall, the game lacks in content. There are 50 unique cars, but the game has the Gran Turismo syndrome, which means you get 6 Eclipses, 6 Skylines, 6 Celicas, 5 Supras, 5 350Z, 4 Imprezas, 4 RX-7s, 3 Jettas, 2 RX-8s, 2 Golfs, 2 IS200s, 2 Evos, 2 MR-2s and a lonely AE86.  The races take place on 3 different maps (LA, Miami and Philadelphia) but not only are the maps tiny, you can only freeroam in LA. Not that you will want to do that, as the cops are always watching you (sometimes engaging pursuit as soon as you leave an event -- or when speeding), you will have to pay for repairs and there's no GPS to guide you to any event. Freeroaming is more annoying than engaging.
"Girlfriends", another selling point of game, are useless. Unless you enjoy heavily dithered low res pictures of not particularly good looking asian women, 240p videos of them dancing at really, really ♥♥♥♥♥♥ songs and insultingly low quality models of them doing the start routine thing in street races. Instead of spending budget on paying the girls, paying artists to model them, paying photographs to take all the pictures and paying the music they dance to, the devs should have focused on more actual content. At least the challenges they give you are fun to play through.
Which brings us on to graphics and audio. The game is old, and the graphics clearly show their age, but it's not too shocking. You get 2003-like shine on everything, bad sun sprites blocking the view and blank interiors but it's holding up rather nicely. Apart from the character models. They aged like milk. Engines sound like drones, the rolling sound from the tires is a bit too pronounced (unless that was the sound from the engine, I can't really tell) and the music is really, really bad. "I muted it in less than 5 minutes" levels of bad.

Oh boy, this game brings so many memories. I remember when I got it in circa 2008 on a DVD with a computer magazine I used to love.
I read the little "review" in the magazine and jumped on the game. Since I was a little girl still I was blown away by the game, honestly. All these shiny cars, so many posibilities how to tune up your car, I could even "own" girls. It was simply awesome for me. I could say that I played some solid 100 hours on it. I wanted 100% progress no matter what.
And here I am after 7 years. I got it with a bundle for 0,99$. Bargain for a game I used to love so much.
You know how sometimes people tell you to not expect much from things you used to love so much and you come back to them? Yeah, there is a good reason for that.
When I first started the game after so long I already noticed that this game is pretty cringy. The music is simply horrible, let's be honest. I had to turn it off after some while and just play my own music over it. Only listenable track is "Madhouse". I mean, yeah I get it there wasn't much cash left for a decent music, but gosh, you could slap some better music over it that wasn't that bad. Nevermind!
Also the gameplay is pretty easy. It isn't really hard to get on the top with a car you got as a starter. I am not trying to say you will finish the whole game with just Subaru Impreza but yeah, you will surive with that car untill you save for that Nissan Skyline loved by everyone (This game made me fall in love with that car even tho I know batshit about cars...).
Anyways, the graphics are acceptable. Always could be better tho. I don't like comparing two completely different games but look at Half life 2 and graphics of this game! Nevermind, let's keep on rolling.
Overall this game is still playable and I must admit I do enjoy it even after all these years but it isn't what it used to be.
Even after this all it will still stay in my heart <3

After patches and updates to 1.3 I'm finally writing a review. The game still has one of the most boring gameloops ever created. Also last update reset all the mind numbing fetch quests simply to rename a few items and add a few more. I have no motivation to go back through the mind numbing fetch quests to get the same stuff with different names. Probably never reach the end of the base quest lines again.
Graphics have improved a ton but the core gameplay loop is as hollow as its ever been. Base building makes zero sense and looks to be added just because the fan base wanted it because it does not fit into the game at all. Clunky mechanics were added to support the idea of having a base yet being able to travel around. However one jump can put you 400 light years from your base and my questions is.....why would you want to go back? You are supposed to keep moving. Base building has no point and there is no reason for it in the grand scheme of the game....which is barely a game. Planets and eye candy serve to cover an empty shell of a concept. They are mere window dressing that tries to cover a fundamental problem. There is nothing noteworthy to do in the game.
There is no challenge in this game that equates to more than keeping little bars full so you don't die. That is NMS in a nutshell. It is a very boring game loop. All games are loops but this loop isn't fun. Do not believe any review that says the experience is chill. It isn't. You are constantly annoyed by your suit telling you this is low or that is low or this needs X. So annoying. If it were real life I would have ripped my suit off and let myself die just to get some peace and quiet. NASA space suits have enough oxygen for 8 hours yet in this game your suit barely has enough resources to fend off cold, heat or anything else for more than 5 minutes. Ridiculous. Next time you want to feel what this would be like go scuba diving yet only take enough oxygen for about 5 minutes. Let me know how that works out for you.

My description for this might seem really odd, but it's actually a pretty fantastic blend of the match-3 puzzler and RPG genres.
Using your party of 4 heroes [Fighter, Mage, Healer and Archer, of course], you manipulate the Fatestream [the game board] to drag, drop and click incoming hero tiles in groups of 3 to create attack tiles that you can click again to attack the enemy you're facing. Set up combos of these tiles and unmatched hero tiles to do bigass combos to deal extra damage [which means clearing a stage faster]. Once you beat a baddy, you use the same techniques to level up your characters, building your way up to skills that can affect your enemy or even the Fatestream itself, depending on the character. Keeping with the JRPG theme, your characters all have HP as well, that you have to keep an eye on. If a character gets killed, their tiles will still be generated on the board, but they'll be useless, and just get in the way of your other tiles.
It's this kind of interaction between the player characters, the tiles coming at you and the board itself where this game shines. Enemy attack tiles will slide down the board toward your characters along with the color-coded hero tiles. You can counter them with your own attacks, of course, but some enemies may have higher defense than others, which means that more grey, neutral tiles are in the way of your hero tiles, making it harder to position your attacks right to break those nasty attack tiles. Or they might be particularly speedy, throwing tons of attacks your way, or they might be a mage that freezes your characters on a hit, rendering those hero tiles immobile or whatever flavor your enemies have on your run to get to the Big Bad.
It can get pretty crazy in the later levels.
With unlockable soundtracks and hero upgrades you can purchase, there's a lot of replay value in it too, so you can keep going back for more and appreciate the gameplay with powerful rewards.
The only question I have is why in the hell is your hero information stored in the 'Beastiary'?

I want to slam this game for outright false advertising. I’m mean “Racer 8”? The thumbnail image is a collection of Micro Machine like cars plastered on a huge logo that looks like it’s right off a shelf at Toys R’ Us. Everything about it gives the vibe of a Micro Machine knock off. So what is Racer 8? It’s a tile rotating puzzle game.
Was it my fault for judging this book by it’s cover and booting it up for the first time without looking at even a single screenshot? Absolutely. But I don’t care, this game was an outright disappointment. Not because it wasn't what I expected, I can learn to enjoy a lot of games regardless of my personal expectations, but even as a puzzle game Racer 8 is dreadful.
Being a driving/racing themed game it needs speed; contrasting this is the fact that a puzzle game of this nature need to be slowly paced in order to give the player a fair chance at being able to think through and solve the board. When you bring these two things together it just causes a train wreck. I would love to see a game bring such opposite concepts together in a very natural and appealing way. Racer 8 is not that game.

Before the fans and supporters get upset that it's a not recommend...it's from a singleplayer perspective...let me explain why:
I got Running with Rifles after one of my buddies told me it was one of the best top shooters he has ever played. I looked at it and looked at it before my girlfriend said "Dude, just buy it already."
Going into it I didn't have high expectations...and I was happily surprised.
I like describing this game as a top down Arma. The maps are really big, there is a ton of soldiers on the ground at one time and it makes you feel like you are in an intense war situation.
Basically how the game works, those who are unaware, is you pick a faction from three: Green Belts, Grey Collars and Brownpants. Each faction has their own arsenal and arguable own play style. You then play a game of Capture the Objectives [think Battlefield or Domination] while completely side objectives [resuce prisoners, collect cargo and things like that]. You can call in artillery, reinforcements, you name it. You start out as a private and work up the ranks. Rank lets you have more people to command in your squad.
There is small little mechanics I won't go into such as stealth and the money/RP system. Just know, the game is bigger than it seems in the screenshots.
So I start playing Solo, and here is where the issues lay:
1. Prepare to Grind
Now, I've played Dark Souls a lot on console and other grind heavy games. The difference between those and RWR is how well it is done. In RWR you may be stuck on the first map, stuck on one objective until you rank up, get a lot of RP then get access to the weapons needed to supress the enemy. Your Allies will die quick, and you'll find only you and your squad pushing. Finally, you get bomb the hell out of the enemy with arty and finally finish a map.
2. Long Battles
Going back to Arma, I've been in really long fights. Some ranged from 30mins to 2 hours. I absolutely love long battles. The only problem with RWR is it's the same 2hours. Think world war one. One side charges, gets mowed down, the other side charges. It's a game of tug-o-war and it gets boring fast if Solo like me.
3. Final Missions [Maybe Spoiler?]
In the last final missions of a campaign you get the most ridiculously hard crap in this game. This whole game is difficult, but I found it fair up until this point. Final Mission 1, you are by YOURSELF pitted against a whole town of enemies. It's unbearable difficult.
Final Mission 2 is where I got stuck and stopped playing. Mortars respawn, so do turrets. So even when me and my small squad of soldiers destroyed the defenses of the enemy, they come back and push us alllllll the way to the start. Rinse and Repeat. It's so fustrating and annoying to the point it made me quit. These missions, are just way, way too hard.
Conclusion:
If Solo, probably shouldn't buy this game

I want to recommend this game. I really do. It accomplishes everything it sets out to do, and it does it well. Running With Rifles puts you in the boots of an average, unremarkable soldier in the ranks of other, somewhat less remarkable soldiers as you fight across various battlefields and attempt to capture territory for your various faction. You have a variety of weapons, equipment, and vehicles at your disposal, with access limited to your rank. The game excels at making the battles seem huge, and even moments of extreme heroism will have little impact in the overall conflict. RWR is about steady gains over time more than anything else. While this aspect is one of the game's greatest strengths, it is also its biggest weakness. You see, this style of conflict turns battles into repetitve slugfests, and you will often find yourself stuck taking and retaking the same obejctives, only to have to backtrack because a sudden enemy push has stolen an objective you secured half an hour ago on the other side of the map. One mission has you take and hold a single objective for 10 minutes (or 600 seconds, as the game states); this mission has taken me several hours due to an enemy push coming while my A.I. teammates are either dead or wandering off. Overall, while the game is interesting and has a unique feel, the player has to tear moments of fun from waves of tedious frustration and repitition.

The music reminds me of classic sci fi, and the planets/space stations are a combination of the JJ Abrams Star Trek movies and the artwork of Syd Mead. There is nothing more relaxing than just flying from planet to planet dodging space pirates, and then landing on those planets and seeing the weird life forms found there.

Ah, SRS, an oldie, and to some, a goodie as well!
Street Racing Syndicate has been out for about 11 years now, and taking in perspective of the times since then, in all honestly, this game hasn't aged as well as those who've played the game years ago would hope. But that doesn't mean it's no longer a good game.
I first played this game around the time it was new for the PS2, and the main things about this game that I wanted to experience again for the PC, several years later have you, was the feel of being in the import racing scene. It's not as immersive or as replayable as let's say Need for Speed: Undergound 2, but for those who are playing it for the first time, it'll likely keep you occupied for quite some time before you move on to the next game. The only real thing that stood out to me in this game (aside from the women, of course!) was how you can wager money with other racers, and with no restarts, you either win, or lose. And winning is just as beneficial to your career progression as losing is harmful, mostly because you'll be low on cash. But other than wagering and entering race series in the game, the only real use of money is to buy new cars and upgrade them.
That's probably the best part of the game: the car customization. Although the car selection isn't bad (some good cars and variations of the cars are nice, but there's not much variety in cars in general to choose from), when you do go to the garage, you're welcomed with performance upgrades, visual (cosmetic) upgrades, the dyno, and repairing your car if it's damaged. Which, of course, costs money as well, but a broken car doesn't hinder your car's performance. You have a good amount of options to choose from, though if car customization is what you're after, you're better off with Need for Speed Underground 2. Taking away the comparison of the two games, it's definitely an aspect of SRS that I enjoy, sometimes more than actually driving the car.
Let's not forget to mention, there's cops in the Free Roam of Street Mode (career mode basically)!  The Arcade Mode is fun as well, and you can unlock cars for completing Iron Man and Checkpoint challenges in that mode for Street Mode. And yes, they're customized and ready to be driven as soon as you unlock them! I haven't touched Multiplayer, but I definitely wouldn't recommend getting this game hoping it still works.
Here's where the downfalls come in. First off, the game is slow. I'm not talking about the game's progress is slow. No, when you're driving fast, it feels slow. Even with motion blur it feels as if going 180 mph is about the same as going 90 mph. I'm not exaggerating either. It's the main reason why racing feels less exciting than the other racing games of its time. Let's not even compare it to the newer games. Another downfall is the game's graphics. Sure, not bad for its time, but the textures is the only real downside to it. Frame rate is fine, and even View Replays look nice when they're focused on your car most of the time. This is with the highest settings too. There's also the physics of the game, not the best, not the worst, but the tuning options for each car in the game are there to make the physics more bearable. What car customization won't fix is how much respect points you need to move forward into the career mode. Once you get stuck, it a pain to go back and re-do events to get more respect points, even if you have some of the fastest cars and alot of girlfriends in the game.
The sounds in this game is a split, for me, at least. The cars and the environment sound nice, when they're not chopped up (that's an issue I had as well as a video I saw, could just be on my end though). The music, however, gets repetitive, and eventually it's best to turn it off, or play your own music on the side. The soundtrack isn't the best either, maybe one or two good tracks, but that's about it.
Overall, Street Racing Syndicate is a game to try out for it's price. It definitely won't feel like a waste of $10 (I heard it was 99 cents at one point, but it was $10 when I purchased it). You'll be able to enjoy what the game has to offer, but that's about it, really. The slow pace of the game and the narrow options of cars to choose from is part of what makes this game feel outdated, even for its time it wasn't considered any of the best games out there of the import tuner racing genre. If you've played this game before, it's a nice nostalgia ride.

This has been the most anticpated game of the year for me, and I was really skeptical if it would hold up to the goden standards of The New Order........ And I'm very happy to say that it does and in my opinion supercedes it..
Pros :
1. A more run n gun favoring level design than The New Order with a lot of corridors and great inter-connecting levels akin to classic old school shooters.
2. Better movement physics... It just feels great to run n gun in these levels.
3. Side missions... You can revisit levels that you've already visited to kill Ober Kommandos (Nazi high ranking officers basically), where enemy placement is different, thus giving you a more varied combat experience than what you had in the main missions. Though the levels are the same, it plays entirely different because of new enemy placements, so you get twice the replay value right there.
4. 3 cool super powers which are damn fun to use and alters your playstyle to keep combat varied and interesting.
5. Good story, though I don't much care for it. But like in TNO, the characters are well realized, and BJ Blaskowicz's voice is still great to hear.
Cons :
1. Slightly less punchier guns than TNO. (Though gunplay is a notch down, gameplay is still a notch up thanks to the level design which keeps it entertaining every moment.)
2. Some boring sections in the Nazi U Boat, which acts as your resistance base.
3. Some cut scenes that are supposed to be funny didn't make me laugh, and some cringey moments. (But then again, there were more great moments than bad ones in my opinion, though I preferred the always serious tone of TNO).
Optimization is decent, but not great. Using a gtx 970 I got 40-60 fps on High settings @ 2560 x 1080 ultrawide resolution. All in all, it has some ups and downs compared to TNO, but overall a damn worthy sequel and a damn QUALITY game.

What an amazing port in a world where we're used to being disappointed.
No issues at all besides the already mentioned bug that causes your game to crash if you go into network play with a long steam name. Game runs fine, no issues with controllers, netplay is relatively smooth, overall a great game.
Did I mention the waifus? There's a lot of waifus.

-First off, how's the port?
I've experienced no detrimental problems in my time with the game. No slowdowns, crashes, or anything for me. Game natively recognized every controller I threw at it (x360, ps3 stick, even a gamecube controller), and I was able to rebind everything. And I highly reccomend using some kind of controller for this game.
-Okay, so the game runs. What about the gameplay?
So far so good. Game is REALLY fun. REALLY REALLY fun. Especially when you get the hang of the homing system. I've had multiple times when playing something happens, and I just say "You can do that? THAT'S AWESOME!"
All the characters are really unique and feel fresh, and all of the arcanas are really neat. (I can stop time? Yes please)
Music is pretty good.
-Now: The netcode.
From my experience so far, it works very well. Matches have ranged from BUTTERY SMOOTH to slightly rough. Sometimes the worse connections can take a few seconds to get going, but once they do it's completely playable. You can't expect to to have smooth matches with people from out of the country, or if they just have a bad connection. No amount of netcode wizardry will fix that.
Oh yeah it's also got cute girls
You like those, right?
TL;DR
It's good. Buy it and come play with us.

I like puzzle games quite a bit, so on the surface Dungeon Hearts looks like it would fit pretty well for me in that Candy Crush/Bejeweled corner of my game library.  Heck, even the anime characters don't even phase me that much.  They're pretty harmless and fairly low key as far as such characters go.  The thing that landed Dungeon Hearts is the game play.
The puzzle style of Dungeon Hearts is not hard to figure out.  In theory, it's actually a pretty decent puzzle system.  Match 3 or more colors to clear gems off the moving game board, each color representing a different character who then does damage to your enemy.  Combine gems of different colors on different levels, double your attack score!  My frustrations come mostly from my self;  I just don't feel fast enough to be any good at the game.
The learning curve starts out simple enough, but it doesn't take long before you're in the full mix of battle and for me, I started to fumble my gems very quickly. This led to frustration, which led to resentment towards a game I wanted to be casual and ultimately lead to it's being removed from the hard drive.
I'ts not a bad game by any means, it's just not for me.

Well, here are the nitpicks I've generated so far:
The FoV slider is affecting the menu screens. It used to do that in HL2 and the episodes, until the SteamPipe update stopped that from happening, and I thought that was wonderful when it happened.
The intro cutscene...well, it needs to be put back to normal. Nothing should have been changed about that. Now the Gman's face looks red. It's probably just the lighting that was changed, because I can distinctly tell that in vanilla there is a green light coming from the left, covering his right cheek and the right side of his nose, but in Update those areas are just in shadow. But the *entire* face looks very red even though the Gman is usually portrayed as being extremely pale.
The commentary nodes seem to make all NPC action stop completely. This makes the whole experience unnecessarily slow.
Moving to the second map made me crash (with commentary on, didn't try it with commentary off). I had to use "map d1_trainstation_02", or the game would have been 4 minutes long. After that it's been smooth so far...
(very verrrry minor one: The magnifying glass in Kleiner's lab was moved, which kills the small possibility of seeing his head through it when he bends down...I liked trying to line it up :p )
Small visual bug in the final map of Route Kanal: shooting the SMG at certain areas of the toxic sludge create dark lines across the screen. It seemed to happen only on the near side of the plank you walk across to get to the boat room (left of the plank when facing the boat), not the far side.
The sky in the Gravity Gun training yard is too dark. Perhaps it's more realistic or something, but in vanilla I thought that scene was awesome for how you could see the swarm of scanners sweeping over, and I can't see them at all against the darker colored sky.
That's as far as I've played...I'm sure more things like this will come up, but my main point is that certain changes from the original (the sky color and the Gman lighting) might have unforeseen effects on the aesthetic qualities of important visual pieces.
It's not all bad of course. The lighting detail reworks, while they still feel like they're limited by the engine itself, are definitely an improvement and really remove some of the apparent age of this game. And the extra dead trees in Water Hazard, oh my, I never would have thought of doing that and it's AMAZING. But the best thing by far has to be the selective music fadeouts. Particularly at the point where CP Violation leads into the box with the rebel + Vort + Gman TV, because now I don't have to deliberately slow myself down if I want the scene to play out properly, but also all the fadeouts before loading screens make everything so much smoother. :)

Half Life 2: Update provides overhauled graphics to HL2 including enhanced lighting and shading effects, better water & fog, as well as many other things. This paired with a kickass Community Commentary, where the mod developers and several members of Did You Know Gaming and Ross Scott provide insight into the area you are in, while also discussing some of the finer details and cut content, which is a very intriguing thing to hear about while playing. A majority of the time, these commentaries aren't intrusive, and stop NPCs from proceeding without you as you observe the environment and listen to whoever might be doing the current commentary. This is a great survival game, and I can only imagine it will get even better before release. It takes a while to figure out how things work, but I never object to that in a game, I like a challenge.
The weather and seasons are great. I absolutely love the ambient insect and animal life, even though some of them startle the blorp out of me occasionally. Staying alive through winter actually feels like an achievement, especially if you underestimate how cold it is going to get (and are a real cheapskate like me, who don't want to use your resources on making shoddy clothing that don't last terribly long).
There are plenty of enemies to fight, but you can also avoid them if you just want to focus on surviving the world. Unlike games like 7 Days to Die, enemies do not constantly seek you out, so your base seems to be safe enough. The creatures in the game are also very believable. They look good, move well (I am VERY impressed with how the deer flee if you try to hunt them). The hostile ones have made short work of me, particularly when I want to "just look a little further, even though my health is at 24%". Curiosity killed the cat, but satisfaction brought it back. At least if said cat had a statue of ressurection placed in some nice spot.
This is also a game that sucks me in, alllowing me to forget my troubles when I require it. I may think I've been playing for a few minutes, but suddenly, hours have passed. Which is invaluable when I have a bad day, one that I need to get through with a minimum of fuss.
SPOILERS:
*Unless you live in the desert, save your smelting and baking for the winter. You're going to need that extra heat then anyway.
*Find a good pine forest to go lumberjacking in, in order to get enough tree sap; you're going to want those water barrels.
*When the mists come, stay where you are, or go straight back to your base. You'll get hopelessly lost if you're not careful. When it's dark, you can at least see the horizon and keep track of your position, but in the mist, all you can see are your closest surroundings.
*If you don't live in a dense leafy forest, you will want to harvest clay during your first summer. Midsummer may be the only time water level is low enough.

Given that I'm a fan of the series, it was obvious from the onset that I'd be comparing SRS to Need For Speed. SRS feels like a watered-down version of NFS Carbon (in the open world and impromptu races) and Underground (in the hot women starting the races and in the customization). I say "watered down" because it fails to accomplish what either of those NFS games did.
The graphics are unfortunately a product of the game's time. 2004 doesn't look so good in 2015, and the max resolution (which I can't even remember right now) is too low for today's standards. Thankfully, though, they didn't tax my computer like a lot of old games do for some reason, so at least there's that. And the cars look relatively nice compared to the scenery. Character models and cutscenes are horrible, though.
Gameplay shouldn't be too difficult - it's a racing game. Speed up, slow down, switch gears, get the position and win the thing. The nitrous works odd here, though; instead of having a limited supply that replenishes, you have a large supply that doesn't replenish. The handling also seems a little off than typical, cars are really floaty at times. Performance upgrades might change that, but the menu UI isn't exactly intuitive enough for me to tell which upgrades are actually good and which aren't. On the topic of menu UI, the entire game UI is really dated and uses odd keys like spacebar for some selections. Controller support is limited - it works, but you can't rebind all keys, and the UI doesn't show any controller buttons.
Music and sound effects are meh. That's all I have to say about them.
If you're looking for a good racing game, get a PS2 (or emulator) and one of the older NFS games. Underground, Underground 2, Most Wanted, and Carbon are very good ones, the latter two being much better than SRS in every way.

Pretentious Game is an indie puzzle platformer. The game’s aesthetic is incredibly minimalistic, reminding me strongly of “Thomas Was Alone”,  and I initially thought the game would be a simple go from A to B across numerous levels with increasing levels of infuriating difficulty. I quickly realised however that beneath the simple art style there is some depth (and pretentiousness!) to Pretentious Game.
The game has been released in chapters, with 5 released so far and apparently more to come. You play as a movable square block that has to somehow get to the opposite side of the screen. How you do this is (generally) revealed by lines of text accompanying each ‘level’. These helpful hints also reveal the plot of the game, hence the hidden depth I referred to earlier. Accompanying your playthrough is soft, simple, melodic music of a slightly depressing tone. While the music is nice I also think it’s potentially a bit too simple and it would have been nice if each chapter had a bit more music variety to it.
In terms of the storyline I would say that, while I do like the clever way in which it is told, it’s a bit too cliché for my liking, with the first chapter literally being a boy-meets-girl affair and the plot doesn’t really get that much more innovative later on. Having said that, I did find myself keen to find out what the next line of text would say and hoping that the blocks found a happy ending. It didn’t take too long to find out that ending though because the game really is very short and I’m guessing it won’t get much longer even with additional chapters.
Overall: I enjoyed playing through Pretentious Game but I feel a little more effort on an innovative storyline and a bit more time making more interesting platforming would have made the game much better. Despite that, I think it’s well worth picking up in the sale if you want to while away an hour or so playing a game with some simple fun.

Had there not been greater games like Divinity Original Sin 2 in 2017, Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice would easily win my heart away for 2017. It’s not often wise to believe the immense praise surrounding a game, but with HSS the accolades it has earned are well-justified.
In the solemn wake of Visceral Studios and of many publishers shifting away from single-player titles, Ninja Team manages not only to vindicate the excellence of well-crafted, scripted experiences but also to compete in quality with AAA games as a budgeted, indie title. On top of all these merits, HSS also manages to tastefully handle its taboo subject matter of mental illness in the medium of video-games where no publisher would dare explore for fear of alienating consumers. No section, however repetitive it may seem, feels like padding on the journey, and it’s because of this focused design that the ideas/themes explored are handled with as much respect as perfection for its craft. As a finely tuned linear experience, HSS can truly let the audience embrace the absolute turmoil and the horrors of Senua that no film can ever hope to replicate through sights, sound and bonding with characters on a screen.
Though there are legitimate issues with the core design, perhaps the most worthless is its focused design being a bad thing, the thing that prevents the game being undermined by its mechanics is how spread out they are to keep Hellblade from becoming tedious. Linearity is the saving grace of HSS that is the cornerstone of why it is successful. In many ways, the gameplay design is not only thematically appropriate given its subject matter but also mechanically varied as HSS focuses on its schizophrenic ideas tied loosely together on two foundations, fighting and focusing (puzzles). Beats in the story and levels may utilize one element or the other, or a mixture of the two, and its diversity keeps the failures of its basic combat or its puzzles from overstaying its welcome.
This idea goes back to the days of Half-Life 1&2 where levels are more about introducing and mastering new mechanics rather than being level-packs reiterating the same gameplay. One area might focus on introducing a new enemy type from the limited roster of seven (technically eight, one of which you cannot fight), it also might introduce world-shifting perspectives, or it may create several survival horror sequences to disarm you. Sometimes these concepts are one-time encounters or reoccurring obstacles you slowly come to master. Like the descent into madness of Senua, it’s an experience that always keeps you guessing and adapting to the situation in order to press onward.
HSS also makes a subtle change to the linearity problem cited in these single-player games by adding some branching paths that tie into the unreliability of the narrator, Senua, which only makes replaying the game more enjoyable. It would easy to lambaste the gameplay as a simplified DmC (made by the same developers)—or, ironically, a simplified take on the new God of War given its Norse mythology—yet the real brilliance is how the designers masquerade its faults that immerse the player only further into its world and into Senua’s journey.
Admittedly, the first time I heard Hellblade would tackle mental illness, especially psychosis-related conditions like schizophrenia, it was not something I believed a game could handle without compromising its authenticity. This is largely due to previous experiences in games like Dead Space 2 as well as studying childhood psychology around mental health issues, which often exposes how people attempt to prescribe a problem rather than identify the real issue. While DS2 pushed the line of tackling this taboo, its execution always felt pre-medicated as it followed the stages of grief too sterilely as if madness was a linear progression, and in some games the affliction itself is only a temporary matter that gets resolved completely.
However, what Hellblade manages to achieve is one of the most convincing portrayals of mental health because it never holds back its punches from its disturbing imagery, its sound-design, its unreliable narrator and its usage of game mechanics to explore Senua’s dissociation with reality. Audio especially plays a major role as Senua disassociates her voice as many characters such as the narrator, the speaker as well as her audience, both belittling and encouraging her at every moment. The narrative also utilizes subtle connections to psychology such as the exploration of the id with the superego voices of Druth, her mother, and Dillion contrasted with her alter-ego of The Beast/Fenrix, Hera and her father to spice up the voice-acting from being a one man show. Moments of Senua’s past are told out of order in response to traumatic situations or in the pursuit of overcoming them. Lastly, the game design itself uses mechanics all centered around the manipulation of perception from reading symbols into the environment or twisting reality with her own mental state to reiterate her descending state of her mind and the many obstacles she faces.
What is perhaps the most surprising is how the narrative remains easy to understand despite all the complexities thrown in with Senua as an unreliable narrator. The story itself, , which admittedly never communicates in-game all its subtitles like Senua being a Celtic character venturing into a Norse area of myth, follows a traditional epic quest that blends her own personal struggle with the awe of legends as Senua travels into the Norse underworld, Hel, which seems shaped by her own twisted state to torment her. Mysteries and unresolved queries from Senua’s flashbacks still retain their luster like thinking of the objective plot, but they never cloud it from the real story of Senua learning to overcome her own limitations and the acceptance that she has to live with her own problems.
Any other game burdened under the pressure of its publishers would think twice of tackling as many macabre elements and disturbing imagery as Team Ninja. None of which would end the story as Hellblade does where madness itself is not the final boss; it’s rather a living wound, a badge symbolizing the victory for another day, and accepting this condition is the penultimate lesson learned on a journey of self-revelation.
If the game’s authenticity and heartfelt dedication had not won me over, then the credits song featuring my favorite band of all time was the icing on the surprise that is Hellblade. Words can only begin to describe the sublime journey this game creates, far more than I have managed to communicate all the intricacies of mastership that Team Ninja displays. Games like Hellblade are more than worth your time given their brevity; they’re worth revisiting, again, and again—the insanity itself of wishing to spend more time together only is curtailed by the spoken words of goodbye of someone ready to move on, hoping that not only is she not changed but the world itself has not changed to forget her.
