Darksiders II = Zelda + jumping + leveling up.
To be more serious, Darksiders II is the game that matches Zelda in its fundamentals (dungeons, puzzles, monsters and bosses), but successfully develops its own theme and style.
This game is better than Zelda in the following ways:
* More intense battles. Death has a surprising large number of different moves, creating endless possibilities for combos, delivering an action battle experience comparable even to that of Devil May Cry.
* More wall action. Death can run along or jump off from walls, an ability that makes walls much more than room dividers.
* Level system, equipments and quest system.
On the other hand, Darksiders II is inferior to Zelda in the following ways:
* Limited camera adjustment. In aiming mode you cannot aim more than about 45 degrees up or down from horizontal. When clinging to walls, sometimes the camera is in such an awkward position that you cannot see the next target that you should jump to, and it's almost not movable at all, leaving you wondering if you hit a dead end.
* Focusing on one enemy does not stop others from attacking. Yes I know that Zelda: Ocarina of Time did this because player had little control over camera position, and in Darksiders II now we have that control. However here the camera is so close to Death that, at any time a forgotten enemy may jump out from behind the camera and give Death an unforeseen, unavoidable attack. It feels not fair.
* Crashes, glitches and soft locks. There had been once when I got locked in a room, because one enemy failed to appear, and I was supposed to defeat that enemy to proceed. Just imagine how much time I wasted examining everything in the room.
In conclusion, I do see the developers paying tribute to Zelda games (heavily so). They did learn and copy the Zelda spirit perfectly, throwing in their own creativity here and there, but there are also unignorable problems that affect the player experience. Had improvements been made, this game could become perfect.
+ Zelda elements
+ Intense battles
- Awkward camera
- Glitches

Dungeon Hearts really is able to capture my attention.
A seemingly simple turn based RPG with a twist, yet very fun. If you have played Magical Drop or pattern-matching games, you'll be familiar with this one. You need to match tiles, and explode them to do damage to enemies. Chain more special tiles to do moar damage. Yes, reflex and quick coordination are necessities to progress.
Your team consists of four characters, each has personal special attacks and abilities that you can invoke after reaching certain levels. Enemies can also attack you using their special moves, poison or hex that weakens your char. That's it, RPG style.
Graphic is great and can please my eyes. I'm kinda selective when it comes to graphic quality, but hey for this one I don't even complain. Not hi-tech like that of Diablo 3, but it does its job. Background graphic is kinda boring and repetitive, but during battles who gives a damn looking at background?
Soundtrack is included, much to my joy! And what's more, they're not forgettable. These OSTs are your typical RPGs' OST, fast paced and intense. Bosses' OSTs are even more awesome. My personal fav: Troublesome Foe.
Normal campaign has 3 difficulty levels. If you want challenge, start no less than normal. Hard is for experienced players.
What's more, if you've beaten the game and want more, we have Endless mode.
Overall, you can't go wrong buying the game. Someone mentioned this is optimized for mobile devices, but who cares? The Developer is active and listening to suggestions, worth every penny (and it's cheap!).

Deutsches Reich (German: [ˈdɔʏtʃəs ˈʀaɪç]) was the official name for the German nation state from 1871 to 1943 in the German language. It translates literally to "German Empire", with a context approximating that of "German Realm".[1] From 1943 to 1945, the official name was – but not formally proclaimed – Großdeutsches Reich ("Greater German Reich") on account of the new territories annexed into the state's administration during the Second World War.
To refer to the entire period, the partially translated "German Reich" /ˈdʒɜːrmən ˈraɪk/, which has no monarchical connotations, is often used,[2] with "German Realm" being a more appropriate direct translation of the official title.[1] Informally, this nation was also known simply as Germany.

It really pains me to say that I think you should wait a bit before purchasing this game. The game has a lot of depth and detail, but next to no polish. HOWEVER, if you're willing to put up with an unpolished game, and are more interested in the complexities once you get a house built and such, then buy it and try it for yourself. PROS:
- Fairly pretty
- Very good tooltips
- Plenty of detail (ie; hunger and thirst, temperature, weather, food spoiling, etc. - typical survival things)
- REAL WEATHER *AND* ALL 4 SEASONS
- Fairly good building system
CONS:
- Limited language support in its alpha stage (the Devs have mentioned they're going to fix this for the full release; when  the game stops changing so rapidly)
- Lack of polish (looking through objects, unreliable interactions, bad animations, river sounds are coming through the wrong speakers depending on direction, etc.)
- Currently no multiplayer in it's alpha stage (going to be added upon full release)
Now, this game has been in development for a little bit and they have shoved in a lot of content. But if you're looking for a good survival game that is more complete or has more polish so that it's more enjoyable; look somewhere else. If you're looking for a game to invest some money and time into and want to watch it grow and evolve, than buy this game now and support the developers!
Personally I am going to wait until they get into at least the beta stage before investing a lot of time into this game. Not because it's bad; but because I know that there is plenty of potential here and I don't want to ruin my perspective.

This is a unique survival game. This one has seasons and flooding. Like most survival games you have to worry about the basics. Food-Water-Shelter. Because of the seasons you have to plan ahead. Stock pile food and wood. Winter is harsh. Have to keep a fire going to stay warm. Make clothing to help resist the elements.
Make a shelter.

Yes there are caves, and abandoned settlements that contain good resources, however they are usually guarded by unfriendly NPC (Spiders, maneating worms, demon dog, dwarve archers) and other unknown mobs.
There is a "lives system" in effect. There are these resurrection statues that represent your character lives.
You start off with 2 or 3. You may build more, but if you run out of lives you can't respawn. (Unless you go to main menu and click continue)
Currently only Singleplayer, with Online in the works.
The game is in Alpha so it still needs a lot of work to make it more enjoyable.

So I pre-ordered this.
At the time, when I first played it, I came to regret that as a mistake. I sank a couple hours in here and there, but I just couldn't get into it. The story felt dull, the landscapes were just... off, and it just wasn't what was advertised.
I cast it aside, too late to refund.
Base building came out, along with vehicles, creative mode, and a camera. I played around with them, and they were fun - but the survival still felt lackluster. Creative mode got boring fast, and the camera (probably one of my favourite game features at the time) was hardly worth going into the game to use just for screenshots.
And now, after the Waking Titan ARG - we have Atlas Rises.
To be honest - I'm impressed. Suddenly, I find myself wanting to play survival because it's fun. Hell, I find myself wanting to play the game itself because I enjoy it now, not because I'm bored and need to sink time into something. The story is interesting and I want to see more, dozens of tiny little things that weren't there suddenly are...
It's a new experience.
In all honesty, I would have much preferred to see the game in this state on release. That way I would have been spared a year of disappointment. Hello Games has done what few developers would have done after the disaster of the release, and has spent time and effort making this game into something they can be proud of. It's clear they believe in the potential of No Man's Sky, and I find that inspiring.
I can finally, in good conscience, recommend this game.
I think the price is still too steep - but I would recommend it on half price.
They fixed most of the problems seen at launch and added loads of content that should have been in the launch. A year down the line, its a completely different and better game.

Only get this game if you liked Sunless Sea's writing so much you'd play it even if you had to do it while sitting on the world's most uncomfortable chair with someone poking you with a fork every few seconds.
The writing in this game is very good. A lot of the quests are poorly designed but the overall story feels stronger and more consequential than Sunless Sea, and the locations are creative and diverse.
But that's not what you're dealing with for the vast majority of your game experience. This consists of driving a train thing that handles like a 1930s tractor through very ugly (the art in this game ranges from awful to serviceable) procedurally generated rooms filled with obstacles that cause you small amounts of damage if you run into them. It's not challenging, it's mindless and repetitive, literally some of the most annoying content-spacing-filler I've ever encountered. Sunless Sea's long, empty stretches of ocean eventually grew on me, but not this.
Combat is equally stupid. I found myself in a fully upgraded ship constantly dodging small bandits because I didn't want to sit through the game's clunky turn-based combat system any more than I had to. This is even aside from the bug that randomly makes your gunners disappear for no apparent reason.
Yes, there are bugs (the game crashes constantly) but they're generally not game-breaking if you save. The real problem is the fact that the Sunless Sea engine is really poorly suited for some of what this game is trying to do. Every time there's a choice with a lot of options you have to scroll through pages and pages (no mouse wheel support); every time you acquire an item with an action associated with it your start page for every location expands, making every minor decision that much more irritating. The map is useless, too large even at max resolution, and the protocol for finding new locations sometimes just doesn't tell you where they are.
Anyway, a frustrating game. Just play Sunless Sea instead.

I'm not very far into this yet, but I can already tell I'mma like it. The only way I can think of to describe it, is a cyber-punk post-apocalytic-style RPG with better combat mechanics. (My boyfriend watched me play a couple fights and says they're like Sid Meier Pirates, but honestly, I have no idea. You control your whole ship, shoot guns, board the other vessel.) Combat tripped me up for a while because I couldn't figure out how to control my people (left click to select, *right* click to designate where to go), and I'm still far too weak to actually enter combat much at this point, but I think it'll be fun.
But I'm sitting here after a couple hours of play with a notepad covered in tables of where the cheapest places to buy things are, and where best to sell my secrets and stories to, according to monetary reward, and needed Rep. I don't know, something about a game where min-maxing requires making heaps of notes really revs my engine.
But don't think you *have* to do it - that's why I call it min-maxing. If you're happy to just pay the extra 5-10g (that's guineas, not gold), then you needn't be so anal.
The main point, though, is the quests. Like a traditional RPG, or a JRPG, there's a main plotline (escape the House! Maybe. Or burn it to the ground. Or something.) that has you driving round, discovering other cities and settlements, and striking out into the untamed wilds. But there are aso side quests. My first run-through, I spent 30 minutes without a single quest because I kept my starter crew and didn't manage to tag an event. Second run-through, on the advice of a guide, I hired an all-new crew and I have about ten side-quests that I'm working on simultaneously. So if you enjoy DO ALL THE THINGS style gameplay, that's here for you.
I don't know if the plots end up being rewarding, or if the story ends up being worth the journey, but I'm still willing to give a recc, just because I'm having fun on the way.

A House of Many Doors is imaginative and interesting to explore. There are many choices to make, areas to investigate, quests, and even romance, if you're into it and the NPCs are as well. A player can easily spend dozens of hours on this game. The music is decent, and the art is too.
Yet, despite these good things, there are problems. Travel is irritating, and there are bugs, typos, and story holes. The sad part is that most of these flaws probably would've been easily fixable -- at least, easily fixable in comparison to the amount of time/effort it took to make the game. Beta-testing probably would've been the way to go, since the story branches out into an ambitious amount of directions. Perhaps this means that if patches are applied in the future, then it will get better.
The most noticeable issue is traveling. It takes a while to navigate from place-to-place: you are a trackless train on many legs ("kintopede"), and skittering about a massive "house." For atmospheric purposes, long travel-times make sense. However, after several hours of encountering this design choice, travel becomes less of an aesthetic pleasure and more of a grinding chore. A teleport item ("fetch mirror") can be bought to partially circumvent this. It will teleport the player to some key points of interest, but not all of them, and not to random, empty rooms that have been visited before.
The 2nd biggest problem is in the game's bugs. These come up sporadically, but they harm immersion. For example, during a major plot-point (heist), alarms were disabled, and a guard showed up. My choices were to either trick the guard, let an NPC do it, or let another NPC kill the guard. I knew that my own character's Guile stat was high, and that I ought to bluff/charm the guard instead of an NPC in my party. I didn't want to kill the guard if it wasn't necessary, either. I made my choice: I would trick the guard. Instead of this working, clicking the choice looped back to the prior dialogue. I had to re-read the part about the alarms being disabled. I was then given the options for the guard again. The game was stuck on a loop. I had to choose the option to kill the guard to break the loop. That instance harmed what ought to have been a tense, narrative moment.
Sometimes bugs ruined settings, too. For instance, there's a room called, "A Room of Memories." It's hard to find and I was curious, wondering what it would contain. I explored it. I looked at the portraits on the wall. The text read, "With a jolt, you recognize the subjects of some of the portraits. Crewmembers who died while under your care. [Name]. Sitting on the wall, framed in gold. Exactly as they looked when alive. There is something accusing about their stare." ...That was odd to read, considering that the crewmember in question never died. He was alive, retired from my crew, pursuing his passion, and was working happily. I visited him afterward to make sure. (I'm not putting the name in order to avoid spoilers for the character.)

As for the "story holes," what I mean by the phrase is, "gaps which affect the game." I'm hesitant to call them plot holes, but they do weaken the story. For instance, you can rescue a lost child and have pets, but if you manage to escape, then there's no mention of what becomes of them. Considering that the child is human, a part of the crew (the "mascot"), is acquired from a subplot, can be interacted with (to increase sanity) -- well, it's weird that she just vanishes. She disappears without a mention, if the game ends this way, but she was supposed to mean something to the crew. Similarly, if you make a choice an NPC disagrees with at one point, then he'll make a speech and ditch you. The speech is the same whether or not he's married to you or just a friend. You can't attempt to stop him, reason with him, change your own mind based on his feelings/thoughts, or anything like that, either. There's no discussion. Unless you want to outright kill him, then he dramatically heads off. You can't even chase after him, but it's implied that he's probably going to die if he goes out alone. I call moments like these "holes" or "gaps," because they aren't flaws in the main plot itself, but they do weaken NPCs, and leave gaps in the emotional narrative that the story was weaving. At other points, it's just weird (like when an Aspect of the Trickster can remain in your party, despite completing an achievement that should have made them leave.)
I got AHOMD on sale for $2.74, though. I felt like I got a bargain, played it for many hours, and I still do recommend the game. If you like exploration games and RPGs, then this is probably worth playing. Despite its flaws, the world is interesting, the writing is decent, and the amount of choice is better than I've found in most games. The side-quests are also varied. You can do everything from bounty hunting, to ferrying around passengers, exploring hidden depths below cities, to ****ing an oil rig. This breadth of scope is why I liked it, because sometimes I was surprised at what I was able to do. I would often save, try something, and then reload my save, just because there was a zany option and I wanted to see what would happen.
The trouble is that going on about these positive parts would ruin them. If I explain them too deeply, then the surprise of finding them is ruined. Hopefully, my playtime of 50+ hours will speak for itself, and underline the fact that the positive to find in this game does outweigh the negative, because I wanted to play it as much as I did despite the negatives.
Sometimes when you stare into an abyss, the abyss will stare back. Sometimes it will tell you a story.

This is a rich, wonderful world to explore, creepy and fascinating with a tremendous amount of things to discover.
The inevitable Sunless Sea discussion: yes, you'll see similarities; think of them as two games in the same tightly-defined genre, where some of the mechanics and assumptions hold true from one game to another. HoMD is much more forgiving in its gameplay than SSea in a few key senses: it's much easier to come up with enough money to keep your kinetopede fueled, and it's much easier to avoid combat when you're not prepared for it (and win it when you are).
And that's absolutely fine. HoMD isn't about the roguelike race to accomplish what you can before inevitable death; instead it's about exploring and uncovering the dozens of interconnected stories of the House's various rooms and denizens. Death, insanity, and maiming are all possibilities, sure, but they're risks that you can manage and avoid if you don't want to see what happens when things go Very Wrong for your hapless captain. Learning what you can of the far-flung corners of the House is key to advancing -- the information and emotional experiences you gather on your adventures become the fuel for both financial gain (when you practice your craft as a journalist) and character stat growth (when you come home and "write" procedurally generated poems to gain the Apprehensions you pour into skill points). It's an excellent instance of designing the mechanics to reward a key non-combat conceit. Not to mention the computer comes up with some really entertaining poems. My favorite so far of my character's efforts was a gothic piece called "Hark! The Hell."
There are so many beautiful and terrible things happening in the House, and it's thrilling to know that at 23 hours of gameplay I haven't seen anywhere near all of them. What a delight.

Inevitably, A House Of Many Doors must be compared to Sunless Sea. So I'll compare and contrast the core common aspects of both games:
Exploration: There's a serious problem with the concept of open-world freedom when your map is unbounded but your tiles are; your centipede train must pass through one of up to four doors per tile, each of which is a self-contained map of randomly generated objects that can get in your way. On the other hand, there's a lot more to do here than just put your vehicle in autopilot - the map system truly feels like an exploration system thanks to said uniformity, and random events / points of interest are far more frequent with deeper reprecussions, allowing for a deeper experience while you're driving. Also, you're in a giant mechanical centipede :P
Combat: Undeniably superior to Sunless Sea, or even Sunless Skies, though it has a few major flaws. You and your opponent get four actions per turn. You shoot each other with fairly innacurate but extremely deadly (and varied) homing missiles, and can board each others' vessels in close-combat. In addition to hull and crew damage, you can also target the headlights for sanity (Terror) damage - crew members with low sanity tend to act like Darkest Dungeon characters and waste their turns flipping the ♥♥♥♥ out, running into random rooms and slitting their wrists or losing themselves to further madness. Naturally, you can blow up the enemy (and the win explosion is utterly satisfying) or kill the crew first and salvage better loot. Ultimately, the level of challenge is always context dependent and thus appropriate - Sunless Sea has a serious easy mode in the form of flanking from behind, but here and in the right context, any fight can be a routine pushover or a desperate panicking retreat. It's horror exploration combat at its finest.
Story: Holy.♥♥♥♥♥♥ Once you get past the cliche "Ancestors were trapped with aliens in another dimension, want to leave" base plot, there's enough story and mythology to make this a standalone universe. Eldritch monsters have dates with river goddesses. Sultans bask in the shadow of a derelict spaceship cast by a tiny sun a few clicks north. An entire city has gone to war with its own mirror reflection! Hearts ar literally stolen, ghouls roam in pirate ships, angels pray to the reich, rattus fabers illegally finish stories in a library of unfinished books! There are Sweeny Todds, kitsunes, and Uncle Vernons on your ship! You're the victim of brain theft and you retrieved the wrong memory! It doesn't matter if it was based on Fallen London, it's simply too complete to be anything less than its own epic!
So in conclusion, it is a whole game. You want a break from your local mythos? Read if you dare.

Well that game can not be bad because it is a sequel to the new order which was good....I was wrong and I will be reviewing wolfenstein 2: the new colossus in a pro/ con style and end with my conclusion.
Pro:
The games graphics are amazing. There are many moments in which the developers did an outstanding job in how the in game world looks like and how cutscenes are well designed. The game looks phenomenal.
The music is nice. It has some really catchy tunes for combat but the best part of all the return of house of the rising sun for the audio collectable. That is a really good song.
Con:
The combat is a let down. At the start you play with 50 hp so initially your a very squishy sponge but later in the game you earn 100 hp and still your as squishy as ever. The problem is that the developers made the character so weak and the enemies bullet sponges on higher difficulties. It is not a very enjoyable challenge.
None of the characters are enjoyable. The main character inparticular is also in a moody mood every since a specific character died. That character was not a huge deal compaired to his wife that is pregnant with twins...So for about half of the game you always have monologues about woe is me that this one character died. Other characters specifically the newer characters are awful. The mad black afro girl is always following that stereotype to which she is always fighting verbal confertations which extends the cutscene lenght. It does not make her a likeable character at all and everytime a cutscene revolves around her I cant help but feel annoyed. The other new character is a crazy dude that is hyped up about aliens and such. He is interesting in short bursts but in these cutscenes his enjoyment factor goes down the drain with how annoying he is in the long run. Finally a new character that we meet is some drunk guy. He is ok but what was the point of making him if he does not impact the game much at all, he is barely if ever present in any future missions which surprise is like 3.
Cutscenes are ungodly long. Cutscenes range around 15 minutes which is not too bad if done right but the issue is that the cutscenes deal with characters that are unenjoyable to see or hear from.
Theres the KKK. That is not a bad thing in my eyes because the new colossus is building a world of evil and if evil takes over the world then the evils like the KKK would most likely be present. That was a cool idea but the issue is that they show up for a minor walk by interaction and were never built upon ever through out the game. You dont fight the KKK or interact with them at all which is a missed opportunity to give the world more depth than nazi stabby shooty time.
The world is shallow like a puddle. There is nothing unique about the world we are trying to save. Most of the levels are ruin cities, labs, and space station. There is not diversity in the world or much in visual interest that gives the world meaning to either the character or player.
Whats the end goal? Not sure, the game didnt give me much insentive to care about a whole lot about the game, characters, the world, whatever. What is my insentive to play if the game does not give me goals to go for?
No chapter selection. Yea a pretty nice feature that was present in the previous title the new order. It gave the player the ability to choose what level to go to and re experience the story or specific moments of the story they enjoyed. That is missing in this game. Rather we get a mission overworld that we can revisit previous levels but at the expense of going through moments of the story we want to revisit. That is bad design because if I want to go back to venus and re-experience the hitler scene then guess what...i need to redo an entire new playthrough just for me to go back and enjoy a moment i want to enjoy. No thanks game.
Melee combat is awful. In general my idea of the game is that even if we are squishy maybe doing melee kills with give us back hp much like how doom did it...nope, rather than help the player your more punished by the fact that the melee animation takes about 3 seconds so that is 3 seconds for you to sit down and watch your hp drop from 100 to 0 with no way of defending yourself. Stay away from melee kills, that is the fastest way to getting yourself killed.
There is alot of collectables that ammount to nothing. So through the game you can grab alot of objects like gold, toys, concept art, star cards, and death cards. All they do is grant the player concept art. So all the collectables in the game add up to say it with me "100% completion." Not that the collectables help with my survival like how in the new order there were collectables that increased max hp or armor which helped in later levels or difficulties. That is not present here which is disappointing because i would like to know that my efforts for doing or collecting things ment more than artistic stuff.
Conclusion:

I don't think I have ever written a review, but I felt it necessary because this game is getting a bad rap and I don't think it's deserved at all. This game is awesome and well worth the full price. The story is great, the acting is absolutely first rate, and the shooting action is very satisfying. It's definitely not for kids though. It has very adult content and some nudity. I didn't play the first one, so I didn't have any expectations relating to that. After reading some of the negative reviews, I was hesitant to buy it. But when it went on sale for $29.99 I decided to give it a try. I'm very glad I did. It seems like the main complaints against this game have to do with three things - so I'll address them here:
1) Many say that the game is buggy. I bought the game a few weeks ago, and from start to finish I did not experience a single glitch or crash or whatever. I played it on a gaming laptop with a Geforce GTX 1070 and i7 7700hq. It ran perfectly and consistenty at 60 fps at maximum settings.
2) Some complained that the game was short. It took me 19 hours. I thought that was perfect. It wasn't long enough so that you start to feel like the game is a chore. It was the perfect length for a satisfying experience; and I still have a lot to do if I wanted to continue doing the kill missions and collecting items. Or I could go back and make some different choices and change up the play style if I was into that sort of thing. It definitely has some replay value because it's fun.
3) Some complained about the cutscenes. Yes, the game does have cutscenes. But they are brilliantly produced in my opinion, and they add to the overall story substantially. One person described the game as very little playing with mostly cutscenes. He must have really raced through the game to have that experience. I thought the cut scenes were timed right, appropriate length, and were great quality. One complaint though is that I don't think you can pause the cutscenes, and that isn't good if you get interrupted with real life.
In conclusion, I would say that if you're the type of gamer that holds the run button down and races through games trying to finish them as fast as you can and can't be bothered with the overall experience maybe this isn't for you. If you're the type of person that has to get 100% completion in games and appreciates collecting items and exploring everything, you'll love it. If you're like me and you're somewhere in the middle - you like to explore most of the game, kill all the bad guys, and collect a good amount of the weapons upgrades, but are not really concerned with completion you'll love it.
Overall, in my opinion Bethesda and the very talented team of people that created this masterpiece deserve to be recognized for an outstanding game. Great job! I would rate the game 9/10 stars.

I recommend the game but understand that it has some pretty glaring issues that could turn away those looking for TNO gameplay. I finished this game in roughly 2 days (which is not a problem, I like to no-life games, y'know?) and while it was fun, I found the game teasing more and more but not delivering.
The gunplay is still there, nice and responsive with familiar tools such as throwing hatchets and takedowns. However, the actual variety of the weapons only cater to certain styles of playing the game. The game gives you the Pistol 1960, an SMG, the Sturmgewehr rifle, the Shockhammer shotgun, a modified Laserkraftwerk (if you took Fergus' path), and a Kampfpistole grenade launcher that you will never use because it's supplied with no ammunition, not counting the heavy weapons wielded by Super Soldiers.  Out of all the weapons, I found myself absolutely wrecking face with just the SMG as the weapon upgrade kits no longer provide a unique alternate function to a weapon but rather straight upgrades that surpass other weapons. For instance, in The New Order, the Sturmgewehr could swap between a standard assault rifle and an underslung rocket launcher. In Colossus, that's done away with and the Sturmgewehr can get armor-piercing rounds, a marksman mode optic, and two mags taped together to reduce reload time.
Even with these upgrades, I never even bothered using the gun because it's overshadowed by the SMG, which can get a 90-round magazine, a slow-firing but incredibly powerful ammo type that can down Super Soldiers with ease, and a suppressor that makes it incredibly useful for just cleaving through the area without breaking a sweat. This is fun but it really prevents you from exploring other weapons on higher difficulties. Why use the assault rifle's armor piercing rounds when you can just one-shot a Super Soldier with the laser rifle or mow him down with a few upgraded rounds from the SMG?
---
Speaking of Super Soldiers, they're thrown at you just as often as regular Nazi troops. In TNO, they were essentially minibosses for big action setpieces and just one Super Soldier could kick your butt up and down the block. But in Colossus, they're as resilient as wet paper and can be killed with a few nailgun rounds (the  damage upgrade) from the SMG. Don't worry about getting attacked by one, their AI is absolute garbage and can't seem to ever aim their laser beams or napalm launchers at a standing target.
In fact, a lot of the special, heavy enemies from TNO are just downright cannon fodder in Colossus. Drones have poor aim and really only serve as a way to alarm Nazi commanders, the Super Soldiers are no better than normal Nazi soldiers in terms of difficulty, attacks dogs are a rare sight, and nearly every different Nazi soldier (rocket troopers, flame troopers) are either removed or just replaced with shotgunners. The only real threatening enemy types I've encountered is the new robotic humanoid enemy, the "robo-dog" that is introduced in the second-to-last level, the Panzerhund because of it sheer health, and the big stompy bots that can launch missiles at you. Everything else either dies too quickly or gets assblasted by the Laser Rifle in one shot.
And yes. The laser rifle is perhaps the best gun in the game.
---
The story is immersive, and I'll be honest in that it made me laugh or gasp a few times. I love Wolfenstein but The New Colossus leaves a lot to be desired. The actual campaign is short, incredibly short, and consist mostly of rising actions and zero resolutions. When I reached the end of the game (which, by the way, I wasn't even picking up as being the actual END of the game), I thought it was going to continue and get to the part I'm really interested in. Instead, I hit a button, the game builds up a big cutscene, and then credits roll. Nothing is resolved. The game just ends on a cliffhanging, sequel-baiting cutscene when it should have been the second half or final part of the game.
Instead, you're dropped back into the game and, instead of any kind of endgame story, you're just given a series of minigames and 2-5 minute long sidemissions that award you with a whole lot of nothing.
---
One minor thing that got me was how late some gameplay elements were introduced. By the time they introduce a certain type of new gadget, you've already finished the game. Colossus is fun and cathartic but seems to deal with feature creep.
---
The soundtrack by Mick Gordon is delicious, however, but that's because I'm a sound artist and love that kind of stuff. I don't usually turn up my games but the New Orleans and the Courthouse fights (you know the one if you've played the game) was probably the best part of the whole thing, music especially.
---

Shower With Your Dad Simulator takes place in the ancient city of Mapungubwe (meaning 'hill of the jackal'), an Iron Age archaeological site in the Limpopo Province on the border between South Africa, Zimbabwe and Botswana, 75 km from Messina. It sits close to the point where the Limpopo and Shashe Rivers meet. One thousand years ago, Mapungubwe appears to have been the centre of the largest known kingdom in the African sub-continent. The civilization thrived as a sophisticated trading center from around 1200 to 1300 AD, trading gold and ivory with China, India and Egypt.
Your goal is to transform this small city into a nation. Barbaric tribes will try to raid your areas, and European invaders along with other African nations will rival you for land.
The site was 'discovered' on 31 December 1932, when a local informant, Mowena, led E.S.J. van Graan (farmer and prospector), his son and three others, to Greefswald farm on Mapungubwe Hill. On the hill they noticed stone walls and on closer inspection, they recovered gold and iron artifacts, pottery and glass beads. Van Graan's son recognized the academic value of the site and contacted the head history department at the University of Pretoria, Professor Leo FouchÁƒÂƒ©. As a result of his intervention, the University negotiated with the owner of the property, E.E. Collins. In a legal agreement the University took ownership of the gold and other artifacts and secured an option and contract for excavation rights. The University also successfully requested a postponement of prospecting, mining and related activities on Greefswald. In June 1933, Greefswald was bought by the Government and excavation rights were granted to the University of Pretoria. The University established an Archaeological Committee, which from 1933 to 1947 oversaw research and excavations (read more about the excavations).
The find initially received wide publicity in the media, but soon the archaeological digs and discoveries made by the University were kept fairly secret and were only made public after 1994. Possibly because the discovery provided evidence of a civilization that existed and flourished years before European occupation.
Mapungubwe hill is 300m long, broad at one end, tapering at the other. It is only accessible by means of two very steep and narrow paths that twist their way to the summit, and yet 2 000 tons of soil were been artificially transported to the very top by a prehistoric people of unknown identity.
Archaeological enquiry uncovered the remnants of numerous dwellings, which had been built on the ruins of predecessors over many generations, resulting in a series of habitation phases. Radiocarbon dates show that the first buildings were erected below the hill at the beginning of the 11th century AD. But adjacent to Mapungubwe is the sister site of Bambadyanalo, which was settled even earlier. It seems that the centre of the state shifted from Bambandyanalo to Mapungubwe hill in about 1045 AD, when the town most probably became overcrowded. It was also at about this time that hills and mountains became associated with royalty and the noble classes began to build their structure on high ground. This is an important observation as it provided evidence of the extensive wealth and social differentiation of the people of Mapungubwe, in other words this ancient civilization was class-based.
The gold findings are also evidence of early gold smelting. A large amount of artifacts from the royal family were discovered at Mapungubwe. The best known of these objects is the golden rhinoceros. All in all, the amount of gold from this burial amounted to 7 503 ounces.
In the 1400's it appears that all the citizens of the kingdom left leaving palaces and the settlements behind. We don't know exactly why the people of Mapungubwe moved away, but the ruins give us a good idea of how these people lived and how their society and political structures grew over the years. Scholars believe that the climate in the area changed, which made it much harder to grow crops and feed animals, this might have caused the civilization to move.
Greefswald farm remained the property of the State from the 1930s. Management of the farm was taken over by the provincial Department of Nature Conservation in 1992 and control was transferred to SANParks in 1999. Mapungubwe was declared a World Heritage Site by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) in July 2003.

I felt quite emotional when I played this. Going "aww" and "oh no..."
That said, this is a pretty neat game that I played twice just to let the whole story sink in.
Pros;
+ Easy to play. You learn what you need to do very quickly.
+ Puzzles are relatively simple. The levels only become different in small steps. The text/phrases you get every level are enough to hint what you need to do.
+ Some of the puzzles are very clever and brilliantly thought up. This game doesn't only make you use your arrowkeys, but also makes you experiment, use the mouse, the mute button, etc. The game mechanism really enhances the strength of the story and doesn't hold it back.
+ The story is told in a minimalistic art style which made it easy to understand.
+ And the story is pretty good. It was a bit simple, but made me very emotional because of it.
Cons;
- I had a lot of difficulty at the (hidden?) fourth chapter that featured the two children. This was because of a jump trick you needed to do several times in a row. Needless to say, it made me suffer immensely and I never want to play that chapter ever again.
- The game is short (but sweet!). I replayed the first three chapters and managed to entertain myself for 101 minutes total. Sometimes I wish the game was a bit longer.
- I really hate how sudden the car scenes were and the (short) noises that came with it. I am a very sensitive gamer, so noises like that and sudden motions make me very uncomfortable. It was a bit of a jumpscare for me.
So is this game worth your money? Depends on if you think the price of the game is worth around 1~2 hours of gaming entertainment. For me it was worth it. Despite all the negativity in my review, I am very happy to have played this and the story will probably stick in my mind for a week or so.
I think this game is great for the casual gamer. Please give it a try if you can.

This is an early review of the game based on limited time so far.  However, since there is only one other review at this time, I thought I would add another viewpoint.
The game's graphics are very nice, although there are one or two textures that still need a little work.  The effect of the wind on the scenery is well done.  I also have not experience lag or frame rate issues.  So far, the game has proven to be difficult with respect to trying to determine which items can be eaten without getting food poisoning and every creature is much stronger when you start; all of which makes the game interesting.  The objective of a survivial game is, after all, determining how to survive.
I am looking forward to seeing how the change of the seasons affects the game; this is a unique aspect compared with most of the current survival games.   In moving around the landscape, it looks like there is an underlying plot that may prove interesting, but I am not far enough along to know yet how developed the plot is.
In looking through the discussions, the developers appear active and responding to comments which is always an important aspect of any early access game.
My opinon so far, the game shows strong promise. I am looking forward to playing it more and seeing how it develops.
Update:
Ok, I am a little further along, including having died and restarted a few times :)
The seasons add a very nice aspect to the game.  The flooding that occurs is also well done.  It is nice that the weather (wind, etc) affects how cold/warm you are.  Shading under trees and wetness also matters.  As the seasons change, the fruit and mushrooms become scarce, which is a nice aspect.  However, it is difficult to gather enough food and not have it go bad prior to the change of the seasons (which change slowly as you play). I am still working on how to survive this change in the availability of food.  The effects of injury and food poisoning are severe and absolutely must be avoided, which is realistic.  Although, in the beginning, avoiding them while learning the basics, is very challenging, expect to have to restart a few times as you learn the ropes.  There is crafting in the game.  Food can be cooked. Weapons, clothing, armor, etc. can be crafted.  It is possible to build buildings, but it takes a fair amount of work to harvest enough supplies (which is also realistic I suppose).  The trees seem to grow (at least they seem to, I have not stayed still and just watched one to be sure that is what is happening).
The game is hard...  it is a survival game, so that comes with the territory.
The developers are active, following the discussions, responding to questions/comments, and are providing updates already.  They also have plans for future development, based on some of the responses.
As far as this survival game compared to the many others in my inventory, this one shows great promise.  Certain aspects are still being deployed, but the aspects that are there are well done.  In my opinion, the seasons, the effects of weather on the player, and the effects of the seasons on the availability of food all make this game unique and well worth adding to the collection.
Second update:
I now have close to 50 hours in on this game.  Since the game's release, the developers have remained very active, adding new content and responding to both suggestions and bugs reports.  Since I started playing Crossworlds, I have seen many of the suggestions made by the community implemented in the game.  The crafting system has been further developed with seeds & garden plots, beds, and other items added.  The developers have also responded to the criticisms regarding difficulty, etc. in so far as several aspects of the game can now be tweeked, depending on the degree of difficulty that you are looking for.  The rate of food consumption and thrist can be altered, the length of the seasons can be changed, as well as several other aspects that affect game play.  Based on responses from the developers, additional parameters will also be adjustable in the near future.
All in all, this game is continually evolving and the steam community is playing a role in the development, just as all of us are hoping for when we choose to participate in an alpha release.
If you are looking for a survival game that has several unique traits, this is one well worth looking at.  A few of the items that I have found to be fairly unique include:  the seasons change (i.e., leaves appear in the spring and drop in the fall).  The snow builds up on the ground in the winter, it snows and the lakes freezes so that you can walk on them.  The rate of food production for mushrooms, berries, etc. is also season dependent as well as the amount of leaves that you gather from chopping trees.  Wind, rain, wetness, and shade (yes, the shade of a tree) all make a difference in how warm or cold you feel.  The water level of the lake rises and falls due to flooding.  Trees actually grow (not just appear as happens in most survival games).  Different items burn at different rates (branches, logs, coal).
Some aspects found in other games that are also in this one:  items have durability (although a somewhat unique aspect here is that durability affects function, i.e., a worn axe does not chop a tree as fast as a new axe), you can build a home, a campfire, a forge, etc.  One interesting aspect of a house though, it makes a difference in the winter if you leave the door open (or don't have one).  Another common aspect, if you run, you use up food and water faster.  And many more.
Overall, I highly recommend considering adding this game to your collection if you are considering acquiring an additional survival game.

I usually only play games that are heavy on story and rather short, like Alien: Isolation, SOMA and the like. Games that are overly grindy or where you do the same thing over and over are not really my thing.
This is why I hesitated for a long time before I took the plunge and bought this game. I had originally only heard of it in some kind of pre-release footage that showed a seamless planet landing. I completely skipped all the hype and letdown during release, didn't hear about it at all. A few months ago I searched for this elusive game that had the seamless planet landings and found No Man's Sky again. When I saw that it had mostly negative reviews but still a pretty steep price I hesitated. Eventually I took the plunge during a PS4 sale and bought it there.
What can I say, I haven't been disappointed at all. I've played the game on PS4 for at least 80-100 hours. I started at 1.2 and now 1.3 was released and made the game even better.

It has to be your cup of tea, to be sure, but if it is, you'll be in for a treat!

Its interesting at first, with unique looking visuals. The sound is hit and miss. It show potential.
That potential is ruined by highly questionable gameplay design. Forget about exciting dogfights. The enemy is weak and nonthreatening. There really isn't a need to upgrade your ship since your starting ship can easily handle the completely random times you get jumped. You can build a base, which you never really have to defend. A base is mostly a farm, a storage place, and a roof to get out of the acid rain or hostile elements. Sometimes creatures nip at you, but never pose much of a threat. When you shoot stuff to gather materials, these sentinal robot ball things come out and shoot at you.
Yep. Real exciting stuff.
Games like this are going to make me think twice about buying anything that says "procedural generation" in the description. It means the content is going to be a mishmash or random garbage that gets boring and repetitive fast.
Also, do not even get me started on the community. If you even suggest something could be better, the forums get toxic fast, and you will get bashed and flamed without any courtesy whatsoever. It is truely a fanboy game that will make you want to give up vdeo gaming forever to go play horseshoes or shuffleboard with the shallowest flakey people you can find.
A really grand idea in this game is repairing your ships hit points. You can build antimatter in your backpack, but you can't fix your ship's damaged hull with the materials you find. You fix your ship by saving your game, quitting, then reloading. I asked about this on the message board, and got flamed immediately. I was told not to get shot up as a strategy. That should tell you immediately the fans of this game just want to argue, and won't listen to any reason.
The aliens are real exciting as well. They stand around, and enjoy their existance as immobile statues that take forever to understand thanks to the "language grinding system".
You would be better served buying 60 dollars worth of plastic toys and run them over with your lawnmower for a laugh.

This game is absorbing and fascinating, and I recommend it without the slightest hesitation. It inspires the imagination and stimulates creativity and contemplation. There's so much to think about and so much to consider. The setting is evocative, its difficulty is not unforgiving (and it even suggests the "enjoyable" difficulty to start), and the very concept is absolutely enthralling. I was drawn in immediately, and I found it a great deal to comprehend at first, but found myself essentially living a life in this game, not just pursuing the next quest marker mindlessly.
That said, I must issue a caveat or two: if you don't enjoy games where your imagination is a large part of the experience, where you illustrate the unseen with your mind, you probably won't like this. There are also a handful of concerns, such as an apparent inability to heal crew members outside of combat and some seemingly arbitrary limitations of even visiting with people in your own home more than once, as well as assorted bugs that exist in the game. There is also, evidently, an extremely meta storyline that, once completed, can interfere with your ability to play the game, and that is by design. My feelings over it are conflicted, since it's between art and entertainment.
This is certainly an artistic game, and it does truly stoke the fires of the creative drive. I love it for that. If you are a creative person, if you like a little darkness in your games, and if you're fond of losing yourself in a setting, you'll probably have quite a good time with this game. It's worth full price, but it's absolutely worth sale price, to see if you like it. I wish there were more games like this, honestly. I haven't found myself wishing that in quite a while.

Just completed Helllade, and all I have to say is it was quite an experience. Ninja Theory really took care, and paid great attention to make this indie title.  I had discovered it by accident whhile searching "most graphically demanding games" on the web to test the  mettle of my rig.  It looked interesting, and I watched all the diaries on youtube.  Usually I want for games to go on sale (Havn't bought a game full price in quite some time)  Nut the diaries just got me so excited to experience this, I just bought it full price.  But for 30 bucks you really can't go wrong.  And of course it just went on sale again, but my experience was so great, I am not even mad about that.  Also I wanted to support the devs of this awesome experience.
The graphics were perfect.  They really nailed face animations, and movement very well.  It was a little unusual to see Senua in CG, then actual footage of an actor talking to her in the background, but this happened few and far between. and never lasted long.  Sound is downright awesome.  Everyone suggested to play it with earphones, and I will do the same.  You really get the 3d sound experience with phones.  Also you can hear the vioces in Senua's head much better.  Combat is simple, but a satisfying experience.  It is tight and responsive.  There were many parts that got my adrenaline going because Senua is faced with waves, and waves of enemies, with all the while Viking music is playing in the background.  I havn't enjoyed a game soundtrack this much since Skyrim.
If I had any gripes, it would be that the rune puzzles could get a bit tedious, and the enemies were not varied enough.  Once I got down the pattern of the 4 to 5 different demons of Hellheim, it was pretty easy to defeat them one on one, or two on one.  When they start to form a mob around Senua is when it got difficult.  I am a Dark Souls trilogy battle hardened veteran, and I found the combat to be not like the Souls series, if you are worried about that.  I have heard reviewers compare the combat to Souls, and I would say that is unfair.  Yes it is time based, and you have to learn your enemies' patterns, but that is about it.
In conclusion, I would say it was a great privelage to take this Celtic warrior with a huge heart all the way to the heart of Hellheim.  I wold absolutley play the sequel if there ever is one.  I will even play this one again even though it doesn't have much replay value.  Ninja Theory knocked it out of the park.  Forget Indie game of the year, Hellblade deserves GOTY 2017 period.  Get it, you won't regret it.  And no "How to?" guides, do it on your own....lol

Darksiders II = Zelda + jumping + leveling up.
To be more serious, Darksiders II is the game that matches Zelda in its fundamentals (dungeons, puzzles, monsters and bosses), but successfully develops its own theme and style.
This game is better than Zelda in the following ways:
* More intense battles. Death has a surprising large number of different moves, creating endless possibilities for combos, delivering an action battle experience comparable even to that of Devil May Cry.
* More wall action. Death can run along or jump off from walls, an ability that makes walls much more than room dividers.
* Level system, equipments and quest system.
On the other hand, Darksiders II is inferior to Zelda in the following ways:
* Limited camera adjustment. In aiming mode you cannot aim more than about 45 degrees up or down from horizontal. When clinging to walls, sometimes the camera is in such an awkward position that you cannot see the next target that you should jump to, and it's almost not movable at all, leaving you wondering if you hit a dead end.
* Focusing on one enemy does not stop others from attacking. Yes I know that Zelda: Ocarina of Time did this because player had little control over camera position, and in Darksiders II now we have that control. However here the camera is so close to Death that, at any time a forgotten enemy may jump out from behind the camera and give Death an unforeseen, unavoidable attack. It feels not fair.
* Crashes, glitches and soft locks. There had been once when I got locked in a room, because one enemy failed to appear, and I was supposed to defeat that enemy to proceed. Just imagine how much time I wasted examining everything in the room.
In conclusion, I do see the developers paying tribute to Zelda games (heavily so). They did learn and copy the Zelda spirit perfectly, throwing in their own creativity here and there, but there are also unignorable problems that affect the player experience. Had improvements been made, this game could become perfect.
+ Zelda elements
+ Intense battles
- Awkward camera
- Glitches
7 out of 10, good.

This is one of those few games that manages to nail both gameplay and story. Play The New Order first if you haven't already, otherwise you'll miss out on the story (of both games).
Gameplay: great guns with plenty of variety through mods and dual wielding any combination of guns. They all feel pretty powerful in different ways, so there's not a single one that feels superfluous. You can play this game stealthy or guns blazing, or a combination of the two. Think twice about cranking up the difficulty level though. Enemies become quite strong so just shooting everything you see becomes less of a viable play style. Doing the side missions early might make the story missions more enjoyable by unlocking more possibilities. You can still do them after completing the main storyline though, so you're not really missing out if you decide to skip them at first.
Story: the story continues where TNO left off, so you should definitely play that one first (TOB is not needed). They really managed to create a living game world, with a home that felt even more alive than the hideout in TNO. The addition of optional side missions also gives the world a more real feel. Maps are physical places and not just some scenery that you quickly rush through during the main missions. Also rare in games like these is the character development that they managed to squeeze in. The only thing that felt kind of off were the bad attempts at humour, they really felt out of place in an otherwise believable universe.

If you're a big fan of Half-Life 2 and/or you have an eye for detail, the differences between this update and the original game are definitely noticeable. Interior lighting in particular is hugely different in some places, having been relit with radiosity from natural light sources (such as windows), rather than the fake invisible light sources that were used to approximate natural lighting in the original game. I actually think the lighting could use a little more work, but as it stands it's definitely a significant improvement.
I've noticed several bugs/exploits from the original game have been fixed, and while I've heard reports of new bugs and crashes in this mod, I haven't experienced any myself after playing it for several hours straight.
The commentary is well-spoken and very insightful, although if you're a hardcore fan, you probably won't learn much that isn't already covered in existing resources (such as the excellent behind-the-scenes book,
). If you are interested in learning about the design process that drove the development of Half-Life 2, then it's definitely worth listening to (as are the official developer commentaries for Episode 1 and 2).
Overall, this is a pretty good update as long as you don't go into it with the expectation of an HD remaster (which it is not intended to be). Unlike other modifications such as the highly controversial
by FakeFactory,
is extremely restrained in its attempt to improve the game's visuals, with the goal of perfectly preserving the visual design and gameplay experience of Half-Life 2.

To the Moon surprised me quite a bit. I read about the game beforehand, as I usually do, and I thought the emotional element of the narrative may be overblown, as the game was made with RPGMaker, a platform notorious for rehashed titles.
I was pleasantly surprised by the lucidity of the story. It's not terribly complex, though a little far-fetched, it does tug on the heartstrings just enough to make it memorable. Two co-workers set out to grant a dying man's final wish, and to do so they explore his memories. What they discover, and how it all comes together, is very touching. I think the most overlooked element in the narrative is a certain realization relating to another person. Neither protagonist comments on it, to my recollection, which I thought was strange. It was the first thing that I thought about while viewing the ending.
To the Moon is a pretty slow-paced game, and there isn't much gameplay to speak of. While I recommend it, understand that you're getting into a linear story, and that story is really what you're paying for. If you're looking for something with more decision-making or action, To the Moon will certainly disappoint. If you're looking for an experience, you may just enjoy it.

Shower With Your Dad Simulator takes place in the ancient city of Mapungubwe (meaning 'hill of the jackal'), an Iron Age archaeological site in the Limpopo Province on the border between South Africa, Zimbabwe and Botswana, 75 km from Messina. It sits close to the point where the Limpopo and Shashe Rivers meet. One thousand years ago, Mapungubwe appears to have been the centre of the largest known kingdom in the African sub-continent. The civilization thrived as a sophisticated trading center from around 1200 to 1300 AD, trading gold and ivory with China, India and Egypt.
Your goal is to transform this small city into a nation. Barbaric tribes will try to raid your areas, and European invaders along with other African nations will rival you for land.
The site was 'discovered' on 31 December 1932, when a local informant, Mowena, led E.S.J. van Graan (farmer and prospector), his son and three others, to Greefswald farm on Mapungubwe Hill. On the hill they noticed stone walls and on closer inspection, they recovered gold and iron artifacts, pottery and glass beads. Van Graan's son recognized the academic value of the site and contacted the head history department at the University of Pretoria, Professor Leo FouchÁƒÂƒ©. As a result of his intervention, the University negotiated with the owner of the property, E.E. Collins. In a legal agreement the University took ownership of the gold and other artifacts and secured an option and contract for excavation rights. The University also successfully requested a postponement of prospecting, mining and related activities on Greefswald. In June 1933, Greefswald was bought by the Government and excavation rights were granted to the University of Pretoria. The University established an Archaeological Committee, which from 1933 to 1947 oversaw research and excavations (read more about the excavations).
The find initially received wide publicity in the media, but soon the archaeological digs and discoveries made by the University were kept fairly secret and were only made public after 1994. Possibly because the discovery provided evidence of a civilization that existed and flourished years before European occupation.
Mapungubwe hill is 300m long, broad at one end, tapering at the other. It is only accessible by means of two very steep and narrow paths that twist their way to the summit, and yet 2 000 tons of soil were been artificially transported to the very top by a prehistoric people of unknown identity.
Archaeological enquiry uncovered the remnants of numerous dwellings, which had been built on the ruins of predecessors over many generations, resulting in a series of habitation phases. Radiocarbon dates show that the first buildings were erected below the hill at the beginning of the 11th century AD. But adjacent to Mapungubwe is the sister site of Bambadyanalo, which was settled even earlier. It seems that the centre of the state shifted from Bambandyanalo to Mapungubwe hill in about 1045 AD, when the town most probably became overcrowded. It was also at about this time that hills and mountains became associated with royalty and the noble classes began to build their structure on high ground. This is an important observation as it provided evidence of the extensive wealth and social differentiation of the people of Mapungubwe, in other words this ancient civilization was class-based.
The gold findings are also evidence of early gold smelting. A large amount of artifacts from the royal family were discovered at Mapungubwe. The best known of these objects is the golden rhinoceros. All in all, the amount of gold from this burial amounted to 7 503 ounces.
In the 1400's it appears that all the citizens of the kingdom left leaving palaces and the settlements behind. We don't know exactly why the people of Mapungubwe moved away, but the ruins give us a good idea of how these people lived and how their society and political structures grew over the years. Scholars believe that the climate in the area changed, which made it much harder to grow crops and feed animals, this might have caused the civilization to move.
Greefswald farm remained the property of the State from the 1930s. Management of the farm was taken over by the provincial Department of Nature Conservation in 1992 and control was transferred to SANParks in 1999. Mapungubwe was declared a World Heritage Site by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation (UNESCO) in July 2003.

I write this recommendation with some hesitance. I know that people who buy games expect ones to take up a decent amount of their time. I once thought that if a game was longer, that made it better, and would criticize shorter games based on their length (my arguement against Over the Void, and my criticism of the original Portal come to mind), but I think in some ways I've changed my stance on that view. But I know plenty of other people haven't. That's fine. They can suck it.
Pretentious Game is a game without about as much length and content as Over the Void, but the biggest difference between the two that keeps me from changing my recommendation from a "no" to a "yes" on Over the Void, is the type of content each contains. Don't get me wrong, these two games have nothing similar, apart from their hour's worth of playtime. But between games like these and even Hook, is that Pretentious Game intends to tell a story, and uses it's mechanics not only to teach the player what they need to do to beat a level, but also tell them the context of what's going on.
Sure, there are bits, where I had no idea that the red blocks were supposed to be a car. I personally the mechanics and story got a little wobbly during the third and fourth chapters. But the first and second were pure gold for me, and I couldn't stop playing. Sure, it can pick up mechanics and later drop them oddly enough. Some mechanics don't fit well into the story (Hangliding? Really!?), but what Pretentious Game succeeds at, it does well. The nonlinear storytelling between the three chapters sets up what might at first seem to be a simple story, but gradually branches out and explains everything. Did I like chapter four at all? No. Not really. It kinda stunk of BS, and had little to do with the events of the preceding chapters, other than the kids were related to the one woman.
But Pretentious Game is pretentious, as much as it is a game. It's a little too overdramatic, and little cheesey here and there, but it has some pretty dark imagery for a game where the art is all made of pixels. You'll only get about an hour's worth of gameplay (and there is little replay value), but if a fifth chapter were released, I'd still install it again just to find out what happens next.

There is nothing to find, and you will travel on and on before either reloading or warping to a city. Events are somewhat similarly flawed -- loading a save seems to force restart the events of the city you are currently in and will make it easy to either break your game or completely lose track of what you were doing.
But here's the crux of my thumbs down: I invested so much time into this game, became incredibly immersed, overlooked the bugs, but, despite the enormous amount of good will the positive parts of this game engendered, I encountered a bug at the end of the game that just left me traveling outside of the normal map thinking that the next screen would trigger the event that would tie everything together, give me some small sense of satisfaction, and cause the credits to roll.

If you dislike fighting, just increase your Guile (evasion skill) and avoid enemies. On the other hand, you can keep a txt file and note prices in every city, gathering money for the best weapons in the game.
In my opinion, the only bad thing about HOMD is extremely repetitive landscapes. However, in the late game you can mostly use teleportation (Fetch Mirror) to reduce travel time.
Despite this shortcoming, I genuinely enjoyed House of Many Doors and want to recommend it to those who love solid worldbuilding and interesting stories.

Remember me is just one of those games you kind of have to go into without any super high expectations to get the most out of the experience. I just happened to buy the game when I was bored one day and boy I didn't regret it. The premise lured me in as the main theme revolves around good and bad memories, and whether society as a whole should promote the loss of bad memories in favour of good ones even if they're artificial. As for the main story, it had its high and lows, but it kept me interested enough to finish the game. The characters were pretty cool as well. Nilin (the main character) was designed quite well in terms of visuals and story, and made her to be quite awesome instead of plain fan servicing. Although some of the other characters do not have much depth to them, but they did focus on the people closest to Nilin and the key enemies within the game. The visuals for the game were pleasing in my opinion, it definitely suited the environment and characters within the game. As for the last positive, the soundtrack was nice to listen to. As for the negatives, starting soft is the combat. I had a love hate relationship with it as it was a fun thing to play around with at the start, but then it becomes monotonous in the end. So the driving thing about the combat is to alter the combat movesets to fit the enemies that you fight (ie., a boss which requires you to use your skills more thus focusing on cooldown reduction movesets, or using a power based moveset for bosses that require a ton of it). The camera has been getting criticised quite a lot and I would agree with it to a degree. I had no substantial issues with it aside from the fast camera movements it does at times which is a negligible issue. Where this becomes problematic is when I want to grab the collectibles. It takes a bit of time to adjust the camera and it takes away from the experience. Lastly, the game is designed to be quite linear which isn't much of an issue for me but some people do not like linear adventures which is fair enough. Overall, this game was excellent in many departments with a few flaws which are not that big of an issue in my opinion.

Is this a joke? This must be a joke.
^ That would probably be what I would be saying if I followed the hype of the game throughout and played it when it first launched.
[Content] I will firstly address, on the vast scale of things what was promised in comparison to what we have right now...
1) OPEN UNIVERSE. Progress - 0%. There is no open universe. The farthest you'll get to the game being open is a solar system with a skybox and NOT actual stars, galaxies, planets etc. that you can fly to outside of the system. The sun isn't even a real star, planets don't rotate around one another, immersion breaks a second after you feel you have become immersed. The galactic map is a lie; it's a level selection screen, not an actual representation of the cosmic map that you can travel through with your ship. And SPOILER: if you want to get to another galaxy, you must reach the center, which... does it in a stupidest way possible, basically you having your entire journey erased, more or less, and starting almost fresh, just with a galaxy name changed. No change in procedural generation between galaxies, no different levels of different creature/robot infestations around the galaxy overall; nothing. Same old♥♥♥♥♥♥over and over again. On planets, things that look the same are not even ever the same type of a thing. And when they do look the same, none of them ever are on different planets. Which itself would already be some more depth in terms of things already discoved, but nope, not gonna get that!
2) ALTERNATE UNIVERSES. Progress - 0%. There were hints of multiverse systems being implemented in the game. I first thought it was going to be portals that would allow us to do this. But it ended up being disappointing as hell. We already had teleportation mechanics between bases and space stations, which I find to be quite ridiculous already. What is the point of having to travel anywhere via ship, when you can go between galaxies through the portal if you know the coordinates? A good game would make the journey interesting to follow from point A to point B. NMS isn't a good game. That's why it resorts to fast-travel. Having the choice between fast travel and manual travel is an idiotic concept, because that defeats the whole purpose of game design; letting the game guide you instead of presenting you with choices that ruin or make the experience meaningless, which is what fast travel does best. The Waking Titan was a hype for no reason other than possible story that I have not yet gone through myself, but have heard that is basically getting from one point to another and reading a bunch of text. This game never shows you anything, it's all text, because the developers are inept as ♥♥♥♥. One guy made Space Engine. One. Bloody. Guy. And 4 - 16 people have worked on No Man's Sky. Did Sean Murray have any idea how you would even go about making an infinite universe space amount or anything major that he hinter at and promised? May be he should get advice from the guy who made Space Engine, since he seriously doesn't seem to know what he's doing.
3) BIOLOGICAL PHYSICS AND CHEMISTRY. Progress - 0%. Just a bunch of manually made elements and products, no proceduration whatsoever. If you wanted to craft your own tank, space ship that you have designed in your head or even some-what on paper/computer or some other machinery/tool, was expecting animals to have highly complex biology, everything being minable and scannable.
4) ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE. Progress - 0%. Do I need to go any further? Sentinels, animals, "intelligent" alien races are all objects that have programmed conditions to do certain things, sometimes procedurally (i.e. the animals), but even that is bare bones when you find a planet full of hostile creatures. You wouldn't find a giant snake that would try to strangle you, in fact, you wouldn't find any snake-like creatures at all, and if you did, I assure you, it would be a basic animation of it biting you and taking away certain number of healthpoints for your shield or own health, because this game's mechanics have the depth of a puddle. It wouldn't be the snake biting your arm, injecting poison which then, by the scanning of your suit would warn you of the poison, where it's located and how long until your vital organs get damaged, nah, that's too complex, even for a game that was trying to demonstrate itself to be going somewhere along the lines of that complexity. There's a lot you could do with mechanics like in Powder Toy, or even if it's bare bones like the Scrap Mechanic, or god forbid Roblox, but no, the best you'll get in terms of complexity to being able to craft and immerse yourself in is crafting a built-in product 10 times over while the suit lady tells you "product constructed" every time you do and being "bitten" by one of the animals that attack you like any other hostile creature would in the game; playing attack animation and taking away a bit of your health. Complexity may often be too complex for a player to handle if implemented, but if done right, it could be the most immersive thing that you could get your hands on with in terms of the virtual world.
5) MANUAL INPUT. Progress - 1%. I'll be honest and say that there is some room for manual input. The way procedural content can be created and the way AI can learn is if you give them input to tamper with. That is the only way they can learn by themselves, but they can't do it, if you separate it from them. Procedural generation exists in the game on a bare -bones recolour level only and that doesn't even apply to most things like freighters, ground vehicles, barely to ship designs and space stations and especially it doesn't apply to base building, which is single handedly the worst feature about the game. Not because it exists, but because it's executed the worst out of everything in the worst way possible; you can't build anywhere, you have a certain amount of land on a planet you can build on and you can only build using the objects already pre-made by the company itself. You can't design anything within the game and build it like in a 3D modelling software with the resources you collect or craft blueprints for them to sell on the market where an alien would analyse your blueprint and tell you how much they'll give you for it. That's not the depth of this game. If any progress was done with the points above and the one below, then the manual input percentage would have been higher, because if you're just putting in manual content within a game that aims to do things procedurally, you'll be making something else and will probably ending it up being♥♥♥♥♥♥ like this game.
6) PROCEDURAL GENERATION. Progress - 2%. There are quite a bit of stuff that has procedural generation, however it is not complex enough and doesn't have enough input and doesn't apply to enough things (i.e. basically everything except may be yourself, your original ship and sentinels). Imagine seeing a giant yellow whirpool in a system you just arrived in, all happening because of the physics + procedural generation working together, and the developers having no idea anyone else would find it, because they didn't know that's what the program would create, because they never created it in the first place, as it happened due to semi-random selection of elements by the program. Now THAT would be a discovery and the way you would want to handle procedural generation for a game that covers itself in its name, but not the sloppy code pile that is the game's current state.
7) MULTIPLAYER. Progress - 5%. They actually put it in, but it doesn't really mean anything; you can't see each other as playable characters, nor can you see each others' ships, do things together, see the other mine, destroy or build things and there's nothing mechanical you can share really other than a beam of light that marks your position of meeting within one contained leve.. I mean a solar system!
