I honestly can't remember when I received the game, but I for sure looked at Remember Me with interest. After playing almost 8.5 hours, I've run into a well-known bug, and can no longer progress.
Besides this bug, which seems to be related to having a graphics setting besides the default, I will discuss the other parts to the game.
The first fact I'll bring up is the fighting. No, I'm not talking about the enemies here, as there is some well designed variance in them – it's the struggle you go through with the camera controls
. If you touch the camera controls, expect serious and heavy resistance. This becomes even more evident when in combat, where a targeted shot results in a miss purely because the camera decided to snap to the wrong enemy. Furthermore, the FOV is so restrictive, it feels as if the developers are ashamed to show of their work.
The second is the game play. Up to the 8.4 hour mark, I can say that the game has been predominately constant hand holding, follow the leader, and other menial tasks besides the 2 memory remixes, 3 or 4 puzzles, and the standard boss battles. This mirrors the plot in many departments, as it is very predictable, boring, and very lack luster. There were many avenues to explore such as the "outcasts" (but opted to make them simple savages), moral implications of changing memories (besides the monologues by the primary character), and so on. Between the game play and plot, Remember Me felt very scripted, and any deviance from that script causes issues. You do not set the pace in this game, the game controls every aspect of it.
When I sat down to play the game, I thought Remember Me would be similar to Mirror's Edge, with it's unique art style, and smaller focus on combat, but major coverage in the puzzles department and so on. As it turns out, the game acts like a poor copy of Mirror's Edge. Sure, the music and the art are interesting, those two however could not save from the failings of game. Had Remember Me added a RPG component of sorts (just as the developers did with This Life Is Strange), the failings could be overlooked, but this is not the case. This was the third and final nail in the coffin which made me put the game down. I don't think I will ever return, Remember Me has left a bad taste in my mouth.
In the end, I feel cheated in many regards, and will not be recommending this game to anyone. I can't, if a game breaking bug is repeatable with no cure in sight, it is not worth anyone's frustration to play 8 hours and then find themselves stuck because of poor testing. There isn’t enough substance in the title to mitigate the feeling after encountering the bug.

The New Colossus is a good sequel to The New Order. While I would have liked some new gameplay (simply mixing dual wield is not sufficient on its own), it has been refined and tightened to provide a more fluid experience. In this respect I think it approaches more of the run-and-gun that Doom 2016 brought to the table; that being said it is still easy to go down if you expose yourself for too long, but still dual-wielding feels a lot more rewarding in this game as it can make a difference rather than simply adding more chaos like in TNO. For the most part levels are structured like TNO - you have a generally linear level with plenty of cover and vertical dimensions. And much like TNO you'll have "stealth" components which will involve terminating officers to prevent reinforcements, though again like TNO you're free to approach this in anyway you see fit.
And if you happen to not be familiar with the franchise, there is no multiplayer. Outside of the single player there are challenge missions (as were done in TNO and The Old Blood) which are set in the levels which you go through in the game. Needless to say if you're expecting a multiplayer experience you are looking in the wrong place.
The id Tech 6 engine that powered Doom has made a good impression to me here as well, especially with the lighting. I did not have problems with running the game at release for my part so I cannot comment on that part much; I will say that as far as scalability goes it is more flexible than TNO's settings. It seems however that the engine was not as finetuned for this game as it was for Doom, and I hope that it can be smoothed out for other users over time.
As far as the story is concerned, it is a good one, though I feel that it didn't have me as engaged as TNO. This may be because TNO also came out of nowhere and was a genuine surprise to playthrough the first time, whereas we all expected a sequel to TNO at somepoint and it unfortunately follows a lot of the same beats in terms of character development and plot. Don't mistake this for saying that it's a bland experience - there are plenty of awesome moments and setpieces in this game like in TNO, but that it didn't innovate much on this front as it had when TNO came out. Still miles ahead of story presentation in other shooters though.
The only thing I would have liked is probably just one more major area. Without spoiling much, essentially the game has a number of locales further subdivided into levels you go through during the game. I think if one more had been added, that would have probably brought the game to a more suitable length for me. There's a bit of a post-game which will open up one more unique level, though to unlock this you have to replay the other levels again. However the post-game consists of playing the same levels with some cosmetic story-related changes and usually proceeds from the original end point back to the start. This adds more gameplay of course but I felt this was just padding out the length to get to the last unique level.
There will be more new content coming up in the next several months consisting of levels with new locales. These don't involve BJ but are kind of in-game fictional stories with different characters who have a special ability (though these are taken from the three upgrades you get in the main game so it won't be unique). I think in this respect if you are holding out on buying the game and are not in a hurry to play it, then getting it when the inevitable Game+DLC package is released and later on sale is probably your best bet for getting the most mileage out of the game. Otherwise I'm sure the base game will be put on sale alot (and already has been) as will the season pass.

As someone who has experienced mental health issues, I can appreciate the care that Ninja Theory put into creating a believable and empathetic exploration of an often taboo topic. The world that they have created is enthralling not just in its breathtaking environments, but also in how those environments are shaped and distorted by Senua's personal struggle. The actors involved clearly had solid direction, and Senua's actress in particular demonstrates a great honesty with the subject matter at hand.
However, as a game, Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice falls too short to recommend. Senua trudges through the environments at a snail's pace, and quite a few puzzles suffer from confusing design that will probably leave most players needlessly backtracking. The "lore" collectibles break up the narrative flow too much, and they can be easily missed with no way of going back to recover them (which wouldn't be a significant issue if they didn't impact the ending).
The combat is by far the game's biggest weakness. Your movement and skillset are too limited, and the camera and targetting are too rigid, to have satisfying exchanges with enemies. You'll find yourself simply mashing buttons and receiving cheap hits that you couldn't have possibly dodged. There are plenty of non-combat sequences that do a better job of creating and sustaining tension where it's needed. Most of the combat sequences only upset the game's pacing and artificially pad its length. I would have rather the developers removed these sequences entirely.
Unfortunately, the core gameplay wears out its welcome well before the ending, leaving more mechanically-minded players to slog through the tail end of the game with a slight tinge of annoyance constantly clawing at them. For this reason, I would not recommend the game unless you are particularly forgiving of bad design decisions.

Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice has opened my eyes to a new way of gaming. I've been a shooter gamer for quite a while now and this story-driven psychological warfare was both new to me and blew my mind! I had that feeling of not wanting to play the game beause of how real it was regarding a severe mental illness (and a little bit of the horror aspect) but I kept picking it back up anyway until I finished it. If you enjoy story telling and love "feeling" a game, you won't be disappointed.

It is a walking simulator with a 16-bit, twee artstyle. I'm not opposed to this style of game - some games do it pretty well (i.e. The Vanishing of Ethan Carter). This game presents us with a story that superficially tugs on the heart-strings. Yeah, it is sad and may make you cry, but for what end? It all just feels so inconsequential, trite and purposefully sad. Its cool if you got something out of this - the story seems to have resonated with a lot of people, but this style of game is just not for me. If you prefer a game with proper gameplay, like I do, you will want to pass on this. Not recommended.
"If two hearts are meant to be together, no matter how long it takes, how far they go, how tough it seems, fate will bring them together to share their love forever."  ❤

Worth playing if you want a really visceral, gritty depiction of suffering to watch for a few hours. You'll get to experience the protagonists inner workings/mental illness first hand in a remarkably real and cruel. This is a game that you play for the plot and the graphics, and it doesn't disappoint in those regards. If you're even slightly interested, I'd recommend picking it up. It's only 6~8 hours, and there's not exactly a huge catalog of games the explore and depict psychosis.

My review for Half-Life 2 can be seen here:
I'll be covering the updates down below.
While most of the games visuals have been updated there were still some blocky shadows in a Ravenholm. At one point even on my GTX 980 SC ACX 2.0 and an AMD fx-8350 (Now replaced with an i7 4790k Devils Canyon) I suffered awful frame drops that it would seem have since been fixed. It improves the visuals a lot of small ways "that make all the difference in the world". The horrible pop in that occured on a large bridge has been fixed/is nonexistant now and it would seen that the developer has set the r_lod to 0 which means that the pop in or fading is nonexistant on the props now. It's not just as simple as that though. He fixed props that were transparent even from really close up and gave them proper modern day render distances by tweaking the props in questions lod's and fade/draw distance and also realigned the water,fog and skybox on some maps to hide seams that popped up and became more apparent on higher resolutions or on subsequent playthroughs. While it's impressive that thus update was all made by one man I still wish that things like crossbow viewmodel had it's massive error fixed ( You can easily notice that it's still missing half of it's model as it would seem they didn't prepare it for widescreen resolutions.) or that whatever few blotchy shadows remaining got an easy cubemap fix. The water splashes created by player/object impacts could have used a small update too. Here I ported the Left 4 Dead splash effect material:

Otherwise it's a proper update that does what the title suggests and stays true to the original acting like a real patch you would expect the original developers pf Half-Life 2 to release unlike the impressive but unfaithful and obtrusive Cinematic mod.

Okay, I had high hopes for this game and it turned out to be absolutely ridiculous. Music is great, graphics are great as well, but in their chase to catch the trend of "super hard games" the developers went way too far. There are several basic problems that made me simply give up on the game.
1. The block is useless. The more you hold the block button, the more damage it lets through, so the only use of it is to tap it just when the enemy is about to hit you, in order to stun them into a counter attack. The problem is...
2. Counters require split-second timing. And I mean it. There is barely any wiggle room at all, and that is with addition of the fact that the enemies have somewhat awkward, slow animations that really trick you into thinking that it is *now* when it isn't. The problem is, the same applies to enemies that rely on counters to be killed. Exactly the same thing with bouncing back projectiles.
3. Dash is mostly useless. This is because you can only dash back, and most of the time you will be cornered by enemies, your back to the abyss or a trap. You dash, you die. As a bonus: you get hit, you fly back, you die.
4. Combat is beyond simplistic. You have one button to mash, half-useful dash, useless block and a tough to execute counter. Oh, and a projectile attack, probably the best of them all, but even then, combat doesn't feel any meaty, satisfying or even fun.
5. Visual cue issues. I went to the level with witches, got a flaming sword I should be using against them. Great, but the animation of the sword swing obfuscates enemies to the point where it is really damn hard to tell if they are attacking!
6. Controller implementation is lack-luster. It lacks the slight dead zone that prevents the character moving to the opposite direction when you release the stick. It killed me way too many times.

A beautiful game, tailored for a very specific audience.
What I enjoyed:
1. Elegant, literary prose that brings the world to life, and delivers strong emotional beats that drive a compelling plot.
2. Complex and emotionally resonant characters whose stories I became invested in, and whose personalities are developed through small interactions and flavor text as well as conversation and personal stories.
3. A deeply built out and magnificently creative world, and a huge selection of choices and ways to engage with it: seduce gods, argue with poets, topple civilizations, marry into aristocracy, own a dog that's also a fish, etc...
4. Gorgeous watercolor-style art for every cityscape.
5. An initially simple but pleasantly deep combat system, with lots of weapons and tactics to combine, and a couple different enemy AI settings to try out
What I did not enjoy:
1. The tutorial is poorly integrated into the game and fails to mention vital information. Even if you don't know how to play, it might be best to skip it and look up a guide on Steam instead.
2. There are a selection of small mechanical glitches, bugs, and loose ends. Nothing game-breaking or obnoxious, but it is somewhat vexing.
3. The game's small budget means that the procedurally generated no-man's-land between cities is lacking in unique art assets, musical tracks, and random encounters. There's enough to maintain variety for a while, but by the time you're halfway through the game you'll have seen just about every combination.
4. The system for assigning fast-travel waypoints seems... strange. Some areas have a waypoint in every city, but whole sections of the map don't have any waypoints at all. This would be as much of a problem if it were not for the aforementioned lack of procedural generation assets.

This has quickly shot to the top of my favorite games of all time list, and about 6 months after release it's still there. That said, gonna do my best to be relatively objective about its good and bad points:
aHoMD has an amazing setting and top-notch worldbuilding, and digging through the narrative and trying to understand what has happened and will happen is as big a part of the exploration in this game as the physical exploration aspect itself. The House is a bizarre, fascinating place, so if you're a fan of surreal fantasy, magical realism, and slipstream works that toss you a totally alien place and tell you to infer everything from scratch, you'll absolutely love this. Additionally, the game tweaks quite a lot of itself based on your actions and choices, and much of what you do has consequences, from the innocuous to the absolutely devastating. I feel like each one of the characters I play is really a different character because of that.
The biggest thing that puts aHoMD above its cousin Sunless Sea (whose creators gave this game their blessing and support...) for me is the focus on its characters. Sunless Sea is more a game about your captain's journey and the isolation that comes along with being out on a dark, fearsome and alien ocean in a lil' boat, and the characters have stories and personalities but they're also far from the game's focus. In comparison, aHoMD's characters are likeable, bizarre, fascinating, funny, and sometimes detestable. Despite the dark backdrop they're set against, aHoMD's cast is colorful and memorable, and they're a big part of the reason I wish the game had a larger fanbase, so I could talk about and doodle and write fic about all of them.
Some of the crew are romanceable, and that brings me into the fact that this is a game that does representation well and doesn't feel like it's pandering to me (a queer person...) Your captain has a portrait and name but no set portrait and pronouns, and all the romanceable characters, as a result, are all functionally bi/pan+. There are a handful of other explicitely LGBT+ characters who aren't romanceable as well, in and out of your crew, and there's even an polyamorous character, which blew my mind, because how many times do you see that addressed in a way that doesn't feel like it's judging someone, or just having it be ignored altogether!? Blew my mind, man.
The gameplay itself isn't bad, but it's not what you're gonna want to buy the game for. The exploration of the House can be tedious once you get hours into it and know where everything is, but in the beginning it can be frightening and wonderous and fascinating, and even now I still find myself surprised by some events that pop up. The combat is unfortunately pretty poorly explained, but once you get the hang of it there's some decent strategy to it (like FTL but turn based kind of...), but it feels like it's missing a lot that could have made it on par with the aforementioned FTL. That said, one of the "final boss" fights is Mother 3 levels of RPG battle mechanics-as-metaphor and it's absolutely masterful. As with many narrative-heavy games, these mechanics are more of a means to wrap the narrative in theme and feeling and aesthetic. If you play games primarily for their mechanics, I'm not sure this is your kind of game.
Music and art are wonderful, by the way. The background music in particular is wonderful at blending ambient noise into the bgm, as well as evoking emotion once you get near the end of the game and have really come to understand what it all means. The painterly style of the art and somewhat monochromatic background art is rather unique, and the way the game itself uses lighting is nice.
In terms of differences from Sunless Sea, it's a much easier game, no permadeath, and while navigating the House can feel more tedious than sailing around the Neath, there's a fast travel option that cuts substantial time off of travelling to certain areas, and it's a lifesaver.
One final big issue with the game - it's somewhat buggy and unpolished. It used to be a lot worse, I've heard, but there's times where the graphics will be whacked out, or some option that should be there for me isn't (or visa versa.) It's less frustrating because the game autosaves, thank god, but if this is something that's a dealbreaker for you, probably don't invest in this. Otherwise, if this kind of game is your thing, please dear god buy it this game needs to be enjoyed by more people

Racer 8's interface was designed with mobile devices in mind, and it shows it.  You scroll through over-sized menu items by dragging the box up and down, ignoring the arrows which appear only to indicate you can.  The game starts windowed, and while a standard Alt+Enter grants you a less messy-looking fullscreen option, this only makes it harder to find the close window option, which you will want shortly after your first level.
The game itself gives you a puzzle, ala Pipe Mania (circa 1989), except where your little car needs to travel is not clear from the start.  In fact, you have to mess around waiting for objectives to appear, so planning in advance is an option available only to better games than this.  As far as I can tell, there are no differences in the levels (I admit to not having played that many, wishing to retain a semblance of sanity in order to write this review) although it was raining on one level which I'm sure was nice.
A special shout-out has to go to the Auto-Pilot "upgrade", which makes assumptions about you wanting to hit walls and fail, so changes routes for you accordingly.
As a special treat, you can connect this game to your Facebook account.  The developers are clearly in touch with the demands of modern gaming, and should of course be applauded.
Full disclosure: I got this game for free, though still feel a little over-charged.

There is also a shop where you can purchase useful boosts at the beginning of each race, with the coins granted from winning races.
Racer 8 does nothing particularly well. The graphics, gameplay & sound are all very generic. There isn’t anything to hold your interest longer than a couple minutes at a time.

This is it. This is the game that shows that pure passion for gaming still exists. Thank you so much Ninja Theory for us gamers that there are still people in the industry with resources to make a game that exceeds all expectations without the horrible constraints of oppressive publishers that only care about their shareholder dividends.
Hellblade is an authentic journey into the mind of a tormented psyche and it is done so well that it is the only that has given me shivers down my spine.  Ninja Theory has done their due diligence in researching not only an authentic as possible story, but also in the realm of psychosis. They worked in concert with people who have experienced the types of psychosis that Senua went through and was able to present a third person action adventure game which pushes the boundaries of what games are able to represent. IMHO using quality headphones (not gaming branded trash) and a soundcard is almost necessary to truly live this game as it was meant to be experienced. The visuals are that of a AAA game and the auditory finesse is something beyond anything I have experienced in any game to date.
This game is definitely not for every one as some might think that it is too much of a "walking simulator" although there are many enemies and bosses to fight this game is primarily an exploration of what someone goes through when they are already tormented by psychosis and then a seriously traumatic event happens in their life toppling them over into a complete psychotic episode. If you like games as a medium to tell and experience stories better than any movie or book could in terms of immersion with a splash of puzzle solving and fighting this is the game for you.
Hellblade: Senua's Sacrifice shows the world that a truly breathtaking game can be made without the need of a big money publisher and that passion still exists in the industry of gaming at a larger than indie level. From the depths of my inner gamer I say thank you to Ninja Theory for breathing life back into the largely stale bigger budget segment of the gaming industry.

Pros
+ Leveling System (The higher your rank, the more items you have access to)
+ Combat/Stealth (Be a soldier on the front line, or go behind the enemy lines to destroy key enemy buildings/supplies)
+ Community (Over-all good community, you won't see much in terms of TK's or bad sportsmanship, most the time they will go out of their way to help you understand what you need to do, if you ask)

Cons
- Desyncing is a big problem, and seemingly random. One moment the game will run fine, the next you are stuck in place. (Do note that the game doesn't seem to have much in terms of desync on some days/ the start of the week, but as a week moves on the time between desyncs decreases, causing desyncs to occur continuously.)
- Enemy Health/Damage (Some enemies seem to be somewhat invincible at times, either that or they bug out and stay in place, could relate to desync.)
- Accuracy (Accuracy in this game is based solely on sliders, meaning skill alone will not suffice, you have to hope the odds are in your favor.)
Overall a great little game, if of course you enjoy multiplayer. Worth the price and worth the time.

While I did quite like this game and the story that it had to tell, I unfortunately wouldn't recommend this game considering the price and short length. I think you can even just play the chapters online if you looked it up! It's neat how the game puts together the narrative with the gameplay, which will give the player a hint on how to progress, but other than that nothing much about this game is very praise worthy. It really is a Pretentious Game.
Pretentious Game focuses on the story of this small cast of characters represented with colored squares that slide along the ground with no walking animation (just like all those crappy horror games the internet loves so much!). The story centers on the conflicts of relationships and love, and it serves its purpose of invoking emotion in people who actually pay attention to the story. It's nothing groundbreaking or special, really, but it's unique in the way that it gives a single hint in the form of a sentence for the players to continue on.
Though that's where some of the game's faults can be found. In one part, in which you expect the narrative to lead the way, you have to somehow figure out there's invisible platforms to get to the end goal of the chapter's level. As much as I hate invisible platforms, it was made way worse when the narrative doesn't seem to have anything to do with how the level should work.
The fourth chapter has to be one of my least favorite chapters, really. It kind of repeats characteristics for these two characters, adding nothing really to the story. Yeah, I get it, they're very close and help each other out. This chapter was  also the hardest in my opinion. Yet, it seems very unnecessary, like it was just the creator running out of ideas and having to fill the space with this whole chapter. Not to mention that it leaves players on a "cliffhanger" of sorts, teasing for another chapter which still has yet to be delivered. The other chapters didn't even have this cliffhanger before, and they felt complete on their own. This one, however, has all this filler just to have the last part of the chapter actually add something to the story.
Anyway, I would not recommed buying this game on Steam. It doesn't even have any achievements or any added content to make it more enjoyable. Just look it up and play it on your web-browser if you want to.

This is one of those games that intrigued me at the start, but then failed to maintain my interest.
If that was all I had to say on the matter, I'd give it a thumbs up. But, unfortunately, the more I played the game the more I came to realize why it wasn't worth continuing and, worse, why I feel I wasted my time.
At it's base there are several poor game design decisions that ends my interest in this game. Specifically, when you get hit you don't have a significant (or any?) invincibility frames to recover. You know, like how old school games would knock your character back and have him flash for a few seconds, indicating invincibility, and giving you a chance to respond to whatever killed you.
Nope, not in this game. If you're caught in a swarm of enemies, you'll just take hit after hit after hit and become frustrated. It's OK to be frustrated at your own inadequacies, but when you're frustrated by poor mechanics that could otherwise be fixed with a few lines of code, then the onus is on the developer.
There are a few other oddities that are similar simple issues that nonetheless kill the experience.
For example, crouching. You can crouch and swipe at enemies, and in some cases this is exactly what you'd want to do (that's why the ability is, in fact, in the game). However, if you try to stay crouching and turn in the opposite direction guess what happens? Your sprite flips on it's X-axis and keeps your character crouching? Nope. Your character rises out of crouch and starts moving in that direction, which will probably kill you since you were likely crouching to avoid something above you.
This isn't just a problem in this one narrow situation, however. If you happen to subtley move in a direction while crouching (which is easy to do since you can hit a horizontal direction easily when going into crouch or even while in crouch) you, again, stand straight up and start moving!
Again, all of this being easy to fix with  a few lines of code. This isn't idle speculation either since the game was made in Unity and myself and even beginner developer and hobbyists know exactly how this fix would look in code.
Anyhow, all of these issues just added up to frustration and a mild regret to have spent hours in the game. The art and music is interesting, however fails to elevate the overall experience which is, at it's base, flawed and repetitive.
With that said, I am interested in this developer's next effort as I'm sure they learned a lot from the experience and surely will have a better effort the next time around.

While I commend the effort put into designing this game, I still have mixed feelings about the end result. So, you wanted to make a game that was half a movie and half a game? Well then, you had better deliver on a solid conclusion that made the process worth it. Did they do it? Mostly, no. The conclusion to this story leaves the player feeling like they've done little in the way that matters. They just say the message, "Wake up America. Now it's your turn to play rebellion."
I wouldn't recommend this game above the price tag of $40. If I wanted to spend half of my time watching cutscenes, I'd prefer to watch a gripping movie or television show compared to this game. I'm estimating that I spent only about 30% of the game actually killing Nazis and *doing* something. Instead, I'm tasked with solving a lot of problems for incompetent people. I feel like a tool during this game; and it's not very enjoyable.
Oh, and can we please note how f***ing ridiculous it is that there are cutscenes where my pregnant wife is in battle, throwing grenades? What is this rubbish?!
And then I rationalized the DLC, thinking, "Okay, now they get to show American citizens' efforts to dismantle the Reich." Nope. Just your typical trash DLC offering nothing new or exciting to continue the story. They spent so much time making things looked polished and "eye-catching" that distorted the overall message of the game. Again, only recommended at a sale price.

Gameplay
TBH I expected more combat, like in Devil May Cry. I'm disappointed it's actually more of a parkour Zelda, but that's nothing against the game. Hunting the chests is fun. The dungeons and puzzles are well designed so far. Scaling walls and mastering the climbing is rewarded.
I'm wary about backtracking. I hate intended backtracking. The world design lead me straight to an interesting dungeon I had no business attempting. It turns out the boss in there is an optional bounty, intended for characters lv6-12. I was barely level 2. I barely knew I or enemies _had_ levels yet. Yup. It's by the first cool merchant in the open world, and entices you with a chest. Why? Just block it off with an NPC or the hooks that already made me skip several chests.
Combat is fairly rewarding. Small groups of mooks are frequent and trivial, but that's expected. So far the boss fights have been neat and somewhat unique. As easy as it is to just mash light and heavy attack, encounters start to take some thought about dodge direction and how to utilize your active skills. So far most encounters are small and short. Maybe that will change. I'm not far.
This all said, it's fun and I probably will play it through. Secondary weapons seem to somewhat matter. Loot is cool. The demonic weapon upgrading is neat. The skill tree seems decent. I like you can respec, but it has a low-reasonable currency cost. Some old posts online imply you can actually have a 'build' by the end between the trees and gear. Not all solo ARPGs let you differentiate that much.
Graphics
I'm impressed. It looks and runs great. I like the art style a lot.
The first ice boss has a cool model and looked sharp. In game looks better than the video, more like the provided screenshots. I'm not experiencing the performance issues that generated most of the negative reviews. I assume they've been fixed. That said, I'm < 6hrs in as of this review.
Controls/Mechanics
Combat is smooth.
Lock-on could have been a toggle instead of a hold, but it's fine. I would have preferred trigger+button for assigned powers over bumber+button, but also fine.
As much as I love the look and idea of the horse, I wish they would have just given a sprint. The horse is allowed in very limited locations. Also, while I'm impressed they did seemingly pretty fluid mounted combat, it doesn't end up working. One hit knocks you off the horse, and unmounted (standard) combat is too far superior to be messing around on horseback anyway. I find myself moving through many areas wishing I could run faster, especially when retracing steps for a chest or to find/restart a climbing puzzle.
Climbing is generally impressively smooth.
Honestly, I expected ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t like missing beams or constantly jumping 90 degrees off of my intended jump angle. That's actually quite rare, and usually my fault when it does happen.
My only complaint here is when you can't jump onto or scale surfaces you definitely should be able to. Sometimes they're well under the standard jump height, with a gap in the walls/railing and everything. Just be aware there are well designed paths with generally obvious objects/textures, and you will be using them, even if it means going around or reconsidering dungeon rooms. Think more Drake's Fortune treasure puzzles, less Assassin's Creed.
This was a steal at $3. It's probably worth full price.

House of Many Doors is essentially a text adventure with elements inspired by the Indie game FTL. You play as the captain of a kinetopede, a cross between a train and a centipede you use to explore The House, a "parasite dimension" which is comprised of things and places absorbed from other worlds, creating a landscape of bizarre and varied ruling powers and arbitrary laws of the universe.
You begin the game in the middle of nowhere, your head bleeding from an attack by memory pirates who've drilled into your skull, capturing one of your memories to sell as a commodity. Naturally you prefer your thoughts remain your own so you set off with your intrepid crew to try and retrieve it and then continue on with your goal to attempt to escape The House.
Gameplay generally falls into one of 3 categories: exploration, combat, and most importantly, dialogue. Your success and failure in most activity is determined by your stats which are modified by your crew members who have their own stories and histories but can be swapped out with others as you see fit.
Exploration may the game's weakest aspect. You scuttle along in your kinetopede map tile by map-tiles ala-Zelda 1, each screen being procedurally generated with a few assets, and occasionally another vessel to encounter or some curio to explore. The art is very rudimentary, and the procedural generation results in the same assets being pasted in a row at times making the environments look quite tacky. Encounters are easily avoided due to your speed which can be upgraded as the game progresses and there's nothing much worth seeing in these tiles, so you generally just spend your time trying to get to the next point of interest as quickly as possible. Combat doesn't improve on visuals either, the game is pretty ugly outside of the hand drawn art shown at places of interest.
Combat is similar to FTL's crew-and-rooms progression, being able to destroy parts and kill crew with varying effects on what you target. There's an action point system limiting your options within your turn, forcing you to make choice between approaching to board the enemy and engage in hand to hand combat or bombarding them from afar; all the while needing to keep crew alive and your systems running.
Combat is by the large, optional. I encountered one optional quest which required combat, the main storyline I played required none. When I did fight however I didn't see much reason to do anything else but fire away. Your ships crew is rather crowded together in the kinetopede and since moving each one takes an action point the best course of action is to simply blow the other vessel up before they kill your members or blow you up. Boarding vessels was only beneficial if your guards outnumbered theirs and you could kill their gunners quickly. Luckily mildly clever maneuvering can avoid combat altogether so you can get to your destination safely.
The game's true focus is its imaginative writing. When the dialogue windows open you're treated to some of the most interesting writing I've seen in video games in a long time. Each location you find is a new and strange land, inspiring wonder and curiosity. Some are bustling hubs of bizarre denizens with strange ways of life, and others are deserted mysteries of unknown purport.
As you take on quests and advance plots, checks are made against your various stats in order to determine success or failure. Attempting to pick a lock might test your guile while a attempting to make a rousing speech will call your spirit into question. The situations vary greatly, throwing you into fascinating scenarios. Quests are not only found in cities, but by your crew members themselves. I helped my ships surgeon work for a cure to a plague by developing a means to communicate with the sickness as a sentient being. Meanwhile I worked with royalty from multiple nations to prevent a civil war over the abolition of slavery.
As you progress the game has an interesting system of using thoughts, experiences, and tales as currency, some being sold outright for money, others being used as options in dialogue with NPC's. As you progress you gain Apprehensions which are used to increase your stats or advance the main plotline. You can work as a freelance writer, selling reports of other cities to the papers or write your own poetry (which procedurally generates actual stanzas) for more apprehensions to spend on stats.
HOMD's variety-show of writing was enough to keep me guessing and wanting more. Each advancement of a plot made seek its conclusion; skittering across the foreboding darkness of The House to collect supplies for rituals while I learned more about my crew creates a deep narrative experience that's easy to get addicted to. The game has 2 mutually exclusive plot paths to pursue and I hardly explored everything and it took me 15-20 hours to complete. Different backgrounds on character creation and outcomes from quests, as well as being able to find different crew members gives some potential for replayability.
Lovers of myriad universes such as Planescape: Torment will find lots to appreciate in HOMD, but those looking for more "game" in their game will find it lacking. That being said I played non stop until I beat it. Good writing in video games is hard to find these days and I ate it up as much as I could. The real conclusion is that HOMD is a better choose-your-own-adventure book than it is a video game. I'd love to see the gameplay cleaned up and fleshed out for a more wholesome experience. At somewhere between $5-15 it's time in is well worth the cash if you like what the game has to offer. 'Til then, play HOMD for the story, and FTL for the combat.

First of all, to the people comparing this game to Sunless Sea: the maker of this game literally made it from the Sunless Sea creators' offices with their full permission. So yes, the game borrows most mechanics and interface from SS, the story and setting are heavily inspired by SS as well. All of that shouldn't bother you (unless you hated SS).
The great:
+ The writing. This is a heavily narrative-driven game and the setting, the story, the characters and the prose are all up to the task. I can't say it's any less engaging than the wonderful Neath of Sunless Sea/Fallen London.
+ The art. City backgrounds are marvellous. Character portraits are quirky and charismatic, as are their owners.
+ The music. Atmospheric if a little repetitive.
The bad:
- Exploration. The majority of the game you'll spend riding your mechanical centipede across empty boring rooms. This at times is almost enough to cancel any joy you'll be having from the story.
- Combat. Just like SS, the least interesting and most useless game mechanic.
- Pretty much most of game mechanics. The games' mechanical side is pretty rough around the edges and at best doesn't add much to the experience.
All in all this game would probably benefit from stripping the majority of its 'gameplay' mechanics and just sticking with the amazing story and lore in the best CYOA fashion.
I still recommend it because as far as weird narrative-driven CYOA games go, it's one of the gems.
P.S. It also has a wonderful ending.

This game is a love letter to the storytelling embodied in games like Sunless Sea, and shows some of the great potential for heavily-branching player-driven narrative. There is no real action, unless one counts the essentially turn-based combat where one transport vessel's occupants repeatedly attempt to maim the body or occupants of another transport vessel. There is no real system of crafting absurdly specific equipment with which one can go to do battle.
Instead, there is a profoundly long yarn being spun, used to weave a thick and deep image of an ethereal and fascinating realm. There is a slew of cast members whose characters are as varied and complex as any real personality. There are disturbing and endearing places imagined and then brought to life by a strange and peculiar developer. There are many, many hours of adventures to be had in pursuit of inhuman deities and their convoluted scheming.
This game is not simply good; it is compelling. Fans of quality narrative need to at least look at A House of Many Doors.

A Game To Remember.
Remember Me is a solid action fighting platforming story game with a unique mechanic and idea that I don't remember seeing in another video game as of yet.
The fighting system rewards you for doing combos (long combos specifically) and you can customize these combos in a way to make them do more damage, cooldown your abilities faster, or heal you.  It's a very easy system to get the hang of after a little bit and there's a few paths you can go with.  I did a farming/skill intensive build which had the combos do little damage but give me more points to unlock variations in which tree i want subscribed to that combo.  The enemies don't vary a whole lot for the most part which is a little unfortunate but the animations and battling never really gets old throughout the game.  As a side note I did use an xbox 360 controller to play this and suspect that it's much easier to play with that vs the keyboard and mouse.
The platforming is simple but solid.  You won't really be confused as to where to jump next because there's an arrow that shows you grabbable ledges when you are near them.  This system actually works really well to keep you moving and appreciating the sights and animations.
The story is actually pretty interesting and serves some intriguing ideas.  I wouldn't be surprised to see this idea explored in a future episodes of black mirror or something of the sorts.  The ending is a little on the odd side but it was a very fun and entertaining ride throughout with no slow or boring parts that I could note.  The locations you run around in are also nicely detailed and varying which helps to keep everything interesting as you go through the game.
There's a couple other smaller mechanics that the game introduces a limited amount of.  There's some simplish riddles that you have to solve to continue for some parts of the game, one I actually got stuck on for a bit.  Though the game does a good job of hinting as to what you should do when it realizes you've been stuck on a part for a bit.  There's the remix mechanic (which I don't want to detail too much) which is an amazingly interesting and fun mechanic that I have not yet seen in another game.  It both opens some very interesting story ideas and the implementation of it is really well done.  The only part I could complain about is that I'd have loved to have done more remixes and potentially explored some darker possibilities with what the game can imply with a mechanic like that.
Overall if you like action games with a decent story, are craving some new interesting ideas, Remember Me is an absolutely solid choice.

To sum it up in a word, Exploration.  With a capital 'E'.
I rarely get hooked into a game on this level.  I recently went at least two years without experiencing it.  The dry spell is now over.
The last game similar to this I spent any time in was Freelancer.  This is an improvement over that in just about every imaginable way.
I have read a lot of reviews.  I'm learning that they often paint a distorted picture.  This game obviously has a unique history in that regard, since they launched it half-finished at full price a year ago.  Glad I didn't get it then (I've developed a habit of not buying anything at release).  The reason I picked it up was that I heard the Atlas Rises patch/expansion was awesome, and it was on sale.
Holy what the wow.  For my 25 bukaruus or so, I have now gotten over 27 hours of pretty much nonstop enjoyable gameplay, and I'm only 8 achievements in, still on my first ship, and haven't ventured more than 2 warp-jumps away from where I started (with one quest-related exception).
I'll say it again-- the free, open Exploration is unmatched.  Going from fumbling around to fix your sad, broken junk to mastering multiple levels of ship control and continually acquiring new ways to overcome challenges is a powerful feeling.  It stays with you; I'm even looking at the real world differently.  Beyond this, the art and music are fantastic, the writing is way beyond what I expected (to the point of messing with your head, I love it), and I always feel like there's something more to look forward to.
Downsides?  If you don't like resource gathering (i.e. Minecraft) you may have trouble with this one.  However, there are a lot of things to gather for different reasons, and you can choose how much of that you want to do to some extent.  Inventory space is cramped, and you will have to manage the heck out of it, at least initially.  I personally like this pressure - it forces you to streamline and incentivizes seeking upgrades - but some may find it tedious.  It would be nice if sentient NPCs had better A.I. (they're more like Morrowind than Oblivion/Skyrim), but dialogue and animation are quite good and there's so much else to do that I honestly don't miss it.
Is it worth full price?  At this point, it would have been for me.  I had no idea going in, though.  If you're an explorer type who likes sci-fi, enjoyed Minecraft and had fun with any of the Elder Scrolls games, DEFINITELY buy it if it's on sale.  You get elements of all those, plus a spaceship to fly and fight with in different ways.  You can even forget everything else and just play your own version of Asteroids while building up hoards of cash and ship upgrades-- a simple home base and finding a spaceport are all you need.
I'm just having such a blast for the first time in a long while and wanted to share it with the world.  I quit a nearly 3-year Hearthstone addiction (the main game I kept playing during this time) and I'm so glad.  If you're still unsure about buying it, put it on your wishlist NOW.  It will be waiting.

Lets look at some of the pros and cons of this masterpiece
Pros:
-Bullets can knock you down in 1 shot, just like the real world
-Battles can take anywhere from 15 minutes to a couple hours to complete
-Snow can go from vanilla white, to blood red in a matter of minutes
-You actually have to think tactically
-Large gun selection, if you take 5 enemy guns of the same type (e.g. 5 AK-47's) you unlock that weapon for your faction
-Tanks and vehicles can really change how the game is played
-Multiple maps
-AI arent as dumb as you think, they actually call mortar strikes on you
-Low system requirements, decent graphics
Now that all the pros are done lets see the
Cons:
-Can get frustrating if you end up in a stalemate that lasts 6 hours
Overall this game is great. For $16 I would really recommend it. Worth every penny

Despite the updated look of the game (shadows, lighting, etc) being its main point of intrigue, my principal interest was the community commentary - and while I'm only partway in, it's already quite enjoyable to explore and listen to. The various commentators read their parts well, with subtitles to go along with them, placed along the levels to bring insight and information to things you'll either remember from your previous playthroughs of the game or things you never noticed before. If you're interested in the Half-Life lore or the development of the game, I'd recommend this Update just for the commentary alone. The updated engine tweaks like lighting, fog, and bugfixes are a great cherry on the top too. Plus it's free - all you need to have is Half-Life 2 on your account, and if you don't, you're probably not going to be interested in this Update anyway.

A prime example of what the possible future for cinematic gaming should be. Ninja Theory absolutely respected their fanbase and themselves with this triple A quality bombshell. I was able to endearingly put myself in the perspective of Senua. With thick narratives, hair raising 3 demensional sounds, and addictive combat I gladly paid Ninja Theory's price tag as a sign of mutual respect. I wish there was a steel case copy of Hellblade because it would be more than welcome in my gleeming collection of games on my shelf. This is more than fetch quests, more than leveling up, finally a game you can differentiate from other games.
A timeless piece of originality that will make you feel.
Highly recomended for those who yearn to be understood. Cause afterall, that's all Senua ever wanted.
P.S. Wear Headphones.
